Distribution kernels

Definition 1 (Distribution kernel) For a variable of interest z, a kernel is the part of a density or mass function that depends on z. Thus f(z)\propto k(z) means f(z)=c\,k(z) for a constant c that does not depend on z. A factor that is constant for one calculation may need to be retained in another.

title: Reference formulas and problem-solving workflow
section: A workflow for an unseen Bayesian problem
text:
A workflow for an unseen Bayesian problem

State the sampling model, its support, and the conditional independence assumptions.
Write the likelihood with all constants once. Then mark which factors are constant in the parameter currently being analysed.
State the prior and its parameterisation. Check support and propriety.
Multiply likelihood and prior. Combine exponents before naming a distribution.
If a known kernel appears, restore its normalising constant and state the posterior. Otherwise decide whether quadrature, Gibbs sampling, or Metropolis–Hastings is appropriate.
For a marginal likelihood, keep constants that depend on the model even when they do not depend on the model’s parameter.
Distinguish a region of one parameter space from a separate model of lower dimension.
Match the posterior summary to the scientific question: mean, MAP, credible interval, tail probability, predictive probability, or decision under a stated loss.
Check limiting cases, dimensions, and parameter conventions. A one-unit error in a Gamma or Beta shape is usually an exponent error.
If using MCMC, inspect convergence, dependence, effective sample size, and sensitivity to initialisation and tuning.

Kernels can be rebuilt. The transferable skill is to write the density, identify what is fixed, combine the powers and exponential terms, and recognise the resulting kernel. Recognising the distribution is part of the calculation; memorising its normalising constant is not. If the kernel is unfamiliar, the same setup still tells us what must be integrated or sampled. A formula forgotten under pressure can be rebuilt; a confused conditioning argument cannot.

title: Reference formulas and problem-solving workflow
text:
Corrections and distinctions

Remark 2 (Corrections and distinctions). 

In the mode-based pseudo-count convention, \operatorname{Beta}(5,5) contributes four heads and four tails relative to \operatorname{Beta}(1,1): eight trials in total.
Under the stated shape–rate prior \operatorname{Gamma}(12,1), the fruit posterior is \operatorname{Gamma}(189,21). The quoted probability 0.9232 instead corresponds to \operatorname{Gamma}(190,21); see the convention check in Chapter 6.
Equal-tailed, minimum-width, and highest-density intervals are different constructions unless symmetry makes them coincide.
A continuous MAP estimate is obtained by optimisation, not by taking the most common MCMC draw.
Empirical Bayes fixes estimated hyperparameters and is therefore often over-precise. Full Bayes integrates over their posterior uncertainty.
Uniform Dirichlet density means uniform over the simplex; it does not mean that the probability vector is fixed at its barycentre.
Gibbs uses exact full conditionals and accepts every update. Metropolis–Hastings accepts or rejects proposals and requires proposal-scale tuning. Grid Monte Carlo uses independent draws from a discretised density and is not MCMC.
In Gaussian regression, \widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} is normally distributed before studentisation, the marginal posterior shape for \sigma^2 is (n-p)/2, and drawing from p(\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{y}})p({\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid\sigma^2,{\boldsymbol{y}}) is direct iid simulation rather than Gibbs sampling.

title: Reference formulas and problem-solving workflow
text:
Where the argument has been
The chapters form one connected argument:

Remark 3 (A road map). 

Bayes’ rule turns priors and likelihoods into posterior distributions.
Conjugate families make several important updates analytic.
Nonconjugate and multiparameter models motivate Markov-chain Monte Carlo.
Posterior probabilities handle regions of one parameter space, while Bayes factors compare genuinely different models through marginal likelihoods.
Exponential families explain why many conjugate updates have the same algebra.
Hierarchical models turn prior parameters into uncertain population parameters and use MCMC or numerical integration to propagate that extra uncertainty.
Bayesian linear regression lifts the normal model to a vector of means, with least-squares geometry producing analytic coefficient, variance, and predictive distributions.

title: Q59. Gibbs sampling with a weighted count
text:
Topic: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 59 of 59 ‹ Q58

[10 marks]
Let X\in\{0,1,\ldots,8\} and \theta\in(0,1) have joint probability mass/density function \pi(x,\theta)\propto
\binom8x3^x\theta^{x+1}(1-\theta)^{10-x},
\qquad x=0,1,\ldots,8,\quad0<\theta<1.
(a) Find and identify the full conditional distribution X\mid\theta, including its parameters. [3 marks]
(b) Find and identify the full conditional distribution \theta\mid X=x, including its parameters. [3 marks]
(c) Hence write pseudocode for a Gibbs sampler that generates a Markov chain with equilibrium distribution \pi(x,\theta). [3 marks]
(d) Explain why Gibbs sampling does not require an acceptance–rejection step. [1 mark]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. A full conditional is proportional to the joint as a function of the variable being updated, with the other variable fixed. For x=0,\ldots,n, the Binomial kernel can be written \binom nx\{p/(1-p)\}^x. The Beta kernel is \theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1} on (0,1), with a,b>0. Here n=8, and (t) labels a complete sequential Gibbs sweep.
(a) Full conditional of X. For fixed \theta\in(0,1), the marginal density \pi(\theta) does not depend on x, so \pi(x\mid\theta)=\frac{\pi(x,\theta)}{\pi(\theta)}
\propto\binom8x3^x\theta^{x+1}(1-\theta)^{10-x}. Use \theta^{x+1}=\theta\theta^x and (1-\theta)^{10-x}=(1-\theta)^{10}(1-\theta)^{-x} to obtain \begin{aligned}
\pi(x\mid\theta)
&\propto\theta(1-\theta)^{10}\binom8x
\left(\frac{3\theta}{1-\theta}\right)^x\\
&\propto\binom8x\left(\frac{3\theta}{1-\theta}\right)^x,
\qquad x=0,\ldots,8.
\end{aligned} Only the factor \theta(1-\theta)^{10} was dropped: it is constant in x. In contrast, 3^x depends on x and must be retained.
A \operatorname{Binomial}(8,p) probability mass function satisfies \binom8x p^x(1-p)^{8-x}
=(1-p)^8\binom8x\left(\frac p{1-p}\right)^x
\propto\binom8x\left(\frac p{1-p}\right)^x. Match the odds and solve for p: \begin{aligned}
\frac p{1-p}&=\frac{3\theta}{1-\theta},\\
p(1-\theta)&=3\theta(1-p),\\
p-p\theta&=3\theta-3\theta p,\\
p(1+2\theta)&=3\theta.
\end{aligned} Therefore \boxed{X\mid\theta\sim
\operatorname{Binomial}\!\left(8,\frac{3\theta}{1+2\theta}\right),
\qquad X\in\{0,\ldots,8\}.} For 0<\theta<1, the success probability lies strictly between zero and one. The factor 3^x multiplies the Binomial odds by three; it does not simply replace the success probability by 3\theta.
(b) Full conditional of \theta. Now hold x fixed. Both \binom8x and 3^x are constants in \theta, so \pi(\theta\mid x)\propto\pi(x,\theta)
\propto\theta^{x+1}(1-\theta)^{10-x},\qquad0<\theta<1. The \operatorname{Beta}(a,b) kernel is \theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}. Matching exponents gives a-1=x+1\ \Longrightarrow\ a=x+2,\qquad
b-1=10-x\ \Longrightarrow\ b=11-x. Thus \boxed{\theta\mid X=x\sim\operatorname{Beta}(x+2,11-x),
\qquad0<\theta<1.} Both shape parameters are positive for every x\in\{0,\ldots,8\}. Here 3^x can be dropped because the conditioning variable x is fixed.
(c) Gibbs sampler. Choose any valid initial state x^{(0)}\in\{0,\ldots,8\},\qquad\theta^{(0)}\in(0,1), for example (x^{(0)},\theta^{(0)})=(0,1/2). For t=1,\ldots,T:
1. Update X using the previous value of \theta: X^{(t)}\sim\operatorname{Binomial}\!\left(
        8,\frac{3\theta^{(t-1)}}{1+2\theta^{(t-1)}}\right).
2. Update \theta using the newly generated X: \theta^{(t)}\sim
        \operatorname{Beta}\!\left(X^{(t)}+2,11-X^{(t)}\right).
3. Store the completed pair (X^{(t)},\theta^{(t)}).
Use fresh random numbers for each conditional draw. Step 2 conditions on X^{(t)}, not X^{(t-1)}.
Each full-conditional update leaves the joint target invariant, and so does their composition. Both conditionals are positive throughout their respective supports, allowing the chain to move throughout the target support. The resulting Gibbs chain converges to \pi(x,\theta) from a valid starting state. Allow for convergence before using the output for target-distribution summaries.
Equilibrium does not mean independence: successive pairs generally remain dependent because the next X is drawn using the preceding \theta. This is a Markov-chain sampler, not a sequence of independent draws from the joint distribution.
(d) Why no acceptance–rejection step? Each update draws directly from the exact full conditional. It can be viewed as a Metropolis–Hastings update whose proposal is that full conditional, making the acceptance probability one.
For example, when updating X while holding \theta fixed, propose x' from q(x'\mid x,\theta)=\pi(x'\mid\theta). Since \pi(x,\theta)=\pi(\theta)\pi(x\mid\theta), the acceptance ratio is \begin{aligned}
R
&=\frac{\pi(x',\theta)\pi(x\mid\theta)}
        {\pi(x,\theta)\pi(x'\mid\theta)}\\
&=\frac{\pi(\theta)\pi(x'\mid\theta)\pi(x\mid\theta)}
        {\pi(\theta)\pi(x\mid\theta)\pi(x'\mid\theta)}
=1.
\end{aligned} The same cancellation holds for the \theta update. Hence \alpha=\min\{1,R\}=1: every Gibbs update is accepted, so no separate Metropolis accept/reject decision is required.

Key result. The same joint distribution produces different conditional kernels because a different variable is held fixed. Retain 3^x when updating X; drop it when updating \theta. Always use the latest available conditioning values in a sequential Gibbs sweep.

title: Q57. Negative-binomial canonical link
text:
Topic: Introduction to generalised linear models · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 57 of 59 ‹ Q56 Q58 ›

[6 marks]
Let Y have a negative-binomial distribution with probability mass function f(y;\theta)
=\binom{y+r-1}{r-1}\theta^r(1-\theta)^y,
\qquad y=0,1,2,\ldots, where r>0 is known and 0<\theta<1.
(a) Show that this distribution belongs to the linear exponential family by expressing its probability mass function in the form f(y;\theta)
        =\exp\left\{
        \frac{y\,b(\theta)+c(\theta)}{e(\phi)}+d(y;\phi)
        \right\}. Identify the natural parameter b(\theta). [3 marks]
(b) Given that \mu=\mathbb{E}(Y)=\frac{r(1-\theta)}{\theta}, derive the canonical link function g(\mu). [3 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Here Y counts failures, with support \{0,1,2,\ldots\}, known r>0, and 0<\theta<1. For non-integer r, interpret the binomial coefficient as \binom{y+r-1}{r-1}=\Gamma(y+r)/\{\Gamma(r)\Gamma(y+1)\}. In the stated linear exponential-family form, the natural parameter is b(\theta); the canonical link is g(\mu)=b\{\theta(\mu)\}. We use scale convention e(\phi)=1.
(a) Exponential-family representation. The support \{0,1,2,\ldots\} does not depend on \theta. Take logarithms of the supplied mass function: \begin{aligned}
\log f(y;\theta)
&=\log\left\{\binom{y+r-1}{r-1}\theta^r(1-\theta)^y\right\}\\
&=y\log(1-\theta)+r\log\theta
  +\log\binom{y+r-1}{r-1}.
\end{aligned} Since r is known, there is no free dispersion parameter to estimate here. Choose e(\phi)=1 and identify \boxed{
b(\theta)=\log(1-\theta),\qquad
c(\theta)=r\log\theta,\qquad e(\phi)=1,
} \boxed{d(y;\phi)=\log\binom{y+r-1}{r-1}.} The symbol \phi is redundant in this choice: d depends on the known r, not on the unknown \theta. Substitution gives f(y;\theta)
=\exp\left\{y\log(1-\theta)+r\log\theta+
\log\binom{y+r-1}{r-1}\right\}, exactly the required form. In particular, \boxed{\eta=b(\theta)=\log(1-\theta)<0.} The natural parameter is \log(1-\theta), not \log\theta: it is the coefficient multiplying the observation y.
The Gamma-function convention in Definitions makes this representation valid for every stated r>0.
(b) Canonical link. Start with the supplied mean and solve for the original parameter: \begin{aligned}
\mu&=\frac{r(1-\theta)}{\theta},\\
\mu\theta&=r-r\theta,\\
(\mu+r)\theta&=r,\\
\theta&=\frac r{\mu+r},\qquad
1-\theta=\frac{\mu}{\mu+r}.
\end{aligned} Now substitute into the natural parameter from part (a): \boxed{
g(\mu)=b\{\theta(\mu)\}
=\log\left(\frac{\mu}{\mu+r}\right)
=\log\mu-\log(\mu+r),\qquad\mu>0.
} Thus a canonical-link regression would set \eta_i=\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta=g(\mu_i), with \eta_i<0 to keep the means valid. Solving for the mean gives e^\eta=\frac{\mu}{\mu+r}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mu(1-e^\eta)=re^\eta
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\boxed{\mu=\frac{re^\eta}{1-e^\eta},\qquad\eta<0.}
Independent check from the normalising term. Write the log mass function as \log f(y;\eta)=y\eta-A(\eta)+d(y),
\qquad A(\eta)=-r\log(1-e^\eta). Differentiating the identity \sum_y f(y;\eta)=1 gives 0=\sum_y\{y-A'(\eta)\}f(y;\eta), so \mathbb{E}(Y)=A'(\eta). Here A'(\eta)=\frac{re^\eta}{1-e^\eta}, which is exactly the inverse link just derived.
A log link can be chosen for a negative-binomial regression, but it is not the canonical link derived here.

title: Q55. Gamma GLM for reaction times
Q53. Poisson flaws and posterior odds
text:
Topic: Bayesian hypotheses and model comparison · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 53 of 59 ‹ Q52 Q54 ›

[12 marks]
A textile manufacturer counts flaws in equal-length rolls of fabric. Assume X_i\mid\theta\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Poisson}(\theta),
\qquad i=1,\ldots,10, where \theta is the mean number of flaws per roll.
Ten inspected rolls contain 32 flaws in total. The prior is \theta\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(8,2), using the shape–rate convention: \pi(\theta)=\frac{2^8}{\Gamma(8)}\theta^7e^{-2\theta},
\qquad\theta>0. The manufacturer considers the process acceptable if \theta\le4.
(a) Form the likelihood and derive the posterior distribution of \theta. [4 marks]
(b) Find the posterior mean. Show that it lies between the prior mean and the observed sample mean. [2 marks]
(c) Define H_0:\theta\le4,\qquad H_1:\theta>4. Write an integral for \mathbb P(H_0\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}), including the normalising constant. Hence express the posterior odds in favour of H_0. You do not need to evaluate the integral. [3 marks]
(d) A colleague argues:

“The posterior mean is below 4, so the probability that the process is acceptable must be 1.”

Explain why this is incorrect. Would changing H_0 to \theta<4 change its posterior probability? Justify your answer. [3 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. For Gamma shape–rate parameters (A,B), the density is B^A\theta^{A-1}e^{-B\theta}/\Gamma(A) on \theta>0 and the mean is A/B. Here n=10, \sum_i x_i=32, and the prior is \operatorname{Gamma}(8,2). Write q=\mathbb P(\theta\le4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}). Posterior odds in favour of this event over its complement are q/(1-q).
(a) Likelihood and posterior. Conditional independence gives, for observed nonnegative integer counts, \begin{aligned}
L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=\prod_{i=1}^{10}\frac{e^{-\theta}\theta^{x_i}}{x_i!}
=\frac{\theta^{\sum_i x_i}e^{-10\theta}}{\prod_{i=1}^{10}x_i!}\\
&\propto\theta^{32}e^{-10\theta},\qquad\theta>0.
\end{aligned} The factorial term does not depend on \theta, so only the total count is needed for this likelihood kernel. Multiplying by the prior kernel, \begin{aligned}
\pi(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})\pi(\theta)\\
&\propto\theta^{32}e^{-10\theta}\theta^7e^{-2\theta}
=\theta^{39}e^{-12\theta}.
\end{aligned} Matching \theta^{A-1}e^{-B\theta} gives A=40 and B=12. Thus \boxed{\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(40,12)
\quad\text{(shape--rate)},\qquad\theta>0,} with normalised posterior density \boxed{\pi(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\frac{12^{40}}{\Gamma(40)}\theta^{39}e^{-12\theta},
\qquad\theta>0.}
(b) Posterior mean and shrinkage. The prior mean, sample mean, and posterior mean are respectively \mathbb{E}[\theta]=\frac82=4,\qquad
\bar x=\frac{32}{10}=3.2,\qquad
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}]=\frac{40}{12}=\frac{10}{3}.} In particular, 3.2<10/3<4. More explicitly, \mathbb{E}[\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}]
=\frac{8+32}{2+10}
=\frac{2}{12}\left(\frac82\right)
+\frac{10}{12}\left(\frac{32}{10}\right)
=\frac16\mathbb{E}[\theta]+\frac56\bar x. The weights are positive and sum to one, so the posterior mean lies strictly between the two distinct means.
(c) Posterior probability and odds. Let q=\mathbb P(H_0\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}). Integrating the normalised posterior density over the acceptable region gives \boxed{q=\mathbb P(\theta\le4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\frac{12^{40}}{\Gamma(40)}
\int_0^4\theta^{39}e^{-12\theta}\,d\theta.} The two hypotheses exhaust the parameter space, so \mathbb P(H_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=1-q. Therefore the posterior odds in favour of H_0 are q:(1-q), or, as a ratio, \boxed{
\frac{\mathbb P(H_0\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})}{\mathbb P(H_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})}
=\frac{q}{1-q}
=\frac{\displaystyle\int_0^4\theta^{39}e^{-12\theta}\,d\theta}
       {\displaystyle\int_4^\infty\theta^{39}e^{-12\theta}\,d\theta}.
} The common normalising constant cancels in the odds ratio, but it is required in the probability integral above. No numerical evaluation is needed.
(d) A mean below the threshold does not imply certainty. The posterior mean is an average of possible values of \theta, not an upper bound on them. Although \mathbb{E}[\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}]=10/3<4, the \operatorname{Gamma}(40,12) density is strictly positive for every \theta>0, including values above 4. Consequently, \mathbb P(\theta>4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\frac{12^{40}}{\Gamma(40)}
\int_4^\infty\theta^{39}e^{-12\theta}\,d\theta>0, so \mathbb P(\theta\le4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})<1. A point estimate below the threshold does not eliminate posterior uncertainty about acceptability.
Replacing \theta\le4 by \theta<4 does not change the posterior probability. The posterior is continuous, and hence \mathbb P(\theta=4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=0. Therefore \boxed{\mathbb P(\theta<4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\mathbb P(\theta\le4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}).}

Key result. The posterior mean answers “what is the posterior average of \theta?” The posterior probability of H_0 answers “how much posterior probability lies at or below 4?” These are different summaries.

title: Q51. Three-variable Gibbs sampling
text:
Topic: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 51 of 59 ‹ Q50 Q52 ›

[10 marks]
Consider the joint probability mass/density function \begin{aligned}
f(x,y,z)&\propto\binom nx\binom my
z^{x+y+\alpha-1}(1-z)^{n+m-x-y+\beta-1}\\
&\qquad\times\gamma^{m-y}(1-\gamma)^{n-x}
\delta^x(1-\delta)^y,
\end{aligned} where x\in\{0,1,\ldots,n\},\qquad
y\in\{0,1,\ldots,m\},\qquad 0<z<1. Here n,m are known positive integers, and \alpha,\beta>0 and 0<\gamma,\delta<1 are known constants.
(a) Derive the following full conditional distributions, identifying each by name and specifying its parameters and support: X\mid Y=y,Z=z,\qquad
        Y\mid X=x,Z=z,\qquad
        Z\mid X=x,Y=y. [6 marks]
(b) Using your answers to part (a), give pseudocode for a Gibbs sampler targeting f(x,y,z). Specify a valid initial state and make clear which iteration’s values are used in each update. [3 marks]
(c) Suppose the chain has reached equilibrium. Are successive sampled triples independent observations from f(x,y,z)? Briefly justify your answer. [1 mark]
No implementation or numerical simulation is required.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. A weighted Binomial kernel \binom nx a^xb^{n-x} normalises to success probability a/(a+b) for a,b>0. A \operatorname{Beta}(A,B) kernel is z^{A-1}(1-z)^{B-1} on (0,1). Here X\in\{0,\ldots,n\}, Y\in\{0,\ldots,m\}, and 0<Z<1; n,m are positive integers, \alpha,\beta>0, and 0<\gamma,\delta<1. Superscript (t) indexes complete Gibbs sweeps.
(a) Full conditional distributions.
Conditional distribution of X. Holding y and z fixed, \begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(X=x\mid Y=y,Z=z)
&\propto\binom nx z^x(1-z)^{n-x}(1-\gamma)^{n-x}\delta^x\\
&=\binom nx(z\delta)^x\{(1-z)(1-\gamma)\}^{n-x}.
\end{aligned} For positive weights a,b, the binomial theorem gives \sum_{j=0}^n\binom nj a^j b^{n-j}=(a+b)^n. Dividing the kernel by this sum yields a Binomial mass function with success probability a/(a+b). Here define p_X(z)=\frac{z\delta}{z\delta+(1-z)(1-\gamma)}. Consequently, \boxed{X\mid Y=y,Z=z\sim\operatorname{Binomial}\{n,p_X(z)\},
\qquad x\in\{0,\ldots,n\}.} The conditional does not depend on y.
Conditional distribution of Y. Holding x and z fixed, the y-dependent kernel is \begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(Y=y\mid X=x,Z=z)
&\propto\binom my z^y(1-z)^{m-y}\gamma^{m-y}(1-\delta)^y\\
&=\binom my\{z(1-\delta)\}^y\{(1-z)\gamma\}^{m-y}.
\end{aligned} The normalising sum is \{z(1-\delta)+(1-z)\gamma\}^m. Thus, with p_Y(z)=\frac{z(1-\delta)}{z(1-\delta)+(1-z)\gamma}, we obtain \boxed{Y\mid X=x,Z=z\sim\operatorname{Binomial}\{m,p_Y(z)\},
\qquad y\in\{0,\ldots,m\}.} This conditional does not depend on x. In fact, the joint kernel for (X,Y) at fixed z factors into these two Binomial kernels, so X and Y are conditionally independent given Z.
Conditional distribution of Z. Holding x and y fixed leaves f(z\mid x,y)\propto
z^{\alpha+x+y-1}(1-z)^{\beta+n+m-x-y-1},\qquad0<z<1. Matching the Beta kernel gives \boxed{Z\mid X=x,Y=y\sim
\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+x+y,\ \beta+n+m-x-y),\qquad0<z<1.} Both Beta parameters are positive. Also, 0<p_X(z),p_Y(z)<1 under the stated assumptions, so all three conditional distributions are valid.
(b) Gibbs sampler. Use the functions p_X and p_Y from part (a). A valid initial state is \boxed{(x^{(0)},y^{(0)},z^{(0)})=(0,0,1/2).} Choose a run length T. For t=1,\ldots,T, perform one complete sweep:
1. Update X using the previous Z: x^{(t)}\sim\operatorname{Binomial}\!\left(
        n,\frac{z^{(t-1)}\delta}
        {z^{(t-1)}\delta+(1-z^{(t-1)})(1-\gamma)}\right). This is the full conditional given y^{(t-1)},z^{(t-1)}; its formula does not depend on y^{(t-1)}.
2. Update Y using the previous Z: y^{(t)}\sim\operatorname{Binomial}\!\left(
        m,\frac{z^{(t-1)}(1-\delta)}
        {z^{(t-1)}(1-\delta)+(1-z^{(t-1)})\gamma}\right). The latest available conditioning values are x^{(t)},z^{(t-1)}; the formula does not depend on x^{(t)}.
3. Update Z using both newly sampled counts: z^{(t)}\sim\operatorname{Beta}\!\left(
        \alpha+x^{(t)}+y^{(t)},\
        \beta+n+m-x^{(t)}-y^{(t)}\right).
4. Store the completed triple (x^{(t)},y^{(t)},z^{(t)}).
Use fresh random numbers for each conditional draw. Each full-conditional update leaves the target distribution invariant, and therefore so does the complete sweep. No accept/reject step is needed because the draws are directly from the full conditionals.
An arbitrary valid starting state is not necessarily an equilibrium draw; allow for convergence before treating the output as representative of the target distribution.
(c) Independence at equilibrium. No. At equilibrium each completed triple has the target distribution, but successive triples are dependent: the new counts are sampled using the preceding value of Z, and the next Z is then sampled using those counts. Reaching equilibrium does not remove this dependence.

Key result. Conditional independence of X and Y given Z is not independence between successive Gibbs-sampler triples. Stationary output has the correct distribution, but it is not an iid sample.

title: Q49. A Gibbs full conditional under independent priors
text:
Topic: Conjugate analysis for normal models · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 49 of 59 ‹ Q48 Q50 ›

[6 marks]
Suppose X_i\mid\mu,\tau\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}
N\!\left(\mu,\frac1\tau\right),\qquad i=1,\ldots,n, where \mu\in\mathbb R and \tau>0 are unknown.
Assign independent priors \mu\sim N\!\left(\mu_0,\frac1{\kappa_0}\right),
\qquad \tau\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a_0,b_0), where all hyperparameters are known and \kappa_0,a_0,b_0>0. The Gamma distribution is parametrised by shape and rate.
(a) Derive the full conditional distribution \tau\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}}. Show its kernel and identify the distribution and parameters. [4 marks]
(b) Does this full conditional depend explicitly on \mu_0 or \kappa_0? Explain why or why not. [2 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Precision is \tau=1/\sigma^2. N(m,v) uses variance v, and \operatorname{Gamma}(a,b) uses shape a and rate b, with kernel \tau^{a-1}e^{-b\tau} on \tau>0. The full conditional for \tau holds \mu and the data fixed, so only factors that vary with \tau remain.
Assumptions. The priors are independent: \mu\sim N(\mu_0,1/\kappa_0) and \tau\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a_0,b_0), with \kappa_0,a_0,b_0>0. In particular, the prior variance of \mu does not depend on \tau; this distinguishes the question from a Normal–Gamma conditional prior.
(a) Full conditional for \tau. The Normal density with precision \tau is f(x_i\mid\mu,\tau)
=\left(\frac\tau{2\pi}\right)^{1/2}
\exp\left\{-\frac\tau2(x_i-\mu)^2\right\}. Therefore the likelihood kernel is L(\mu,\tau;{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto
\tau^{n/2}\exp\left\{-\frac\tau2\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2\right\}. The independent priors give the joint posterior kernel \begin{aligned}
p(\mu,\tau\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto
\tau^{n/2}\exp\left\{-\frac\tau2\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2\right\}\\
&\quad\times\exp\left\{-\frac{\kappa_0}{2}(\mu-\mu_0)^2\right\}
\tau^{a_0-1}e^{-b_0\tau}.
\end{aligned} For fixed \mu, its prior factor is constant with respect to \tau. Dropping that factor and collecting powers and exponents gives \boxed{
p(\tau\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto
\tau^{a_0+n/2-1}
\exp\left[-\left\{b_0+\frac12\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2\right\}\tau\right],
\quad\tau>0.
} Hence \boxed{
\tau\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{Gamma}\!\left(
a_0+\frac n2,\ b_0+\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2\right)
\quad\text{(shape--rate)}.
}
(b) Dependence on \mu_0 and \kappa_0. No: the full conditional has no explicit dependence on these two hyperparameters. Under the independent priors, p(\mu,\tau)=p(\mu)p(\tau), and once \mu is conditioned on, p(\mu) is a positive constant in the conditional kernel for \tau. It cancels on normalisation.
This does not mean that the prior for \mu is irrelevant to all inference about \tau. It affects the posterior distribution of \mu, and thus can affect the marginal posterior of \tau after \mu is integrated out.

Key result. Do not silently replace the independent prior with \mu\mid\tau\sim N(\mu_0,1/(\kappa_0\tau)). That is a different model whose prior contributes additional \tau-dependent factors to the full conditional.

title: Q47. Overdispersion and quasi-Poisson inference
text:
Topic: Underdispersion, positive responses, and quasi-likelihood · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 47 of 59 ‹ Q46 Q48 ›

[10 marks]
For independent counts, suppose \mathbb{E}(Y_i)=\mu_i=\exp(\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta),
\qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\phi\mu_i.
(a) Explain what \phi>1 means relative to a Poisson model. [2 marks]
(b) Using the quasi-score U(\boldsymbol\beta)
        =\sum_i\frac{Y_i-\mu_i}{\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)}
        \frac{\partial\mu_i}{\partial\boldsymbol\beta}, show why the coefficient estimates coincide with the Poisson estimates when the data and mean model are unchanged. [3 marks]
(c) A coefficient has Poisson standard error 0.10. If \hat\phi=4, find its quasi-Poisson standard error. Explain the effect on a Wald statistic. [2 marks]
(d) Does specifying the mean and variance above determine a complete probability distribution? Explain why an ordinary likelihood-ratio test cannot automatically be applied. [3 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Let \mu_i=e^{\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta}, where \mathbf x_i is a fixed predictor column vector. The dispersion \phi>0 scales variance to \phi\mu_i. A quasi-score weights residuals by the inverse assumed variance and the derivative of the mean; it is an estimating equation, not necessarily the derivative of a full log-likelihood. Standard error is the square root of an estimated coefficient variance.
Assumptions. Compare fits to the same data using the same unpenalised log-linear mean, conditionally independent observations, and a common dispersion \phi. The design and fitted solution must support finite, identifiable coefficient estimates and the stated covariance calculation. Equality of estimates is not asserted for different mean models, penalties, or observation-specific dispersion.
(a) Meaning of \phi>1. A Poisson model has \operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\mathbb{E}(Y_i)=\mu_i. Here \operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\phi\mu_i, so \phi>1 means overdispersion: at the same expected count, the variance is \phi times the Poisson variance.
(b) Equality of the coefficient estimates. For \mu_i=e^{\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta}, \frac{\partial\mu_i}{\partial\boldsymbol\beta}=\mu_i\mathbf x_i. Substitution into the supplied quasi-score gives \begin{aligned}
U(\boldsymbol\beta)
&=\sum_i\frac{Y_i-\mu_i}{\phi\mu_i}\mu_i\mathbf x_i\\
&=\frac1\phi\sum_i\mathbf x_i(Y_i-\mu_i)
=\boxed{\frac1\phi S_{\mathrm{Poisson}}(\boldsymbol\beta)}.
\end{aligned} Because \phi>0 is a common scalar, U(\boldsymbol\beta)=\mathbf0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
S_{\mathrm{Poisson}}(\boldsymbol\beta)=\mathbf0. The same data and mean model therefore give the same fitted coefficients, when the estimates exist and are well defined. Estimating the common dispersion does not change these estimating equations’ roots.
(c) Standard error and Wald statistic. The usual model-based covariance matrix is multiplied by \hat\phi: \widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_{\mathrm{quasi}}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})
=\hat\phi(X^\top\widehat WX)^{-1},
\qquad \widehat W=\operatorname{diag}(\widehat\mu_i). Thus standard errors are multiplied by \sqrt{\hat\phi}, not by \hat\phi itself: \boxed{\operatorname{SE}_{\mathrm{quasi}}=\sqrt4(0.10)=0.20.} For a fixed null value \beta_{j,0}, the signed Wald statistic becomes z_{\mathrm{quasi}}
=\frac{\widehat\beta_j-\beta_{j,0}}{0.20}
=\frac12z_{\mathrm{Poisson}}. Its squared version is one quarter as large. Against the same reference distribution, this gives weaker evidence against the null; it does not necessarily change a particular reject/non-reject decision.
(d) Is a full probability distribution specified? No. A mean and variance alone do not determine all the count probabilities. Quasi-Poisson inference specifies these moments and an estimating equation, not a unique probability mass function. There is therefore no ordinary full likelihood supplied by these assumptions from which to construct an ordinary likelihood-ratio test automatically. A valid test needs an appropriate quasi-likelihood calibration or an additional fully specified distributional model; a Poisson likelihood-ratio test cannot simply ignore the overdispersion.

title: Q45. Gamma regression from the exponential-family form
text:
Topic: Underdispersion, positive responses, and quasi-likelihood · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 45 of 59 ‹ Q44 Q46 ›

[12 marks]
Independent positive responses have density f(y_i\mid\mu_i,k)
=\frac{k^k}{\Gamma(k)\mu_i^k}
y_i^{k-1}\exp\left(-\frac{ky_i}{\mu_i}\right),
\qquad y_i>0, where \mu_i>0 and k>0.
(a) Express the density in the course form f(y;\theta,\phi)
        =\exp\left\{
        \frac{a(y)b(\theta)+c(\theta)}{e(\phi)}+d(y;\phi)
        \right\}, taking \theta=\mu and \phi=1/k. Identify all five functions. [4 marks]
(b) Find \mathbb{E}(Y_i) and \operatorname{Var}(Y_i). [2 marks]
(c) Under the model \log\mu_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i, interpret \beta_1 and derive the ratio of expected responses at x+1 and x. [2 marks]
(d) Derive the score vector for \boldsymbol\beta, treating k as known. [3 marks]
(e) Explain why this model does not assert that \log Y_i is Normally distributed. [1 mark]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. A Gamma variable with shape k and rate k/\mu has mean \mu and variance \mu^2/k; set \phi=1/k. In the course’s exponential-family form, b(\theta) is the coefficient paired with the statistic a(y) after division by e(\phi). For regression, \mathbf X_i=(1,x_i)^\top, \boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_0,\beta_1)^\top, and \mu_i=e^{\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta}. Responses are independent and covariates fixed; the score calculation holds k>0 known.
(a) Exponential-family representation. For one observation, taking logarithms gives \log f(y\mid\mu,k)
=k\log k-\log\Gamma(k)-k\log\mu+(k-1)\log y-\frac{ky}{\mu}. With \theta=\mu and \phi=1/k, rearrange this as \log f(y;\theta,\phi)
=\frac{-y/\theta-\log\theta}{\phi}
+\frac1\phi\log\frac1\phi-\log\Gamma\!\left(\frac1\phi\right)
+\left(\frac1\phi-1\right)\log y. One valid identification of the five functions is \boxed{
a(y)=y,\qquad b(\theta)=-\frac1\theta,\qquad
c(\theta)=-\log\theta,\qquad e(\phi)=\phi,
} \boxed{
d(y;\phi)=\frac1\phi\log\frac1\phi
-\log\Gamma\!\left(\frac1\phi\right)
+\left(\frac1\phi-1\right)\log y.
} The support is y>0, with \theta>0 and \phi>0.
(b) Mean and variance. The given density is Gamma with shape k and rate k/\mu_i. Therefore \boxed{\mathbb{E}(Y_i)=\frac{k}{k/\mu_i}=\mu_i,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\frac{k}{(k/\mu_i)^2}
=\frac{\mu_i^2}{k}=\phi\mu_i^2.}
(c) Interpretation of the coefficient. The log link gives \mu(x)=e^{\beta_0+\beta_1x}, so \boxed{\frac{\mathbb{E}(Y\mid x+1)}{\mathbb{E}(Y\mid x)}
=\frac{e^{\beta_0+\beta_1(x+1)}}{e^{\beta_0+\beta_1x}}
=e^{\beta_1}.} Thus a one-unit increase in x multiplies the expected response by e^{\beta_1}, corresponding to a percentage change 100(e^{\beta_1}-1)\%. The coefficient \beta_1 itself is the change in the log of the mean, not an additive change in the response.
(d) Score vector. Let \mathbf X_i=(1,x_i)^\top and \boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_0,\beta_1)^\top, so that \mu_i=e^{\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta}. Treating k as known, \ell(\boldsymbol\beta)
=-k\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\log\mu_i+\frac{y_i}{\mu_i}\right)+C, where C does not depend on \boldsymbol\beta. Differentiate each summand with respect to its mean and apply the chain rule: \frac{\partial\ell_i}{\partial\mu_i}
=-\frac{k}{\mu_i}+\frac{ky_i}{\mu_i^2},
\qquad
\frac{\partial\mu_i}{\partial\boldsymbol\beta}=\mu_i\mathbf X_i. It follows that \begin{aligned}
S(\boldsymbol\beta)
&=\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(-\frac{k}{\mu_i}+\frac{ky_i}{\mu_i^2}\right)\mu_i\mathbf X_i\\
&=\boxed{k\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf X_i\left(\frac{y_i}{\mu_i}-1\right)}.
\end{aligned} In components, S(\boldsymbol\beta)
=k\begin{pmatrix}
\sum_i(y_i/\mu_i-1)\\[3pt]
\sum_i x_i(y_i/\mu_i-1)
\end{pmatrix}.
(e) Why this is not a lognormal model. The model specifies a Gamma distribution for Y_i and a linear predictor for \log\mu_i=\log\mathbb{E}(Y_i). It does not specify a Normal distribution for \log Y_i. Applying a log link to a conditional mean is not the same operation as transforming the response and assuming Normal errors.

Key result. Keep the response distribution and the link separate: Gamma response plus log link does not mean lognormal response.

title: Q43. Unknown Normal mean and variance: conditional versus marginal
text:
Topic: Conjugate analysis for normal models · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 43 of 59 ‹ Q42 Q44 ›

[14 marks]
Suppose X_1,\ldots,X_n\mid\mu,v
\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(\mu,v),
\qquad p(\mu,v)\propto\frac1v, where \mu\in\mathbb R, v>0, n\ge2, and S=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2>0. Use the inverse-Gamma convention f(v)\propto v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v}.
(a) Establish the identity \sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2=S+n(\mu-\bar x)^2. [2 marks]
(b) Derive the full conditional distributions \mu\mid v,{\boldsymbol{x}} and v\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}}. [4 marks]
(c) Integrate out \mu to derive p(v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}). Explain why it differs from p(v\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}}). [4 marks]
(d) Describe a Gibbs sampler using part (b). A student instead samples v from its marginal posterior, then \mu conditional on that draw, repeating with fresh random numbers. Is this also a valid way to sample the joint posterior? Are its resulting pairs independent? [4 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write v=\sigma^2, \bar x=n^{-1}\sum_i x_i, and S=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2, the unnormalised sum of squares. We use N(m,v) with variance v and \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b) with kernel v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v} on v>0. A full conditional fixes the other parameter; a marginal posterior integrates it out.
Assumptions. The Normal observations are conditionally iid, with prior p(\mu,v)\propto1/v relative to d\mu\,dv. Because this prior is improper, require n\ge2 and S>0 for the posterior below to be proper.
(a) Sum-of-squares identity. Write x_i-\mu=(x_i-\bar x)+(\bar x-\mu) and expand: \begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2
&=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2
+2(\bar x-\mu)\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)
+n(\bar x-\mu)^2\\
&=\boxed{S+n(\mu-\bar x)^2},
\end{aligned} because \sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=0.
(b) Full conditional distributions. The likelihood and joint posterior kernels are L(\mu,v;{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto
v^{-n/2}\exp\left\{-\frac{S+n(\mu-\bar x)^2}{2v}\right\}, p(\mu,v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto
v^{-n/2-1}\exp\left\{-\frac{S+n(\mu-\bar x)^2}{2v}\right\},
\qquad \mu\in\mathbb R,\ v>0. For fixed v, retain only factors involving \mu: p(\mu\mid v,{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto
\exp\left\{-\frac{n(\mu-\bar x)^2}{2v}\right\}. Recognising a Normal kernel, \boxed{\mu\mid v,{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim N\!\left(\bar x,\frac vn\right).} For fixed \mu, retain all the v-dependent factors: p(v\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto
v^{-n/2-1}\exp\left\{-\frac{S+n(\mu-\bar x)^2}{2v}\right\}. Under the stated inverse-Gamma convention, \boxed{
v\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim
\operatorname{InvGamma}\!\left(\frac n2,\frac{S+n(\mu-\bar x)^2}{2}\right).
} Its support is v>0. In this conditional distribution, \mu is held fixed; it has not been replaced by \bar x or integrated out.
(c) Marginal posterior for v. Integrate the joint posterior kernel over all \mu\in\mathbb R: \begin{aligned}
p(v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto v^{-n/2-1}e^{-S/(2v)}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\exp\left\{-\frac{n(\mu-\bar x)^2}{2v}\right\}\,d\mu\\
&=v^{-n/2-1}e^{-S/(2v)}\sqrt{\frac{2\pi v}{n}}\\
&\propto v^{-(n-1)/2-1}e^{-S/(2v)}.
\end{aligned} Therefore \boxed{v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\!\left(\frac{n-1}{2},\frac S2\right),
\qquad v>0.} The assumptions n\ge2 and S>0 make both parameters positive, so the posterior is proper despite the improper prior.
The marginal distribution accounts for uncertainty in \mu by integrating over it. The integral contributes a factor v^{1/2}, changing the shape from n/2 to (n-1)/2. Even setting \mu=\bar x in the full conditional does not produce the marginal posterior, because it misses this factor.
(d) Gibbs sampling and direct joint sampling. Start from any \mu^{(0)}\in\mathbb R and v^{(0)}>0. At iteration t=1,\ldots,T, draw \mu^{(t)}\sim N\!\left(\bar x,\frac{v^{(t-1)}}n\right), v^{(t)}\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\!\left(
\frac n2,\frac{S+n(\mu^{(t)}-\bar x)^2}{2}\right). Each update uses the latest available value of the other parameter. The resulting Markov chain has the joint posterior as its equilibrium distribution; successive pairs are generally dependent, and convergence from the chosen starting value must be assessed.
The student’s alternative is also valid. Independently for each repetition, draw v^{(t)}\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\!\left(\frac{n-1}{2},\frac S2\right),
\qquad
\mu^{(t)}\mid v^{(t)}\sim N\!\left(\bar x,\frac{v^{(t)}}n\right). This samples the factorisation p(\mu,v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=p(v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})p(\mu\mid v,{\boldsymbol{x}}) directly. With fresh independent random numbers for each repetition, the pairs are iid joint-posterior draws, with no burn-in required. The two components within a pair are not independent: the conditional variance of \mu depends on v.

title: Q39. A generalised linear mixed model
text:
Topic: Random slopes, and a binary mixed model · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 39 of 59 ‹ Q38 Q40 ›

[6 marks]
Patients receive treatment A or B and are assessed at weeks 0,4,8,12. The response is 1 if infection is present and 0 otherwise. Treatment A is the reference category.
glmer(
  infection ~ treatment * weeks + (1 | patientID),
  family = binomial
)
(a) Write down explicitly the complete model corresponding to this code. Define the patient and visit indices, and state the relevant distributional and independence assumptions.
(b) Briefly explain why including a patient-specific random intercept is sensible.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Let i=1,\ldots,m index patients and j=1,\ldots,4 index visits. Y_{ij} is the infection indicator, t_{ij}\in\{0,4,8,12\} is time in weeks, and G_i=0 for treatment A or 1 for B. b_i is a patient-specific random intercept, with conditional infection probability p_{ij}(b_i)=\mathbb P(Y_{ij}=1\mid b_i,G_i,t_{ij}). The logit is \log\{p/(1-p)\}; N(0,\tau^2) uses variance \tau^2.
(a) Model statement. The conditional response model is Y_{ij}\mid b_i,G_i,t_{ij}
\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}\{p_{ij}(b_i)\}. Responses are conditionally independent given all random effects and covariates. The R term treatment * weeks expands to treatment, weeks, and their interaction, so \boxed{
\log\left(\frac{p_{ij}(b_i)}{1-p_{ij}(b_i)}\right)
=\beta_0+\beta_GG_i+\beta_Tt_{ij}
+\beta_{GT}G_it_{ij}+b_i.
} The random effects satisfy \boxed{b_i\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,\tau^2).} They are assumed independent of the covariates, and different patients are independent. Repeated responses within a patient are generally not independent after the random effect is integrated out.
(b) Why include a patient-specific random intercept? Patients can have persistent differences in infection propensity that treatment and time do not explain. The shared b_i represents this baseline heterogeneity across all visits for patient i.
To see the induced dependence, let X collect the covariates and consider two distinct visits j\ne k. By the law of total covariance, \begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{ij},Y_{ik}\mid X)
&=\mathbb{E}\{\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{ij},Y_{ik}\mid b_i,X)\mid X\}\\
&\quad+\operatorname{Cov}\{
\mathbb{E}(Y_{ij}\mid b_i,X),\mathbb{E}(Y_{ik}\mid b_i,X)\mid X\}\\
&=\operatorname{Cov}\{p_{ij}(b_i),p_{ik}(b_i)\mid X\}.
\end{aligned} The first term is zero by conditional independence, but the remaining covariance is generally nonzero.
Conclusion: The random intercept accounts for persistent between-patient differences and dependence among repeated observations from the same patient.

title: Q35. Logistic regression and an adjusted effect
text:
Topic: Introduction to generalised linear models · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 35 of 59 ‹ Q34 Q36 ›

[4 marks]
For independent patients, disease is coded 1 for disease and 0 otherwise. The variable group is coded 0 for group A and 1 for group B.
glm(disease ~ group + cholesterol, family = binomial)
(a) Write down explicitly the statistical model corresponding to this code.
(b) The estimated coefficient of group is 0.70. Interpret this estimate after accounting for cholesterol.
(c) Does the estimate mean that group B has a disease probability 0.70 greater than group A? Explain.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Let Y_i=1 indicate disease, g_i=0 for group A and g_i=1 for group B, and c_i denote cholesterol. Write p_i=\mathbb P(Y_i=1\mid g_i,c_i). The odds of probability p are p/(1-p) and its logit is \log\{p/(1-p)\}. An odds ratio compares odds, not probabilities; comparisons here hold cholesterol fixed.
(a) Model statement. Conditional on the fixed covariates, Y_i\mid g_i,c_i\overset{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}
\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_i),
\qquad p_i=\mathbb{P}(Y_i=1\mid g_i,c_i), with \boxed{
\log\left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\right)
=\beta_0+\beta_Gg_i+\beta_Cc_i=\eta_i.
} Equivalently, exponentiating and solving for p_i gives \frac{p_i}{1-p_i}=e^{\eta_i}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
p_i=e^{\eta_i}(1-p_i)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
p_i=\frac{e^{\eta_i}}{1+e^{\eta_i}}.
(b) Interpretation of \widehat\beta_G=0.70. For two patients with the same cholesterol, \frac{\widehat{\operatorname{odds}}(Y=1\mid g=1,c)}
     {\widehat{\operatorname{odds}}(Y=1\mid g=0,c)}
=e^{\widehat\beta_G}=e^{0.70}\approx2.01. Conclusion: Group B has approximately 2.01 times the fitted odds of disease of group A, after accounting for cholesterol. The estimate is an association; it is not automatically a causal effect.
(c) Why this is not a probability increase of 0.70. The coefficient acts on log odds, not directly on probability. If p_A is the fitted probability for group A at a given cholesterol and r=e^{0.70}, then \frac{p_B}{1-p_B}=r\frac{p_A}{1-p_A}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\boxed{p_B=\frac{rp_A}{1-p_A+rp_A}.} The difference p_B-p_A therefore depends on p_A. For example, if p_A=0.20, then p_B\approx0.335, a difference of about 0.135, not 0.70.

title: Q33. Score, Hessian, and information identity
Q31. Interpreting Poisson regression coefficients
text:
Topic: Standard errors, and models for counts · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 31 of 59 ‹ Q30 Q32 ›

[4 marks]
The model in Question 30 produces:



Term
Estimate




Intercept
1.50


distance
-0.04


log(area)
0.60



(a) Interpret the intercept in the context of the study.
(b) Interpret the distance coefficient on the scale of the expected species count.
(c) Compare two lakes at the same distance from the coast, where one has twice the area of the other. What does the model predict about their expected species counts?
(d) Assess this statement: “An extra hectare increases the expected species count by 60%.”






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Let \widehat\mu(d,A) be the fitted expected count at distance d kilometres and area A>0 hectares. A log link gives a mean ratio \mu_2/\mu_1=\exp(\eta_2-\eta_1), where \eta=\log\mu. For a logged covariate, the coefficient is an elasticity: the change in \log\mu per unit change in \log A. Each comparison below holds the other predictor fixed.
The fitted mean at distance d and area A is \widehat\mu(d,A)=\exp\{1.50-0.04d+0.60\log A\}.
(a) Intercept. At d=0 and \log A=0, so that A=1 hectare, \widehat\mu(0,1)=e^{1.50}\approx4.48. Conclusion: A one-hectare lake at the coast has a fitted expected species count of approximately 4.48. This is a reference prediction; it may involve extrapolation if such lakes are not represented in the data.
(b) Distance coefficient. Holding area fixed, increasing distance by one kilometre gives \frac{\widehat\mu(d+1,A)}{\widehat\mu(d,A)}
=\frac{e^{1.50-0.04(d+1)+0.60\log A}}
       {e^{1.50-0.04d+0.60\log A}}
=e^{-0.04}\approx0.9608. Conclusion: Each additional kilometre from the coast is associated with approximately 100(1-e^{-0.04})=3.92\% fewer expected species, holding lake area fixed.
(c) Doubling the area. At the same distance from the coast, \frac{\widehat\mu(d,2A)}{\widehat\mu(d,A)}
=e^{0.60\{\log(2A)-\log A\}}
=e^{0.60\log2}=2^{0.60}\approx1.516. Conclusion: The lake with twice the area has approximately 51.6\% more expected species.
(d) Assessing the extra-hectare claim. The statement is incorrect: the predictor is \log A, not A. An increase from A to A+1 hectares gives the ratio \frac{\widehat\mu(d,A+1)}{\widehat\mu(d,A)}
=\left(\frac{A+1}{A}\right)^{0.60}, which depends on the original area. The coefficient 0.60 is an elasticity: \frac{\partial\log\mu}{\partial\log A}=0.60. For a small percentage increase in area, the expected count increases by approximately 0.60 times that percentage, holding distance fixed.

title: Q29. Comparing Exponential and Gamma lifetime models
text:
Topic: Bayesian hypotheses and model comparison · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 29 of 59 ‹ Q28 Q30 ›

[20 marks]
Researchers observed lifetimes {\boldsymbol{x}}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n), with each x_i>0, for a sample of n medical devices. Two models are proposed, with conditionally iid observations under each model: M_1:\quad X_i\mid\lambda\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda),
\qquad
M_2:\quad X_i\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(3,\theta). Prior experiments suggest the parameter priors \lambda\mid M_1\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(1,3),
\qquad
\theta\mid M_2\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(1,1). Parameterisation: all Gamma distributions use shape–rate notation, and the exponential parameter is its rate.
(i) [6 marks] Find p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_1), the marginal likelihood of the data under model M_1.
(ii) [6 marks] Find p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_2), the marginal likelihood of the data under model M_2.
(iii) [4 marks] Obtain an expression for BF_{12}, the Bayes factor comparing M_1 with M_2. For the observed data, BF_{12}=1.347. Briefly interpret this number. Based on this evidence alone, which model is preferred?
(iv) [4 marks] Suppose the researchers’ prior belief is that M_2 is three times as likely as M_1. What are the posterior model odds? Which model is now preferred?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write S=\sum_i x_i and Q=\prod_i x_i^2. \operatorname{Exp}(\lambda) uses rate \lambda; \operatorname{Gamma}(a,b) uses shape a and rate b. For model M_j, the marginal likelihood is m_j({\boldsymbol{x}})=\int L_j(\vartheta;{\boldsymbol{x}})p_j(\vartheta)\,d\vartheta and BF_{12}=m_1/m_2. Use the same positive, conditionally independent lifetime sample and the stated proper priors in both models.
A marginal likelihood averages the fully normalised likelihood over the parameter prior. Unlike posterior kernel matching, this calculation must retain all multiplicative constants, including factors involving only the data.
Both calculations use the Gamma integral \int_0^\infty t^{A-1}e^{-Bt}\,dt
=\frac{\Gamma(A)}{B^A},\qquad A,B>0.
(i) Marginal likelihood under M_1. For an exponential distribution with rate \lambda, p(x_i\mid\lambda,M_1)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x_i},\qquad x_i>0. Therefore the likelihood and normalised prior are p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\lambda,M_1)=\lambda^n e^{-\lambda S},
\qquad p(\lambda\mid M_1)=3e^{-3\lambda},\quad\lambda>0. Integrating their product, \begin{aligned}
p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_1)
&=\int_0^\infty p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\lambda,M_1)
p(\lambda\mid M_1)\,d\lambda\\
&=3\int_0^\infty\lambda^n e^{-(S+3)\lambda}\,d\lambda\\
&=\boxed{\frac{3\Gamma(n+1)}{(S+3)^{n+1}}.}
\end{aligned} The power \lambda^n corresponds to Gamma shape n+1, not n. The leading 3 comes from the normalised prior and cannot be omitted.
(ii) Marginal likelihood under M_2. For a Gamma distribution with shape 3 and rate \theta, p(x_i\mid\theta,M_2)
=\frac{\theta^3}{\Gamma(3)}x_i^2e^{-\theta x_i}
=\frac{\theta^3}{2}x_i^2e^{-\theta x_i},\qquad x_i>0. Thus p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta,M_2)=\frac{Q}{2^n}\theta^{3n}e^{-\theta S},
\qquad p(\theta\mid M_2)=e^{-\theta},\quad\theta>0. Integrating gives \begin{aligned}
p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_2)
&=\int_0^\infty p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta,M_2)
p(\theta\mid M_2)\,d\theta\\
&=\frac{Q}{2^n}\int_0^\infty\theta^{3n}e^{-(S+1)\theta}\,d\theta\\
&=\boxed{\frac{Q\,\Gamma(3n+1)}{2^n(S+1)^{3n+1}}.}
\end{aligned} Although Q/2^n does not involve \theta, it remains part of the marginal likelihood. Dropping it would give the wrong model comparison.
(iii) Bayes factor and its interpretation. By definition, \begin{aligned}
BF_{12}
&=\frac{p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_1)}{p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_2)}\\
&=\frac{3\Gamma(n+1)}{(S+3)^{n+1}}
\frac{2^n(S+1)^{3n+1}}{Q\,\Gamma(3n+1)}.
\end{aligned} Hence \boxed{BF_{12}
=\frac{3\cdot2^n\Gamma(n+1)(S+1)^{3n+1}}
{\Gamma(3n+1)(S+3)^{n+1}\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_i^2}.} The observed value BF_{12}=1.347 means that the marginal likelihood of the data under M_1 is 1.347 times that under M_2, using the specified parameter priors. The data therefore favour M_1, but only slightly. This is not a posterior probability of either model.
Based on the marginal evidence alone, M_1 is preferred. If the prior model probabilities were equal, its posterior probability would be \mathbb{P}(M_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{1.347}{1+1.347}\approx0.574. Different prior model odds can reverse that posterior preference.
(iv) Unequal prior model probabilities. The prior belief in the question gives \frac{\mathbb{P}(M_1)}{\mathbb{P}(M_2)}=\frac13. Posterior odds equal the Bayes factor times prior odds, so \boxed{
\frac{\mathbb{P}(M_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})}{\mathbb{P}(M_2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})}
=1.347\left(\frac13\right)=0.449.
} Thus the posterior odds are 0.449:1 in favour of M_1 relative to M_2, or approximately 2.227:1 in favour of M_2. With these two models as the alternatives, \mathbb{P}(M_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{0.449}{1+0.449}\approx0.310, \mathbb{P}(M_2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac1{1+0.449}\approx0.690. Model M_2 is now preferred. The Bayes factor moves the odds toward M_1, but the evidence is too weak to overcome the prior three-to-one preference for M_2.

Key result. Keep the normalising constants when integrating likelihoods. A Bayes factor updates model odds; it is not itself a posterior model probability.

title: Q27. Machine downtime and a Gamma prior
text:
Topic: Exponential families and conjugacy · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 27 of 59 ‹ Q26 Q28 ›

[25 marks]
Suppose the proportion of time X that a production machine is down during its daily shift follows a \operatorname{Beta}(1,\theta) distribution: f(x\mid\theta)=\theta(1-x)^{\theta-1},
\qquad 0<x<1,\quad\theta>0. Let X_i denote the proportion of downtime on day i, for i=1,\ldots,n, and assume the observations are conditionally iid given \theta. Use the \operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha,\beta) prior in shape–rate form, p(\theta)=\frac{\beta^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)}
\theta^{\alpha-1}e^{-\beta\theta},
\qquad\theta>0,\quad\alpha,\beta>0.
(a) [1 mark] State, without derivation, the prior mean.
(b) [8 marks] Obtain an expression for the posterior distribution of \theta given the data {\boldsymbol{x}}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n), and identify its distribution.
(c) [2 marks] State, without derivation, the posterior mean.
(d) [9 marks] Explain what happens to the posterior mean:
(i) as n\to\infty, with the prior fixed;
(ii) as \alpha,\beta\to0, with the data fixed;
(iii) as \alpha,\beta\to\infty, with the data fixed.
State any additional conditions required for a definite limit.
(e) [5 marks] Interpret the posterior mean by completing:

“The effect of the prior hyperparameters \alpha and \beta on the posterior mean of \theta is like …”

Support your interpretation with an appropriate expression for the posterior mean.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. The sampling density \theta(1-x)^{\theta-1} is \operatorname{Beta}(1,\theta) on (0,1). The prior \operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha,\beta) uses shape \alpha>0 and rate \beta>0, so its kernel is \theta^{\alpha-1}e^{-\beta\theta} and its mean is \alpha/\beta. The observations are conditionally iid with n\ge1. The transformed sum S=-\sum_i\log(1-x_i) is positive and is not the raw total downtime.
(a) Prior mean. The prior is Gamma in shape–rate form, so \boxed{\mathbb{E}(\theta)=\frac{\alpha}{\beta}.}
(b) Posterior distribution. For conditionally iid observations, the likelihood is \begin{aligned}
L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\theta(1-x_i)^{\theta-1}\\
&=\theta^n\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1-x_i)^{\theta-1}\\
&=\theta^n\exp\!\left\{(\theta-1)
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log(1-x_i)\right\}.
\end{aligned} Define the positive statistic S=-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log(1-x_i)>0. Then L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})
=e^S\theta^ne^{-S\theta}
\propto\theta^ne^{-S\theta},\qquad\theta>0, where only e^S, which does not involve \theta, has been discarded. Multiplying by the Gamma prior gives \begin{aligned}
p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})p(\theta)\\
&\propto\theta^ne^{-S\theta}
\theta^{\alpha-1}e^{-\beta\theta}\\
&=\theta^{\alpha+n-1}e^{-(\beta+S)\theta}.
\end{aligned} Matching the shape–rate Gamma kernel gives \boxed{\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim
\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha+n,\beta+S),\qquad\theta>0.} The normalised posterior density is \boxed{p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\frac{(\beta+S)^{\alpha+n}}{\Gamma(\alpha+n)}
\theta^{\alpha+n-1}e^{-(\beta+S)\theta},\qquad\theta>0.} Equivalently, the posterior rate is \beta-\sum_i\log(1-x_i). It is positive: each \log(1-x_i) is negative.
(c) Posterior mean. \boxed{\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{\alpha+n}{\beta+S}
=\frac{\alpha+n}{\beta-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log(1-x_i)}.}
(d) Limiting behaviour. First identify the maximum-likelihood estimate. From the log-likelihood \ell(\theta)=n\log\theta-S\theta+\text{constant}, we have \ell'(\theta)=\frac n\theta-S,\qquad
\ell''(\theta)=-\frac n{\theta^2}<0. Consequently, \widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}=\frac nS.
(i) Increasing sample size with a fixed prior. Write S_n=-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log(1-X_i) to make its dependence on n explicit. The posterior mean is \frac{\alpha+n}{\beta+S_n}
=\frac{1+\alpha/n}{S_n/n+\beta/n}. If the data arise from the stated model at a true value \theta_0>0, then Z_i=-\log(1-X_i) are iid \operatorname{Exp}(\theta_0) variables. For z\geq0, \mathbb{P}(Z_i>z\mid\theta_0)
=\mathbb{P}(X_i>1-e^{-z}\mid\theta_0)=e^{-\theta_0z}. Thus \mathbb{E}(Z_i\mid\theta_0)=1/\theta_0, and the law of large numbers gives S_n/n\to1/\theta_0. Hence \boxed{\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid X_1,\ldots,X_n)\longrightarrow\theta_0.} The MLE n/S_n has the same limit, and the fixed prior’s influence vanishes. It would be incorrect to let n increase while holding S_n fixed in this sampling argument: new observations also change the sum.
(ii) \alpha,\beta\to0 with the data fixed. For n\geq1 and observed 0<x_i<1, we have S>0. Therefore \boxed{\frac{\alpha+n}{\beta+S}\longrightarrow\frac nS
=\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}.} The proper Gamma priors have the formal limiting kernel 1/\theta, not a uniform density; the resulting limiting posterior is the proper \operatorname{Gamma}(n,S) distribution.
(iii) \alpha,\beta\to\infty with the data fixed. Compare the posterior mean with the prior mean: \frac{(\alpha+n)/(\beta+S)}{\alpha/\beta}
=\frac{1+n/\alpha}{1+S/\beta}\longrightarrow1. Thus the posterior mean follows the prior mean asymptotically. To claim a specific finite limit, specify the limiting ratio. If \alpha/\beta\to m_0\in(0,\infty), then \boxed{\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\longrightarrow m_0.} In particular, this holds when the prior mean is kept fixed at m_0 while its concentration increases. Both prior and posterior variances then tend to zero. Without a condition on \alpha/\beta, there is no unique limit: \alpha=\beta\to\infty gives limit 1, whereas \alpha=2\beta\to\infty gives limit 2; other paths can diverge or fail to converge.
(e) Interpreting the prior’s effect. The posterior mean can be written exactly as \begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=\frac{\alpha+n}{\beta+S}\\
&=\frac{\beta}{\beta+S}\frac{\alpha}{\beta}
+\frac{S}{\beta+S}\frac nS.
\end{aligned} Hence \boxed{\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=w\,\mathbb{E}(\theta)+(1-w)\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}},
\qquad w=\frac{\beta}{\beta+S}.} Since 0<w<1 and the weights sum to one, the posterior mean lies between the prior mean and the MLE.
An exam-style completion of the sentence is:

“The effect of the prior hyperparameters \alpha and \beta on the posterior mean of \theta is like adding prior information that pulls the data-based estimate n/S toward the prior mean \alpha/\beta, with prior weight \beta/(\beta+S).”

Keeping \alpha/\beta fixed while increasing \alpha,\beta increases the prior weight. Increasing the amount of data increases S under the model and reduces that weight.
There is also a pseudo-data interpretation on the transformed scale Z_i=-\log(1-X_i), where Z_i\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\theta). The likelihood estimate is the observation count divided by total transformed exposure, n/S. In the posterior-mean formula, \alpha adds to the count and \beta adds to the transformed exposure: \frac{n+\text{prior pseudo-count}}{S+\text{prior exposure}}
=\frac{n+\alpha}{S+\beta}. These are contributions to the posterior mean, not necessarily a literal integer number of extra observations. This interpretation concerns the transformed downtime, not the raw sum \sum_i x_i.

Key result. The posterior is Gamma with shape \alpha+n and rate \beta-\sum_i\log(1-x_i). A strong prior dominates only toward the mean specified by its ratio \alpha/\beta.

title: Q25. Gibbs, Metropolis–Hastings, and Monte Carlo error
text:
Topic: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 25 of 59 ‹ Q24 Q26 ›

[25 marks]
Consider two random variables X and Y with joint density f(x,y)\propto x^3y\exp(-xy-2x-3y),
\qquad x>0,\quad y>0, and zero density elsewhere.
Support clarification: the supplied screenshot does not state the support. This question uses the positive quadrant.
(a) [10 marks] Describe a Gibbs sampler to generate samples from the above joint density.
(b) [10 marks] Describe a random-walk Metropolis–Hastings algorithm to generate samples from the above joint density, using proposal increments distributed as N_2(\mathbf 0,\sigma^2I_2), where I_2 is the identity matrix and \sigma>0 is fixed.
(c) [5 marks] Briefly describe how you would obtain an approximate 95% confidence interval for \mathbb{E}(Y) from the simulation output.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Take the joint support to be x,y>0. We use \operatorname{Gamma}(a,b) in shape–rate form, with kernel z^{a-1}e^{-bz} on z>0. N_2(\mathbf m,\Sigma) uses a covariance matrix \Sigma, and I_2 is the 2\times2 identity. The estimand in (c) is the fixed target mean \mu_Y=\mathbb{E}_f(Y); its simulation uncertainty is measured by a Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE).
(a) Gibbs sampler. For the conditional distribution of X, fix y>0 and retain all factors involving x: \begin{aligned}
f(x\mid y)&\propto x^3y\exp(-xy-2x-3y)\\
&\propto x^3\exp\{-(y+2)x\},\qquad x>0.
\end{aligned} The power 3=4-1 identifies shape 4, and the coefficient of x in the negative exponential is the rate y+2. Thus \boxed{X\mid Y=y\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(4,y+2).} Similarly, fixing x>0 gives f(y\mid x)\propto y\exp\{-(x+3)y\},\qquad y>0, and hence \boxed{Y\mid X=x\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(2,x+3).} The corresponding normalised conditional densities are f(x\mid y)=\frac{(y+2)^4}{\Gamma(4)}x^3e^{-(y+2)x},
\qquad
f(y\mid x)=\frac{(x+3)^2}{\Gamma(2)}y e^{-(x+3)y}.
Choose any valid initial pair (x^{(0)},y^{(0)}) with both coordinates positive. A systematic-scan Gibbs sampler is:
1. For t=1,\ldots,T, draw X^{(t)}\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(4,Y^{(t-1)}+2).
2. Using this newly drawn value, draw Y^{(t)}\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(2,X^{(t)}+3).
3. Record the pair (X^{(t)},Y^{(t)}) and repeat.
Every draw is from an exact full conditional, so there is no accept–reject step. Each conditional update preserves the target joint distribution; their composition therefore has f(x,y) as an equilibrium distribution. After checking convergence and allowing suitable warm-up, retained pairs can be used to approximate target expectations. Successive pairs are generally dependent, not iid.
(b) Random-walk Metropolis–Hastings. Let the current state be (x,y) with x,y>0. Draw an increment \boldsymbol\varepsilon\sim N_2(\mathbf 0,\sigma^2I_2) and propose (x',y')=(x,y)+\boldsymbol\varepsilon. Equivalently, the proposed state is N_2((x,y)^\top,\sigma^2I_2). The zero-mean normal distribution describes the increment, not an independence proposal centred at the origin.
The proposal is symmetric: q\bigl((x',y')\mid(x,y)\bigr)
=q\bigl((x,y)\mid(x',y')\bigr), because reversing the increment leaves its squared length unchanged. Thus the proposal densities cancel from the Metropolis–Hastings ratio. For a proposal in the positive quadrant, \begin{aligned}
r&=\frac{f(x',y')}{f(x,y)}\\
&=\frac{(x')^3y' e^{-x'y'-2x'-3y'}}{x^3y e^{-xy-2x-3y}}\\
&=\left(\frac{x'}x\right)^3\frac{y'}y
\exp\{-x'y'+xy-2(x'-x)-3(y'-y)\}.
\end{aligned} Therefore the acceptance probability is \boxed{
a\bigl((x,y),(x',y')\bigr)=
\begin{cases}
\min\{1,r\},&x'>0,\ y'>0,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}} The unknown normalising constant of f cancels in the target-density ratio.
Start from a valid positive pair. For each iteration t=1,\ldots,T:
1. Draw an independent N_2(\mathbf0,\sigma^2I_2) increment and add it to (X^{(t-1)},Y^{(t-1)}) to obtain (x',y').
2. If either proposed coordinate is nonpositive, reject the proposal. Otherwise compute a above and draw U\sim U(0,1) independently; accept if U\leq a.
3. On acceptance set (X^{(t)},Y^{(t)})=(x',y'); on rejection set (X^{(t)},Y^{(t)})=(X^{(t-1)},Y^{(t-1)}).
4. Record the state, including repeated states caused by rejection.
An out-of-support proposal is rejected, not repeatedly redrawn until it is positive: such redrawing would change the proposal distribution and its acceptance ratio. Assess convergence before using the retained output.
(c) A 95% confidence interval for \mathbb{E}(Y). The target is the fixed number \mu_Y=\mathbb{E}_f(Y), estimated using a Monte Carlo average. After suitable warm-up and convergence checks, retain N consecutive values Y_1,\ldots,Y_N and calculate \bar Y_N=\frac1N\sum_{t=1}^{N}Y_t. These values are generally autocorrelated, so the iid standard error s_Y/\sqrt N is not generally valid.
One practical method is batch means. Write N=ab, with a non-overlapping batches of length b, and calculate \bar Y_k^{\mathrm{batch}}=
\frac1b\sum_{t=(k-1)b+1}^{kb}Y_t,\qquad k=1,\ldots,a, s_B^2=\frac1{a-1}\sum_{k=1}^{a}
\bigl(\bar Y_k^{\mathrm{batch}}-\bar Y_N\bigr)^2. With batches long relative to the chain’s dependence and sufficiently many batches, the batch averages are approximately independent and approximately normal under the usual Markov-chain central limit conditions. An estimated Monte Carlo standard error is \widehat{\operatorname{MCSE}}(\bar Y_N)=\frac{s_B}{\sqrt a}. An approximate 95% confidence interval is then \boxed{\bar Y_N\ \pm\ t_{0.975,a-1}\frac{s_B}{\sqrt a}.} For large a, the t quantile can be replaced by 1.96. The simulation should be long enough for the interval to be reasonably stable when the batch length is increased.
Equivalently, for a stationary chain satisfying a central limit theorem, \sqrt N(\bar Y_N-\mu_Y)\ \xrightarrow{d}\ N(0,\tau_Y^2), where the long-run variance is \tau_Y^2=\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k,
\qquad \gamma_k=\operatorname{Cov}(Y_t,Y_{t+k}). Batch means estimates this variance by \widehat\tau_Y^2=b s_B^2, giving the same standard error \sqrt{\widehat\tau_Y^2/N}=s_B/\sqrt a.

Key result. This interval measures Monte Carlo error in estimating \mathbb{E}(Y). The empirical 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the Y_t values instead give an interval for the variable Y; they are not a confidence interval for its mean.

title: Q23. Rat-tumour studies and hierarchical shrinkage
text:
Topic: Hierarchical Bayes · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 23 of 59 ‹ Q22 Q24 ›

[12 marks]
Suppose J related studies record tumour counts Y_j\mid\theta_j\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n_j,\theta_j),
\qquad j=1,\ldots,J, independently conditional on the study rates. Assume \theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta
\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta),
\qquad
\alpha\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1),\quad
\beta\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1), where the two hyperpriors are independent. Write \mathbf y=(y_1,\ldots,y_J); the sample sizes n_j are known. You may use B(a,b)=\int_0^1 t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}\,dt,
\qquad
f(\theta\mid a,b)=\frac{\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}}{B(a,b)}.
(a) [2 marks] Derive and identify the full conditional distribution \theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y.
(b) [3 marks] For this part only, fix \alpha=2 and \beta=8. Two studies report (y_1,n_1)=(4,10),\qquad (y_2,n_2)=(40,100). Calculate both posterior means. Although both observed proportions equal 0.4, explain why the posterior means differ and identify which study experiences stronger shrinkage.
(c) [4 marks] Return to unknown \alpha,\beta. Integrate out the study rates to derive:
(i) the marginal probability \mathbb{P}(Y_j=y_j\mid\alpha,\beta);
(ii) the marginal posterior kernel p(\alpha,\beta\mid\mathbf y).
Express your answers using Beta functions. Explain why the Beta prior’s normalising factor cannot be discarded when deriving this hyperparameter posterior.
(d) [3 marks] Explain how the full Bayesian model allows studies to share information. What uncertainty is omitted if \alpha,\beta are instead estimated from the data and then treated as known?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Study j has observed count y_j, known size n_j, and unknown rate \theta_j; \alpha,\beta>0 are shared hyperparameters. A \operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta) density is \theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1}/B(\alpha,\beta) on (0,1), where B(a,b)=\int_0^1u^{a-1}(1-u)^{b-1}\,du. \operatorname{Exp}(1) uses rate one. Partial pooling allows different study rates linked through a common population distribution.
Assumptions. The hierarchy assumes conditional independence of studies given their rates, and iid Beta rates given \alpha,\beta. Thus its joint density factors as p(\alpha)p(\beta)\prod_jp(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta)p(y_j\mid\theta_j), with independent rate-one exponential hyperpriors. Only in part (b) are the hyperparameters fixed at the supplied values.
(a) Full conditional for a study rate. Holding \alpha,\beta fixed, the factors involving \theta_j are \begin{aligned}
p(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y)
&\propto p(y_j\mid\theta_j)p(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta)\\
&\propto\theta_j^{y_j}(1-\theta_j)^{n_j-y_j}
\theta_j^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta_j)^{\beta-1}\\
&=\theta_j^{\alpha+y_j-1}(1-\theta_j)^{\beta+n_j-y_j-1}.
\end{aligned} Therefore \boxed{\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y
\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+y_j,\beta+n_j-y_j),\qquad 0<\theta_j<1.} Conditional on the hyperparameters and data, the study rates are independent. Other studies’ observations affect this study’s marginal posterior through learning \alpha,\beta, not through an additional factor in this full conditional.
(b) Posterior means and shrinkage. For fixed \alpha=2, \beta=8, the population mean is \frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}=\frac2{10}=0.2. The two posteriors are \theta_1\mid\alpha=2,\beta=8,\mathbf y\sim\operatorname{Beta}(6,14), \theta_2\mid\alpha=2,\beta=8,\mathbf y\sim\operatorname{Beta}(42,68). Thus their posterior means are \boxed{\mathbb{E}(\theta_1\mid\alpha=2,\beta=8,\mathbf y)=\frac6{20}=0.3,} \boxed{\mathbb{E}(\theta_2\mid\alpha=2,\beta=8,\mathbf y)=\frac{42}{110}
\approx0.3818.} To see the shrinkage explicitly, write \frac{\alpha+y_j}{\alpha+\beta+n_j}
=\frac{\alpha+\beta}{\alpha+\beta+n_j}
\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}
+\frac{n_j}{\alpha+\beta+n_j}\frac{y_j}{n_j}. Both sample proportions equal 0.4, but study 1 puts weight 10/20=1/2 on the population mean, whereas study 2 puts only 10/110=1/11 on it. The smaller study therefore experiences stronger shrinkage toward 0.2. The larger study has more information about its own rate, so its posterior mean remains closer to its observed proportion.
(c) Integrating out the study rates. For one study, retain the normalising factor of the Beta density: \begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(Y_j=y_j\mid\alpha,\beta)
&=\int_0^1 p(y_j\mid\theta_j)p(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta)\,d\theta_j\\
&=\binom{n_j}{y_j}\frac1{B(\alpha,\beta)}
\int_0^1\theta_j^{y_j+\alpha-1}
(1-\theta_j)^{n_j-y_j+\beta-1}\,d\theta_j\\
&=\boxed{\binom{n_j}{y_j}
\frac{B(\alpha+y_j,\beta+n_j-y_j)}{B(\alpha,\beta)}.}
\end{aligned} This is a Beta–Binomial marginal distribution, with y_j\in\{0,\ldots,n_j\}.
The independent rate-one exponential hyperpriors give p(\alpha,\beta)=e^{-\alpha-\beta},\qquad \alpha>0,\quad\beta>0. The studies remain independent conditional on the hyperparameters after their individual rates have been integrated out. Consequently, \begin{aligned}
p(\alpha,\beta\mid\mathbf y)
&\propto p(\alpha,\beta)
\prod_{j=1}^{J}\mathbb{P}(Y_j=y_j\mid\alpha,\beta)\\
&\propto e^{-(\alpha+\beta)}
\prod_{j=1}^{J}
\frac{B(\alpha+y_j,\beta+n_j-y_j)}{B(\alpha,\beta)}.
\end{aligned} Hence \boxed{
p(\alpha,\beta\mid\mathbf y)
\propto e^{-(\alpha+\beta)}B(\alpha,\beta)^{-J}
\prod_{j=1}^{J}B(\alpha+y_j,\beta+n_j-y_j),
\quad \alpha,\beta>0.
} The binomial coefficients can be dropped because the observed y_j and known n_j make them constant with respect to \alpha,\beta. However, 1/B(\alpha,\beta) depends on the hyperparameters, so it must remain. A factor constant in \theta_j need not be constant in \alpha,\beta.
(d) Sharing information and hyperparameter uncertainty. Every study contributes to the posterior for the common population parameters \alpha,\beta. That posterior then contributes to each study-specific posterior through p(\theta_j\mid\mathbf y)
=\int_0^\infty\!\int_0^\infty
p(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y)
p(\alpha,\beta\mid\mathbf y)\,d\alpha\,d\beta. This is partial pooling: study rates can differ, but they are connected by a population distribution learned from all the studies. The model does not force them to be identical, and it does not treat them as unrelated.
Replacing \alpha,\beta by fixed estimates is an empirical-Bayes plug-in analysis. It omits uncertainty about the population distribution’s parameters. For example, the law of total variance gives \begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(\theta_j\mid\mathbf y)
={}&\mathbb{E}\!\left[
\operatorname{Var}(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y)
\mid\mathbf y\right]\\
&+\operatorname{Var}\!\left[
\mathbb{E}(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y)
\mid\mathbf y\right].
\end{aligned} The second term represents variation in the conditional mean as the hyperparameters vary under their posterior. A plug-in calculation does not propagate this variation and can therefore give an overly precise account of uncertainty.

Key result. Conditional conjugacy does not eliminate uncertainty in the hyperparameters. Full Bayes learns their distribution and averages over it.

title: Q21. Evidence and posterior model probabilities
Q19. Assessing a Metropolis–Hastings sampler
text:
Topic: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 19 of 59 ‹ Q18 Q20 ›

[4 marks]
A researcher runs a random-walk Metropolis–Hastings sampler using a Normal proposal centred at the current state. The proposal standard deviation is very small, and approximately 99% of proposals are accepted. The researcher concludes that the sampler is highly efficient.
Explain why the acceptance rate alone does not justify this conclusion. Describe the behaviour you would expect from this sampler and identify one additional feature of its output that you would examine.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. The acceptance rate is the fraction of proposed moves accepted. Autocorrelation measures dependence between draws at different lags. For a chosen posterior summary, effective sample size is the number of independent target draws giving comparable Monte Carlo precision. Efficiency concerns that precision per unit of computation, not the acceptance fraction alone.
An acceptance rate of 99% does not by itself demonstrate efficiency. With a very small proposal standard deviation, proposed values lie close to the current state. The target density changes little across such a short move, so most proposals are accepted; however, each accepted move advances the chain only a small distance.
The expected consequences are slow exploration of the posterior and strong autocorrelation between successive draws. A large recorded sample may then contain information equivalent to a much smaller independent sample.
In addition to acceptance rate, useful diagnostics include:

a trace plot, to assess whether the chain explores the full target region;
the autocorrelation function, to measure serial dependence; and
the effective sample size, to quantify the independent information represented by the chain.

Thus a very high acceptance rate may indicate that the proposal scale is too small, not that the sampler is highly efficient.
An exact independent draw from the target would also have acceptance probability one and would be efficient. High acceptance is therefore neither sufficient evidence of efficiency nor inherently a fault; the movement and dependence matter.

title: Q17. Choosing a conjugate prior
text:
Topic: The Beta–Binomial model · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 17 of 59 ‹ Q16 Q18 ›

[3 marks]
Explain what it means for a prior family to be conjugate to a sampling model, and give one practical advantage of using such a family.
A researcher instead chooses a nonconjugate prior because it better represents the available background information. Does this make the Bayesian analysis invalid? Explain what computational difficulty may arise.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. A prior family is conjugate when multiplication by the likelihood and normalisation return a member of that family. For the example below, the Binomial likelihood kernel is \theta^x(1-\theta)^{n-x} and the Beta prior kernel is \theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1} on (0,1), with a,b>0. A valid posterior requires a finite, positive normalising integral.
For example, multiplying the Binomial and Beta kernels adds their success and failure exponents. Thus X\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,\theta),
\qquad
\theta\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a,b) implies \theta\mid X=x
\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a+x,b+n-x). One practical advantage is that posterior updating reduces to updating the hyperparameters. Posterior summaries and predictive calculations can often be obtained analytically, without numerical integration.
A nonconjugate prior does not make the analysis invalid. It may be preferable when it represents the available prior information more faithfully. However, the posterior may not have a standard form, and its normalising constant or required expectations may be difficult to calculate. Numerical quadrature, grid approximation, importance sampling, or MCMC may then be required.

title: Q15. Prior beliefs and conflicting data
text:
Topic: Bayesian foundations · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 15 of 59 ‹ Q14 Q16 ›

[3 marks]
A researcher models independent observations as Bernoulli with unknown success probability \theta. The researcher chooses a prior that is uniform on (0,1/2).
Of 100 observed trials, 80 are successes. The researcher argues that these data should make the posterior probability of \theta>1/2 large.
Is this reasoning correct? Explain what happens and whether collecting more observations can overcome the restriction imposed by this prior.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Let L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})=p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta) and let m({\boldsymbol{x}})=\int L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})p(\theta)\,d\theta be the marginal likelihood. Bayes’ update is p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})p(\theta)/m({\boldsymbol{x}}), provided 0<m({\boldsymbol{x}})<\infty. The prior here excludes the entire region \theta>1/2, not merely a single value.
The reasoning is incorrect. The prior density is zero for every \theta>1/2. Bayes’ theorem gives p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
\propto p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta)p(\theta), so p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=0
\qquad\text{whenever }\theta>1/2. Hence \boxed{
\mathbb{P}(\theta>1/2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=0.
