} This remains true regardless of how many observations are collected. The likelihood can redistribute posterior mass only among parameter values to which the prior assigns positive density; it cannot create support in a region excluded by the prior.
The observed proportion 80/100=0.8 instead reveals serious conflict between the data and the assumed model–prior combination. The researcher should reconsider the restricted prior, or investigate whether the Bernoulli model is appropriate. With the restriction left unchanged, additional data cannot make the posterior probability above 1/2 positive.

title: Q13. Bayesian German tank problem
Q11. Bayes factors and posterior odds
text:
Topic: Bayesian hypotheses and model comparison · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 11 of 59 ‹ Q10 Q12 ›

Suppose X\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,\theta). Consider M_0:\theta=\frac12,
  \qquad
  M_1:\theta\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1). Under M_1, the stated distribution is the prior for \theta. Write m_j(x)=p(x\mid M_j).
(a) Derive m_0(x) and m_1(x). Retain the constants in the binomial probability mass function. [4 marks]
(b) Obtain B_{10}=\frac{m_1(x)}{m_0(x)}. Explain how it relates prior model odds to posterior model odds. [3 marks]
(c) Suppose n=3, x=3, and \mathbb{P}(M_1)=1/5. Calculate B_{10} and \mathbb{P}(M_1\mid x). Explain how the data can favour M_1 while M_0 still has the larger posterior probability. [3 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. M_0 fixes \theta=1/2; M_1 assigns \theta\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1,1). Write m_j(x)=\mathbb P(X=x\mid M_j) for the marginal likelihood and B_{10}=m_1(x)/m_0(x) for the Bayes factor favouring M_1. The Beta integral is B(a,b)=\int_0^1u^{a-1}(1-u)^{b-1}\,du. Prior probabilities of the two models are distinct from their priors for \theta.

(a) Marginal likelihoods
Under M_0, the marginal probability of observing X=x is m_0(x)
=
\mathbb{P}(X=x\mid M_0)
=
\binom{n}{x}\left(\frac12\right)^x
\left(\frac12\right)^{n-x}
=
\boxed{\binom{n}{x}2^{-n}}.
Under M_1, integrate the likelihood with respect to the uniform prior: \begin{aligned}
m_1(x)
&=
\mathbb{P}(X=x\mid M_1)\\
&=
\binom{n}{x}
\int_0^1\theta^x(1-\theta)^{n-x}\,d\theta\\
&=
\binom{n}{x}B(x+1,n-x+1)\\
&=
\binom{n}{x}
\frac{x!(n-x)!}{(n+1)!}\\
&=
\boxed{\frac{1}{n+1}}.
\end{aligned}


(b) Bayes factor
The Bayes factor in favour of M_1 over M_0 is \boxed{
B_{10}
=
\frac{m_1(x)}{m_0(x)}
=
\frac{2^n}{(n+1)\binom{n}{x}}.
} Values greater than one favour M_1, while values less than one favour M_0.


(c) Posterior model odds
Posterior odds equal the Bayes factor multiplied by prior odds: \boxed{
\frac{\mathbb{P}(M_1\mid x)}{\mathbb{P}(M_0\mid x)}
=
B_{10}
\frac{\mathbb{P}(M_1)}{\mathbb{P}(M_0)}.
}


(d) Numerical comparison
For n=3 and x=3, m_0(3)=\frac18,
\qquad
m_1(3)=\frac14,
\qquad
B_{10}=2. Thus the observed data are twice as probable under M_1 as under M_0, so the data favour M_1.
If \mathbb{P}(M_1)=\frac15,
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(M_0)=\frac45, then the prior odds for M_1 are 1/4. Hence \frac{\mathbb{P}(M_1\mid x)}{\mathbb{P}(M_0\mid x)}
=2\left(\frac14\right)
=\frac12. Therefore \boxed{
\mathbb{P}(M_1\mid x)=\frac13,
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(M_0\mid x)=\frac23.
} The data favour M_1, but the prior favoured M_0 by four to one. The evidence from this small sample is not strong enough to overturn that prior preference, so M_0 remains more probable a posteriori.

title: Q9. Gibbs sampling for a correlated normal target
text:
Topic: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 9 of 59 ‹ Q8 Q10 ›

Consider the joint posterior density p(\theta_1,\theta_2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
  \propto
  \exp\left[
    -\frac{\theta_1^2-2\rho\theta_1\theta_2+\theta_2^2}
           {2(1-\rho^2)}
  \right], where \theta_1,\theta_2\in\mathbb{R} and -1<\rho<1 is known.
(a) Derive the two full conditional distributions, identifying their means and variances. [4 marks]
(b) Give pseudocode for a Gibbs sampler with this equilibrium density. Make clear which current or updated value is used at each step. [3 marks]
(c) Suppose the initial pair is drawn exactly from the equilibrium distribution. Are the subsequent sampled pairs necessarily independent? Explain. [2 marks]
(d) When \rho is close to 1, explain why this sampler may move slowly through the joint posterior, even though every Gibbs update is accepted. [3 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. The target coordinates \theta_1,\theta_2 have zero means, unit marginal variances, and correlation \rho, with -1<\rho<1. A full conditional holds the other coordinate and the data x fixed. The Normal kernel \exp\{-(u-m)^2/(2v)\} identifies mean m and variance v>0. Superscript (t) labels the Gibbs sweep.
The joint density has kernel \pi(\theta_1,\theta_2\mid x)
\propto
\exp\left\{
-\frac{1}{2(1-\rho^2)}
\left(\theta_1^2-2\rho\theta_1\theta_2+\theta_2^2\right)
\right\}.

(a) Full conditional distributions
For the first full conditional, p(\theta_1\mid\theta_2,x)
=
\frac{p(\theta_1,\theta_2\mid x)}{p(\theta_2\mid x)}
\propto p(\theta_1,\theta_2\mid x)
\quad\text{as a function of }\theta_1. The denominator is constant when \theta_2 and x are held fixed. Thus the joint kernel is sufficient: terms involving \theta_1 must be kept, while terms free of \theta_1 may be absorbed into the proportionality constant.
We aim to match the Normal kernel \exp\left\{-\frac{(\theta_1-m)^2}{2v}\right\}, where m is the mean and v is the variance. Treat the quadratic form in the joint exponent as a quadratic in \theta_1. Completing the square gives \begin{aligned}
\theta_1^2-2\rho\theta_1\theta_2+\theta_2^2
&=(\theta_1-\rho\theta_2)^2
  -\rho^2\theta_2^2+\theta_2^2\\
&=(\theta_1-\rho\theta_2)^2
  +(1-\rho^2)\theta_2^2.
\end{aligned} Substitution into the joint kernel gives \begin{aligned}
p(\theta_1\mid\theta_2,x)
&\propto
\exp\left\{
-\frac{(\theta_1-\rho\theta_2)^2+(1-\rho^2)\theta_2^2}
{2(1-\rho^2)}
\right\}\\
&=
\exp\left\{-\frac{(\theta_1-\rho\theta_2)^2}
{2(1-\rho^2)}\right\}
\exp\left\{-\frac{\theta_2^2}{2}\right\}\\
&\propto
\exp\left\{-\frac{(\theta_1-\rho\theta_2)^2}
{2(1-\rho^2)}\right\}.
\end{aligned} The factor \exp(-\theta_2^2/2) is dropped because it is constant with respect to \theta_1. Matching the remaining expression to the Normal kernel yields \boxed{
\theta_1\mid\theta_2,x
\sim N\left(\rho\theta_2,\,1-\rho^2\right).
} The condition -1<\rho<1 ensures that the conditional variance 1-\rho^2 is positive.
For the other coordinate, the same calculation gives \theta_2^2-2\rho\theta_1\theta_2+\theta_1^2
=
(\theta_2-\rho\theta_1)^2+(1-\rho^2)\theta_1^2. Hence, by symmetry, \boxed{
\theta_2\mid\theta_1,x
\sim N\left(\rho\theta_1,\,1-\rho^2\right).
}


(b) Gibbs sampler
Starting from any valid pair (\theta_1^{(0)},\theta_2^{(0)})\in\mathbb{R}^2, repeat for t=1,\ldots,T:
1. Draw \theta_1^{(t)}
    \sim N\left(\rho\theta_2^{(t-1)},\,1-\rho^2\right).
2. Draw \theta_2^{(t)}
    \sim N\left(\rho\theta_1^{(t)},\,1-\rho^2\right).
3. Store (\theta_1^{(t)},\theta_2^{(t)}).
Each update is sampled directly from a full conditional distribution, so no accept–reject step is required.


(c) Equilibrium and independence
If the chain is started in equilibrium, every stored pair has the required joint distribution. The pairs are nevertheless generally not independent, because the distribution of the next pair depends on the current pair through the Gibbs updates.
When \rho=0, the coordinates are independent and fresh conditional draws produce independent pairs across full sweeps. This exception does not apply to a correlated target.


(d) Effect of strong correlation
When \rho is close to 1, the joint density is concentrated around the diagonal \theta_1=\theta_2, while the conditional variance 1-\rho^2 is close to zero. Each Gibbs update therefore makes only a small move along the narrow high-density region. This produces strong autocorrelation and slow mixing. Thus, although every Gibbs proposal is accepted, an acceptance rate of one does not imply efficient exploration of the target distribution.

title: Q7. Normal estimation and prediction
text:
Topic: Conjugate analysis for normal models · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 7 of 59 ‹ Q6 Q8 ›

Suppose that, conditionally on \mu, X_1,\ldots,X_n\mid\mu
  \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2), where \sigma^2>0 is known. Use the prior \mu\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_0,\tau^2), where \tau^2>0 is known.
(a) By completing the square in \mu, derive its posterior distribution. Denote the posterior mean and variance by m and v. [4 marks]
(b) Let X_{\mathrm{new}} be a further observation, independent of the observed sample given \mu. Derive its posterior predictive distribution. Explain the two sources of its variance. [4 marks]
(c) As n\to\infty, with \sigma^2 and the prior fixed, what happens to the posterior variance of \mu and the predictive variance of X_{\mathrm{new}}? Explain why they behave differently. [2 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. The notation N(m,v) uses mean m and variance v; precision is 1/v. The data have known variance \sigma^2>0, and the mean prior is N(\mu_0,\tau^2) with \tau^2>0. Write \bar x=n^{-1}\sum_i x_i. Posterior prediction averages a new observation’s sampling distribution over the parameter posterior; that observation is independent of the original sample conditional on \mu.

(a) Posterior distribution of \mu
Start from independence and the specified prior: L(\mu;{\boldsymbol{x}})=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}
\exp\left[-\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right],
\qquad
p(\mu)\propto\exp\left[-\frac{(\mu-\mu_0)^2}{2\tau^2}\right]. The identity \sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2+n(\mu-\bar x)^2 follows by expanding around \bar x; the cross term is zero because \sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=0. Bayes’ theorem multiplies these two kernels. Ignoring terms that do not depend on \mu, \begin{aligned}
  p(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
  &\propto
  \exp\left[
    -\frac{n}{2\sigma^2}(\mu-\bar{x})^2
    -\frac{1}{2\tau^2}(\mu-\mu_0)^2
  \right]\\
  &\propto
  \exp\left[
    -\frac12
    \left\{
      \left(\frac{n}{\sigma^2}+\frac{1}{\tau^2}\right)\mu^2
      -2\left(
        \frac{n\bar{x}}{\sigma^2}+\frac{\mu_0}{\tau^2}
      \right)\mu
    \right\}
  \right].
\end{aligned} Define v=\left(\frac{n}{\sigma^2}+\frac{1}{\tau^2}\right)^{-1},
  \qquad
  m=v\left(
    \frac{n\bar{x}}{\sigma^2}+\frac{\mu_0}{\tau^2}
  \right). Completing the square gives p(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
  \propto
  \exp\left[-\frac{(\mu-m)^2}{2v}\right], so \boxed{\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(m,v)}. Equivalently, v=\frac{\sigma^2\tau^2}{n\tau^2+\sigma^2},
  \qquad
  m=\frac{n\tau^2\bar{x}+\sigma^2\mu_0}
          {n\tau^2+\sigma^2}.


(b) Posterior predictive distribution
Conditional on \mu, X_{\mathrm{new}}=\mu+\varepsilon,
  \qquad
  \varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2), where \varepsilon is independent of \mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}. Since \mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(m,v), \boxed{
    X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
    \sim\mathcal{N}(m,\sigma^2+v)
  }. The predictive variance can also be obtained from \begin{aligned}
  \operatorname{Var}(X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
  &=
  \mathbb{E}\!\left[
    \operatorname{Var}(X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}})
    \mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
  \right]\\
  &\quad+
  \operatorname{Var}\!\left(
    \mathbb{E}[X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}}]
    \mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
  \right)\\
  &=\sigma^2+v.
\end{aligned} Here \sigma^2 is future-observation noise and v is uncertainty about the unknown mean.


(c) Limiting variances
As n\to\infty, v=\left(\frac{n}{\sigma^2}+\frac{1}{\tau^2}\right)^{-1}
  \longrightarrow0, whereas \operatorname{Var}(X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
  =\sigma^2+v
  \longrightarrow\sigma^2. Increasing n removes uncertainty about \mu, but it does not remove the irreducible sampling variation in a new observation.

title: Q5. Random-walk Metropolis-Hastings
text:
Topic: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 5 of 59 ‹ Q4 Q6 ›

Let the target density be \pi(x)\propto x^2e^{-x},
  \qquad x>0. We wish to sample from \pi using a random-walk Metropolis-Hastings algorithm with proposal Y\mid X^{(t-1)}=x\sim\mathcal{N}(x,\sigma^2), where \sigma>0 is fixed.
(a) [3 marks] Show that the Metropolis-Hastings acceptance probability is \alpha(x,y)
          =
          \begin{cases}
            \displaystyle
            \min\left\{
              \left(\frac{y}{x}\right)^2 e^{-(y-x)},1
            \right\}, & y>0,\\[1.2em]
            0, & y\leq0.
          \end{cases} Explain why the proposal-density terms cancel.
(b) [2 marks] Calculate the acceptance probability for each proposed move. You may leave your answers in exact exponential form.
1. Current state x=2, proposed state y=3.
2. Current state x=3, proposed state y=2.
(c) [3 marks] Write pseudocode for a random-walk Metropolis-Hastings sampler generating T observations from the target distribution. Begin from a valid initial value x^{(0)}>0.
(d) [1 mark] Explain why the unknown normalising constant of \pi(x) is not required.
(e) [2 marks] Are the sampled values X^{(1)},X^{(2)},\ldots,X^{(T)} independent? Briefly explain.
(f) [2 marks] Explain what is likely to happen if:
1. \sigma is extremely small;
2. \sigma is extremely large.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write q(y\mid x) for the density of a proposal y from current state x, and \alpha(x,y) for its acceptance probability. The target kernel is x^2e^{-x} on x>0 and zero elsewhere. N(x,\sigma^2) uses variance \sigma^2, held fixed and positive throughout the run; start with x^{(0)}>0.
As a recognition check, \pi(x)\propto x^{3-1}e^{-1\cdot x},
  \qquad x>0, is the kernel of a \operatorname{Gamma}(3,1) distribution under the shape-rate convention. The exercise nevertheless asks us to construct a Metropolis-Hastings sampler for this target.

(a) Acceptance probability
For a proposal density q(y\mid x), the Metropolis-Hastings acceptance probability is \alpha(x,y)
  =\min\left\{
    \frac{\pi(y)q(x\mid y)}{\pi(x)q(y\mid x)},1
  \right\}. The normal random-walk proposal is symmetric because q(y\mid x)
  =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}
   \exp\left[-\frac{(y-x)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right]
  =q(x\mid y). The proposal-density terms therefore cancel. If y>0, the target-density ratio is \frac{\pi(y)}{\pi(x)}
  =\frac{y^2e^{-y}}{x^2e^{-x}}
  =\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)^2e^{-(y-x)}. If y\leq0, then y is outside the support of the target and the proposal must be rejected. Hence \boxed{
    \alpha(x,y)
    =
    \begin{cases}
      \displaystyle
      \min\left\{
        \left(\frac{y}{x}\right)^2e^{-(y-x)},1
      \right\}, & y>0,\\[1.2em]
      0, & y\leq0.
    \end{cases}
  }


(b) Acceptance probabilities for the two moves
1. For x=2 and y=3, \alpha(2,3)
          =\min\left\{\left(\frac32\right)^2e^{-1},1\right\}
          =\boxed{\frac{9}{4e}\approx0.828}, since 9/(4e)<1. Thus the move is accepted with probability about 82.8\%.
2. For x=3 and y=2, \alpha(3,2)
          =\min\left\{\left(\frac23\right)^2e,1\right\}
          =\min\left\{\frac{4e}{9},1\right\}
          =\boxed{1}, since 4e/9>1. This move goes to a point of higher target density and is always accepted.
This illustrates the basic Metropolis rule: moves to higher target density are accepted automatically, while moves to lower target density may still be accepted with positive probability.


(c) Random-walk Metropolis-Hastings pseudocode
Choose an initial state x^{(0)}>0. For t=1,2,\ldots,T:
1. Generate a proposal Y\sim\mathcal{N}\bigl(x^{(t-1)},\sigma^2\bigr).
2. Calculate a=
          \begin{cases}
            \displaystyle
            \min\left\{
              \left(\frac{Y}{x^{(t-1)}}\right)^2
              e^{-(Y-x^{(t-1)})},1
            \right\}, & Y>0,\\[1.2em]
            0, & Y\leq0.
          \end{cases}
3. Independently generate U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1).
4. Set X^{(t)}=
          \begin{cases}
            Y, & U\leq a,\\
            X^{(t-1)}, & U>a.
          \end{cases}
5. Store X^{(t)}.
A rejection does not mean that nothing is recorded: the chain stores the current value again, so X^{(t)}=X^{(t-1)}. After a suitable burn-in, the stored values are approximately distributed according to \pi.


(d) Unknown normalising constant
If \pi(x)=\widetilde{\pi}(x)/C, then \frac{\pi(y)}{\pi(x)}
  =\frac{\widetilde{\pi}(y)/C}{\widetilde{\pi}(x)/C}
  =\frac{\widetilde{\pi}(y)}{\widetilde{\pi}(x)}. Thus the same unknown constant appears in the numerator and denominator and cancels from the acceptance ratio. Metropolis-Hastings therefore requires the target only up to proportionality, which is especially useful for posterior distributions with an intractable marginal likelihood.


(e) Independence of the sampled values
No. Each proposal is generated from the previous state, and a rejected move gives X^{(t)}=X^{(t-1)}. The samples therefore form a Markov chain and are generally serially dependent, even after the chain has reached equilibrium. At equilibrium, each X^{(t)} has marginal distribution \pi, but having the correct marginal distribution does not imply independence.


(f) Effect of the proposal scale
1. If \sigma is extremely small, proposals stay close to the current state and are usually accepted. However, the chain moves slowly through the target distribution, producing high autocorrelation and poor mixing.
2. If \sigma is extremely large, many proposals fall outside the support or in regions of very low target density. The acceptance rate becomes small, so the chain often repeats its current value and again mixes poorly.

title: Q3. Confidence and credible intervals
text:
Topic: Bayesian foundations · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 3 of 59 ‹ Q2 Q4 ›

[6 marks]
Explain the difference between a frequentist confidence interval and a Bayesian credible interval. In your answer:
1. state what is regarded as random in each framework;
2. give the correct interpretation of a 95% confidence interval;
3. give the correct interpretation of a 95% credible interval; and
4. explain why the two intervals may sometimes have the same numerical endpoints but still have different interpretations.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Let X denote a random sample and x its observed value; C(X)=(L(X),U(X)) is an interval-producing procedure. Its coverage is \mathbb P_\theta\{\theta\in C(X)\}, calculated over samples at fixed \theta. A posterior credible interval instead has probability content \int_{C(x)}p(\theta\mid x)\,d\theta under the specified model and prior.
1. What is random?
In frequentist inference, the parameter \theta is fixed but unknown. Before observing the sample, the data X are random, so the interval endpoints L(X) and U(X) are also random.
In Bayesian inference, uncertainty about \theta is described by its posterior distribution p(\theta\mid x). Once we condition on the observed data x, those data are treated as fixed and \theta has a posterior probability distribution.
2. Interpretation of a 95% confidence interval.
A 95% confidence-interval procedure satisfies \mathbb{P}_{\theta}\!\left\{L(X)<\theta<U(X)\right\}=0.95, where the probability is taken over repeated samples generated with the same fixed value of \theta. Therefore, in repeated sampling, 95% of the intervals produced by the procedure would contain the true parameter.
After observing the data, the realised interval is fixed. In the frequentist framework, it is therefore incorrect to say that there is a 95% probability that the fixed parameter lies in this particular observed interval.
3. Interpretation of a 95% credible interval.
A Bayesian 95% credible interval (a,b) satisfies \mathbb{P}(a<\theta<b\mid x)=0.95. Conditional on the observed data, model, and prior, there is 95% posterior probability that \theta lies between a and b.
4. Why identical endpoints do not imply identical meanings.
The two methods can produce the same numerical endpoints in some simple models, or approximately the same endpoints in large samples. Their interpretations remain different because they use different probability statements:

5. confidence refers to the long-run coverage of a random interval procedure under repeated sampling;
6. credibility refers to posterior probability for \theta conditional on the observed data and the assumed prior and model.


Key result. Exam-safe sentence. A 95% confidence interval has 95% long-run coverage under repeated sampling, whereas a 95% credible interval contains 95% of the posterior probability for the parameter given the observed data.

title: Q1. Rayleigh conjugate prior
text:
Topic: Exponential families and conjugacy · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 1 of 59 Q2 ›

Suppose X_1,\ldots,X_n\mid\theta
  \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Rayleigh}(\theta), with density f(x\mid\theta)
  =\frac{x}{\theta}\exp\left(-\frac{x^2}{2\theta}\right),
  \qquad x>0,\quad \theta>0.
Using the general exponential-family conjugacy result, find a conjugate prior for \theta and derive the posterior distribution.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. For observed {\boldsymbol{x}}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n), L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}}) is the sampling density viewed as a function of \theta. A kernel omits only factors constant in that parameter. Conjugacy means that prior and posterior belong to the same family. We use \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b):\quad p(\theta)\propto\theta^{-a-1}e^{-b/\theta},
\qquad \theta>0,\quad a,b>0, with shape a and inverse-Gamma scale b. The Rayleigh observations are conditionally iid and positive.
The general exponential-family form used in the course is f(x\mid\theta)
  =b(x)\frac{\exp\{c(\theta)T(x)\}}{a(\theta)}, for which a conjugate prior has kernel \pi(\theta)
  \propto
  \frac{\exp\{\alpha c(\theta)\}}{a(\theta)^\beta}.
For the Rayleigh density, f(x\mid\theta)
  =x\,
    \frac{\exp\left\{-\dfrac{1}{\theta}\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right\}}
         {\theta}. Thus, we identify b(x)=x,
  \qquad
  T(x)=\frac{x^2}{2},
  \qquad
  c(\theta)=-\frac{1}{\theta},
  \qquad
  a(\theta)=\theta.
Substitution into the conjugate-prior kernel gives \pi(\theta)
  \propto
  \frac{\exp(-\alpha/\theta)}{\theta^\beta}
  =\theta^{-\beta}\exp\left(-\frac{\alpha}{\theta}\right). Matching this to the inverse-Gamma kernel in Definitions gives a=\beta-1,
  \qquad
  b=\alpha. Therefore, a conjugate prior is \boxed{\theta\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(\beta-1,\alpha)}, with \alpha>0 and \beta>1 for a proper prior.
For an iid sample, the likelihood is \begin{aligned}
  L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})
  &=\prod_{i=1}^n
    \frac{x_i}{\theta}
    \exp\left(-\frac{x_i^2}{2\theta}\right)\\
  &\propto
    \theta^{-n}
    \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\theta}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2\right).
\end{aligned} Multiplying the likelihood by the prior gives \begin{aligned}
  \pi(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
  &\propto L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})\pi(\theta)\\
  &\propto
    \theta^{-n}
    \exp\left(-\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2}{2\theta}\right)
    \theta^{-\beta}
    \exp\left(-\frac{\alpha}{\theta}\right)\\
  &\propto
    \theta^{-(\beta+n)}
    \exp\left[
      -\frac{\alpha+\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2}{\theta}
    \right].
\end{aligned} Recognising the inverse-Gamma kernel, \boxed{
    \theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
    \sim
    \operatorname{InvGamma}\left(
      \beta+n-1,
      \alpha+\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2
    \right)
  }.
Equivalently, if the prior is written directly as \theta\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b), then

Key result. \boxed{
    \theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
    \sim
    \operatorname{InvGamma}\left(
      a+n,
      b+\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2
    \right)
  }. This is the form worth remembering after working through the derivation.

title: Question 20. Toenail infection GLMM
text:
Topic: Random slopes, and a binary mixed model · more questions on this topic
Source: Final preparation, question 20 of 22 ‹ Question 19 Question 21 ›

2024 examination, Question 4 (20 marks).
In this trial, 294 patients were randomised to terbinafine (250 mg/day) or itraconazole (200 mg/day), and assessed at weeks 0,4,8,12,24,36,48. The binary outcome is moderate or severe onycholysis (1) versus none or mild (0). The command and summary output for the first fit are reproduced below.
fit1 = glmer(outcome ~ treatment*weeks + (1|patientID), family=binomial)

Random effects:
 Groups     Name        Variance Std.Dev.
 patientID  (Intercept)   21.05    4.588
Number of obs: 1908, groups: patientID, 294

Fixed effects:
                              Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept)                   -2.54669    0.78251  -3.255  0.00114 **
treatmentTerbinafine          -0.25799    0.69136  -0.373  0.70902
weeks                         -0.10343    0.01214  -8.517   <2e-16 ***
treatmentTerbinafine:weeks    -0.04059    0.01840  -2.207  0.02735 *
(a) [2 marks] Why is a patient-specific random intercept sensible?
(b) [6 marks] Write the GLMM corresponding to the first command.
(c) [5 marks] Interpret the five reported values, on the scale of the model.
(d) [2 marks] Is there a treatment difference in the first fit, and which treatment looks better?
The second fit allows a patient-specific week slope:
fit2 = glmer(outcome ~ treatment*weeks + (weeks|patientID), family=binomial)

Random effects:
 Groups     Name        Variance Std.Dev. Corr
 patientID  (Intercept) 7380.733   85.911
            weeks          9.124    3.021 -0.30
Number of obs: 1908, groups: patientID, 294

Fixed effects:
                              Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept)                  -12.68683    1.21837 -10.413   <2e-16 ***
treatmentterbinafine          -0.06899    1.56848  -0.044    0.965
weeks                         -2.80367    0.31638  -8.862   <2e-16 ***
treatmentterbinafine:weeks    -0.27229    0.27409  -0.993    0.321
(e) [2 marks] How does the second model differ from the first?
(f) [3 marks] Does the second fit show a treatment difference? How can the two conclusions be reconciled?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Let j index patients, i index visits, t_{ji} be week, and T_j=1 for terbinafine or 0 for itraconazole. The response Y_{ji}=1 indicates moderate or severe onycholysis. The conditional probability is p_{ji}(\alpha_j)=\mathbb{P}(Y_{ji}=1\mid T_j,t_{ji},\alpha_j). The logit is \log\{p/(1-p)\} and its inverse is \operatorname{expit}(\eta)=e^\eta/(1+e^\eta). Fixed effects describe the population predictor; random effects describe patient departures from it.
(a) Each patient is assessed at seven visits, so the responses are repeated measures on the same person. A patient intercept is a draw from a population of patients: one variance, rather than a separate mean for each of the 294 named people. The trial is about the treatments in that population. Two visits on the same patient share the intercept, so they are dependent. Conditional on the intercept they are independent. Assigning the treatment at random does not remove that dependence.
For two distinct visits on the same patient, the law of total covariance gives

\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{ji},Y_{jk}\mid X)
&=\mathbb{E}\{\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{ji},Y_{jk}\mid\alpha_j,X)\mid X\}\\
&\quad+\operatorname{Cov}\{p_{ji}(\alpha_j),p_{jk}(\alpha_j)\mid X\}.
\end{aligned}

The first term is zero under conditional independence. The second is generally nonzero because both probabilities change with the same latent intercept. This is the mechanism by which the model accounts for repeated-measure dependence.
(b) Let T_j=1 for terbinafine and T_j=0 for itraconazole, and let visit i of patient j have response Y_{ji}. Naming binomial and not naming a link selects the logit. The model is

\begin{aligned}
Y_{ji}\mid \alpha_j
&\sim
\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_{ji}),\\
\operatorname{logit}(p_{ji})
&=
\beta_0+\beta_1 T_j+\beta_2\,\mathrm{weeks}_{ji}
+\beta_3 T_j\,\mathrm{weeks}_{ji}+\alpha_j,\\
\alpha_j
&\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}
\operatorname{N}(0,\sigma_A^2),
\end{aligned}

with visits conditionally independent given \alpha_j, patients independent of one another, and random intercepts independent of the assigned treatment. Equivalently, p_{ji} is the expit of the linear predictor. The normal distribution is a model for a latent intercept on the log-odds scale. It is not a claim that a normal measurement was observed. The likelihood integrates \alpha_j out, and there is no closed form.
For patient j the likelihood contribution is the one-dimensional integral of the product of the visit-specific Bernoulli masses against the normal random-intercept density. Integration is performed once per patient, since all visits share that intercept. Similarly, the population-averaged probability is \mathbb{E}_{\alpha_j}\{p_{ji}(\alpha_j)\}. Because expit is nonlinear, this generally differs from setting \alpha_j=0 in the predictor.
(c) Every coefficient below holds the patient’s intercept fixed. A unit change is a change in log-odds, and \exp(\beta) multiplies the odds. It is not a change in probability.
The standard deviation 4.588 is the standard deviation of \alpha_j on the log-odds scale. Holding fixed covariates constant, a one-standard-deviation increase in the latent intercept multiplies conditional odds by \exp(4.588)\approx98. It is a scale of between-patient heterogeneity, not a standard deviation of observed binary responses or disease probabilities.
The intercept -2.547 is the log-odds for a typical patient, \alpha_j=0, on itraconazole at week 0. Week 0 is a real visit. The probability is

\frac{\exp(-2.547)}{1+\exp(-2.547)}\approx 0.073.

The terbinafine coefficient -0.258 is the week-0 contrast for a given patient. Terbinafine multiplies the odds of moderate or severe onycholysis by \exp(-0.258)\approx 0.77 relative to itraconazole. The z statistic is -0.37 and p=0.71, so this is not a detected difference.
The weeks coefficient -0.103 is the per-week change for a patient on itraconazole. One extra week multiplies the odds by \exp(-0.103)\approx 0.90, at that patient’s intercept. The z statistic is -8.5.
The interaction -0.0406 is the extra weekly change under terbinafine. Each extra week multiplies the terbinafine-versus-itraconazole odds ratio by \exp(-0.0406)\approx 0.96. The weekly multiplier itself is \exp(-0.144)\approx 0.87 on terbinafine and \exp(-0.103)\approx 0.90 on itraconazole. The z statistic is -2.21 and p=0.027, past the usual 5\% line.
One can obtain all these interpretations by writing the two fitted predictors separately:

\eta_I(t,\alpha)=-2.547-0.103t+\alpha,\qquad
\eta_T(t,\alpha)=-2.805-0.144t+\alpha.

Subtracting them at a common week and random-intercept value gives \log\operatorname{OR}_{T:I}(t)=\beta_1+\beta_3t. Differentiating with respect to week gives the two log-odds slopes and their difference \beta_3. This avoids confusing a baseline contrast, a time slope and a difference in slopes.
(d) There is evidence of a difference in the rate, with a steeper decline under terbinafine. The week-0 contrast has p=0.71 and describes baseline differences before treatment, not the difference in improvement. The treatment-by-weeks interaction has p=0.027 and addresses that difference. At week 48, which is a visit in the trial, the subject-specific log-odds contrast is

-0.258+48(-0.0406)=-2.21,

so the odds of moderate or severe onycholysis under terbinafine are \exp(-2.21)\approx 0.11 times the odds under itraconazole, for a given patient.
This is a fitted contrast, not a significance test at week 48. Its standard error would require \operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1)+48^2\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_3)+96\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\beta_1,\hat\beta_3), and the covariance is not printed. The interaction test itself is H_0:\beta_3=0; equality of the treatment predictors at every week would require the joint null \beta_1=\beta_3=0.
(e) (weeks|patientID) adds a random slope on weeks and a covariance between that slope and the intercept. In the notation of (b),

\operatorname{logit}(p_{ji})
=
X_{ji}^{\top}\beta+Z_{ji}^{\top}\alpha_j,
\qquad
\alpha_j\sim \operatorname{N}(0,\Sigma_A),

where Z_{ji}=(1,\mathrm{weeks}_{ji})^{\top} and \Sigma_A holds two variances and one covariance. The first model is the special case with the slope variance equal to zero. Patients may then differ in baseline and in rate. The fixed effects remain the population constants. The \alpha_j are draws.
Writing \alpha_j=(\alpha_{0j},\alpha_{1j})^\top, patient j’s log-odds slope is \beta_2+\beta_3T_j+\alpha_{1j}. If the two random-effect variances are \tau_0^2,\tau_1^2 and their covariance is \tau_{01}, the covariance between the random parts of that patient’s predictors at weeks s,t is \tau_0^2+(s+t)\tau_{01}+st\tau_1^2. The model therefore changes the time-dependent covariance structure as well as allowing different trajectories.
(f) In the second fit the treatment coefficient has p=0.965 and the treatment-by-weeks interaction has p=0.321. It therefore gives no clear evidence that the two drugs differ in either baseline log-odds or rate of change. Both fitted weekly slopes are negative, but this alone does not establish a causal improvement for either drug. The first fit forces all patients in a treatment group to share a time slope; the second allows patient-specific slopes. Some variation attributed to the fixed interaction in the first fit can instead be represented by those individual trajectories. The interaction standard error rises from 0.018 to 0.274, so the second estimate is much less precise.
The fitted intercept–slope correlation is -0.30. On the model’s log-odds scale, patients with a higher random intercept tend to have a more negative random slope, hence a steeper decline; the association is modest and does not itself explain a treatment contrast. Alan’s central point is that allowing different patient trajectories changes the treatment comparison. The very large fitted random-effect standard deviations also warrant a fit check. Neither fit proves that the drugs are equally effective.
For example, an approximate 95\% Wald interval for the second interaction is -0.27229\pm1.96(0.27409), or about (-0.810,0.265). It includes zero and substantial nonzero differences in slopes. The changed conclusion is therefore about the precision of the treatment comparison under a different dependence model. Adding random slopes does not universally increase every standard error, and the change in a p-value alone does not establish which random-effects structure is adequate.

title: Question 17. Hierarchical Poisson model
text:
Topic: Hierarchical Bayes · more questions on this topic
Source: Final preparation, question 17 of 22 ‹ Question 16 Question 18 ›

Suppose J factories manufacture components. Factory j produces n_j observations of the number of defective components per batch.
Assume

Y_{ij}\mid\theta_j\stackrel{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}\operatorname{Poisson}(\theta_j),
\qquad i=1,\ldots,n_j,\quad j=1,\ldots,J.

Here, \theta_j>0 represents the expected number of defects per batch in factory j.
Rather than modelling the factory rates independently, we assume

\theta_j\mid\lambda\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Gamma}(a,\lambda),

where a>0 is known and \lambda>0 is an unknown common hyperparameter.
Finally, assign the hyperprior

\lambda\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(c,d),

where c,d>0 are known.
All Gamma distributions use the shape–rate parameterisation:

f(x\mid a,b)=\frac{b^{a}}{\Gamma(a)}x^{a-1}e^{-bx},
\qquad x>0.

(a) Write down the joint density p({\boldsymbol{Y}},{\boldsymbol{\theta}},\lambda) up to proportionality in the unknown parameters.
(b) Derive the full conditional distribution p(\theta_j\mid\lambda,{\boldsymbol{Y}}) for each factory j. Identify its distribution and parameters.
(c) Derive the full conditional distribution p(\lambda\mid{\boldsymbol{\theta}},{\boldsymbol{Y}}). Identify its distribution and parameters.
(d) Using your results from (b) and (c), describe a Gibbs sampling algorithm targeting p({\boldsymbol{\theta}},\lambda\mid{\boldsymbol{Y}}).
(e) Explain how the hierarchical model allows observations from one factory to influence inference about another factory’s defect rate.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Y_{ij} is the count from batch i in factory j, \theta_j is that factory’s mean count, and \lambda is a shared unknown gamma rate. The known shape is a, while c,d define the shape–rate gamma hyperprior on \lambda. Write s_j=\sum_iY_{ij} and \bar Y_j=s_j/n_j. The conditional hierarchy is \lambda\longrightarrow{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\longrightarrow{\boldsymbol{Y}}.
(a) Let s_j=\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}Y_{ij}. Since {\boldsymbol{Y}}\perp\lambda\mid{\boldsymbol{\theta}},

p({\boldsymbol{Y}},{\boldsymbol{\theta}},\lambda)
=
p({\boldsymbol{Y}}\mid{\boldsymbol{\theta}})\,p({\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mid\lambda)\,p(\lambda).

For \theta_j>0 and \lambda>0,

\begin{aligned}
p({\boldsymbol{Y}}\mid{\boldsymbol{\theta}})
&=
\Biggl(\prod_{j=1}^{J}\prod_{i=1}^{n_j}\frac{1}{Y_{ij}!}\Biggr)
\prod_{j=1}^{J}e^{-n_j\theta_j}\theta_j^{s_j},\\
p({\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mid\lambda)
&=
\Biggl(\frac{\lambda^{a}}{\Gamma(a)}\Biggr)^{J}
\prod_{j=1}^{J}\theta_j^{a-1}e^{-\lambda\theta_j},\\
p(\lambda)
&=
\frac{d^{c}}{\Gamma(c)}\lambda^{c-1}e^{-d\lambda}.
\end{aligned}

The factors 1/Y_{ij}!, \Gamma(a)^{-J} and d^{c}/\Gamma(c) do not depend on ({\boldsymbol{\theta}},\lambda). Dropping them leaves

\boxed{
p({\boldsymbol{Y}},{\boldsymbol{\theta}},\lambda)
\propto
\lambda^{aJ+c-1}e^{-d\lambda}
\prod_{j=1}^{J}
\theta_j^{s_j+a-1}e^{-(n_j+\lambda)\theta_j}.
}

(b) In the kernel from (a), the factors containing \theta_j are

\theta_j^{s_j+a-1}e^{-(n_j+\lambda)\theta_j}
=
\theta_j^{(s_j+a)-1}e^{-(n_j+\lambda)\theta_j},
\qquad\theta_j>0.

No other rate appears. Here s_j+a>0 because a>0 and s_j\ge 0, and n_j+\lambda>0 because \lambda>0. This is a shape–rate gamma kernel, so

\boxed{
\theta_j\mid\lambda,{\boldsymbol{Y}}
\sim
\operatorname{Gamma}\!\left(a+\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}Y_{ij},\ n_j+\lambda\right).
}

(c) In the kernel from (a), the factors containing \lambda are

\lambda^{aJ+c-1}
\exp\Bigl(-\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{J}\theta_j\Bigr)e^{-d\lambda}
=
\lambda^{(aJ+c)-1}
\exp\Bigl(-\Bigl(d+\sum_{j=1}^{J}\theta_j\Bigr)\lambda\Bigr),

for \lambda>0. Given {\boldsymbol{\theta}}, the observations do not appear. The shape aJ+c>0, and the rate d+\sum_j\theta_j>0 because d>0. Thus

\boxed{
\lambda\mid{\boldsymbol{\theta}},{\boldsymbol{Y}}
\sim
\operatorname{Gamma}\!\left(c+aJ,\ d+\sum_{j=1}^{J}\theta_j\right).
}

(d) By (b) and (c), start from \lambda^{(0)}>0 and repeat the following sweep. For each j=1,\ldots,J, draw

\theta_j^{(t+1)}
\sim
\operatorname{Gamma}\!\left(a+\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}Y_{ij},\ n_j+\lambda^{(t)}\right),

using \lambda^{(t)} and factory j’s counts. By (b) this draw does not use the other rates, so the J draws may be made in any order from the same \lambda^{(t)}. Then draw

\lambda^{(t+1)}
\sim
\operatorname{Gamma}\!\left(c+aJ,\ d+\sum_{j=1}^{J}\theta_j^{(t+1)}\right),

using the updated rates and not \lambda^{(t)}.

\therefore
\text{these full-conditional updates are a Gibbs sampler targeting }
p({\boldsymbol{\theta}},\lambda\mid{\boldsymbol{Y}}).

(e) By (b), \theta_j depends on the other factories only through \lambda. Counts from factory k update \theta_k, and by (c) every rate enters the conditional distribution of the shared \lambda. That \lambda is the second parameter of \theta_j. This dependence through the common hyperparameter is borrowing strength: observations from one factory inform the defect rate at another.
At a fixed \lambda, the conditional posterior mean makes the shrinkage explicit:

\mathbb{E}(\theta_j\mid\lambda,{\boldsymbol{Y}})
=\frac{s_j+a}{n_j+\lambda}
=\frac{n_j}{n_j+\lambda}\bar Y_j
+\frac{\lambda}{n_j+\lambda}\frac a\lambda.

It averages factory j’s sample mean and the common prior mean a/\lambda. A small factory receives more pooling for a given \lambda. To obtain the marginal posterior mean, average this expression over p(\lambda\mid{\boldsymbol{Y}}); that hyperposterior is informed by every factory. Fixing \lambda externally would remove this particular route by which other factories’ observations influence \theta_j. Integrating a shared uncertain \lambda also makes the factory rates generally dependent in the joint posterior.

title: Question 2. Normal variance, known mean
text:
Topic: Conjugate analysis for normal models · more questions on this topic
Source: Final preparation, question 2 of 22 ‹ Question 1 Question 3 ›

Let

X_i\mid\sigma^2\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^2),

with \mu known and

\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(\alpha_0,\beta_0),

in the shape–rate parameterisation

f(\sigma^2)\propto(\sigma^2)^{-\alpha_0-1}\exp(-\beta_0/\sigma^2).

(a) Write the posterior distribution of \sigma^2, and state what is added to each parameter.
(b) State the posterior mean and mode of \sigma^2, including the conditions under which each exists.
(c) Explain why that mean and mode generally differ.
(d) Explain why the variance update uses squared deviations from the known mean \mu, rather than from \bar x.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Put v=\sigma^2 and Q_\mu=\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2, with \mu known. Our \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b) convention has density b^a v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v}/\Gamma(a) for v>0. Equivalently, 1/v\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a,b) in shape–rate form. Specifying the kernel avoids ambiguity about the second parameter.
(a) Independence gives the likelihood kernel L(v)\propto v^{-n/2}e^{-Q_\mu/(2v)}. Multiplication by the prior gives

p(v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto
v^{-n/2}e^{-Q_\mu/(2v)}v^{-\alpha_0-1}e^{-\beta_0/v}
=v^{-(\alpha_0+n/2)-1}e^{-(\beta_0+Q_\mu/2)/v}.

Let \alpha_n=\alpha_0+n/2 and \beta_n=\beta_0+Q_\mu/2. Recognising this kernel,

\boxed{
\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim
\operatorname{InvGamma}(\alpha_n,\beta_n).
}

Each observation adds 1/2 to the shape. Half the sum of squared deviations from the known mean is added to the rate.
(b) For this shape–rate kernel, and for \beta_n>0,

\mathbb{E}(\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{\beta_n}{\alpha_n-1}
\quad\text{when }\alpha_n>1,
\qquad
\operatorname{mode}(\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{\beta_n}{\alpha_n+1}
\quad\text{when }\alpha_n>0.

The mode solves (-\alpha_n-1)/v+\beta_n/v^2=0. The mean is the gamma integral of v\cdot v^{-\alpha_n-1}e^{-\beta_n/v}, which converges only for \alpha_n>1.
More explicitly, substituting u=\beta_n/v into the expectation gives \mathbb{E}(v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\beta_n\Gamma(\alpha_n-1)/\Gamma(\alpha_n)=\beta_n/(\alpha_n-1). When 0<\alpha_n\le1, the posterior is still a proper distribution, but its right tail is too heavy to have a finite mean. Posterior propriety and existence of a posterior moment are separate requirements.
(c) For \alpha_n>1,

\frac{\beta_n}{\alpha_n-1}-\frac{\beta_n}{\alpha_n+1}
=
\frac{2\beta_n}{(\alpha_n-1)(\alpha_n+1)}>0.

The inverse-gamma density is right-skewed, so the long right tail pulls the mean above the mode.
(d) Under the sampling model, \operatorname{Var}(X_i\mid\sigma^2)=\mathbb{E}[(X_i-\mu)^2\mid\sigma^2]. The sufficient statistic for \sigma^2, with \mu known, is \sum(x_i-\mu)^2. Since

\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2
=
\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2-n(\bar x-\mu)^2,

centring at \bar x omits the term n(\bar x-\mu)^2.
When the mean is known, departures of the sample mean from that value are evidence about the observation variance too. For example, a tightly clustered sample far from the known mean has small \sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2 but large Q_\mu. Replacing Q_\mu by the centred sum of squares would discard that evidence and change the likelihood.

title: Question 1. Normal mean, known variance
text:
Topic: Conjugate analysis for normal models · more questions on this topic
Source: Final preparation, question 1 of 22 Question 2 ›

Let

X_i\mid\mu\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^2),

with \sigma^2 known and \mu\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu_0,\sigma_0^2).
(a) Using only the precision-addition rule and the precision-weighted mean, write the two updated parameters of the posterior for \mu.
(b) Define the prior equivalent sample size, and state what it counts.
(c) Explain why the posterior mean is a precision-weighted average of the prior mean and the sample mean.
(d) State and interpret the limiting posterior mean and variance as n\to\infty, with the prior parameters fixed and \bar X_n\to\mu^{\ast}.
(e) State the posterior predictive distribution of one new observation X_{\mathrm{new}}, conditionally independent of the sample given \mu.
(f) Explain why the posterior predictive variance is larger than the posterior variance of \mu.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write \bar x=n^{-1}\sum_i x_i. A normal distribution \operatorname{N}(m,v) has mean m and variance v; its precision is 1/v. Here \sigma^2 is the known observation variance, \sigma_0^2 is the prior variance of the unknown mean, and \sigma_1^2 will be its posterior variance. These are variances of different objects.
(a) The data precision of n observations is n/\sigma^2, and the prior precision is 1/\sigma_0^2. Precision addition gives

\frac1{\sigma_1^2}
=
\frac n{\sigma^2}+\frac1{\sigma_0^2}.

The posterior mean is the precision-weighted average of \bar x and \mu_0:

\mu_1
=
\frac{(n/\sigma^2)\bar x+(1/\sigma_0^2)\mu_0}{n/\sigma^2+1/\sigma_0^2}
=
\frac{n\bar x\,\sigma_0^2+\mu_0\sigma^2}{n\sigma_0^2+\sigma^2}.


\boxed{\mu\mid x\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2).}

(b)

\kappa_0=\frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma_0^2}.

It counts how many observations of variance \sigma^2 have the same precision as the prior, since 1/\sigma_0^2=\kappa_0/\sigma^2.
Consequently, \mu_1=(n\bar x+\kappa_0\mu_0)/(n+\kappa_0) and \sigma_1^2=\sigma^2/(n+\kappa_0). The equivalent sample size measures information about the common mean. It need not be an integer or represent actual previous observations.
(c) Up to an additive constant free of \mu, the log posterior is

-\frac{n}{2\sigma^2}(\bar x-\mu)^2-\frac{1}{2\sigma_0^2}(\mu-\mu_0)^2.

Its derivative is (n/\sigma^2)(\bar x-\mu)-(1/\sigma_0^2)(\mu-\mu_0). Setting the derivative equal to zero balances the two pulls, so

\mu_1
=
\frac{(n/\sigma^2)\bar x+(1/\sigma_0^2)\mu_0}{n/\sigma^2+1/\sigma_0^2}.

The second derivative is -n/\sigma^2-1/\sigma_0^2<0, so this stationary point is the unique posterior mode. The posterior is normal, hence its mode equals its mean. This derives the weighting rule: moving away from a more precise source incurs a larger quadratic penalty. The two weights are nonnegative and sum to one, so the posterior mean lies between \bar x and \mu_0.
(d) Let w_n=(n/\sigma^2)/(n/\sigma^2+1/\sigma_0^2). Then w_n\to 1 and

\mu_1=w_n\bar X_n+(1-w_n)\mu_0\to\mu^{\ast},
\qquad
\sigma_1^2=\Bigl(\frac n{\sigma^2}+\frac1{\sigma_0^2}\Bigr)^{-1}\to 0.

With the prior held fixed, the data precision dominates. The posterior concentrates at the limiting sample mean.
This conclusion uses the stated convergence \bar X_n\to\mu^\ast. Under the iid normal model with true mean \mu^\ast, that convergence follows from the law of large numbers. A fixed prior contributes a fixed amount of precision, while the likelihood contributes an amount growing linearly with n.
(e) Given \mu, X_{\mathrm{new}} is independent of the sample and X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid\mu\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^2). Since \mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2),

\boxed{X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu_1,\sigma^2+\sigma_1^2).}

To see the distributional result, write X_{\mathrm{new}}=\mu+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{new}}, where \varepsilon_{\mathrm{new}}\sim\operatorname{N}(0,\sigma^2) is independent of the posterior draw of \mu. Conditional on the observed sample, this is a sum of two independent normal variables. Merely replacing \mu by \mu_1 would omit uncertainty about the unknown mean.
(f) By the law of total variance,

\operatorname{Var}(X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=
\mathbb{E}[\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}]+\operatorname{Var}(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=
\sigma^2+\sigma_1^2.

The term \sigma_1^2 is uncertainty about \mu. The term \sigma^2 is the variance of a new observation even if \mu is known. Both are positive, so the predictive variance exceeds the posterior variance of \mu.

title: Question 18. Bayesian model selection
text:
Topic: Bayesian hypotheses and model comparison · more questions on this topic
Source: Final preparation, question 18 of 22 ‹ Question 17 Question 19 ›

Suppose Y_1,\ldots,Y_n are independent observations, with observed data {\boldsymbol{y}}=(y_1,\ldots,y_n). A researcher wishes to compare two competing models.
Under model M_1,

Y_i\mid\theta,M_1\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{N}(\theta,1),

where the unknown mean has prior distribution

\theta\mid M_1\sim \operatorname{N}(0,\tau^2).

Under model M_2,

Y_i\mid\mu,\sigma^2,M_2\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^2),

where the unknown mean and variance have prior distributions

\mu\mid\sigma^2,M_2\sim \operatorname{N}\Bigl(0,\frac{\sigma^2}{\kappa}\Bigr),
\qquad
\sigma^2\mid M_2\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(\alpha,\beta).

Assume that n\geq 2, and \tau^2,\kappa,\alpha,\beta are known positive constants.
The inverse-gamma distribution is parameterised by

f(v;a,b)=\frac{b^{a}}{\Gamma(a)}v^{-a-1}\exp\Bigl(-\frac{b}{v}\Bigr),
\qquad v>0.

Define

\bar y=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}y_i,
\qquad
S=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\bar y)^{2}.

You may use the identity

\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\eta)^{2}=S+n(\bar y-\eta)^{2}

and the result

\int_{0}^{\infty}v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v}\,dv=\frac{\Gamma(a)}{b^{a}},
\qquad a,b>0.

(a) Write down the likelihood functions L_1(\theta;{\boldsymbol{y}}) and L_2(\mu,\sigma^2;{\boldsymbol{y}}) under models M_1 and M_2, respectively. [2 marks]
(b) Using the prior distribution of \theta, derive an expression for the marginal likelihood p({\boldsymbol{y}}\mid M_1). The derivation should explicitly show the integration over \theta, including any completion of the square required. [5 marks]
(c) The marginal likelihood under model M_2 is given by

p({\boldsymbol{y}}\mid M_2)
=
\int_0^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
p({\boldsymbol{y}}\mid\mu,\sigma^2,M_2)\,
p(\mu\mid\sigma^2,M_2)\,
p(\sigma^2\mid M_2)\,d\mu\,d\sigma^2.

(i) Integrate out \mu to obtain an expression for p({\boldsymbol{y}}\mid\sigma^2,M_2). [4 marks]
(ii) Hence integrate out \sigma^2 to derive the marginal likelihood p({\boldsymbol{y}}\mid M_2). [4 marks]
(d)
(i) Obtain an expression for the Bayes factor

B_{12}=\frac{p({\boldsymbol{y}}\mid M_1)}{p({\boldsymbol{y}}\mid M_2)}.

(ii) Suppose the prior model probabilities are P(M_1)=0.25 and P(M_2)=0.75. Express the posterior odds in favour of M_1 in terms of B_{12}.
[3 marks]
(e)
(i) Explain why normalising constants that do not depend on the unknown parameters must nevertheless be retained when calculating marginal likelihoods.
(ii) State the conditions under which the Bayes factor is well-defined. Explain briefly why replacing the proper parameter priors with unspecified improper priors can cause difficulties in Bayesian model comparison.
[2 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. \operatorname{N}(\eta,v) has mean \eta and variance v. Write \bar y=n^{-1}\sum_i y_i and S=\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2. Model M_1 has known variance one and unknown mean \theta; M_2 has unknown mean and variance with a dependent normal–inverse-gamma prior. The quantity B_{12}=p({\boldsymbol{y}}\mid M_1)/p({\boldsymbol{y}}\mid M_2) compares prior predictive densities of the same data, and each parameter prior is distinct from the prior probability of its model.
(a) By the given sum-of-squares identity, for \theta\in\mathbb{R},

\boxed{
L_1(\theta;{\boldsymbol{y}})
=
(2\pi)^{-n/2}
\exp\Bigl(-\tfrac12\bigl[S+n(\bar y-\theta)^{2}\bigr]\Bigr).
}

For \mu\in\mathbb{R} and \sigma^{2}>0,

\boxed{
L_2(\mu,\sigma^{2};{\boldsymbol{y}})
=
(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{-n/2}
\exp\Bigl(-\frac{S+n(\bar y-\mu)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\Bigr).
}

(b) The \operatorname{N}(0,\tau^{2}) prior has density (2\pi\tau^{2})^{-1/2}\exp(-\theta^{2}/(2\tau^{2})). Thus

\begin{aligned}
p({\boldsymbol{y}}\mid M_1)
&=
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}L_1(\theta;{\boldsymbol{y}})\,(2\pi\tau^{2})^{-1/2}e^{-\theta^{2}/(2\tau^{2})}\,d\theta\\
&=
(2\pi)^{-n/2}(2\pi\tau^{2})^{-1/2}e^{-S/2}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\exp\Bigl(-\tfrac12\Bigl[n(\bar y-\theta)^{2}+\frac{\theta^{2}}{\tau^{2}}\Bigr]\Bigr)\,d\theta.
\end{aligned}

The expression in brackets is

n(\bar y-\theta)^{2}+\frac{\theta^{2}}{\tau^{2}}
=
\Bigl(n+\frac1{\tau^{2}}\Bigr)\theta^{2}-2n\bar y\,\theta+n\bar y^{2}.

Set A=n+1/\tau^{2}. Then A>0, because n\geq 2 and \tau^{2}>0, and \tau^{2}A=1+n\tau^{2}. Completing the square,

\begin{aligned}
A\theta^{2}-2n\bar y\,\theta+n\bar y^{2}
&=
A\Bigl(\theta-\frac{n\bar y}{A}\Bigr)^{2}
+n\bar y^{2}\frac{A-n}{A}\\
&=
A\Bigl(\theta-\frac{n\bar y}{A}\Bigr)^{2}
+\frac{n\bar y^{2}}{1+n\tau^{2}},
\end{aligned}

where A-n=1/\tau^{2}. The integral equals

\exp\Bigl(-\frac{n\bar y^{2}}{2(1+n\tau^{2})}\Bigr)
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\exp\Bigl(-\frac A2\Bigl(\theta-\frac{n\bar y}{A}\Bigr)^{2}\Bigr)\,d\theta
=
\exp\Bigl(-\frac{n\bar y^{2}}{2(1+n\tau^{2})}\Bigr)
\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{A}},

since A>0. The remaining normalising factors simplify by \tau^{2}A=1+n\tau^{2}:

(2\pi\tau^{2})^{-1/2}\sqrt{2\pi/A}=(1+n\tau^{2})^{-1/2}.


\boxed{
p({\boldsymbol{y}}\mid M_1)
=
(2\pi)^{-n/2}(1+n\tau^{2})^{-1/2}
\exp\Bigl(-\frac12\Bigl[S+\frac{n\bar y^{2}}{1+n\tau^{2}}\Bigr]\Bigr).
}

(c)
(i) The conditional prior of \mu has density (\kappa/(2\pi\sigma^{2}))^{1/2}\exp(-\kappa\mu^{2}/(2\sigma^{2})). Therefore

\begin{aligned}
p({\boldsymbol{y}}\mid\sigma^{2},M_2)
&=
(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{-n/2}\Bigl(\frac{\kappa}{2\pi\sigma^{2}}\Bigr)^{1/2}e^{-S/(2\sigma^{2})}\\
&\qquad\times
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\exp\Bigl(-\frac{n(\bar y-\mu)^{2}+\kappa\mu^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\Bigr)\,d\mu.
\end{aligned}

Since n+\kappa>0,

\begin{aligned}
n(\bar y-\mu)^{2}+\kappa\mu^{2}
&=
(n+\kappa)\Bigl(\mu-\frac{n\bar y}{n+\kappa}\Bigr)^{2}
+n\bar y^{2}\frac{\kappa}{n+\kappa}.
\end{aligned}

The integral is

\exp\Bigl(-\frac{n\kappa\bar y^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}(n+\kappa)}\Bigr)
\sqrt{\frac{2\pi\sigma^{2}}{n+\kappa}}.

Multiplying by the constant prefactor, the factors (2\pi\sigma^{2})^{\pm 1/2} cancel, and

\boxed{
p({\boldsymbol{y}}\mid\sigma^{2},M_2)
=
(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{-n/2}\Bigl(\frac{\kappa}{n+\kappa}\Bigr)^{1/2}
\exp\Bigl(-\frac{Q}{2\sigma^{2}}\Bigr),
}

where Q=S+n\kappa\bar y^{2}/(n+\kappa).
(ii) By (i) and the inverse-gamma prior,

\begin{aligned}
p({\boldsymbol{y}}\mid M_2)
&=
(2\pi)^{-n/2}\Bigl(\frac{\kappa}{n+\kappa}\Bigr)^{1/2}
\frac{\beta^{\alpha}}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\\
&\qquad\times
\int_0^{\infty}
(\sigma^{2})^{-(\alpha+n/2)-1}
\exp\Bigl(-\frac{\beta+Q/2}{\sigma^{2}}\Bigr)\,d\sigma^{2}.
\end{aligned}

Here \alpha+n/2>0 because \alpha>0 and n\geq 2, and \beta+Q/2>0 because \beta>0 and Q\geq 0. The given integral with these values yields

\boxed{
p({\boldsymbol{y}}\mid M_2)
=
(2\pi)^{-n/2}\Bigl(\frac{\kappa}{n+\kappa}\Bigr)^{1/2}
\frac{\beta^{\alpha}\,\Gamma(\alpha+n/2)}{\Gamma(\alpha)\,(\beta+Q/2)^{\alpha+n/2}},
}

with Q as in (i).
The two integrations under M_2 have different roles. Integrating over \mu combines the sampling information about the mean with its conditional normal prior, producing the adjustment n\kappa\bar y^2/(n+\kappa). Integrating over \sigma^2 then averages over uncertainty in the common variance. Neither step replaces an unknown by its maximum likelihood estimate. The factor \sqrt{\kappa/(n+\kappa)} is one of the normalisation factors that would be lost by keeping only an exponential kernel.
(d)
(i) By (b) and (c)(ii), the factors (2\pi)^{-n/2} cancel, so

\boxed{
B_{12}
=
(1+n\tau^{2})^{-1/2}
\exp\Bigl(-\frac12\Bigl[S+\frac{n\bar y^{2}}{1+n\tau^{2}}\Bigr]\Bigr)
\Bigl(\frac{n+\kappa}{\kappa}\Bigr)^{1/2}
\frac{\Gamma(\alpha)\,(\beta+Q/2)^{\alpha+n/2}}{\beta^{\alpha}\,\Gamma(\alpha+n/2)},
}

where Q=S+n\kappa\bar y^{2}/(n+\kappa).
(ii)

\frac{\mathbb{P}(M_1\mid{\boldsymbol{y}})}{\mathbb{P}(M_2\mid{\boldsymbol{y}})}
=
B_{12}\,\frac{\mathbb{P}(M_1)}{\mathbb{P}(M_2)}
=
B_{12}\,\frac{0.25}{0.75}
=
\frac{B_{12}}{3}.


\therefore
\text{the posterior odds in favour of }M_1\text{ are }B_{12}/3.

Therefore the posterior favours M_1 only if B_{12}>3, rather than merely B_{12}>1. If the two models exhaust the alternatives, \mathbb{P}(M_1\mid{\boldsymbol{y}})=B_{12}/(B_{12}+3). A Bayes factor above one says that the data shift the odds towards M_1; it need not make M_1 the more probable model after accounting for the prior odds.
(e)
(i) A constant free of the parameters cancels in the posterior distribution within one model. It does not cancel between M_1 and M_2, because the two marginal likelihoods need not contain the same constant. Those factors remain in B_{12}.
(ii) B_{12} is well-defined when 0<p({\boldsymbol{y}}\mid M_k)<\infty for k=1,2. That holds here: both parameter priors are proper, n\geq 2, and \tau^{2},\kappa,\alpha,\beta>0, so the integrals in (b) and (c) converge. An unspecified improper prior is determined only up to an arbitrary positive multiple. That multiple remains in the marginal likelihood, so the Bayes factor is not uniquely defined.
A marginal likelihood is a prior-weighted average of likelihood values, so it depends on both fit and how much prior mass lies in parameter regions that fit the data. Broadening a proper prior can change this average even when the posterior within a model changes little. Sensitivity to the stated prior scales is therefore part of interpreting the model comparison; a proper posterior by itself does not justify a Bayes factor based on an unspecified improper prior.

title: Question 14. Inverse-gamma waiting time
text:
Topic: Exponential families and conjugacy · more questions on this topic
Source: Final preparation, question 14 of 22 ‹ Question 13 Question 15 ›

The waiting time until the mth animal at location i has density

f(x_i\mid\theta)
=
\frac{1}{\Gamma(m)\,\theta^{m}}x_i^{m-1}e^{-x_i/\theta},
\quad x_i>0,

so \theta>0 is a scale. The prior is

f(\theta)
=
\frac{\beta_0^{\alpha_0}}{\Gamma(\alpha_0)}\theta^{-\alpha_0-1}e^{-\beta_0/\theta},
\quad\alpha_0>0,\ \beta_0>0.

The exam states that the maximum likelihood estimator is \hat\theta=\bar x/m.
(i) State the prior mean. [1 mark]
(ii) Find and identify the posterior distribution of \theta. [5 marks]
(iii) State the posterior mean, and show that it is a weighted sum of the prior mean and \hat\theta. [5 marks]
(iv) What happens to the posterior mean as m\to\infty? [2 marks]
(v) What happens if \alpha_0,\beta_0\to 0? [2 marks]
(vi) Complete: “The effect of the prior hyperparameters \alpha_0 and \beta_0 on the posterior mean of \theta is like…” [2 marks]
(vii) Describe a posterior 100(1-\alpha)\% credible interval for \theta. [5 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Here m is a known gamma shape and \theta is its unknown scale: the sampling kernel in \theta is \theta^{-m}\exp(-x/\theta). This differs from a gamma rate parameterisation. Write T=\sum_i x_i and use \operatorname{InvGamma}(\alpha_0,\beta_0) with kernel \theta^{-\alpha_0-1}e^{-\beta_0/\theta}. The estimator \hat\theta=T/(nm) has the same units as \theta.
The sampling density is gamma with shape m and scale \theta, so \mathbb{E}(X_i\mid\theta)=m\theta and the supplied estimator \hat\theta=\bar x/m is the maximum likelihood estimator.
(i) For \alpha_0>1,

\mathbb{E}(\theta)=\beta_0/(\alpha_0-1).

(ii) The likelihood contributes

\theta^{-nm}\exp\bigl(-(\textstyle\sum_i x_i)/\theta\bigr).

The prior contributes

\theta^{-\alpha_0-1}\exp(-\beta_0/\theta).

Hence

\boxed{\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(\alpha_0+nm,\;\beta_0+\textstyle\sum_i x_i).}

(iii) For \alpha_0+nm>1,

\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=
\frac{\beta_0+\sum x_i}{\alpha_0+nm-1}
=
\frac{(\alpha_0-1)\,\mathbb{E}(\theta)+nm\,\hat\theta}{(\alpha_0-1)+nm}.

Writing the mean explicitly as a convex combination gives

\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\underbrace{\frac{\alpha_0-1}{\alpha_0+nm-1}}_{w_0}\mathbb{E}(\theta)
+\underbrace{\frac{nm}{\alpha_0+nm-1}}_{w_n}\hat\theta.

For \alpha_0>1, both weights are nonnegative and w_0+w_n=1. The data contribution is nm, the total number of captured animals across the n locations.
(iv) With n and the prior fixed, m\to\infty makes w_0\to0 and w_n\to1. If \hat\theta=\bar x/m remains bounded, as it does in probability under the stated sampling model at a fixed true scale, the posterior mean approaches \hat\theta.
(v) Taking \alpha_0,\beta_0\to0 in the posterior expression gives \sum_i x_i/(nm-1)=\{nm/(nm-1)\}\hat\theta, provided nm>1. It is close to, but not exactly, the MLE. This is a formal weak-prior limit: the proper inverse-gamma prior’s mean does not exist along the path once \alpha_0\leq1, so the weighted-average formula involving that mean cannot be used to take this limit.
(vi) When \alpha_0>1, the hyperparameters act like prior information that pulls the MLE toward the prior mean \beta_0/(\alpha_0-1), with weight w_0. In the posterior-mean ratio, \alpha_0-1 plays a pseudo-count role beside the observed nm, and \beta_0 plays a prior total-waiting-time role beside \sum_i x_i. These need not represent literal extra animals.
(vii) Let a=\alpha_0+nm and b=\beta_0+\sum x_i. The central credible interval is the \alpha/2 and 1-\alpha/2 quantiles of \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b).
Equivalently, let q_u be the u-quantile of \operatorname{Gamma}(a,b) in shape–rate form. Since 1/\theta has this gamma posterior, the interval is [1/q_{1-\alpha/2},1/q_{\alpha/2}]. The reversal of endpoints follows because taking reciprocals is decreasing. Conditional on the data and model, the interval contains posterior probability 1-\alpha; it describes uncertainty about the common scale, not the waiting time of a future animal.

title: Question 12. Improper prior for a normal sample
text:
Topic: Conjugate analysis for normal models · more questions on this topic
Source: Final preparation, question 12 of 22 ‹ Question 11 Question 13 ›

The prior and the sample are

f(\mu,\sigma^{2})\propto 1/\sigma^{2},
\qquad
x_1,\ldots,x_n\mid\mu,\sigma^{2}\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2}),

with n\geq 2.
(i) Derive the joint posterior kernel of (\mu,\sigma^{2}). [2 marks]
(ii) Show that \sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\mu)^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar x)^{2}+n(\mu-\bar x)^{2}. [2 marks]
(iii) Show that \mu\mid\sigma^{2},{\boldsymbol{x}} is normal, and give its mean and variance. [2 marks]
(iv) Show that \sigma^{2}\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}} is inverse-gamma, and give its shape and rate. [2 marks]
(v) Describe how to sample from the joint posterior. [4 marks]
(vi) Describe 90\% posterior credible intervals for \mu and for \sigma^{2}. [2 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write v=\sigma^2, \bar x=n^{-1}\sum_i x_i and S=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2, the unnormalised sum of squares. The prior p(\mu,v)\propto1/v is a density kernel relative to d\mu\,dv, and \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b) has kernel v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v}. Take the observed sample to be nonconstant (S>0), as required for a proper posterior with this improper prior.
(i) The likelihood contributes (\sigma^{2})^{-n/2}\exp\bigl(-\sum(x_i-\mu)^{2}/(2\sigma^{2})\bigr), and the prior contributes \sigma^{-2}. For \sigma^{2}>0,

f(\mu,\sigma^{2}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
\propto
(\sigma^{2})^{-n/2-1}
\exp\Bigl(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\mu)^{2}\Bigr).

(ii)

\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\mu)^{2}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar x+\bar x-\mu)^{2}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar x)^{2}+n(\mu-\bar x)^{2},

because \sum(x_i-\bar x)=0.
(iii) Let S=\sum(x_i-\bar x)^{2}. By (ii), the kernel in \mu is \exp\bigl(-n(\mu-\bar x)^{2}/(2\sigma^{2})\bigr). Thus

\mu\mid\sigma^{2},{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim \operatorname{N}(\bar x,\,\sigma^{2}/n).

(iv) The kernel in \sigma^{2} is

(\sigma^{2})^{-(n/2)-1}
\exp\Bigl(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\mu)^{2}\Bigr).


\boxed{\sigma^{2}\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim
\operatorname{InvGamma}\Bigl(\frac n2,\;\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\mu)^{2}\Bigr).}

(v) The two full conditionals give a valid Gibbs sampler, but direct independent draws are available. Integrate the joint kernel over \mu. By (ii), the normal integral contributes \sqrt{2\pi v/n}, so

\begin{aligned}
p(v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto v^{-n/2-1}e^{-S/(2v)}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-n(\mu-\bar x)^2/(2v)}\,d\mu\\
&\propto v^{-(n-1)/2-1}e^{-S/(2v)}.
\end{aligned}

Thus v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}((n-1)/2,S/2) when S>0. For each independent posterior pair, draw v from this marginal and then \mu\mid v,{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{N}(\bar x,v/n). This samples p(\mu,v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=p(v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})p(\mu\mid v,{\boldsymbol{x}}) exactly, with no burn-in. The pairs are independent across draws, though \mu and v within a pair are dependent. The marginal shape (n-1)/2 differs from the full-conditional shape n/2 because integrating over \mu contributes v^{1/2}.
If using Gibbs instead, initialise v^{(0)}>0 and alternate

\mu^{(t)}\sim\operatorname{N}(\bar x,v^{(t-1)}/n),\qquad
v^{(t)}\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\left(\frac n2,\frac{S+n(\mu^{(t)}-\bar x)^2}{2}\right).

These are dependent Markov-chain draws, so convergence must be assessed. Setting \mu=\bar x in the variance full conditional would not give the marginal variance posterior: it would still have shape n/2 and would miss the integration factor above.
(vi) Let F_{\mathrm{IG}} be the CDF of \operatorname{InvGamma}((n-1)/2,S/2). A central 90\% credible interval for v=\sigma^2 is [F_{\mathrm{IG}}^{-1}(0.05),F_{\mathrm{IG}}^{-1}(0.95)]. Integrating v out gives \mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}} a Student-t distribution with n-1 degrees of freedom, centre \bar x and scale \sqrt{S/[n(n-1)]}. Hence its central 90\% interval is

\boxed{\bar x\ \pm\ t_{0.95,n-1}\sqrt{\frac{S}{n(n-1)}}.}

Empirical 5\% and 95\% quantiles of the direct draws are an alternative approximation to these intervals.

title: Question 6. Geometric–beta Gibbs sampler
text:
Topic: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings · more questions on this topic
Source: Final preparation, question 6 of 22 ‹ Question 5 Question 7 ›

Consider X and Y with joint density

f(x,y)\propto y^{\alpha}(1-y)^{x+\beta-1},

for x=1,2,3,\ldots and 0<y<1, where \alpha>0 and \beta>0. Describe a Gibbs sampler for this joint density.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. This target has one discrete coordinate X\in\{1,2,\ldots\} and one continuous coordinate Y\in(0,1). Here \operatorname{Geom}(p) counts trials up to and including the first success, with mass p(1-p)^{x-1}. A \operatorname{Beta}(a,b) density is proportional to y^{a-1}(1-y)^{b-1}. When finding a full conditional, keep all factors involving the coordinate being updated and normalise over that coordinate’s support.
For 0<y<1, the factors in x are (1-y)^{x-1}. For r=1-y\in(0,1),

\sum_{x=1}^{\infty}r^{x-1}=\frac{1}{1-r}=\frac{1}{y},

so

X\mid y\sim\operatorname{Geom}(y),
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(X=x\mid y)=y(1-y)^{x-1},\quad x=1,2,\ldots.

The factors in y are y^{(\alpha+1)-1}(1-y)^{(x+\beta)-1}, so

Y\mid x\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+1,\,x+\beta).

Record the completed pair. Each draw is from an exact full conditional, so there is no acceptance step. To see why an update preserves the joint target, suppose a pair already has density f: leaving Y unchanged and redrawing X from f(x\mid Y) gives f_Y(y)f(x\mid y)=f(x,y) again. The same reasoning applies to the other coordinate and hence to their composition. Convergence from the chosen start still needs assessment, and successive sweeps are generally dependent.
The target is proper: summing its kernel over x leaves y^{\alpha-1}(1-y)^\beta, which has a finite beta integral for the stated positive parameters. In fact, this also identifies Y\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta+1) marginally. It provides a useful check on a Gibbs simulation; it is different from the full conditional Y\mid X.
Support and mixing checks. Correct full conditionals alone do not guarantee useful exploration. For example, take a target uniform on the two disjoint squares (0,1)^2 and (2,3)^2. Updating one coordinate while holding the other fixed cannot leave the current square, so a single-coordinate Gibbs chain cannot explore the whole target. The present geometric–beta target is positive over its product support and has no such hard separation. Strong dependence can nevertheless make exploration slow; a longer discarded prefix does not fix poor mixing. If implementing the first draw with R’s rgeom, add one because R counts failures before success.

title: Question 19. Poisson regression for fish species
text:
Topic: Standard errors, and models for counts · more questions on this topic
Source: Final preparation, question 19 of 22 ‹ Question 18 Question 20 ›

2024 examination, Question 3 (20 marks).
Barbour and Brown recorded the number Y_i of fish species in n=70 lakes, together with latitude and area. The scatterplots show the observed counts against the two covariates.



Species counts against latitude and log lake area, as shown in the 2024 examination.


Consider

Y_i\mid X_i\stackrel{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}\operatorname{Poisson}(\mu_i=\exp(X_i^{\top}\beta)),
\qquad
X_i^{\top}\beta=\beta_0+\beta_1\,\mathrm{latitude}_i+\beta_2\log(\mathrm{area}_i).

(a) [1 mark] Briefly argue why \log(\mathrm{area}_i) is preferable to \mathrm{area}_i in the linear predictor.
(b) [2 marks] Show that the log-likelihood is

\ell(\beta\mid X,Y)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl\{Y_i(X_i^{\top}\beta)-\exp(X_i^{\top}\beta)\bigr\}+\text{constant}.

(c) [2 marks] Derive the score and show that

S(\beta)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Y_i-\mu_i(X_i^{\top}\beta)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid X_i)}\,\mu_i'(X_i^{\top}\beta)\,X_i.

(d) [1 mark] Show that S(\beta) is unbiased.
(e) [2 marks] Verify \operatorname{Var}(S(\beta))=-\mathbb{E}[\partial S(\beta)/\partial\beta].
The first statistician fits the linear Poisson model:
fit1 = glm(species ~ latitude + log(area), family=poisson)

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept)  2.5949644  0.0668158   38.84   <2e-16 ***
latitude    -0.0149475  0.0008788  -17.01   <2e-16 ***
log(area)    0.2092975  0.0068808   30.42   <2e-16 ***

(Dispersion parameter for poisson family taken to be 1)
Null deviance:     2646.1 on 69 degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 1249.9 on 67 degrees of freedom
AIC: 1616.4
(f) [5 marks] Interpret the intercept, the latitude and \log(\mathrm{area}) coefficients, the null deviance and the residual deviance.
The second statistician replaces the latitude slope with a smooth:
library(mgcv)
fit2 = gam(species ~ s(latitude) + log(area), family=poisson)

Parametric coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept)  2.064885   0.065793   31.39   <2e-16 ***
log(area)    0.202381   0.007701   26.28   <2e-16 ***

Approximate significance of smooth terms:
             edf Ref.df Chi.sq p-value
s(latitude) 8.881  8.996  463.2  <2e-16 ***



Fitted latitude smooth and uncertainty bands from the 2024 examination.


(g) [1 mark] Interpret the edf value 8.881.
(h) [2 marks] Comparing the two fits, is a linear function of latitude enough after accounting for lake area?
(i) [4 marks] Summarise the main findings in one short paragraph.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Y_i is the species count in lake i, and X_i=(1,\mathrm{latitude}_i,\log\mathrm{area}_i)^\top is its fixed covariate vector. The model assumes independent Y_i\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\mu_i) with \mu_i=\exp(X_i^\top\beta). Thus \mathbb{E}(Y_i\mid X_i)=\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid X_i)=\mu_i, with dispersion fixed at one. The score is the gradient of the log-likelihood, and Fisher information measures its expected curvature, or equivalently its covariance under the model.
(a) \log(\mathrm{area}) transforms a covariate; the log link transforms the response mean. These are separate choices. Logging area compresses its range and represents multiplicative area comparisons by additive differences: one unit of \log(\mathrm{area}) multiplies area by e. With a log link and a log-area predictor,

\mu_i=e^{\beta_0+\beta_1\mathrm{latitude}_i}\,
\mathrm{area}_i^{\beta_2}.

This is a power-law area effect, whereas using raw area in the same log-link GLM gives an exponential area effect. The observed plot and scientific context should guide that choice; logging a covariate does not by itself establish model adequacy. Neither choice requires taking \log Y_i, so zero species counts pose no transformation problem for the response.
(b) The Poisson log-likelihood contribution is Y_i\log\mu_i-\mu_i-\log(Y_i!). The factorial term does not depend on \beta. With the log link, \log\mu_i=X_i^{\top}\beta and \mu_i=\exp(X_i^{\top}\beta), so

\ell(\beta\mid X,Y)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl\{Y_i(X_i^{\top}\beta)-\exp(X_i^{\top}\beta)\bigr\}
+\text{constant}.

(c) Differentiate (b). Since \partial\mu_i/\partial\beta=\mu_i X_i,

S(\beta)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i-\mu_i)X_i.

For every GLM the score is the same residual, reweighted by the variance and by the slope of the mean:

S(\beta)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\frac{Y_i-\mu_i}{\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid X_i)}
\,\mu_i'(X_i^{\top}\beta)\,X_i.

Here \operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid X_i)=\mu_i. Under the log link, \mu_i'=\mu_i, so the weight equals 1 and the general score reduces to the sum above. Setting S(\beta)=0 is still nonlinear in \beta, because \mu_i=\exp(X_i^{\top}\beta). The fit is Fisher scoring of that equation, not a closed form.
(d) At the \beta in the model, \mathbb{E}(Y_i\mid X_i)=\mu_i. Each summand then has conditional mean zero, and \mathbb{E}[S(\beta)]=0.
Explicitly, with the design held fixed,

\mathbb{E}\{S(\beta)\mid X\}
=\sum_iX_i\{\mathbb{E}(Y_i\mid X)-\mu_i\}=0.

This identity concerns repeated samples at the true parameter. The fitted score S(\hat\beta)=0 instead follows from maximising the observed likelihood; the two zeroes arise for different reasons.
(e) From the reduced score and \partial\mu_i/\partial\beta^{\top}=\mu_i X_i^{\top},

\frac{\partial S(\beta)}{\partial\beta}
=
-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mu_i X_iX_i^{\top}.

The right-hand side does not depend on Y, so

-\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\partial S(\beta)}{\partial\beta}\right]
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mu_i X_iX_i^{\top}.

Calculate the score covariance separately. Conditional independence removes cross-covariances, and the Poisson variance is \operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid X)=\mu_i, so

\operatorname{Var}\{S(\beta)\mid X\}
=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid X)X_iX_i^{\top}
=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mu_iX_iX_i^{\top}.

This matches the negative expected Hessian above. The common matrix is the Fisher information. For the Poisson log link the observed and expected information agree; overdispersion or dependence would change the score covariance even if the mean formula remained correct.
(f) The intercept 2.595 is the log mean at latitude 0 (the equator) and \log(\mathrm{area})=0 (unit area), so the fitted mean there is \exp(2.595)\approx 13.4 species. This is the model’s reference lake, not a general mean for the sampled lakes.
The latitude coefficient -0.01495 is a multiplicative effect at fixed log area. One extra degree away from the equator multiplies the mean count by \exp(-0.01495)\approx 0.985. A degree is a small unit: ten degrees multiply the mean by \exp(-0.1495)\approx 0.861. Those are the same fit. The coefficient looks small because the unit is one degree.
The coefficient 0.2093 is the effect of one unit of \log(\mathrm{area}) at fixed latitude. Multiplying area by e multiplies the mean count by \exp(0.2093)\approx 1.233.
For any positive multiplier c, the fitted mean ratio is c^{0.2093}. Doubling area therefore multiplies the fitted mean by about 1.16, rather than by 1.23. The coefficient is an elasticity: a small 1\% increase in area corresponds to approximately a 0.2093\% increase in the expected count, holding latitude fixed.
The null deviance 2646.1 on 69 degrees of freedom is the deviance of the intercept-only model, one mean for every lake. The deviance is twice the drop in log-likelihood from the saturated fit to the model under discussion,

D(Y;\hat\mu)=2\bigl\{\ell(Y;Y)-\ell(\hat\mu;Y)\bigr\},

with Poisson dispersion fixed at 1. The degrees of freedom are n-1=69.
The residual deviance 1249.9 on 67 degrees of freedom is the deviance of the fitted three-parameter model, n-3=67. For the Poisson,

D
=
2\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left\{
Y_i\log\frac{Y_i}{\hat\mu_i}-(Y_i-\hat\mu_i)
\right\}.

The value is about 19 times its degrees of freedom, so the Poisson model fits poorly relative to its stated mean–variance assumptions. This can reflect overdispersion, a misspecified mean function, influential lakes or dependence; the deviance alone does not identify which. A quasi-Poisson fit with \operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid X_i)=\phi\mu_i would retain these fitted coefficients while adjusting their standard errors, but it would not repair a wrong mean function.
The saturated fit has one fitted mean per observation, \hat\mu_i=Y_i, and hence no residual degrees of freedom. The null and residual degrees of freedom reveal n=70 and three fitted regression coefficients. In the deviance formula use 0\log(0/\hat\mu_i)=0 when Y_i=0. Comparing deviance to degrees of freedom is a diagnostic, not a proof that one particular assumption failed; sparse counts can also make a nominal chi-squared approximation inaccurate.
(g) The value 8.881 is the effective degrees of freedom of the fitted latitude smooth. It measures the smooth’s effective flexibility after penalisation, roughly comparable to a high-order polynomial fit; the fitted function is not literally a polynomial of degree 8.881. A value near 1 would indicate an approximately straight effect on the log-mean scale. Here the fitted effect is substantially more flexible.
The GAM keeps the Poisson response distribution and log link but replaces \beta_1\mathrm{latitude} by a fitted function g(\mathrm{latitude}). A smooth can be represented by basis functions with a penalty discouraging excessive wiggliness. The edf describes the flexibility remaining after that penalty, rather than the number of knots or an ordinary polynomial degree. The plotted ordinate is the smooth’s contribution to the log mean; obtaining a predicted count also requires the intercept and log-area contribution.
(h) The plotted effect of latitude rises and falls several times, so a single straight line on the log-mean scale misses its shape. The edf of 8.881 is also far above the near-linear value of 1. The printed \chi^2 test concerns whether the smooth is absent, not specifically whether it departs from a line. A direct formal comparison of linear and smooth latitude fits would address that narrower hypothesis. The log-area coefficient is similar in the two fits, 0.209 and 0.202.
(i) At a fixed latitude, multiplying lake area by e multiplies the fitted mean species count by about 1.23; the log-area coefficient stays close to 0.20 in the GAM. The smooth suggests high diversity near the equator, a dip around 20–25 degrees away, a rise around 30–40 degrees, and lower diversity towards the poles. A single latitude slope misses this pattern. The linear Poisson fit reduces deviance from 2646.1 to 1249.9, but the residual deviance remains far above 67 degrees of freedom. Check the mean function, the Poisson variance assumption and influential lakes before relying on its printed standard errors and z tests.

title: Question 8. Exponential versus gamma lifetimes
text:
Topic: Bayesian hypotheses and model comparison · more questions on this topic
Source: Final preparation, question 8 of 22 ‹ Question 7 Question 9 ›
