The lifetimes of n devices are {\boldsymbol{x}}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n). Two models are proposed,

M_1\colon X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda),
\qquad
M_2\colon X\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(3,\theta),

with priors \lambda\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(1,3) and \theta\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(1,1). Gamma and exponential distributions use the shape–rate sheet: a \operatorname{Gamma}(3,\theta) density is \theta^{3}x^{2}e^{-\theta x}/2.
(i) Find the marginal likelihood f({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_1). [6 marks]
(ii) Find the marginal likelihood f({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_2). [6 marks]
(iii) Obtain BF_{12}=f({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_1)/f({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_2). For these data BF_{12}=1.347. Interpret this number and state which model it prefers. [4 marks]
(iv) The researchers believe M_2 is three times as likely as M_1 a priori. What are the posterior odds? Which model is preferred? [4 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write S=\sum_i x_i and Q=\prod_i x_i^2. Both \lambda and \theta are rates. The marginal likelihood f({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_k) is the prior predictive density of the entire observed sample under model M_k. The Bayes factor BF_{12} is the ratio of these densities, in the stated order.
A marginal likelihood integrates the normalised likelihood against the normalised parameter prior, so factors involving only the data must be retained. Both integrations use \int_0^\infty t^{A-1}e^{-Bt}\,dt=\Gamma(A)/B^A for A,B>0. This identity follows by setting u=Bt in the defining gamma integral.
(i) The \operatorname{Exp}(\lambda) likelihood is \lambda^{n}e^{-\lambda\sum x_i}, and the \operatorname{Gamma}(1,3) prior density is 3e^{-3\lambda}. Hence

f({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_1)
=
3\int_0^{\infty}\lambda^{n}e^{-\lambda(\sum x_i+3)}\,d\lambda
=
\boxed{\dfrac{3\,n!}{\bigl(3+\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\bigr)^{n+1}}.}

(ii) A \operatorname{Gamma}(3,\theta) observation has density \theta^{3}x^{2}e^{-\theta x}/2. The prior density of \theta is e^{-\theta}. Therefore

\begin{aligned}
f({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_2)
&=
\frac{\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_i^{2}}{2^{n}}
\int_0^{\infty}\theta^{3n}e^{-\theta(\sum x_i+1)}\,d\theta\\
&=
\boxed{\dfrac{\bigl(\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_i^{2}\bigr)\,\Gamma(3n+1)}{2^{n}\bigl(1+\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\bigr)^{3n+1}}.}
\end{aligned}

(iii) Substituting (i) and (ii) into BF_{12}=f({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_1)/f({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_2) gives

\boxed{BF_{12}
=\frac{3\,2^n\Gamma(n+1)(S+1)^{3n+1}}
{\Gamma(3n+1)(S+3)^{n+1}Q}.}

For the observed sample this is 1.347: the marginal likelihood under M_1 is 1.347 times that under M_2. The data therefore favour M_1, but only slightly. The Bayes factor is not a posterior model probability.
For a continuous sample these are densities, not probabilities of the exact observed vector. Their ratio compares how strongly the two prior predictive distributions support the same observed data. Optimising each likelihood and taking the ratio would instead compare maximised likelihoods and would not calculate this Bayes factor.
(iv) Prior odds of M_1 to M_2 are 1/3. Posterior odds of M_1 to M_2 are BF_{12}/3=1.347/3=0.449:1, or about 2.23:1 in favour of M_2. Thus M_2 is preferred once the prior odds are included.
The governing identity is posterior odds = Bayes factor \times prior odds. The data shift the odds towards M_1, but the shift is too small to overcome the prior preference for M_2. If these are the only two models under consideration, their posterior probabilities are approximately 0.310 and 0.690, respectively.

title: Question 13. Binomial–beta Gibbs sampler
text:
Topic: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings · more questions on this topic
Source: Final preparation, question 13 of 22 ‹ Question 12 Question 14 ›

For x=0,1,\ldots,n and 0\leq\theta\leq 1, with \alpha,\beta>0,

f(x,\theta)
=
\binom{n}{x}\theta^{x+\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{n-x+\beta-1}.

(i) Find and name the conditional distribution of x\mid\theta. The kernel is enough. [4 marks]
(ii) Find and name the conditional distribution of \theta\mid x. The kernel is enough. [4 marks]
(iii) Describe a Gibbs sampler for f(x,\theta). [7 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. The target is a joint distribution of a count X\in\{0,\ldots,n\} and a probability \theta\in(0,1). For positive \alpha,\beta, the kernel factors as a \operatorname{Bin}(n,\theta) mass times a \operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta) kernel. In finding X\mid\theta, normalisation is a sum over counts; for \theta\mid X, it is an integral over (0,1).
The displayed joint expression is a kernel: summing it over x gives \theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1}, whose integral is B(\alpha,\beta). The normalising factor 1/B(\alpha,\beta) cancels from both full conditionals.
(i) With \theta fixed, \theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1} is constant in x, but \binom{n}{x} is not. The remaining kernel is \binom{n}{x}\theta^x(1-\theta)^{n-x}. Therefore

x\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,\theta).

(ii) The factors in \theta are \theta^{x+\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{n-x+\beta-1}. Therefore

\theta\mid x\sim\operatorname{Beta}(x+\alpha,\,n-x+\beta).

(iii) Choose x^{(0)}\in\{0,\ldots,n\} and \theta^{(0)}\in(0,1). For t=1,\ldots,T, draw

X^{(t)}\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,\theta^{(t-1)}),
\qquad
\theta^{(t)}\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+X^{(t)},\beta+n-X^{(t)}),

in that order, and record the completed pair. The second update uses the new count. Each exact full-conditional update preserves the joint target, so no Metropolis acceptance step is needed; successive recorded pairs are generally dependent.
The target also admits a useful simulation check. Its marginal for \theta is \operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta), because summing the binomial mass over x gives one. Drawing \theta from this marginal and then X\mid\theta would generate independent joint pairs directly. The Gibbs algorithm answers the question using full conditionals, but its long-run \theta histogram should agree with that beta marginal.

title: C50. ARCH and GARCH
text:
Topic: Dependence along a series · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 50 of 50 ‹ C49

What do ARCH and GARCH models describe? What additional dependence does GARCH include?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. ARCH (autoregressive conditional heteroscedasticity) models let the current conditional variance depend on past squared mean-adjusted responses (shocks), describing changing volatility rather than only the conditional mean. GARCH (generalised ARCH) additionally includes lagged conditional variances in that variance equation.

title: C48. Invertibility
text:
Topic: Dependence along a series · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 48 of 50 ‹ C47 C49 ›

What does invertibility mean for a moving-average model? State the root condition for a finite-order model.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. An MA model is invertible when its innovations can be recovered as a stable, convergent linear filter of current and past observations. For a finite-order model with MA polynomial b(z)=1+b_1z+\cdots+b_qz^q, the usual invertibility condition is that every root has modulus greater than one.

title: C46. AR, MA and ARMA orders
text:
Topic: Dependence along a series · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 46 of 50 ‹ C45 C47 ›

What are AR(p), MA(q) and ARMA(p,q) models? What do their orders count?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. An ARMA(p,q) representation combines p lagged responses with the current and q lagged white-noise innovations: X_t=c+\sum_{j=1}^p a_jX_{t-j}+\varepsilon_t+
\sum_{k=1}^q b_k\varepsilon_{t-k}, with intercept c. AR(p) sets q=0, MA(q) sets p=0, and the orders are the largest included lags, not the number of observations.

title: C44. White noise is not necessarily independent
text:
Topic: Dependence along a series · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 44 of 50 ‹ C43 C45 ›

Does white noise necessarily consist of independent observations? Give the moment definition of white noise.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. White noise \{\varepsilon_t\} has zero mean, a common finite variance \sigma^2 and zero covariance between distinct times. These moment conditions do not imply independence, although jointly Gaussian white noise is independent.

title: C42. Process and realisation
text:
Topic: Dependence along a series · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 42 of 50 ‹ C41 C43 ›

What is a stochastic process, and how does an observed time series relate to it?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. A stochastic process is a collection of random variables \{X_t:t\in\mathcal T\} indexed by time or another index set \mathcal T. An observed time series is a finite portion of one realisation (sample path), not a collection of independent realisations of the whole process.

title: C40. Sandwich robustness
text:
Topic: Marginal models, and two responses at once · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 40 of 50 ‹ C39 C41 ›

What misspecification can the GEE sandwich covariance estimator tolerate? Does it repair an incorrect mean model?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. The sandwich estimator estimates the sampling covariance of the GEE coefficient estimator using empirical cluster residual variation, allowing the working covariance to be misspecified. It does not repair an incorrect mean model: its usual robustness is asymptotic with many independent clusters, a correct marginal mean, valid estimating equations and regularity conditions, not a guarantee for small samples or informative missingness.

title: C38. Generalised estimating equations
text:
Topic: Marginal models, and two responses at once · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 38 of 50 ‹ C37 C39 ›

What are generalised estimating equations, and what mean-model parameters do they estimate?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. GEE are estimating equations for the coefficients of a marginal (population-average) mean model for correlated responses, constructed using derivatives of the mean and a working within-cluster covariance. They require no full joint response distribution, but assume independent clusters and, for consistency under standard regularity conditions, a correctly specified marginal mean.

title: C36. Conditional versus marginal dependence
text:
Topic: Marginal models, and two responses at once · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 36 of 50 ‹ C35 C37 ›

How can responses be independent conditional on a random effect but correlated marginally?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. Conditional independence fixes the shared random effect, whereas marginalisation averages over it. For Y_{ij}=m_{ij}+b_i+\varepsilon_{ij} with fixed m_{ij}, independent errors and b_i independent of all errors, \operatorname{Cov}(Y_{ij},Y_{ik})=\operatorname{Var}(b_i) for j\ne k: the unobserved shared intercept induces marginal correlation.

title: C34. Fixed and random effects
text:
Topic: Random intercepts · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 34 of 50 ‹ C33 C35 ›

What are fixed effects and random effects in a mixed model?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. Fixed effects are unknown coefficients treated as constants; random effects are latent group-specific quantities modelled as draws from a shared distribution, commonly a multivariate normal. Their variance parameters describe between-group heterogeneity, whereas the realised group effects are predicted.

title: C32. Roughness penalty
text:
Topic: Smooth means · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 32 of 50 ‹ C31 C33 ›

Why penalise \int\{f''(x)\}^2\,dx when fitting a smooth? What happens as its penalty weight increases?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. For a smooth f, the roughness measure J(f)=\int\{f''(x)\}^2\,dx penalises curvature when fitting by maximising \ell(f)-\lambda J(f)/2, with \lambda\ge0. Larger \lambda favours less wiggle; as \lambda\to\infty the fit approaches the penalty’s linear null space, where an admissible limiting fit exists.

title: C30. Significance is not adequacy
text:
Topic: Paired comparisons, and how far a fit is from the data · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 30 of 50 ‹ C29 C31 ›

Does a significant predictor establish that a GLM fits adequately? Name one separate diagnostic check.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. A coefficient significance test addresses a specified null hypothesis about that coefficient within the assumed model; adequacy concerns whether the model describes the data sufficiently well. Significance does not establish adequacy: for example, inspect Pearson residuals (y_i-\hat\mu_i)/\sqrt{\hat\phi V(\hat\mu_i)} against fitted values for unexplained patterns or changing spread.

title: C28. Dispersion
text:
Topic: Underdispersion, positive responses, and quasi-likelihood · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 28 of 50 ‹ C27 C29 ›

What is the dispersion parameter \phi in \operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid x_i)=\phi V(\mu_i)? Define overdispersion and underdispersion relative to \phi=1.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. In \operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid x_i)=\phi V(\mu_i), the function V specifies the variance’s dependence on the mean and the positive scalar \phi scales that variance. Relative to the baseline \phi=1, overdispersion means \phi>1 and underdispersion means 0<\phi<1; for quasi-Poisson, V(\mu)=\mu.

title: C26. Bradley–Terry
text:
Topic: Paired comparisons, and how far a fit is from the data · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 26 of 50 ‹ C25 C27 ›

What is the Bradley–Terry model for a head-to-head contest with no ties?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. For a contest with no ties, assign real-valued log-abilities \lambda_j; the model specifies \mathbb{P}(j\text{ beats }k)=e^{\lambda_j}/(e^{\lambda_j}+e^{\lambda_k}), equivalently odds e^{\lambda_j-\lambda_k}. Only ability differences are identifiable, so a reference such as \lambda_1=0 is needed.

title: C24. Categorical response types
text:
Topic: Categorical responses · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 24 of 50 ‹ C23 C25 ›

What are nominal and ordinal responses? What probabilities does a baseline-category logit compare?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. Nominal categories have no intrinsic ordering; ordinal categories have an ordering but not necessarily meaningful numerical gaps. A baseline-category logit compares category probabilities with a fixed reference: \log(p_k/p_0)=\beta_{0k}+x^\top\beta_k, where p_k=\mathbb{P}(Y=k\mid x) and k\ne0.

title: C22. Negative-binomial variation
text:
Topic: Standard errors, and models for counts · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 22 of 50 ‹ C21 C23 ›

Why can a negative-binomial model handle overdispersed counts that a Poisson model cannot?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. The Poisson model has \operatorname{Var}(Y)=\mu, whereas a negative-binomial model with mean \mu>0 and size \nu>0 has \operatorname{Var}(Y)=\mu+\mu^2/\nu. The extra positive term allows greater variation than Poisson at the same mean, as arises from Gamma mixing of Poisson intensities; the Poisson limit is recovered as \nu\to\infty.

title: C20. Logit, probit and odds
text:
Topic: Introduction to generalised linear models · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 20 of 50 ‹ C19 C21 ›

How do the logit and probit links differ? Define the odds associated with a success probability p.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. For success probability 0<p<1, odds are p/(1-p), the logit is \log\{p/(1-p)\}, and the probit is \Phi^{-1}(p), where \Phi is the standard normal CDF. These are different links for the same Bernoulli mean p, giving different probability curves and coefficient interpretations.

title: C18. Score and information
text:
Topic: Introduction to generalised linear models · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 18 of 50 ‹ C17 C19 ›

What are the score vector and the expected Fisher information matrix for a log-likelihood?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. For log-likelihood \ell(\beta), the score is its gradient S(\beta)=\partial\ell/\partial\beta and expected Fisher information is I(\beta)=-\mathbb{E}_\beta[\partial^2\ell/\partial\beta\,\partial\beta^\top], with expectation under the model and covariates fixed. Under the usual differentiability and interchange conditions, \mathbb{E}_\beta[S(\beta)]=0 and I(\beta)=\operatorname{Var}_\beta(S(\beta)).

title: C16. The GLM components
text:
Topic: Introduction to generalised linear models · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 16 of 50 ‹ C15 C17 ›

What are the three components of a GLM? State the usual conditional-independence assumption.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. A GLM specifies an exponential-family response distribution, a linear predictor \eta_i=x_i^\top\beta, and a link g(\mu_i)=\eta_i, where \mu_i=\mathbb{E}(Y_i\mid x_i). Responses are assumed independent conditional on the fixed covariates and model parameters.

title: C14. Metropolis–Hastings cancellations
text:
Topic: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 14 of 50 ‹ C13 C15 ›

Why can Metropolis–Hastings use an unnormalised target? When do its proposal-density terms cancel?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. Let \pi(z)=k(z)/Z be the target and q(y\mid x) the proposal density from current state x to candidate y. The acceptance probability is \min\{1,k(y)q(x\mid y)/[k(x)q(y\mid x)]\} because Z cancels; the proposal terms cancel only when q(y\mid x)=q(x\mid y), as for a fixed-scale symmetric random walk.

title: C12. Markov property and invariance
text:
Topic: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 12 of 50 ‹ C11 C13 ›

What is the Markov property? What does it mean for a distribution to be invariant for a chain?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. The Markov property says that the conditional distribution of the next state, given the whole past, depends only on the current state. A distribution \pi is invariant if one transition preserves it: X^{(t)}\sim\pi implies X^{(t+1)}\sim\pi; this alone does not establish convergence from every initial state.

title: C10. Gamma and inverse-Gamma kernels
text:
Topic: Conjugate analysis for normal models · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 10 of 50 ‹ C9 C11 ›

State the kernels and support of shape–rate \operatorname{Gamma}(a,b) and \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b).






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. A kernel omits only factors constant in the variable of interest; for t>0 and a,b>0, shape–rate \operatorname{Gamma}(a,b) has kernel t^{a-1}e^{-bt}, whereas \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b) has kernel t^{-a-1}e^{-b/t}. The parameter b is the Gamma rate; under the stated inverse-Gamma convention, 1/T\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a,b) when T\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b).

title: C8. Evidence and model odds
text:
Topic: Bayesian hypotheses and model comparison · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 8 of 50 ‹ C7 C9 ›

What are marginal likelihoods and Bayes factors? How does a Bayes factor update model odds?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. For model M_j with a proper parameter prior, its marginal likelihood is m_j(x)=\int p(x\mid\theta_j,M_j)p(\theta_j\mid M_j)\,d\theta_j, and BF_{12}=m_1(x)/m_2(x) is the Bayes factor for M_1 against M_2. Posterior model odds equal BF_{12} times prior model odds; the Bayes factor alone is not a posterior model probability.

title: C6. Two kinds of interval
text:
Topic: Bayesian foundations · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 6 of 50 ‹ C5 C7 ›

How do the probability statements for a 95% credible interval and a 95% confidence interval differ?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. A 95% credible interval C(x) satisfies \mathbb{P}(\theta\in C(x)\mid x)=0.95 under the specified model and prior. A 95% confidence procedure I(X) has 95% repeated-sampling coverage of a fixed \theta (exactly or approximately, as stated), rather than 95% posterior probability for its observed interval.

title: C4. Exponential family
text:
Topic: Exponential families and conjugacy · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 4 of 50 ‹ C3 C5 ›

What is an exponential family? Identify its natural parameter and statistic.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. An exponential family has density or mass function f(x\mid\theta)=b(x)\exp\{c(\theta)^\top T(x)\}/a(\theta), where c(\theta) is the natural parameter, T(x) the natural statistic, b(x) a parameter-free base factor and a(\theta) the normalising function. In the regular form used here, the support is independent of \theta.

title: C2. Conjugacy
text:
Topic: The Beta–Binomial model · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 2 of 50 ‹ C1 C3 ›

What is a conjugate prior family? Give one prior–sampling-model example.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. A prior family is conjugate for a sampling model if Bayesian updating keeps the posterior in that family, with updated hyperparameters. For example, a \operatorname{Beta}(a,b) prior for a binomial success probability yields \operatorname{Beta}(a+x,b+n-x) after x successes in n trials, where a,b>0.

text:

title: Sufficiency and the posterior
text:
Topic: Exponential families and conjugacy · more questions on this topic

Let {\boldsymbol{X}}=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)^{\mathsf T} have likelihood p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta) and prior p(\theta). If U({\boldsymbol{X}}) is sufficient for \theta, use the Fisher–Neyman factorisation theorem and Bayes’ rule to show that the posterior depends on the observed sample only through U({\boldsymbol{x}}). Retain the normalising integral in the derivation.






Worked answer (click to show)





Question. Let {\boldsymbol{X}}=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)^{\mathsf T} have likelihood p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta) and prior p(\theta). If U({\boldsymbol{X}}) is sufficient for \theta, use the Fisher–Neyman factorisation theorem and Bayes’ rule to show that the posterior depends on the observed sample only through U({\boldsymbol{x}}). Retain the normalising integral in the derivation.
Solution. By the Fisher–Neyman factorisation theorem, sufficiency of U({\boldsymbol{X}}) implies that there are nonnegative functions g and h such that

p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta)=g\{U({\boldsymbol{x}}),\theta\}h({\boldsymbol{x}}),

where h does not depend on \theta. Bayes’ rule, including its normalising integral, gives \begin{align*}
p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=\frac{p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta)p(\theta)}
{\displaystyle\int p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid t)p(t)\,\mathrm{d} t}\\
&=\frac{g\{U({\boldsymbol{x}}),\theta\}h({\boldsymbol{x}})p(\theta)}
{\displaystyle\int g\{U({\boldsymbol{x}}),t\}h({\boldsymbol{x}})p(t)\,\mathrm{d} t}\\
&=\boxed{
\frac{g\{U({\boldsymbol{x}}),\theta\}p(\theta)}
{\displaystyle\int g\{U({\boldsymbol{x}}),t\}p(t)\,\mathrm{d} t}}.
\end{align*} Every occurrence of the observed sample is through U({\boldsymbol{x}}); the factor h({\boldsymbol{x}}) cancels because it is constant with respect to the integration variable and the parameter.

title: Normal–inverse-\chi^2 conjugacy
A logit-normal prior for a coin
text:

Suppose X\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,\theta) and prior knowledge favours heads. Consider the logit-normal prior

p(\theta)=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\theta(1-\theta)}
\exp\!\left[-\frac12\{\operatorname{logit}(\theta)-1\}^2\right],
\qquad 0<\theta<1,

where \operatorname{logit}(\theta)=\log\{\theta/(1-\theta)\}.

Plot the prior on a grid and describe its shape.
Generate 100{,}000 prior draws by taking Y\sim\operatorname{N}(1,1) and \theta=\exp(Y)/\{1+\exp(Y)\}. Add a kernel-density estimate from the draws to the exact prior curve.
Explain how the draws approximate the prior mean.
After observing x heads in n tosses, show that


p(\theta\mid x)\propto
\theta^{x-1}(1-\theta)^{n-x-1}
\exp\!\left[-\frac12\{\operatorname{logit}(\theta)-1\}^2\right].

Explain why this posterior is not Beta.






Worked answer (click to show)





Question. Suppose X\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,\theta) and prior knowledge favours heads. Consider the logit-normal prior

p(\theta)=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\theta(1-\theta)}
\exp\!\left[-\frac12\{\operatorname{logit}(\theta)-1\}^2\right],
\qquad 0<\theta<1,

where \operatorname{logit}(\theta)=\log\{\theta/(1-\theta)\}.

Plot the prior on a grid and describe its shape.
Generate 100{,}000 prior draws by taking Y\sim\operatorname{N}(1,1) and \theta=\exp(Y)/\{1+\exp(Y)\}. Add a kernel-density estimate from the draws to the exact prior curve.
Explain how the draws approximate the prior mean.
After observing x heads in n tosses, show that


p(\theta\mid x)\propto
\theta^{x-1}(1-\theta)^{n-x-1}
\exp\!\left[-\frac12\{\operatorname{logit}(\theta)-1\}^2\right].

Explain why this posterior is not Beta.
Solution. Let Y=\operatorname{logit}(\theta). Then

\theta=\frac{e^Y}{1+e^Y},
\qquad
\frac{\,\mathrm{d} Y}{\,\mathrm{d}\theta}
=\frac1\theta+\frac1{1-\theta}
=\frac1{\theta(1-\theta)}.

Transforming Y\sim\operatorname{N}(1,1) therefore produces exactly the stated prior.

The density is unimodal, concentrated above 1/2, and has a longer left tail than right tail. Its mode is near 0.84. The exact curve and a simulation check can be produced together by the following code.

dlogitnormal <- function(theta) {
  ok <- theta > 0 & theta < 1
  ans <- numeric(length(theta))
  ans[ok] <- dnorm(qlogis(theta[ok]), mean = 1, sd = 1) /
             (theta[ok] * (1 - theta[ok]))
  ans
}

set.seed(3500)
theta_grid <- seq(0.001, 0.999, length.out = 1000)
theta_draw <- plogis(rnorm(100000, mean = 1, sd = 1))

plot(theta_grid, dlogitnormal(theta_grid), type = "l",
     xlab = expression(theta), ylab = expression(p(theta)))
lines(density(theta_draw, from = 0, to = 1), col = "steelblue")

The overlaid kernel-density estimate should follow the exact curve. Agreement is a useful check both of the transformation and of the Jacobian in the displayed density.
By the law of large numbers,


\widehat{\mathbb{E}(\theta)}
=\frac1L\sum_{l=1}^L\theta^{(l)}
\longrightarrow \mathbb{E}(\theta).

For L=100{,}000 the answer varies slightly with the seed; numerical integration gives \mathbb{E}(\theta)\approx0.6967.

The binomial likelihood kernel is


p(x\mid\theta)\propto\theta^x(1-\theta)^{n-x}.

Multiplying by the prior gives \begin{align*}
p(\theta\mid x)
&\propto p(x\mid\theta)p(\theta)\\
&\propto
\theta^x(1-\theta)^{n-x}
\frac1{\theta(1-\theta)}
\exp\!\left[-\frac12\{\operatorname{logit}(\theta)-1\}^2\right]\\
&=\boxed{
\theta^{x-1}(1-\theta)^{n-x-1}
\exp\!\left[-\frac12\{\operatorname{logit}(\theta)-1\}^2\right]}.
\end{align*} A Beta kernel consists only of powers of \theta and 1-\theta. The extra factor involving the squared logit cannot be absorbed into those powers, so the posterior is not Beta.

title: An IQ threshold
text:
Topic: Bayesian hypotheses and model comparison · more questions on this topic
Source: Book exercise from Bayesian hypotheses and model comparison ‹ Two routes to the same table Factorisation and data reduction ›

Model population IQ by \mu\sim\operatorname{N}(100,15^2). Conditional on a person’s true IQ \mu, a standardised test score satisfies X\mid\mu\sim\operatorname{N}(\mu,10^2). A candidate obtains x=135, and the classification threshold for “gifted” is 130.

Find an equal-tailed 95\% posterior credible interval for \mu.
For H_0:\mu<130 and H_1:\mu\geq130, calculate the posterior odds \mathbb{P}(H_0\mid x)/\mathbb{P}(H_1\mid x) and state which hypothesis they favour.
Calculate \operatorname{BF}_{01} and reconcile its direction with that of the posterior odds by examining the prior odds.







Worked answer (click to show)





Question. Model population IQ by \mu\sim\operatorname{N}(100,15^2). Conditional on a person’s true IQ \mu, a standardised test score satisfies X\mid\mu\sim\operatorname{N}(\mu,10^2). A candidate obtains x=135, and the classification threshold for “gifted” is 130.

Find an equal-tailed 95\% posterior credible interval for \mu.
For H_0:\mu<130 and H_1:\mu\geq130, calculate the posterior odds \mathbb{P}(H_0\mid x)/\mathbb{P}(H_1\mid x) and state which hypothesis they favour.
Calculate \operatorname{BF}_{01} and reconcile its direction with that of the posterior odds by examining the prior odds.

Solution. The normal prior and likelihood give posterior precision

\frac1{v_1}=\frac1{15^2}+\frac1{10^2}
=\frac1{225}+\frac1{100}
=\frac{325}{22500}.

Hence

v_1=\frac{22500}{325}=69.2308.

The posterior mean is \begin{align*}
m_1
&=v_1\left(\frac{100}{15^2}+\frac{135}{10^2}\right)\\
&=\frac{15^2(135)+10^2(100)}{15^2+10^2}\\
&=\frac{30375+10000}{325}\\
&=124.2308.
\end{align*} Therefore

\boxed{\mu\mid x=135\sim\operatorname{N}(124.2308,69.2308)}.


The posterior standard deviation is \sqrt{69.2308}=8.3205. Thus the equal-tailed interval is \begin{align*}
m_1\pm z_{0.975}\sqrt{v_1}
&=124.2308\pm1.959964(8.3205)\\
&=\boxed{(107.923,140.539)}.
\end{align*}
Under the posterior, \begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}(H_0\mid x)
&=\mathbb{P}(\mu<130\mid x)\\
&=\Phi\!\left(\frac{130-124.2308}{8.3205}\right)\\
&=0.7560,
\end{align*} so \mathbb{P}(H_1\mid x)=1-0.7560=0.2440. The posterior odds are


\boxed{
\frac{\mathbb{P}(H_0\mid x)}{\mathbb{P}(H_1\mid x)}
=\frac{0.7560}{0.2440}=3.0977}.

On posterior odds alone, H_0 is favoured by about 3.1:1.

Under the prior, \begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}(H_0)
&=\mathbb{P}(\mu<130)\\
&=\Phi\!\left(\frac{130-100}{15}\right)\\
&=\Phi(2)=0.97725.
\end{align*} The prior odds are therefore


\frac{\mathbb{P}(H_0)}{\mathbb{P}(H_1)}
=\frac{0.97725}{1-0.97725}
=42.9558.

Consequently \begin{align*}
\operatorname{BF}_{01}
&=\frac{\text{posterior odds for $H_0$}}
{\text{prior odds for $H_0$}}\\
&=\frac{3.0977}{42.9558}\\
&=\boxed{0.0721}.
\end{align*} Equivalently, \operatorname{BF}_{10}=1/0.0721\approx13.87: the score is about fourteen times more probable under H_1 than under H_0 after averaging within each hypothesis. The posterior nevertheless favours H_0 because the prior odds favoured it by about 43:1. The Bayes factor records the movement supplied by the data; the posterior odds also contain the starting odds.

title: An independent Gamma proposal
Exponential observations parameterised by rate
text:
Topic: Exponential families and conjugacy · more questions on this topic
Source: Book exercise from Exponential families and conjugacy ‹ Sufficiency and the posterior Exponential observations parameterised by mean ›

For X\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\theta), take \theta to be the rate, so that

p(x\mid\theta)=\theta e^{-\theta x}\mathbf{1}_{\{x\geq0\}}.

Write this model in the chapter’s a(\theta), b(x), c(\theta), T(x) form and use that form to find a conjugate prior. Then give the posterior for an iid sample x_1,\ldots,x_n.






Worked answer (click to show)





Question. For X\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\theta), take \theta to be the rate, so that

p(x\mid\theta)=\theta e^{-\theta x}\mathbf{1}_{\{x\geq0\}}.

Write this model in the chapter’s a(\theta), b(x), c(\theta), T(x) form and use that form to find a conjugate prior. Then give the posterior for an iid sample x_1,\ldots,x_n.
Solution. For one observation,

p(x\mid\theta)=\theta e^{-\theta x}\mathbf{1}_{\{x\geq0\}}
=\frac{b(x)\exp\{c(\theta)T(x)\}}{a(\theta)}

with

\boxed{
b(x)=\mathbf{1}_{\{x\geq0\}},\quad
T(x)=x,\quad
c(\theta)=-\theta,\quad
a(\theta)=\frac1\theta}.

The chapter’s generic conjugate-prior kernel is therefore \begin{align*}
p(\theta\mid\alpha,\beta)
&\propto
\frac{\exp\{c(\theta)\alpha\}}{a(\theta)^\beta}\\
&=\frac{e^{-\alpha\theta}}{(1/\theta)^\beta}\\
&=\theta^\beta e^{-\alpha\theta}.
\end{align*} For \alpha>0 and \beta>-1, this is

\theta\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\beta+1,\alpha)

in the book’s shape–rate convention.
For an iid sample let S({\boldsymbol{x}})=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i. Then \begin{align*}
p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto
\left\{\prod_{i=1}^n\theta e^{-\theta x_i}\right\}
\theta^\beta e^{-\alpha\theta}\\
&=\theta^n e^{-\theta S({\boldsymbol{x}})}
\theta^\beta e^{-\alpha\theta}\\
&=\theta^{\beta+n}
e^{-\{\alpha+S({\boldsymbol{x}})\}\theta}.
\end{align*} Thus

\boxed{\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{Gamma}\bigl(\beta+n+1,\alpha+S({\boldsymbol{x}})\bigr)}.

Equivalently, if the prior is written in the standard shape–rate form \operatorname{Gamma}(a_0,b_0), then

\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim
\operatorname{Gamma}\bigl(a_0+n,b_0+S({\boldsymbol{x}})\bigr).

title: A bivariate-normal Gibbs sampler
text:
Topic: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings · more questions on this topic
Source: Book exercise from Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings ‹ Adapt, discard, fix Metropolis–Hastings for the logit-normal posterior ›

Let {\boldsymbol{X}}=(X_1,X_2)^{\mathsf T} have a bivariate normal distribution with mean zero, unit marginal variances, and correlation \rho, so that

{\boldsymbol{X}}\sim\operatorname{N}_2\!\left(
\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\end{bmatrix},
\begin{bmatrix}1&\rho\\ \rho&1\end{bmatrix}
\right),\qquad |\rho|<1.


Derive the conditional distributions of X_1\mid X_2 and X_2\mid X_1.
Write pseudocode for a systematic-scan Gibbs sampler.
Implement it in R or Python.
From a chosen initial vector, generate 10{,}000 dependent draws for \rho=0, 0.7, and 0.97. Plot the draws and explain how \rho affects serial movement even though the stationary marginal variance remains one.







Worked answer (click to show)





Question. Let {\boldsymbol{X}}=(X_1,X_2)^{\mathsf T} have a bivariate normal distribution with mean zero, unit marginal variances, and correlation \rho, so that

{\boldsymbol{X}}\sim\operatorname{N}_2\!\left(
\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\end{bmatrix},
\begin{bmatrix}1&\rho\\ \rho&1\end{bmatrix}
\right),\qquad |\rho|<1.


Derive the conditional distributions of X_1\mid X_2 and X_2\mid X_1.
Write pseudocode for a systematic-scan Gibbs sampler.
Implement it in R or Python.
From a chosen initial vector, generate 10{,}000 dependent draws for \rho=0, 0.7, and 0.97. Plot the draws and explain how \rho affects serial movement even though the stationary marginal variance remains one.

Solution. The joint density has kernel

p(x_1,x_2)\propto
\exp\!\left[-\frac{x_1^2-2\rho x_1x_2+x_2^2}
{2(1-\rho^2)}\right].

When x_2 is held fixed, \begin{align*}
x_1^2-2\rho x_1x_2+x_2^2
&=(x_1-\rho x_2)^2-\rho^2x_2^2+x_2^2\\
&=(x_1-\rho x_2)^2+(1-\rho^2)x_2^2.
\end{align*} The final term is constant as a function of x_1, so \begin{align*}
p(x_1\mid x_2)
&\propto
\exp\!\left[-\frac{(x_1-\rho x_2)^2}{2(1-\rho^2)}\right],\\
&\boxed{X_1\mid X_2=x_2\sim\operatorname{N}(\rho x_2,1-\rho^2)}.
\end{align*} Symmetry gives

\boxed{X_2\mid X_1=x_1\sim\operatorname{N}(\rho x_1,1-\rho^2)}.

Starting from (x_1^{(0)},x_2^{(0)}), one systematic Gibbs sweep is \begin{align*}
x_1^{(t)}&\sim\operatorname{N}\!\left(\rho x_2^{(t-1)},1-\rho^2\right),\\
x_2^{(t)}&\sim\operatorname{N}\!\left(\rho x_1^{(t)},1-\rho^2\right).
\end{align*} The newest available coordinate is used in the second update.
gibbs_bvn <- function(rho, iterations = 10000, initial = c(1, 1)) {
  stopifnot(abs(rho) < 1)
  out <- matrix(NA_real_, iterations, 2,
                dimnames = list(NULL, c("x1", "x2")))
  out[1, ] <- initial
  conditional_sd <- sqrt(1 - rho^2)

  for (t in 2:iterations) {
    out[t, 1] <- rnorm(1, rho * out[t - 1, 2], conditional_sd)
    out[t, 2] <- rnorm(1, rho * out[t, 1], conditional_sd)
  }
  out
}

set.seed(3500)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
for (rho in c(0, 0.7, 0.97)) {
  z <- gibbs_bvn(rho)
  plot(z, pch = 20, cex = 0.35,
       xlab = expression(x[1]), ylab = expression(x[2]),
       main = bquote(rho == .(rho)))
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
When \rho=0, each conditional is \operatorname{N}(0,1) and a sweep produces a new independent pair. When \rho=0.97, the conditional variance is

1-0.97^2=1-0.9409=0.0591,

far smaller than the marginal variance one. The chain therefore moves in small, strongly correlated steps along the narrow diagonal ellipse. The stationary marginal distributions remain \operatorname{N}(0,1); what deteriorates is the effective information per iteration.

title: Hierarchical Bayes
text:
Part of Bayesian statistics · 9 questions on this topic · What links here
This chapter develops Bayesian models for related groups. The central idea is not conjugacy: a hierarchy can be conjugate or nonconjugate. Its defining feature is that group-specific parameters are connected through a shared population distribution, allowing partial pooling while preserving genuine between-group variation.

title: Hierarchical Bayes
text:
Why hierarchical Bayes?

Definition 1 (Hierarchical Bayesian model) Hierarchical Bayes is ordinary Bayes for data that arrive in related groups. Each group is allowed to have its own parameter, but those group parameters are modelled as draws from a common population distribution. This structure is useful whenever complete equality between groups is implausible, yet treating them as unrelated would discard real information.
Article: Hierarchical Bayesian model →


From one tutorial class to many
For one tutorial class, let Y_i be the mark of student i and let \theta be the class’s unknown true mean. With a known within-class variance \sigma^2, an ordinary Bayesian model is

Y_i\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{N}(\theta,\sigma^2),
\qquad
\theta\sim\operatorname{N}(\mu_0,\tau_0^2).

The sampling distribution describes variation between students, whereas the prior describes uncertainty about the class mean. Bayes’ rule combines the two sources of information.
Now suppose there are J tutorial classes. Give class j its own mean \theta_j: 
Y_{ij}\mid\theta_j,\sigma^2
\sim\operatorname{N}(\theta_j,\sigma^2),
\qquad i=1,\ldots,n_j,\qquad j=1,\ldots,J.
\qquad(1) Estimating every \theta_j separately ignores that all the classes belong to the same course. A second level connects them: 
\theta_j\mid\mu,\tau^2
\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{N}(\mu,\tau^2),
\qquad j=1,\ldots,J.
\qquad(2) Here \mu is the overall course mean and \tau^2 measures genuine between-class variation. The hierarchy is

(\mu,\tau^2)\longrightarrow\theta_j\longrightarrow Y_{ij}.

The first arrow describes variation between class means; the second describes variation between students within a class. Confusing these two levels would attribute sampling noise among students to real differences among classes.

Definition 2 (Hyperparameter) For a fully Bayesian analysis, the population-level quantities are also unknown and receive priors, for example

\mu\sim\operatorname{N}(m_0,s_0^2),
\qquad
\tau^2\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b).

The quantities controlling the distribution of the \theta_j’s are called hyperparameters, or higher-level parameters. Once priors are assigned to them, their uncertainty is propagated into every class-specific posterior.
Article: Hyperparameter →



Complete pooling, no pooling, and partial pooling
The modelling choice can be organised into three cases.







Approach
Assumption and consequence




Complete pooling
Set \theta_1=\cdots=\theta_J=\theta and analyse all students as though every class has exactly the same mean.


No pooling
Estimate each \theta_j from class j alone; information from the other classes is discarded.


Partial pooling
Retain distinct \theta_j’s but connect them through the shared distribution in Equation 2.



Hierarchical Bayes produces partial pooling. A large class can speak mostly for itself. A small class has a noisy sample mean, so its estimate is pulled more strongly toward the population centre. This movement is called shrinkage or borrowing strength.


Where the shrinkage weight comes from
Condition for the moment on known \mu, \tau^2, and \sigma^2. The sample mean in class j satisfies

\overline Y_j\mid\theta_j
\sim\operatorname{N}\!\left(\theta_j,\frac{\sigma^2}{n_j}\right).

After observing \overline y_j, multiply its likelihood by the second-level prior: \begin{align*}
p(\theta_j\mid\overline y_j,\mu,\tau^2,\sigma^2)
&\propto
\exp\!\left\{-\frac{n_j}{2\sigma^2}
       (\overline y_j-\theta_j)^2\right\}
\exp\!\left\{-\frac{1}{2\tau^2}
       (\theta_j-\mu)^2\right\}\\
&=\exp\!\left\{-\frac12\left[
    \frac{n_j}{\sigma^2}(\theta_j^2-2\overline y_j\theta_j
       +\overline y_j^2)
   +\frac1{\tau^2}(\theta_j^2-2\mu\theta_j+\mu^2)
   \right]\right\}\\
&\propto\exp\!\left\{-\frac12\left[
   \left(\frac{n_j}{\sigma^2}+\frac1{\tau^2}\right)\theta_j^2
   -2\left(\frac{n_j\overline y_j}{\sigma^2}
            +\frac\mu{\tau^2}\right)\theta_j
   \right]\right\}.
\end{align*} Set

A_j=\frac{n_j}{\sigma^2}+\frac1{\tau^2},
\qquad
B_j=\frac{n_j\overline y_j}{\sigma^2}+\frac\mu{\tau^2}.

Completing the square gives \begin{align*}
A_j\theta_j^2-2B_j\theta_j
&=A_j\left(\theta_j^2-2\frac{B_j}{A_j}\theta_j\right)\\
&=A_j\left[
   \left(\theta_j-\frac{B_j}{A_j}\right)^2
   -\left(\frac{B_j}{A_j}\right)^2
   \right].
\end{align*}

Proposition 1 (Normal hierarchical shrinkage) The final term is constant in \theta_j. The remaining kernel is normal, so 
\theta_j\mid\overline y_j,\mu,\tau^2,\sigma^2
\sim\operatorname{N}\!\left(
   \frac{B_j}{A_j},\frac1{A_j}\right).
\qquad(3) Its variance is \begin{align*}
\frac1{A_j}
&=\frac1{n_j/\sigma^2+1/\tau^2}\\
&=\frac{\sigma^2\tau^2}{\sigma^2+n_j\tau^2},
\end{align*} and its mean can be rearranged without omitting any terms: \begin{align*}
\frac{B_j}{A_j}
&=\frac{n_j\overline y_j/\sigma^2+\mu/\tau^2}
         {n_j/\sigma^2+1/\tau^2}\\
&=\frac{n_j\tau^2\overline y_j+\sigma^2\mu}
         {\sigma^2+n_j\tau^2}\\
&=\frac{n_j\tau^2}{\sigma^2+n_j\tau^2}\overline y_j
   +\frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2+n_j\tau^2}\mu\\
&=w_j\overline y_j+(1-w_j)\mu,
\end{align*} where 
w_j=\frac{n_j\tau^2}{\sigma^2+n_j\tau^2},
\qquad
1-w_j=\frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2+n_j\tau^2}.
\qquad(4) Thus

\mathbb{E}(\theta_j\mid\overline y_j,\mu,\tau^2,\sigma^2)
=w_j\overline y_j+(1-w_j)\mu.

Article: Normal hierarchical shrinkage →

If n_j is large, then w_j is close to one and class j mainly trusts its own data. If n_j is small, then w_j is smaller and the estimate moves toward \mu. If the class means are genuinely heterogeneous, then \tau^2 is large and the model shrinks less. In a full Bayesian fit, the data from all classes learn \mu and \tau^2, so the amount of sharing is itself uncertain rather than fixed in advance.

Example 1 (Large and small tutorial classes) Suppose the overall mean is \mu=70, the within-class standard deviation is \sigma=10, and the between-class standard deviation is \tau=5. Class A has 100 students and \overline y_A=75, while Class B has only two students and \overline y_B=95.
Question. Compute the two shrinkage weights and posterior means, treating \mu, \sigma^2, and \tau^2 as fixed, and explain why the more extreme sample mean need not produce the more extreme posterior mean.
Solution. For Class A, \begin{align*}
w_A&=\frac{100(25)}{100+100(25)}=\frac{25}{26}\approx0.962,\\
\mathbb{E}(\theta_A\mid\overline y_A,\mu,\tau^2,\sigma^2)
&=\frac{25}{26}(75)+\frac1{26}(70)\approx74.81.
\end{align*} For Class B, \begin{align*}
w_B&=\frac{2(25)}{100+2(25)}=\frac13,\\
\mathbb{E}(\theta_B\mid\overline y_B,\mu,\tau^2,\sigma^2)
&=\frac13(95)+\frac23(70)\approx78.33.
\end{align*} The extreme average from the small class is not ignored, but it is recognised as much less precise.







Key idea



Each group gets its own parameter, while the group parameters come from a shared population distribution. Information does not pass directly from one class to another. Every class helps learn the common population quantities, and those quantities then influence every group-specific posterior. Groups therefore learn from their own data while borrowing strength from the others.


“Borrowing strength” can sound more mysterious than it is. Class A does not hand observations directly to Class B. Both classes help estimate the shared population distribution, and that distribution changes what is plausible for each class. The gain is largest for small groups, but the same mechanism can over-shrink genuinely unusual groups if the population model is too rigid. Partial pooling is powerful because it compromises; the adequacy of that compromise still has to be checked.

title: Hierarchical Bayes
section: A first hierarchy: TG5 cattle studies
text:
A first hierarchy: TG5 cattle studies
Genetics is among the most statistically sophisticated applied fields, but that sophistication is often hidden behind software. A scientist may be using a recently developed Monte Carlo method because it has appeared in a software package, without knowing how the method works. Someone nevertheless has to establish that the computation and its assumptions are sound. That is a fairly concrete use for statistical expertise. 1
The practical difficulty begins even earlier. A proper meta-analysis tries to find every relevant study, including studies with small or null effects that were never published. In this case much of the material was unpublished, and the data were obtainable largely because a company already had commercial relationships with the breeders. The available records were study summaries rather than the complete farm-level records. Commercial questions and scientific questions were not always the same. Getting the data is not as easy as it sounds.

Example 2 (TG5 cattle hierarchy) A cattle-genetics meta-analysis illustrates hierarchical Bayes. The search was not exhaustive, but it recovered 14 independent studies, many of them unpublished, which produced 19 standardised estimates of a TG5 genotype effect on beef marbling. The studies covered four breed groups and four marbling measurements, so treating every estimate as an exchangeable replicate would erase scientifically meaningful structure.
The original study-level analyses compared the CC and TT genotypes with CT, then divided each contrast by its residual standard deviation. A schematic version of the hierarchy is \begin{align*}
y_{ij}\mid\delta_i,w_{ij}
&\sim\operatorname{N}(\delta_i,w_{ij}^{-1}),\\
\delta_i\mid\mu_{b(i)},\tau_{\mathrm{study}}
&\sim\operatorname{N}(\mu_{b(i)},\tau_{\mathrm{study}}^{-1}),\\
\mu_b\mid\mu_0,\tau_{\mathrm{breed}}
&\sim\operatorname{N}(\mu_0,\tau_{\mathrm{breed}}^{-1}),\\
\mu_0&\sim\operatorname{N}(0,\xi^2),
\qquad \xi^2\text{ large}.
\end{align*} Here w_{ij} records the within-study information, \delta_i is a study effect, and \mu_b is a breed-group effect. Precision parameters were given diffuse scaled inverse-\chi^2-type priors in the applied analysis. The diagrammatic flow is

\text{overall effect}\longrightarrow
\text{breed effect}\longrightarrow
\text{study effect}\longrightarrow
\text{observed contrast}.

The hierarchy performs partial pooling at more than one level. The reported posterior for TT minus CC lay mostly above zero, with a smaller shift for one T copy, but the important methodological point is that every conclusion and every uncertainty interval came from one coherent multilevel fit. The example connects Bayesian random parameters to mixed models. The analysis was fitted in WinBUGS using a Gibbs sampler; the “GS” in the software name stands for Gibbs sampling.

title: Hierarchical Bayes
text:
Rat tumours: why a hierarchy?

Example 3 (Rat-tumour hierarchy) Tumour rates in female F344 rats supply a second hierarchical example. In a current control study, y=4 of n=14 rats developed one or more tumours over two years.2 A one-study model is

Y\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Bin}(14,\theta),
\qquad
\theta\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta),

giving

\theta\mid Y=4
\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+4,\beta+10).

The question is how to choose (\alpha,\beta) when 70 earlier control studies are available.
Let study j contribute y_j tumour-bearing rats from n_j animals. The hierarchical model is 
Y_j\mid\theta_j,n_j\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n_j,\theta_j),
\qquad
\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta
\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta),
\quad j=1,\ldots,J.
\qquad(5) Each study has its own rate, but all study rates are drawn from a common population distribution.

Good applied statistics begins before the algebra. Downloading a data set without understanding why the experiment was conducted, how an outcome was defined, or which sources of variation changed between studies is not enough. The hierarchy should represent the scientific design we actually have, not a generic stack of random effects added after the fact. The version of the rat example used here follows the account in Gelman’s book.3

title: Hierarchical Bayes
text:
Exchangeability

Definition 3 (Exchangeability) The parameters \theta_1,\ldots,\theta_J are exchangeable if their joint density is invariant to every permutation \pi:

p(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_J)
=p(\theta_{\pi(1)},\ldots,\theta_{\pi(J)}).

Conditional iid sampling from a common Beta distribution implies exchangeability:

p({\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mid\alpha,\beta)
=\prod_{j=1}^Jp(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta).

The scientific claim is that study labels do not encode systematic differences in strain, laboratory, protocol, calendar time, or tumour definition. The sample sizes n_j may differ; exchangeability requires the latent rates not to be systematically related to those sizes.
Article: Exchangeability →

Exchangeability is a judgement made before seeing the outcomes, not permission to ignore everything known about the groups. If laboratory, breed, protocol, or calendar time plausibly changes the rates, that information should enter the hierarchy rather than be hidden by a common label. We assume exchangeability when the remaining labels carry no reason for a systematic ordering; learning more about the data can reveal that a richer grouping is needed.

title: Hierarchical Bayes
text:
Empirical hyperparameters by moment matching

Definition 4 (Empirical Bayes) An empirical Bayes analysis estimates prior or population-level hyperparameters from data and then treats those estimates as fixed in a lower-level Bayesian update. A full Bayesian analysis instead assigns the hyperparameters a prior and propagates their posterior uncertainty.
Article: Empirical Bayes →

The observed historical proportions \widehat\theta_j=y_j/n_j had empirical mean m=0.136 and standard deviation s=0.103. A \operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta) variable has

m=\frac\alpha{\alpha+\beta},
\qquad
s^2=\frac{\alpha\beta}
{(\alpha+\beta)^2(\alpha+\beta+1)}.

Let t=\alpha+\beta. Since \alpha=mt and \beta=(1-m)t, \begin{align*}
s^2
&=\frac{(mt)((1-m)t)}{t^2(t+1)}\\
&=\frac{m(1-m)}{t+1}.
\end{align*} Solving, \begin{align*}
s^2(t+1)&=m(1-m),\\
t+1&=\frac{m(1-m)}{s^2},\\
t&=\frac{m(1-m)}{s^2}-1,\\
\alpha&=mt,
\qquad
\beta=(1-m)t.
\end{align*} Substituting m=0.136 and s=0.103 gives approximately

(\alpha,\beta)\approx(1.37,8.7).

The values (1.370,8.693) differ slightly from that approximation; the difference is attributable to rounding in the reported historical standard deviation.
Using these values as if known gives the current-study posterior

\theta_{\mathrm{current}}\mid y=4,n=14
\sim\operatorname{Beta}(5.370,18.693),

with mean

\frac{5.370}{5.370+18.693}
\approx0.223.

This lies between the historical mean 0.136 and the current proportion 4/14\approx0.286. That movement is partial pooling.
The plug-in calculation has three limitations:

the empirical variance of y_j/n_j contains both real between-study variation and binomial sampling variation;
treating estimated (\alpha,\beta) as known omits hyperparameter uncertainty; and
historical and current studies may not be exchangeable.

There are two related but distinct reuse issues. For the 70 historical studies, empirical Bayes estimates (\alpha,\beta) from the same y_j values whose study rates are then re-estimated, so treating the fitted hyperparameters as fixed understates uncertainty. Applying that historical fit to a separate current 4/14 study does not literally reuse the current data, but it still ignores uncertainty in the population distribution. Full Bayes repairs both calculations by propagating the posterior uncertainty in (\alpha,\beta).
Empirical Bayes is often a sensible first analysis, but its apparent precision can be deceptive. Once estimated hyperparameters are treated as fixed, the lower-level posterior forgets that the population distribution was itself learned from finite data. A full Bayesian model restores that uncertainty. The trade-off is computational rather than philosophical: we gain a coherent uncertainty calculation at the cost of a larger joint posterior.

title: Hierarchical Bayes
Hierarchical Bayes
Hierarchical Bayes
text:
Hyperprior and transformations
One proper choice is independent exponential hyperpriors,

\alpha\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda),
\qquad
\beta\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda),
\qquad
\alpha\perp\beta.

The choice \lambda=1 is a plain starting point. Its implications are clearer after writing

u=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta},
\qquad t=\alpha+\beta,
\qquad
\alpha=ut,
\qquad \beta=(1-u)t.

Because

\left|\frac{\partial(\alpha,\beta)}{\partial(u,t)}\right|=t,

the transformed density is \begin{align*}
p(u,t)
&=\lambda^2e^{-\lambda t}t\\
&=\mathbf{1}\{0<u<1\}
   \frac{\lambda^2}{\Gamma(2)}t^{2-1}e^{-\lambda t}.
\end{align*} Thus u\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1), t\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(2,\lambda), and u\perp t. The prior is proper and its rate has an interpretable effect: \mathbb{E}(t)=2/\lambda. Calling a smaller rate “more diffuse” is incomplete, because it also favours larger total concentration and therefore more tightly clustered study rates conditional on u.
Gelman’s alternative improper prior is 
p(\alpha,\beta)\propto(\alpha+\beta)^{-5/2},
\qquad \alpha,\beta>0.
\qquad(9) It can be motivated by a uniform prior on

u=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta},
\qquad
v=\frac1{\sqrt{\alpha+\beta}}.

Let t=\alpha+\beta. The forward derivatives are

\frac{\partial u}{\partial\alpha}=\frac\beta{t^2},
\quad
\frac{\partial u}{\partial\beta}=-\frac\alpha{t^2},
\quad
\frac{\partial v}{\partial\alpha}
=\frac{\partial v}{\partial\beta}
=-\frac12t^{-3/2}.

Hence \begin{align*}
\left|\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(\alpha,\beta)}\right|
&=\left|
\frac\beta{t^2}\left(-\frac12t^{-3/2}\right)
-\left(-\frac\alpha{t^2}\right)
  \left(-\frac12t^{-3/2}\right)
\right|\\
&=\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2t^{7/2}}\\
&=\frac12t^{-5/2}.
\end{align*} A constant density in (u,v) therefore transforms to p(\alpha,\beta)\propto t^{-5/2}, as claimed. Because the prior is improper, posterior propriety must be established for the data configuration being analysed.
The transformation is derived here. It does not make an improper prior uniquely noninformative, and it does not remove the need to state the domain.

Remark 1 (Uniformity depends on a domain). The Jacobian calculation is local; calling the prior “uniform in (u,v)” also requires a stated domain. Over an unbounded or boundary-touching domain the density is improper, so the transformed expression is a modelling choice, not an automatic noninformative prior.
Article: Uniformity depends on a domain →

The grid calculation uses

z_1=\log(\alpha/\beta),
\qquad
z_2=\log(\alpha+\beta).

Let t=e^{z_2} and r=e^{z_1}. Solving \alpha/\beta=r and \alpha+\beta=t gives 
\alpha=t\frac{r}{1+r},
\qquad
\beta=t\frac1{1+r}.
\qquad(10) Equivalently, let m=r/(1+r). The Jacobians are

\left|\frac{\partial(\alpha,\beta)}{\partial(m,t)}\right|=t,
\qquad
\left|\frac{\partial(m,t)}{\partial(z_1,z_2)}\right|
=m(1-m)t.

Therefore \begin{align*}
\left|\frac{\partial(\alpha,\beta)}
              {\partial(z_1,z_2)}\right|
&=t^2m(1-m)\\
&=(tm)(t(1-m))\\
&=\alpha\beta.
\end{align*} Under Equation 9, the transformed prior is therefore 
p(z_1,z_2)
\propto \alpha\beta(\alpha+\beta)^{-5/2},
\qquad(11) where (\alpha,\beta) are obtained from Equation 10.

title: Hierarchical Bayes
text:
Grid approximation and posterior simulation
The calculation begins with a rectangular grid over (z_1,z_2), evaluates the unnormalised transformed hyperposterior at each cell, and expands the grid if substantial mass lies against an edge. The first trial used approximately

z_1\in[-2.5,-1],
\qquad
z_2\in[1.5,3],

and clipped part of the high-density region. An illustrative adjusted range was approximately

z_1\in[-2.35,0.3],
\qquad
z_2\in[1,5].

The grid method is deliberately visible. Modern MCMC software can hide much of this computation, but it still faces the same posterior geometry. A grid forces us to inspect the transformed scale, the Jacobian, the region carrying mass, and whether density is being clipped at a boundary. In two dimensions that transparency is often worth more than a more sophisticated black box.

Definition 5 (Grid Monte Carlo approximation) Let w_{ab} be the unnormalised hyperposterior value at grid cell (a,b), including the Jacobian \alpha\beta. The discrete approximation is

\widehat p_{ab}=\frac{w_{ab}}{\sum_{r,s}w_{rs}}.

Sampling from the approximate full posterior proceeds as follows.

Flatten the grid weights into a one-dimensional list, form cumulative probabilities, draw U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1), and select the first cell whose cumulative probability exceeds U. Equivalently, draw a grid cell (Z_1,Z_2) with probabilities \widehat p_{ab}. Optionally add independent uniform jitter within the selected cell.
Transform (Z_1,Z_2) to (\alpha,\beta) using Equation 10.
For each study, draw independently


  \theta_j\sim\operatorname{Beta}(y_j+\alpha,n_j-y_j+\beta)

using Equation 7.

Repeat to obtain (\alpha^{(l)},\beta^{(l)},{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(l)}), l=1,\ldots,L.

These grid-cell draws are independent; this is Monte Carlo from a piecewise-constant approximation, not Markov-chain Monte Carlo. A 100\times100 grid has 10^4 cells and remains practical because only two hyperparameters are integrated numerically. A comparable grid over all J+2 unknowns would be impossible.
Article: Grid Monte Carlo approximation →

Here is the corresponding calculation. The vectors y and n_trials contain the tumour counts y_j and sample sizes n_j for the 71 studies. The logarithmic calculation is important: subtracting the largest log weight before exponentiating prevents numerical underflow without changing the normalised probabilities.
z <- expand.grid(
  z1 = seq(-2.35, 0.30, length.out = 100),
  z2 = seq( 1.00, 5.00, length.out = 100)
)
total <- exp(z$z2)
mean_rate <- plogis(z$z1)
z$alpha <- total * mean_rate
z$beta  <- total * (1 - mean_rate)

log_w <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(z)), function(k) {
  a <- z$alpha[k]
  b <- z$beta[k]
  -2.5 * log(a + b) +
    sum(lbeta(y + a, n_trials - y + b) - lbeta(a, b)) +
    log(a) + log(b)              # Jacobian alpha * beta
}, numeric(1))

prob <- exp(log_w - max(log_w))
prob <- prob / sum(prob)

set.seed(3500)
M <- 1000L
cell <- sample.int(nrow(z), M, replace = TRUE, prob = prob)
alpha <- z$alpha[cell]
beta  <- z$beta[cell]
theta <- vapply(seq_along(y), function(j) {
  rbeta(M, y[j] + alpha, n_trials[j] - y[j] + beta)
}, numeric(M))
Each row of theta is one draw of all 71 study rates. Summarising a column marginalises (\alpha,\beta) automatically because the corresponding hyperparameter draws are simply not retained in that summary. Before using the result, plot the grid weights and check that appreciable mass does not meet an edge; a grid whose boundary cuts through the density fails precisely that check.






Figure 1: Contours of the rat-tumour hyperposterior in the transformed (z_1,z_2) coordinates, including the Jacobian \alpha\beta. The dashed outline marks a grid whose boundary cuts through the density. Its upper edge cuts through appreciable density, so enlarging the numerical domain is part of the calculation rather than a plotting preference. The gold point is the largest evaluated grid value on the expanded domain.



For a posterior expectation,

\mathbb{E}(\alpha\mid{\boldsymbol{y}})
\approx\frac1L\sum_{l=1}^L\alpha^{(l)}.

If the inferential target is only {\boldsymbol{\theta}}, marginalise the hyperparameters by ignoring their sampled coordinates and summarising {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(1)},\ldots,{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(L)}. This is Monte Carlo marginalisation, not a claim that hyperparameter uncertainty is absent.
Study-specific posterior medians and 95\% intervals, ordered by the raw rates y_j/n_j, do not follow the 45-degree line: small and noisy studies move toward the population centre. This is shrinkage, also called borrowing strength. No observation is literally passed from one study to another. All studies help estimate the shared population quantities, and those quantities then influence every study-specific posterior. The model does not force the rates to be equal; the amount of movement is learned from the between-study spread and each study’s sample size.
Compared with plugging in one estimate of (\alpha,\beta), full Bayes usually widens the marginal intervals for \theta_j because it adds the variance due to hyperparameter uncertainty. Omitting that variance component makes the intervals over-precise.






Key idea



The hierarchy shares information without forcing all studies to have the same rate. Full Bayes propagates uncertainty in the population of rates into every study-specific posterior. The grid sampler works because only two hyperparameters require numerical integration; in higher dimensions one would normally return to Gibbs or Metropolis–Hastings.








Figure 2: Raw rates and marginal posterior medians under the full grid approximation. Segments show movement from the no-shrinkage line; the current 4/14 study is red and point size records n_j.

title: Bayesian hypotheses and model comparison

title: Bayesian hypotheses and model comparison
text:
Probability statements and decisions

Definition 1 (Posterior hypothesis probability) Suppose a parameter space \Omega is partitioned into regions \Omega_0 and \Omega_1. The posterior hypothesis probabilities are \begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}(H_0\mid x)
&=\mathbb{P}(\theta\in\Omega_0\mid x)
=\int_{\Omega_0}p(\theta\mid x)\,\mathrm{d}\theta,\\
\mathbb{P}(H_1\mid x)
&=\mathbb{P}(\theta\in\Omega_1\mid x)
=\int_{\Omega_1}p(\theta\mid x)\,\mathrm{d}\theta.
\end{align*} If the two regions exhaust the support, the probabilities sum to one.
Article: Posterior hypothesis probability →


Proposition 1 (Bayes action for two hypotheses) These probabilities do not by themselves define an action. If choosing action a_0 when H_1 is true costs L_{01} and choosing a_1 when H_0 is true costs L_{10}, the posterior expected losses are

\rho(a_0\mid x)=L_{01}\mathbb{P}(H_1\mid x),
\qquad
\rho(a_1\mid x)=L_{10}\mathbb{P}(H_0\mid x).

Choose a_0 when \begin{align*}
L_{01}\mathbb{P}(H_1\mid x)
&<L_{10}\mathbb{P}(H_0\mid x)\\
\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\frac{\mathbb{P}(H_0\mid x)}{\mathbb{P}(H_1\mid x)}
&>\frac{L_{01}}{L_{10}}.
\end{align*} Equal losses reduce the threshold to one. This separates the probability calculation from the decision rule.
Article: Bayes action for two hypotheses →

The Bayesian calculation need not force an all-or-nothing verdict. A useful practice is to report the posterior support for each hypothesis and to let the action depend on the real consequences of being wrong. If a decision is compulsory, losses provide the threshold. Reporting evidence and choosing an action are related tasks, but they are not the same task. This is also why Bayesians are often less enthusiastic about compulsory model selection than about reporting posterior model probabilities.1
In frequentist design, type-I and type-II error rates \alpha and \beta are properties of repeated use of a test. Values such as 0.05 and 0.20 are planning choices, not scientific constants, and sample-size calculations also require an effect size worth detecting.

title: Bayesian hypotheses and model comparison
text:
Poisson imperfect-fruit example

Example 1 (Imperfect-fruit decision) Let X_i be the number of imperfect pieces in box i, with about 100 pieces per box. “Imperfect” must be defined before the data are collected so that producer and analyst classify fruit in the same way. The model is

X_i\mid\theta\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Poisson}(\theta),
\qquad
H_0:\theta\leq10,
\quad H_1:\theta>10.

For the observed sample, n=20 and S=\sum_i x_i=177; the stated prior is \theta\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(12,1) in shape–rate form.
Question. Find the posterior distribution, the posterior probabilities and odds for H_0 and H_1, and an equal-tailed 95\% credible interval. Explain why the interval may cross 10 even when most posterior mass lies below it.
Solution. Because the posterior for \theta is continuous,

\mathbb{P}(\theta=10\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=0.

Consequently it makes no numerical difference whether equality is assigned to H_0 or H_1. This is a statement about the continuous parameter, even though the observed fruit counts are discrete.
For n boxes and S=\sum_i x_i, the likelihood is 
\begin{aligned}
p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta)
&=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{e^{-\theta}\theta^{x_i}}{x_i!}\\
&=\left(\prod_{i=1}^n\frac1{x_i!}\right)
   e^{-n\theta}\theta^{\sum_i x_i}\\
&\propto e^{-n\theta}\theta^S.
\end{aligned}
\qquad(1) The working total is S=177 for n=20.
The stated prior is \theta\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(12,1) in the standard shape–rate convention, so

p(\theta)=\frac1{\Gamma(12)}\theta^{12-1}e^{-\theta}
\propto\theta^{11}e^{-\theta}.

Multiplying by the likelihood gives \begin{align*}
p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto
\theta^S e^{-n\theta}\theta^{11}e^{-\theta}\\
&=\theta^{S+11}e^{-(n+1)\theta}\\
&=\theta^{189-1}e^{-21\theta}.
\end{align*} Therefore the internally consistent shape–rate update is 
\boxed{\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(189,21)}.
\qquad(2) Its posterior mean is

\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{189}{21}=9.

The MLE is S/n=177/20=8.85. Although the prior mean 12 lies above the boundary 10, the data move the posterior centre below it.
Let \gamma(a,z)=\int_0^zt^{a-1}e^{-t}\,\mathrm{d} t be the lower incomplete Gamma function. If T\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a,b), then

\mathbb{P}(T\leq t)=\frac{\gamma(a,bt)}{\Gamma(a)}.

Consequently, \begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}(H_0\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=\mathbb{P}(\theta\leq10\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\\
&=\frac{\gamma(189,21\cdot10)}{\Gamma(189)}\\
&=0.93298381,\\
\mathbb{P}(H_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})&=1-0.93298381=0.06701619.
\end{align*} The posterior odds are

\frac{\mathbb{P}(H_0\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})}{\mathbb{P}(H_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})}
=\frac{0.93298381}{0.06701619}
\approx13.92.

The equal-tailed 95\% credible interval is approximately (7.76,10.33). It crosses 10, while 93.3\% of posterior mass lies at or below 10. These are different summaries: interval inclusion does not produce a general accept/reject rule for an interval hypothesis.






Figure 1: The fruit posterior \operatorname{Gamma}(189,21), with the region \theta\leq10 shaded. The two summaries disagree in appearance only. The equal-tailed interval must leave 2.5\% in each tail, so its upper endpoint is pushed past 10; the shaded area answers a different question and puts 93.3\% of the mass at or below the boundary. Reading the crossing as a rejection substitutes one summary for the other.









Parameterisation check



A convention check uses the other Gamma convention. Writing a prior kernel p(\theta)\propto\theta^\alpha e^{-\beta\theta} with \alpha=12 describes \operatorname{Gamma}(13,1), not the stated \operatorname{Gamma}(12,1). That alternative gives \theta\mid x\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(190,21), posterior mean 190/21\approx9.05, \mathbb{P}(\theta\leq10\mid x)=0.92320087, odds 12.02, and interval (7.81,10.38). The main calculation above follows the stated shape–rate prior; the alternative is retained here so that neither that result nor the convention error is hidden.

title: Bayesian hypotheses and model comparison
text:
Posterior odds and Bayes factors

Theorem 1 (Posterior-odds factorisation) For two models M_1 and M_2, Bayes’ rule gives

\mathbb{P}(M_j\mid x)
=\frac{p(x\mid M_j)\mathbb{P}(M_j)}{p(x)}.

Taking the ratio cancels the common evidence p(x): 
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathbb{P}(M_1\mid x)}{\mathbb{P}(M_2\mid x)}
&=\frac{p(x\mid M_1)\mathbb{P}(M_1)/p(x)}
         {p(x\mid M_2)\mathbb{P}(M_2)/p(x)}\\
&=\underbrace{\frac{p(x\mid M_1)}{p(x\mid M_2)}}_{
      \operatorname{BF}_{12}}
   \underbrace{\frac{\mathbb{P}(M_1)}{\mathbb{P}(M_2)}}_{
      \text{prior odds}}.
\end{aligned}
\qquad(3)
Article: Posterior-odds factorisation →


Definition 2 (Marginal likelihood and Bayes factor) The marginal likelihood in model M_j is 
p(x\mid M_j)
=\int p(x\mid\theta_j,M_j)
       p(\theta_j\mid M_j)\,\mathrm{d}\theta_j.
\qquad(4) It averages the likelihood over the parameter prior; it does not evaluate the likelihood at a fitted maximum. The Bayes factor comparing M_1 with M_2 is \operatorname{BF}_{12}=p(x\mid M_1)/p(x\mid M_2).
Article: Marginal likelihood and Bayes factor →

A Bayes factor compares whole models, not merely their best-fitting parameter values. The marginal likelihood averages over each model’s prior parameter space, so diffuse priors can spread support across many poor explanations and change the comparison. Equal prior model probabilities are a transparent modelling choice, not a mathematical requirement. Model probabilities, parameter priors, and the set of models under consideration must all be stated before a numerical ratio can be interpreted responsibly.

Remark 1 (A hypothesis region is not a separate model). Two constructions must not be confused:

If H_0 and H_1 are regions of one parameter space, compute one posterior and integrate it over the regions.
If M_1 and M_2 have different dimensions or parameterisations, each model needs its own parameter prior and marginal likelihood. A continuous prior on the larger space assigns probability zero to a lower-dimensional surface.

The fruit example is the first construction. Independence in the advertising table is the second.
Article: A hypothesis region is not a separate model →

title: Bayesian hypotheses and model comparison
section: Bayes factor for independence in the 2\times3 table
text:
Bayes factor for independence in the 2\times3 table
Let M_1 be the unrestricted six-cell multinomial and M_2 impose independence of gender and response. We assign equal model probabilities, so the prior odds are one. This is a stated modelling choice, not an automatic default.

Unrestricted model M_1
Under

{\boldsymbol{p}}\mid M_1\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(1,1,1,1,1,1),

the prior density is

\frac{\Gamma(6)}{\Gamma(1)^6}=120.

The fact that a uniform density equals 120 rather than 1 reflects the volume of the five-dimensional simplex.
Let C=501!/\prod_{k=1}^6x_k! be the multinomial coefficient. Then 
\begin{aligned}
p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_1)
&=\int C\prod_{k=1}^6p_k^{x_k}\,120\,\mathrm{d}{\boldsymbol{p}}\\
&=120C\,B(x_1+1,\ldots,x_6+1)\\
&=120\frac{501!}{\prod_kx_k!}
   \frac{\prod_k\Gamma(x_k+1)}{\Gamma(501+6)}\\
&=120\frac{501!}{\prod_kx_k!}
   \frac{\prod_kx_k!}{\Gamma(507)}\\
&=\frac{501!\Gamma(6)}{\Gamma(507)}\\
&=\binom{506}{5}^{-1}\\
&=3.690091\times10^{-12}.
\end{aligned}
\qquad(5) The cell factorials cancel, so this prior predictive probability is the same for every six-cell count vector with total 501.


Independence model M_2
Write

p_{ij}=r_i c_j,
\qquad r_1+r_2=1,
\qquad c_1+c_2+c_3=1.

Use independent uniform priors

(r_1,r_2)\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(1,1),
\qquad
(c_1,c_2,c_3)\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(1,1,1).

Their joint density is

\frac{\Gamma(2)}{\Gamma(1)^2}
\frac{\Gamma(3)}{\Gamma(1)^3}=1\cdot2=2.

Substituting p_{ij}=r_ic_j into the cell likelihood and grouping row and column exponents gives \begin{align*}
\prod_{i=1}^2\prod_{j=1}^3p_{ij}^{x_{ij}}
&=\prod_{i,j}(r_ic_j)^{x_{ij}}\\
&=\prod_i r_i^{\sum_jx_{ij}}
   \prod_j c_j^{\sum_ix_{ij}}\\
&=r_1^{257}r_2^{244}
   c_1^{146}c_2^{95}c_3^{260}.
\end{align*} The marginal likelihood separates into two Dirichlet integrals: 
\begin{aligned}
p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_2)
&=2C
   \int r_1^{257}r_2^{244}\,\mathrm{d}{\boldsymbol{r}}
   \int c_1^{146}c_2^{95}c_3^{260}\,\mathrm{d}{\boldsymbol{c}}\\
&=2C\,B(258,245)B(147,96,261)\\
&=9.212201\times10^{-15}.
\end{aligned}
\qquad(6)
The Bayes factor is therefore \begin{align*}
\operatorname{BF}_{12}
&=\frac{3.690091\times10^{-12}}
         {9.212201\times10^{-15}}\\
&=400.57.
\end{align*} With equal prior odds, the posterior odds are 400.57:1, giving

\mathbb{P}(M_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\frac{400.57}{1+400.57}\approx0.9975,
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(M_2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\approx0.0025.

Under the specified models and priors, the table is strong evidence that response depends on gender.
A frequentist likelihood-ratio or Pearson \chi^2 analysis of the same table would probably reach the same qualitative conclusion by different workings. A frequentist comparison is not carried out here, so this is calibration, not a claim that the two inferential statements or their assumptions are identical.
The departure is visible in the raw rates:

\frac{147}{257}\approx0.572,
\qquad
\frac{113}{244}\approx0.463.

Under independence, the expected male-negative count based on observed margins is

\frac{257\cdot146}{501}\approx74.9,

compared with 53 observed.
Bayes factors automatically average over unused parameter space, creating a complexity penalty. They are also sensitive to parameter priors because Equation 4 averages over the whole prior. A responsible model comparison therefore checks defensible alternatives such as uniform, Jeffreys, and weakly informative Dirichlet concentrations.

title: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings
text:
Markov chains and equilibrium

Definition 1 (Markov chain) A stochastic process X_0,X_1,\ldots is a Markov chain if 
\mathbb{P}(X_{t+1}\in A\mid X_t,X_{t-1},\ldots,X_0)
=\mathbb{P}(X_{t+1}\in A\mid X_t)
\qquad(1) for every measurable set A. In a discrete state space, write q(y\mid x) for the transition probability from x to y; in a continuous state space it is a transition density.
Article: Markov chain →


Definition 2 (Stationarity and detailed balance) A distribution \pi is stationary if a state distributed as \pi remains distributed as \pi after one transition. The global balance equation is 
\pi(y)=\sum_x\pi(x)q(y\mid x)
\quad\text{or}\quad
\pi(y)=\int\pi(x)q(y\mid x)\,\mathrm{d} x.
\qquad(2) A stronger sufficient condition is detailed balance: 
\pi(x)q(y\mid x)=\pi(y)q(x\mid y)
\quad\text{for all }x,y.
\qquad(3)
Article: Stationarity and detailed balance →


Theorem 1 (Detailed balance implies stationarity) If a transition kernel q satisfies Equation 3 for a probability distribution \pi, then \pi satisfies global balance and is a stationary distribution of the chain.
Article: Detailed balance implies stationarity →


Proof. Proof. Integrate both sides of Equation 3 in x: \begin{align*}
\int\pi(x)q(y\mid x)\,\mathrm{d} x
&=\int\pi(y)q(x\mid y)\,\mathrm{d} x\\
&=\pi(y)\int q(x\mid y)\,\mathrm{d} x\\
&=\pi(y).
\end{align*} The last equality holds because a transition density integrates to one.

Stationarity alone is not enough for simulation. One also needs conditions such as irreducibility and aperiodicity so that the chain can reach the whole target support and converge to its stationary distribution. These are grouped informally under ergodicity in this chapter.
MCMC is not intrinsically Bayesian. It is a general method for sampling difficult distributions, and it has deep roots in statistical physics as well as major uses in machine learning. Bayesian posterior calculation is one particularly natural application. The practical migration came at about 1990: methods long used in statistical physics, particularly condensed-matter problems involving large interacting systems, were taken up for posterior calculations that had previously been restricted largely to analytically convenient models. The recipe is to construct a chain whose equilibrium distribution is the posterior, then use its dependent output as a Monte Carlo sample.1
crumbs: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis--Hastings

title: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings
text:
A four-state random walk

Example 1 (Four-state random walk) Question. Consider states 1,2,3,4 arranged in a line. At every state the chain stays put with probability 1/2. From an endpoint it moves to the only neighbour with probability 1/2; from an interior state it moves left or right with probability 1/4 each. With columns indexing the current state and rows the next state, construct the transition matrix and find the stationary distribution.
Solution. The transition matrix is

{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{Q}}=
\begin{pmatrix}
1/2&1/4&0&0\\
1/2&1/2&1/4&0\\
0&1/4&1/2&1/2\\
0&0&1/4&1/2
\end{pmatrix}.

Detailed balance between states 1 and 2 requires

\pi_1\frac12=\pi_2\frac14
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\pi_2=2\pi_1.

Similarly,

\pi_2\frac14=\pi_3\frac14
\Longrightarrow\pi_3=\pi_2,
\qquad
\pi_3\frac14=\pi_4\frac12
\Longrightarrow\pi_3=2\pi_4.

Hence

{\boldsymbol{\pi}}=(\pi_1,\pi_2,\pi_3,\pi_4)^{\mathsf T}
\propto(1,2,2,1)^{\mathsf T}.

Normalising by 1+2+2+1=6 gives

\boxed{{\boldsymbol{\pi}}=(1/6,2/6,2/6,1/6)^{\mathsf T}}.
