title: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings
text:
Gibbs sampling

Definition 3 (Systematic-scan Gibbs sampler) Suppose the target is a joint density \pi(x_1,\ldots,x_p) that is difficult to sample from directly, while every full conditional is available. One Gibbs sweep updates coordinates in order: \begin{align*}
X_1^{(t+1)}&\sim
\pi(x_1\mid X_2^{(t)},\ldots,X_p^{(t)}),\\
X_2^{(t+1)}&\sim
\pi(x_2\mid X_1^{(t+1)},X_3^{(t)},\ldots,X_p^{(t)}),\\
&\ \vdots\\
X_p^{(t+1)}&\sim
\pi(x_p\mid X_1^{(t+1)},\ldots,X_{p-1}^{(t+1)}).
\end{align*} Each update uses the newest available coordinate values. Under standard ergodicity conditions, X^{(t)} converges in distribution to \pi. For a full conditional, the other coordinates are held fixed. Therefore

\pi(x_i\mid x_{-i})
=\frac{\pi(x_i,x_{-i})}{\pi(x_{-i})}
\propto\pi(x_i,x_{-i})
\quad\text{as a function of }x_i.

Terms involving only x_{-i} may be dropped, but any term that still contains x_i must remain. Gibbs accepts every coordinate draw because it samples from the exact conditional rather than proposing and rejecting a candidate.
Article: Systematic-scan Gibbs sampler →


Bivariate exponential example

Example 2 (Bivariate exponential target) The target is

\pi(x_1,x_2)\propto
e^{-x_1x_2-x_1-x_2},
\qquad x_1,x_2\geq0.

Question. Derive both full conditional distributions and use them to specify a systematic-scan Gibbs sampler.
Solution. To obtain X_1\mid X_2=x_2, hold x_2 fixed: \begin{align*}
\pi(x_1\mid x_2)
&\propto\pi(x_1,x_2)\\
&\propto e^{-x_1x_2-x_1-x_2}\\
&\propto e^{-x_1(x_2+1)},
\qquad x_1\geq0.
\end{align*} The omitted factor e^{-x_2} is constant in x_1. Normalising gives

\pi(x_1\mid x_2)=(x_2+1)e^{-(x_2+1)x_1},

so

X_1\mid X_2=x_2\sim\operatorname{Exp}(x_2+1).

By symmetry,

X_2\mid X_1=x_1\sim\operatorname{Exp}(x_1+1).

Starting from any nonnegative pair (x_1^{(0)},x_2^{(0)}), the sampler is \begin{align*}
x_1^{(t+1)}&\sim\operatorname{Exp}(x_2^{(t)}+1),\\
x_2^{(t+1)}&\sim\operatorname{Exp}(x_1^{(t+1)}+1).
\end{align*}



Running the Gibbs sampler
The full conditionals above are the part to derive. Once they are correct, the sampler itself is a short computation. The newest value of x_1 must be used in the update of x_2; using the old value in both lines would define a different transition rule.
gibbs_exp <- function(iterations) {
  out <- matrix(0, iterations, 2)  # start at (0, 0)
  for (t in 2:iterations) {
    out[t, 1] <- rexp(1, rate = out[t - 1, 2] + 1)
    out[t, 2] <- rexp(1, rate = out[t, 1] + 1)
  }
  out
}
set.seed(3500)
draw <- gibbs_exp(20000)
keep <- draw[-seq_len(1000), ]
matplot(keep, type = "l", lty = 1)
acf(keep[, 1])
The trace plot and autocorrelation function are not substitutes for the stationarity argument. They address the separate practical question of whether this finite run appears to have explored the target well enough for the posterior summary at hand.


Normal mean and variance example

Example 3 (Normal mean and variance) Question. For the joint normal-model posterior in Equation (4) in Conjugate analysis for normal models, describe a systematic Gibbs sampler and state how retained draws estimate the posterior mean of \mu.
Solution. For the joint posterior in Equation (4) in Conjugate analysis for normal models, alternate \begin{align*}
\mu^{(t+1)}&\sim
p(\mu\mid\sigma^{2(t)},{\boldsymbol{x}})
\quad\text{using (5)},\\
\sigma^{2(t+1)}&\sim
p(\sigma^2\mid\mu^{(t+1)},{\boldsymbol{x}})
\quad\text{using (6)}.
\end{align*} After discarding a warm-up segment, Monte Carlo estimates use the retained draws. For example,

\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\frac1L\sum_{t=B+1}^{B+L}\mu^{(t)},

where B is the number of discarded iterations. Because the draws are dependent, L correlated draws contain less information than L independent draws. Autocorrelation, trace plots, multiple chains, and effective sample size are therefore part of a serious analysis.



Initialisation, warm-up, and dependence

Remark 1 (Warm-up is not a convergence proof). The chain should be initialised in a plausible region when one is available. A start many standard deviations from the typical set can require a long time to return, while a start at the mean of a separated mixture can lie in a low-density gap. Multiple dispersed chains help reveal failure to explore all modes; they do not repair it automatically.
Discarding early draws is called warm-up or burn-in. It limits dependence on the chosen initial state, but it is not a proof of convergence. Strong posterior correlation produces staircase-like Gibbs paths and high autocorrelation. Separated modes are harder still because a coordinate-wise move may have to cross a low-density barrier.
Thinning by retaining every kth draw reduces storage and visible serial dependence, but usually throws away usable information. Unless storage or an expensive downstream calculation is the constraint, retain all post-warm-up draws and quantify their effective sample size. Posterior means, probabilities, and equal-tailed intervals are computed from those draws; a continuous MAP is found by optimisation, not by asking which simulated value occurred most often.
Article: Warm-up is not a convergence proof →







Figure 1: One Gibbs path through a bivariate normal target with correlation 0.95. Updating X_1\mid X_2 moves horizontally and updating X_2\mid X_1 moves vertically. The narrow diagonal target therefore turns exact conditional simulation into a staircase: every update is valid, but successive states remain strongly dependent.



Burn-in is a practical attempt to reduce the memory of a poor starting point; it is not a theorem that the retained chain has converged. A very long run can make an initial mistake negligible, but separated modes may still defeat a sampler that never travels between them. The central question is not merely how many iterations were produced, but whether the chain explored every region whose posterior mass matters often enough to estimate their relative weights.
The deliberately absurd comparison is between 100{,}000 draws and 100 billion draws. A fixed number of poor initial draws becomes negligible as a proportion of an enormous run. That arithmetic does not help if an important remote mode is never visited: the question is whether such a region would appear in a run of that length, not merely whether the denominator is large.
Raising a target density to a power, \pi(x)^c, sharpens it for c>1 and flattens it for 0<c<1. Simulated annealing gradually changes such a power or temperature so that sampling increasingly resembles optimisation. 2

title: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings
text:
Metropolis–Hastings

Why another sampler is needed
Gibbs sampling is wonderfully direct when every full conditional is a distribution from which we can simulate. Often it is not. The logit-normal coin model in the logit-normal Metropolis–Hastings exercise, for example, has posterior kernel

f(\theta)
=\theta^{x-1}(1-\theta)^{n-x-1}
   \exp\!\left[-\frac12\{\operatorname{logit}(\theta)-1\}^2\right],
\qquad 0<\theta<1.

This is not a Beta kernel, nor another standard density from which we can draw directly. We can nevertheless evaluate f(\theta) at any admissible value. Writing

\pi(\theta)=\frac{f(\theta)}{C},
\qquad
C=\int_0^1 f(t)\,\mathrm{d} t,

makes the computational problem precise: we want draws from \pi using pointwise evaluations of f, without first calculating the intractable normalising constant C.
The Metropolis–Hastings strategy is to construct a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is \pi. After warm-up, its dependent states can be used to estimate posterior quantities. The design problem is therefore not to sample from \pi in one step, but to devise a transition rule that preserves \pi.


Deriving the acceptance probability
Begin with any proposal density q(y\mid x) that is easy to simulate. It will not generally satisfy detailed balance for \pi:

\pi(x)q(y\mid x)\neq \pi(y)q(x\mid y).

We correct the imbalance by accepting a proposed move x\to y with probability a(x,y). For y\neq x, the resulting transition density is

q_{\mathrm{MH}}(y\mid x)=q(y\mid x)a(x,y).

Detailed balance will hold if

\pi(x)q(y\mid x)a(x,y)
=\pi(y)q(x\mid y)a(y,x).

Consequently the paired acceptance probabilities must obey 
\frac{a(x,y)}{a(y,x)}
=\frac{\pi(y)q(x\mid y)}{\pi(x)q(y\mid x)}
=:r(x,y).
\qquad(4) Only their ratio is prescribed. Since rejection wastes a possible move, take the largest probabilities compatible with Equation 4 and with 0\leq a\leq1. If r(x,y)\leq1, set a(x,y)=r(x,y) and a(y,x)=1; if r(x,y)>1, set a(x,y)=1 and a(y,x)=1/r(x,y). Both cases are 
a(x,y)=\min\!\left\{
  1,
  \frac{\pi(y)q(x\mid y)}{\pi(x)q(y\mid x)}
\right\}.
\qquad(5)

Definition 4 (Metropolis–Hastings update) Let \pi(x) be a target density known only up to proportionality. Given X_t=x:

propose Y=y from a proposal density q(y\mid x);
calculate r(x,y) from Equation 4 and put a(x,y)=\min\{1,r(x,y)\};
draw U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1) and set


  X_{t+1}=
  \begin{cases}
   y,&U\leq a(x,y),\\
   x,&U>a(x,y).
  \end{cases}

If \pi(x)=f(x)/C for unknown C, then

\frac{\pi(y)}{\pi(x)}
=\frac{f(y)/C}{f(x)/C}
=\frac{f(y)}{f(x)},

so the normalising constant cancels.
Article: Metropolis–Hastings update →

For a posterior, the evidence p(\text{data}) is precisely such a constant, so the ratio needs only likelihood times prior. In computation we normally evaluate the log ratio and accept when

\log U\leq \min\{0,\log r(x,y)\}.

This avoids numerical underflow when an unnormalised target is a product of many small terms.
This cancellation is why Metropolis methods became central in statistical physics. An Ising model on m binary sites has 2^m configurations, making its partition function impractical to sum, but ratios of unnormalised target weights are immediate. The original Metropolis algorithm used symmetric proposals; Hastings’ generalisation supplied the proposal-density correction in Equation 5.3
The wartime history surrounding Los Alamos also includes Leó Szilárd.4
For y\neq x, the Metropolis–Hastings transition density is

q_{\mathrm{MH}}(y\mid x)=q(y\mid x)a(x,y).

For y=x, the transition probability includes the total rejection probability:

q_{\mathrm{MH}}(x\mid x)
=1-\int_{z\neq x}q(z\mid x)a(x,z)\,\mathrm{d} z.

Thus a rejected proposal is not thrown away in search of another proposal: the current value is recorded again. If instead we redraw until a proposal is accepted, the transition density becomes

\widetilde q(y\mid x)
=\frac{q(y\mid x)a(x,y)}{A(x)},
\qquad
A(x)=\int q(z\mid x)a(x,z)\,\mathrm{d} z.

The extra normaliser depends on the current state. This altered chain is in detailed balance with a density proportional to \pi(x)A(x), not generally with \pi(x), and therefore targets the wrong distribution.


Detailed-balance proof without skipped cases

Theorem 2 (Metropolis–Hastings invariance) The Metropolis–Hastings transition defined by Equation 5 satisfies detailed balance with respect to \pi. Consequently, \pi is stationary.
Article: Metropolis–Hastings invariance →


Proof. Proof. Let

r(x,y)=\frac{\pi(y)q(x\mid y)}
              {\pi(x)q(y\mid x)}.

For y\neq x, \begin{align*}
\pi(x)q_{\mathrm{MH}}(y\mid x)
&=\pi(x)q(y\mid x)\min\{r(x,y),1\}.
\end{align*} There are two cases.
If r(x,y)\leq1, then \begin{align*}
\pi(x)q_{\mathrm{MH}}(y\mid x)
&=\pi(x)q(y\mid x)r(x,y)\\
&=\pi(x)q(y\mid x)
   \frac{\pi(y)q(x\mid y)}{\pi(x)q(y\mid x)}\\
&=\pi(y)q(x\mid y).
\end{align*} Since r(y,x)=1/r(x,y)\geq1, the reverse move is accepted with probability one, so

\pi(y)q_{\mathrm{MH}}(x\mid y)
=\pi(y)q(x\mid y).

If r(x,y)>1, then the forward move is accepted with probability one:

\pi(x)q_{\mathrm{MH}}(y\mid x)=\pi(x)q(y\mid x).

Now r(y,x)<1, so \begin{align*}
\pi(y)q_{\mathrm{MH}}(x\mid y)
&=\pi(y)q(x\mid y)r(y,x)\\
&=\pi(y)q(x\mid y)
   \frac{\pi(x)q(y\mid x)}{\pi(y)q(x\mid y)}\\
&=\pi(x)q(y\mid x).
\end{align*} Thus detailed balance holds in both cases. For x=y, both sides of the detailed-balance equation are identical. Therefore \pi is stationary. 

The theorem establishes invariance, not convergence from an arbitrary starting value and not efficiency. The ergodicity conditions stated earlier are still needed for convergence, while proposal design determines how much useful information the dependent output contains.

title: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings
text:
Random-walk and independent proposals
For a random-walk proposal Y=x+Z with a distribution symmetric about zero,

q(y\mid x)=q(x\mid y),

so Equation 5 reduces to

a(x,y)=\min\!\left\{1,\frac{\pi(y)}{\pi(x)}\right\}.

Every proposed move to higher target density is accepted; a move to a point with two-thirds as much density is accepted with probability 2/3.
For an independent proposal q(y\mid x)=g(y),

a(x,y)=\min\!\left\{
1,\frac{\pi(y)g(x)}{\pi(x)g(y)}
\right\}.

Equivalently, with w(z)=\pi(z)/g(z),

a(x,y)=\min\!\left\{1,\frac{w(y)}{w(x)}\right\}.

The Hastings factor g(x)/g(y) corrects for the fact that g may propose some regions too often and others too rarely. It must not be discarded merely because the proposal is independent of the current state. An independent proposal can jump between separated modes, but it performs poorly if g under-covers a region where \pi is large. A local random walk can represent local shape well but may become trapped in one mode. Proposal scale is therefore a genuine tuning decision, not a cosmetic one.

Gibbs sampling as an always-accepted MH update
The connection with Gibbs sampling can be made exact. Suppose the current state is {\boldsymbol{x}}=(x_1,x_2)^{\mathsf T} and we update only the first coordinate by proposing

{\boldsymbol{y}}=(y_1,x_2)^{\mathsf T},
\qquad
y_1\sim\pi(\,\cdot\mid x_2).

Then

q({\boldsymbol{y}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\pi(y_1\mid x_2),
\qquad
q({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid{\boldsymbol{y}})=\pi(x_1\mid x_2).

Using joint equals conditional times marginal, the Hastings ratio is \begin{align*}
r({\boldsymbol{x}},{\boldsymbol{y}})
&=\frac{\pi(y_1,x_2)\pi(x_1\mid x_2)}
         {\pi(x_1,x_2)\pi(y_1\mid x_2)}\\
&=\frac{\pi(y_1\mid x_2)\pi(x_2)
          \pi(x_1\mid x_2)}
         {\pi(x_1\mid x_2)\pi(x_2)
          \pi(y_1\mid x_2)}\\
&=1.
\end{align*} Every Gibbs coordinate proposal is therefore accepted. This does not imply that every Gibbs sampler moves efficiently. In the bivariate-normal example, as |\rho|\to1 the conditional standard deviation \sqrt{1-\rho^2} tends to zero: acceptance remains one while successive states move only a very short distance.
Proposal design is an art because local and global exploration pull in different directions. Tiny random-walk steps are accepted but travel slowly; huge steps travel far but are mostly rejected. An independent proposal can jump between modes, yet it wastes effort if it puts mass where the target has almost none. The Hastings correction guarantees the right equilibrium under the required conditions; it does not guarantee an efficient journey there.






Figure 2: Three random-walk Metropolis chains with the same \operatorname{N}(0,1) target and different proposal standard deviations s_q. The tiny proposal is accepted almost every time but advances slowly; the huge proposal repeats its current value through long runs of rejections. A moderate acceptance rate is useful only because it accompanies larger moves and much weaker autocorrelation. The displayed acceptance rate is a.





Pilot adaptation and a fixed proposal
Adaptive proposals are a practical response to this tuning problem. A conservative version has two stages:

run a pilot calculation to learn a plausible centre, scale, or covariance for the proposal;
discard the pilot output, fix the learned proposal, restart the chain, and use only the second-stage draws for inference.

Conditional on the now-fixed proposal, the ordinary Metropolis–Hastings invariance argument applies to the retained chain.
Some adaptive schemes retain the history and continue changing the proposal during the run. Then the transition rule depends on time and on more than the current state, so the fixed-kernel proof given above no longer establishes the result. Such methods can be valid, but they require additional conditions and theory. Validity does not follow merely from the fact that the proposal seems to improve.

title: The Beta–Binomial model
text:
Coin tossing and the likelihood
Let Y_i=1 denote a head on toss i and Y_i=0 a tail. Conditional on the unknown probability \theta,

  Y_i\mid\theta\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Bern}(\theta),
  \qquad 0\leq\theta\leq1.

For an observed sequence y_1,\ldots,y_n with x=\sum_{i=1}^ny_i heads, \begin{align*}
  p(y_1,\ldots,y_n\mid\theta)
  &=\prod_{i=1}^n\theta^{y_i}(1-\theta)^{1-y_i}\\
  &=\theta^{\sum_i y_i}(1-\theta)^{\sum_i(1-y_i)}\\
  &=\theta^x(1-\theta)^{n-x}.
\end{align*} If only the count X=\sum_iY_i is observed, then all \binom{n}{x} sequences with x heads are collected together: 
p(x\mid\theta)=\binom{n}{x}\theta^x(1-\theta)^{n-x}.
\qquad(1) The combinatorial term matters for probabilities of X, but it is constant in \theta and can be removed from the likelihood kernel.

title: The Beta–Binomial model
text:
The Beta prior

Definition 1 (Beta distribution) For \alpha,\beta>0, the Beta density is 
p(\theta\mid\alpha,\beta)
  =\frac{1}{B(\alpha,\beta)}
   \theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1},
  \qquad 0<\theta<1,
\qquad(2) where

  B(\alpha,\beta)
  =\int_0^1t^{\alpha-1}(1-t)^{\beta-1}\,\mathrm{d} t
  =\frac{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)}
         {\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)}.

Article: Beta distribution →

Three symmetric priors make the contrast concrete:

\operatorname{Beta}(5,5), concentrated around 1/2;
\operatorname{Beta}(1,1), uniform on [0,1]; and
\operatorname{Beta}(0.6,0.6), with greater density near 0 and 1.

For an ordinary circulating coin, \operatorname{Beta}(5,5) is the most defensible of these three: manufacturing makes values near 1/2 more plausible than values near 0 or 1, while symmetry does not favour heads over tails. If the experiment itself supplies no preferred face, that symmetry is the stable description. A uniform prior assigns equal mass to every interval of the same width, including physically extreme intervals near the endpoints. The U-shaped prior instead represents suspicion that the coin is strongly biased, not ignorance in a neutral sense.
There is no context-free “correct prior for a coin.” The population of coins matters. A newly minted circulating coin, a stage magician’s coin, and a coin selected because it behaved strangely are different prior problems. Calling a prior neutral does not make it so: even the uniform prior gives substantial weight to physically extreme biases. The defensible choice is the one whose implications match how the object entered the experiment.
Persi Diaconis made the same contextual point with a mechanical coin-flipping machine: what looks random at one level may be largely determined once the initial conditions are controlled.1
Rare data remain possible. Under a fair coin, ten heads in ten tosses has probability 2^{-10}=1/1024; it is surprising, not logically impossible. For \alpha,\beta>1,

  \mathbb{E}(\theta)=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta},
  \qquad
  \operatorname{mode}(\theta)
  =\frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha+\beta-2},

and for all \alpha,\beta>0,

  \operatorname{Var}(\theta)
  =\frac{\alpha\beta}
  {(\alpha+\beta)^2(\alpha+\beta+1)}.

title: The Beta–Binomial model
section: Conjugate update with every constant shown

title: The Beta–Binomial model
text:
Worked prior-sensitivity calculation
For n=10 tosses and x=3 heads, these three priors give \begin{align*}
  \operatorname{Beta}(5,5)&\longrightarrow\operatorname{Beta}(8,12),\\
  \operatorname{Beta}(1,1)&\longrightarrow\operatorname{Beta}(4,8),\\
  \operatorname{Beta}(0.6,0.6)&\longrightarrow\operatorname{Beta}(3.6,7.6).
\end{align*} For example, under the uniform prior,

  \mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)=\frac4{12}=\frac13,
  \qquad
  \widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MAP}}
  =\frac{4-1}{4+8-2}=\frac3{10}=0.3.

The posterior probability of downward bias is

  \mathbb{P}(\theta<0.5\mid x)
  =\int_0^{0.5}\frac{\theta^3(1-\theta)^7}{B(4,8)}\,\mathrm{d}\theta.

With n=100 and x=30 heads, the same priors give \begin{align*}
  \operatorname{Beta}(5,5)&\longrightarrow\operatorname{Beta}(35,75),\\
  \operatorname{Beta}(1,1)&\longrightarrow\operatorname{Beta}(31,71),\\
  \operatorname{Beta}(0.6,0.6)&\longrightarrow\operatorname{Beta}(30.6,70.6).
\end{align*} The relative effect of the prior is smaller because the data contribute 100 counts while the first prior contributes a fixed amount.






Figure 1: The three priors, then the posteriors they produce on the two datasets above. Both datasets have the same observed proportion 0.3, marked by the dashed vertical line, so moving to the right changes only how much weight the data carry. Ten tosses leave three visibly different posteriors; one hundred leave three that have nearly closed on each other and on x/n. Disagreement about the prior is a disagreement about small samples. The \operatorname{Beta}(0.6,0.6) prior is unbounded at 0 and 1, so its curve leaves the top of the first panel.









Parameterisation check



Direct substitution of x=30 in Equation 4 gives the first shape parameters 35, 31, and 30.6 written above. The values 36, 32, and 31.6 are one unit larger and do not follow from that substitution. The second shape parameters that match x=30 are 75, 71, and 70.6.

title: The Beta–Binomial model
text:
Pseudo-counts and sequential updating
The posterior mean is \begin{align*}
  \mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)
  &=\frac{x+\alpha}{n+\alpha+\beta}\\
  &=\frac{n}{n+\alpha+\beta}\frac{x}{n}
    +\frac{\alpha+\beta}{n+\alpha+\beta}
      \frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}.
\end{align*} Thus \alpha+\beta acts as a prior sample size for the posterior mean, with \alpha prior heads and \beta prior tails.
For the posterior mode, \begin{align*}
  \widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MAP}}
  &=\frac{x+\alpha-1}{n+\alpha+\beta-2}\\
  &=\frac{n}{n+\alpha+\beta-2}\frac{x}{n}
    +\frac{\alpha+\beta-2}{n+\alpha+\beta-2}
     \frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha+\beta-2},
\end{align*} provided the updated parameters exceed one. Hence \alpha-1 and \beta-1 are the natural pseudo-counts for mode calculations. The two conventions do not contradict each other; they correspond to different posterior summaries.

Remark 1 (Two pseudo-count conventions). For posterior means, (\alpha,\beta) act as prior success and failure counts. For an interior posterior mode, the corresponding counts are (\alpha-1,\beta-1). A pseudo-count statement is incomplete unless the posterior summary being interpreted is also named.
Article: Two pseudo-count conventions →







Parameterisation check



Relative to \operatorname{Beta}(1,1), the prior \operatorname{Beta}(5,5) contributes four additional heads and four additional tails in the mode-based convention. That is eight prior trials, not “four heads in four trials.”



Proposition 2 (Sequential coherence) Sequential updating is exact. If data arrive in batches (x_1,n_1) and (x_2,n_2), then \begin{align*}
  \theta\mid x_1
  &\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+x_1,\beta+n_1-x_1),\\
  \theta\mid x_1,x_2
  &\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+x_1+x_2,
                 \beta+n_1+n_2-x_1-x_2),
\end{align*} which is the same posterior obtained by combining both batches first.
Article: Sequential coherence →

title: The Beta–Binomial model
text:
Nonconjugate priors

Remark 2 (Conjugacy is optional). Conjugacy is convenient, not compulsory. A prior concentrated around 1/2 could be obtained by truncating a Laplace density:

  p(\theta)\propto
  \exp\!\left(-\frac{|\theta-1/2|}{b}\right)
  \mathbf{1}\{0\leq\theta\leq1\}.

The posterior kernel is then

p(\theta\mid x)
\propto
\theta^x(1-\theta)^{n-x}
\exp\!\left(-\frac{|\theta-1/2|}{b}\right)
\mathbf{1}\{0\leq\theta\leq1\}.

If equality rather than proportionality is needed, symmetry supplies the normalising constant without numerical integration: \begin{align*}
\int_0^1\exp\!\left(-\frac{|\theta-1/2|}{b}\right)\,\mathrm{d}\theta
&=2\int_0^{1/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{1/2-\theta}{b}\right)\,\mathrm{d}\theta\\
&=2\left[b\exp\!\left(-\frac{1/2-\theta}{b}\right)\right]_{\theta=0}^{1/2}\\
&=2b\left(1-e^{-1/(2b)}\right).
\end{align*} Thus the proper truncated-Laplace prior has multiplier ([2b{1-e^{-1/(2b)}}]^{-1}). The resulting posterior is not a named standard density, so its normalising integral and summaries must be evaluated numerically. The later MCMC chapters provide a general route when direct integration becomes difficult.
Article: Conjugacy is optional →

The difficulty scales with dimension. A one-dimensional posterior can be normalised by quadrature; a direct grid with m points in each of d coordinates requires m^d evaluations. This exponential growth is the computational reason that nonconjugate multiparameter models lead to Monte Carlo methods.
Conjugacy is a computational convenience, not a modelling command. It was especially attractive when integration and simulation were expensive, and it remains valuable because it exposes the update algebra. But if a scientifically sensible prior is nonconjugate, the right response is usually to improve the computation rather than replace the prior merely to obtain a named posterior. Likewise, the MAP can be useful, particularly in optimisation, but one point is not a substitute for the posterior uncertainty that motivated Bayesian analysis in the first place.

title: The Beta–Binomial model
text:
Beta–Binomial prediction
The prior predictive probability of X=x is already given by Equation 3. Expanding the Beta functions gives the Beta–Binomial mass function:

  p(x)
  =\binom{n}{x}
   \frac{\Gamma(x+\alpha)\Gamma(n-x+\beta)}
        {\Gamma(n+\alpha+\beta)}
   \frac{\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)}
        {\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)}.

For one future toss \widetilde Y, conditional independence gives \begin{align*}
  \mathbb{P}(\widetilde Y=1\mid x)
  &=\int_0^1\mathbb{P}(\widetilde Y=1\mid\theta)
     p(\theta\mid x)\,\mathrm{d}\theta\\
  &=\int_0^1\theta p(\theta\mid x)\,\mathrm{d}\theta\\
  &=\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)\\
  &=\frac{x+\alpha}{n+\alpha+\beta}.
\end{align*} For m future tosses and \widetilde X future heads, \begin{align*}
  p(\widetilde x\mid x)
  &=\int_0^1
    \binom{m}{\widetilde x}
    \theta^{\widetilde x}(1-\theta)^{m-\widetilde x}
    \frac{\theta^{x+\alpha-1}
          (1-\theta)^{n-x+\beta-1}}
         {B(x+\alpha,n-x+\beta)}\,\mathrm{d}\theta\\
  &=\binom{m}{\widetilde x}
    \frac{B(\widetilde x+x+\alpha,
            m-\widetilde x+n-x+\beta)}
         {B(x+\alpha,n-x+\beta)}.
\end{align*} This is a Beta–Binomial posterior predictive distribution.

Proposition 3 (Beta–Binomial posterior prediction) If \theta\mid x\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a,b) and, conditionally on \theta, \widetilde X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(m,\theta), then

\mathbb{P}(\widetilde X=k\mid x)
=\binom mk\frac{B(k+a,m-k+b)}{B(a,b)},
\qquad k=0,\ldots,m.

For one future Bernoulli observation, \mathbb{P}(\widetilde Y=1\mid x)=a/(a+b).
Article: Beta–Binomial posterior prediction →


Numerical example: five future tosses

Example 1 (Five future tosses) Suppose the prior is \theta\sim\operatorname{Beta}(2,2) and the observed data contain x=8 heads in n=10 tosses.
Question. Find the posterior predictive probability of a head on the next toss and the probability of at least four heads in five future tosses. Derive the predictive variance for the five-toss count and compare it with the variance obtained by plugging the posterior mean of \theta into a Binomial model.
Solution. The posterior calculation gives

\theta\mid x
\sim\operatorname{Beta}(2+8,2+10-8)
=\operatorname{Beta}(10,4).

For the very next toss, \begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}(\widetilde Y=1\mid x)
&=\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)\\
&=\frac{10}{10+4}\\
&=\frac57\\
&\approx0.714.
\end{align*} The raw sample proportion is 8/10=0.8. The prediction is less extreme because it averages over the posterior produced by the data and the \operatorname{Beta}(2,2) prior.
Now let \widetilde X be the number of heads in m=5 future tosses. With a=10, b=4, and T=a+b=14, 
\mathbb{P}(\widetilde X=k\mid x)
=\binom5k\frac{B(k+a,5-k+b)}{B(a,b)},
\qquad k=0,\ldots,5.
\qquad(5) For the rising factorial

(c)^{\overline r}
=c(c+1)\cdots(c+r-1),
\qquad
(c)^{\overline 0}=1,

the Beta-function ratio satisfies

\frac{B(k+a,5-k+b)}{B(a,b)}
=\frac{(a)^{\overline k}(b)^{\overline{5-k}}}
       {(a+b)^{\overline5}}.

Therefore the probability of at least four heads is \begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}(\widetilde X\geq4\mid x)
&=\mathbb{P}(\widetilde X=4\mid x)
   +\mathbb{P}(\widetilde X=5\mid x)\\
&=\frac{
   \binom54(10)^{\overline4}(4)^{\overline1}
   +\binom55(10)^{\overline5}(4)^{\overline0}}
   {(14)^{\overline5}}\\
&=\frac{
   5(10\cdot11\cdot12\cdot13)(4)
   +(10\cdot11\cdot12\cdot13\cdot14)}
   {14\cdot15\cdot16\cdot17\cdot18}\\
&=\frac{583440}{1028160}\\
&\approx0.567.
\end{align*}
This example also shows exactly why posterior prediction is more dispersed than a plug-in Binomial distribution. Conditional on \theta,

\mathbb{E}(\widetilde X\mid\theta)=5\theta,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\widetilde X\mid\theta)=5\theta(1-\theta).

For \theta\mid x\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a,b) with T=a+b,

\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)=\frac aT,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\theta\mid x)=\frac{ab}{T^2(T+1)}.

Moreover, \begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}\{\theta(1-\theta)\mid x\}
&=\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)-\mathbb{E}(\theta^2\mid x)\\
&=\frac aT-\frac{a(a+1)}{T(T+1)}\\
&=\frac{a(T+1)-a(a+1)}{T(T+1)}\\
&=\frac{a(T-a)}{T(T+1)}\\
&=\frac{ab}{T(T+1)}.
\end{align*} Applying Equation (3) in Bayesian foundations, \begin{align*}
\operatorname{Var}(\widetilde X\mid x)
&=\mathbb{E}\{5\theta(1-\theta)\mid x\}
   +\operatorname{Var}(5\theta\mid x)\\
&=\frac{5ab}{T(T+1)}
   +\frac{25ab}{T^2(T+1)}\\
&=\frac{5ab(T+5)}{T^2(T+1)}\\
&=\frac{5(10)(4)(19)}{14^2(15)}\\
&=\frac{190}{147}\\
&\approx1.293.
\end{align*} If one instead plugs in the posterior mean \widehat\theta=10/14, the variance would be only

5\widehat\theta(1-\widehat\theta)
=5\left(\frac{10}{14}\right)\left(\frac4{14}\right)
=\frac{50}{49}
\approx1.020.

The difference is the second term in Equation (3) in Bayesian foundations: uncertainty about \theta.

title: Dependence along a series
text:
Part of Time series · 7 questions on this topic · What links here
Clustered data are dependent because they share a block. A time series is dependent because it is ordered. Today’s observation can depend on yesterday’s observation, or on yesterday’s surprise. The aim is less “describe this sample” than “say what happens next”. A perfect fit to the past, with one parameter per time point, does not forecast.

title: Dependence along a series
text:
Autoregression and moving averages
An autoregression of order 1 writes 
X_t=\beta X_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t,
 with the innovations \varepsilon_t independent of each other. A random walk is the case \beta=1, and it wanders off. A spring temperature might have \beta a little above 1, a drift toward summer, plus a daily innovation. A winter temperature might have \beta a little below 1. The best guess of today’s temperature, before the day is observed, is often yesterday’s. A Markov chain is the same skeleton: the next state depends on the current state and a draw.
A moving average of order 1 depends on the previous innovation rather than the previous level: 
X_t=\alpha\varepsilon_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t.
 Stock that did not sell yesterday, discounted and sold today, plus a new surplus, is that equation. So is a weather forecast whose credibility today depends on how wrong it was yesterday, with \alpha the weight on yesterday’s error.






Figure 1: Three series simulated from the same innovations. The AR(1) stays near its mean. The random walk wanders off, which is why \beta=1 is not weakly stationary. The MA(1) is a short, jagged dependence on the previous surprise.



A series we record is a finite piece of a process that could have been running for a long time, and often in continuous time. A city’s midday temperature on 365 days is a sample from a continuous temperature path, taken at one hour of each day. The whole process can be studied first, and finite collections of times examined afterwards, which is the probabilist’s direction. Or a model can be written for the finite collection observed, which is the statistical direction. If every finite subcollection is multivariate normal, the continuous-time process is a Gaussian process, and the converse holds too. That equivalence is special to the normal. It is also why a Gaussian-process prior has become a fashionable smoother: one draw of the process is a curve, and a penalty on how irregular the draw is plays the role of \lambda in the smoothing chapters.

title: Dependence along a series
text:
Stationarity
Without some repetition, a series of length T does not identify a different mean at every time and a different covariance for every pair. Strict stationarity says that any block of observations has the same joint distribution as the same block shifted by \tau. The path changes. The distribution does not. Weak stationarity asks only for two moments: a mean \mu that does not depend on time, and a covariance that depends on the two times only through their difference, 
\gamma_{t-s}=\mathrm{Cov}(X_s,X_t).
 The lag-zero value \gamma_0=\mathrm{Var}(X_t) is then constant as well. The autocorrelation is \gamma_h/\gamma_0, which lies in [-1,1]. For a Gaussian process, weak stationarity and strict stationarity are the same statement. Otherwise weak is weaker.
The variogram looks at the change rather than the level: 
\mathrm{Var}(X_s-X_t)=2(\gamma_0-\gamma_{t-s})
 when the process is weakly stationary. People often care about how much tomorrow moves from today, not about the variance of today’s temperature in isolation. A variogram can exist when the covariance function does not, because the difference X_s-X_t can be well behaved when X_t itself is not.

Theorem 1 If \{X_t\} is weakly stationary with mean zero, then 
X_t=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} a_j\varepsilon_{t-j}+\nu_t,
 where the \varepsilon_t are uncorrelated with mean zero and variance \sigma^2, the coefficients a_j are constants, \nu_t is linearly determined by its own past, and the innovations are uncorrelated with \nu_t. If the mean is \mu, add \mu to the right-hand side.
Article: Wold decomposition →

Every weakly stationary series is a moving average of infinite order, plus a deterministic piece. In practice the mean is subtracted first and put back at the end. The modelling choices are then which of those pieces we keep: is the dependence Markov, or seasonal, or both; is the season only in the mean; are the lags added or multiplied? A multiplicative series is often logged, and then the forecast is on the log scale. Jensen’s inequality says \mathrm{E}(\log X)\neq\log\mathrm{E}(X). Exponentiating a forecast of the log is not a forecast of the mean on the original scale.
White noise is the building block inside that sum: uncorrelated innovations with mean zero and constant variance. The next chapter is a forecasting application rather than a further derivation of white noise, AR(p), and MA(q).

An AR(1) with coefficient 1 is a random walk. Say what happens to the variance of X_t as t grows, and why that process cannot be weakly stationary.
For a weakly stationary series, show \mathrm{Var}(X_s-X_t)=2(\gamma_0-\gamma_{|t-s|}) from the definition of \gamma.
Why does a time series of length T, with a different mean at each time and a free covariance for every pair, run out of degrees of freedom? What does weak stationarity put in place of those free parameters?

title: Three species on one hillside
text:
Part of Correlated data · What links here
The burn example had two different kinds of measurement on one child. This chapter stays with a vector response, but now every component is binary.
Thomas Yee’s VGAM package fits vector generalised linear models in which every component has the same type. It will not take one binary margin and one continuous margin, which is why the burn data were fitted by hand. It will take three binary margins. The Hunua ranges data record, at 392 locations, whether each of three New Zealand plants was present: Cyathea dealbata (cyadea), Beilschmiedia tawa (beitaw), and Knightia excelsa (kniexc). Altitude is the covariate. The plants may prefer different heights, and they may help or crowd each other, so the three binary responses at one location are not independent. The association is not forced to be positive.
Each margin is a logistic regression with its own intercept and its own slope on altitude: 
\mathrm{P}(Y_k=1\mid \text{altitude})
=\frac{\exp(\beta_{k0}+\beta_{k1}\,\text{altitude})}{1+\exp(\beta_{k0}+\beta_{k1}\,\text{altitude})},
 and the working variance is the Bernoulli variance \mu_k(1-\mu_k). The working association between each pair is a log odds ratio: the odds of finding species k when species k' is present, divided by the odds of finding species k when species k' is absent. That is a two-way interaction. A three-way odds ratio, all three plants at once, can be written down but has no clear interpretation, so the working model stops at pairs. Any three species on a hillside do interact as a triple. The working model is therefore wrong. It does not have to be right for the slopes, once the sandwich standard errors are used.
vglm with the trivariate binary family loglinb3 returns model-based standard errors that assume the working variance and the working odds ratios. The sandwich is a plug-in on top of that fit. Altitude in the table is scaled by 10^3. In the coefficient vector, predictor 1 is Cyathea, 2 is Beilschmiedia, and 3 is Knightia. Predictors 4 to 6 are the pairwise log odds ratios. The slope table below keeps the three species intercepts and the three altitude slopes. The Std. Error column from summary is the naive standard error. The sandwich column in that table is the robust standard error.
At sea level the log-odds of Cyathea are -0.977, so the probability is \exp(-0.977)/(1+\exp(-0.977))\approx 0.27. Each extra kilometre of altitude multiplies those odds by \exp(-0.570)=0.57, but a sandwich z of -0.70 is not a claim of an altitude effect for Cyathea. Beilschmiedia is uncommon at sea level, probability \exp(-1.890)/(1+\exp(-1.890))\approx 0.13, and it prefers height: \exp(3.85)\approx 47 times the odds per kilometre, with sandwich z=4.42. In Figure 1 that climb is the steep curve. Knightia is the intermediate case, and its altitude slope is not detected (z=1.36). The naive and sandwich standard errors are the same order of magnitude, which is consistent with a working model that is not wildly wrong. It is still a pairwise model on a three-species hillside, so the sandwich column is the one to trust, not because the odds ratios are correct, but because those standard errors do not need them to be.
The fitted probabilities at the first location, the eight possible presence patterns of the three plants, start at 0.267 for “none of them”. Those eight probabilities are a joint distribution under the working model. They are not required for the slope estimates.

title: Random slopes, and a binary mixed model
text:
Part of Correlated data · 6 questions on this topic · What links here
A shared intercept is the smallest mixed model. Blocks can also change slopes. This chapter fits that model to a sleep-deprivation study, and then replaces the normal residual by a Bernoulli likelihood for a contraception survey.
crumbs: Random slopes, and a binary mixed model

title: Random slopes, and a binary mixed model
section: A slope that belongs to the block
text:
A slope that belongs to the block
Write {\boldsymbol{Z}}_{ji} for the covariates whose effects are allowed to vary by block. They may be the same as {\boldsymbol{X}}_{ji}, or a subset, or something else. 
Y_{ji}
={\boldsymbol{X}}_{ji}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}
+{\boldsymbol{Z}}_{ji}^\top\boldsymbol{\alpha}_j
+\varepsilon_{ji},
 
\boldsymbol{\alpha}_j\stackrel{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}\mathrm{N}({\boldsymbol{0}},{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_A),
\qquad
\varepsilon_{ji}\stackrel{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}\mathrm{N}(0,\sigma^2).
 {\color{blue}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_A holds the variances of the random intercept and the random slopes, and the covariances between them. Dropping every random slope returns the model of the previous chapter. We start from the larger model when a covariate might interact with the block: some hospitals are better at some treatments, some drivers deteriorate faster when they are not allowed to sleep.
A fixed effect is a constant. Repeat the experiment and it is the same constant. A random effect is a draw. Repeat the sleep study and eighteen different drivers are drawn, and the eighteen intercepts and slopes are new. We estimate the mean and the covariance of that population. Predicting the eighteen draws we happened to get is a different task, and it is a prediction of a random variable, not an estimate of a fixed parameter. With the variances known, that prediction is the best linear unbiased predictor. With the variances estimated, it is the empirical version of the same thing. Software computes it. We do not derive it by hand.
crumbs: Random slopes, and a binary mixed model

title: Random slopes, and a binary mixed model
text:
Sleep deprivation
Eighteen subjects, treated as a sample of long-distance drivers rather than as eighteen named people, were restricted to three hours of sleep a night for ten days. Each day their reaction time was an average of several ruler-drop trials, in milliseconds. Most people slow down. One or two stay flat, and one seems to get slightly faster, which is the pattern if three hours was more sleep than they usually had. Before looking, the reasonable model is a person-specific intercept and a person-specific slope on day. Reflexes differ, and so does the damage from another night of three hours.
need <- function(pkg) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  }
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(pkg, character.only = TRUE))
}
need("lme4")
data(sleepstudy, package = "lme4")
fit <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (Days | Subject), data = sleepstudy)
summary(fit)
fit0 <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 | Subject), data = sleepstudy)
anova(fit0, fit)
round(ranef(fit)$Subject[c("308", "309", "370"), ], 1)
The (Days | Subject) term is a random intercept and a random slope on day, with a correlation between them. The fit is by restricted maximum likelihood. The estimates are
Random effects:
 Subject  (Intercept)   variance 612.09    sd 24.74
          Days          variance  35.07    sd  5.92    corr 0.07
 Residual               variance 654.94    sd 25.59

Fixed effects:
 (Intercept)   251.41     se 6.83
 Days           10.47     se 1.55
These are statements about the population the eighteen were drawn from, not about the eighteen. The average driver starts at 251 milliseconds and slows by 10.5 milliseconds per day of deprivation. A typical driver sits 25 milliseconds away from that starting value, and a typical slope sits 5.9 milliseconds per day away from 10.5. The correlation between a driver’s intercept and slope is 0.07. Someone who is slow on day zero is not, in any important way, someone who deteriorates faster.
Whether the random slopes are needed is a comparison of this fit with Reaction ~ Days + (1 | Subject). The likelihood-ratio statistic is 42.1 on 2 degrees of freedom, and the printed p-value is 7\times 10^{-10}. That p-value is not an exact chi-squared tail probability. The null hypothesis puts a variance on the boundary of the parameter space, at zero, so the usual asymptotic distribution does not apply. The printed tail probability is conservative: it is larger than the p-value from the correct mixture of chi-squared laws. A conservative p-value this small is still small. The slopes stay. Had the printed value been 0.07, it would not be clear which side of 0.05 the proper test sat on, and the term would not be dropped on the strength of the printed value.
The empirical predictors of the eighteen deviations are a different object again. Subject 308 is predicted about 2 milliseconds slower than the population intercept and about 9 milliseconds per day steeper than the population slope. Subject 309 is about 40 milliseconds faster at the start and has a slope about 8 below the average, which is why that series looks flat: 10.5-8 is nearly zero. Subject 370 starts faster than average and then falls away faster than average.






Figure 1: Reaction time for the eighteen subjects. The black line is the population fit, about 251 milliseconds plus 10.5 milliseconds a day. Subjects 308, 309 and 370 are marked. Subject 309 is the flat series.



Repeat the study and none of these eighteen numbers returns. The fixed effects 251 and 10.5 are the quantities that are supposed to.
crumbs: Random slopes, and a binary mixed model

title: Random slopes, and a binary mixed model
text:
A Bernoulli response
The outer distribution does not have to be normal. Keep the linear predictor, random intercept and random slopes included, and let 
Y_{ji}\mid {\boldsymbol{X}}_{ji},\boldsymbol{\alpha}_j
\stackrel{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}
\mathrm{Bernoulli}\!\left(
\mu\bigl({\boldsymbol{X}}_{ji}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}+{\boldsymbol{Z}}_{ji}^\top\boldsymbol{\alpha}_j\bigr)
\right),
 with \boldsymbol{\alpha}_j still multivariate normal on the link scale. For a logit, \mu is the expit. The normal distribution on \boldsymbol{\alpha}_j is a modelling choice about a latent intercept, not a claim that we observed a normal measurement. It is a distribution we can interpret, and there is no stronger reason, before seeing the data, to pick a different one. The likelihood integrates the random effects out. There is no closed form, and no single algorithm that is guaranteed to find the maximum in every data set. When the numerical answer is in doubt, we fit the model more than one way, and we trust an agreement.
The 1989 Bangladesh fertility survey has 1934 women and a binary response: currently using contraception, or not. Age is centred and enters as a quadratic, because use should rise and then fall rather than climb forever. ch records whether she already has a living child. urban records urban against rural. district is the cluster. Women in the same district share facilities and customs, so a district intercept is the natural random effect. If every district in the country were in the sample, “a draw from a population of districts” would be a fiction about the boundaries of districts rather than about a sampling frame. We still use it. The districts that exist are one way of cutting the map.
need <- function(pkg) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  }
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(pkg, character.only = TRUE))
}
need("lme4")
need("mlmRev")
data(Contraception, package = "mlmRev")
# age is already centred in this copy of the survey
Contraception$ch <- as.integer(Contraception$livch != "0")
Contraception$age2 <- Contraception$age^2
# a warning about rescaling age and age2 can appear; the estimates are the table below
summary(glmer(use ~ age + age2 + urban + ch + (1 | district),
              data = Contraception, family = binomial))
There are 60 districts. The district intercept has estimated standard deviation 0.474 on the log-odds scale: from district to district, at a fixed age, urban status, and child status, the log-odds of use move by about half a unit. The fixed effects are
(Intercept)  -1.006    se 0.169    z -5.95
age           0.0063   se 0.0079   z  0.79
age2         -0.00464  se 0.00072  z -6.43
urbanY        0.693    se 0.121    z  5.74
ch            0.860    se 0.148    z  5.80
Age has a positive linear term that is not itself significant and a negative square that is. Together they are the upside-down parabola.






Figure 2: Fitted probability of contraceptive use against centred age, in a typical district, for a woman who already has a living child. Urban sits above rural. The two curves are one parabola, not two separate age effects.



The linear coefficient is not interpreted on its own. Urban women have odds of use \exp(0.693)=2.00 times those of rural women in the same district, at the same age and the same child status. A woman who already has a living child has odds \exp(0.860)=2.36 times those of a woman who does not. The district standard deviation is a typical shift, not a comparison of two named districts.
The urban contrast need not be the same in every district. A large city can have a rural fringe that is not very different from the centre. A small regional centre can have a sharp drop just outside the town. Some districts in the file are entirely urban, so a rural contrast for them is a prediction about a place that is not there.
need <- function(pkg) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  }
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(pkg, character.only = TRUE))
}
need("lme4")
need("mlmRev")
data(Contraception, package = "mlmRev")
Contraception$ch <- as.integer(Contraception$livch != "0")
Contraception$age2 <- Contraception$age^2
summary(glmer(use ~ age + age2 + urban + ch + (urban | district),
              data = Contraception, family = binomial))
The average urban coefficient is now 0.770 (z=4.69): across districts, urban versus rural is a factor of \exp(0.77)\approx 2.16 on the odds. The district-level standard deviation of that contrast is 0.74, almost as large as the average contrast itself. Some districts have essentially no urban gap. Some have a much larger one. The correlation between the district intercept and the district urban slope is -0.79. A district that already has high use has a smaller urban-rural gap. Where use is common, rural and urban are not far apart, and where use is uncommon the town centre and the countryside are. The likelihood-ratio comparison with the random-intercept-only model is small enough, even as a conservative boundary p-value, that the extra random slope stays. It is an interaction. The effect of living in town depends on the district.
Marginal models, which describe the population average without a mechanism for the correlation, are the next chapter.

The sleep-study random-slope variance is 35.07. Convert it to a standard deviation and say what “a typical driver” means for the daily change in reaction time.
Why is the p-value on \sigma^2_{\text{slope}}=0 not a chi-squared tail probability, and in which direction is the printed value wrong?
From the contraception fit with a random intercept only, compute \exp(0.693) and \exp(0.860) and state both as odds ratios with the covariates that are being held fixed.
The correlation between a district’s intercept and its urban slope is -0.79. Give the direction of that statement in one sentence, without using the word “significant”.

title: Additive smooths
text:
Part of Smoothing · 2 questions on this topic · What links here
A smooth function of one covariate was enough to let kyphosis rise and fall with age. This chapter puts more than one covariate into that smooth.

title: Additive smooths
text:
Sums of smooth functions
A completely free surface g(x_1,x_2,x_3) can be fitted, and in four covariates it cannot even be pictured. We do not use it. The model that stays readable replaces the linear predictor by a sum of univariate smooths, one per covariate. On the logit scale for kyphosis, 
\mathrm{logit}\,\mathrm{P}(\text{kyphosis})
=\beta_0+g_1(\text{number})+g_2(\text{start})+g_3(\text{age}).
 Each g_j has its own penalty. Nothing forces them to be equally smooth. This is a generalised additive model, in the sense of Hastie and Tibshirani: additive in the smooths, not linear in the covariates. Number takes only the values 1 through 8, and Start only sixteen vertebral positions, so a smooth cannot have more knots than there are distinct values.
need <- function(pkg) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  }
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(pkg, character.only = TRUE))
}
need("mgcv")
need("rpart")
data(kyphosis, package = "rpart")
kyphosis$Kyphosis <- as.numeric(kyphosis$Kyphosis == "present")
summary(gam(Kyphosis ~ s(Number, k = 8) + s(Start, k = 16) + s(Age),
            family = binomial, data = kyphosis))
The equivalent degrees of freedom are about 1.19 for the number of vertebrae, 2.04 for the starting position, and 2.21 for age.






Figure 1: The three smooths in the additive kyphosis model, on the log-odds scale and centred at zero. Number of vertebrae is close to a straight line. Starting position is flat through the upper vertebrae and then falls. Age still rises and then eases.



In Figure 1, number is almost a straight line on the log-odds scale: more vertebrae in the same operation, higher odds of kyphosis. Start is flat from the top of the spine through about the sixth vertebra and then falls. Surgery that begins low on the back has the smaller risk. Age, now conditional on the other two, still rises and then eases, a little less dramatically than when it was the only covariate.
Each curve is the effect of moving that one covariate while the others are held fixed. Holding the starting vertebra at 16 and imagining ten vertebrae below it is not a spine that exists. The sentence is conditional on a hypothetical, and some of those hypotheticals are empty.
A free function of all three covariates together would fit a surface we could not explain to a surgeon. Two-way interactions are already hard. Three-way interactions are where we stop. The compromise is a partially linear model: a coefficient for the term you want a unit-change sentence about, and a smooth for the terms you are only adjusting for. Ambient temperature in a lab, or the weight of a patient in a trial of two treatments, is the second kind. Dose and treatment are the first kind.
Number of vertebrae looked linear, so force it to be a slope and leave start and age smooth:
need <- function(pkg) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  }
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(pkg, character.only = TRUE))
}
need("mgcv")
need("rpart")
data(kyphosis, package = "rpart")
kyphosis$Kyphosis <- as.numeric(kyphosis$Kyphosis == "present")
summary(gam(Kyphosis ~ Number + s(Start, k = 16) + s(Age),
            family = binomial, data = kyphosis))
The slope on number is 0.333 with standard error 0.232 (z=1.43, p=0.15). Once start and age are in the model, the number of vertebrae is not detected. We would drop it. Start remains, with equivalent degrees of freedom about 2.03. One printout gave p=0.013 for start and p=0.071 for age; mgcv 1.8 prints about 0.015 and 0.078. Age stays borderline either way, and we keep it for the same reason as in the previous chapter. The important covariate is where the operation starts. On the plotted smooth, the log-odds for a start among vertebrae 1 to 5 sit several units above the log-odds for a start at the bottom of the spine. That gap can be read as a factor of about \exp(5)=148 on the odds scale. A gap of 4, which is also a fair reading of the same curve, is \exp(4)\approx 55. We will not pretend the graph yields one integer. The comparison is large, it favours starting lower, and it is conditional on age.






Key idea



Smooth the covariates you are adjusting for and do not need a one-sentence answer about. Keep a parametric term for the covariate whose unit change you intend to report. A smooth of everything is a picture, not an effect.



In the additive kyphosis model, Number has equivalent degrees of freedom 1.19. Say what that number claims about the shape on the log-odds scale, and why k = 8 is a ceiling rather than a target.

title: Probability-integral residuals
text:
Part of Generalised linear models · What links here
A Pearson plot of a binary or a count fit is striped. The stripes are the values the response is allowed to take, not a missed term. This is the last diagnostic that still belongs with generalised linear models. It replaces that plot with a transform that does not care what the distribution was.
Suppose Y has continuous distribution function F. Then U=F(Y) is uniform on (0,1). The probability of falling below the value you actually observed, scored by the distribution that generated it, is a uniform draw. If F is discrete the same idea uses a generalised inverse, and F(Y) is only approximately uniform. The approximation improves as the fitted distribution spreads over more values. A Bernoulli is the worst case. A Poisson with a large mean is kinder.
After a model has been fitted, plug in \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} and compute F(y_i;\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) for each observation. These are not exactly uniform, for the same reason a residual divided by \hat\sigma is not exactly standard normal: the parameters were estimated. If the model is adequate they should still look like a uniform sample. Order them and plot them against the uniform quantiles 1/n,2/n,\ldots,n/n. Those quantiles are equally spaced, which is the one pleasant feature of the uniform that the normal does not share. A straight line is what you want.
Bend the line and the fit is wrong in a readable way. If the plotted residuals bow above the diagonal through the middle of the sample, the middle observations are larger than the fitted distribution expected: the mean is too low in the middle of the range. The opposite bow means the fit is too high there. Either shape is a reason to change the mean, not to stare harder at a banded Pearson plot.
The same construction works when the data really are normal. F is then a normal distribution function, and the uniform plot is that normal probability transformed one more time. The classical residual plots remain the right tool when Y is continuous and the variance function is the thing in doubt.
The next question is what to do when no straight line, on any link, is a shape you are willing to write down in advance.

title: Categorical responses
text:
Part of Generalised linear models · 3 questions on this topic · What links here
A response that can only land in one of K fixed categories is polytomous. There is no mean of the category labels that we are willing to interpret. A grade of 7 is not seven times a grade of 1, and the average of “rugby”, “cricket”, and “netball” is not a sport. What is well defined is the probability of each category.
Three kinds of scale show up in practice.
Write p_k=\mathrm{P}(Y\text{ is in category }k). For an ordinal scale we would rather work with the upper tail, because “at least this good” is the question people ask: 
\gamma_k=\mathrm{P}(Y\ge k).
 The tails determine the category probabilities and the other way around. \gamma_1=1 if category 1 is the bottom of the scale, because everyone is at least in the lowest category. Cumulative probabilities are meaningless if the labels have no order. For a nominal response we stay with the p_k.
“Association” is the word. “Correlation” is for two numerical variables. A grade is not numerical, so hours of study are associated with higher grades. They are not correlated with the grade labels.

title: Categorical responses
section: Ordinal data, built from binary splits
text:
Ordinal data, built from binary splits
Food scores, pain scores, and agreement scales have cutpoints that are partly conventional. If we collapse “strongly agree” into “agree”, the form of the model should survive. The estimates will change, because information was thrown away. The equation should be the same kind of equation. That requirement is what forces cumulative probabilities rather than a separate model for each p_k.
Three categories are enough to see it. In the pneumonia experiment, animals were exposed to a bacterium for a logged time x=\log(\text{exposure in seconds}), and the response was 1 none, 2 mild, 3 severe. Sample size falls as the dose rises, which is the ethical constraint you would hope for. The rows, with x=\log t, are

Suppose the only question is whether any pneumonia occurred. Mild and severe collapse into one category, and the problem is binary: 
\mathrm{P}(Y\ge 2)=\frac{\exp(\beta_{0,\mathrm{ms}}+\beta_{1,\mathrm{ms}} x)}{1+\exp(\beta_{0,\mathrm{ms}}+\beta_{1,\mathrm{ms}} x)}.
 Suppose instead that mild disease is treatable and only severe disease is the event. None and mild collapse, and again the problem is binary, with its own intercept and slope, for \mathrm{P}(Y\ge 3). The only model for three ordered categories that collapses to a logistic regression on every neighbouring split is a logistic regression for each upper tail: \begin{align*}
\mathrm{P}(Y\ge 3)&=\frac{\exp(\beta_{03}+\beta_{13}x)}{1+\exp(\beta_{03}+\beta_{13}x)},\\
\mathrm{P}(Y\ge 2)&=\frac{\exp(\beta_{02}+\beta_{12}x)}{1+\exp(\beta_{02}+\beta_{12}x)},\\
\mathrm{P}(Y\ge 1)&=1.
\end{align*} That is an interaction: every cutpoint has its own slope. It is as hard to read as a set of non-parallel lines. The model we fit forces the slopes to be common and lets only the intercepts differ.

Definition 1 A proportional-odds model for ordered categories 1,\ldots,K and covariates {\boldsymbol{x}} is 
\mathrm{logit}\,\mathrm{P}(Y\ge k\mid {\boldsymbol{x}})=\beta_{0k}+{\boldsymbol{x}}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta},
\qquad k=2,\ldots,K,
 with \beta_{02}\ge\beta_{03}\ge\cdots\ge\beta_{0K}. A unit increase in a covariate multiplies the odds of being in category k or higher by e^{\beta_j}, and that factor does not depend on k.
Article: Proportional-odds model →

The intercepts have to decrease as k increases, because \mathrm{P}(Y\ge 2)\ge\mathrm{P}(Y\ge 3)\ge\cdots. For a university grade, one extra hour of study multiplies the odds of a 4 or better, a 5 or better, and a 7, by the same factor. If those factors differed, you would have a non-proportional odds model, which is the interaction above, and we would not lead with it.
The response at each x is a vector of counts, so the fit is a vector GLM. In the VGAM package:1
need <- function(pkg) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  }
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(pkg, character.only = TRUE))
}
need("VGAM")
data(pneumo, package = "VGAM")
pneumo$none <- pneumo$normal
pneumo$x <- log(pneumo$exposure.time)
summary(vglm(cbind(none, mild, severe) ~ x, family = propodds, data = pneumo))
              Estimate Std. Error z value
(Intercept):1  -9.6761     1.3241   -7.31
(Intercept):2 -10.5817     1.3454   -7.86
x               2.5968     0.3811    6.81
The first linear predictor is \mathrm{logit}\,\mathrm{P}(Y\ge 2). The second is \mathrm{logit}\,\mathrm{P}(Y\ge 3). So \begin{align*}
\widehat{\mathrm{P}}(Y\ge 2)
&=\frac{\exp(-9.6761+2.5968\,x)}{1+\exp(-9.6761+2.5968\,x)},\\
\widehat{\mathrm{P}}(Y\ge 3)
&=\frac{\exp(-10.5817+2.5968\,x)}{1+\exp(-10.5817+2.5968\,x)}.
\end{align*}






Figure 1: Fitted cumulative probabilities against exposure time. The severe curve stays below the curve for mild or severe, and the two curves share a slope on the logit scale. Points are the proportions in the table.



At x=0, which is one second of exposure if x is a natural log of seconds, the odds of severe pneumonia are e^{-10.58}, of order 10^{-5}. The odds of mild or severe are e^{-9.68}, larger, as they must be, because that event contains the severe cases. Both are negligible, which is the right answer for an animal that was barely exposed.
A unit increase in x is a factor of e\approx 2.7 in exposure time, roughly a threefold increase. It multiplies the odds of crossing either cut by 
\exp(2.5968)=13.4.
 The z statistic on that slope is 6.81. Exposure time is strongly associated with worse pneumonia, and the multiplier is the same for “any pneumonia” and for “severe pneumonia”. That is the proportional-odds claim.
Replacing the logit by the complementary log-log gives a proportional-hazards model, 
\log\bigl(-\log(1-\gamma_k)\bigr)=\beta_{0k}+{\boldsymbol{x}}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta},
 with the same parallel-slope constraint and the same ordering of intercepts. The coefficient is a log hazard, not a log odds ratio. We can say what an odds ratio is. A hazard is a definition we can write down and a quantity we cannot usually explain. The call that forces the cumulative, reversed, parallel, complementary-log-log model is
need <- function(pkg) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  }
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(pkg, character.only = TRUE))
}
need("VGAM")
data(pneumo, package = "VGAM")
pneumo$none <- pneumo$normal
pneumo$x <- log(pneumo$exposure.time)
fit <- vglm(cbind(none, mild, severe) ~ x,
            family = cumulative(reverse = TRUE, parallel = TRUE, link = "cloglog"),
            data = pneumo)
summary(fit)
deviance(fit)
logLik(fit)
and it returns intercepts -8.60 and -9.35, with slope 2.21 (z=7.06). The residual deviance is 6.65 against 5.03 for the proportional-odds fit, and the log-likelihood is -25.90 against -25.09. The odds model fits this table a little better. The two models are not nested, so that comparison is not a likelihood-ratio test. It is the same kind of absolute comparison as an AIC when the parameter count matches, which here it does.

title: Categorical responses
text:
Nominal categories
If the labels can be written in any order, cumulative tails are not available. Start again from the binary logit. With categories 0 and 1, 
\log\frac{p_1}{p_0}=\beta_0+{\boldsymbol{x}}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}.
 With three nominal categories, say rugby =0, cricket =1, netball =2, there are three pairwise log-odds, but only two are free. If cricket is twice as likely as rugby and netball is three times as likely as rugby, then netball is 1.5 times as likely as cricket. In equations, 
\log\frac{p_2}{p_1}
=\log\frac{p_2}{p_0}-\log\frac{p_1}{p_0},
 so the third comparison is the difference of the two comparisons against the baseline, and it has the same linear form. Once every category is compared with category 0, every other pair is determined. That is the same bookkeeping as knowing everyone’s mark relative to the lowest mark in the class.

Definition 2 For nominal categories 0,1,\ldots,K-1, the baseline-category logit model is 
\log\frac{p_k}{p_0}=\beta_{0k}+{\boldsymbol{x}}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}_k,
\qquad k=1,\ldots,K-1.
 The log-odds of category k against category k' are (\beta_{0k}-\beta_{0k'})+{\boldsymbol{x}}^\top(\boldsymbol{\beta}_k-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{k'}).
Article: Baseline-category logit model →

There are K-1 linear predictors, each with its own intercept and its own slopes. The covariates may be the same. The coefficients are not.

Addiction categories
A German survey interviewed 712 people about addiction and classified the answers in three categories that we will not put in an order: 0 weak-willed, 1 addiction by disease, 2 both.2 The covariates are sex (female =1), age in years, and an indicator for being a university academic. The first rows look like this: illness 1, female, age 61, not academic; then illness 0, female, 43, not academic; then illness 2, male, 44, not academic.
multinomial(refLevel = 1) takes the lowest level of ill, which is 0, as the reference, even though that level is stored as the number 0. The numbering in the coefficient names is the predictor number, not the illness code.
need <- function(pkg) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  }
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(pkg, character.only = TRUE))
}
need("catdata")
need("VGAM")
data(addiction, package = "catdata")
addiction$ill <- factor(addiction$ill)
summary(vglm(ill ~ gender + age + university,
             family = multinomial(refLevel = 1),
             data = addiction))
               Estimate Std. Error z value
(Intercept):1   -1.1607     0.2654   -4.37
(Intercept):2   -2.0156     0.3076   -6.55
gender:1         0.4366     0.1938    2.25
gender:2         0.2879     0.2208    1.30
age:1            0.0299     0.0062    4.80
age:2            0.0421     0.0068    6.17
university:1     1.6220     0.2535    6.40
university:2     1.0673     0.2891    3.69
Predictor 1 is \log(\hat p_1/\hat p_0), disease versus weak-willed. Predictor 2 is \log(\hat p_2/\hat p_0), both versus weak-willed. Written out, \begin{align*}
\log\frac{\hat p_1}{\hat p_0}
&=-1.161+0.437\,\mathrm{female}+0.0299\,\mathrm{age}+1.622\,\mathrm{university},\\
\log\frac{\hat p_2}{\hat p_0}
&=-2.016+0.288\,\mathrm{female}+0.0421\,\mathrm{age}+1.067\,\mathrm{university}.
\end{align*} Reading those coefficients as odds ratios, and the comparison of category 2 against category 1, is the next chapter. The fit itself is the multinomial likelihood with these two linear predictors, dispersion fixed at 1: one independent choice of a single category per person. If a questionnaire let you tick several categories, that 1 would be the wrong dispersion, and this would be the wrong model.

From the proportional-odds intercepts, check that \widehat{\mathrm{P}}(Y\ge 2)>\widehat{\mathrm{P}}(Y\ge 3) at x=0, and say why a reversal would have meant the fit was impossible rather than merely a bad fit.
Show that collapsing mild and severe into one category recovers a single logistic regression from the proportional-odds model, with the same slope \beta.
For the three-category nominal model, derive \log(p_2/p_1) from \log(p_2/p_0) and \log(p_1/p_0), and confirm that the result is still a linear predictor.

title: Standard errors, and models for counts
text:
Part of Generalised linear models · 7 questions on this topic · What links here
The previous chapter stopped once Fisher scoring had produced the cholesterol coefficients. Estimation is the less interesting half. This chapter is about the precision of those coefficients, and then about what changes when the response is a count rather than a coin toss.
crumbs: Standard errors, and models for counts

title: Standard errors, and models for counts
text:
Standard errors in a GLM
For a regular model and a large enough sample, the maximum likelihood estimator \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} is asymptotically normal, centred at the true value \boldsymbol{\beta}^\star, with covariance equal to the inverse Fisher information at that true value: 
\mathrm{cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\approx {\color{blue}\boldsymbol{I}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^\star)^{-1}.
\qquad(1) We never know \boldsymbol{\beta}^\star. The usable matrix plugs in \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}: 
{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{I}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
=\sum_{i=1}^n
\frac{\bigl(\mu'({\boldsymbol{X}}_i^\top\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\bigr)^2}{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(Y_i)}\,
{\boldsymbol{X}}_i{\boldsymbol{X}}_i^\top.
\qquad(2) The standard error of \hat\beta_j is the square root of the jth diagonal entry of {\color{blue}\boldsymbol{I}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})^{-1}. A marginal interval is 
\hat\beta_j\pm z_{\alpha/2}\,\widehat{\mathrm{se}}(\hat\beta_j).
 For a GLM we use z, not t. The normal approximation is already a large-sample statement. Once the residual degrees of freedom are past thirty or forty, a t cutoff and 1.96 are not meaningfully different, and the theory that delivers Equation 1 is a central limit theorem, not an exact normal linear model. For 95%, use 1.96.






Key idea



The estimated coefficients come from Fisher scoring. Their standard errors come from the inverse Fisher information, evaluated at those coefficients. Intervals and tests for a GLM use z, not t.



Cholesterol, with standard errors
chol_file <- "data/cholest.csv"
if (!file.exists(chol_file)) {
  stop("Could not find data/cholest.csv. Set the working directory to the book folder.")
}
chol <- read.csv(chol_file)
summary(glm(disease ~ gender + cholesterol, data = chol, family = binomial))
summary(glm(disease ~ cholesterol, data = chol, family = binomial))
prints
            Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept) -9.3203     2.1714  -4.292  1.77e-05
gender      -0.1094     0.4873  -0.224  0.822
cholesterol  1.5842     0.3836   4.130  3.63e-05
The dispersion is reported as 1. For a binomial, that is a reminder, not an estimate: \mathrm{Var}=p(1-p) exactly, with no free \phi.
Cholesterol has a clear positive association with the log-odds of disease. Sex, given cholesterol, does not: the estimate is a tenth of its standard error. The simpler model drops sex.
            Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept) -9.2012     2.0992  -4.383  1.17e-05
cholesterol  1.5549     0.3592   4.329  1.50e-05
A 95% interval for the cholesterol slope is 
1.5549\pm 1.96\times 0.3592=(0.85,\ 2.26).
 On the odds scale, a one-unit increase in cholesterol multiplies the odds of disease by something between \exp(0.85)=2.34 and \exp(2.26)=9.58. The curve on the probability scale is still an S, flat near 0 and near 1. Drawing the fitted curve at the two endpoints 0.85 and 2.26 is a pointwise band for that single slope. A simultaneous band, allowing the intercept to move as well, is a different object, and it is unnecessary for this one-slope model.
Over the short window from about 4.5 to 7, a straight line and the logistic curve are not dramatically different. That is not a reason to fit the line. A cholesterol of 4.2 or 7.2 would push a straight line outside (0,1). The logistic curve is a valid probability for every cholesterol you might hand it later. If the effect were steeper, the S would be obvious and the line would fail even inside the window. The philosophical objection stands either way.






Figure 1: Probability of disease against cholesterol. Points are jittered off 0 and 1. The shaded window runs from 4.5 to 7. The solid curve is the fitted logistic. The dashed curves keep that intercept and use the endpoints 0.85 and 2.26 of the slope interval. The straight line is least squares, extended until it leaves (0,1).

title: Standard errors, and models for counts
text:
Binomial counts
Often we do not record a zero or a one for every beetle, patient, or firm. We apply a treatment to a group and count the successes. Group sizes need not match. If the members of a group are independent, the likelihood is the Bernoulli likelihood multiplied by a binomial coefficient that does not depend on \boldsymbol{\beta}. The maximiser is unchanged. The data can be stored as two columns, successes and failures, and glm recognises that layout.
Bliss (1935) exposed beetles to carbon disulphide for five hours. The dose on the page is already \log_{10} of concentration, so one unit is a tenfold increase.
