killed <- c(6, 13, 18, 28, 52, 53, 61, 60)
notkilled <- c(53, 47, 48, 28, 11, 6, 1, 0)
response <- cbind(killed, notkilled)
summary(glm(response ~ dose, family = binomial))
The fit, in four Fisher-scoring iterations, is
            Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept)  -61.249      5.206  -11.76   <2e-16
dose           34.555      2.926   11.81   <2e-16
A coefficient of 34.6 per unit of \log_{10} dose is a statement about a tenfold change in concentration, and the experiment only runs from 1.69 to 1.88.






Figure 2: Proportion of beetles killed against log dose, with binomial standard errors. One unit on the horizontal axis is a tenfold change in concentration. The experiment covers only the short stretch drawn here.



Quoting a one-unit effect is like quoting a one-kilometre effect in a study of human height. Bring the unit back to the data. For an increase of 0.01 in log-dose, 
\exp(0.3456)=1.41,
 so the odds of being killed are multiplied by about 1.41. The standard error scales the same way, 2.926\times 0.01=0.02926, and \begin{align*}
\exp(0.3456-1.96\times 0.02926)&=\exp(0.288)=1.33,\\
\exp(0.3456+1.96\times 0.02926)&=\exp(0.403)=1.50.
\end{align*} Rounding can put the upper endpoint at 1.49 rather than 1.50. Either rounding is the same scientific sentence: a small step up in log-dose raises the odds of death by roughly 30 to 50 percent, and the interval sits entirely above 1.
crumbs: Standard errors, and models for counts

title: Standard errors, and models for counts
text:
Counts
A count is a non-negative integer: insurance claims in a year, particles in a Geiger counter, episodes of a behaviour. The mean has to stay non-negative for every covariate. The natural link, and the canonical one, is the log: 
\log\mu_i={\boldsymbol{X}}_i^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}
\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
\mu_i=\exp({\boldsymbol{X}}_i^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}).
\qquad(3) The identity link \mu_i={\boldsymbol{X}}_i^\top\boldsymbol{\beta} is the second thing people reach for. It can look acceptable on a short stretch of x, where an exponential and a straight line are hard to tell apart. It is still not a model we will use. Somewhere outside the window the line is negative, and a mean count cannot be. The log link is a legitimate model for any {\boldsymbol{X}} and any \boldsymbol{\beta}.
The outer distribution for a count, as a starting point, is Poisson: 
Y_i\mid {\boldsymbol{X}}_i\stackrel{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}\mathrm{Poisson}\!\left(\mu_i=\exp({\boldsymbol{X}}_i^\top\boldsymbol{\beta})\right).
 Poisson is the French for fish.1 There is a precise limit behind the “rare events” slogan. If Y\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(n,p) and n\to\infty with p=\lambda/n, then Y converges in distribution to \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda). Five runs in a week is, in that caricature, a coin tossed once a second for 604{,}800 seconds with success probability 5/604800, provided every second is independent of every other second and the probability never changes. Those are the Poisson-process assumptions, and they are the reason a real count is so often not Poisson. A Geiger counter has a dead time after each click. Incidents in a behavioural study arrive in spurts. Even a careful laboratory has a rate that wobbles. The variance is then not exactly the mean.

Quasi-Poisson
Unless there is a strong reason to insist on a pure Poisson process, use 
\mathrm{Var}(Y_i\mid {\boldsymbol{X}}_i)=\phi\mu_i=\phi\exp({\boldsymbol{X}}_i^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}).
\qquad(4) Here \phi>1 is overdispersion and \phi<1 is underdispersion. The case \phi=1 is the Poisson. This is a quasi-Poisson model. The variance function is a legitimate description of spread. Inside the exponential family, a variance exactly proportional to the mean forces the Poisson, so there is no exponential-family distribution with a free \phi in Equation 4. You cannot simulate a new count from a quasi-Poisson specification alone. We will use it as a description. A stricter view, which reserves the name model for something one can simulate from, would refuse the name. We will come back to that distinction when we treat quasi-likelihood properly. For fitting, glm only needs the mean and the variance, so family = quasipoisson runs.


Reading a log-linear coefficient
Two covariates are enough: 
\log\mu=\beta_0+\beta_1 x_1+\beta_2 x_2.
 Increase x_1 by one unit and hold x_2 fixed. The mean is multiplied by e^{\beta_1}. The same sentence with the labels swapped is \beta_2. The intercept is the mean when every covariate is at its baseline, \exp(\beta_0), and it is meaningful only when that baseline is a real situation. Do not judge a slope by whether the coefficient looks small. A small coefficient may be a large effect written in a small unit, and the comparison that matters is with the standard error.


Mine injuries
Myers, Montgomery, and Vining report injuries in the upper seam of 44 West Virginia coal mines. Three covariates survived their selection: inner burden thickness in feet (x_1), the percent already extracted from the seam below (x_2), and years the mine has been open (x_3). The fitted mean used for the interpretation is 
\hat\mu=\exp(-3.2707-0.0015 x_1+0.0627 x_2-0.0317 x_3).
\qquad(5) The glm summary from the fit below prints an intercept of -3.7207, with slopes -0.00148, 0.06270, and -0.03165. The slopes match the rounded values in Equation 5. The intercepts do not: -3.2707 and -3.7207 differ by a transposition. The reading below follows Equation 5 as written, and the standard errors and the dispersion are taken from the printed summary, where the slopes are the quantities being tested.2
On Equation 5, the intercept is the mean number of injuries when the inner burden is 0 feet, nothing has been extracted below, and the mine is brand new: \exp(-3.2707)=0.038. A new mine and a mine with nothing extracted below are imaginable. Zero inner burden is a hole at the surface, which is not a mine. The intercept is algebra, not a sentence to publish.
A one-foot increase in inner burden multiplies the mean by \exp(-0.0015)=0.999. A foot is about thirty centimetres. A per-foot effect is not worth quoting. Per ten feet the coefficient is -0.015, and the mean is multiplied by \exp(-0.015)\approx 0.985. Still a small multiplicative change, and still something to compare with a standard error rather than with 1 by eye.
One extra percentage point of extraction below multiplies injuries by \exp(0.0627)=1.065. One extra year of age multiplies them by \exp(-0.0317)=0.969, which is about 1.03 times fewer injuries. The sign is not the story you might have expected. A dangerous mine may have been closed before it could appear in a data set of mines that are still open. Age in this table is entangled with having survived.
The Poisson log-likelihood is \sum_i\{y_i\log\mu_i-\mu_i\}, up to a constant. Differentiating and setting the score to zero produces 
\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{y_i-\mu_i}{\mu_i}\,\mu_i\,{\boldsymbol{X}}_i
=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\mu_i)\,{\boldsymbol{X}}_i={\boldsymbol{0}}
 when the link is log, because then \mu'=\mu and \mathrm{Var}=\mu, so the two cancel. It is still nonlinear in \boldsymbol{\beta}, because \mu_i=\exp({\boldsymbol{X}}_i^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}). The general score from the previous chapter is the same equation before that cancellation. Software does the iteration.
need <- function(pkg) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  }
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(pkg, character.only = TRUE))
}
need("locfit")
data(mine, package = "locfit")
mines <- data.frame(
  y = mine$frac,
  x1 = mine$inb,
  x2 = mine$extrp,
  x3 = mine$time
)
fit1 <- glm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, data = mines, family = poisson)
fit2 <- glm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, data = mines, family = quasipoisson)
summary(fit1)
summary(fit2)
The Poisson summary is
              Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept) -3.72068    0.97888   -3.801  0.000144
x1          -0.001479   0.000824  -1.794  0.0728
x2           0.06270    0.01227    5.110  3.2e-07
x3          -0.03165    0.01631   -1.941  0.0523
with dispersion fixed at 1. Inner burden and mine age are borderline. Percent extraction is not. The quasi-Poisson summary has the same four estimates. Only the standard errors change, because the estimated dispersion is 0.905, a bit under 1: given these three covariates, the injury counts vary less than a Poisson process. The quasi-Poisson standard errors are smaller by about \sqrt{0.905}, the t statistics move accordingly, and mine age now sits below 0.05 (p=0.048) while inner burden remains borderline (p=0.067). All three terms stay in the model. A term that is hovering on the boundary, and that still carries information, is not dropped. The underdispersion fits the selection story: mines that would have been wild never stayed open long enough to be counted, so the ones we see are a little more deterministic than a pure count process.

title: Standard errors, and models for counts
section: Two models with a real distribution
text:
Two models with a real distribution
A quasi-Poisson variance is not, by itself, a distribution you can draw from. If you want a distribution, and you only need extra variation in the direction of overdispersion, the usual next model is the negative binomial. One construction is a gamma mixture of Poissons: draw a rate from a gamma distribution, then draw a Poisson count at that rate. The mean and variance are 
\mathrm{E}(Y)=\mu,
\qquad
\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\mu+\frac{\mu^2}{\nu},
\qquad \nu>0.
\qquad(6) This is quadratic in the mean, not a constant times the mean. It is always at least the Poisson variance. As \nu\to\infty the extra term vanishes and the Poisson returns. The parameter \nu is traditionally called a dispersion, but a larger \nu concentrates the counts, so it behaves as a concentration. The negative binomial is an exponential family in \mu only when \nu is held fixed. The fit in MASS::glm.nb is a profile: fix \nu, solve the GLM for the mean, move \nu, and repeat.
That mixture cannot produce underdispersion. Counts that are tighter than a Poisson need a different family. The Conway–Maxwell–Poisson distribution has been available since Conway and Maxwell (1962), from queueing theory with dependent waiting times, and it was brought back into statistical use by Shmueli and coauthors in 2005. In the original scaling, 
f(y;\lambda,\nu)\propto \frac{\lambda^y}{(y!)^\nu},
\qquad y=0,1,2,\ldots,
 with \nu<1 overdispersed, \nu=1 exactly Poisson, and \nu>1 underdispersed. Calling \nu a dispersion runs the name backwards: larger \nu means a tighter distribution. The serious defect is that \lambda is not the mean. There is no closed form for \mathrm{E}(Y) or \mathrm{Var}(Y), so a regression on \lambda cannot be compared with a Poisson or negative-binomial regression on \mu.
A repair from 2017 puts the mean in the parameter and solves backwards for the rate: 
f(y;\mu,\nu)\propto \frac{\lambda(\mu,\nu)^y}{(y!)^\nu}.
 Now \mu is exactly the mean, the same parameter as in the Poisson and the negative binomial, and the variance still has no closed form. That is acceptable if the mean is what you came to estimate. The variance is needed for standard errors, and those can be computed after the fit. The bankruptcy-bids example, which is strongly underdispersed once the covariates are in the model, is the next chapter. The point to keep from this chapter is why the mean parameterisation exists: without it, a better AIC on the \lambda scale is not a comparison with a model for the mean.

For the beetle fit, recompute \exp(0.3456\pm 1.96\times 0.02926) and state the interval as a multiplicative change in odds per 0.01 of log-dose. Explain, in one sentence, why the unscaled coefficient 34.6 is a bad unit for that sentence.
The Poisson score set to zero is \sum_i(y_i-\mu_i){\boldsymbol{X}}_i={\boldsymbol{0}} under the log link. Show the cancellation, starting from the general GLM score (y_i-\mu_i)\,\mu'({\boldsymbol{X}}_i^\top\boldsymbol{\beta})/\mathrm{Var}(Y_i).
In the mine regression, the quasi-Poisson estimates match the Poisson estimates and the standard errors do not. Explain why, using the fact that \phi factors out of the score and is estimated afterwards.
State one thing the negative binomial variance Equation 6 can represent that Equation 4 cannot, and one thing the Conway–Maxwell–Poisson can represent that the negative binomial cannot.

title: Warm-up is not a convergence proof
text:
Remark taught in Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings, part of Bayesian statistics
The chain should be initialised in a plausible region when one is available. A start many standard deviations from the typical set can require a long time to return, while a start at the mean of a separated mixture can lie in a low-density gap. Multiple dispersed chains help reveal failure to explore all modes; they do not repair it automatically.
Discarding early draws is called warm-up or burn-in. It limits dependence on the chosen initial state, but it is not a proof of convergence. Strong posterior correlation produces staircase-like Gibbs paths and high autocorrelation. Separated modes are harder still because a coordinate-wise move may have to cross a low-density barrier.
Thinning by retaining every kth draw reduces storage and visible serial dependence, but usually throws away usable information. Unless storage or an expensive downstream calculation is the constraint, retain all post-warm-up draws and quantify their effective sample size. Posterior means, probabilities, and equal-tailed intervals are computed from those draws; a continuous MAP is found by optimisation, not by asking which simulated value occurred most often.

title: Warm-up is not a convergence proof
text:
Examples

Concept check: C15. Warm-up and dependence

Question page: C15. Warm-up and dependence

Does discarding MCMC warm-up guarantee convergence or make the retained draws independent? Explain briefly.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. Warm-up (burn-in) is an initial segment discarded to reduce the influence of initialisation. Discarding it neither proves convergence nor removes serial dependence: even a chain at equilibrium generally has dependent successive states, so mixing and Monte Carlo precision still need assessment.





Practice set: Q19. Assessing a Metropolis–Hastings sampler

Question page: Q19. Assessing a Metropolis–Hastings sampler

[4 marks]
A researcher runs a random-walk Metropolis–Hastings sampler using a Normal proposal centred at the current state. The proposal standard deviation is very small, and approximately 99% of proposals are accepted. The researcher concludes that the sampler is highly efficient.
Explain why the acceptance rate alone does not justify this conclusion. Describe the behaviour you would expect from this sampler and identify one additional feature of its output that you would examine.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. The acceptance rate is the fraction of proposed moves accepted. Autocorrelation measures dependence between draws at different lags. For a chosen posterior summary, effective sample size is the number of independent target draws giving comparable Monte Carlo precision. Efficiency concerns that precision per unit of computation, not the acceptance fraction alone.
An acceptance rate of 99% does not by itself demonstrate efficiency. With a very small proposal standard deviation, proposed values lie close to the current state. The target density changes little across such a short move, so most proposals are accepted; however, each accepted move advances the chain only a small distance.
The expected consequences are slow exploration of the posterior and strong autocorrelation between successive draws. A large recorded sample may then contain information equivalent to a much smaller independent sample.
In addition to acceptance rate, useful diagnostics include:

a trace plot, to assess whether the chain explores the full target region;
the autocorrelation function, to measure serial dependence; and
the effective sample size, to quantify the independent information represented by the chain.

Thus a very high acceptance rate may indicate that the proposal scale is too small, not that the sampler is highly efficient.
An exact independent draw from the target would also have acceptance probability one and would be efficient. High acceptance is therefore neither sufficient evidence of efficiency nor inherently a fault; the movement and dependence matter.

title: Three easy confusions
text:
Remark

The marginal variance posterior has inverse-Gamma shape (n-p)/2, not (n+p)/2. The p/2 belongs to the coefficient normalising constant and must be subtracted from the original power.
Drawing first from p(\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{y}}) and then from p({\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid\sigma^2,{\boldsymbol{y}}) produces iid posterior draws. A genuine Gibbs sampler instead uses p(\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{y}}) and therefore produces a Markov chain.

title: Systematic-scan Gibbs sampler
text:
Definition taught in Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings, part of Bayesian statistics
Suppose the target is a joint density \pi(x_1,\ldots,x_p) that is difficult to sample from directly, while every full conditional is available. One Gibbs sweep updates coordinates in order: \begin{align*}
X_1^{(t+1)}&\sim
\pi(x_1\mid X_2^{(t)},\ldots,X_p^{(t)}),\\
X_2^{(t+1)}&\sim
\pi(x_2\mid X_1^{(t+1)},X_3^{(t)},\ldots,X_p^{(t)}),\\
&\ \vdots\\
X_p^{(t+1)}&\sim
\pi(x_p\mid X_1^{(t+1)},\ldots,X_{p-1}^{(t+1)}).
\end{align*} Each update uses the newest available coordinate values. Under standard ergodicity conditions, X^{(t)} converges in distribution to \pi. For a full conditional, the other coordinates are held fixed. Therefore
\pi(x_i\mid x_{-i})
=\frac{\pi(x_i,x_{-i})}{\pi(x_{-i})}
\propto\pi(x_i,x_{-i})
\quad\text{as a function of }x_i.
Terms involving only x_{-i} may be dropped, but any term that still contains x_i must remain. Gibbs accepts every coordinate draw because it samples from the exact conditional rather than proposing and rejecting a candidate.

title: Systematic-scan Gibbs sampler
text:
Properties

Full conditionals under independent priors

Main article: Full conditionals under independent priors

Holding \sigma^2 fixed, the calculation from Equation (1) in Conjugate analysis for normal models applies verbatim: 
\boxed{
\mu\mid\sigma^2,{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{N}\!\left(
\frac{n\overline x\,\sigma_0^2+\mu_0\sigma^2}
      {n\sigma_0^2+\sigma^2},
\frac{\sigma^2\sigma_0^2}{n\sigma_0^2+\sigma^2}
\right)}.
 Holding \mu fixed, the calculation from Equation (3) in Conjugate analysis for normal models applies: 
\boxed{
\sigma^2\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\!\left(
\alpha_0+\frac n2,
\beta_0+\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2
\right)}.



Warm-up is not a convergence proof

Main article: Warm-up is not a convergence proof

The chain should be initialised in a plausible region when one is available. A start many standard deviations from the typical set can require a long time to return, while a start at the mean of a separated mixture can lie in a low-density gap. Multiple dispersed chains help reveal failure to explore all modes; they do not repair it automatically.
Discarding early draws is called warm-up or burn-in. It limits dependence on the chosen initial state, but it is not a proof of convergence. Strong posterior correlation produces staircase-like Gibbs paths and high autocorrelation. Separated modes are harder still because a coordinate-wise move may have to cross a low-density barrier.
Thinning by retaining every kth draw reduces storage and visible serial dependence, but usually throws away usable information. Unless storage or an expensive downstream calculation is the constraint, retain all post-warm-up draws and quantify their effective sample size. Posterior means, probabilities, and equal-tailed intervals are computed from those draws; a continuous MAP is found by optimisation, not by asking which simulated value occurred most often.

title: Systematic-scan Gibbs sampler
text:
Examples

Bivariate exponential target

Worked example from Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings

The target is

\pi(x_1,x_2)\propto
e^{-x_1x_2-x_1-x_2},
\qquad x_1,x_2\geq0.

Question. Derive both full conditional distributions and use them to specify a systematic-scan Gibbs sampler.
Solution. To obtain X_1\mid X_2=x_2, hold x_2 fixed: \begin{align*}
\pi(x_1\mid x_2)
&\propto\pi(x_1,x_2)\\
&\propto e^{-x_1x_2-x_1-x_2}\\
&\propto e^{-x_1(x_2+1)},
\qquad x_1\geq0.
\end{align*} The omitted factor e^{-x_2} is constant in x_1. Normalising gives

\pi(x_1\mid x_2)=(x_2+1)e^{-(x_2+1)x_1},

so

X_1\mid X_2=x_2\sim\operatorname{Exp}(x_2+1).

By symmetry,

X_2\mid X_1=x_1\sim\operatorname{Exp}(x_1+1).

Starting from any nonnegative pair (x_1^{(0)},x_2^{(0)}), the sampler is \begin{align*}
x_1^{(t+1)}&\sim\operatorname{Exp}(x_2^{(t)}+1),\\
x_2^{(t+1)}&\sim\operatorname{Exp}(x_1^{(t+1)}+1).
\end{align*}


Normal mean and variance

Worked example from Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings

Question. For the joint normal-model posterior in Equation (4) in Conjugate analysis for normal models, describe a systematic Gibbs sampler and state how retained draws estimate the posterior mean of \mu.
Solution. For the joint posterior in Equation (4) in Conjugate analysis for normal models, alternate \begin{align*}
\mu^{(t+1)}&\sim
p(\mu\mid\sigma^{2(t)},{\boldsymbol{x}})
\quad\text{using (5)},\\
\sigma^{2(t+1)}&\sim
p(\sigma^2\mid\mu^{(t+1)},{\boldsymbol{x}})
\quad\text{using (6)}.
\end{align*} After discarding a warm-up segment, Monte Carlo estimates use the retained draws. For example,

\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\frac1L\sum_{t=B+1}^{B+L}\mu^{(t)},

where B is the number of discarded iterations. Because the draws are dependent, L correlated draws contain less information than L independent draws. Autocorrelation, trace plots, multiple chains, and effective sample size are therefore part of a serious analysis.


Practice set: Q4. Gibbs sampling from full conditionals

Question page: Q4. Gibbs sampling from full conditionals

Let X\in\{0,1,\ldots,10\} and 0<\theta<1 have joint density/mass function \pi(x,\theta)
  \propto
  \binom{10}{x}\theta^{x+1}(1-\theta)^{12-x}.
(a) [2 marks] Find and identify the conditional distribution of X\mid\theta.
(b) [2 marks] Find and identify the conditional distribution of \theta\mid X=x.
(c) [3 marks] Hence write pseudocode for a Gibbs sampler that generates a Markov chain with equilibrium distribution \pi(x,\theta). Begin from an arbitrary valid starting value (x^{(0)},\theta^{(0)}).
(d) [2 marks] Explain why there is no accept-reject step in this Gibbs sampler.
(e) [1 mark] Are the resulting pairs \bigl(X^{(1)},\theta^{(1)}\bigr),
          \bigl(X^{(2)},\theta^{(2)}\bigr),\ldots independent? Briefly explain.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. A full conditional is obtained by normalising the joint in the variable being updated; the other variable is fixed. The relevant kernels are \operatorname{Bin}(n,p):\ \binom nx p^x(1-p)^{n-x},\quad x=0,\ldots,n, \operatorname{Beta}(a,b):\ u^{a-1}(1-u)^{b-1},\quad 0<u<1,\quad a,b>0. Here n=10; superscript (t) denotes a completed Gibbs iteration.

(a) Conditional distribution of X\mid\theta
Holding \theta fixed and retaining the terms that depend on x, \begin{aligned}
  \pi(x\mid\theta)
  &\propto
    \binom{10}{x}\theta^{x+1}(1-\theta)^{12-x}\\
  &=\theta(1-\theta)^2
    \binom{10}{x}\theta^x(1-\theta)^{10-x}\\
  &\propto
    \binom{10}{x}\theta^x(1-\theta)^{10-x}.
\end{aligned} The discarded factor \theta(1-\theta)^2 is constant with respect to x. Therefore, \boxed{X\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Bin}(10,\theta)}.


(b) Conditional distribution of \theta\mid X=x
Holding x fixed, \pi(\theta\mid x)
  \propto
  \theta^{x+1}(1-\theta)^{12-x},
  \qquad 0<\theta<1. The kernel of a \operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta) distribution is \theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1}. Matching powers gives \alpha=x+2,
  \qquad
  \beta=13-x. Hence, \boxed{
    \theta\mid X=x
    \sim\operatorname{Beta}(x+2,13-x)
  }.


(c) Gibbs-sampler pseudocode
Choose any valid starting values x^{(0)}\in\{0,1,\ldots,10\},
  \qquad
  \theta^{(0)}\in(0,1). For t=1,2,\ldots,T:
1. Generate X^{(t)}
          \sim\operatorname{Bin}\bigl(10,\theta^{(t-1)}\bigr).
2. Using the newly generated X^{(t)}, generate \theta^{(t)}
          \sim\operatorname{Beta}\bigl(X^{(t)}+2,13-X^{(t)}\bigr).
3. Store \bigl(X^{(t)},\theta^{(t)}\bigr).
After a suitable burn-in, the stored states have approximately the target equilibrium distribution \pi(x,\theta).


(d) Why there is no accept-reject step
Each update is sampled directly from its exact full conditional distribution. The generated value therefore already has the required conditional distribution and is always accepted. Equivalently, Gibbs sampling is a special case of Metropolis-Hastings whose acceptance probability is 1.


(e) Independence of the sampled pairs
No. The update X^{(t)} depends on \theta^{(t-1)}, and \theta^{(t)} then depends on X^{(t)}. Successive states therefore form a Markov chain and are generally serially dependent. Once the chain is in equilibrium, each individual state has marginal distribution \pi(x,\theta), but this does not make the states independent.

Key result. The two full conditionals are \boxed{
    X\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Bin}(10,\theta),
    \qquad
    \theta\mid X=x\sim\operatorname{Beta}(x+2,13-x)
  }. At each iteration, sample from these in order using the newest available value. Exact full-conditional draws require no rejection, but successive Gibbs states are not independent.







Practice set: Q9. Gibbs sampling for a correlated normal target

Question page: Q9. Gibbs sampling for a correlated normal target

Consider the joint posterior density p(\theta_1,\theta_2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
  \propto
  \exp\left[
    -\frac{\theta_1^2-2\rho\theta_1\theta_2+\theta_2^2}
           {2(1-\rho^2)}
  \right], where \theta_1,\theta_2\in\mathbb{R} and -1<\rho<1 is known.
(a) Derive the two full conditional distributions, identifying their means and variances. [4 marks]
(b) Give pseudocode for a Gibbs sampler with this equilibrium density. Make clear which current or updated value is used at each step. [3 marks]
(c) Suppose the initial pair is drawn exactly from the equilibrium distribution. Are the subsequent sampled pairs necessarily independent? Explain. [2 marks]
(d) When \rho is close to 1, explain why this sampler may move slowly through the joint posterior, even though every Gibbs update is accepted. [3 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. The target coordinates \theta_1,\theta_2 have zero means, unit marginal variances, and correlation \rho, with -1<\rho<1. A full conditional holds the other coordinate and the data x fixed. The Normal kernel \exp\{-(u-m)^2/(2v)\} identifies mean m and variance v>0. Superscript (t) labels the Gibbs sweep.
The joint density has kernel \pi(\theta_1,\theta_2\mid x)
\propto
\exp\left\{
-\frac{1}{2(1-\rho^2)}
\left(\theta_1^2-2\rho\theta_1\theta_2+\theta_2^2\right)
\right\}.

(a) Full conditional distributions
For the first full conditional, p(\theta_1\mid\theta_2,x)
=
\frac{p(\theta_1,\theta_2\mid x)}{p(\theta_2\mid x)}
\propto p(\theta_1,\theta_2\mid x)
\quad\text{as a function of }\theta_1. The denominator is constant when \theta_2 and x are held fixed. Thus the joint kernel is sufficient: terms involving \theta_1 must be kept, while terms free of \theta_1 may be absorbed into the proportionality constant.
We aim to match the Normal kernel \exp\left\{-\frac{(\theta_1-m)^2}{2v}\right\}, where m is the mean and v is the variance. Treat the quadratic form in the joint exponent as a quadratic in \theta_1. Completing the square gives \begin{aligned}
\theta_1^2-2\rho\theta_1\theta_2+\theta_2^2
&=(\theta_1-\rho\theta_2)^2
  -\rho^2\theta_2^2+\theta_2^2\\
&=(\theta_1-\rho\theta_2)^2
  +(1-\rho^2)\theta_2^2.
\end{aligned} Substitution into the joint kernel gives \begin{aligned}
p(\theta_1\mid\theta_2,x)
&\propto
\exp\left\{
-\frac{(\theta_1-\rho\theta_2)^2+(1-\rho^2)\theta_2^2}
{2(1-\rho^2)}
\right\}\\
&=
\exp\left\{-\frac{(\theta_1-\rho\theta_2)^2}
{2(1-\rho^2)}\right\}
\exp\left\{-\frac{\theta_2^2}{2}\right\}\\
&\propto
\exp\left\{-\frac{(\theta_1-\rho\theta_2)^2}
{2(1-\rho^2)}\right\}.
\end{aligned} The factor \exp(-\theta_2^2/2) is dropped because it is constant with respect to \theta_1. Matching the remaining expression to the Normal kernel yields \boxed{
\theta_1\mid\theta_2,x
\sim N\left(\rho\theta_2,\,1-\rho^2\right).
} The condition -1<\rho<1 ensures that the conditional variance 1-\rho^2 is positive.
For the other coordinate, the same calculation gives \theta_2^2-2\rho\theta_1\theta_2+\theta_1^2
=
(\theta_2-\rho\theta_1)^2+(1-\rho^2)\theta_1^2. Hence, by symmetry, \boxed{
\theta_2\mid\theta_1,x
\sim N\left(\rho\theta_1,\,1-\rho^2\right).
}


(b) Gibbs sampler
Starting from any valid pair (\theta_1^{(0)},\theta_2^{(0)})\in\mathbb{R}^2, repeat for t=1,\ldots,T:
1. Draw \theta_1^{(t)}
    \sim N\left(\rho\theta_2^{(t-1)},\,1-\rho^2\right).
2. Draw \theta_2^{(t)}
    \sim N\left(\rho\theta_1^{(t)},\,1-\rho^2\right).
3. Store (\theta_1^{(t)},\theta_2^{(t)}).
Each update is sampled directly from a full conditional distribution, so no accept–reject step is required.


(c) Equilibrium and independence
If the chain is started in equilibrium, every stored pair has the required joint distribution. The pairs are nevertheless generally not independent, because the distribution of the next pair depends on the current pair through the Gibbs updates.
When \rho=0, the coordinates are independent and fresh conditional draws produce independent pairs across full sweeps. This exception does not apply to a correlated target.


(d) Effect of strong correlation
When \rho is close to 1, the joint density is concentrated around the diagonal \theta_1=\theta_2, while the conditional variance 1-\rho^2 is close to zero. Each Gibbs update therefore makes only a small move along the narrow high-density region. This produces strong autocorrelation and slow mixing. Thus, although every Gibbs proposal is accepted, an acceptance rate of one does not imply efficient exploration of the target distribution.






Final preparation: Question 6. Geometric–beta Gibbs sampler

Question page: Question 6. Geometric–beta Gibbs sampler

Consider X and Y with joint density

f(x,y)\propto y^{\alpha}(1-y)^{x+\beta-1},

for x=1,2,3,\ldots and 0<y<1, where \alpha>0 and \beta>0. Describe a Gibbs sampler for this joint density.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. This target has one discrete coordinate X\in\{1,2,\ldots\} and one continuous coordinate Y\in(0,1). Here \operatorname{Geom}(p) counts trials up to and including the first success, with mass p(1-p)^{x-1}. A \operatorname{Beta}(a,b) density is proportional to y^{a-1}(1-y)^{b-1}. When finding a full conditional, keep all factors involving the coordinate being updated and normalise over that coordinate’s support.
For 0<y<1, the factors in x are (1-y)^{x-1}. For r=1-y\in(0,1),

\sum_{x=1}^{\infty}r^{x-1}=\frac{1}{1-r}=\frac{1}{y},

so

X\mid y\sim\operatorname{Geom}(y),
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(X=x\mid y)=y(1-y)^{x-1},\quad x=1,2,\ldots.

The factors in y are y^{(\alpha+1)-1}(1-y)^{(x+\beta)-1}, so

Y\mid x\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+1,\,x+\beta).

Record the completed pair. Each draw is from an exact full conditional, so there is no acceptance step. To see why an update preserves the joint target, suppose a pair already has density f: leaving Y unchanged and redrawing X from f(x\mid Y) gives f_Y(y)f(x\mid y)=f(x,y) again. The same reasoning applies to the other coordinate and hence to their composition. Convergence from the chosen start still needs assessment, and successive sweeps are generally dependent.
The target is proper: summing its kernel over x leaves y^{\alpha-1}(1-y)^\beta, which has a finite beta integral for the stated positive parameters. In fact, this also identifies Y\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta+1) marginally. It provides a useful check on a Gibbs simulation; it is different from the full conditional Y\mid X.
Support and mixing checks. Correct full conditionals alone do not guarantee useful exploration. For example, take a target uniform on the two disjoint squares (0,1)^2 and (2,3)^2. Updating one coordinate while holding the other fixed cannot leave the current square, so a single-coordinate Gibbs chain cannot explore the whole target. The present geometric–beta target is positive over its product support and has no such hard separation. Strong dependence can nevertheless make exploration slow; a longer discarded prefix does not fix poor mixing. If implementing the first draw with R’s rgeom, add one because R counts failures before success.

title: Statistic and estimator
text:
Definition taught in Exponential families and conjugacy, part of Bayesian statistics
Write the complete sample as {\boldsymbol{X}}=(X_1,\ldots,X_n) and its realised value as {\boldsymbol{x}}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n). A statistic is any function
T=T({\boldsymbol{X}})
of the random data alone. It cannot contain an unknown parameter. An estimator is a statistic used to estimate a parameter or a function of one, so every estimator is a statistic but not every statistic is introduced for estimation. For example, \overline X, \max_iX_i, and \sum_i(X_i-\overline X)^2 are all statistics.

title: Sequential coherence
text:
Proposition taught in The Beta–Binomial model, part of Bayesian statistics
Sequential updating is exact. If data arrive in batches (x_1,n_1) and (x_2,n_2), then \begin{align*}
  \theta\mid x_1
  &\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+x_1,\beta+n_1-x_1),\\
  \theta\mid x_1,x_2
  &\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+x_1+x_2,
                 \beta+n_1+n_2-x_1-x_2),
\end{align*} which is the same posterior obtained by combining both batches first.

title: Proportional-odds model
text:
Definition taught in Categorical responses, part of Generalised linear models
A proportional-odds model for ordered categories 1,\ldots,K and covariates {\boldsymbol{x}} is 
\mathrm{logit}\,\mathrm{P}(Y\ge k\mid {\boldsymbol{x}})=\beta_{0k}+{\boldsymbol{x}}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta},
\qquad k=2,\ldots,K,
 with \beta_{02}\ge\beta_{03}\ge\cdots\ge\beta_{0K}. A unit increase in a covariate multiplies the odds of being in category k or higher by e^{\beta_j}, and that factor does not depend on k.

title: Prior and posterior predictive distributions
text:
Definition taught in Bayesian foundations, part of Bayesian statistics
Before data are observed, a new observation \widetilde x is generated by first drawing \theta from its prior and then drawing \widetilde x from the sampling model. Marginalising \theta gives the prior predictive density: \begin{align*}
  p(\widetilde x)
  &=\int p(\widetilde x,\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta\\
  &=\int p(\widetilde x\mid\theta)p(\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta.
\end{align*}
After observing x, the analogous calculation uses the posterior: \begin{align*}
  p(\widetilde x\mid x)
  &=\int p(\widetilde x,\theta\mid x)\,\mathrm{d}\theta\\
  &=\int p(\widetilde x\mid\theta,x)p(\theta\mid x)\,\mathrm{d}\theta\\
  &=\int p(\widetilde x\mid\theta)p(\theta\mid x)\,\mathrm{d}\theta.
\end{align*} The last equality uses conditional independence of future and observed data given \theta. Prediction therefore averages the sampling model over parameter uncertainty instead of plugging in a single estimate.
The prior predictive distribution asks what data the complete model regarded as plausible before seeing the observations. It is therefore useful for study design and for detecting a prior that places most of its mass on scientifically absurd data. The posterior predictive distribution asks what future data are plausible after learning from x. It is used for forecasting and for posterior predictive model checks. Although both are mixtures of the sampling distribution, they mix with different distributions for \theta: p(\theta) before the data and p(\theta\mid x) after the data.

title: Prior and posterior predictive distributions
text:
Properties

Predictive-variance decomposition

Main article: Predictive-variance decomposition

Under the conditional-independence assumption above, 
\boxed{
\operatorname{Var}(\widetilde X\mid x)
=\underbrace{\mathbb{E}\{v(\theta)\mid x\}}_{\textnormal{future-observation noise}}
+\underbrace{\operatorname{Var}\{m(\theta)\mid x\}}_{\textnormal{parameter uncertainty}}.}



Beta–Binomial posterior prediction

Main article: Beta–Binomial posterior prediction

If \theta\mid x\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a,b) and, conditionally on \theta, \widetilde X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(m,\theta), then

\mathbb{P}(\widetilde X=k\mid x)
=\binom mk\frac{B(k+a,m-k+b)}{B(a,b)},
\qquad k=0,\ldots,m.

For one future Bernoulli observation, \mathbb{P}(\widetilde Y=1\mid x)=a/(a+b).


Posterior prediction under the reference prior

Main article: Posterior prediction under the reference prior


\boxed{
\widetilde Y\mid{\boldsymbol{y}},{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}},\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim t_{n-p}\!\left(
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}^\top\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},
s\sqrt{1+h(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}})}\right).}
 For the unknown mean response itself, there is no new observational error: 
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}^\top{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid{\boldsymbol{y}},{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}
\sim t_{n-p}\!\left(
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}^\top\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},
s\sqrt{h(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}})}\right).

title: Prior and posterior predictive distributions
text:
Examples

Practice set: Q7. Normal estimation and prediction

Question page: Q7. Normal estimation and prediction

Suppose that, conditionally on \mu, X_1,\ldots,X_n\mid\mu
  \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2), where \sigma^2>0 is known. Use the prior \mu\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_0,\tau^2), where \tau^2>0 is known.
(a) By completing the square in \mu, derive its posterior distribution. Denote the posterior mean and variance by m and v. [4 marks]
(b) Let X_{\mathrm{new}} be a further observation, independent of the observed sample given \mu. Derive its posterior predictive distribution. Explain the two sources of its variance. [4 marks]
(c) As n\to\infty, with \sigma^2 and the prior fixed, what happens to the posterior variance of \mu and the predictive variance of X_{\mathrm{new}}? Explain why they behave differently. [2 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. The notation N(m,v) uses mean m and variance v; precision is 1/v. The data have known variance \sigma^2>0, and the mean prior is N(\mu_0,\tau^2) with \tau^2>0. Write \bar x=n^{-1}\sum_i x_i. Posterior prediction averages a new observation’s sampling distribution over the parameter posterior; that observation is independent of the original sample conditional on \mu.

(a) Posterior distribution of \mu
Start from independence and the specified prior: L(\mu;{\boldsymbol{x}})=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}
\exp\left[-\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right],
\qquad
p(\mu)\propto\exp\left[-\frac{(\mu-\mu_0)^2}{2\tau^2}\right]. The identity \sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2+n(\mu-\bar x)^2 follows by expanding around \bar x; the cross term is zero because \sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=0. Bayes’ theorem multiplies these two kernels. Ignoring terms that do not depend on \mu, \begin{aligned}
  p(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
  &\propto
  \exp\left[
    -\frac{n}{2\sigma^2}(\mu-\bar{x})^2
    -\frac{1}{2\tau^2}(\mu-\mu_0)^2
  \right]\\
  &\propto
  \exp\left[
    -\frac12
    \left\{
      \left(\frac{n}{\sigma^2}+\frac{1}{\tau^2}\right)\mu^2
      -2\left(
        \frac{n\bar{x}}{\sigma^2}+\frac{\mu_0}{\tau^2}
      \right)\mu
    \right\}
  \right].
\end{aligned} Define v=\left(\frac{n}{\sigma^2}+\frac{1}{\tau^2}\right)^{-1},
  \qquad
  m=v\left(
    \frac{n\bar{x}}{\sigma^2}+\frac{\mu_0}{\tau^2}
  \right). Completing the square gives p(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
  \propto
  \exp\left[-\frac{(\mu-m)^2}{2v}\right], so \boxed{\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(m,v)}. Equivalently, v=\frac{\sigma^2\tau^2}{n\tau^2+\sigma^2},
  \qquad
  m=\frac{n\tau^2\bar{x}+\sigma^2\mu_0}
          {n\tau^2+\sigma^2}.


(b) Posterior predictive distribution
Conditional on \mu, X_{\mathrm{new}}=\mu+\varepsilon,
  \qquad
  \varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2), where \varepsilon is independent of \mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}. Since \mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(m,v), \boxed{
    X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
    \sim\mathcal{N}(m,\sigma^2+v)
  }. The predictive variance can also be obtained from \begin{aligned}
  \operatorname{Var}(X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
  &=
  \mathbb{E}\!\left[
    \operatorname{Var}(X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}})
    \mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
  \right]\\
  &\quad+
  \operatorname{Var}\!\left(
    \mathbb{E}[X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}}]
    \mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
  \right)\\
  &=\sigma^2+v.
\end{aligned} Here \sigma^2 is future-observation noise and v is uncertainty about the unknown mean.


(c) Limiting variances
As n\to\infty, v=\left(\frac{n}{\sigma^2}+\frac{1}{\tau^2}\right)^{-1}
  \longrightarrow0, whereas \operatorname{Var}(X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
  =\sigma^2+v
  \longrightarrow\sigma^2. Increasing n removes uncertainty about \mu, but it does not remove the irreducible sampling variation in a new observation.






Practice set: Q20. Estimation and prediction

Question page: Q20. Estimation and prediction

[4 marks]
Suppose measurements are conditionally independent with X_i\mid\mu\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2), where \sigma^2>0 is known, and a proper Normal prior is used for \mu.
Explain the difference between the posterior distribution of \mu and the posterior predictive distribution of one new measurement. As the number of observations becomes very large, would you expect uncertainty about both quantities to approach zero? Explain your reasoning.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. \mu is the population mean and \widetilde X is a new observation. Write \mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim N(m_n,v_n), where v_n is the posterior variance. The known observation variance is \sigma^2>0; conditional on \mu, the new Normal observation is independent of the original sample. A predictive distribution averages over parameter uncertainty as well as new-observation noise.
The posterior distribution p(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}) describes remaining uncertainty about the unknown population mean \mu after observing the data. The posterior predictive distribution p(\widetilde x\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\int p(\widetilde x\mid\mu)
p(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\,d\mu describes uncertainty about a future observation \widetilde X. It includes both uncertainty about \mu and the new observation’s sampling variation around \mu.
If \mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(m_n,v_n), then \boxed{
\widetilde X\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\mathcal{N}(m_n,\sigma^2+v_n).
} As n\to\infty, under the model and standard regularity conditions, v_n\longrightarrow0. Hence posterior uncertainty about \mu approaches zero. By contrast, \operatorname{Var}(\widetilde X\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{new-observation noise}}
+\underbrace{v_n}_{\text{parameter uncertainty}}
\longrightarrow\sigma^2. Predictive uncertainty therefore does not vanish: even if \mu were known exactly, a future measurement would still vary randomly around it.

title: Precision weighting
text:
Remark taught in Conjugate analysis for normal models, part of Bayesian statistics
Writing
w=\frac{\sigma^2}{n\sigma_0^2+\sigma^2}
turns Equation (2) in Conjugate analysis for normal models into
\mu_1=(1-w)\overline x+w\mu_0.
The posterior mean is therefore a precision-weighted average. Equivalently, if \kappa_0=\sigma^2/\sigma_0^2, then
\mu_1=\frac{n\overline x+\kappa_0\mu_0}{n+\kappa_0}.
Thus the prior behaves like \kappa_0 observations whose mean is \mu_0. In the special case \sigma_0^2=\sigma^2, it behaves like one extra observation at \mu_0.

title: Precision weighting
text:
Examples

Final preparation: Question 1. Normal mean, known variance

Question page: Question 1. Normal mean, known variance

Let

X_i\mid\mu\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^2),

with \sigma^2 known and \mu\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu_0,\sigma_0^2).
(a) Using only the precision-addition rule and the precision-weighted mean, write the two updated parameters of the posterior for \mu.
(b) Define the prior equivalent sample size, and state what it counts.
(c) Explain why the posterior mean is a precision-weighted average of the prior mean and the sample mean.
(d) State and interpret the limiting posterior mean and variance as n\to\infty, with the prior parameters fixed and \bar X_n\to\mu^{\ast}.
(e) State the posterior predictive distribution of one new observation X_{\mathrm{new}}, conditionally independent of the sample given \mu.
(f) Explain why the posterior predictive variance is larger than the posterior variance of \mu.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write \bar x=n^{-1}\sum_i x_i. A normal distribution \operatorname{N}(m,v) has mean m and variance v; its precision is 1/v. Here \sigma^2 is the known observation variance, \sigma_0^2 is the prior variance of the unknown mean, and \sigma_1^2 will be its posterior variance. These are variances of different objects.
(a) The data precision of n observations is n/\sigma^2, and the prior precision is 1/\sigma_0^2. Precision addition gives

\frac1{\sigma_1^2}
=
\frac n{\sigma^2}+\frac1{\sigma_0^2}.

The posterior mean is the precision-weighted average of \bar x and \mu_0:

\mu_1
=
\frac{(n/\sigma^2)\bar x+(1/\sigma_0^2)\mu_0}{n/\sigma^2+1/\sigma_0^2}
=
\frac{n\bar x\,\sigma_0^2+\mu_0\sigma^2}{n\sigma_0^2+\sigma^2}.


\boxed{\mu\mid x\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2).}

(b)

\kappa_0=\frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma_0^2}.

It counts how many observations of variance \sigma^2 have the same precision as the prior, since 1/\sigma_0^2=\kappa_0/\sigma^2.
Consequently, \mu_1=(n\bar x+\kappa_0\mu_0)/(n+\kappa_0) and \sigma_1^2=\sigma^2/(n+\kappa_0). The equivalent sample size measures information about the common mean. It need not be an integer or represent actual previous observations.
(c) Up to an additive constant free of \mu, the log posterior is

-\frac{n}{2\sigma^2}(\bar x-\mu)^2-\frac{1}{2\sigma_0^2}(\mu-\mu_0)^2.

Its derivative is (n/\sigma^2)(\bar x-\mu)-(1/\sigma_0^2)(\mu-\mu_0). Setting the derivative equal to zero balances the two pulls, so

\mu_1
=
\frac{(n/\sigma^2)\bar x+(1/\sigma_0^2)\mu_0}{n/\sigma^2+1/\sigma_0^2}.

The second derivative is -n/\sigma^2-1/\sigma_0^2<0, so this stationary point is the unique posterior mode. The posterior is normal, hence its mode equals its mean. This derives the weighting rule: moving away from a more precise source incurs a larger quadratic penalty. The two weights are nonnegative and sum to one, so the posterior mean lies between \bar x and \mu_0.
(d) Let w_n=(n/\sigma^2)/(n/\sigma^2+1/\sigma_0^2). Then w_n\to 1 and

\mu_1=w_n\bar X_n+(1-w_n)\mu_0\to\mu^{\ast},
\qquad
\sigma_1^2=\Bigl(\frac n{\sigma^2}+\frac1{\sigma_0^2}\Bigr)^{-1}\to 0.

With the prior held fixed, the data precision dominates. The posterior concentrates at the limiting sample mean.
This conclusion uses the stated convergence \bar X_n\to\mu^\ast. Under the iid normal model with true mean \mu^\ast, that convergence follows from the law of large numbers. A fixed prior contributes a fixed amount of precision, while the likelihood contributes an amount growing linearly with n.
(e) Given \mu, X_{\mathrm{new}} is independent of the sample and X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid\mu\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^2). Since \mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2),

\boxed{X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu_1,\sigma^2+\sigma_1^2).}

To see the distributional result, write X_{\mathrm{new}}=\mu+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{new}}, where \varepsilon_{\mathrm{new}}\sim\operatorname{N}(0,\sigma^2) is independent of the posterior draw of \mu. Conditional on the observed sample, this is a sum of two independent normal variables. Merely replacing \mu by \mu_1 would omit uncertainty about the unknown mean.
(f) By the law of total variance,

\operatorname{Var}(X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=
\mathbb{E}[\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}]+\operatorname{Var}(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=
\sigma^2+\sigma_1^2.

The term \sigma_1^2 is uncertainty about \mu. The term \sigma^2 is the variance of a new observation even if \mu is known. Both are positive, so the predictive variance exceeds the posterior variance of \mu.

title: Posterior predictive target
text:
Definition taught in Bayesian linear regression, part of Bayesian statistics
Prediction requires a new random quantity; estimating a fitted mean and predicting a new observation are not the same problem. For a new predictor vector \widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}, suppose 
\widetilde Y\mid{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2,\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{N}(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}^\top{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2).
 The posterior predictive density is 
p(\widetilde y\mid{\boldsymbol{y}},{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}},\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\int_0^\infty\int_{\mathbb{R}^p}
p(\widetilde y\mid{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2,\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}})
p({\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{y}},{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})
\,\mathrm{d}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\,\mathrm{d}\sigma^2.

title: Posterior predictive target
text:
Examples

Practice set: Q24. Bayesian regression and prediction

Question page: Q24. Bayesian regression and prediction

[12 marks]
Consider the regression model Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad
\varepsilon_i\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2), with reference prior p(\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma^2)\propto1/\sigma^2 for (\beta_0,\beta_1)\in\mathbb{R}^2 and \sigma^2>0. For n=10 observations, the design matrix has rows (1,x_i), and \widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
(X^\top X)^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1/10&0\\0&1/40\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \operatorname{SSE}=16. The observed predictor values range from -3 to 3.
You may use the standard regression posterior formulas under this prior. Use the inverse-Gamma convention f(v)\propto v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v}. Write t_\nu(m,s) for a Student-t distribution with location m and scale s, and use t_{0.975,8}=2.306.
(a) [2 marks] State the marginal posterior distribution of \sigma^2 and calculate \mathbb{E}(\sigma^2\mid\mathbf y,X).
(b) [3 marks] State the marginal posterior distribution of the slope \beta_1, and calculate its equal-tailed 95% credible interval.
(c) [4 marks] At x_*=0, derive the posterior distributions and equal-tailed 95% intervals for:
(i) the unknown mean response \mu_*=\beta_0+\beta_1x_*;
(ii) a new observation \widetilde Y.
Explain precisely why the second interval is wider.
(d) [3 marks] Calculate h(x_*)=(1,x_*)(X^\top X)^{-1}(1,x_*)^\top at x_*=0 and x_*=4. Compare the posterior predictive scales at these points and explain how the calculation reflects uncertainty from extrapolation.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write D=(\mathbf y,X), v=\sigma^2, and \operatorname{SSE}=\|\mathbf y-X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\|^2. The inverse-Gamma kernel is v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v} on v>0. t_\nu(m,s) denotes location m, scale s, and \nu degrees of freedom: (T-m)/s\sim t_\nu. A scale is not a variance; t_{q,\nu} denotes the q quantile of standard t_\nu.
Assumptions. Use independent Normal errors, fixed covariates, full column rank X, n>p, positive SSE, and the reference prior p(\boldsymbol\beta,v)\propto1/v with respect to d\boldsymbol\beta\,dv. These rank and residual conditions ensure a proper posterior despite the improper prior.
There are p=2 regression coefficients, including the intercept. Define \nu=n-p=8,\qquad
s^2=\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}{n-p}=\frac{16}{8}=2,
\qquad C=(X^\top X)^{-1}. Here s^2 is the residual variance estimate; it is not the posterior mean of \sigma^2.
Why the regression posterior has this form. The likelihood times the reference prior gives p(\boldsymbol\beta,v\mid D)
\propto v^{-n/2-1}
\exp\{-\|\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta\|^2/(2v)\},
\qquad v=\sigma^2>0. Expand about the least-squares estimate. The cross term vanishes because X^\top(\mathbf y-X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})=\mathbf0, giving \|\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta\|^2
=\operatorname{SSE}
+(\boldsymbol\beta-\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})^\top
X^\top X(\boldsymbol\beta-\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}). The second term is a Normal quadratic. At fixed v it identifies \boldsymbol\beta\mid v,D\sim
N_p(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},vC). Its unnormalised exponential integrates to (2\pi v)^{p/2}|X^\top X|^{-1/2}, which explains the v^{p/2} factor in the variance marginal below.
(a) Marginal variance posterior. Under the stated reference prior, \sigma^2\mid D\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\left(\frac{n-p}{2},
\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}2\right). Thus \boxed{\sigma^2\mid D\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(4,8),\qquad\sigma^2>0.} An \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b) variable has mean b/(a-1) when a>1, so \boxed{\mathbb{E}(\sigma^2\mid D)=\frac8{4-1}=\frac83\approx2.6667.} For completeness, integrating the coefficient kernel out of the joint posterior contributes a factor (\sigma^2)^{p/2}. Therefore p(\sigma^2\mid D)
\propto (\sigma^2)^{-(n/2+1)}(\sigma^2)^{p/2}
\exp\!\left(-\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}{2\sigma^2}\right)
=(\sigma^2)^{-5}e^{-8/\sigma^2}, confirming the shape 4, not n/2=5.
(b) Slope posterior and credible interval. The conditional coefficient posterior is \boldsymbol\beta\mid\sigma^2,D
\sim N_2(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},\sigma^2 C). The slope entry of C is 1/40, so \beta_1\mid\sigma^2,D\sim N\!\left(2,\frac{\sigma^2}{40}\right). Integrating over \sigma^2\mid D gives \boxed{\beta_1\mid D\sim t_8\!\left(2,\sqrt{\frac2{40}}\right)
=t_8(2,\sqrt{0.05}).} Equivalently, (\beta_1-2)/\sqrt{0.05}\mid D\sim t_8. The equal-tailed 95% credible interval is therefore 2\pm2.306\sqrt{0.05}=2\pm0.5156,
\qquad\boxed{(1.484,\,2.516).} The second argument of t_8 is a scale, not a variance. There is no additional division by \sqrt n: sample-size information is already in C.
(c) Mean response versus a new observation at x_*=0. For a general predictor value, set \mathbf z_*=(1,x_*)^\top and write m_*=\mathbf z_*^\top\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},
\qquad h(x_*)=\mathbf z_*^\top C\mathbf z_*. The linear-transformation rule for a normal vector gives \mu_*\mid\sigma^2,D
\sim N\bigl(m_*,\sigma^2 h(x_*)\bigr). For a new response \widetilde Y=\mu_*+\widetilde\varepsilon, the new error is independent of the coefficient uncertainty conditional on \sigma^2,D, and has variance \sigma^2. Thus \widetilde Y\mid\sigma^2,D,x_*
\sim N\bigl(m_*,\sigma^2\{1+h(x_*)\}\bigr). Integrating over the inverse-Gamma variance posterior gives \mu_*\mid D\sim t_8\bigl(m_*,s\sqrt{h(x_*)}\bigr), \widetilde Y\mid D,x_*\sim t_8\bigl(m_*,s\sqrt{1+h(x_*)}\bigr). At x_*=0, m_*=(1,0)\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}=1,
\qquad h(0)=\frac1{10}. Therefore the unknown mean response has posterior \boxed{\mu_*\mid D\sim t_8(1,\sqrt{0.2}),} with equal-tailed 95% credible interval 1\pm2.306\sqrt{0.2}=1\pm1.0313,
\qquad\boxed{(-0.031,\,2.031).} The new observation has posterior predictive distribution \boxed{\widetilde Y\mid D,x_*=0\sim t_8(1,\sqrt{2.2}),} with equal-tailed 95% predictive interval 1\pm2.306\sqrt{2.2}=1\pm3.4204,
\qquad\boxed{(-2.420,\,4.420).} Both intervals have the same centre and use the same t_8 quantile. The predictive interval is wider because a new observation includes both uncertainty about the regression mean and fresh observational noise. That additional noise produces the extra 1 in 1+h(x_*).
(d) Extrapolation and predictive scale. Using the supplied diagonal matrix, \begin{aligned}
h(x_*)&=(1,x_*)
\begin{pmatrix}1/10&0\\0&1/40\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}1\\x_*\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\frac1{10}+\frac{x_*^2}{40}.
\end{aligned} Hence \boxed{h(0)=0.1,\qquad h(4)=0.1+\frac{16}{40}=0.5.} The corresponding predictive scales are \boxed{s_{\mathrm{pred}}(0)=\sqrt{2(1+0.1)}=\sqrt{2.2}\approx1.4832,} \boxed{s_{\mathrm{pred}}(4)=\sqrt{2(1+0.5)}=\sqrt3\approx1.7321.} At x_*=4, the predicted centre is 1+2(4)=9, so the predictive distribution is t_8(9,\sqrt3). Its interval is wider than at x_*=0 because it has the same degrees of freedom but a larger scale.
The value 4 lies outside the observed range [-3,3]. Uncertainty about the slope has a greater effect on the fitted mean farther from the centred design, increasing h(x_*). The future-error contribution is unchanged; the increased width comes from greater parameter uncertainty in the prediction. This calculation assumes the linear model remains appropriate beyond the observed range; it does not account for possible failure of that model there.

Key result. The mean-response scale is s\sqrt h; the new-observation scale is s\sqrt{1+h}. The extra 1 represents new observational noise, while h measures uncertainty about the fitted mean.

title: Posterior point summaries
text:
Definition taught in Bayesian foundations, part of Bayesian statistics
For a scalar parameter, common point summaries include
\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)=\int\theta p(\theta\mid x)\,\mathrm{d}\theta,
  \qquad
  \widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MAP}}
  =\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\theta}p(\theta\mid x),
the posterior median, and posterior quantiles. These summaries need not agree for a skewed distribution.

title: Posterior point summaries
text:
Properties

Posterior summaries from draws

Main article: Posterior summaries from draws

Let \theta^{(1)},\ldots,\theta^{(L)} be posterior draws and let \theta_{(1)}\leq\cdots\leq\theta_{(L)} be their order statistics. Then \begin{align*}
\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(\theta\mid x)
&=\frac1L\sum_{l=1}^L\theta^{(l)},\\
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\theta\mid x)
&=\frac1{L-1}\sum_{l=1}^L
   \left(\theta^{(l)}-\overline\theta\right)^2,\\
\widehat{\mathbb{P}}(\theta<c\mid x)
&=\frac1L\sum_{l=1}^L\mathbf{1}\{\theta^{(l)}<c\}.
\end{align*} The posterior median and equal-tailed interval are estimated by the corresponding empirical quantiles. With L=1000, the median can be estimated by the average of \theta_{(500)} and \theta_{(501)}, and a direct 95\% interval approximation by [\theta_{(25)},\theta_{(975)}]. The precise indices vary slightly with a software package’s quantile convention.

title: Posterior point summaries
text:
Examples

Book exercise: Posterior mean under squared-error loss

Question page: Posterior mean under squared-error loss

For observed data {\boldsymbol{x}}, consider the posterior mean squared error of a point estimate d=d({\boldsymbol{x}}),

R(d\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(d-\theta)^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\bigr].

Show, without omitting the quadratic expansion or the minimisation step, that the posterior mean d=\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}) is the minimum-mean-square-error estimator of \theta.






Worked answer (click to show)





Question. For observed data {\boldsymbol{x}}, consider the posterior mean squared error of a point estimate d=d({\boldsymbol{x}}),

R(d\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(d-\theta)^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\bigr].

Show, without omitting the quadratic expansion or the minimisation step, that the posterior mean d=\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}) is the minimum-mean-square-error estimator of \theta.
Solution. Once {\boldsymbol{x}} has been observed, d=d({\boldsymbol{x}}) is a fixed number and only \theta is random under the posterior. Therefore \begin{align*}
R(d\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(d-\theta)^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\bigr]\\
&=\mathbb{E}\bigl[d^2-2d\theta+\theta^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\bigr]\\
&=d^2-2d\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})+\mathbb{E}(\theta^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}).
\end{align*} Put m=\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}). Adding and subtracting m^2 gives \begin{align*}
R(d\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=d^2-2dm+m^2+\mathbb{E}(\theta^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})-m^2\\
&=(d-m)^2+\operatorname{Var}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}).
\end{align*} The posterior variance does not depend on d, and (d-m)^2\geq0 with equality exactly when d=m. Equivalently,

\frac{\partial R}{\partial d}=2d-2m,
\qquad
\frac{\partial^2 R}{\partial d^2}=2>0.

Thus the unique minimiser is

\boxed{d_{\mathrm{MMSE}}({\boldsymbol{x}})=\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})}.






Concept check: C7. MAP and squared-error loss

Question page: C7. MAP and squared-error loss

How does a MAP estimate differ from a Bayes estimate under squared-error loss?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. The MAP maximises p(\theta\mid x), whereas a Bayes estimate minimises the posterior expected loss for a specified loss function. Under squared-error loss and a finite posterior second moment, \mathbb{E}[(\theta-d)^2\mid x]=\operatorname{Var}(\theta\mid x)+(\mathbb{E}[\theta\mid x]-d)^2, so the Bayes estimate is the posterior mean, not generally the mode.

title: Posterior hypothesis probability
text:
Definition taught in Bayesian hypotheses and model comparison, part of Bayesian statistics
Suppose a parameter space \Omega is partitioned into regions \Omega_0 and \Omega_1. The posterior hypothesis probabilities are \begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}(H_0\mid x)
&=\mathbb{P}(\theta\in\Omega_0\mid x)
=\int_{\Omega_0}p(\theta\mid x)\,\mathrm{d}\theta,\\
\mathbb{P}(H_1\mid x)
&=\mathbb{P}(\theta\in\Omega_1\mid x)
=\int_{\Omega_1}p(\theta\mid x)\,\mathrm{d}\theta.
\end{align*} If the two regions exhaust the support, the probabilities sum to one.

title: Posterior hypothesis probability
Posterior hypothesis probability
text:
Examples

Imperfect-fruit decision

Worked example from Bayesian hypotheses and model comparison

Let X_i be the number of imperfect pieces in box i, with about 100 pieces per box. “Imperfect” must be defined before the data are collected so that producer and analyst classify fruit in the same way. The model is

X_i\mid\theta\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Poisson}(\theta),
\qquad
H_0:\theta\leq10,
\quad H_1:\theta>10.

For the observed sample, n=20 and S=\sum_i x_i=177; the stated prior is \theta\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(12,1) in shape–rate form.
Question. Find the posterior distribution, the posterior probabilities and odds for H_0 and H_1, and an equal-tailed 95\% credible interval. Explain why the interval may cross 10 even when most posterior mass lies below it.
Solution. Because the posterior for \theta is continuous,

\mathbb{P}(\theta=10\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=0.

Consequently it makes no numerical difference whether equality is assigned to H_0 or H_1. This is a statement about the continuous parameter, even though the observed fruit counts are discrete.
For n boxes and S=\sum_i x_i, the likelihood is 
\begin{aligned}
p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta)
&=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{e^{-\theta}\theta^{x_i}}{x_i!}\\
&=\left(\prod_{i=1}^n\frac1{x_i!}\right)
   e^{-n\theta}\theta^{\sum_i x_i}\\
&\propto e^{-n\theta}\theta^S.
\end{aligned}
 The working total is S=177 for n=20.
The stated prior is \theta\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(12,1) in the standard shape–rate convention, so

p(\theta)=\frac1{\Gamma(12)}\theta^{12-1}e^{-\theta}
\propto\theta^{11}e^{-\theta}.

Multiplying by the likelihood gives \begin{align*}
p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto
\theta^S e^{-n\theta}\theta^{11}e^{-\theta}\\
&=\theta^{S+11}e^{-(n+1)\theta}\\
&=\theta^{189-1}e^{-21\theta}.
\end{align*} Therefore the internally consistent shape–rate update is 
\boxed{\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(189,21)}.
 Its posterior mean is

\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{189}{21}=9.

The MLE is S/n=177/20=8.85. Although the prior mean 12 lies above the boundary 10, the data move the posterior centre below it.
Let \gamma(a,z)=\int_0^zt^{a-1}e^{-t}\,\mathrm{d} t be the lower incomplete Gamma function. If T\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a,b), then

\mathbb{P}(T\leq t)=\frac{\gamma(a,bt)}{\Gamma(a)}.

Consequently, \begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}(H_0\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=\mathbb{P}(\theta\leq10\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\\
&=\frac{\gamma(189,21\cdot10)}{\Gamma(189)}\\
&=0.93298381,\\
\mathbb{P}(H_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})&=1-0.93298381=0.06701619.
\end{align*} The posterior odds are

\frac{\mathbb{P}(H_0\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})}{\mathbb{P}(H_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})}
=\frac{0.93298381}{0.06701619}
\approx13.92.

The equal-tailed 95\% credible interval is approximately (7.76,10.33). It crosses 10, while 93.3\% of posterior mass lies at or below 10. These are different summaries: interval inclusion does not produce a general accept/reject rule for an interval hypothesis.






Figure 1: The fruit posterior \operatorname{Gamma}(189,21), with the region \theta\leq10 shaded. The two summaries disagree in appearance only. The equal-tailed interval must leave 2.5\% in each tail, so its upper endpoint is pushed past 10; the shaded area answers a different question and puts 93.3\% of the mass at or below the boundary. Reading the crossing as a rejection substitutes one summary for the other.









Parameterisation check



A convention check uses the other Gamma convention. Writing a prior kernel p(\theta)\propto\theta^\alpha e^{-\beta\theta} with \alpha=12 describes \operatorname{Gamma}(13,1), not the stated \operatorname{Gamma}(12,1). That alternative gives \theta\mid x\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(190,21), posterior mean 190/21\approx9.05, \mathbb{P}(\theta\leq10\mid x)=0.92320087, odds 12.02, and interval (7.81,10.38). The main calculation above follows the stated shape–rate prior; the alternative is retained here so that neither that result nor the convention error is hidden.




Practice set: Q21. Evidence and posterior model probabilities

Question page: Q21. Evidence and posterior model probabilities

[4 marks]
An analysis produces a Bayes factor of 4 in favour of model M_1 over model M_0. Before observing the data, the researcher regarded M_0 as nine times as probable as M_1. The researcher concludes:

“The Bayes factor favours M_1, so M_1 must now have the greater posterior probability.”

Assess this conclusion. Explain how the Bayes factor changes the model odds, and identify which model has the greater posterior probability.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. The Bayes factor is B_{10}=p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_1)/p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_0). Odds in favour of M_1 are \mathbb P(M_1)/\mathbb P(M_0), with the analogous conditional ratio for posterior odds. The two models exhaust the comparison, so their probabilities sum to one. Here B_{10}=4 and the prior odds are 1:9.
A Bayes factor updates prior model odds according to \frac{\mathbb{P}(M_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})}{\mathbb{P}(M_0\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})}
=B_{10}
\frac{\mathbb{P}(M_1)}{\mathbb{P}(M_0)}. Because M_0 was initially nine times as probable as M_1, the prior odds in favour of M_1 are \frac{\mathbb{P}(M_1)}{\mathbb{P}(M_0)}=\frac19. With B_{10}=4, the posterior odds become \boxed{
\frac{\mathbb{P}(M_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})}{\mathbb{P}(M_0\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})}
=4\left(\frac19\right)=\frac49.
} Therefore, \mathbb{P}(M_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac4{13},
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(M_0\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac9{13}. The data favour M_1 relative to the prior because B_{10}>1, but the evidence is not strong enough to overcome the initial nine-to-one odds in favour of M_0. Thus \boxed{
\mathbb{P}(M_0\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})>
\mathbb{P}(M_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}).
} The researcher’s conclusion is therefore incorrect: a Bayes factor favouring M_1 does not necessarily make M_1 the more probable model a posteriori.





Concept check: C8. Evidence and model odds

Question page: C8. Evidence and model odds

What are marginal likelihoods and Bayes factors? How does a Bayes factor update model odds?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. For model M_j with a proper parameter prior, its marginal likelihood is m_j(x)=\int p(x\mid\theta_j,M_j)p(\theta_j\mid M_j)\,d\theta_j, and BF_{12}=m_1(x)/m_2(x) is the Bayes factor for M_1 against M_2. Posterior model odds equal BF_{12} times prior model odds; the Bayes factor alone is not a posterior model probability.

title: Normal–Normal model
text:
Definition taught in Conjugate analysis for normal models, part of Bayesian statistics
Assume
X_1,\ldots,X_n\mid\mu
  \stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^2),
where \sigma^2 is known, and use the prior
\mu\sim\operatorname{N}(\mu_0,\sigma_0^2).

title: Normal–Normal model
text:
Properties

Normal–Normal conjugacy

Main article: Normal–Normal conjugacy


\boxed{
  \mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{N}(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)},
 with 
\begin{aligned}
\sigma_1^2
&=\frac1A
=\left(\frac n{\sigma^2}+\frac1{\sigma_0^2}\right)^{-1}
=\frac{\sigma^2\sigma_0^2}{n\sigma_0^2+\sigma^2},
\\
\mu_1
&=\frac BA
=\frac{\sum_i x_i/\sigma^2+\mu_0/\sigma_0^2}
        {n/\sigma^2+1/\sigma_0^2}\\
&=\frac{n\overline x\,\sigma_0^2+\mu_0\sigma^2}
        {n\sigma_0^2+\sigma^2}.
\end{aligned}



Precision weighting

Main article: Precision weighting

Writing

w=\frac{\sigma^2}{n\sigma_0^2+\sigma^2}

turns Equation (2) in Conjugate analysis for normal models into

\mu_1=(1-w)\overline x+w\mu_0.

The posterior mean is therefore a precision-weighted average. Equivalently, if \kappa_0=\sigma^2/\sigma_0^2, then

\mu_1=\frac{n\overline x+\kappa_0\mu_0}{n+\kappa_0}.

Thus the prior behaves like \kappa_0 observations whose mean is \mu_0. In the special case \sigma_0^2=\sigma^2, it behaves like one extra observation at \mu_0.

title: Normal–Normal model
text:
Examples

Final preparation: Question 1. Normal mean, known variance

Question page: Question 1. Normal mean, known variance

Let

X_i\mid\mu\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^2),

with \sigma^2 known and \mu\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu_0,\sigma_0^2).
(a) Using only the precision-addition rule and the precision-weighted mean, write the two updated parameters of the posterior for \mu.
(b) Define the prior equivalent sample size, and state what it counts.
(c) Explain why the posterior mean is a precision-weighted average of the prior mean and the sample mean.
(d) State and interpret the limiting posterior mean and variance as n\to\infty, with the prior parameters fixed and \bar X_n\to\mu^{\ast}.
(e) State the posterior predictive distribution of one new observation X_{\mathrm{new}}, conditionally independent of the sample given \mu.
(f) Explain why the posterior predictive variance is larger than the posterior variance of \mu.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write \bar x=n^{-1}\sum_i x_i. A normal distribution \operatorname{N}(m,v) has mean m and variance v; its precision is 1/v. Here \sigma^2 is the known observation variance, \sigma_0^2 is the prior variance of the unknown mean, and \sigma_1^2 will be its posterior variance. These are variances of different objects.
(a) The data precision of n observations is n/\sigma^2, and the prior precision is 1/\sigma_0^2. Precision addition gives

\frac1{\sigma_1^2}
=
\frac n{\sigma^2}+\frac1{\sigma_0^2}.

The posterior mean is the precision-weighted average of \bar x and \mu_0:

\mu_1
=
\frac{(n/\sigma^2)\bar x+(1/\sigma_0^2)\mu_0}{n/\sigma^2+1/\sigma_0^2}
=
\frac{n\bar x\,\sigma_0^2+\mu_0\sigma^2}{n\sigma_0^2+\sigma^2}.


\boxed{\mu\mid x\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2).}

(b)

\kappa_0=\frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma_0^2}.

It counts how many observations of variance \sigma^2 have the same precision as the prior, since 1/\sigma_0^2=\kappa_0/\sigma^2.
Consequently, \mu_1=(n\bar x+\kappa_0\mu_0)/(n+\kappa_0) and \sigma_1^2=\sigma^2/(n+\kappa_0). The equivalent sample size measures information about the common mean. It need not be an integer or represent actual previous observations.
(c) Up to an additive constant free of \mu, the log posterior is

-\frac{n}{2\sigma^2}(\bar x-\mu)^2-\frac{1}{2\sigma_0^2}(\mu-\mu_0)^2.

Its derivative is (n/\sigma^2)(\bar x-\mu)-(1/\sigma_0^2)(\mu-\mu_0). Setting the derivative equal to zero balances the two pulls, so

\mu_1
=
\frac{(n/\sigma^2)\bar x+(1/\sigma_0^2)\mu_0}{n/\sigma^2+1/\sigma_0^2}.

The second derivative is -n/\sigma^2-1/\sigma_0^2<0, so this stationary point is the unique posterior mode. The posterior is normal, hence its mode equals its mean. This derives the weighting rule: moving away from a more precise source incurs a larger quadratic penalty. The two weights are nonnegative and sum to one, so the posterior mean lies between \bar x and \mu_0.
(d) Let w_n=(n/\sigma^2)/(n/\sigma^2+1/\sigma_0^2). Then w_n\to 1 and

\mu_1=w_n\bar X_n+(1-w_n)\mu_0\to\mu^{\ast},
\qquad
\sigma_1^2=\Bigl(\frac n{\sigma^2}+\frac1{\sigma_0^2}\Bigr)^{-1}\to 0.

With the prior held fixed, the data precision dominates. The posterior concentrates at the limiting sample mean.
This conclusion uses the stated convergence \bar X_n\to\mu^\ast. Under the iid normal model with true mean \mu^\ast, that convergence follows from the law of large numbers. A fixed prior contributes a fixed amount of precision, while the likelihood contributes an amount growing linearly with n.
(e) Given \mu, X_{\mathrm{new}} is independent of the sample and X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid\mu\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^2). Since \mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2),

\boxed{X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu_1,\sigma^2+\sigma_1^2).}

To see the distributional result, write X_{\mathrm{new}}=\mu+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{new}}, where \varepsilon_{\mathrm{new}}\sim\operatorname{N}(0,\sigma^2) is independent of the posterior draw of \mu. Conditional on the observed sample, this is a sum of two independent normal variables. Merely replacing \mu by \mu_1 would omit uncertainty about the unknown mean.
(f) By the law of total variance,

\operatorname{Var}(X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=
\mathbb{E}[\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}]+\operatorname{Var}(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=
\sigma^2+\sigma_1^2.

The term \sigma_1^2 is uncertainty about \mu. The term \sigma^2 is the variance of a new observation even if \mu is known. Both are positive, so the predictive variance exceeds the posterior variance of \mu.





Practice set: Q7. Normal estimation and prediction

Question page: Q7. Normal estimation and prediction

Suppose that, conditionally on \mu, X_1,\ldots,X_n\mid\mu
  \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2), where \sigma^2>0 is known. Use the prior \mu\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_0,\tau^2), where \tau^2>0 is known.
(a) By completing the square in \mu, derive its posterior distribution. Denote the posterior mean and variance by m and v. [4 marks]
(b) Let X_{\mathrm{new}} be a further observation, independent of the observed sample given \mu. Derive its posterior predictive distribution. Explain the two sources of its variance. [4 marks]
(c) As n\to\infty, with \sigma^2 and the prior fixed, what happens to the posterior variance of \mu and the predictive variance of X_{\mathrm{new}}? Explain why they behave differently. [2 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. The notation N(m,v) uses mean m and variance v; precision is 1/v. The data have known variance \sigma^2>0, and the mean prior is N(\mu_0,\tau^2) with \tau^2>0. Write \bar x=n^{-1}\sum_i x_i. Posterior prediction averages a new observation’s sampling distribution over the parameter posterior; that observation is independent of the original sample conditional on \mu.

(a) Posterior distribution of \mu
Start from independence and the specified prior: L(\mu;{\boldsymbol{x}})=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}
\exp\left[-\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right],
\qquad
p(\mu)\propto\exp\left[-\frac{(\mu-\mu_0)^2}{2\tau^2}\right]. The identity \sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2+n(\mu-\bar x)^2 follows by expanding around \bar x; the cross term is zero because \sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=0. Bayes’ theorem multiplies these two kernels. Ignoring terms that do not depend on \mu, \begin{aligned}
  p(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
  &\propto
  \exp\left[
    -\frac{n}{2\sigma^2}(\mu-\bar{x})^2
    -\frac{1}{2\tau^2}(\mu-\mu_0)^2
  \right]\\
  &\propto
  \exp\left[
    -\frac12
    \left\{
      \left(\frac{n}{\sigma^2}+\frac{1}{\tau^2}\right)\mu^2
      -2\left(
        \frac{n\bar{x}}{\sigma^2}+\frac{\mu_0}{\tau^2}
      \right)\mu
    \right\}
  \right].
\end{aligned} Define v=\left(\frac{n}{\sigma^2}+\frac{1}{\tau^2}\right)^{-1},
  \qquad
  m=v\left(
    \frac{n\bar{x}}{\sigma^2}+\frac{\mu_0}{\tau^2}
  \right). Completing the square gives p(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
  \propto
  \exp\left[-\frac{(\mu-m)^2}{2v}\right], so \boxed{\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(m,v)}. Equivalently, v=\frac{\sigma^2\tau^2}{n\tau^2+\sigma^2},
  \qquad
  m=\frac{n\tau^2\bar{x}+\sigma^2\mu_0}
          {n\tau^2+\sigma^2}.


(b) Posterior predictive distribution
Conditional on \mu, X_{\mathrm{new}}=\mu+\varepsilon,
  \qquad
  \varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2), where \varepsilon is independent of \mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}. Since \mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(m,v), \boxed{
    X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
    \sim\mathcal{N}(m,\sigma^2+v)
  }. The predictive variance can also be obtained from \begin{aligned}
  \operatorname{Var}(X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
  &=
  \mathbb{E}\!\left[
    \operatorname{Var}(X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}})
    \mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
  \right]\\
  &\quad+
  \operatorname{Var}\!\left(
    \mathbb{E}[X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}}]
    \mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
  \right)\\
  &=\sigma^2+v.
\end{aligned} Here \sigma^2 is future-observation noise and v is uncertainty about the unknown mean.


(c) Limiting variances
As n\to\infty, v=\left(\frac{n}{\sigma^2}+\frac{1}{\tau^2}\right)^{-1}
  \longrightarrow0, whereas \operatorname{Var}(X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
  =\sigma^2+v
  \longrightarrow\sigma^2. Increasing n removes uncertainty about \mu, but it does not remove the irreducible sampling variation in a new observation.

\boxed{
\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\!\left(
   \alpha_0+\frac n2,
