title: Normal–inverse-Gamma variance update
text:
Examples

Final preparation: Question 2. Normal variance, known mean

Question page: Question 2. Normal variance, known mean

Let

X_i\mid\sigma^2\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^2),

with \mu known and

\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(\alpha_0,\beta_0),

in the shape–rate parameterisation

f(\sigma^2)\propto(\sigma^2)^{-\alpha_0-1}\exp(-\beta_0/\sigma^2).

(a) Write the posterior distribution of \sigma^2, and state what is added to each parameter.
(b) State the posterior mean and mode of \sigma^2, including the conditions under which each exists.
(c) Explain why that mean and mode generally differ.
(d) Explain why the variance update uses squared deviations from the known mean \mu, rather than from \bar x.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Put v=\sigma^2 and Q_\mu=\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2, with \mu known. Our \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b) convention has density b^a v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v}/\Gamma(a) for v>0. Equivalently, 1/v\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a,b) in shape–rate form. Specifying the kernel avoids ambiguity about the second parameter.
(a) Independence gives the likelihood kernel L(v)\propto v^{-n/2}e^{-Q_\mu/(2v)}. Multiplication by the prior gives

p(v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto
v^{-n/2}e^{-Q_\mu/(2v)}v^{-\alpha_0-1}e^{-\beta_0/v}
=v^{-(\alpha_0+n/2)-1}e^{-(\beta_0+Q_\mu/2)/v}.

Let \alpha_n=\alpha_0+n/2 and \beta_n=\beta_0+Q_\mu/2. Recognising this kernel,

\boxed{
\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim
\operatorname{InvGamma}(\alpha_n,\beta_n).
}

Each observation adds 1/2 to the shape. Half the sum of squared deviations from the known mean is added to the rate.
(b) For this shape–rate kernel, and for \beta_n>0,

\mathbb{E}(\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{\beta_n}{\alpha_n-1}
\quad\text{when }\alpha_n>1,
\qquad
\operatorname{mode}(\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{\beta_n}{\alpha_n+1}
\quad\text{when }\alpha_n>0.

The mode solves (-\alpha_n-1)/v+\beta_n/v^2=0. The mean is the gamma integral of v\cdot v^{-\alpha_n-1}e^{-\beta_n/v}, which converges only for \alpha_n>1.
More explicitly, substituting u=\beta_n/v into the expectation gives \mathbb{E}(v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\beta_n\Gamma(\alpha_n-1)/\Gamma(\alpha_n)=\beta_n/(\alpha_n-1). When 0<\alpha_n\le1, the posterior is still a proper distribution, but its right tail is too heavy to have a finite mean. Posterior propriety and existence of a posterior moment are separate requirements.
(c) For \alpha_n>1,

\frac{\beta_n}{\alpha_n-1}-\frac{\beta_n}{\alpha_n+1}
=
\frac{2\beta_n}{(\alpha_n-1)(\alpha_n+1)}>0.

The inverse-gamma density is right-skewed, so the long right tail pulls the mean above the mode.
(d) Under the sampling model, \operatorname{Var}(X_i\mid\sigma^2)=\mathbb{E}[(X_i-\mu)^2\mid\sigma^2]. The sufficient statistic for \sigma^2, with \mu known, is \sum(x_i-\mu)^2. Since

\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2
=
\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2-n(\bar x-\mu)^2,

centring at \bar x omits the term n(\bar x-\mu)^2.
When the mean is known, departures of the sample mean from that value are evidence about the observation variance too. For example, a tightly clustered sample far from the known mean has small \sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2 but large Q_\mu. Replacing Q_\mu by the centred sum of squares would discard that evidence and change the likelihood.





Practice set: Q28. Lognormal variance and conjugate inference

Question page: Q28. Lognormal variance and conjugate inference

[20 marks]
The size X of a certain type of particle can be modelled by a lognormal distribution with density f(x\mid\mu,\sigma^2)
=\frac1{x\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}
\exp\!\left\{-\frac{(\log x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right\},
\qquad x>0. Note that if X\sim\operatorname{logN}(\mu,\sigma^2), then Y=\log X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2). Assume that \mu is known and \sigma^2>0 is unknown. For the posterior calculations, let X_1,\ldots,X_n be conditionally iid observations from this model.
(i) [4 marks] Show that this lognormal model belongs to the exponential family.
(ii) [4 marks] Find the form of a conjugate prior for \sigma^2 and identify the distribution.
(iii) [5 marks] Find the posterior distribution of \sigma^2 given the observed data {\boldsymbol{x}}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n).
(iv) [4 marks] State, without derivation, the posterior mean and posterior mode. Explain their behaviour as n\to\infty, with the prior fixed.
(v) [3 marks] Briefly describe how you would construct a 90% credible interval for \sigma^2.






Worked answer (click to show)





Taking logs converts this to a Normal model with known mean and unknown variance.
Definitions. Write v=\sigma^2 and S=\sum_i(\log x_i-\mu)^2. The log observations have Normal mean \mu and variance v; \mu is known. An \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b) density has kernel v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v} on v>0. Throughout, Gamma distributions of the precision 1/v use shape–rate parameters. The positive observations are conditionally iid; prior propriety and moment conditions are stated below.
(i) Exponential-family form. The density can be written as f(x\mid v)
=\frac1{x\sqrt{2\pi}}
\frac{\exp\!\left\{-\dfrac1v\,
\dfrac{(\log x-\mu)^2}{2}\right\}}{\sqrt v},
\qquad x>0,\quad v>0. Comparing with the course’s form f(x\mid v)=b(x)\frac{\exp\{c(v)T(x)\}}{a(v)}, we identify \boxed{
\begin{gathered}
b(x)=\frac1{x\sqrt{2\pi}},\qquad
T(x)=\frac{(\log x-\mu)^2}{2},\\
c(v)=-\frac1v,\qquad a(v)=\sqrt v.
\end{gathered}} Here \mu is known, so T(x) involves no unknown parameter. The support x>0 also does not depend on v. This establishes the required one-parameter exponential-family representation.
(ii) Conjugate prior. For this representation, the general conjugate prior has kernel \pi(v)\propto\frac{\exp\{\eta c(v)\}}{a(v)^\kappa}
=v^{-\kappa/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac\eta v\right),\qquad v>0. Compare this with the inverse-Gamma kernel \pi(v)\propto v^{-a_0-1}e^{-b_0/v}. Matching the power and exponential term gives a_0=\frac\kappa2-1,\qquad b_0=\eta. Thus a convenient parameterisation of the conjugate prior is \boxed{\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(a_0,b_0),\qquad a_0,b_0>0,} with normalised density \pi(v)=\frac{b_0^{a_0}}{\Gamma(a_0)}
v^{-a_0-1}e^{-b_0/v},\qquad v>0. In the general conjugacy parameters, propriety requires \eta>0 and \kappa>2. The prior is on the variance \sigma^2, not on the standard deviation \sigma.
(iii) Posterior distribution. Define the sum of squared deviations on the log scale, S=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\log x_i-\mu)^2. The likelihood is \begin{aligned}
L(v;{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac1{x_i\sqrt{2\pi v}}
\exp\!\left\{-\frac{(\log x_i-\mu)^2}{2v}\right\}\\
&=(2\pi)^{-n/2}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac1{x_i}\right)
v^{-n/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{S}{2v}\right)\\
&\propto v^{-n/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{S}{2v}\right).
\end{aligned} The factors omitted in the last line do not depend on v. Multiplying by the inverse-Gamma prior, \begin{aligned}
\pi(v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto v^{-n/2}e^{-S/(2v)}v^{-a_0-1}e^{-b_0/v}\\
&=v^{-(a_0+n/2)-1}
\exp\!\left\{-\frac{b_0+S/2}{v}\right\}.
\end{aligned} Let A_n=a_0+\frac n2,\qquad B_n=b_0+\frac S2. Recognising the inverse-Gamma kernel gives \boxed{\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(A_n,B_n),\qquad\sigma^2>0.} Its normalised density is \pi(v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{B_n^{A_n}}{\Gamma(A_n)}
v^{-A_n-1}e^{-B_n/v},\qquad v>0.
(iv) Posterior mean, mode, and large-sample behaviour. The posterior summaries are \boxed{\mathbb{E}(\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{B_n}{A_n-1}
=\frac{b_0+S/2}{a_0+n/2-1},\qquad A_n>1,} \boxed{\widehat{\sigma^2}_{\mathrm{MAP}}=\frac{B_n}{A_n+1}
=\frac{b_0+S/2}{a_0+n/2+1}.} If A_n\leq1, the posterior mean is not finite; the mode exists for all A_n,B_n>0.
For fixed prior parameters and data generated at true variance \sigma_0^2, the law of large numbers gives \frac{S_n}{n}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\log X_i-\mu)^2
\longrightarrow\sigma_0^2. Both posterior summaries approach S_n/n and hence \sigma_0^2: the fixed prior’s influence vanishes. Since \mu is known, S_n/n is the usual likelihood estimate; there is no need to estimate \mu or replace it by the sample log-mean.
(v) A 90% credible interval for the variance. One valid choice is an equal-tailed interval. Let F_{\mathrm{IG}} be the CDF of the posterior \operatorname{InvGamma}(A_n,B_n). Choose its 5% and 95% quantiles: \boxed{\left[F_{\mathrm{IG}}^{-1}(0.05),
F_{\mathrm{IG}}^{-1}(0.95)\right].} This leaves posterior probability 0.05 below the interval and 0.05 above it, so the interval contains 0.90 posterior probability.
Equivalently, use the reciprocal precision W=\frac1{\sigma^2},\qquad
W\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(A_n,B_n)
\quad\text{in shape--rate form}. If q_{0.05} and q_{0.95} are the corresponding Gamma quantiles, then \mathbb{P}(q_{0.05}\leq W\leq q_{0.95}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=0.90. Taking reciprocals reverses the inequalities, giving \boxed{\left[\frac1{q_{0.95}},\frac1{q_{0.05}}\right]} as the same 90% credible interval for \sigma^2. The quantiles can be computed numerically, or approximated by the empirical 5% and 95% quantiles of a large sample drawn from the inverse-Gamma posterior.
This interval is for the unknown variance, not for a new particle size. It is an equal-tailed interval; it need not be the shortest or highest-posterior-density interval.

Key result. Take logs, recognise a normal model with known mean, and update a_0\mapsto a_0+n/2 and b_0\mapsto b_0+\tfrac12\sum_i(\log x_i-\mu)^2.

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid\sigma^2,{\boldsymbol{y}}
\sim\operatorname{N}_p({\boldsymbol{m}}_n,\sigma^2{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{V}}_n),
\qquad

title: Normal–inverse-Gamma conjugacy
text:
Examples

Final preparation: Question 5. Normal–inverse-\chi^2 regression

Question page: Question 5. Normal–inverse-\chi^2 regression

Suppose

y\mid\beta,\sigma^2,X\sim \operatorname{N}_n(X\beta,\sigma^2 I_n),

with prior

\beta\mid\sigma^2\sim \operatorname{N}_p(\beta_0,\sigma^2\Sigma_0),
\qquad
\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{Inv\text{-}\chi^2}(\mu_0,\sigma_0^2).

Here X is known, \Sigma_0 is positive definite, and \mu_0,\sigma_0^2>0. The inverse-\chi^2 convention is

\frac{\mu_0\sigma_0^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_{\mu_0}.

(a) State the inverse-\chi^2 prior kernel and its equivalent inverse-gamma parameters.
(b) State the updated parameters \Sigma_n and \beta_n.
(c) State the updated parameters \mu_n and \sigma_n^2.
(d) Express the joint posterior through a conditional posterior for \beta and a marginal posterior for \sigma^2.
(e) Express the updated scale using a residual sum of squares and a prior penalty. Explain why it is positive.
(f) Is \Sigma_n the conditional covariance matrix of \beta? Is \sigma_n^2 the posterior mean of \sigma^2? Give the correct expressions and the posterior mode of \sigma^2.
(g) State the full conditional posterior of \sigma^2\mid\beta,y,X. How does it differ from its marginal posterior?
(h) Without consulting the updates, complete the square to reconstruct them. Explain why the marginal degrees of freedom are \mu_0+n.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. There are n responses and p regression coefficients; X is an n\times p known design matrix. Write v=\sigma^2. The matrix \Sigma_0 scales the conditional prior covariance v\Sigma_0. In this question \mu_0 denotes prior degrees of freedom, not a normal mean. Our \operatorname{Inv\text{-}\chi^2}(\nu,s^2) convention means \nu s^2/v\sim\chi^2_\nu, or equivalently v\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(\nu/2,\nu s^2/2).
(a) The transformation \mu_0\sigma_0^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_{\mu_0} has kernel

\pi(\sigma^2)
\propto
(\sigma^2)^{-\mu_0/2-1}
\exp\Bigl(-\frac{\mu_0\sigma_0^2}{2\sigma^2}\Bigr),
\qquad\sigma^2>0.

Matching (\sigma^2)^{-a-1}\exp(-b/\sigma^2) gives a=\mu_0/2 and b=\mu_0\sigma_0^2/2.
For completeness, if U=\mu_0\sigma_0^2/v, then |dU/dv|=\mu_0\sigma_0^2/v^2. Multiplying the \chi^2_{\mu_0} density at U by this Jacobian gives the displayed inverse-gamma kernel. The Jacobian supplies the power v^{-2} and must be retained.

\boxed{
\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\Bigl(\frac{\mu_0}{2},\frac{\mu_0\sigma_0^2}{2}\Bigr).
}

(b) Since \Sigma_0^{-1} is positive definite and X^\top X is positive semidefinite, \Sigma_n^{-1} is positive definite. Precision addition gives

\boxed{\Sigma_n^{-1}=X^\top X+\Sigma_0^{-1},}
\qquad
\boxed{\beta_n=\Sigma_n(X^\top y+\Sigma_0^{-1}\beta_0).}

The data and prior precision contributions add, and their combined precision determines the posterior centre.
At fixed v, the likelihood contributes X^\top X/v to the precision of \beta, and the prior contributes \Sigma_0^{-1}/v. Their sum is \Sigma_n^{-1}/v. A proper positive-definite prior therefore gives a proper conditional update even if X is not of full column rank; an unregularised least-squares inverse (X^\top X)^{-1} is not needed.
(c)

\boxed{\mu_n=\mu_0+n,}
\qquad
\boxed{
\sigma_n^2
=
\frac{
\mu_0\sigma_0^2+y^\top y+\beta_0^\top\Sigma_0^{-1}\beta_0
-\beta_n^\top\Sigma_n^{-1}\beta_n
}{\mu_n}.
}

(d)

\boxed{\beta\mid\sigma^2,y,X\sim \operatorname{N}_p(\beta_n,\sigma^2\Sigma_n),}
\qquad
\boxed{\sigma^2\mid y,X\sim\operatorname{Inv\text{-}\chi^2}(\mu_n,\sigma_n^2).}

Together these specify a normal–inverse-\chi^2 joint posterior.
This is a conditional–marginal factorisation. To draw an independent posterior pair, draw v from the marginal inverse-\chi^2 distribution and then \beta from its normal distribution conditional on that v. The components within a pair are dependent through the conditional covariance, even though different pairs can be generated independently.
(e) Equivalently,

\mu_n\sigma_n^2
=
\mu_0\sigma_0^2
+(y-X\beta_n)^\top(y-X\beta_n)
+(\beta_n-\beta_0)^\top\Sigma_0^{-1}(\beta_n-\beta_0).

Both quadratic forms are nonnegative and \mu_0\sigma_0^2>0, so \sigma_n^2>0. The algebra is completed in (h).
(f) No. The conditional covariance is \sigma^2\Sigma_n, not \Sigma_n:

\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(\beta\mid\sigma^2,y,X)=\sigma^2\Sigma_n.}

The parameter \sigma_n^2 is a scale. By the inverse-gamma equivalence in (a),

\boxed{
\mathbb{E}(\sigma^2\mid y,X)
=
\frac{\mu_n\sigma_n^2}{\mu_n-2},
\qquad\mu_n>2,
}

and

\boxed{
\operatorname{mode}(\sigma^2\mid y,X)
=
\frac{\mu_n\sigma_n^2}{\mu_n+2}.
}

(g)

\boxed{
\sigma^2\mid\beta,y,X
\sim
\operatorname{Inv\text{-}\chi^2}\!\left(
\mu_n+p,\;
\frac{\mu_n\sigma_n^2+(\beta-\beta_n)^\top\Sigma_n^{-1}(\beta-\beta_n)}{\mu_n+p}
\right).
}

The full conditional fixes \beta. The marginal posterior integrates \beta out, which removes p from the degrees of freedom.
The difference comes from the normal density’s factor v^{-p/2}. It remains when \beta is fixed and therefore adds p/2 to the inverse-gamma shape. Integrating over \beta instead contributes a factor v^{p/2}, cancelling it. Substituting \beta=\beta_n in the full conditional would leave the wrong degrees of freedom.
(h) Expand the likelihood quadratic and the prior quadratic:

\begin{aligned}
&(y-X\beta)^\top(y-X\beta)
+(\beta-\beta_0)^\top\Sigma_0^{-1}(\beta-\beta_0)\\
&\quad=
\beta^\top(X^\top X+\Sigma_0^{-1})\beta
-2\beta^\top(X^\top y+\Sigma_0^{-1}\beta_0)
+y^\top y+\beta_0^\top\Sigma_0^{-1}\beta_0\\
&\quad=
(\beta-\beta_n)^\top\Sigma_n^{-1}(\beta-\beta_n)
+y^\top y+\beta_0^\top\Sigma_0^{-1}\beta_0
-\beta_n^\top\Sigma_n^{-1}\beta_n.
\end{aligned}

Adding \mu_0\sigma_0^2, the terms free of \beta are the numerator of \mu_n\sigma_n^2 in (c), with \mu_n=\mu_0+n. Thus

\boxed{
Q(\beta)
=
(\beta-\beta_n)^\top\Sigma_n^{-1}(\beta-\beta_n)
+\mu_n\sigma_n^2.
}

The joint posterior kernel is

(\sigma^2)^{-(\mu_0+n+p)/2-1}
\exp\Bigl(-\frac{Q(\beta)}{2\sigma^2}\Bigr).

The integral over \beta of the normal kernel equals (2\pi\sigma^2)^{p/2}|\Sigma_n|^{1/2}. The remaining power of \sigma^2 is

-\frac{\mu_0+n+p}{2}-1+\frac p2
=
-\frac{\mu_0+n}{2}-1.


\therefore
\text{the marginal inverse-}\chi^2\text{ degrees of freedom are }\mu_0+n.






Practice set: Q58. Joint Normal conjugacy and exact sampling

Question page: Q58. Joint Normal conjugacy and exact sampling

[20 marks; approximately 25 minutes]
Let X_1,\ldots,X_n\mid\mu,\sigma^2
\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(\mu,\sigma^2), with both \mu\in\mathbb R and \sigma^2>0 unknown, and n\ge1. Write \theta=(\mu,\sigma^2). Prior densities below are with respect to d\mu\,d\sigma^2. Use the inverse-Gamma convention p(v)\propto v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v} for v>0.
(i) Show the Normal belongs to the exponential family in the form f(x\mid\theta)
        =\frac{b(x)\exp\{c_1(\theta)T_1(x)+c_2(\theta)T_2(x)\}}
        {a(\theta)}. Identify b,a,c_1,c_2,T_1,T_2 (signs go in the c_j). Hence write the likelihood of the whole sample in terms of \sum_i x_i and \sum_i x_i^2. [4 marks]
(ii) The conjugate prior for this family is \pi(\theta)\propto
        \frac{\exp\{c_1(\theta)\alpha_1+c_2(\theta)\alpha_2\}}
        {a(\theta)^\beta}. Write it out explicitly in \mu and \sigma^2. By completing the square in \mu, show it factorises as \mu\mid\sigma^2\sim N\!\left(m_0,\frac{\sigma^2}{\kappa_0}\right),
        \qquad\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(a_0,b_0), and find m_0,\kappa_0,a_0,b_0 in terms of \alpha_1,\alpha_2,\beta. State the conditions on the hyperparameters for a proper distribution. [6 marks]
(iii) Show that the posterior is in the same family, with hyperparameters (\alpha_1+\sum_i x_i,\,\alpha_2+\sum_i x_i^2,\,\beta+n). Then give the posterior m_n,\kappa_n,a_n,b_n in terms of \bar x, s^2=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2, and the prior quantities. Here s^2 denotes the unnormalised sum of squares, not the sample variance. [4 marks]
(iv) Show that \mathbb{E}[\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}] is a weighted average of m_0 and \bar x, and give the weights. What happens as n\to\infty with fixed prior hyperparameters? [3 marks]
(v) Describe how to draw exact (non-MCMC) samples from the joint posterior of (\mu,\sigma^2), and explain why it works. Assess the claim: “With a flat prior on \mu and an independent inverse-Gamma prior on \sigma^2, exact sampling is unavailable and a Gibbs sampler is necessary.” [3 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write v=\sigma^2, \bar x=n^{-1}\sum_i x_i, and s^2=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2. Here s^2 is the unnormalised sum of squares, not the sample variance. N(m,v) uses variance v; \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b) has kernel v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v} on v>0. A Normal–inverse-Gamma factorisation means p(\mu,v)=p(v)p(\mu\mid v), not independence of \mu and v.
Assumptions. Use the specified conditionally iid Normal model with n\ge1. The joint prior density is with respect to d\mu\,dv and has exactly the kernel stated in the question. Changing to precision, or starting with a density in natural-parameter coordinates, would require a Jacobian; no such change is made here.
(i) Exponential-family form and likelihood. Expanding (x-\mu)^2=x^2-2\mu x+\mu^2 gives f(x\mid\mu,v)
=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi v}}
\exp\left(-\frac{x^2}{2v}+\frac{\mu x}{v}-\frac{\mu^2}{2v}\right)
=\frac{(2\pi)^{-1/2}\exp\{(\mu/v)x-x^2/(2v)\}}
{\sqrt v\exp\{\mu^2/(2v)\}}. One valid identification, with signs in the c_j, is \boxed{\begin{aligned}
b(x)&=(2\pi)^{-1/2},& a(\theta)&=\sqrt v\exp\{\mu^2/(2v)\},\\
T_1(x)&=x,&c_1(\theta)&=\frac\mu v,\\
T_2(x)&=x^2,&c_2(\theta)&=-\frac1{2v}.
\end{aligned}} Let S_1=\sum_i x_i and S_2=\sum_i x_i^2. Then \boxed{L(\mu,v;{\boldsymbol{x}})
=(2\pi v)^{-n/2}
\exp\left[-\frac{S_2-2\mu S_1+n\mu^2}{2v}\right].} Thus the sample enters the likelihood through (S_1,S_2).
(ii) Conjugate prior and parameter matching. Substitution into the given prior formula yields the joint density kernel \pi(\mu,v)
\propto v^{-\beta/2}
\exp\left[-\frac{\beta\mu^2-2\alpha_1\mu+\alpha_2}{2v}\right]. For \beta>0, complete the square: \beta\mu^2-2\alpha_1\mu+\alpha_2
=\beta\left(\mu-\frac{\alpha_1}{\beta}\right)^2
+\alpha_2-\frac{\alpha_1^2}{\beta}. Set \boxed{m_0=\frac{\alpha_1}{\beta},\qquad
\kappa_0=\beta,\qquad a_0=\frac{\beta-3}{2},\qquad
b_0=\frac12\left(\alpha_2-\frac{\alpha_1^2}{\beta}\right).} To see the shape parameter, factor the kernel as \pi(\mu,v)\propto
\underbrace{v^{-1/2}
\exp\left[-\frac{\kappa_0(\mu-m_0)^2}{2v}\right]}
_{\text{Normal conditional kernel, including its }v^{-1/2}\text{ factor}}
\underbrace{v^{-(\beta-1)/2}e^{-b_0/v}}
_{\text{inverse-Gamma marginal kernel}}. The Normal factor has a normalising multiplier \sqrt{\kappa_0/(2\pi)} that does not depend on v. The remaining exponent therefore satisfies a_0+1=(\beta-1)/2, giving a_0=(\beta-3)/2. Hence \mu\mid v\sim N(m_0,v/\kappa_0) and v\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(a_0,b_0).
The necessary and sufficient conditions for a proper prior are \boxed{\alpha_1\in\mathbb R,\qquad\beta>3,\qquad
\alpha_2>\frac{\alpha_1^2}{\beta}.} They ensure \kappa_0,a_0,b_0>0. The specified three-hyperparameter prior is a subfamily of the general Normal–inverse-Gamma family: it imposes \kappa_0=2a_0+3.
(iii) Posterior update. Multiplying the prior kernel by the likelihood gives \pi(\mu,v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
\propto v^{-(\beta+n)/2}
\exp\left[-\frac{(\beta+n)\mu^2
-2(\alpha_1+S_1)\mu+(\alpha_2+S_2)}{2v}\right]. This has exactly the same form, with \boxed{\alpha_1'=\alpha_1+S_1,\qquad
\alpha_2'=\alpha_2+S_2,\qquad\beta'=\beta+n.} Using S_1=n\bar x, S_2=s^2+n\bar x^2, and the prior identities \alpha_1=\kappa_0m_0 and \alpha_2=2b_0+\kappa_0m_0^2, we obtain \boxed{\begin{aligned}
\kappa_n&=\kappa_0+n,\\
m_n&=\frac{\kappa_0m_0+n\bar x}{\kappa_0+n},\\
a_n&=a_0+\frac n2,\\
b_n&=b_0+\frac12\left[s^2+
\frac{\kappa_0n}{\kappa_0+n}(\bar x-m_0)^2\right].
\end{aligned}} In particular, the final update follows from \begin{aligned}
b_n
&=\frac12\left[\alpha_2+S_2-
\frac{(\alpha_1+S_1)^2}{\beta+n}\right]\\
&=b_0+\frac12\left[s^2+\kappa_0m_0^2+n\bar x^2
-\frac{(\kappa_0m_0+n\bar x)^2}{\kappa_0+n}\right]\\
&=b_0+\frac12\left[s^2+
\frac{\kappa_0n}{\kappa_0+n}(\bar x-m_0)^2\right].
\end{aligned} Therefore \boxed{\mu\mid v,{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim N(m_n,v/\kappa_n),\qquad
v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(a_n,b_n).} The v distribution here is the marginal posterior, with \mu integrated out. All updates remain proper when the prior is proper.
(iv) Posterior mean and weights. For n\ge1 and a proper prior, a_n=a_0+n/2>1/2, which ensures that the marginal posterior mean of \mu exists. Iterated expectation gives \mathbb{E}[\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}]
=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathbb{E}[\mu\mid v,{\boldsymbol{x}}]\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\right]
=m_n. Consequently, \boxed{\mathbb{E}[\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}]
=\underbrace{\frac{\kappa_0}{\kappa_0+n}}_{w_0}m_0
+\underbrace{\frac n{\kappa_0+n}}_{w_x}\bar x.} The weights are positive and sum to one. For fixed prior hyperparameters, w_0\to0 and w_x\to1: the prior contribution vanishes and the posterior mean approaches the sample mean. Under iid sampling at fixed true parameters, \bar x\to\mu_{\mathrm{true}} almost surely, so m_n\to\mu_{\mathrm{true}} almost surely as well.
(v) Exact joint-posterior sampling. For each j=1,\ldots,M, independently of all previous pairs:
1. Draw v^{(j)}\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(a_n,b_n) from the marginal posterior of v=\sigma^2.
2. Draw \mu^{(j)}\sim N(m_n,v^{(j)}/\kappa_n), conditional on that newly drawn variance.
3. Store (\mu^{(j)},v^{(j)}).
For example, step 1 can use G^{(j)}\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a_n,b_n) in shape–rate form and set v^{(j)}=1/G^{(j)}. With fresh random numbers in each repetition, this produces iid pairs from the joint posterior because p(\mu,v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=p(v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\,p(\mu\mid v,{\boldsymbol{x}}). The two coordinates within a pair are generally dependent, but distinct pairs are independent. There is no Markov-chain convergence, burn-in, or accept/reject step to manage in this construction.
Assessing the flat-prior claim. The claim is false for a flat mean prior and an independent inverse-Gamma variance prior. To distinguish its hyperparameters from those above, suppose p(\mu)\propto1,\qquad
v\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(a_*,b_*),\qquad a_*,b_*>0. Although this joint prior is improper in \mu, for n\ge1 the posterior is proper. Using \sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2=s^2+n(\mu-\bar x)^2, its kernel is p(\mu,v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
\propto v^{-a_*-1-n/2}
\exp\left[-\frac{b_*+s^2/2}{v}
          -\frac{n(\mu-\bar x)^2}{2v}\right]. Integrating over \mu contributes a factor proportional to \sqrt v, since \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\exp\left[-\frac{n(\mu-\bar x)^2}{2v}\right]d\mu
=\sqrt{\frac{2\pi v}{n}}. Hence \boxed{v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim
\operatorname{InvGamma}\!\left(a_*+\frac{n-1}{2},\ b_*+\frac{s^2}{2}\right),
\qquad\mu\mid v,{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim N(\bar x,v/n).} One can again draw from the variance marginal and then the Normal conditional, producing independent exact posterior pairs. Gibbs sampling is valid here, but not necessary. The same distinction appears in Question 43 for p(\mu,v)\propto1/v, with its stated propriety conditions.

Key result. Exact direct sampling uses a marginal then a conditional. Gibbs sampling alternates full conditionals. The key issue is whether the needed marginal is available for direct sampling, not merely whether the prior was described as independent.

title: Normal distribution
text:
Properties

Normal–Normal conjugacy

Main article: Normal–Normal conjugacy


\boxed{
  \mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{N}(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)},
 with 
\begin{aligned}
\sigma_1^2
&=\frac1A
=\left(\frac n{\sigma^2}+\frac1{\sigma_0^2}\right)^{-1}
=\frac{\sigma^2\sigma_0^2}{n\sigma_0^2+\sigma^2},
\\
\mu_1
&=\frac BA
=\frac{\sum_i x_i/\sigma^2+\mu_0/\sigma_0^2}
        {n/\sigma^2+1/\sigma_0^2}\\
&=\frac{n\overline x\,\sigma_0^2+\mu_0\sigma^2}
        {n\sigma_0^2+\sigma^2}.
\end{aligned}



Normal–inverse-Gamma variance update

Main article: Normal–inverse-Gamma variance update


\boxed{
\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\!\left(
   \alpha_0+\frac n2,
   \beta_0+\frac12S_\mu
\right)}.



Full conditionals under independent priors

Main article: Full conditionals under independent priors

Holding \sigma^2 fixed, the calculation from Equation (1) in Conjugate analysis for normal models applies verbatim: 
\boxed{
\mu\mid\sigma^2,{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{N}\!\left(
\frac{n\overline x\,\sigma_0^2+\mu_0\sigma^2}
      {n\sigma_0^2+\sigma^2},
\frac{\sigma^2\sigma_0^2}{n\sigma_0^2+\sigma^2}
\right)}.
 Holding \mu fixed, the calculation from Equation (3) in Conjugate analysis for normal models applies: 
\boxed{
\sigma^2\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\!\left(
\alpha_0+\frac n2,
\beta_0+\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2
\right)}.



Precision weighting

Main article: Precision weighting

Writing

w=\frac{\sigma^2}{n\sigma_0^2+\sigma^2}

turns Equation (2) in Conjugate analysis for normal models into

\mu_1=(1-w)\overline x+w\mu_0.

The posterior mean is therefore a precision-weighted average. Equivalently, if \kappa_0=\sigma^2/\sigma_0^2, then

\mu_1=\frac{n\overline x+\kappa_0\mu_0}{n+\kappa_0}.

Thus the prior behaves like \kappa_0 observations whose mean is \mu_0. In the special case \sigma_0^2=\sigma^2, it behaves like one extra observation at \mu_0.

title: Normal distribution
text:
Examples

Practice set: Q7. Normal estimation and prediction

Question page: Q7. Normal estimation and prediction

Suppose that, conditionally on \mu, X_1,\ldots,X_n\mid\mu
  \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2), where \sigma^2>0 is known. Use the prior \mu\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_0,\tau^2), where \tau^2>0 is known.
(a) By completing the square in \mu, derive its posterior distribution. Denote the posterior mean and variance by m and v. [4 marks]
(b) Let X_{\mathrm{new}} be a further observation, independent of the observed sample given \mu. Derive its posterior predictive distribution. Explain the two sources of its variance. [4 marks]
(c) As n\to\infty, with \sigma^2 and the prior fixed, what happens to the posterior variance of \mu and the predictive variance of X_{\mathrm{new}}? Explain why they behave differently. [2 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. The notation N(m,v) uses mean m and variance v; precision is 1/v. The data have known variance \sigma^2>0, and the mean prior is N(\mu_0,\tau^2) with \tau^2>0. Write \bar x=n^{-1}\sum_i x_i. Posterior prediction averages a new observation’s sampling distribution over the parameter posterior; that observation is independent of the original sample conditional on \mu.

(a) Posterior distribution of \mu
Start from independence and the specified prior: L(\mu;{\boldsymbol{x}})=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}
\exp\left[-\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right],
\qquad
p(\mu)\propto\exp\left[-\frac{(\mu-\mu_0)^2}{2\tau^2}\right]. The identity \sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2+n(\mu-\bar x)^2 follows by expanding around \bar x; the cross term is zero because \sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=0. Bayes’ theorem multiplies these two kernels. Ignoring terms that do not depend on \mu, \begin{aligned}
  p(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
  &\propto
  \exp\left[
    -\frac{n}{2\sigma^2}(\mu-\bar{x})^2
    -\frac{1}{2\tau^2}(\mu-\mu_0)^2
  \right]\\
  &\propto
  \exp\left[
    -\frac12
    \left\{
      \left(\frac{n}{\sigma^2}+\frac{1}{\tau^2}\right)\mu^2
      -2\left(
        \frac{n\bar{x}}{\sigma^2}+\frac{\mu_0}{\tau^2}
      \right)\mu
    \right\}
  \right].
\end{aligned} Define v=\left(\frac{n}{\sigma^2}+\frac{1}{\tau^2}\right)^{-1},
  \qquad
  m=v\left(
    \frac{n\bar{x}}{\sigma^2}+\frac{\mu_0}{\tau^2}
  \right). Completing the square gives p(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
  \propto
  \exp\left[-\frac{(\mu-m)^2}{2v}\right], so \boxed{\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(m,v)}. Equivalently, v=\frac{\sigma^2\tau^2}{n\tau^2+\sigma^2},
  \qquad
  m=\frac{n\tau^2\bar{x}+\sigma^2\mu_0}
          {n\tau^2+\sigma^2}.


(b) Posterior predictive distribution
Conditional on \mu, X_{\mathrm{new}}=\mu+\varepsilon,
  \qquad
  \varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2), where \varepsilon is independent of \mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}. Since \mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(m,v), \boxed{
    X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
    \sim\mathcal{N}(m,\sigma^2+v)
  }. The predictive variance can also be obtained from \begin{aligned}
  \operatorname{Var}(X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
  &=
  \mathbb{E}\!\left[
    \operatorname{Var}(X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}})
    \mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
  \right]\\
  &\quad+
  \operatorname{Var}\!\left(
    \mathbb{E}[X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}}]
    \mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
  \right)\\
  &=\sigma^2+v.
\end{aligned} Here \sigma^2 is future-observation noise and v is uncertainty about the unknown mean.


(c) Limiting variances
As n\to\infty, v=\left(\frac{n}{\sigma^2}+\frac{1}{\tau^2}\right)^{-1}
  \longrightarrow0, whereas \operatorname{Var}(X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
  =\sigma^2+v
  \longrightarrow\sigma^2. Increasing n removes uncertainty about \mu, but it does not remove the irreducible sampling variation in a new observation.






Final preparation: Question 1. Normal mean, known variance

Question page: Question 1. Normal mean, known variance

Let

X_i\mid\mu\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^2),

with \sigma^2 known and \mu\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu_0,\sigma_0^2).
(a) Using only the precision-addition rule and the precision-weighted mean, write the two updated parameters of the posterior for \mu.
(b) Define the prior equivalent sample size, and state what it counts.
(c) Explain why the posterior mean is a precision-weighted average of the prior mean and the sample mean.
(d) State and interpret the limiting posterior mean and variance as n\to\infty, with the prior parameters fixed and \bar X_n\to\mu^{\ast}.
(e) State the posterior predictive distribution of one new observation X_{\mathrm{new}}, conditionally independent of the sample given \mu.
(f) Explain why the posterior predictive variance is larger than the posterior variance of \mu.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write \bar x=n^{-1}\sum_i x_i. A normal distribution \operatorname{N}(m,v) has mean m and variance v; its precision is 1/v. Here \sigma^2 is the known observation variance, \sigma_0^2 is the prior variance of the unknown mean, and \sigma_1^2 will be its posterior variance. These are variances of different objects.
(a) The data precision of n observations is n/\sigma^2, and the prior precision is 1/\sigma_0^2. Precision addition gives

\frac1{\sigma_1^2}
=
\frac n{\sigma^2}+\frac1{\sigma_0^2}.

The posterior mean is the precision-weighted average of \bar x and \mu_0:

\mu_1
=
\frac{(n/\sigma^2)\bar x+(1/\sigma_0^2)\mu_0}{n/\sigma^2+1/\sigma_0^2}
=
\frac{n\bar x\,\sigma_0^2+\mu_0\sigma^2}{n\sigma_0^2+\sigma^2}.


\boxed{\mu\mid x\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2).}

(b)

\kappa_0=\frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma_0^2}.

It counts how many observations of variance \sigma^2 have the same precision as the prior, since 1/\sigma_0^2=\kappa_0/\sigma^2.
Consequently, \mu_1=(n\bar x+\kappa_0\mu_0)/(n+\kappa_0) and \sigma_1^2=\sigma^2/(n+\kappa_0). The equivalent sample size measures information about the common mean. It need not be an integer or represent actual previous observations.
(c) Up to an additive constant free of \mu, the log posterior is

-\frac{n}{2\sigma^2}(\bar x-\mu)^2-\frac{1}{2\sigma_0^2}(\mu-\mu_0)^2.

Its derivative is (n/\sigma^2)(\bar x-\mu)-(1/\sigma_0^2)(\mu-\mu_0). Setting the derivative equal to zero balances the two pulls, so

\mu_1
=
\frac{(n/\sigma^2)\bar x+(1/\sigma_0^2)\mu_0}{n/\sigma^2+1/\sigma_0^2}.

The second derivative is -n/\sigma^2-1/\sigma_0^2<0, so this stationary point is the unique posterior mode. The posterior is normal, hence its mode equals its mean. This derives the weighting rule: moving away from a more precise source incurs a larger quadratic penalty. The two weights are nonnegative and sum to one, so the posterior mean lies between \bar x and \mu_0.
(d) Let w_n=(n/\sigma^2)/(n/\sigma^2+1/\sigma_0^2). Then w_n\to 1 and

\mu_1=w_n\bar X_n+(1-w_n)\mu_0\to\mu^{\ast},
\qquad
\sigma_1^2=\Bigl(\frac n{\sigma^2}+\frac1{\sigma_0^2}\Bigr)^{-1}\to 0.

With the prior held fixed, the data precision dominates. The posterior concentrates at the limiting sample mean.
This conclusion uses the stated convergence \bar X_n\to\mu^\ast. Under the iid normal model with true mean \mu^\ast, that convergence follows from the law of large numbers. A fixed prior contributes a fixed amount of precision, while the likelihood contributes an amount growing linearly with n.
(e) Given \mu, X_{\mathrm{new}} is independent of the sample and X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid\mu\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^2). Since \mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2),

\boxed{X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu_1,\sigma^2+\sigma_1^2).}

To see the distributional result, write X_{\mathrm{new}}=\mu+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{new}}, where \varepsilon_{\mathrm{new}}\sim\operatorname{N}(0,\sigma^2) is independent of the posterior draw of \mu. Conditional on the observed sample, this is a sum of two independent normal variables. Merely replacing \mu by \mu_1 would omit uncertainty about the unknown mean.
(f) By the law of total variance,

\operatorname{Var}(X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=
\mathbb{E}[\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}]+\operatorname{Var}(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=
\sigma^2+\sigma_1^2.

The term \sigma_1^2 is uncertainty about \mu. The term \sigma^2 is the variance of a new observation even if \mu is known. Both are positive, so the predictive variance exceeds the posterior variance of \mu.

title: Multinomial distribution
text:
Properties

Multinomial central limit theorem

Main article: Multinomial central limit theorem

Let {\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{Multinomial}(n,{\boldsymbol{p}}) and \widehat{\boldsymbol{p}}={\boldsymbol{x}}/n. For fixed interior {\boldsymbol{p}}, define the covariance matrix

{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}({\boldsymbol{p}})
=\operatorname{diag}({\boldsymbol{p}})-{\boldsymbol{p}}{\boldsymbol{p}}^{\mathsf T}.

Then

\sqrt n\,(\widehat{\boldsymbol{p}}-{\boldsymbol{p}})
\xrightarrow{\mathcal D}
\operatorname{N}_K\!\left(
  {\boldsymbol{0}},
  {\color{blue}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}({\boldsymbol{p}})
\right).

The covariance matrix is singular because the components of \widehat{\boldsymbol{p}}-{\boldsymbol{p}} sum to zero. On the (K-1)-dimensional simplex, the count cloud therefore tightens at the usual n^{-1/2} rate and becomes locally normal.


Dirichlet–Multinomial conjugacy

Main article: Dirichlet–Multinomial conjugacy

After division by this evidence, 
\boxed{
{\boldsymbol{p}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1+x_1,\ldots,\alpha_K+x_K)}.

title: Multinomial distribution
text:
Examples

Practice set: Q22. Advertising responses and Dirichlet inference

Question page: Q22. Advertising responses and Dirichlet inference

[10 marks]
An advertising campaign records responses from 60 independently sampled people:




Negative
Neutral
Positive




Male
8
6
16


Female
12
4
14



Let \mathbf p=(p_{MN},p_{MU},p_{MP},p_{FN},p_{FU},p_{FP}) be the six population cell probabilities, with U denoting a neutral response. Model the counts as multinomial and use \mathbf p\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(1,1,1,1,1,1). You may use the Dirichlet kernel f(\mathbf p)\propto\prod_{k=1}^{K}p_k^{\alpha_k-1},
\qquad p_k>0,\quad \sum_{k=1}^{K}p_k=1.
(a) [2 marks] Derive the posterior distribution of \mathbf p, stating its parameters and support.
(b) [2 marks] Find the posterior mean of p_{MP} and its component of the joint MAP estimate of \mathbf p. Explain why that MAP component equals the observed cell proportion here.
(c) [2 marks] Find the posterior predictive probability that one new person responds positively, regardless of gender. Express it as a posterior expectation before calculating it.
(d) [2 marks] For that new person, calculate \mathbb{P}(\text{positive response}\mid\text{female},\text{data}). Explain why this differs from \mathbb{P}(\text{female and positive response}\mid\text{data}).
(e) [2 marks] Are the six components of \mathbf p independent under the posterior? Explain using their constraint.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Let D be the observed table and \mathbf p its six population cell probabilities. The labels M,F denote male and female; N,U,P denote negative, neutral, and positive. With parameters a_1,\ldots,a_K>0, a Dirichlet density has kernel \prod_k p_k^{a_k-1} on the simplex p_k>0, \sum_kp_k=1. The joint MAP maximises this density over the entire simplex, not a one-component marginal density.
(a) Posterior distribution. Write the counts in the stated order as \mathbf x=(8,6,16,12,4,14),\qquad n=60. The multinomial likelihood is L(\mathbf p;D)=\frac{60!}{\prod_{k=1}^{6}x_k!}
\prod_{k=1}^{6}p_k^{x_k}
\propto\prod_{k=1}^{6}p_k^{x_k}. The Dirichlet prior has kernel \prod_k p_k^{1-1}=1 on the simplex. Consequently, p(\mathbf p\mid D)\propto
\prod_{k=1}^{6}p_k^{x_k+1-1}, which is the Dirichlet kernel with parameters x_k+1. Thus \boxed{\mathbf p\mid D\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(9,7,17,13,5,15).} Its density is supported on the simplex p_k>0, \sum_{k=1}^6p_k=1; the boundary has probability zero. The posterior concentration is A=9+7+17+13+5+15=66.
(b) Posterior mean and MAP. For a Dirichlet vector with parameters a_1,\ldots,a_K and A=\sum_k a_k, \mathbb{E}(p_k)=\frac{a_k}{A},\qquad
\widehat p_{k,\mathrm{MAP}}=\frac{a_k-1}{A-K}
\quad\text{when every }a_k>1. Here every posterior parameter exceeds one, so \boxed{\mathbb{E}(p_{MP}\mid D)=\frac{17}{66}\approx0.2576,}
\qquad
\boxed{\widehat p_{MP,\mathrm{MAP}}=
\frac{17-1}{66-6}=\frac{16}{60}\approx0.2667.} The MAP component is taken from the mode of the joint posterior for \mathbf p. Since the prior density is constant on the simplex, maximising the posterior is equivalent to maximising the likelihood, giving the observed cell proportions.
(c) Predicting a positive response. Conditional on \mathbf p, the probability of a positive response is p_{MP}+p_{FP}. Averaging over posterior uncertainty gives \begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(\text{positive}\mid D)
&=\int (p_{MP}+p_{FP})p(\mathbf p\mid D)\,d\mathbf p\\
&=\mathbb{E}(p_{MP}+p_{FP}\mid D)\\
&=\frac{17}{66}+\frac{15}{66}
=\boxed{\frac{16}{33}\approx0.4848.}
\end{aligned} Prediction uses posterior averaging, not substitution of the MAP estimate.
(d) Conditioning on the new person being female. First calculate the two relevant posterior predictive probabilities: \mathbb{P}(\text{female and positive}\mid D)=\mathbb{E}(p_{FP}\mid D)=\frac{15}{66}, \mathbb{P}(\text{female}\mid D)
=\mathbb{E}(p_{FN}+p_{FU}+p_{FP}\mid D)
=\frac{13+5+15}{66}=\frac{33}{66}. By the definition of conditional probability, \boxed{
\mathbb{P}(\text{positive}\mid\text{female},D)
=\frac{15/66}{33/66}=\frac5{11}\approx0.4545.
} By contrast, the joint probability is \boxed{\mathbb{P}(\text{female and positive}\mid D)
=\frac{15}{66}=\frac5{22}\approx0.2273.} The conditional probability restricts attention to the female row; the joint probability refers to both events occurring for a person sampled from the whole population.
(e) Posterior dependence. No. The probabilities must satisfy \sum_k p_k=1 exactly. Increasing one component leaves less total probability for the others. More formally, if they were independent, then 0=\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^{6}p_k\,\middle|\,D\right)
=\sum_{k=1}^{6}\operatorname{Var}(p_k\mid D)>0, a contradiction, since each component has positive posterior variance. Indeed, distinct Dirichlet components have \operatorname{Cov}(p_j,p_k\mid D)
=-\frac{a_ja_k}{A^2(A+1)}<0,\qquad j\ne k.

Key result. Add counts to the Dirichlet parameters; average probabilities for prediction; and distinguish a joint cell probability from a probability conditional on a row.

With {\boldsymbol{x}}\mid{\boldsymbol{p}}\sim\operatorname{Multinomial}(123,{\boldsymbol{p}}) and {\boldsymbol{p}}\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_4), identify the posterior.
Last week’s percentages were 44.79\%, 27.60\%, 7.36\%, and 20.25\%. Explain how to use these proportions to choose the direction of {\boldsymbol{\alpha}}, and how a chosen total concentration records the weight given to last week.
Using a prior equivalent, for posterior-mean purposes, to last week’s proportions plus one baseline count in each category, report posterior means and equal-tailed 95\% credible intervals for p_1, p_4, p_1+p_2+p_3, and p_1-p_4.







Worked answer (click to show)





Question. A restaurant observed the following numbers of orders yesterday:

Let {\boldsymbol{p}}=(p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4) be the corresponding population proportions.

With {\boldsymbol{x}}\mid{\boldsymbol{p}}\sim\operatorname{Multinomial}(123,{\boldsymbol{p}}) and {\boldsymbol{p}}\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_4), identify the posterior.
Last week’s percentages were 44.79\%, 27.60\%, 7.36\%, and 20.25\%. Explain how to use these proportions to choose the direction of {\boldsymbol{\alpha}}, and how a chosen total concentration records the weight given to last week.
Using a prior equivalent, for posterior-mean purposes, to last week’s proportions plus one baseline count in each category, report posterior means and equal-tailed 95\% credible intervals for p_1, p_4, p_1+p_2+p_3, and p_1-p_4.

Solution.

The Dirichlet–Multinomial update adds the observed cell counts to the corresponding concentration parameters. Since 63+19+3+38=123, \begin{align*}
{\boldsymbol{p}}&\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3,\alpha_4),\\
{\boldsymbol{x}}\mid{\boldsymbol{p}}&\sim\operatorname{Multinomial}(123,{\boldsymbol{p}}),\\
&\boxed{{\boldsymbol{p}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(63+\alpha_1,19+\alpha_2,3+\alpha_3,38+\alpha_4)}.
\end{align*}
Write last week’s proportions as


{\boldsymbol{q}}=(0.4479,0.2760,0.0736,0.2025).

A Dirichlet prior centred exactly at {\boldsymbol{q}} can be written {\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\kappa{\boldsymbol{q}}, where \kappa>0 is the total prior concentration. Increasing \kappa preserves the prior mean but increases the weight assigned to last week.
The construction used here instead combines 100 fractional counts with one baseline count in each category:

{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
=(44.79,27.60,7.36,20.25)+(1,1,1,1)
=(45.79,28.60,8.36,21.25).

Its concentration is 104 and its mean is {\boldsymbol{\alpha}}/104, which is slightly closer to (1/4,1/4,1/4,1/4) than {\boldsymbol{q}}. Thus the direction and concentration should both be reported; percentages alone determine only the direction.

The posterior parameters are \begin{align*}
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^\ast
&=(63,19,3,38)+(45.79,28.60,8.36,21.25)\\
&=\boxed{(108.79,47.60,11.36,59.25)},
\end{align*} with total concentration \alpha_0^\ast=108.79+47.60+11.36+59.25=227. Thus


\mathbb{E}(P_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{108.79}{227}=0.4793,
\qquad
\mathbb{E}(P_4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{59.25}{227}=0.2610.

Also,

\mathbb{E}(P_1+P_2+P_3\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=1-\mathbb{E}(P_4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=0.7390

and

\mathbb{E}(P_1-P_4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\frac{108.79-59.25}{227}=0.2182.

The Dirichlet marginal results give \begin{align*}
P_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}&\sim\operatorname{Beta}(108.79,118.21),\\
P_4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}&\sim\operatorname{Beta}(59.25,167.75),\\
P_1+P_2+P_3\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}&\sim\operatorname{Beta}(167.75,59.25).
\end{align*} Their intervals can therefore be obtained with Beta quantiles. The difference P_1-P_4 has no such Beta form, so simulation handles all four quantities uniformly:
rdirichlet_base <- function(n, alpha) {
  z <- sapply(alpha, function(a) rgamma(n, shape = a, rate = 1))
  z / rowSums(z)
}

set.seed(3500)
alpha_post <- c(108.79, 47.60, 11.36, 59.25)
p <- rdirichlet_base(100000, alpha_post)
summaries <- cbind(
  p1 = p[, 1],
  p4 = p[, 4],
  p123 = rowSums(p[, 1:3]),
  difference = p[, 1] - p[, 4]
)
rbind(
  mean = colMeans(summaries),
  lower = apply(summaries, 2, quantile, 0.025),
  upper = apply(summaries, 2, quantile, 0.975)
)

Concept check: C14. Metropolis–Hastings cancellations

Question page: C14. Metropolis–Hastings cancellations

Why can Metropolis–Hastings use an unnormalised target? When do its proposal-density terms cancel?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. Let \pi(z)=k(z)/Z be the target and q(y\mid x) the proposal density from current state x to candidate y. The acceptance probability is \min\{1,k(y)q(x\mid y)/[k(x)q(y\mid x)]\} because Z cancels; the proposal terms cancel only when q(y\mid x)=q(x\mid y), as for a fixed-scale symmetric random walk.

title: Markov chain
text:
Definition taught in Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings, part of Bayesian statistics
A stochastic process X_0,X_1,\ldots is a Markov chain if 
\mathbb{P}(X_{t+1}\in A\mid X_t,X_{t-1},\ldots,X_0)
=\mathbb{P}(X_{t+1}\in A\mid X_t)
 for every measurable set A. In a discrete state space, write q(y\mid x) for the transition probability from x to y; in a continuous state space it is a transition density.

title: Markov chain
text:
Properties

Detailed balance implies stationarity

Main article: Detailed balance implies stationarity

If a transition kernel q satisfies Equation (3) in Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings for a probability distribution \pi, then \pi satisfies global balance and is a stationary distribution of the chain.


Metropolis–Hastings invariance

Main article: Metropolis–Hastings invariance

The Metropolis–Hastings transition defined by Equation (5) in Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings satisfies detailed balance with respect to \pi. Consequently, \pi is stationary.

title: Markov chain
text:
Examples

Four-state random walk

Worked example from Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings

Question. Consider states 1,2,3,4 arranged in a line. At every state the chain stays put with probability 1/2. From an endpoint it moves to the only neighbour with probability 1/2; from an interior state it moves left or right with probability 1/4 each. With columns indexing the current state and rows the next state, construct the transition matrix and find the stationary distribution.
Solution. The transition matrix is

{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{Q}}=
\begin{pmatrix}
1/2&1/4&0&0\\
1/2&1/2&1/4&0\\
0&1/4&1/2&1/2\\
0&0&1/4&1/2
\end{pmatrix}.

Detailed balance between states 1 and 2 requires

\pi_1\frac12=\pi_2\frac14
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\pi_2=2\pi_1.

Similarly,

\pi_2\frac14=\pi_3\frac14
\Longrightarrow\pi_3=\pi_2,
\qquad
\pi_3\frac14=\pi_4\frac12
\Longrightarrow\pi_3=2\pi_4.

Hence

{\boldsymbol{\pi}}=(\pi_1,\pi_2,\pi_3,\pi_4)^{\mathsf T}
\propto(1,2,2,1)^{\mathsf T}.

Normalising by 1+2+2+1=6 gives

\boxed{{\boldsymbol{\pi}}=(1/6,2/6,2/6,1/6)^{\mathsf T}}.



Practice set: Q18. Equilibrium and independence

Question page: Q18. Equilibrium and independence

[4 marks]
A Gibbs sampler targets a bivariate posterior in which the two parameters are strongly correlated. Its initial state is drawn exactly from the target posterior. A student states:

“The chain starts at equilibrium, so its successive sampled pairs can be treated as independent posterior observations.”

Explain what starting at equilibrium guarantees. Does independence follow? Justify your answer by referring to how Gibbs updates are generated.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. An invariant or equilibrium distribution is preserved by the chain’s transition. Starting from it makes the chain stationary: every iteration has the same marginal target distribution. This is weaker than independence across iterations. Here one Gibbs sweep updates each coordinate once from its exact full conditional, using the newest available conditioning value.
To see invariance directly, start with a pair having density p(\theta_1,\theta_2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}). Updating \theta_1 while leaving \theta_2 unchanged gives density p(\theta_2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\,
p(\theta_1'\mid\theta_2,{\boldsymbol{x}})
=p(\theta_1',\theta_2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}). The second conditional update reconstructs the same joint density in the same way. Therefore the full sweep preserves the target. Starting at equilibrium guarantees stationarity. If (\theta_1^{(0)},\theta_2^{(0)})
\sim p(\theta_1,\theta_2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}), then \boxed{
(\theta_1^{(t)},\theta_2^{(t)})
\sim p(\theta_1,\theta_2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
\quad\text{for every }t\geq0.
} Thus no convergence from an incorrectly distributed initial state is needed.
Independence does not follow. A systematic Gibbs update has the form \theta_1^{(t+1)}
\sim p(\theta_1\mid\theta_2^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{x}}), followed by \theta_2^{(t+1)}
\sim p(\theta_2\mid\theta_1^{(t+1)},{\boldsymbol{x}}). The new pair is generated using components of the current pair, so successive states are generally serially dependent. This dependence can be particularly strong when the target parameters are strongly correlated. Starting at equilibrium gives the correct marginal distribution at every iteration, but it does not turn the Markov chain into independent posterior draws.





Concept check: C12. Markov property and invariance

Question page: C12. Markov property and invariance

What is the Markov property? What does it mean for a distribution to be invariant for a chain?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. The Markov property says that the conditional distribution of the next state, given the whole past, depends only on the current state. A distribution \pi is invariant if one transition preserves it: X^{(t)}\sim\pi implies X^{(t+1)}\sim\pi; this alone does not establish convergence from every initial state.

Practice set: Q24. Bayesian regression and prediction

Question page: Q24. Bayesian regression and prediction

[12 marks]
Consider the regression model Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad
\varepsilon_i\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2), with reference prior p(\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma^2)\propto1/\sigma^2 for (\beta_0,\beta_1)\in\mathbb{R}^2 and \sigma^2>0. For n=10 observations, the design matrix has rows (1,x_i), and \widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
(X^\top X)^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1/10&0\\0&1/40\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \operatorname{SSE}=16. The observed predictor values range from -3 to 3.
You may use the standard regression posterior formulas under this prior. Use the inverse-Gamma convention f(v)\propto v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v}. Write t_\nu(m,s) for a Student-t distribution with location m and scale s, and use t_{0.975,8}=2.306.
(a) [2 marks] State the marginal posterior distribution of \sigma^2 and calculate \mathbb{E}(\sigma^2\mid\mathbf y,X).
(b) [3 marks] State the marginal posterior distribution of the slope \beta_1, and calculate its equal-tailed 95% credible interval.
(c) [4 marks] At x_*=0, derive the posterior distributions and equal-tailed 95% intervals for:
(i) the unknown mean response \mu_*=\beta_0+\beta_1x_*;
(ii) a new observation \widetilde Y.
Explain precisely why the second interval is wider.
(d) [3 marks] Calculate h(x_*)=(1,x_*)(X^\top X)^{-1}(1,x_*)^\top at x_*=0 and x_*=4. Compare the posterior predictive scales at these points and explain how the calculation reflects uncertainty from extrapolation.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write D=(\mathbf y,X), v=\sigma^2, and \operatorname{SSE}=\|\mathbf y-X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\|^2. The inverse-Gamma kernel is v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v} on v>0. t_\nu(m,s) denotes location m, scale s, and \nu degrees of freedom: (T-m)/s\sim t_\nu. A scale is not a variance; t_{q,\nu} denotes the q quantile of standard t_\nu.
Assumptions. Use independent Normal errors, fixed covariates, full column rank X, n>p, positive SSE, and the reference prior p(\boldsymbol\beta,v)\propto1/v with respect to d\boldsymbol\beta\,dv. These rank and residual conditions ensure a proper posterior despite the improper prior.
There are p=2 regression coefficients, including the intercept. Define \nu=n-p=8,\qquad
s^2=\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}{n-p}=\frac{16}{8}=2,
\qquad C=(X^\top X)^{-1}. Here s^2 is the residual variance estimate; it is not the posterior mean of \sigma^2.
Why the regression posterior has this form. The likelihood times the reference prior gives p(\boldsymbol\beta,v\mid D)
\propto v^{-n/2-1}
\exp\{-\|\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta\|^2/(2v)\},
\qquad v=\sigma^2>0. Expand about the least-squares estimate. The cross term vanishes because X^\top(\mathbf y-X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})=\mathbf0, giving \|\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta\|^2
=\operatorname{SSE}
+(\boldsymbol\beta-\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})^\top
X^\top X(\boldsymbol\beta-\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}). The second term is a Normal quadratic. At fixed v it identifies \boldsymbol\beta\mid v,D\sim
N_p(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},vC). Its unnormalised exponential integrates to (2\pi v)^{p/2}|X^\top X|^{-1/2}, which explains the v^{p/2} factor in the variance marginal below.
(a) Marginal variance posterior. Under the stated reference prior, \sigma^2\mid D\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\left(\frac{n-p}{2},
\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}2\right). Thus \boxed{\sigma^2\mid D\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(4,8),\qquad\sigma^2>0.} An \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b) variable has mean b/(a-1) when a>1, so \boxed{\mathbb{E}(\sigma^2\mid D)=\frac8{4-1}=\frac83\approx2.6667.} For completeness, integrating the coefficient kernel out of the joint posterior contributes a factor (\sigma^2)^{p/2}. Therefore p(\sigma^2\mid D)
\propto (\sigma^2)^{-(n/2+1)}(\sigma^2)^{p/2}
\exp\!\left(-\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}{2\sigma^2}\right)
=(\sigma^2)^{-5}e^{-8/\sigma^2}, confirming the shape 4, not n/2=5.
(b) Slope posterior and credible interval. The conditional coefficient posterior is \boldsymbol\beta\mid\sigma^2,D
\sim N_2(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},\sigma^2 C). The slope entry of C is 1/40, so \beta_1\mid\sigma^2,D\sim N\!\left(2,\frac{\sigma^2}{40}\right). Integrating over \sigma^2\mid D gives \boxed{\beta_1\mid D\sim t_8\!\left(2,\sqrt{\frac2{40}}\right)
=t_8(2,\sqrt{0.05}).} Equivalently, (\beta_1-2)/\sqrt{0.05}\mid D\sim t_8. The equal-tailed 95% credible interval is therefore 2\pm2.306\sqrt{0.05}=2\pm0.5156,
\qquad\boxed{(1.484,\,2.516).} The second argument of t_8 is a scale, not a variance. There is no additional division by \sqrt n: sample-size information is already in C.
(c) Mean response versus a new observation at x_*=0. For a general predictor value, set \mathbf z_*=(1,x_*)^\top and write m_*=\mathbf z_*^\top\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},
\qquad h(x_*)=\mathbf z_*^\top C\mathbf z_*. The linear-transformation rule for a normal vector gives \mu_*\mid\sigma^2,D
\sim N\bigl(m_*,\sigma^2 h(x_*)\bigr). For a new response \widetilde Y=\mu_*+\widetilde\varepsilon, the new error is independent of the coefficient uncertainty conditional on \sigma^2,D, and has variance \sigma^2. Thus \widetilde Y\mid\sigma^2,D,x_*
\sim N\bigl(m_*,\sigma^2\{1+h(x_*)\}\bigr). Integrating over the inverse-Gamma variance posterior gives \mu_*\mid D\sim t_8\bigl(m_*,s\sqrt{h(x_*)}\bigr), \widetilde Y\mid D,x_*\sim t_8\bigl(m_*,s\sqrt{1+h(x_*)}\bigr). At x_*=0, m_*=(1,0)\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}=1,
\qquad h(0)=\frac1{10}. Therefore the unknown mean response has posterior \boxed{\mu_*\mid D\sim t_8(1,\sqrt{0.2}),} with equal-tailed 95% credible interval 1\pm2.306\sqrt{0.2}=1\pm1.0313,
\qquad\boxed{(-0.031,\,2.031).} The new observation has posterior predictive distribution \boxed{\widetilde Y\mid D,x_*=0\sim t_8(1,\sqrt{2.2}),} with equal-tailed 95% predictive interval 1\pm2.306\sqrt{2.2}=1\pm3.4204,
\qquad\boxed{(-2.420,\,4.420).} Both intervals have the same centre and use the same t_8 quantile. The predictive interval is wider because a new observation includes both uncertainty about the regression mean and fresh observational noise. That additional noise produces the extra 1 in 1+h(x_*).
(d) Extrapolation and predictive scale. Using the supplied diagonal matrix, \begin{aligned}
h(x_*)&=(1,x_*)
\begin{pmatrix}1/10&0\\0&1/40\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}1\\x_*\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\frac1{10}+\frac{x_*^2}{40}.
\end{aligned} Hence \boxed{h(0)=0.1,\qquad h(4)=0.1+\frac{16}{40}=0.5.} The corresponding predictive scales are \boxed{s_{\mathrm{pred}}(0)=\sqrt{2(1+0.1)}=\sqrt{2.2}\approx1.4832,} \boxed{s_{\mathrm{pred}}(4)=\sqrt{2(1+0.5)}=\sqrt3\approx1.7321.} At x_*=4, the predicted centre is 1+2(4)=9, so the predictive distribution is t_8(9,\sqrt3). Its interval is wider than at x_*=0 because it has the same degrees of freedom but a larger scale.
The value 4 lies outside the observed range [-3,3]. Uncertainty about the slope has a greater effect on the fitted mean farther from the centred design, increasing h(x_*). The future-error contribution is unchanged; the increased width comes from greater parameter uncertainty in the prediction. This calculation assumes the linear model remains appropriate beyond the observed range; it does not account for possible failure of that model there.

Key result. The mean-response scale is s\sqrt h; the new-observation scale is s\sqrt{1+h}. The extra 1 represents new observational noise, while h measures uncertainty about the fitted mean.






Practice set: Q43. Unknown Normal mean and variance: conditional versus marginal

Question page: Q43. Unknown Normal mean and variance: conditional versus marginal

[14 marks]
Suppose X_1,\ldots,X_n\mid\mu,v
\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(\mu,v),
\qquad p(\mu,v)\propto\frac1v, where \mu\in\mathbb R, v>0, n\ge2, and S=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2>0. Use the inverse-Gamma convention f(v)\propto v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v}.
(a) Establish the identity \sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2=S+n(\mu-\bar x)^2. [2 marks]
(b) Derive the full conditional distributions \mu\mid v,{\boldsymbol{x}} and v\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}}. [4 marks]
(c) Integrate out \mu to derive p(v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}). Explain why it differs from p(v\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}}). [4 marks]
(d) Describe a Gibbs sampler using part (b). A student instead samples v from its marginal posterior, then \mu conditional on that draw, repeating with fresh random numbers. Is this also a valid way to sample the joint posterior? Are its resulting pairs independent? [4 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write v=\sigma^2, \bar x=n^{-1}\sum_i x_i, and S=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2, the unnormalised sum of squares. We use N(m,v) with variance v and \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b) with kernel v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v} on v>0. A full conditional fixes the other parameter; a marginal posterior integrates it out.
Assumptions. The Normal observations are conditionally iid, with prior p(\mu,v)\propto1/v relative to d\mu\,dv. Because this prior is improper, require n\ge2 and S>0 for the posterior below to be proper.
(a) Sum-of-squares identity. Write x_i-\mu=(x_i-\bar x)+(\bar x-\mu) and expand: \begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2
&=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2
+2(\bar x-\mu)\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)
+n(\bar x-\mu)^2\\
&=\boxed{S+n(\mu-\bar x)^2},
\end{aligned} because \sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=0.
(b) Full conditional distributions. The likelihood and joint posterior kernels are L(\mu,v;{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto
v^{-n/2}\exp\left\{-\frac{S+n(\mu-\bar x)^2}{2v}\right\}, p(\mu,v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto
v^{-n/2-1}\exp\left\{-\frac{S+n(\mu-\bar x)^2}{2v}\right\},
\qquad \mu\in\mathbb R,\ v>0. For fixed v, retain only factors involving \mu: p(\mu\mid v,{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto
\exp\left\{-\frac{n(\mu-\bar x)^2}{2v}\right\}. Recognising a Normal kernel, \boxed{\mu\mid v,{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim N\!\left(\bar x,\frac vn\right).} For fixed \mu, retain all the v-dependent factors: p(v\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto
v^{-n/2-1}\exp\left\{-\frac{S+n(\mu-\bar x)^2}{2v}\right\}. Under the stated inverse-Gamma convention, \boxed{
v\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim
\operatorname{InvGamma}\!\left(\frac n2,\frac{S+n(\mu-\bar x)^2}{2}\right).
} Its support is v>0. In this conditional distribution, \mu is held fixed; it has not been replaced by \bar x or integrated out.
(c) Marginal posterior for v. Integrate the joint posterior kernel over all \mu\in\mathbb R: \begin{aligned}
p(v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto v^{-n/2-1}e^{-S/(2v)}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\exp\left\{-\frac{n(\mu-\bar x)^2}{2v}\right\}\,d\mu\\
&=v^{-n/2-1}e^{-S/(2v)}\sqrt{\frac{2\pi v}{n}}\\
&\propto v^{-(n-1)/2-1}e^{-S/(2v)}.
\end{aligned} Therefore \boxed{v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\!\left(\frac{n-1}{2},\frac S2\right),
\qquad v>0.} The assumptions n\ge2 and S>0 make both parameters positive, so the posterior is proper despite the improper prior.
The marginal distribution accounts for uncertainty in \mu by integrating over it. The integral contributes a factor v^{1/2}, changing the shape from n/2 to (n-1)/2. Even setting \mu=\bar x in the full conditional does not produce the marginal posterior, because it misses this factor.
(d) Gibbs sampling and direct joint sampling. Start from any \mu^{(0)}\in\mathbb R and v^{(0)}>0. At iteration t=1,\ldots,T, draw \mu^{(t)}\sim N\!\left(\bar x,\frac{v^{(t-1)}}n\right), v^{(t)}\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\!\left(
\frac n2,\frac{S+n(\mu^{(t)}-\bar x)^2}{2}\right). Each update uses the latest available value of the other parameter. The resulting Markov chain has the joint posterior as its equilibrium distribution; successive pairs are generally dependent, and convergence from the chosen starting value must be assessed.
The student’s alternative is also valid. Independently for each repetition, draw v^{(t)}\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\!\left(\frac{n-1}{2},\frac S2\right),
\qquad
\mu^{(t)}\mid v^{(t)}\sim N\!\left(\bar x,\frac{v^{(t)}}n\right). This samples the factorisation p(\mu,v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=p(v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})p(\mu\mid v,{\boldsymbol{x}}) directly. With fresh independent random numbers for each repetition, the pairs are iid joint-posterior draws, with no burn-in required. The two components within a pair are not independent: the conditional variance of \mu depends on v.

title: Marginal likelihood and Bayes factor
text:
Definition taught in Bayesian hypotheses and model comparison, part of Bayesian statistics
The marginal likelihood in model M_j is 
p(x\mid M_j)
=\int p(x\mid\theta_j,M_j)
       p(\theta_j\mid M_j)\,\mathrm{d}\theta_j.
 It averages the likelihood over the parameter prior; it does not evaluate the likelihood at a fitted maximum. The Bayes factor comparing M_1 with M_2 is \operatorname{BF}_{12}=p(x\mid M_1)/p(x\mid M_2).

title: Marginal likelihood and Bayes factor
Marginal likelihood and Bayes factor
text:
Examples

Practice set: Q11. Bayes factors and posterior odds

Question page: Q11. Bayes factors and posterior odds

Suppose X\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,\theta). Consider M_0:\theta=\frac12,
  \qquad
  M_1:\theta\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1). Under M_1, the stated distribution is the prior for \theta. Write m_j(x)=p(x\mid M_j).
(a) Derive m_0(x) and m_1(x). Retain the constants in the binomial probability mass function. [4 marks]
(b) Obtain B_{10}=\frac{m_1(x)}{m_0(x)}. Explain how it relates prior model odds to posterior model odds. [3 marks]
(c) Suppose n=3, x=3, and \mathbb{P}(M_1)=1/5. Calculate B_{10} and \mathbb{P}(M_1\mid x). Explain how the data can favour M_1 while M_0 still has the larger posterior probability. [3 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. M_0 fixes \theta=1/2; M_1 assigns \theta\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1,1). Write m_j(x)=\mathbb P(X=x\mid M_j) for the marginal likelihood and B_{10}=m_1(x)/m_0(x) for the Bayes factor favouring M_1. The Beta integral is B(a,b)=\int_0^1u^{a-1}(1-u)^{b-1}\,du. Prior probabilities of the two models are distinct from their priors for \theta.

(a) Marginal likelihoods
Under M_0, the marginal probability of observing X=x is m_0(x)
=
\mathbb{P}(X=x\mid M_0)
=
\binom{n}{x}\left(\frac12\right)^x
\left(\frac12\right)^{n-x}
=
\boxed{\binom{n}{x}2^{-n}}.
Under M_1, integrate the likelihood with respect to the uniform prior: \begin{aligned}
m_1(x)
&=
\mathbb{P}(X=x\mid M_1)\\
&=
\binom{n}{x}
\int_0^1\theta^x(1-\theta)^{n-x}\,d\theta\\
&=
\binom{n}{x}B(x+1,n-x+1)\\
&=
\binom{n}{x}
\frac{x!(n-x)!}{(n+1)!}\\
&=
\boxed{\frac{1}{n+1}}.
\end{aligned}


(b) Bayes factor
The Bayes factor in favour of M_1 over M_0 is \boxed{
B_{10}
=
\frac{m_1(x)}{m_0(x)}
=
\frac{2^n}{(n+1)\binom{n}{x}}.
} Values greater than one favour M_1, while values less than one favour M_0.


(c) Posterior model odds
Posterior odds equal the Bayes factor multiplied by prior odds: \boxed{
\frac{\mathbb{P}(M_1\mid x)}{\mathbb{P}(M_0\mid x)}
=
B_{10}
\frac{\mathbb{P}(M_1)}{\mathbb{P}(M_0)}.
}


(d) Numerical comparison
For n=3 and x=3, m_0(3)=\frac18,
\qquad
m_1(3)=\frac14,
\qquad
B_{10}=2. Thus the observed data are twice as probable under M_1 as under M_0, so the data favour M_1.
If \mathbb{P}(M_1)=\frac15,
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(M_0)=\frac45, then the prior odds for M_1 are 1/4. Hence \frac{\mathbb{P}(M_1\mid x)}{\mathbb{P}(M_0\mid x)}
=2\left(\frac14\right)
=\frac12. Therefore \boxed{
\mathbb{P}(M_1\mid x)=\frac13,
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(M_0\mid x)=\frac23.
} The data favour M_1, but the prior favoured M_0 by four to one. The evidence from this small sample is not strong enough to overturn that prior preference, so M_0 remains more probable a posteriori.






Final preparation: Question 15. Battery lifetimes and a Bayes factor

Question page: Question 15. Battery lifetimes and a Bayes factor

Researchers are attempting to determine the distribution of lifetimes of a type of battery. They have measured the lifetimes (years) of n of these batteries, recorded as x_1,\ldots,x_n, which we assume were the result of a random sample and we will assume that the observations could be considered independent and identically distributed. Two models were proposed:

M_1\colon x\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\theta)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
M_2\colon x\sim\operatorname{Weibull}(5,\theta).

This Weibull density is given by

f(x)=5\theta x^{4}e^{-\theta x^{5}},
\qquad\text{for }x>0.

Consider the prior distribution \theta\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1).
(a) Find the marginal likelihood under model M_1. [3 marks]
(b) Find the marginal likelihood under model M_2. [3 marks]
(c) Obtain an expression for the Bayes factor comparing M_1 to M_2. [2 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Under M_1, \theta is an exponential rate. Under M_2, its meaning is fixed by the supplied Weibull density 5\theta x^4e^{-\theta x^5}, rather than by a software scale convention. In both models the prior density is e^{-\theta} on \theta>0. Write S_1=\sum_i x_i, S_5=\sum_i x_i^5 and P_4=\prod_i x_i^4. The marginal likelihood averages a sampling density over the specified parameter prior.
(a) Let S_1=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i. Independence gives, for \theta>0,

p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta,M_1)
=
\prod_{i=1}^{n}\theta e^{-\theta x_i}
=
\theta^{n}e^{-\theta S_1}.

Since S_1+1>0,

p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_1)
=
\int_0^{\infty}\theta^{n}e^{-\theta(S_1+1)}\,d\theta.

Put u=(S_1+1)\theta. Then d\theta=du/(S_1+1) and u runs over (0,\infty), so

\begin{aligned}
p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_1)
&=
(S_1+1)^{-(n+1)}\int_0^{\infty}u^{n}e^{-u}\,du
=
\frac{\Gamma(n+1)}{(S_1+1)^{n+1}}.
\end{aligned}

Here n is a positive integer, so \Gamma(n+1)=n!.

\boxed{p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_1)
=
\dfrac{n!}{\bigl(1+\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\bigr)^{n+1}}.}

(b) Let P_4=\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_i^{4} and S_5=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i^{5}. The given density and independence give

p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta,M_2)
=
\prod_{i=1}^{n}5\theta x_i^{4}e^{-\theta x_i^{5}}
=
5^{n}\theta^{n}P_4 e^{-\theta S_5},
\qquad\theta>0.

Thus

p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_2)
=
5^{n}P_4\int_0^{\infty}\theta^{n}e^{-(S_5+1)\theta}\,d\theta.

Now S_5+1>0. The same substitution as in (a) gives \int_0^{\infty}\theta^{n}e^{-(S_5+1)\theta}\,d\theta=n!/(S_5+1)^{n+1}. The factor 5^{n}P_4 does not depend on \theta, but it belongs to the normalised sampling density, so it remains in the marginal likelihood.

\boxed{p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_2)
=
\dfrac{5^{n}\,n!\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_i^{4}}{\bigl(1+\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i^{5}\bigr)^{n+1}}.}

(c) By (a) and (b),

\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{BF}_{12}
&=
\frac{p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_1)}{p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_2)}
=
\frac{n!/(1+S_1)^{n+1}}{5^{n}n!\,P_4/(1+S_5)^{n+1}}
=
\frac{1}{5^{n}P_4}
\Biggl(\frac{1+S_5}{1+S_1}\Biggr)^{n+1}.
\end{aligned}


\boxed{\operatorname{BF}_{12}
=
\dfrac{1}{5^{n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_i^{4}}
\Biggl(
\dfrac{1+\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i^{5}}{1+\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i}
\Biggr)^{n+1}.}

Thus \operatorname{BF}_{12}>1 favours M_1, and \operatorname{BF}_{12}<1 favours M_2.
The transformation U=X^5 clarifies the second integration: under M_2, U\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\theta). However, the observed data are the x_i, so the transformation Jacobian \prod_i5x_i^4=5^nP_4 remains in their likelihood. Dropping it would compare densities expressed for different observed variables. In posterior inference within M_2 it is constant in \theta and can be omitted; in this model comparison it cannot.
The prior in each model must also be normalised. Using a density proportional to one on the positive line in place of \operatorname{Exp}(1) would introduce an unspecified multiplicative constant into each marginal likelihood. The stated proper priors avoid that ambiguity. Posterior model odds are obtained only after multiplying BF_{12} by the prior model odds.

title: Log-partition moment identities
text:
Proposition taught in Exponential families and conjugacy, part of Bayesian statistics
Whenever c(\theta) can be used as a local parameter and differentiation under the normalising integral is valid,
\nabla_c\log a(\theta)
=\mathbb{E}_\theta\{T(X)\},
\qquad
\nabla_c^2\log a(\theta)
=\operatorname{Cov}_\theta\{T(X)\}.
Here derivatives are taken with respect to c=c(\theta), so a(\theta) is regarded as a function of c through the chosen parametrisation. Consequently \log a(\theta) is convex as a function of c, and the one-observation Fisher information in the natural parameter is \nabla_c^2\log a(\theta).
