title: Inverse-Gamma distribution
text:
Definition taught in Conjugate analysis for normal models, part of Bayesian statistics · Also on the distribution sheet
Under the book’s convention,
\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(\alpha_0,\beta_0),
means that \sigma^2>0 has density
p(\sigma^2)
=\frac{\beta_0^{\alpha_0}}{\Gamma(\alpha_0)}
  (\sigma^2)^{-\alpha_0-1}
\exp\!\left(-\frac{\beta_0}{\sigma^2}\right).

title: Inverse-Gamma distribution
text:
Properties

Normal–inverse-Gamma variance update

Main article: Normal–inverse-Gamma variance update


\boxed{
\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\!\left(
   \alpha_0+\frac n2,
   \beta_0+\frac12S_\mu
\right)}.



Normal–inverse-Gamma conjugacy

Main article: Normal–inverse-Gamma conjugacy


{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid\sigma^2,{\boldsymbol{y}}
\sim\operatorname{N}_p({\boldsymbol{m}}_n,\sigma^2{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{V}}_n),
\qquad
\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{y}}\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(a_n,b_n).



Marginal variance posterior

Main article: Marginal variance posterior


\boxed{
\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{y}},{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}
\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\!\left(
\frac{n-p}{2},\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}2\right).}
 The p/2 from the normalising constant is subtracted from n/2; it is not added. Equivalently, 
\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}{\sigma^2}\mid{\boldsymbol{y}},{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}
\sim\chi^2_{n-p}.
 If n>p+2, the posterior mean exists and is

\mathbb{E}(\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{y}},{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})
=\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}{n-p-2}
=\frac{n-p}{n-p-2}s^2.

The posterior mode is \operatorname{SSE}/(n-p+2). Thus the unbiased estimator s^2 is generally neither the posterior mean nor the posterior mode; calling any one quantity “the estimate” implicitly chooses a loss function.

title: Inverse-Gamma distribution
text:
Examples

Final preparation: Question 2. Normal variance, known mean

Question page: Question 2. Normal variance, known mean

Let

X_i\mid\sigma^2\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^2),

with \mu known and

\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(\alpha_0,\beta_0),

in the shape–rate parameterisation

f(\sigma^2)\propto(\sigma^2)^{-\alpha_0-1}\exp(-\beta_0/\sigma^2).

(a) Write the posterior distribution of \sigma^2, and state what is added to each parameter.
(b) State the posterior mean and mode of \sigma^2, including the conditions under which each exists.
(c) Explain why that mean and mode generally differ.
(d) Explain why the variance update uses squared deviations from the known mean \mu, rather than from \bar x.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Put v=\sigma^2 and Q_\mu=\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2, with \mu known. Our \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b) convention has density b^a v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v}/\Gamma(a) for v>0. Equivalently, 1/v\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a,b) in shape–rate form. Specifying the kernel avoids ambiguity about the second parameter.
(a) Independence gives the likelihood kernel L(v)\propto v^{-n/2}e^{-Q_\mu/(2v)}. Multiplication by the prior gives

p(v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto
v^{-n/2}e^{-Q_\mu/(2v)}v^{-\alpha_0-1}e^{-\beta_0/v}
=v^{-(\alpha_0+n/2)-1}e^{-(\beta_0+Q_\mu/2)/v}.

Let \alpha_n=\alpha_0+n/2 and \beta_n=\beta_0+Q_\mu/2. Recognising this kernel,

\boxed{
\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim
\operatorname{InvGamma}(\alpha_n,\beta_n).
}

Each observation adds 1/2 to the shape. Half the sum of squared deviations from the known mean is added to the rate.
(b) For this shape–rate kernel, and for \beta_n>0,

\mathbb{E}(\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{\beta_n}{\alpha_n-1}
\quad\text{when }\alpha_n>1,
\qquad
\operatorname{mode}(\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{\beta_n}{\alpha_n+1}
\quad\text{when }\alpha_n>0.

The mode solves (-\alpha_n-1)/v+\beta_n/v^2=0. The mean is the gamma integral of v\cdot v^{-\alpha_n-1}e^{-\beta_n/v}, which converges only for \alpha_n>1.
More explicitly, substituting u=\beta_n/v into the expectation gives \mathbb{E}(v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\beta_n\Gamma(\alpha_n-1)/\Gamma(\alpha_n)=\beta_n/(\alpha_n-1). When 0<\alpha_n\le1, the posterior is still a proper distribution, but its right tail is too heavy to have a finite mean. Posterior propriety and existence of a posterior moment are separate requirements.
(c) For \alpha_n>1,

\frac{\beta_n}{\alpha_n-1}-\frac{\beta_n}{\alpha_n+1}
=
\frac{2\beta_n}{(\alpha_n-1)(\alpha_n+1)}>0.

The inverse-gamma density is right-skewed, so the long right tail pulls the mean above the mode.
(d) Under the sampling model, \operatorname{Var}(X_i\mid\sigma^2)=\mathbb{E}[(X_i-\mu)^2\mid\sigma^2]. The sufficient statistic for \sigma^2, with \mu known, is \sum(x_i-\mu)^2. Since

\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2
=
\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2-n(\bar x-\mu)^2,

centring at \bar x omits the term n(\bar x-\mu)^2.
When the mean is known, departures of the sample mean from that value are evidence about the observation variance too. For example, a tightly clustered sample far from the known mean has small \sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2 but large Q_\mu. Replacing Q_\mu by the centred sum of squares would discard that evidence and change the likelihood.





Final preparation: Question 14. Inverse-gamma waiting time

Question page: Question 14. Inverse-gamma waiting time

The waiting time until the mth animal at location i has density

f(x_i\mid\theta)
=
\frac{1}{\Gamma(m)\,\theta^{m}}x_i^{m-1}e^{-x_i/\theta},
\quad x_i>0,

so \theta>0 is a scale. The prior is

f(\theta)
=
\frac{\beta_0^{\alpha_0}}{\Gamma(\alpha_0)}\theta^{-\alpha_0-1}e^{-\beta_0/\theta},
\quad\alpha_0>0,\ \beta_0>0.

The exam states that the maximum likelihood estimator is \hat\theta=\bar x/m.
(i) State the prior mean. [1 mark]
(ii) Find and identify the posterior distribution of \theta. [5 marks]
(iii) State the posterior mean, and show that it is a weighted sum of the prior mean and \hat\theta. [5 marks]
(iv) What happens to the posterior mean as m\to\infty? [2 marks]
(v) What happens if \alpha_0,\beta_0\to 0? [2 marks]
(vi) Complete: “The effect of the prior hyperparameters \alpha_0 and \beta_0 on the posterior mean of \theta is like…” [2 marks]
(vii) Describe a posterior 100(1-\alpha)\% credible interval for \theta. [5 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Here m is a known gamma shape and \theta is its unknown scale: the sampling kernel in \theta is \theta^{-m}\exp(-x/\theta). This differs from a gamma rate parameterisation. Write T=\sum_i x_i and use \operatorname{InvGamma}(\alpha_0,\beta_0) with kernel \theta^{-\alpha_0-1}e^{-\beta_0/\theta}. The estimator \hat\theta=T/(nm) has the same units as \theta.
The sampling density is gamma with shape m and scale \theta, so \mathbb{E}(X_i\mid\theta)=m\theta and the supplied estimator \hat\theta=\bar x/m is the maximum likelihood estimator.
(i) For \alpha_0>1,

\mathbb{E}(\theta)=\beta_0/(\alpha_0-1).

(ii) The likelihood contributes

\theta^{-nm}\exp\bigl(-(\textstyle\sum_i x_i)/\theta\bigr).

The prior contributes

\theta^{-\alpha_0-1}\exp(-\beta_0/\theta).

Hence

\boxed{\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(\alpha_0+nm,\;\beta_0+\textstyle\sum_i x_i).}

(iii) For \alpha_0+nm>1,

\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=
\frac{\beta_0+\sum x_i}{\alpha_0+nm-1}
=
\frac{(\alpha_0-1)\,\mathbb{E}(\theta)+nm\,\hat\theta}{(\alpha_0-1)+nm}.

Writing the mean explicitly as a convex combination gives

\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\underbrace{\frac{\alpha_0-1}{\alpha_0+nm-1}}_{w_0}\mathbb{E}(\theta)
+\underbrace{\frac{nm}{\alpha_0+nm-1}}_{w_n}\hat\theta.

For \alpha_0>1, both weights are nonnegative and w_0+w_n=1. The data contribution is nm, the total number of captured animals across the n locations.
(iv) With n and the prior fixed, m\to\infty makes w_0\to0 and w_n\to1. If \hat\theta=\bar x/m remains bounded, as it does in probability under the stated sampling model at a fixed true scale, the posterior mean approaches \hat\theta.
(v) Taking \alpha_0,\beta_0\to0 in the posterior expression gives \sum_i x_i/(nm-1)=\{nm/(nm-1)\}\hat\theta, provided nm>1. It is close to, but not exactly, the MLE. This is a formal weak-prior limit: the proper inverse-gamma prior’s mean does not exist along the path once \alpha_0\leq1, so the weighted-average formula involving that mean cannot be used to take this limit.
(vi) When \alpha_0>1, the hyperparameters act like prior information that pulls the MLE toward the prior mean \beta_0/(\alpha_0-1), with weight w_0. In the posterior-mean ratio, \alpha_0-1 plays a pseudo-count role beside the observed nm, and \beta_0 plays a prior total-waiting-time role beside \sum_i x_i. These need not represent literal extra animals.
(vii) Let a=\alpha_0+nm and b=\beta_0+\sum x_i. The central credible interval is the \alpha/2 and 1-\alpha/2 quantiles of \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b).
Equivalently, let q_u be the u-quantile of \operatorname{Gamma}(a,b) in shape–rate form. Since 1/\theta has this gamma posterior, the interval is [1/q_{1-\alpha/2},1/q_{\alpha/2}]. The reversal of endpoints follows because taking reciprocals is decreasing. Conditional on the data and model, the interval contains posterior probability 1-\alpha; it describes uncertainty about the common scale, not the waiting time of a future animal.

title: Hyperparameter
text:
Definition taught in Hierarchical Bayes, part of Bayesian statistics
For a fully Bayesian analysis, the population-level quantities are also unknown and receive priors, for example
\mu\sim\operatorname{N}(m_0,s_0^2),
\qquad
\tau^2\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b).
The quantities controlling the distribution of the \theta_j’s are called hyperparameters, or higher-level parameters. Once priors are assigned to them, their uncertainty is propagated into every class-specific posterior.

title: Hyperparameter
text:
Properties

Marginal hyperposterior

Main article: Marginal hyperposterior

The binomial coefficient does not depend on (\alpha,\beta), so the hyperposterior kernel is 
\boxed{
p(\alpha,\beta\mid{\boldsymbol{y}})
\propto p(\alpha,\beta)
\prod_{j=1}^J
\frac{\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)
       \Gamma(y_j+\alpha)
       \Gamma(n_j-y_j+\beta)}
      {\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)
       \Gamma(n_j+\alpha+\beta)}}.
 This expression is available pointwise but is not a familiar normalised density.

title: Hyperparameter
text:
Examples

Rat-tumour hierarchy

Worked example from Hierarchical Bayes

Tumour rates in female F344 rats supply a second hierarchical example. In a current control study, y=4 of n=14 rats developed one or more tumours over two years. A one-study model is

Y\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Bin}(14,\theta),
\qquad
\theta\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta),

giving

\theta\mid Y=4
\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+4,\beta+10).

The question is how to choose (\alpha,\beta) when 70 earlier control studies are available.
Let study j contribute y_j tumour-bearing rats from n_j animals. The hierarchical model is 
Y_j\mid\theta_j,n_j\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n_j,\theta_j),
\qquad
\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta
\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta),
\quad j=1,\ldots,J.
 Each study has its own rate, but all study rates are drawn from a common population distribution.


Practice set: Q23. Rat-tumour studies and hierarchical shrinkage

Question page: Q23. Rat-tumour studies and hierarchical shrinkage

[12 marks]
Suppose J related studies record tumour counts Y_j\mid\theta_j\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n_j,\theta_j),
\qquad j=1,\ldots,J, independently conditional on the study rates. Assume \theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta
\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta),
\qquad
\alpha\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1),\quad
\beta\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1), where the two hyperpriors are independent. Write \mathbf y=(y_1,\ldots,y_J); the sample sizes n_j are known. You may use B(a,b)=\int_0^1 t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}\,dt,
\qquad
f(\theta\mid a,b)=\frac{\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}}{B(a,b)}.
(a) [2 marks] Derive and identify the full conditional distribution \theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y.
(b) [3 marks] For this part only, fix \alpha=2 and \beta=8. Two studies report (y_1,n_1)=(4,10),\qquad (y_2,n_2)=(40,100). Calculate both posterior means. Although both observed proportions equal 0.4, explain why the posterior means differ and identify which study experiences stronger shrinkage.
(c) [4 marks] Return to unknown \alpha,\beta. Integrate out the study rates to derive:
(i) the marginal probability \mathbb{P}(Y_j=y_j\mid\alpha,\beta);
(ii) the marginal posterior kernel p(\alpha,\beta\mid\mathbf y).
Express your answers using Beta functions. Explain why the Beta prior’s normalising factor cannot be discarded when deriving this hyperparameter posterior.
(d) [3 marks] Explain how the full Bayesian model allows studies to share information. What uncertainty is omitted if \alpha,\beta are instead estimated from the data and then treated as known?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Study j has observed count y_j, known size n_j, and unknown rate \theta_j; \alpha,\beta>0 are shared hyperparameters. A \operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta) density is \theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1}/B(\alpha,\beta) on (0,1), where B(a,b)=\int_0^1u^{a-1}(1-u)^{b-1}\,du. \operatorname{Exp}(1) uses rate one. Partial pooling allows different study rates linked through a common population distribution.
Assumptions. The hierarchy assumes conditional independence of studies given their rates, and iid Beta rates given \alpha,\beta. Thus its joint density factors as p(\alpha)p(\beta)\prod_jp(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta)p(y_j\mid\theta_j), with independent rate-one exponential hyperpriors. Only in part (b) are the hyperparameters fixed at the supplied values.
(a) Full conditional for a study rate. Holding \alpha,\beta fixed, the factors involving \theta_j are \begin{aligned}
p(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y)
&\propto p(y_j\mid\theta_j)p(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta)\\
&\propto\theta_j^{y_j}(1-\theta_j)^{n_j-y_j}
\theta_j^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta_j)^{\beta-1}\\
&=\theta_j^{\alpha+y_j-1}(1-\theta_j)^{\beta+n_j-y_j-1}.
\end{aligned} Therefore \boxed{\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y
\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+y_j,\beta+n_j-y_j),\qquad 0<\theta_j<1.} Conditional on the hyperparameters and data, the study rates are independent. Other studies’ observations affect this study’s marginal posterior through learning \alpha,\beta, not through an additional factor in this full conditional.
(b) Posterior means and shrinkage. For fixed \alpha=2, \beta=8, the population mean is \frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}=\frac2{10}=0.2. The two posteriors are \theta_1\mid\alpha=2,\beta=8,\mathbf y\sim\operatorname{Beta}(6,14), \theta_2\mid\alpha=2,\beta=8,\mathbf y\sim\operatorname{Beta}(42,68). Thus their posterior means are \boxed{\mathbb{E}(\theta_1\mid\alpha=2,\beta=8,\mathbf y)=\frac6{20}=0.3,} \boxed{\mathbb{E}(\theta_2\mid\alpha=2,\beta=8,\mathbf y)=\frac{42}{110}
\approx0.3818.} To see the shrinkage explicitly, write \frac{\alpha+y_j}{\alpha+\beta+n_j}
=\frac{\alpha+\beta}{\alpha+\beta+n_j}
\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}
+\frac{n_j}{\alpha+\beta+n_j}\frac{y_j}{n_j}. Both sample proportions equal 0.4, but study 1 puts weight 10/20=1/2 on the population mean, whereas study 2 puts only 10/110=1/11 on it. The smaller study therefore experiences stronger shrinkage toward 0.2. The larger study has more information about its own rate, so its posterior mean remains closer to its observed proportion.
(c) Integrating out the study rates. For one study, retain the normalising factor of the Beta density: \begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(Y_j=y_j\mid\alpha,\beta)
&=\int_0^1 p(y_j\mid\theta_j)p(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta)\,d\theta_j\\
&=\binom{n_j}{y_j}\frac1{B(\alpha,\beta)}
\int_0^1\theta_j^{y_j+\alpha-1}
(1-\theta_j)^{n_j-y_j+\beta-1}\,d\theta_j\\
&=\boxed{\binom{n_j}{y_j}
\frac{B(\alpha+y_j,\beta+n_j-y_j)}{B(\alpha,\beta)}.}
\end{aligned} This is a Beta–Binomial marginal distribution, with y_j\in\{0,\ldots,n_j\}.
The independent rate-one exponential hyperpriors give p(\alpha,\beta)=e^{-\alpha-\beta},\qquad \alpha>0,\quad\beta>0. The studies remain independent conditional on the hyperparameters after their individual rates have been integrated out. Consequently, \begin{aligned}
p(\alpha,\beta\mid\mathbf y)
&\propto p(\alpha,\beta)
\prod_{j=1}^{J}\mathbb{P}(Y_j=y_j\mid\alpha,\beta)\\
&\propto e^{-(\alpha+\beta)}
\prod_{j=1}^{J}
\frac{B(\alpha+y_j,\beta+n_j-y_j)}{B(\alpha,\beta)}.
\end{aligned} Hence \boxed{
p(\alpha,\beta\mid\mathbf y)
\propto e^{-(\alpha+\beta)}B(\alpha,\beta)^{-J}
\prod_{j=1}^{J}B(\alpha+y_j,\beta+n_j-y_j),
\quad \alpha,\beta>0.
} The binomial coefficients can be dropped because the observed y_j and known n_j make them constant with respect to \alpha,\beta. However, 1/B(\alpha,\beta) depends on the hyperparameters, so it must remain. A factor constant in \theta_j need not be constant in \alpha,\beta.
(d) Sharing information and hyperparameter uncertainty. Every study contributes to the posterior for the common population parameters \alpha,\beta. That posterior then contributes to each study-specific posterior through p(\theta_j\mid\mathbf y)
=\int_0^\infty\!\int_0^\infty
p(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y)
p(\alpha,\beta\mid\mathbf y)\,d\alpha\,d\beta. This is partial pooling: study rates can differ, but they are connected by a population distribution learned from all the studies. The model does not force them to be identical, and it does not treat them as unrelated.
Replacing \alpha,\beta by fixed estimates is an empirical-Bayes plug-in analysis. It omits uncertainty about the population distribution’s parameters. For example, the law of total variance gives \begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(\theta_j\mid\mathbf y)
={}&\mathbb{E}\!\left[
\operatorname{Var}(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y)
\mid\mathbf y\right]\\
&+\operatorname{Var}\!\left[
\mathbb{E}(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y)
\mid\mathbf y\right].
\end{aligned} The second term represents variation in the conditional mean as the hyperparameters vary under their posterior. A plug-in calculation does not propagate this variation and can therefore give an overly precise account of uncertainty.

Key result. Conditional conjugacy does not eliminate uncertainty in the hyperparameters. Full Bayes learns their distribution and averages over it.

title: Grid Monte Carlo approximation
text:
Definition taught in Hierarchical Bayes, part of Bayesian statistics
Let w_{ab} be the unnormalised hyperposterior value at grid cell (a,b), including the Jacobian \alpha\beta. The discrete approximation is
\widehat p_{ab}=\frac{w_{ab}}{\sum_{r,s}w_{rs}}.
Sampling from the approximate full posterior proceeds as follows.
\theta_j\sim\operatorname{Beta}(y_j+\alpha,n_j-y_j+\beta)
using Equation (7) in Hierarchical Bayes.
These grid-cell draws are independent; this is Monte Carlo from a piecewise-constant approximation, not Markov-chain Monte Carlo. A 100\times100 grid has 10^4 cells and remains practical because only two hyperparameters are integrated numerically. A comparable grid over all J+2 unknowns would be impossible.

text:

The hyperparameters update as

\alpha\leftarrow

\qquad

title: Generic exponential-family conjugate update
text:
Examples

Poisson natural form and Gamma conjugacy

Worked example from Exponential families and conjugacy

Question. For iid Poisson observations with mean \theta, write the model in the a(\theta), b(x), c(\theta), T(x) form, identify the sufficient statistic, and derive the corresponding conjugate prior and posterior update.
Solution. For one Poisson observation, \begin{align*}
p(x\mid\theta)
&=\frac{e^{-\theta}\theta^x}{x!}\\
&=\frac1{x!}\exp\{x\log\theta\}e^{-\theta}\\
&=\frac{b(x)\exp\{c(\theta)T(x)\}}{a(\theta)},
\end{align*} with

b(x)=\frac1{x!},
\qquad c(\theta)=\log\theta,
\qquad T(x)=x,
\qquad a(\theta)=e^\theta.

For the Poisson model, the definition Equation (4) in Exponential families and conjugacy gives S({\boldsymbol{x}})=\sum_i x_i. The joint likelihood is \begin{align*}
p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta)
&=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{e^{-\theta}\theta^{x_i}}{x_i!}\\
&=\left(\prod_{i=1}^n\frac1{x_i!}\right)
   \exp\{(\log\theta)S({\boldsymbol{x}})-n\theta\}.
\end{align*} The factorisation theorem shows that S({\boldsymbol{X}}) is sufficient for \theta. It is also minimal sufficient by the likelihood-ratio criterion. Because the natural parameter c(\theta)=\log\theta ranges over the open set \mathbb{R}, S({\boldsymbol{X}}) is complete as well.
The generic prior Equation (6) in Exponential families and conjugacy becomes \begin{align*}
p(\theta\mid\alpha,\beta)
&\propto
\frac{\exp\{\alpha\log\theta\}}{(e^\theta)^\beta}\\
&=\theta^\alpha e^{-\beta\theta}.
\end{align*} This is the kernel of \operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha+1,\beta), not \operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha,\beta). Using the sufficient statistic S({\boldsymbol{x}}), \begin{align*}
p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto
\theta^{S({\boldsymbol{x}})} e^{-n\theta}\theta^\alpha e^{-\beta\theta}\\
&=\theta^{S({\boldsymbol{x}})+\alpha}e^{-(n+\beta)\theta},
\end{align*} so 
\boxed{
\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha+S({\boldsymbol{x}})+1,\beta+n)}.
 Its posterior mean is \begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=\frac{\alpha+S({\boldsymbol{x}})+1}{\beta+n}\\
&=\frac{(\alpha+1)+n\overline x}{\beta+n}\\
&=\frac\beta{\beta+n}\frac{\alpha+1}{\beta}
  +\frac n{\beta+n}\overline x.
\end{align*} The prior therefore behaves, for the mean, as \beta prior observations with total count \alpha+1.


Practice set: Q1. Rayleigh conjugate prior

Question page: Q1. Rayleigh conjugate prior

Suppose X_1,\ldots,X_n\mid\theta
  \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Rayleigh}(\theta), with density f(x\mid\theta)
  =\frac{x}{\theta}\exp\left(-\frac{x^2}{2\theta}\right),
  \qquad x>0,\quad \theta>0.
Using the general exponential-family conjugacy result, find a conjugate prior for \theta and derive the posterior distribution.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. For observed {\boldsymbol{x}}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n), L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}}) is the sampling density viewed as a function of \theta. A kernel omits only factors constant in that parameter. Conjugacy means that prior and posterior belong to the same family. We use \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b):\quad p(\theta)\propto\theta^{-a-1}e^{-b/\theta},
\qquad \theta>0,\quad a,b>0, with shape a and inverse-Gamma scale b. The Rayleigh observations are conditionally iid and positive.
The general exponential-family form used in the course is f(x\mid\theta)
  =b(x)\frac{\exp\{c(\theta)T(x)\}}{a(\theta)}, for which a conjugate prior has kernel \pi(\theta)
  \propto
  \frac{\exp\{\alpha c(\theta)\}}{a(\theta)^\beta}.
For the Rayleigh density, f(x\mid\theta)
  =x\,
    \frac{\exp\left\{-\dfrac{1}{\theta}\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right\}}
         {\theta}. Thus, we identify b(x)=x,
  \qquad
  T(x)=\frac{x^2}{2},
  \qquad
  c(\theta)=-\frac{1}{\theta},
  \qquad
  a(\theta)=\theta.
Substitution into the conjugate-prior kernel gives \pi(\theta)
  \propto
  \frac{\exp(-\alpha/\theta)}{\theta^\beta}
  =\theta^{-\beta}\exp\left(-\frac{\alpha}{\theta}\right). Matching this to the inverse-Gamma kernel in Definitions gives a=\beta-1,
  \qquad
  b=\alpha. Therefore, a conjugate prior is \boxed{\theta\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(\beta-1,\alpha)}, with \alpha>0 and \beta>1 for a proper prior.
For an iid sample, the likelihood is \begin{aligned}
  L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})
  &=\prod_{i=1}^n
    \frac{x_i}{\theta}
    \exp\left(-\frac{x_i^2}{2\theta}\right)\\
  &\propto
    \theta^{-n}
    \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\theta}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2\right).
\end{aligned} Multiplying the likelihood by the prior gives \begin{aligned}
  \pi(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
  &\propto L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})\pi(\theta)\\
  &\propto
    \theta^{-n}
    \exp\left(-\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2}{2\theta}\right)
    \theta^{-\beta}
    \exp\left(-\frac{\alpha}{\theta}\right)\\
  &\propto
    \theta^{-(\beta+n)}
    \exp\left[
      -\frac{\alpha+\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2}{\theta}
    \right].
\end{aligned} Recognising the inverse-Gamma kernel, \boxed{
    \theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
    \sim
    \operatorname{InvGamma}\left(
      \beta+n-1,
      \alpha+\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2
    \right)
  }.
Equivalently, if the prior is written directly as \theta\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b), then

Key result. \boxed{
    \theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
    \sim
    \operatorname{InvGamma}\left(
      a+n,
      b+\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2
    \right)
  }. This is the form worth remembering after working through the derivation.






Practice set: Q12. Pareto likelihood and Gamma posterior

Question page: Q12. Pareto likelihood and Gamma posterior

Suppose X_1,\ldots,X_n are conditionally iid with density p(x_i\mid\theta)
  =\theta m^\theta x_i^{-(\theta+1)},
  \qquad x_i\geq m, where m>0 is known and \theta>0 is unknown. Use the prior p(\theta)=\theta e^{-\theta},
  \qquad \theta>0. You may use the fact that a \operatorname{Gamma}(A,B) distribution in shape–rate form has kernel \theta^{A-1}e^{-B\theta}, mean A/B, and mode (A-1)/B when A>1.
[8 marks]
(a) Show that the likelihood can be written L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto\theta^n e^{-\theta S},
          \qquad
          S=\sum_{i=1}^n\log\left(\frac{x_i}{m}\right). [3 marks]
(b) Derive the posterior distribution of \theta. Identify its distribution, parameters, and support. [3 marks]
(c) State the posterior mean and MAP estimate. [2 marks]
Start with part (a). The target expression is supplied, so the task is to show how multiplying the densities produces it.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. The known lower endpoint is m>0, and the observed data satisfy x_i\ge m. We use the shape–rate Gamma kernel \theta^{A-1}e^{-B\theta} for \theta>0, A,B>0, with mean A/B and mode (A-1)/B when A>1. The MAP estimate is this posterior mode. The prior \theta e^{-\theta} is \operatorname{Gamma}(2,1).
Since m is known and the observed sample is valid, the support indicator does not depend on \theta.

(a) Likelihood
By conditional independence, \begin{aligned}
L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=\prod_{i=1}^n
  \left[\theta m^\theta x_i^{-(\theta+1)}\right]\\
&=\theta^n m^{n\theta}
  \prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{-(\theta+1)}.
\end{aligned} The factor m^{n\theta} must be retained because it depends on \theta. Using a^b=e^{b\log a}, \begin{aligned}
L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=\theta^n
  \exp\left(n\theta\log m\right)
  \exp\left[-(\theta+1)\sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i\right]\\
&=\theta^n
  \exp\left[-\sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i\right]
  \exp\left[-\theta\left\{
    \sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i-n\log m
  \right\}\right].
\end{aligned} The first exponential in the final line does not depend on \theta and may be absorbed into the proportionality constant. Also, \sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i-n\log m
=\sum_{i=1}^n\log\left(\frac{x_i}{m}\right)
=S. Therefore, \boxed{
L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto\theta^n e^{-\theta S},
\qquad \theta>0.
}


(b) Posterior distribution
Multiplying the likelihood by the prior gives \begin{aligned}
p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})p(\theta)\\
&\propto
\theta^n e^{-\theta S}\,
\theta e^{-\theta}\\
&=\theta^{n+1}e^{-(S+1)\theta},
\qquad \theta>0.
\end{aligned} Comparing this with the shape–rate Gamma kernel \theta^{A-1}e^{-B\theta}, we obtain A-1=n+1,
\qquad
B=S+1. Hence \boxed{
\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(n+2,S+1)
\quad\text{in shape--rate form},
\qquad \theta>0.
} Because x_i\geq m, each \log(x_i/m)\geq0, so S+1>0 as required.


(c) Posterior mean and MAP estimate
For a shape–rate \operatorname{Gamma}(A,B) distribution, the mean is A/B. Therefore, \boxed{
\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{n+2}{S+1}.
} The MAP estimate is the posterior mode. Since A=n+2>1, \boxed{
\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MAP}}
=\frac{A-1}{B}
=\frac{n+1}{S+1}.
}

title: Gaussian linear model
text:
Definition taught in Bayesian linear regression, part of Bayesian statistics
Let {\boldsymbol{x}}_i^\top denote row i of {\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}. The Gaussian linear model is 
{\boldsymbol{Y}}={\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}},
\qquad
{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}\mid\sigma^2
\sim\operatorname{N}_n({\boldsymbol{0}},\sigma^2{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{I}}_n),
 and hence 
{\boldsymbol{Y}}\mid{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2,{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}
\sim\operatorname{N}_n({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{I}}_n).
 Equivalently, the errors are independent with \varepsilon_i\sim\operatorname{N}(0,\sigma^2), so every response has variance \sigma^2 and distinct responses have zero covariance.
The design matrix is conditioned on and treated as fixed. This does not claim that its entries were never measured; it says that their uncertainty is not part of this particular model.

title: Gaussian linear model
Gaussian linear model
text:
Examples

Eight-point regression

Worked example from Bayesian linear regression

Consider n=8 observations with one predictor and an intercept:

{\boldsymbol{x}}=(1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8)^{\mathsf T},
\qquad
{\boldsymbol{y}}=(2.05,3.40,4.55,5.10,7.20,8.05,9.60,10.80)^\top.

Question. Under the reference-prior analysis developed above, compute \widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}, the fitted sum of squared errors, the posterior distributions of \sigma^2 and {\boldsymbol{\beta}}, and marginal 95\% credible intervals for the two regression coefficients. Then derive posterior predictive distributions at \widetilde x=4.5 and \widetilde x=10 and explain the effect of extrapolation.
Solution. For this example put the intercept first, so the ith row of {\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}} is (1,x_i). Direct summation gives

\sum_i y_i=50.75,
\qquad
\sum_i x_i y_i=280.80,
\qquad
\sum_i y_i^2=387.9175.

Therefore

{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}=
\begin{pmatrix}8&36\\36&204\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\boldsymbol{y}}=
\begin{pmatrix}50.75\\280.80\end{pmatrix}.

The determinant is 8(204)-36^2=336, so

({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})^{-1}
=\frac1{336}\begin{pmatrix}204&-36\\-36&8\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}
0.607143&-0.107143\\
-0.107143&0.023810
\end{pmatrix}.

Multiplying by {\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\boldsymbol{y}}, \begin{align*}
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
&=\frac1{336}
\begin{pmatrix}204&-36\\-36&8\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}50.75\\280.80\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\frac1{336}
\begin{pmatrix}
204(50.75)-36(280.80)\\
-36(50.75)+8(280.80)
\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\begin{pmatrix}0.726786\\1.248214\end{pmatrix}.
\end{align*} The fitted SSE can be calculated without listing every residual: \begin{align*}
\operatorname{SSE}
&={\boldsymbol{y}}^\top{\boldsymbol{y}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\boldsymbol{y}}\\
&=387.9175
-\frac{244.2}{336}(50.75)-\frac{419.4}{336}(280.80)\\
&\approx0.534554.
\end{align*} The exact coefficients are kept here rather than the six-figure decimals printed above. The subtraction cancels almost everything: two quantities near 387.9 leave a remainder near 0.53, so rounding \widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} first costs about four significant figures in \operatorname{SSE}. Summing the squared residuals directly avoids the cancellation entirely.
Thus n-p=6 and

s^2=\frac{0.534554}{6}\approx0.089092.

Under the reference prior, \begin{align*}
\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{y}}
&\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(3,0.267277),\\
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid{\boldsymbol{y}}
&\sim t_6\!\left(
\begin{pmatrix}0.726786\\1.248214\end{pmatrix},
0.089092
\begin{pmatrix}
0.607143&-0.107143\\
-0.107143&0.023810
\end{pmatrix}\right).
\end{align*} The variance summaries illustrate why the loss function matters:

\mathbb{E}(\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{y}})=\frac{0.267277}{3-1}=0.133638,
\qquad
\operatorname{mode}(\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{y}})
=\frac{0.267277}{3+1}=0.066819,

while s^2=0.089092. Using t_{0.975,6}\approx2.447, the marginal 95\% credible intervals are approximately

\beta_0\mid{\boldsymbol{y}}:\ (0.158,1.296),
\qquad
\beta_1\mid{\boldsymbol{y}}:\ (1.136,1.361).

At \widetilde x=4.5, take \widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}=(1,4.5)^\top. Matrix multiplication gives

h(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}})
=(1,4.5)({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})^{-1}
\begin{pmatrix}1\\4.5\end{pmatrix}=0.125,

and the predicted centre is

\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}^\top\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
=0.726786+4.5(1.248214)=6.34375.

Consequently,

\widetilde Y\mid{\boldsymbol{y}},\widetilde x=4.5
\sim t_6\!\left(6.34375,
\sqrt{0.089092(1.125)}\right)
\approx t_6(6.344,0.317).

At \widetilde x=10, the centre is about 13.209 and h(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}})\approx0.845, giving predictive scale about 0.405. The increase from 0.317 is the uncertainty cost of extrapolating beyond the observed predictor range.






Figure 1: The eight observations, the fitted line, and the two bands. The inner band is for the mean response and the outer for a new observation; the gap between them is the extra 1 in the predictive scale, which is why they never meet however small the leverage term becomes. The vertical rules mark the two predictions computed above, at \widetilde x=4.5 inside the data and \widetilde x=10 beyond it. Both bands are narrowest near \overline x and flare outward, so the cost of extrapolation is a feature of the geometry rather than a separate warning to remember.





Practice set: Q24. Bayesian regression and prediction

Question page: Q24. Bayesian regression and prediction

[12 marks]
Consider the regression model Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad
\varepsilon_i\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2), with reference prior p(\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma^2)\propto1/\sigma^2 for (\beta_0,\beta_1)\in\mathbb{R}^2 and \sigma^2>0. For n=10 observations, the design matrix has rows (1,x_i), and \widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
(X^\top X)^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1/10&0\\0&1/40\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \operatorname{SSE}=16. The observed predictor values range from -3 to 3.
You may use the standard regression posterior formulas under this prior. Use the inverse-Gamma convention f(v)\propto v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v}. Write t_\nu(m,s) for a Student-t distribution with location m and scale s, and use t_{0.975,8}=2.306.
(a) [2 marks] State the marginal posterior distribution of \sigma^2 and calculate \mathbb{E}(\sigma^2\mid\mathbf y,X).
(b) [3 marks] State the marginal posterior distribution of the slope \beta_1, and calculate its equal-tailed 95% credible interval.
(c) [4 marks] At x_*=0, derive the posterior distributions and equal-tailed 95% intervals for:
(i) the unknown mean response \mu_*=\beta_0+\beta_1x_*;
(ii) a new observation \widetilde Y.
Explain precisely why the second interval is wider.
(d) [3 marks] Calculate h(x_*)=(1,x_*)(X^\top X)^{-1}(1,x_*)^\top at x_*=0 and x_*=4. Compare the posterior predictive scales at these points and explain how the calculation reflects uncertainty from extrapolation.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write D=(\mathbf y,X), v=\sigma^2, and \operatorname{SSE}=\|\mathbf y-X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\|^2. The inverse-Gamma kernel is v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v} on v>0. t_\nu(m,s) denotes location m, scale s, and \nu degrees of freedom: (T-m)/s\sim t_\nu. A scale is not a variance; t_{q,\nu} denotes the q quantile of standard t_\nu.
Assumptions. Use independent Normal errors, fixed covariates, full column rank X, n>p, positive SSE, and the reference prior p(\boldsymbol\beta,v)\propto1/v with respect to d\boldsymbol\beta\,dv. These rank and residual conditions ensure a proper posterior despite the improper prior.
There are p=2 regression coefficients, including the intercept. Define \nu=n-p=8,\qquad
s^2=\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}{n-p}=\frac{16}{8}=2,
\qquad C=(X^\top X)^{-1}. Here s^2 is the residual variance estimate; it is not the posterior mean of \sigma^2.
Why the regression posterior has this form. The likelihood times the reference prior gives p(\boldsymbol\beta,v\mid D)
\propto v^{-n/2-1}
\exp\{-\|\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta\|^2/(2v)\},
\qquad v=\sigma^2>0. Expand about the least-squares estimate. The cross term vanishes because X^\top(\mathbf y-X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})=\mathbf0, giving \|\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta\|^2
=\operatorname{SSE}
+(\boldsymbol\beta-\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})^\top
X^\top X(\boldsymbol\beta-\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}). The second term is a Normal quadratic. At fixed v it identifies \boldsymbol\beta\mid v,D\sim
N_p(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},vC). Its unnormalised exponential integrates to (2\pi v)^{p/2}|X^\top X|^{-1/2}, which explains the v^{p/2} factor in the variance marginal below.
(a) Marginal variance posterior. Under the stated reference prior, \sigma^2\mid D\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\left(\frac{n-p}{2},
\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}2\right). Thus \boxed{\sigma^2\mid D\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(4,8),\qquad\sigma^2>0.} An \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b) variable has mean b/(a-1) when a>1, so \boxed{\mathbb{E}(\sigma^2\mid D)=\frac8{4-1}=\frac83\approx2.6667.} For completeness, integrating the coefficient kernel out of the joint posterior contributes a factor (\sigma^2)^{p/2}. Therefore p(\sigma^2\mid D)
\propto (\sigma^2)^{-(n/2+1)}(\sigma^2)^{p/2}
\exp\!\left(-\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}{2\sigma^2}\right)
=(\sigma^2)^{-5}e^{-8/\sigma^2}, confirming the shape 4, not n/2=5.
(b) Slope posterior and credible interval. The conditional coefficient posterior is \boldsymbol\beta\mid\sigma^2,D
\sim N_2(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},\sigma^2 C). The slope entry of C is 1/40, so \beta_1\mid\sigma^2,D\sim N\!\left(2,\frac{\sigma^2}{40}\right). Integrating over \sigma^2\mid D gives \boxed{\beta_1\mid D\sim t_8\!\left(2,\sqrt{\frac2{40}}\right)
=t_8(2,\sqrt{0.05}).} Equivalently, (\beta_1-2)/\sqrt{0.05}\mid D\sim t_8. The equal-tailed 95% credible interval is therefore 2\pm2.306\sqrt{0.05}=2\pm0.5156,
\qquad\boxed{(1.484,\,2.516).} The second argument of t_8 is a scale, not a variance. There is no additional division by \sqrt n: sample-size information is already in C.
(c) Mean response versus a new observation at x_*=0. For a general predictor value, set \mathbf z_*=(1,x_*)^\top and write m_*=\mathbf z_*^\top\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},
\qquad h(x_*)=\mathbf z_*^\top C\mathbf z_*. The linear-transformation rule for a normal vector gives \mu_*\mid\sigma^2,D
\sim N\bigl(m_*,\sigma^2 h(x_*)\bigr). For a new response \widetilde Y=\mu_*+\widetilde\varepsilon, the new error is independent of the coefficient uncertainty conditional on \sigma^2,D, and has variance \sigma^2. Thus \widetilde Y\mid\sigma^2,D,x_*
\sim N\bigl(m_*,\sigma^2\{1+h(x_*)\}\bigr). Integrating over the inverse-Gamma variance posterior gives \mu_*\mid D\sim t_8\bigl(m_*,s\sqrt{h(x_*)}\bigr), \widetilde Y\mid D,x_*\sim t_8\bigl(m_*,s\sqrt{1+h(x_*)}\bigr). At x_*=0, m_*=(1,0)\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}=1,
\qquad h(0)=\frac1{10}. Therefore the unknown mean response has posterior \boxed{\mu_*\mid D\sim t_8(1,\sqrt{0.2}),} with equal-tailed 95% credible interval 1\pm2.306\sqrt{0.2}=1\pm1.0313,
\qquad\boxed{(-0.031,\,2.031).} The new observation has posterior predictive distribution \boxed{\widetilde Y\mid D,x_*=0\sim t_8(1,\sqrt{2.2}),} with equal-tailed 95% predictive interval 1\pm2.306\sqrt{2.2}=1\pm3.4204,
\qquad\boxed{(-2.420,\,4.420).} Both intervals have the same centre and use the same t_8 quantile. The predictive interval is wider because a new observation includes both uncertainty about the regression mean and fresh observational noise. That additional noise produces the extra 1 in 1+h(x_*).
(d) Extrapolation and predictive scale. Using the supplied diagonal matrix, \begin{aligned}
h(x_*)&=(1,x_*)
\begin{pmatrix}1/10&0\\0&1/40\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}1\\x_*\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\frac1{10}+\frac{x_*^2}{40}.
\end{aligned} Hence \boxed{h(0)=0.1,\qquad h(4)=0.1+\frac{16}{40}=0.5.} The corresponding predictive scales are \boxed{s_{\mathrm{pred}}(0)=\sqrt{2(1+0.1)}=\sqrt{2.2}\approx1.4832,} \boxed{s_{\mathrm{pred}}(4)=\sqrt{2(1+0.5)}=\sqrt3\approx1.7321.} At x_*=4, the predicted centre is 1+2(4)=9, so the predictive distribution is t_8(9,\sqrt3). Its interval is wider than at x_*=0 because it has the same degrees of freedom but a larger scale.
The value 4 lies outside the observed range [-3,3]. Uncertainty about the slope has a greater effect on the fitted mean farther from the centred design, increasing h(x_*). The future-error contribution is unchanged; the increased width comes from greater parameter uncertainty in the prediction. This calculation assumes the linear model remains appropriate beyond the observed range; it does not account for possible failure of that model there.

Key result. The mean-response scale is s\sqrt h; the new-observation scale is s\sqrt{1+h}. The extra 1 represents new observational noise, while h measures uncertainty about the fitted mean.






Final preparation: Question 5. Normal–inverse-\chi^2 regression

Question page: Question 5. Normal–inverse-\chi^2 regression

Suppose

y\mid\beta,\sigma^2,X\sim \operatorname{N}_n(X\beta,\sigma^2 I_n),

with prior

\beta\mid\sigma^2\sim \operatorname{N}_p(\beta_0,\sigma^2\Sigma_0),
\qquad
\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{Inv\text{-}\chi^2}(\mu_0,\sigma_0^2).

Here X is known, \Sigma_0 is positive definite, and \mu_0,\sigma_0^2>0. The inverse-\chi^2 convention is

\frac{\mu_0\sigma_0^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_{\mu_0}.

(a) State the inverse-\chi^2 prior kernel and its equivalent inverse-gamma parameters.
(b) State the updated parameters \Sigma_n and \beta_n.
(c) State the updated parameters \mu_n and \sigma_n^2.
(d) Express the joint posterior through a conditional posterior for \beta and a marginal posterior for \sigma^2.
(e) Express the updated scale using a residual sum of squares and a prior penalty. Explain why it is positive.
(f) Is \Sigma_n the conditional covariance matrix of \beta? Is \sigma_n^2 the posterior mean of \sigma^2? Give the correct expressions and the posterior mode of \sigma^2.
(g) State the full conditional posterior of \sigma^2\mid\beta,y,X. How does it differ from its marginal posterior?
(h) Without consulting the updates, complete the square to reconstruct them. Explain why the marginal degrees of freedom are \mu_0+n.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. There are n responses and p regression coefficients; X is an n\times p known design matrix. Write v=\sigma^2. The matrix \Sigma_0 scales the conditional prior covariance v\Sigma_0. In this question \mu_0 denotes prior degrees of freedom, not a normal mean. Our \operatorname{Inv\text{-}\chi^2}(\nu,s^2) convention means \nu s^2/v\sim\chi^2_\nu, or equivalently v\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(\nu/2,\nu s^2/2).
(a) The transformation \mu_0\sigma_0^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_{\mu_0} has kernel

\pi(\sigma^2)
\propto
(\sigma^2)^{-\mu_0/2-1}
\exp\Bigl(-\frac{\mu_0\sigma_0^2}{2\sigma^2}\Bigr),
\qquad\sigma^2>0.

Matching (\sigma^2)^{-a-1}\exp(-b/\sigma^2) gives a=\mu_0/2 and b=\mu_0\sigma_0^2/2.
For completeness, if U=\mu_0\sigma_0^2/v, then |dU/dv|=\mu_0\sigma_0^2/v^2. Multiplying the \chi^2_{\mu_0} density at U by this Jacobian gives the displayed inverse-gamma kernel. The Jacobian supplies the power v^{-2} and must be retained.

\boxed{
\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\Bigl(\frac{\mu_0}{2},\frac{\mu_0\sigma_0^2}{2}\Bigr).
}

(b) Since \Sigma_0^{-1} is positive definite and X^\top X is positive semidefinite, \Sigma_n^{-1} is positive definite. Precision addition gives

\boxed{\Sigma_n^{-1}=X^\top X+\Sigma_0^{-1},}
\qquad
\boxed{\beta_n=\Sigma_n(X^\top y+\Sigma_0^{-1}\beta_0).}

The data and prior precision contributions add, and their combined precision determines the posterior centre.
At fixed v, the likelihood contributes X^\top X/v to the precision of \beta, and the prior contributes \Sigma_0^{-1}/v. Their sum is \Sigma_n^{-1}/v. A proper positive-definite prior therefore gives a proper conditional update even if X is not of full column rank; an unregularised least-squares inverse (X^\top X)^{-1} is not needed.
(c)

\boxed{\mu_n=\mu_0+n,}
\qquad
\boxed{
\sigma_n^2
=
\frac{
\mu_0\sigma_0^2+y^\top y+\beta_0^\top\Sigma_0^{-1}\beta_0
-\beta_n^\top\Sigma_n^{-1}\beta_n
}{\mu_n}.
}

(d)

\boxed{\beta\mid\sigma^2,y,X\sim \operatorname{N}_p(\beta_n,\sigma^2\Sigma_n),}
\qquad
\boxed{\sigma^2\mid y,X\sim\operatorname{Inv\text{-}\chi^2}(\mu_n,\sigma_n^2).}

Together these specify a normal–inverse-\chi^2 joint posterior.
This is a conditional–marginal factorisation. To draw an independent posterior pair, draw v from the marginal inverse-\chi^2 distribution and then \beta from its normal distribution conditional on that v. The components within a pair are dependent through the conditional covariance, even though different pairs can be generated independently.
(e) Equivalently,

\mu_n\sigma_n^2
=
\mu_0\sigma_0^2
+(y-X\beta_n)^\top(y-X\beta_n)
+(\beta_n-\beta_0)^\top\Sigma_0^{-1}(\beta_n-\beta_0).

Both quadratic forms are nonnegative and \mu_0\sigma_0^2>0, so \sigma_n^2>0. The algebra is completed in (h).
(f) No. The conditional covariance is \sigma^2\Sigma_n, not \Sigma_n:

\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(\beta\mid\sigma^2,y,X)=\sigma^2\Sigma_n.}

The parameter \sigma_n^2 is a scale. By the inverse-gamma equivalence in (a),

\boxed{
\mathbb{E}(\sigma^2\mid y,X)
=
\frac{\mu_n\sigma_n^2}{\mu_n-2},
\qquad\mu_n>2,
}

and

\boxed{
\operatorname{mode}(\sigma^2\mid y,X)
=
\frac{\mu_n\sigma_n^2}{\mu_n+2}.
}

(g)

\boxed{
\sigma^2\mid\beta,y,X
\sim
\operatorname{Inv\text{-}\chi^2}\!\left(
\mu_n+p,\;
\frac{\mu_n\sigma_n^2+(\beta-\beta_n)^\top\Sigma_n^{-1}(\beta-\beta_n)}{\mu_n+p}
\right).
}

The full conditional fixes \beta. The marginal posterior integrates \beta out, which removes p from the degrees of freedom.
The difference comes from the normal density’s factor v^{-p/2}. It remains when \beta is fixed and therefore adds p/2 to the inverse-gamma shape. Integrating over \beta instead contributes a factor v^{p/2}, cancelling it. Substituting \beta=\beta_n in the full conditional would leave the wrong degrees of freedom.
(h) Expand the likelihood quadratic and the prior quadratic:

\begin{aligned}
&(y-X\beta)^\top(y-X\beta)
+(\beta-\beta_0)^\top\Sigma_0^{-1}(\beta-\beta_0)\\
&\quad=
\beta^\top(X^\top X+\Sigma_0^{-1})\beta
-2\beta^\top(X^\top y+\Sigma_0^{-1}\beta_0)
+y^\top y+\beta_0^\top\Sigma_0^{-1}\beta_0\\
&\quad=
(\beta-\beta_n)^\top\Sigma_n^{-1}(\beta-\beta_n)
+y^\top y+\beta_0^\top\Sigma_0^{-1}\beta_0
-\beta_n^\top\Sigma_n^{-1}\beta_n.
\end{aligned}

Adding \mu_0\sigma_0^2, the terms free of \beta are the numerator of \mu_n\sigma_n^2 in (c), with \mu_n=\mu_0+n. Thus

\boxed{
Q(\beta)
=
(\beta-\beta_n)^\top\Sigma_n^{-1}(\beta-\beta_n)
+\mu_n\sigma_n^2.
}

The joint posterior kernel is

(\sigma^2)^{-(\mu_0+n+p)/2-1}
\exp\Bigl(-\frac{Q(\beta)}{2\sigma^2}\Bigr).

The integral over \beta of the normal kernel equals (2\pi\sigma^2)^{p/2}|\Sigma_n|^{1/2}. The remaining power of \sigma^2 is

-\frac{\mu_0+n+p}{2}-1+\frac p2
=
-\frac{\mu_0+n}{2}-1.


\therefore
\text{the marginal inverse-}\chi^2\text{ degrees of freedom are }\mu_0+n.

title: Full conditionals under independent priors
Full conditionals under independent priors
text:
Examples

Normal mean and variance

Worked example from Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings

Question. For the joint normal-model posterior in Equation (4) in Conjugate analysis for normal models, describe a systematic Gibbs sampler and state how retained draws estimate the posterior mean of \mu.
Solution. For the joint posterior in Equation (4) in Conjugate analysis for normal models, alternate \begin{align*}
\mu^{(t+1)}&\sim
p(\mu\mid\sigma^{2(t)},{\boldsymbol{x}})
\quad\text{using (5)},\\
\sigma^{2(t+1)}&\sim
p(\sigma^2\mid\mu^{(t+1)},{\boldsymbol{x}})
\quad\text{using (6)}.
\end{align*} After discarding a warm-up segment, Monte Carlo estimates use the retained draws. For example,

\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\frac1L\sum_{t=B+1}^{B+L}\mu^{(t)},

where B is the number of discarded iterations. Because the draws are dependent, L correlated draws contain less information than L independent draws. Autocorrelation, trace plots, multiple chains, and effective sample size are therefore part of a serious analysis.


Practice set: Q49. A Gibbs full conditional under independent priors

Question page: Q49. A Gibbs full conditional under independent priors

[6 marks]
Suppose X_i\mid\mu,\tau\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}
N\!\left(\mu,\frac1\tau\right),\qquad i=1,\ldots,n, where \mu\in\mathbb R and \tau>0 are unknown.
Assign independent priors \mu\sim N\!\left(\mu_0,\frac1{\kappa_0}\right),
\qquad \tau\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a_0,b_0), where all hyperparameters are known and \kappa_0,a_0,b_0>0. The Gamma distribution is parametrised by shape and rate.
(a) Derive the full conditional distribution \tau\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}}. Show its kernel and identify the distribution and parameters. [4 marks]
(b) Does this full conditional depend explicitly on \mu_0 or \kappa_0? Explain why or why not. [2 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Precision is \tau=1/\sigma^2. N(m,v) uses variance v, and \operatorname{Gamma}(a,b) uses shape a and rate b, with kernel \tau^{a-1}e^{-b\tau} on \tau>0. The full conditional for \tau holds \mu and the data fixed, so only factors that vary with \tau remain.
Assumptions. The priors are independent: \mu\sim N(\mu_0,1/\kappa_0) and \tau\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a_0,b_0), with \kappa_0,a_0,b_0>0. In particular, the prior variance of \mu does not depend on \tau; this distinguishes the question from a Normal–Gamma conditional prior.
(a) Full conditional for \tau. The Normal density with precision \tau is f(x_i\mid\mu,\tau)
=\left(\frac\tau{2\pi}\right)^{1/2}
\exp\left\{-\frac\tau2(x_i-\mu)^2\right\}. Therefore the likelihood kernel is L(\mu,\tau;{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto
\tau^{n/2}\exp\left\{-\frac\tau2\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2\right\}. The independent priors give the joint posterior kernel \begin{aligned}
p(\mu,\tau\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto
\tau^{n/2}\exp\left\{-\frac\tau2\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2\right\}\\
&\quad\times\exp\left\{-\frac{\kappa_0}{2}(\mu-\mu_0)^2\right\}
\tau^{a_0-1}e^{-b_0\tau}.
\end{aligned} For fixed \mu, its prior factor is constant with respect to \tau. Dropping that factor and collecting powers and exponents gives \boxed{
p(\tau\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto
\tau^{a_0+n/2-1}
\exp\left[-\left\{b_0+\frac12\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2\right\}\tau\right],
\quad\tau>0.
} Hence \boxed{
\tau\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{Gamma}\!\left(
a_0+\frac n2,\ b_0+\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2\right)
\quad\text{(shape--rate)}.
}
(b) Dependence on \mu_0 and \kappa_0. No: the full conditional has no explicit dependence on these two hyperparameters. Under the independent priors, p(\mu,\tau)=p(\mu)p(\tau), and once \mu is conditioned on, p(\mu) is a positive constant in the conditional kernel for \tau. It cancels on normalisation.
This does not mean that the prior for \mu is irrelevant to all inference about \tau. It affects the posterior distribution of \mu, and thus can affect the marginal posterior of \tau after \mu is integrated out.

Key result. Do not silently replace the independent prior with \mu\mid\tau\sim N(\mu_0,1/(\kappa_0\tau)). That is a different model whose prior contributes additional \tau-dependent factors to the full conditional.






Final preparation: Question 3. Normal mean and variance

Question page: Question 3. Normal mean and variance

Let X_i\mid\mu,\sigma^2\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^2), with independent priors

\mu\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu_0,\sigma_0^2),
\qquad
\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(\alpha_0,\beta_0).

(a) Does the joint posterior have this same product form?
(b) Write the full conditional distributions of \mu and of \sigma^2.
(c) Which updating algorithm uses these two distributions as its steps?
(d) Explain why independent priors for \mu and \sigma^2 do not generally give independent posteriors.
(e) Distinguish a full conditional posterior from a marginal posterior.
(f) Explain why a standard full conditional distribution does not imply that the corresponding marginal posterior belongs to the same family.
(g) Explain how a Gibbs sampler uses these full conditional distributions.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write v=\sigma^2, S=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2, and use \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b) with kernel v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v}. Prior independence means p(\mu,v)=p(\mu)p(v). A full conditional fixes the other unknown parameter; a marginal posterior averages over its posterior uncertainty.
(a) No. After the data are observed, \mu and \sigma^2 are dependent, so the joint posterior is not an independent normal times an independent inverse-gamma.
Bayes’ theorem gives the joint kernel

p(\mu,v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto
v^{-(\alpha_0+n/2)-1}
\exp\left\{-\frac{\beta_0+\{S+n(\mu-\bar x)^2\}/2}{v}
-\frac{(\mu-\mu_0)^2}{2\sigma_0^2}\right\}.

The term (\mu-\bar x)^2/v couples the two unknowns. The same discrepancy between \mu and the data is more plausible when the observation variance is larger.
(b) With the other parameter held fixed, the updates are the univariate conjugate posteriors:

\begin{aligned}
\mu\mid\sigma^2,x
&\sim
N\Biggl(
\frac{n\bar x\,\sigma_0^2+\mu_0\sigma^2}{n\sigma_0^2+\sigma^2},\;
\frac{\sigma^2\sigma_0^2}{n\sigma_0^2+\sigma^2}
\Biggr),\\[4pt]
\sigma^2\mid\mu,x
&\sim
\operatorname{InvGamma}\Bigl(
\alpha_0+\frac n2,\;
\beta_0+\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2
\Bigr).
\end{aligned}

The normal variance equals \sigma_1^2 from the known-variance update, because

\Bigl(\frac n{\sigma^2}+\frac1{\sigma_0^2}\Bigr)^{-1}
=
\frac{\sigma^2\sigma_0^2}{n\sigma_0^2+\sigma^2}.

(c) A Gibbs sampler uses these two distributions. Choose v^{(0)}>0. At sweep t, draw \mu^{(t)} from the normal full conditional using v^{(t-1)}, then draw v^{(t)} from the inverse-gamma full conditional using \mu^{(t)}. Record the completed pair. The second draw uses the newly updated mean, rather than its value from the previous sweep.
For compact notation in the algorithm, define

m(v)=\frac{n\bar x/v+\mu_0/\sigma_0^2}{n/v+1/\sigma_0^2},
\qquad V(v)=\left(\frac n v+\frac1{\sigma_0^2}\right)^{-1},
\qquad b(\mu)=\beta_0+\frac12\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2.

Here B is the number of initial sweeps discarded as warm-up, not a guarantee of convergence. Assess mixing from multiple valid starting values, trace plots and autocorrelation, and account for dependence when computing Monte Carlo error. An exact full-conditional draw needs no Metropolis acceptance step.
(d) The prior density factors as p(\mu)\,p(\sigma^2). The likelihood does not. The factor \sigma^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2 depends on both parameters, so

p(\mu,\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})

does not factor into a function of \mu alone times a function of \sigma^2 alone.
(e) A full conditional treats the other parameter as known:

p(\mu\mid\sigma^2,{\boldsymbol{x}})
\quad\text{and}\quad
p(\sigma^2\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}}).

The marginal posteriors integrate that parameter out,

p(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=
\int p(\mu\mid\sigma^2,{\boldsymbol{x}})\,p(\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\,d\sigma^2,
\qquad
p(\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=
\int p(\sigma^2\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}})\,p(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\,d\mu.

(f) The full conditional p(\mu\mid\sigma^2,{\boldsymbol{x}}) is normal at each fixed \sigma^2. The marginal p(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}) mixes those normals over the posterior distribution of \sigma^2; a mixture need not belong to the component family. Here, integrating the joint kernel over v gives

p(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto
\exp\left\{-\frac{(\mu-\mu_0)^2}{2\sigma_0^2}\right\}
\left\{\beta_0+\frac{S+n(\mu-\bar x)^2}{2}\right\}^{-(\alpha_0+n/2)}.

This is generally neither a normal nor a Student-t kernel. Likewise, the marginal variance posterior is a mixture of inverse-gamma full conditionals and is not generally inverse-gamma. Substituting a point estimate for the other unknown does not perform the required integration.
(g) Each Gibbs step draws from one full conditional, using the most recent value of the conditioned parameter. The stationary distribution of the pair is the joint posterior p(\mu,\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}). A marginal posterior is represented by the simulated values of one coordinate, not by a single full-conditional distribution.
After suitable convergence assessment and warm-up, averages of functions of the retained pairs approximate joint-posterior expectations. Keeping only the \mu coordinate approximates its marginal posterior automatically: uncertainty in v has been propagated through the chain. Successive draws are generally correlated, so Monte Carlo standard errors must account for that dependence.

title: Exponential family
text:
Definition taught in Introduction to generalised linear models, part of Generalised linear models
A random variable Y whose distribution depends on a parameter \theta belongs to a (one-parameter) exponential family, with dispersion \phi, if its density or mass function can be written 
f(y;\theta)=\exp\left\{\frac{a(y)\,b(\theta)+c(\theta)}{e(\phi)}+d(y;\phi)\right\},
 where a, b, c, d and e are known functions. The dispersion \phi is treated as a nuisance: often known, and at least constant across observations. It is the family’s variance parameter.

title: Exponential family
text:
Properties

Mean and variance of an exponential family

Main article: Mean and variance of an exponential family

If Y has density or mass function Equation (7) in Introduction to generalised linear models, and if differentiation in \theta may be passed under the integral or the sum, then 
\mathrm{E}(Y)=-c'(\theta),
\qquad
\mathrm{Var}(Y)=-c''(\theta)\,e(\phi).



Log-partition moment identities

Main article: Log-partition moment identities

Whenever c(\theta) can be used as a local parameter and differentiation under the normalising integral is valid,

\nabla_c\log a(\theta)
=\mathbb{E}_\theta\{T(X)\},
\qquad
\nabla_c^2\log a(\theta)
=\operatorname{Cov}_\theta\{T(X)\}.

Here derivatives are taken with respect to c=c(\theta), so a(\theta) is regarded as a function of c through the chosen parametrisation. Consequently \log a(\theta) is convex as a function of c, and the one-observation Fisher information in the natural parameter is \nabla_c^2\log a(\theta).


Generic exponential-family conjugate update

Main article: Generic exponential-family conjugate update

The hyperparameters update as 
\boxed{
\alpha\leftarrow
\alpha+S({\boldsymbol{x}}),
\qquad
\beta\leftarrow\beta+n.}



Pitman–Koopman–Darmois, informal form

Main article: Pitman–Koopman–Darmois, informal form

For regular iid models with parameter-independent support, the theorem says, roughly, that the existence for every n of a sufficient statistic whose dimension stays fixed essentially characterises exponential families. The support condition matters: models such as \operatorname{Uniform}(0,\theta) can have a fixed-dimensional sufficient statistic without having the regular form Equation (3) in Exponential families and conjugacy.

title: Exponential family
text:
Examples

Practice set: Q45. Gamma regression from the exponential-family form

Question page: Q45. Gamma regression from the exponential-family form

[12 marks]
Independent positive responses have density f(y_i\mid\mu_i,k)
=\frac{k^k}{\Gamma(k)\mu_i^k}
y_i^{k-1}\exp\left(-\frac{ky_i}{\mu_i}\right),
\qquad y_i>0, where \mu_i>0 and k>0.
(a) Express the density in the course form f(y;\theta,\phi)
        =\exp\left\{
        \frac{a(y)b(\theta)+c(\theta)}{e(\phi)}+d(y;\phi)
        \right\}, taking \theta=\mu and \phi=1/k. Identify all five functions. [4 marks]
(b) Find \mathbb{E}(Y_i) and \operatorname{Var}(Y_i). [2 marks]
(c) Under the model \log\mu_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i, interpret \beta_1 and derive the ratio of expected responses at x+1 and x. [2 marks]
(d) Derive the score vector for \boldsymbol\beta, treating k as known. [3 marks]
(e) Explain why this model does not assert that \log Y_i is Normally distributed. [1 mark]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. A Gamma variable with shape k and rate k/\mu has mean \mu and variance \mu^2/k; set \phi=1/k. In the course’s exponential-family form, b(\theta) is the coefficient paired with the statistic a(y) after division by e(\phi). For regression, \mathbf X_i=(1,x_i)^\top, \boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_0,\beta_1)^\top, and \mu_i=e^{\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta}. Responses are independent and covariates fixed; the score calculation holds k>0 known.
(a) Exponential-family representation. For one observation, taking logarithms gives \log f(y\mid\mu,k)
=k\log k-\log\Gamma(k)-k\log\mu+(k-1)\log y-\frac{ky}{\mu}. With \theta=\mu and \phi=1/k, rearrange this as \log f(y;\theta,\phi)
=\frac{-y/\theta-\log\theta}{\phi}
+\frac1\phi\log\frac1\phi-\log\Gamma\!\left(\frac1\phi\right)
+\left(\frac1\phi-1\right)\log y. One valid identification of the five functions is \boxed{
a(y)=y,\qquad b(\theta)=-\frac1\theta,\qquad
c(\theta)=-\log\theta,\qquad e(\phi)=\phi,
} \boxed{
d(y;\phi)=\frac1\phi\log\frac1\phi
-\log\Gamma\!\left(\frac1\phi\right)
+\left(\frac1\phi-1\right)\log y.
} The support is y>0, with \theta>0 and \phi>0.
(b) Mean and variance. The given density is Gamma with shape k and rate k/\mu_i. Therefore \boxed{\mathbb{E}(Y_i)=\frac{k}{k/\mu_i}=\mu_i,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\frac{k}{(k/\mu_i)^2}
=\frac{\mu_i^2}{k}=\phi\mu_i^2.}
(c) Interpretation of the coefficient. The log link gives \mu(x)=e^{\beta_0+\beta_1x}, so \boxed{\frac{\mathbb{E}(Y\mid x+1)}{\mathbb{E}(Y\mid x)}
=\frac{e^{\beta_0+\beta_1(x+1)}}{e^{\beta_0+\beta_1x}}
=e^{\beta_1}.} Thus a one-unit increase in x multiplies the expected response by e^{\beta_1}, corresponding to a percentage change 100(e^{\beta_1}-1)\%. The coefficient \beta_1 itself is the change in the log of the mean, not an additive change in the response.
(d) Score vector. Let \mathbf X_i=(1,x_i)^\top and \boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_0,\beta_1)^\top, so that \mu_i=e^{\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta}. Treating k as known, \ell(\boldsymbol\beta)
=-k\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\log\mu_i+\frac{y_i}{\mu_i}\right)+C, where C does not depend on \boldsymbol\beta. Differentiate each summand with respect to its mean and apply the chain rule: \frac{\partial\ell_i}{\partial\mu_i}
=-\frac{k}{\mu_i}+\frac{ky_i}{\mu_i^2},
\qquad
\frac{\partial\mu_i}{\partial\boldsymbol\beta}=\mu_i\mathbf X_i. It follows that \begin{aligned}
S(\boldsymbol\beta)
&=\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(-\frac{k}{\mu_i}+\frac{ky_i}{\mu_i^2}\right)\mu_i\mathbf X_i\\
&=\boxed{k\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf X_i\left(\frac{y_i}{\mu_i}-1\right)}.
\end{aligned} In components, S(\boldsymbol\beta)
=k\begin{pmatrix}
\sum_i(y_i/\mu_i-1)\\[3pt]
\sum_i x_i(y_i/\mu_i-1)
\end{pmatrix}.
(e) Why this is not a lognormal model. The model specifies a Gamma distribution for Y_i and a linear predictor for \log\mu_i=\log\mathbb{E}(Y_i). It does not specify a Normal distribution for \log Y_i. Applying a log link to a conditional mean is not the same operation as transforming the response and assuming Normal errors.

Key result. Keep the response distribution and the link separate: Gamma response plus log link does not mean lognormal response.






Concept check: C4. Exponential family

Question page: C4. Exponential family

What is an exponential family? Identify its natural parameter and statistic.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. An exponential family has density or mass function f(x\mid\theta)=b(x)\exp\{c(\theta)^\top T(x)\}/a(\theta), where c(\theta) is the natural parameter, T(x) the natural statistic, b(x) a parameter-free base factor and a(\theta) the normalising function. In the regular form used here, the support is independent of \theta.

title: Exchangeability
text:
Definition taught in Hierarchical Bayes, part of Bayesian statistics
The parameters \theta_1,\ldots,\theta_J are exchangeable if their joint density is invariant to every permutation \pi:
p(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_J)
=p(\theta_{\pi(1)},\ldots,\theta_{\pi(J)}).
Conditional iid sampling from a common Beta distribution implies exchangeability:
p({\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mid\alpha,\beta)
=\prod_{j=1}^Jp(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta).
The scientific claim is that study labels do not encode systematic differences in strain, laboratory, protocol, calendar time, or tumour definition. The sample sizes n_j may differ; exchangeability requires the latent rates not to be systematically related to those sizes.

title: Exchangeability
text:
Examples

Rat-tumour hierarchy

Worked example from Hierarchical Bayes

Tumour rates in female F344 rats supply a second hierarchical example. In a current control study, y=4 of n=14 rats developed one or more tumours over two years. A one-study model is

Y\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Bin}(14,\theta),
\qquad
\theta\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta),

giving

\theta\mid Y=4
\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+4,\beta+10).

The question is how to choose (\alpha,\beta) when 70 earlier control studies are available.
Let study j contribute y_j tumour-bearing rats from n_j animals. The hierarchical model is 
Y_j\mid\theta_j,n_j\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n_j,\theta_j),
\qquad
\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta
\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta),
\quad j=1,\ldots,J.
 Each study has its own rate, but all study rates are drawn from a common population distribution.


Concept check: C9. Pooling

Question page: C9. Pooling

How does partial pooling in a hierarchical model differ from complete pooling and no pooling?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. Complete pooling uses one common group parameter, no pooling estimates each group separately, and partial pooling connects distinct group parameters through a shared population distribution. This hierarchy allows information to be shared, typically shrinking less precisely estimated group effects more strongly toward the population centre.

title: Empirical Bayes
text:
Definition taught in Hierarchical Bayes, part of Bayesian statistics
An empirical Bayes analysis estimates prior or population-level hyperparameters from data and then treats those estimates as fixed in a lower-level Bayesian update. A full Bayesian analysis instead assigns the hyperparameters a prior and propagates their posterior uncertainty.

title: Empirical Bayes
text:
Properties

Normal hierarchical shrinkage

Main article: Normal hierarchical shrinkage

The final term is constant in \theta_j. The remaining kernel is normal, so 
\theta_j\mid\overline y_j,\mu,\tau^2,\sigma^2
\sim\operatorname{N}\!\left(
   \frac{B_j}{A_j},\frac1{A_j}\right).
 Its variance is \begin{align*}
\frac1{A_j}
&=\frac1{n_j/\sigma^2+1/\tau^2}\\
&=\frac{\sigma^2\tau^2}{\sigma^2+n_j\tau^2},
\end{align*} and its mean can be rearranged without omitting any terms: \begin{align*}
\frac{B_j}{A_j}
&=\frac{n_j\overline y_j/\sigma^2+\mu/\tau^2}
         {n_j/\sigma^2+1/\tau^2}\\
&=\frac{n_j\tau^2\overline y_j+\sigma^2\mu}
         {\sigma^2+n_j\tau^2}\\
&=\frac{n_j\tau^2}{\sigma^2+n_j\tau^2}\overline y_j
   +\frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2+n_j\tau^2}\mu\\
&=w_j\overline y_j+(1-w_j)\mu,
\end{align*} where 
w_j=\frac{n_j\tau^2}{\sigma^2+n_j\tau^2},
\qquad
1-w_j=\frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2+n_j\tau^2}.
 Thus

\mathbb{E}(\theta_j\mid\overline y_j,\mu,\tau^2,\sigma^2)
=w_j\overline y_j+(1-w_j)\mu.

title: Empirical Bayes
text:
Examples

Large and small tutorial classes

Worked example from Hierarchical Bayes

Suppose the overall mean is \mu=70, the within-class standard deviation is \sigma=10, and the between-class standard deviation is \tau=5. Class A has 100 students and \overline y_A=75, while Class B has only two students and \overline y_B=95.
Question. Compute the two shrinkage weights and posterior means, treating \mu, \sigma^2, and \tau^2 as fixed, and explain why the more extreme sample mean need not produce the more extreme posterior mean.
Solution. For Class A, \begin{align*}
w_A&=\frac{100(25)}{100+100(25)}=\frac{25}{26}\approx0.962,\\
\mathbb{E}(\theta_A\mid\overline y_A,\mu,\tau^2,\sigma^2)
&=\frac{25}{26}(75)+\frac1{26}(70)\approx74.81.
\end{align*} For Class B, \begin{align*}
w_B&=\frac{2(25)}{100+2(25)}=\frac13,\\
\mathbb{E}(\theta_B\mid\overline y_B,\mu,\tau^2,\sigma^2)
&=\frac13(95)+\frac23(70)\approx78.33.
\end{align*} The extreme average from the small class is not ignored, but it is recognised as much less precise.

title: Dirichlet moments
Dirichlet moments
text:
Examples

Practice set: Q22. Advertising responses and Dirichlet inference

Question page: Q22. Advertising responses and Dirichlet inference

[10 marks]
An advertising campaign records responses from 60 independently sampled people:




Negative
Neutral
Positive




Male
8
6
16


Female
12
4
14



Let \mathbf p=(p_{MN},p_{MU},p_{MP},p_{FN},p_{FU},p_{FP}) be the six population cell probabilities, with U denoting a neutral response. Model the counts as multinomial and use \mathbf p\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(1,1,1,1,1,1). You may use the Dirichlet kernel f(\mathbf p)\propto\prod_{k=1}^{K}p_k^{\alpha_k-1},
\qquad p_k>0,\quad \sum_{k=1}^{K}p_k=1.
(a) [2 marks] Derive the posterior distribution of \mathbf p, stating its parameters and support.
(b) [2 marks] Find the posterior mean of p_{MP} and its component of the joint MAP estimate of \mathbf p. Explain why that MAP component equals the observed cell proportion here.
(c) [2 marks] Find the posterior predictive probability that one new person responds positively, regardless of gender. Express it as a posterior expectation before calculating it.
(d) [2 marks] For that new person, calculate \mathbb{P}(\text{positive response}\mid\text{female},\text{data}). Explain why this differs from \mathbb{P}(\text{female and positive response}\mid\text{data}).
(e) [2 marks] Are the six components of \mathbf p independent under the posterior? Explain using their constraint.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Let D be the observed table and \mathbf p its six population cell probabilities. The labels M,F denote male and female; N,U,P denote negative, neutral, and positive. With parameters a_1,\ldots,a_K>0, a Dirichlet density has kernel \prod_k p_k^{a_k-1} on the simplex p_k>0, \sum_kp_k=1. The joint MAP maximises this density over the entire simplex, not a one-component marginal density.
(a) Posterior distribution. Write the counts in the stated order as \mathbf x=(8,6,16,12,4,14),\qquad n=60. The multinomial likelihood is L(\mathbf p;D)=\frac{60!}{\prod_{k=1}^{6}x_k!}
\prod_{k=1}^{6}p_k^{x_k}
\propto\prod_{k=1}^{6}p_k^{x_k}. The Dirichlet prior has kernel \prod_k p_k^{1-1}=1 on the simplex. Consequently, p(\mathbf p\mid D)\propto
\prod_{k=1}^{6}p_k^{x_k+1-1}, which is the Dirichlet kernel with parameters x_k+1. Thus \boxed{\mathbf p\mid D\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(9,7,17,13,5,15).} Its density is supported on the simplex p_k>0, \sum_{k=1}^6p_k=1; the boundary has probability zero. The posterior concentration is A=9+7+17+13+5+15=66.
(b) Posterior mean and MAP. For a Dirichlet vector with parameters a_1,\ldots,a_K and A=\sum_k a_k, \mathbb{E}(p_k)=\frac{a_k}{A},\qquad
\widehat p_{k,\mathrm{MAP}}=\frac{a_k-1}{A-K}
\quad\text{when every }a_k>1. Here every posterior parameter exceeds one, so \boxed{\mathbb{E}(p_{MP}\mid D)=\frac{17}{66}\approx0.2576,}
\qquad
\boxed{\widehat p_{MP,\mathrm{MAP}}=
\frac{17-1}{66-6}=\frac{16}{60}\approx0.2667.} The MAP component is taken from the mode of the joint posterior for \mathbf p. Since the prior density is constant on the simplex, maximising the posterior is equivalent to maximising the likelihood, giving the observed cell proportions.
(c) Predicting a positive response. Conditional on \mathbf p, the probability of a positive response is p_{MP}+p_{FP}. Averaging over posterior uncertainty gives \begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(\text{positive}\mid D)
&=\int (p_{MP}+p_{FP})p(\mathbf p\mid D)\,d\mathbf p\\
&=\mathbb{E}(p_{MP}+p_{FP}\mid D)\\
&=\frac{17}{66}+\frac{15}{66}
=\boxed{\frac{16}{33}\approx0.4848.}
\end{aligned} Prediction uses posterior averaging, not substitution of the MAP estimate.
(d) Conditioning on the new person being female. First calculate the two relevant posterior predictive probabilities: \mathbb{P}(\text{female and positive}\mid D)=\mathbb{E}(p_{FP}\mid D)=\frac{15}{66}, \mathbb{P}(\text{female}\mid D)
=\mathbb{E}(p_{FN}+p_{FU}+p_{FP}\mid D)
=\frac{13+5+15}{66}=\frac{33}{66}. By the definition of conditional probability, \boxed{
\mathbb{P}(\text{positive}\mid\text{female},D)
=\frac{15/66}{33/66}=\frac5{11}\approx0.4545.
} By contrast, the joint probability is \boxed{\mathbb{P}(\text{female and positive}\mid D)
=\frac{15}{66}=\frac5{22}\approx0.2273.} The conditional probability restricts attention to the female row; the joint probability refers to both events occurring for a person sampled from the whole population.
(e) Posterior dependence. No. The probabilities must satisfy \sum_k p_k=1 exactly. Increasing one component leaves less total probability for the others. More formally, if they were independent, then 0=\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^{6}p_k\,\middle|\,D\right)
=\sum_{k=1}^{6}\operatorname{Var}(p_k\mid D)>0, a contradiction, since each component has positive posterior variance. Indeed, distinct Dirichlet components have \operatorname{Cov}(p_j,p_k\mid D)
=-\frac{a_ja_k}{A^2(A+1)}<0,\qquad j\ne k.

Key result. Add counts to the Dirichlet parameters; average probabilities for prediction; and distinguish a joint cell probability from a probability conditional on a row.
