title: Direct posterior simulation
text:
Proposition taught in Bayesian linear regression, part of Bayesian statistics
\sigma^{2(m)}\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\!\left(
  \frac{n-p}{2},\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}2\right);
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(m)}\sim\operatorname{N}_p\!\left(
  \widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},
  \sigma^{2(m)}({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})^{-1}\right).
The resulting pairs are iid joint-posterior draws. There is no burn-in, serial dependence, or convergence diagnostic.

title: Direct posterior simulation
text:
Examples

Practice set: Q58. Joint Normal conjugacy and exact sampling

Question page: Q58. Joint Normal conjugacy and exact sampling

[20 marks; approximately 25 minutes]
Let X_1,\ldots,X_n\mid\mu,\sigma^2
\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(\mu,\sigma^2), with both \mu\in\mathbb R and \sigma^2>0 unknown, and n\ge1. Write \theta=(\mu,\sigma^2). Prior densities below are with respect to d\mu\,d\sigma^2. Use the inverse-Gamma convention p(v)\propto v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v} for v>0.
(i) Show the Normal belongs to the exponential family in the form f(x\mid\theta)
        =\frac{b(x)\exp\{c_1(\theta)T_1(x)+c_2(\theta)T_2(x)\}}
        {a(\theta)}. Identify b,a,c_1,c_2,T_1,T_2 (signs go in the c_j). Hence write the likelihood of the whole sample in terms of \sum_i x_i and \sum_i x_i^2. [4 marks]
(ii) The conjugate prior for this family is \pi(\theta)\propto
        \frac{\exp\{c_1(\theta)\alpha_1+c_2(\theta)\alpha_2\}}
        {a(\theta)^\beta}. Write it out explicitly in \mu and \sigma^2. By completing the square in \mu, show it factorises as \mu\mid\sigma^2\sim N\!\left(m_0,\frac{\sigma^2}{\kappa_0}\right),
        \qquad\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(a_0,b_0), and find m_0,\kappa_0,a_0,b_0 in terms of \alpha_1,\alpha_2,\beta. State the conditions on the hyperparameters for a proper distribution. [6 marks]
(iii) Show that the posterior is in the same family, with hyperparameters (\alpha_1+\sum_i x_i,\,\alpha_2+\sum_i x_i^2,\,\beta+n). Then give the posterior m_n,\kappa_n,a_n,b_n in terms of \bar x, s^2=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2, and the prior quantities. Here s^2 denotes the unnormalised sum of squares, not the sample variance. [4 marks]
(iv) Show that \mathbb{E}[\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}] is a weighted average of m_0 and \bar x, and give the weights. What happens as n\to\infty with fixed prior hyperparameters? [3 marks]
(v) Describe how to draw exact (non-MCMC) samples from the joint posterior of (\mu,\sigma^2), and explain why it works. Assess the claim: “With a flat prior on \mu and an independent inverse-Gamma prior on \sigma^2, exact sampling is unavailable and a Gibbs sampler is necessary.” [3 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write v=\sigma^2, \bar x=n^{-1}\sum_i x_i, and s^2=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2. Here s^2 is the unnormalised sum of squares, not the sample variance. N(m,v) uses variance v; \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b) has kernel v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v} on v>0. A Normal–inverse-Gamma factorisation means p(\mu,v)=p(v)p(\mu\mid v), not independence of \mu and v.
Assumptions. Use the specified conditionally iid Normal model with n\ge1. The joint prior density is with respect to d\mu\,dv and has exactly the kernel stated in the question. Changing to precision, or starting with a density in natural-parameter coordinates, would require a Jacobian; no such change is made here.
(i) Exponential-family form and likelihood. Expanding (x-\mu)^2=x^2-2\mu x+\mu^2 gives f(x\mid\mu,v)
=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi v}}
\exp\left(-\frac{x^2}{2v}+\frac{\mu x}{v}-\frac{\mu^2}{2v}\right)
=\frac{(2\pi)^{-1/2}\exp\{(\mu/v)x-x^2/(2v)\}}
{\sqrt v\exp\{\mu^2/(2v)\}}. One valid identification, with signs in the c_j, is \boxed{\begin{aligned}
b(x)&=(2\pi)^{-1/2},& a(\theta)&=\sqrt v\exp\{\mu^2/(2v)\},\\
T_1(x)&=x,&c_1(\theta)&=\frac\mu v,\\
T_2(x)&=x^2,&c_2(\theta)&=-\frac1{2v}.
\end{aligned}} Let S_1=\sum_i x_i and S_2=\sum_i x_i^2. Then \boxed{L(\mu,v;{\boldsymbol{x}})
=(2\pi v)^{-n/2}
\exp\left[-\frac{S_2-2\mu S_1+n\mu^2}{2v}\right].} Thus the sample enters the likelihood through (S_1,S_2).
(ii) Conjugate prior and parameter matching. Substitution into the given prior formula yields the joint density kernel \pi(\mu,v)
\propto v^{-\beta/2}
\exp\left[-\frac{\beta\mu^2-2\alpha_1\mu+\alpha_2}{2v}\right]. For \beta>0, complete the square: \beta\mu^2-2\alpha_1\mu+\alpha_2
=\beta\left(\mu-\frac{\alpha_1}{\beta}\right)^2
+\alpha_2-\frac{\alpha_1^2}{\beta}. Set \boxed{m_0=\frac{\alpha_1}{\beta},\qquad
\kappa_0=\beta,\qquad a_0=\frac{\beta-3}{2},\qquad
b_0=\frac12\left(\alpha_2-\frac{\alpha_1^2}{\beta}\right).} To see the shape parameter, factor the kernel as \pi(\mu,v)\propto
\underbrace{v^{-1/2}
\exp\left[-\frac{\kappa_0(\mu-m_0)^2}{2v}\right]}
_{\text{Normal conditional kernel, including its }v^{-1/2}\text{ factor}}
\underbrace{v^{-(\beta-1)/2}e^{-b_0/v}}
_{\text{inverse-Gamma marginal kernel}}. The Normal factor has a normalising multiplier \sqrt{\kappa_0/(2\pi)} that does not depend on v. The remaining exponent therefore satisfies a_0+1=(\beta-1)/2, giving a_0=(\beta-3)/2. Hence \mu\mid v\sim N(m_0,v/\kappa_0) and v\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(a_0,b_0).
The necessary and sufficient conditions for a proper prior are \boxed{\alpha_1\in\mathbb R,\qquad\beta>3,\qquad
\alpha_2>\frac{\alpha_1^2}{\beta}.} They ensure \kappa_0,a_0,b_0>0. The specified three-hyperparameter prior is a subfamily of the general Normal–inverse-Gamma family: it imposes \kappa_0=2a_0+3.
(iii) Posterior update. Multiplying the prior kernel by the likelihood gives \pi(\mu,v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
\propto v^{-(\beta+n)/2}
\exp\left[-\frac{(\beta+n)\mu^2
-2(\alpha_1+S_1)\mu+(\alpha_2+S_2)}{2v}\right]. This has exactly the same form, with \boxed{\alpha_1'=\alpha_1+S_1,\qquad
\alpha_2'=\alpha_2+S_2,\qquad\beta'=\beta+n.} Using S_1=n\bar x, S_2=s^2+n\bar x^2, and the prior identities \alpha_1=\kappa_0m_0 and \alpha_2=2b_0+\kappa_0m_0^2, we obtain \boxed{\begin{aligned}
\kappa_n&=\kappa_0+n,\\
m_n&=\frac{\kappa_0m_0+n\bar x}{\kappa_0+n},\\
a_n&=a_0+\frac n2,\\
b_n&=b_0+\frac12\left[s^2+
\frac{\kappa_0n}{\kappa_0+n}(\bar x-m_0)^2\right].
\end{aligned}} In particular, the final update follows from \begin{aligned}
b_n
&=\frac12\left[\alpha_2+S_2-
\frac{(\alpha_1+S_1)^2}{\beta+n}\right]\\
&=b_0+\frac12\left[s^2+\kappa_0m_0^2+n\bar x^2
-\frac{(\kappa_0m_0+n\bar x)^2}{\kappa_0+n}\right]\\
&=b_0+\frac12\left[s^2+
\frac{\kappa_0n}{\kappa_0+n}(\bar x-m_0)^2\right].
\end{aligned} Therefore \boxed{\mu\mid v,{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim N(m_n,v/\kappa_n),\qquad
v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(a_n,b_n).} The v distribution here is the marginal posterior, with \mu integrated out. All updates remain proper when the prior is proper.
(iv) Posterior mean and weights. For n\ge1 and a proper prior, a_n=a_0+n/2>1/2, which ensures that the marginal posterior mean of \mu exists. Iterated expectation gives \mathbb{E}[\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}]
=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathbb{E}[\mu\mid v,{\boldsymbol{x}}]\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\right]
=m_n. Consequently, \boxed{\mathbb{E}[\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}]
=\underbrace{\frac{\kappa_0}{\kappa_0+n}}_{w_0}m_0
+\underbrace{\frac n{\kappa_0+n}}_{w_x}\bar x.} The weights are positive and sum to one. For fixed prior hyperparameters, w_0\to0 and w_x\to1: the prior contribution vanishes and the posterior mean approaches the sample mean. Under iid sampling at fixed true parameters, \bar x\to\mu_{\mathrm{true}} almost surely, so m_n\to\mu_{\mathrm{true}} almost surely as well.
(v) Exact joint-posterior sampling. For each j=1,\ldots,M, independently of all previous pairs:
1. Draw v^{(j)}\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(a_n,b_n) from the marginal posterior of v=\sigma^2.
2. Draw \mu^{(j)}\sim N(m_n,v^{(j)}/\kappa_n), conditional on that newly drawn variance.
3. Store (\mu^{(j)},v^{(j)}).
For example, step 1 can use G^{(j)}\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a_n,b_n) in shape–rate form and set v^{(j)}=1/G^{(j)}. With fresh random numbers in each repetition, this produces iid pairs from the joint posterior because p(\mu,v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=p(v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\,p(\mu\mid v,{\boldsymbol{x}}). The two coordinates within a pair are generally dependent, but distinct pairs are independent. There is no Markov-chain convergence, burn-in, or accept/reject step to manage in this construction.
Assessing the flat-prior claim. The claim is false for a flat mean prior and an independent inverse-Gamma variance prior. To distinguish its hyperparameters from those above, suppose p(\mu)\propto1,\qquad
v\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(a_*,b_*),\qquad a_*,b_*>0. Although this joint prior is improper in \mu, for n\ge1 the posterior is proper. Using \sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2=s^2+n(\mu-\bar x)^2, its kernel is p(\mu,v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
\propto v^{-a_*-1-n/2}
\exp\left[-\frac{b_*+s^2/2}{v}
          -\frac{n(\mu-\bar x)^2}{2v}\right]. Integrating over \mu contributes a factor proportional to \sqrt v, since \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\exp\left[-\frac{n(\mu-\bar x)^2}{2v}\right]d\mu
=\sqrt{\frac{2\pi v}{n}}. Hence \boxed{v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim
\operatorname{InvGamma}\!\left(a_*+\frac{n-1}{2},\ b_*+\frac{s^2}{2}\right),
\qquad\mu\mid v,{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim N(\bar x,v/n).} One can again draw from the variance marginal and then the Normal conditional, producing independent exact posterior pairs. Gibbs sampling is valid here, but not necessary. The same distinction appears in Question 43 for p(\mu,v)\propto1/v, with its stated propriety conditions.

Key result. Exact direct sampling uses a marginal then a conditional. Gibbs sampling alternates full conditionals. The key issue is whether the needed marginal is available for direct sampling, not merely whether the prior was described as independent.

title: Credible-region constructions
text:
Definition taught in Bayesian foundations, part of Bayesian statistics
Three interval constructions are worth distinguishing. An equal-tailed 95\% credible interval (l,u) satisfies
\mathbb{P}(\theta<l\mid x)=0.025,
  \qquad
  \mathbb{P}(\theta>u\mid x)=0.025.
The minimum-width interval solves
\min_{l<u}(u-l)
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\int_l^u p(\theta\mid x)\,\mathrm{d}\theta=0.95.
A highest-posterior-density set chooses a level c so that
\mathcal H_c=\{\theta:p(\theta\mid x)\geq c\},
\qquad
\int_{\mathcal H_c}p(\theta\mid x)\,\mathrm{d}\theta=0.95.
Every included point then has density at least as large as every excluded point. For a continuous unimodal posterior this gives the minimum-width interval; for a multimodal posterior the highest-density set can be disjoint. For a symmetric unimodal density, the mean, median, and mode coincide and the common interval constructions often agree.

title: Credible-region constructions
text:
Properties

Posterior summaries from draws

Main article: Posterior summaries from draws

Let \theta^{(1)},\ldots,\theta^{(L)} be posterior draws and let \theta_{(1)}\leq\cdots\leq\theta_{(L)} be their order statistics. Then \begin{align*}
\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(\theta\mid x)
&=\frac1L\sum_{l=1}^L\theta^{(l)},\\
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\theta\mid x)
&=\frac1{L-1}\sum_{l=1}^L
   \left(\theta^{(l)}-\overline\theta\right)^2,\\
\widehat{\mathbb{P}}(\theta<c\mid x)
&=\frac1L\sum_{l=1}^L\mathbf{1}\{\theta^{(l)}<c\}.
\end{align*} The posterior median and equal-tailed interval are estimated by the corresponding empirical quantiles. With L=1000, the median can be estimated by the average of \theta_{(500)} and \theta_{(501)}, and a direct 95\% interval approximation by [\theta_{(25)},\theta_{(975)}]. The precise indices vary slightly with a software package’s quantile convention.

title: Credible-region constructions
text:
Examples

Practice set: Q8. Equal-tailed and highest-density intervals

Question page: Q8. Equal-tailed and highest-density intervals

Suppose a continuous parameter \theta has posterior density p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=2\theta,
  \qquad 0<\theta<1, and zero elsewhere.
(a) Find a 75% equal-tailed posterior credible interval. [3 marks]
(b) Find a minimum-width 75% posterior credible interval. Sketch the posterior density and explain why your interval is a highest-density interval. Exact expressions are sufficient. [3 marks]
(c) A frequentist confidence-interval procedure happens to return the same endpoints as one of your intervals. Explain the difference between a 75% confidence statement and a 75% posterior credible statement. [2 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. For a continuous posterior, F(u)=\mathbb P(\theta\le u\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}) and F^{-1} is its quantile function. An equal-tailed interval puts half the omitted probability in each tail. A highest-density interval (HDI, also called HPD) includes points of at least as high density as those excluded. Here the posterior density is 2\theta on (0,1) and the required probability is 0.75.
For 0<\theta<1, the posterior distribution function is F(\theta)=\int_0^\theta 2u\,du=\theta^2,
  \qquad
  F^{-1}(p)=\sqrt{p}.

(a) Equal-tailed 75% credible interval
An equal-tailed 75% interval leaves probability 0.125 in each tail. Therefore its endpoints are F^{-1}(0.125)=\sqrt{\frac18},
  \qquad
  F^{-1}(0.875)=\sqrt{\frac78}. Thus \boxed{
    \left[\sqrt{\frac18},\sqrt{\frac78}\right]
  } is the 75% equal-tailed posterior credible interval.


(b) Minimum-width 75% credible interval
The posterior density 2\theta increases throughout (0,1), so the highest-density interval must contain the largest values of \theta and end at 1. Let it be [c,1]. Then \mathbb{P}(c\leq\theta\leq1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
  =1-F(c)=1-c^2=0.75, which gives c=1/2. Hence the minimum-width interval is \boxed{\left[\frac12,1\right]}.



Every included point has density at least as large as every excluded point, so [1/2,1] is a highest-density interval. Equivalently, among intervals [a,b] satisfying b^2-a^2=0.75, its width (b-a)=0.75/(a+b) is minimised by taking the largest possible a+b, namely b=1 and a=1/2.


(c) Confidence versus credibility
A 75% confidence procedure has repeated-sampling coverage \mathbb{P}_{\theta}\{L(X)\leq\theta\leq U(X)\}=0.75. The probability refers to the random interval procedure; after observing the data, the realised frequentist interval is fixed.
A 75% credible interval [a,b] satisfies \mathbb{P}(a\leq\theta\leq b\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=0.75. This probability refers directly to the posterior distribution of \theta given the observed data, prior, and model. Identical numerical endpoints do not change these different interpretations.






Practice set: Q13. Bayesian German tank problem

Question page: Q13. Bayesian German tank problem

In the Second World War, Allied statisticians estimated German tank production from the serial numbers on captured tanks. Treat the serial numbers as continuous. Suppose X_1,\ldots,X_n\mid\theta
\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Uniform}(0,\theta),
\qquad \theta>0, and write x_{(n)}=\max_i x_i. Place the Pareto prior p(\theta\mid\alpha,\beta)
=\frac{\alpha\beta^\alpha}{\theta^{\alpha+1}},
\qquad \theta\geq\beta, where \alpha,\beta>0. Here \beta is a known lower bound on production.
[13 marks]
(a) Write the likelihood with every indicator function shown explicitly. Derive the posterior distribution of \theta and show that it is Pareto. State its parameters, and state exactly when the data change the prior lower bound. [4 marks]
(b) Find the posterior mean. The MLE is \widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}=x_{(n)}. Explain why the posterior mean always exceeds it, and why this is sensible rather than a sign of bias in the Bayesian estimate. [2 marks]
(c) Derive the posterior predictive density of one new captured serial number \widetilde X. Show that it is a two-component mixture, and identify both components and their weights. Find \mathbb{P}\!\left(
          \widetilde X>\max\{\beta,x_{(n)}\}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
        \right) and interpret it. [4 marks]
(d) The Pitman–Koopman–Darmois theorem links sufficient statistics of fixed dimension to exponential families. Here x_{(n)} is a one-dimensional sufficient statistic for every n, and a conjugate prior exists. Explain why this does not make \operatorname{Uniform}(0,\theta) an exponential family, and why it does not contradict the theorem. [2 marks]
(e) The captured serials are 19,40,42,60, and the prior has \alpha=1 and \beta=50. Give the posterior mean and a 95% highest-posterior-density interval for \theta. Justify the lower endpoint of the interval. [1 mark]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write x_{(1)}=\min_i x_i and x_{(n)}=\max_i x_i; \mathbf1\{A\} is one when A holds and zero otherwise. Our Pareto convention is p(\theta)=ab^a\theta^{-a-1}\mathbf1\{\theta\ge b\}, with shape a>0 and lower bound b>0. \widetilde X denotes a new serial number, conditionally independent of the sample given \theta. We use the stated continuous, conditionally iid model with n\ge1 and positive observations.
Write a_n=\alpha+n,
\qquad
b_n=\max\{\beta,x_{(n)}\}.

(a) Likelihood and posterior
For observations from \operatorname{Uniform}(0,\theta), \begin{aligned}
L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=\prod_{i=1}^n
  \left[\frac{1}{\theta}\,
  \mathbf{1}\{0<x_i<\theta\}\right]\\
&=\theta^{-n}\,
  \mathbf{1}\{x_{(1)}>0\}
  \prod_{i=1}^n\mathbf{1}\{x_i<\theta\}\\
&=\theta^{-n}\,
  \mathbf{1}\{x_{(1)}>0\}
  \mathbf{1}\{x_{(n)}<\theta\}.
\end{aligned} For a valid observed sample, \mathbf{1}\{x_{(1)}>0\} does not depend on \theta. Hence L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})
\propto\theta^{-n}\mathbf{1}\{\theta>x_{(n)}\}. Multiplying by the prior gives \begin{aligned}
p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto
\theta^{-n}\mathbf{1}\{\theta>x_{(n)}\}
\theta^{-(\alpha+1)}\mathbf{1}\{\theta\geq\beta\}\\
&=\theta^{-(\alpha+n+1)}
  \mathbf{1}\{\theta\geq b_n\}\\
&=\theta^{-(a_n+1)}\mathbf{1}\{\theta\geq b_n\}.
\end{aligned} The distinction between strict and non-strict inequalities at one endpoint is irrelevant for a continuous density. Since \int_{b_n}^{\infty}\theta^{-(a_n+1)}\,d\theta
=\frac{b_n^{-a_n}}{a_n}, the normalised posterior density is p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\frac{a_n b_n^{a_n}}{\theta^{a_n+1}},
\qquad \theta\geq b_n. Therefore, \boxed{
\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{Pareto}\!\left(
\alpha+n,\max\{\beta,x_{(n)}\}
\right).
} The data change the lower bound exactly when x_{(n)}>\beta. Otherwise the lower bound remains \beta, although the shape still changes from \alpha to \alpha+n.


(b) Posterior mean
Because a_n=\alpha+n>1, the posterior mean exists and is \boxed{
\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\frac{a_n b_n}{a_n-1}
=\frac{(\alpha+n)\max\{\beta,x_{(n)}\}}
{\alpha+n-1}.
} Since a_n/(a_n-1)>1 and b_n\geq x_{(n)}, \mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})>b_n\geq x_{(n)}
=\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}. This is sensible. The MLE is the smallest value of \theta compatible with the data because the likelihood decreases for \theta>x_{(n)}. Moreover, X_{(n)}<\theta almost surely and \mathbb{E}(X_{(n)}\mid\theta)=\frac{n}{n+1}\theta, so the sample maximum systematically falls below the true upper endpoint. The posterior mean allows for the unobserved region above the largest captured serial. Frequentist bias is a repeated-sampling property; the posterior mean is instead the Bayes estimate under squared-error loss.


(c) Posterior predictive distribution
For a new serial number \widetilde X, \begin{aligned}
p(\widetilde x\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=\int_{b_n}^{\infty}
  \frac{1}{\theta}\mathbf{1}\{0<\widetilde x<\theta\}
  \frac{a_n b_n^{a_n}}{\theta^{a_n+1}}\,d\theta\\
&=a_n b_n^{a_n}
  \int_{\max\{b_n,\widetilde x\}}^{\infty}
  \theta^{-(a_n+2)}\,d\theta,
  \qquad \widetilde x>0.
\end{aligned} Thus p(\widetilde x\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle
\frac{a_n}{a_n+1}\frac{1}{b_n},
&0<\widetilde x\leq b_n,\\[1.1em]
\displaystyle
\frac{a_n b_n^{a_n}}{(a_n+1)\widetilde x^{a_n+1}},
&\widetilde x>b_n,\\[0.8em]
0,&\widetilde x\leq0.
\end{cases} Equivalently, this is the mixture \boxed{
\frac{a_n}{a_n+1}\operatorname{Uniform}(0,b_n)
+\frac{1}{a_n+1}\operatorname{Pareto}(a_n,b_n).
} The component weights sum to one. The Uniform component has no probability above b_n, whereas the Pareto component lies above b_n almost surely. Therefore, \boxed{
\mathbb{P}(\widetilde X>b_n\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\frac{1}{a_n+1}
=\frac{1}{\alpha+n+1}.
} This is the posterior predictive probability that the next captured serial exceeds whichever is larger: the confirmed lower bound \beta or the current sample maximum.


(d) Why there is no contradiction with the Pitman–Koopman–Darmois theorem
In a regular exponential-family model, the support cannot change with the parameter: a representation of the form p(x\mid\theta)
=b(x)\frac{\exp\{c(\theta)T(x)\}}{a(\theta)} has support determined by b(x), since the exponential term is positive. For the Uniform model, p(x\mid\theta)=\frac{1}{\theta}
\mathbf{1}\{0<x<\theta\}, and the indicator switches on or off as \theta changes. Its support depends on \theta, so this is an irregular model rather than a regular exponential family.
The Pitman–Koopman–Darmois theorem assumes, among other regularity conditions, parameter-independent support. This model violates that assumption and lies outside the theorem’s scope. It may therefore have the fixed-dimensional sufficient statistic x_{(n)} and a conjugate prior without being an exponential family. The existence of a conjugate prior does not by itself imply exponential-family structure.


(e) Numerical posterior and 95% HPD interval
Here n=4, x_{(n)}=60, \alpha=1, and \beta=50, so a_n=5,
\qquad
b_n=60,
\qquad
\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{Pareto}(5,60). The posterior mean is \boxed{
\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{5(60)}{4}=75.
} The posterior density is strictly decreasing on [60,\infty), so its highest-density interval must begin at the posterior mode and lower support boundary, 60. If the upper endpoint is u, then 0.05
=\mathbb{P}(\theta>u\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\left(\frac{60}{u}\right)^5. Hence u=60(20)^{1/5}\approx109.2, and \boxed{
\text{95\% HPD interval}
=\left[60,\,60(20)^{1/5}\right]
\approx[60,109.2].
} The lower endpoint is 60 because values below the largest observed serial are impossible, and the decreasing posterior density is maximised at that boundary.

title: Conditional coefficient posterior
Conditional coefficient posterior
text:
Examples

Practice set: Q24. Bayesian regression and prediction

Question page: Q24. Bayesian regression and prediction

[12 marks]
Consider the regression model Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad
\varepsilon_i\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2), with reference prior p(\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma^2)\propto1/\sigma^2 for (\beta_0,\beta_1)\in\mathbb{R}^2 and \sigma^2>0. For n=10 observations, the design matrix has rows (1,x_i), and \widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
(X^\top X)^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1/10&0\\0&1/40\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \operatorname{SSE}=16. The observed predictor values range from -3 to 3.
You may use the standard regression posterior formulas under this prior. Use the inverse-Gamma convention f(v)\propto v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v}. Write t_\nu(m,s) for a Student-t distribution with location m and scale s, and use t_{0.975,8}=2.306.
(a) [2 marks] State the marginal posterior distribution of \sigma^2 and calculate \mathbb{E}(\sigma^2\mid\mathbf y,X).
(b) [3 marks] State the marginal posterior distribution of the slope \beta_1, and calculate its equal-tailed 95% credible interval.
(c) [4 marks] At x_*=0, derive the posterior distributions and equal-tailed 95% intervals for:
(i) the unknown mean response \mu_*=\beta_0+\beta_1x_*;
(ii) a new observation \widetilde Y.
Explain precisely why the second interval is wider.
(d) [3 marks] Calculate h(x_*)=(1,x_*)(X^\top X)^{-1}(1,x_*)^\top at x_*=0 and x_*=4. Compare the posterior predictive scales at these points and explain how the calculation reflects uncertainty from extrapolation.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write D=(\mathbf y,X), v=\sigma^2, and \operatorname{SSE}=\|\mathbf y-X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\|^2. The inverse-Gamma kernel is v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v} on v>0. t_\nu(m,s) denotes location m, scale s, and \nu degrees of freedom: (T-m)/s\sim t_\nu. A scale is not a variance; t_{q,\nu} denotes the q quantile of standard t_\nu.
Assumptions. Use independent Normal errors, fixed covariates, full column rank X, n>p, positive SSE, and the reference prior p(\boldsymbol\beta,v)\propto1/v with respect to d\boldsymbol\beta\,dv. These rank and residual conditions ensure a proper posterior despite the improper prior.
There are p=2 regression coefficients, including the intercept. Define \nu=n-p=8,\qquad
s^2=\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}{n-p}=\frac{16}{8}=2,
\qquad C=(X^\top X)^{-1}. Here s^2 is the residual variance estimate; it is not the posterior mean of \sigma^2.
Why the regression posterior has this form. The likelihood times the reference prior gives p(\boldsymbol\beta,v\mid D)
\propto v^{-n/2-1}
\exp\{-\|\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta\|^2/(2v)\},
\qquad v=\sigma^2>0. Expand about the least-squares estimate. The cross term vanishes because X^\top(\mathbf y-X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})=\mathbf0, giving \|\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta\|^2
=\operatorname{SSE}
+(\boldsymbol\beta-\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})^\top
X^\top X(\boldsymbol\beta-\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}). The second term is a Normal quadratic. At fixed v it identifies \boldsymbol\beta\mid v,D\sim
N_p(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},vC). Its unnormalised exponential integrates to (2\pi v)^{p/2}|X^\top X|^{-1/2}, which explains the v^{p/2} factor in the variance marginal below.
(a) Marginal variance posterior. Under the stated reference prior, \sigma^2\mid D\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\left(\frac{n-p}{2},
\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}2\right). Thus \boxed{\sigma^2\mid D\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(4,8),\qquad\sigma^2>0.} An \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b) variable has mean b/(a-1) when a>1, so \boxed{\mathbb{E}(\sigma^2\mid D)=\frac8{4-1}=\frac83\approx2.6667.} For completeness, integrating the coefficient kernel out of the joint posterior contributes a factor (\sigma^2)^{p/2}. Therefore p(\sigma^2\mid D)
\propto (\sigma^2)^{-(n/2+1)}(\sigma^2)^{p/2}
\exp\!\left(-\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}{2\sigma^2}\right)
=(\sigma^2)^{-5}e^{-8/\sigma^2}, confirming the shape 4, not n/2=5.
(b) Slope posterior and credible interval. The conditional coefficient posterior is \boldsymbol\beta\mid\sigma^2,D
\sim N_2(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},\sigma^2 C). The slope entry of C is 1/40, so \beta_1\mid\sigma^2,D\sim N\!\left(2,\frac{\sigma^2}{40}\right). Integrating over \sigma^2\mid D gives \boxed{\beta_1\mid D\sim t_8\!\left(2,\sqrt{\frac2{40}}\right)
=t_8(2,\sqrt{0.05}).} Equivalently, (\beta_1-2)/\sqrt{0.05}\mid D\sim t_8. The equal-tailed 95% credible interval is therefore 2\pm2.306\sqrt{0.05}=2\pm0.5156,
\qquad\boxed{(1.484,\,2.516).} The second argument of t_8 is a scale, not a variance. There is no additional division by \sqrt n: sample-size information is already in C.
(c) Mean response versus a new observation at x_*=0. For a general predictor value, set \mathbf z_*=(1,x_*)^\top and write m_*=\mathbf z_*^\top\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},
\qquad h(x_*)=\mathbf z_*^\top C\mathbf z_*. The linear-transformation rule for a normal vector gives \mu_*\mid\sigma^2,D
\sim N\bigl(m_*,\sigma^2 h(x_*)\bigr). For a new response \widetilde Y=\mu_*+\widetilde\varepsilon, the new error is independent of the coefficient uncertainty conditional on \sigma^2,D, and has variance \sigma^2. Thus \widetilde Y\mid\sigma^2,D,x_*
\sim N\bigl(m_*,\sigma^2\{1+h(x_*)\}\bigr). Integrating over the inverse-Gamma variance posterior gives \mu_*\mid D\sim t_8\bigl(m_*,s\sqrt{h(x_*)}\bigr), \widetilde Y\mid D,x_*\sim t_8\bigl(m_*,s\sqrt{1+h(x_*)}\bigr). At x_*=0, m_*=(1,0)\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}=1,
\qquad h(0)=\frac1{10}. Therefore the unknown mean response has posterior \boxed{\mu_*\mid D\sim t_8(1,\sqrt{0.2}),} with equal-tailed 95% credible interval 1\pm2.306\sqrt{0.2}=1\pm1.0313,
\qquad\boxed{(-0.031,\,2.031).} The new observation has posterior predictive distribution \boxed{\widetilde Y\mid D,x_*=0\sim t_8(1,\sqrt{2.2}),} with equal-tailed 95% predictive interval 1\pm2.306\sqrt{2.2}=1\pm3.4204,
\qquad\boxed{(-2.420,\,4.420).} Both intervals have the same centre and use the same t_8 quantile. The predictive interval is wider because a new observation includes both uncertainty about the regression mean and fresh observational noise. That additional noise produces the extra 1 in 1+h(x_*).
(d) Extrapolation and predictive scale. Using the supplied diagonal matrix, \begin{aligned}
h(x_*)&=(1,x_*)
\begin{pmatrix}1/10&0\\0&1/40\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}1\\x_*\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\frac1{10}+\frac{x_*^2}{40}.
\end{aligned} Hence \boxed{h(0)=0.1,\qquad h(4)=0.1+\frac{16}{40}=0.5.} The corresponding predictive scales are \boxed{s_{\mathrm{pred}}(0)=\sqrt{2(1+0.1)}=\sqrt{2.2}\approx1.4832,} \boxed{s_{\mathrm{pred}}(4)=\sqrt{2(1+0.5)}=\sqrt3\approx1.7321.} At x_*=4, the predicted centre is 1+2(4)=9, so the predictive distribution is t_8(9,\sqrt3). Its interval is wider than at x_*=0 because it has the same degrees of freedom but a larger scale.
The value 4 lies outside the observed range [-3,3]. Uncertainty about the slope has a greater effect on the fitted mean farther from the centred design, increasing h(x_*). The future-error contribution is unchanged; the increased width comes from greater parameter uncertainty in the prediction. This calculation assumes the linear model remains appropriate beyond the observed range; it does not account for possible failure of that model there.

Key result. The mean-response scale is s\sqrt h; the new-observation scale is s\sqrt{1+h}. The extra 1 represents new observational noise, while h measures uncertainty about the fitted mean.

title: Categorical and multinomial models
text:
Definition taught in Categorical data and the Dirichlet distribution, part of Bayesian statistics
For two categories, a Bernoulli trial has probabilities (p,1-p) and an aggregated count has a binomial distribution. For K categories, let
{\boldsymbol{p}}=(p_1,\ldots,p_K)^{\mathsf T},
\qquad p_k\geq0,
\qquad \sum_{k=1}^Kp_k=1.
A single observation Y_i\in\{1,\ldots,K\} has
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=k\mid{\boldsymbol{p}})=p_k.
For n conditionally independent observations define
X_k=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf{1}\{Y_i=k\}.
Then \sum_kX_k=n and
{\boldsymbol{x}}\mid{\boldsymbol{p}}\sim\operatorname{Multinomial}(n,{\boldsymbol{p}}).

title: Categorical and multinomial models
text:
Properties

Multinomial central limit theorem

Main article: Multinomial central limit theorem

Let {\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{Multinomial}(n,{\boldsymbol{p}}) and \widehat{\boldsymbol{p}}={\boldsymbol{x}}/n. For fixed interior {\boldsymbol{p}}, define the covariance matrix

{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}({\boldsymbol{p}})
=\operatorname{diag}({\boldsymbol{p}})-{\boldsymbol{p}}{\boldsymbol{p}}^{\mathsf T}.

Then

\sqrt n\,(\widehat{\boldsymbol{p}}-{\boldsymbol{p}})
\xrightarrow{\mathcal D}
\operatorname{N}_K\!\left(
  {\boldsymbol{0}},
  {\color{blue}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}({\boldsymbol{p}})
\right).

The covariance matrix is singular because the components of \widehat{\boldsymbol{p}}-{\boldsymbol{p}} sum to zero. On the (K-1)-dimensional simplex, the count cloud therefore tightens at the usual n^{-1/2} rate and becomes locally normal.


Dirichlet–Multinomial conjugacy

Main article: Dirichlet–Multinomial conjugacy

After division by this evidence, 
\boxed{
{\boldsymbol{p}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1+x_1,\ldots,\alpha_K+x_K)}.

title: Categorical and multinomial models
text:
Examples

Practice set: Q22. Advertising responses and Dirichlet inference

Question page: Q22. Advertising responses and Dirichlet inference

[10 marks]
An advertising campaign records responses from 60 independently sampled people:




Negative
Neutral
Positive




Male
8
6
16


Female
12
4
14



Let \mathbf p=(p_{MN},p_{MU},p_{MP},p_{FN},p_{FU},p_{FP}) be the six population cell probabilities, with U denoting a neutral response. Model the counts as multinomial and use \mathbf p\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(1,1,1,1,1,1). You may use the Dirichlet kernel f(\mathbf p)\propto\prod_{k=1}^{K}p_k^{\alpha_k-1},
\qquad p_k>0,\quad \sum_{k=1}^{K}p_k=1.
(a) [2 marks] Derive the posterior distribution of \mathbf p, stating its parameters and support.
(b) [2 marks] Find the posterior mean of p_{MP} and its component of the joint MAP estimate of \mathbf p. Explain why that MAP component equals the observed cell proportion here.
(c) [2 marks] Find the posterior predictive probability that one new person responds positively, regardless of gender. Express it as a posterior expectation before calculating it.
(d) [2 marks] For that new person, calculate \mathbb{P}(\text{positive response}\mid\text{female},\text{data}). Explain why this differs from \mathbb{P}(\text{female and positive response}\mid\text{data}).
(e) [2 marks] Are the six components of \mathbf p independent under the posterior? Explain using their constraint.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Let D be the observed table and \mathbf p its six population cell probabilities. The labels M,F denote male and female; N,U,P denote negative, neutral, and positive. With parameters a_1,\ldots,a_K>0, a Dirichlet density has kernel \prod_k p_k^{a_k-1} on the simplex p_k>0, \sum_kp_k=1. The joint MAP maximises this density over the entire simplex, not a one-component marginal density.
(a) Posterior distribution. Write the counts in the stated order as \mathbf x=(8,6,16,12,4,14),\qquad n=60. The multinomial likelihood is L(\mathbf p;D)=\frac{60!}{\prod_{k=1}^{6}x_k!}
\prod_{k=1}^{6}p_k^{x_k}
\propto\prod_{k=1}^{6}p_k^{x_k}. The Dirichlet prior has kernel \prod_k p_k^{1-1}=1 on the simplex. Consequently, p(\mathbf p\mid D)\propto
\prod_{k=1}^{6}p_k^{x_k+1-1}, which is the Dirichlet kernel with parameters x_k+1. Thus \boxed{\mathbf p\mid D\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(9,7,17,13,5,15).} Its density is supported on the simplex p_k>0, \sum_{k=1}^6p_k=1; the boundary has probability zero. The posterior concentration is A=9+7+17+13+5+15=66.
(b) Posterior mean and MAP. For a Dirichlet vector with parameters a_1,\ldots,a_K and A=\sum_k a_k, \mathbb{E}(p_k)=\frac{a_k}{A},\qquad
\widehat p_{k,\mathrm{MAP}}=\frac{a_k-1}{A-K}
\quad\text{when every }a_k>1. Here every posterior parameter exceeds one, so \boxed{\mathbb{E}(p_{MP}\mid D)=\frac{17}{66}\approx0.2576,}
\qquad
\boxed{\widehat p_{MP,\mathrm{MAP}}=
\frac{17-1}{66-6}=\frac{16}{60}\approx0.2667.} The MAP component is taken from the mode of the joint posterior for \mathbf p. Since the prior density is constant on the simplex, maximising the posterior is equivalent to maximising the likelihood, giving the observed cell proportions.
(c) Predicting a positive response. Conditional on \mathbf p, the probability of a positive response is p_{MP}+p_{FP}. Averaging over posterior uncertainty gives \begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(\text{positive}\mid D)
&=\int (p_{MP}+p_{FP})p(\mathbf p\mid D)\,d\mathbf p\\
&=\mathbb{E}(p_{MP}+p_{FP}\mid D)\\
&=\frac{17}{66}+\frac{15}{66}
=\boxed{\frac{16}{33}\approx0.4848.}
\end{aligned} Prediction uses posterior averaging, not substitution of the MAP estimate.
(d) Conditioning on the new person being female. First calculate the two relevant posterior predictive probabilities: \mathbb{P}(\text{female and positive}\mid D)=\mathbb{E}(p_{FP}\mid D)=\frac{15}{66}, \mathbb{P}(\text{female}\mid D)
=\mathbb{E}(p_{FN}+p_{FU}+p_{FP}\mid D)
=\frac{13+5+15}{66}=\frac{33}{66}. By the definition of conditional probability, \boxed{
\mathbb{P}(\text{positive}\mid\text{female},D)
=\frac{15/66}{33/66}=\frac5{11}\approx0.4545.
} By contrast, the joint probability is \boxed{\mathbb{P}(\text{female and positive}\mid D)
=\frac{15}{66}=\frac5{22}\approx0.2273.} The conditional probability restricts attention to the female row; the joint probability refers to both events occurring for a person sampled from the whole population.
(e) Posterior dependence. No. The probabilities must satisfy \sum_k p_k=1 exactly. Increasing one component leaves less total probability for the others. More formally, if they were independent, then 0=\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^{6}p_k\,\middle|\,D\right)
=\sum_{k=1}^{6}\operatorname{Var}(p_k\mid D)>0, a contradiction, since each component has positive posterior variance. Indeed, distinct Dirichlet components have \operatorname{Cov}(p_j,p_k\mid D)
=-\frac{a_ja_k}{A^2(A+1)}<0,\qquad j\ne k.

Key result. Add counts to the Dirichlet parameters; average probabilities for prediction; and distinguish a joint cell probability from a probability conditional on a row.

title: Binomial distribution
text:
Properties

Beta–Binomial conjugacy

Main article: Beta–Binomial conjugacy


\boxed{
  \theta\mid x\sim
  \operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+x,\beta+n-x)}.



Beta–Binomial posterior prediction

Main article: Beta–Binomial posterior prediction

If \theta\mid x\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a,b) and, conditionally on \theta, \widetilde X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(m,\theta), then

\mathbb{P}(\widetilde X=k\mid x)
=\binom mk\frac{B(k+a,m-k+b)}{B(a,b)},
\qquad k=0,\ldots,m.

For one future Bernoulli observation, \mathbb{P}(\widetilde Y=1\mid x)=a/(a+b).

title: Binomial distribution
text:
Examples

Five future tosses

Worked example from The Beta–Binomial model

Suppose the prior is \theta\sim\operatorname{Beta}(2,2) and the observed data contain x=8 heads in n=10 tosses.
Question. Find the posterior predictive probability of a head on the next toss and the probability of at least four heads in five future tosses. Derive the predictive variance for the five-toss count and compare it with the variance obtained by plugging the posterior mean of \theta into a Binomial model.
Solution. The posterior calculation gives

\theta\mid x
\sim\operatorname{Beta}(2+8,2+10-8)
=\operatorname{Beta}(10,4).

For the very next toss, \begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}(\widetilde Y=1\mid x)
&=\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)\\
&=\frac{10}{10+4}\\
&=\frac57\\
&\approx0.714.
\end{align*} The raw sample proportion is 8/10=0.8. The prediction is less extreme because it averages over the posterior produced by the data and the \operatorname{Beta}(2,2) prior.
Now let \widetilde X be the number of heads in m=5 future tosses. With a=10, b=4, and T=a+b=14, 
\mathbb{P}(\widetilde X=k\mid x)
=\binom5k\frac{B(k+a,5-k+b)}{B(a,b)},
\qquad k=0,\ldots,5.
 For the rising factorial

(c)^{\overline r}
=c(c+1)\cdots(c+r-1),
\qquad
(c)^{\overline 0}=1,

the Beta-function ratio satisfies

\frac{B(k+a,5-k+b)}{B(a,b)}
=\frac{(a)^{\overline k}(b)^{\overline{5-k}}}
       {(a+b)^{\overline5}}.

Therefore the probability of at least four heads is \begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}(\widetilde X\geq4\mid x)
&=\mathbb{P}(\widetilde X=4\mid x)
   +\mathbb{P}(\widetilde X=5\mid x)\\
&=\frac{
   \binom54(10)^{\overline4}(4)^{\overline1}
   +\binom55(10)^{\overline5}(4)^{\overline0}}
   {(14)^{\overline5}}\\
&=\frac{
   5(10\cdot11\cdot12\cdot13)(4)
   +(10\cdot11\cdot12\cdot13\cdot14)}
   {14\cdot15\cdot16\cdot17\cdot18}\\
&=\frac{583440}{1028160}\\
&\approx0.567.
\end{align*}
This example also shows exactly why posterior prediction is more dispersed than a plug-in Binomial distribution. Conditional on \theta,

\mathbb{E}(\widetilde X\mid\theta)=5\theta,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\widetilde X\mid\theta)=5\theta(1-\theta).

For \theta\mid x\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a,b) with T=a+b,

\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)=\frac aT,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\theta\mid x)=\frac{ab}{T^2(T+1)}.

Moreover, \begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}\{\theta(1-\theta)\mid x\}
&=\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)-\mathbb{E}(\theta^2\mid x)\\
&=\frac aT-\frac{a(a+1)}{T(T+1)}\\
&=\frac{a(T+1)-a(a+1)}{T(T+1)}\\
&=\frac{a(T-a)}{T(T+1)}\\
&=\frac{ab}{T(T+1)}.
\end{align*} Applying Equation (3) in Bayesian foundations, \begin{align*}
\operatorname{Var}(\widetilde X\mid x)
&=\mathbb{E}\{5\theta(1-\theta)\mid x\}
   +\operatorname{Var}(5\theta\mid x)\\
&=\frac{5ab}{T(T+1)}
   +\frac{25ab}{T^2(T+1)}\\
&=\frac{5ab(T+5)}{T^2(T+1)}\\
&=\frac{5(10)(4)(19)}{14^2(15)}\\
&=\frac{190}{147}\\
&\approx1.293.
\end{align*} If one instead plugs in the posterior mean \widehat\theta=10/14, the variance would be only

5\widehat\theta(1-\widehat\theta)
=5\left(\frac{10}{14}\right)\left(\frac4{14}\right)
=\frac{50}{49}
\approx1.020.

The difference is the second term in Equation (3) in Bayesian foundations: uncertainty about \theta.


Practice set: Q6. Beta-Binomial conjugacy and prior influence

Question page: Q6. Beta-Binomial conjugacy and prior influence

Suppose X\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,\theta),
  \qquad
  \theta\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a,b), where n\geq1, a,b>0, and the observed value of X is x.
(a) Derive the posterior density of \theta. Identify its distribution, parameters, and support. [3 marks]
(b) Express the posterior mean as a weighted average of the prior mean and x/n. Explain how the weight on the prior changes as n increases, with a and b fixed. [3 marks]
(c) Another statistician instead uses a prior uniform on (0,1/2). If x/n=4/5, can the posterior assign positive probability to \theta>1/2? Explain why or why not. [2 marks]
(d) Under squared-error loss, explain why the posterior mean is the Bayes estimate. Is it necessarily the Bayes estimate under a different loss? [2 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. For a,b>0, a \operatorname{Beta}(a,b) density is \theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}/B(a,b) on (0,1), where B(a,b)=\int_0^1u^{a-1}(1-u)^{b-1}\,du. Here x is a Binomial success count out of known n. A Bayes estimate is an action d minimising posterior expected loss. Part (c) substitutes a restricted prior; part (d) returns to the Beta prior from (a).

(a) Posterior distribution
The likelihood and prior kernels are p(x\mid\theta)\propto\theta^x(1-\theta)^{n-x},
  \qquad
  p(\theta)\propto\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}. Therefore, \begin{aligned}
  p(\theta\mid x)
  &\propto p(x\mid\theta)p(\theta)\\
  &\propto
    \theta^{a+x-1}(1-\theta)^{b+n-x-1},
    \qquad 0<\theta<1.
\end{aligned} Thus \boxed{
    \theta\mid x\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a+x,b+n-x)
  }. The normalised posterior density is p(\theta\mid x)
  =\frac{\theta^{a+x-1}(1-\theta)^{b+n-x-1}}
         {B(a+x,b+n-x)},
  \qquad 0<\theta<1.


(b) Posterior mean and prior influence
The posterior mean is \mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)=\frac{a+x}{a+b+n}. Since the prior mean is \mathbb{E}(\theta)=a/(a+b), \begin{aligned}
  \mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)
  &=
  \frac{a+b}{a+b+n}\frac{a}{a+b}
  +\frac{n}{a+b+n}\frac{x}{n}\\
  &=
  \boxed{
    \frac{a+b}{a+b+n}\mathbb{E}(\theta)
    +\frac{n}{a+b+n}\frac{x}{n}
  }.
\end{aligned} The two weights sum to one. With a and b fixed, the prior weight (a+b)/(a+b+n) decreases to zero as n\to\infty, while the data weight increases to one.


(c) Restricted prior support
No. A prior uniform on (0,1/2) has density zero for \theta>1/2. Because p(\theta\mid x)\propto p(x\mid\theta)p(\theta), the posterior is also zero wherever the prior is zero. Hence \boxed{\mathbb{P}(\theta>1/2\mid x)=0}, even when x/n=4/5. The likelihood can reweight values inside the prior support, but it cannot create posterior mass outside that support.


(d) Bayes estimate under squared-error loss
Write m=\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x) and expand \theta-d=(\theta-m)+(m-d). The cross term has posterior expectation 2(m-d)\mathbb{E}(\theta-m\mid x)=0. Consequently, for an estimate d, the posterior expected squared loss is \begin{aligned}
  \mathbb{E}\bigl[(\theta-d)^2\mid x\bigr]
  &=
  \operatorname{Var}(\theta\mid x)
  +\bigl\{\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)-d\bigr\}^2.
\end{aligned} The variance term does not depend on d, so this expression is minimised by \boxed{
  \widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{Bayes}}
  =\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)
  =\frac{a+x}{a+b+n}.
  } The Bayes estimate depends on the loss function: for example, absolute-error loss gives a posterior median rather than necessarily the posterior mean.






Practice set: Q44. Testing whether a coin is fair

Question page: Q44. Testing whether a coin is fair

[10 marks]
Suppose X\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,\theta). Compare M_0:\theta=\frac12,
\qquad M_1:\theta\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a,b), with a,b>0 and equal prior model probabilities.
You may use B(a,b)=\int_0^1t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}\,dt.
(a) Derive \mathbb{P}(X=x\mid M_0) and \mathbb{P}(X=x\mid M_1). [4 marks]
(b) Obtain the Bayes factor BF_{01} and the posterior probability \mathbb{P}(M_0\mid X=x). [3 marks]
(c) A student argues:

“Under a continuous Beta posterior, \mathbb{P}(\theta=1/2\mid x)=0, so Bayesian inference always rejects a fair coin.”

Explain the error. [3 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. M_0 fixes \theta=1/2 and M_1 assigns a \operatorname{Beta}(a,b) prior, with a,b>0. Its density is \theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}/B(a,b), where B(a,b)=\int_0^1u^{a-1}(1-u)^{b-1}\,du. BF_{01} is the marginal-likelihood ratio favouring M_0. Prior model probabilities are equal; a model probability is distinct from a point probability within the continuous alternative.
(a) Marginal likelihoods. Under M_0, \theta=1/2 is fixed, so \boxed{\mathbb{P}(X=x\mid M_0)=\binom nx2^{-n}.} Under M_1, average the likelihood over the Beta prior: \begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(X=x\mid M_1)
&=\int_0^1\binom nx\theta^x(1-\theta)^{n-x}
\frac{\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}}{B(a,b)}\,d\theta\\
&=\frac{\binom nx}{B(a,b)}
\int_0^1\theta^{a+x-1}(1-\theta)^{b+n-x-1}\,d\theta\\
&=\boxed{\binom nx\frac{B(a+x,b+n-x)}{B(a,b)}}.
\end{aligned}
(b) Bayes factor and posterior model probability. The Bayes factor in favour of M_0 over M_1 is \boxed{
BF_{01}
=\frac{\mathbb{P}(X=x\mid M_0)}{\mathbb{P}(X=x\mid M_1)}
=2^{-n}\frac{B(a,b)}{B(a+x,b+n-x)}.
} The binomial coefficients cancel in the ratio, but belong in the individual marginal likelihoods. Equal prior model probabilities give prior odds one, so posterior odds equal BF_{01}. Hence \boxed{
\mathbb{P}(M_0\mid X=x)
=\frac{BF_{01}}{1+BF_{01}}
=\frac{2^{-n}B(a,b)}{2^{-n}B(a,b)+B(a+x,b+n-x)}.
}
(c) Error in the student’s argument. Under M_1 alone, \theta\mid x,M_1\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a+x,b+n-x),
\qquad \mathbb{P}(\theta=1/2\mid x,M_1)=0, because this posterior is continuous. Every individual point has probability zero under it; that fact is not a test rejecting that particular value.
The model comparison instead assigns positive prior probability to the separate point-null model M_0. Both marginal likelihoods are positive for valid data, so \mathbb{P}(M_0\mid x)>0. In the combined model, \mathbb{P}(\theta=1/2\mid x)=\mathbb{P}(M_0\mid x), since M_0 places all its probability at 1/2 and M_1 contributes no point mass there. The student has confused a probability conditional on M_1 with the probability after allowing both models.

\mathbb{P}(\widetilde X\geq4\mid x)
&=\mathbb{P}(\widetilde X=4\mid x)
   +\mathbb{P}(\widetilde X=5\mid x)\\
&=\frac{
   \binom54(10)^{\overline4}(4)^{\overline1}
   +\binom55(10)^{\overline5}(4)^{\overline0}}
   {(14)^{\overline5}}\\
&=\frac{
   5(10\cdot11\cdot12\cdot13)(4)
   +(10\cdot11\cdot12\cdot13\cdot14)}
   {14\cdot15\cdot16\cdot17\cdot18}\\
&=\frac{583440}{1028160}\\

\operatorname{Var}(\widetilde X\mid x)
&=\mathbb{E}\{5\theta(1-\theta)\mid x\}
   +\operatorname{Var}(5\theta\mid x)\\
&=\frac{5ab}{T(T+1)}
   +\frac{25ab}{T^2(T+1)}\\
&=\frac{5ab(T+5)}{T^2(T+1)}\\

title: Bayesian credible interval
text:
Definition taught in Bayesian foundations, part of Bayesian statistics
Bayesian analysis introduces a probability distribution for the unknown parameter. Conditional on observed data x, a statement such as
\mathbb{P}\!\left(a(x)<\mu<b(x)\mid x\right)=0.95
is meaningful. The interval (a(x),b(x)) is a 95\% credible interval. This is not a reworded confidence interval: the two calculations can coincide in large samples, but their probability statements condition on different objects.

title: Bayesian credible interval
text:
Properties

Posterior summaries from draws

Main article: Posterior summaries from draws

Let \theta^{(1)},\ldots,\theta^{(L)} be posterior draws and let \theta_{(1)}\leq\cdots\leq\theta_{(L)} be their order statistics. Then \begin{align*}
\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(\theta\mid x)
&=\frac1L\sum_{l=1}^L\theta^{(l)},\\
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\theta\mid x)
&=\frac1{L-1}\sum_{l=1}^L
   \left(\theta^{(l)}-\overline\theta\right)^2,\\
\widehat{\mathbb{P}}(\theta<c\mid x)
&=\frac1L\sum_{l=1}^L\mathbf{1}\{\theta^{(l)}<c\}.
\end{align*} The posterior median and equal-tailed interval are estimated by the corresponding empirical quantiles. With L=1000, the median can be estimated by the average of \theta_{(500)} and \theta_{(501)}, and a direct 95\% interval approximation by [\theta_{(25)},\theta_{(975)}]. The precise indices vary slightly with a software package’s quantile convention.

title: Bayesian credible interval
text:
Examples

Practice set: Q3. Confidence and credible intervals

Question page: Q3. Confidence and credible intervals

[6 marks]
Explain the difference between a frequentist confidence interval and a Bayesian credible interval. In your answer:
1. state what is regarded as random in each framework;
2. give the correct interpretation of a 95% confidence interval;
3. give the correct interpretation of a 95% credible interval; and
4. explain why the two intervals may sometimes have the same numerical endpoints but still have different interpretations.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Let X denote a random sample and x its observed value; C(X)=(L(X),U(X)) is an interval-producing procedure. Its coverage is \mathbb P_\theta\{\theta\in C(X)\}, calculated over samples at fixed \theta. A posterior credible interval instead has probability content \int_{C(x)}p(\theta\mid x)\,d\theta under the specified model and prior.
1. What is random?
In frequentist inference, the parameter \theta is fixed but unknown. Before observing the sample, the data X are random, so the interval endpoints L(X) and U(X) are also random.
In Bayesian inference, uncertainty about \theta is described by its posterior distribution p(\theta\mid x). Once we condition on the observed data x, those data are treated as fixed and \theta has a posterior probability distribution.
2. Interpretation of a 95% confidence interval.
A 95% confidence-interval procedure satisfies \mathbb{P}_{\theta}\!\left\{L(X)<\theta<U(X)\right\}=0.95, where the probability is taken over repeated samples generated with the same fixed value of \theta. Therefore, in repeated sampling, 95% of the intervals produced by the procedure would contain the true parameter.
After observing the data, the realised interval is fixed. In the frequentist framework, it is therefore incorrect to say that there is a 95% probability that the fixed parameter lies in this particular observed interval.
3. Interpretation of a 95% credible interval.
A Bayesian 95% credible interval (a,b) satisfies \mathbb{P}(a<\theta<b\mid x)=0.95. Conditional on the observed data, model, and prior, there is 95% posterior probability that \theta lies between a and b.
4. Why identical endpoints do not imply identical meanings.
The two methods can produce the same numerical endpoints in some simple models, or approximately the same endpoints in large samples. Their interpretations remain different because they use different probability statements:

5. confidence refers to the long-run coverage of a random interval procedure under repeated sampling;
6. credibility refers to posterior probability for \theta conditional on the observed data and the assumed prior and model.


Key result. Exam-safe sentence. A 95% confidence interval has 95% long-run coverage under repeated sampling, whereas a 95% credible interval contains 95% of the posterior probability for the parameter given the observed data.






Practice set: Q16. Interpreting identical interval endpoints

Question page: Q16. Interpreting identical interval endpoints

[4 marks]
A Bayesian analysis produces a 95% posterior credible interval [0.3,0.6] for a parameter \theta. A frequentist analysis happens to produce a 95% confidence interval with the same endpoints.
Explain the interpretation of each interval. Identify what is treated as random in each probability statement and explain why identical endpoints do not imply identical interpretations.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. C(X) denotes an interval computed from a random sample X; C({\boldsymbol{x}}) is its realised value. \mathbb P_\theta describes repeated sampling with \theta fixed. In contrast, \mathbb P(\,\cdot\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}) for the parameter is calculated from its posterior under the chosen model and prior. The stated 95% levels refer respectively to coverage and posterior probability.
For the Bayesian interval, \boxed{
\mathbb{P}(0.3\leq\theta\leq0.6\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=0.95.
} Conditional on the observed data, the assumed model, and the prior, there is 95% posterior probability that \theta lies between 0.3 and 0.6. The observed data are fixed, while uncertainty about \theta is represented by its posterior distribution.
For a frequentist 95% confidence-interval procedure C(X), \boxed{
\mathbb{P}_{\theta}\{\theta\in C(X)\}=0.95.
} Here \theta is fixed and the interval is random because it is calculated from the random sample X. Under repeated sampling at the same true value of \theta, 95% of the intervals generated by the procedure would contain \theta. Once the data have been observed, the realised interval is fixed; the frequentist statement is not that this particular interval contains \theta with probability 0.95.
Therefore identical endpoints do not imply identical interpretations. The credible interval assigns posterior probability to values of \theta given the observed data, whereas the confidence interval describes the long-run coverage of a random interval-producing procedure.

title: Bayes action for two hypotheses
text:
Proposition taught in Bayesian hypotheses and model comparison, part of Bayesian statistics
These probabilities do not by themselves define an action. If choosing action a_0 when H_1 is true costs L_{01} and choosing a_1 when H_0 is true costs L_{10}, the posterior expected losses are
\rho(a_0\mid x)=L_{01}\mathbb{P}(H_1\mid x),
\qquad
\rho(a_1\mid x)=L_{10}\mathbb{P}(H_0\mid x).
Choose a_0 when \begin{align*}
L_{01}\mathbb{P}(H_1\mid x)
&<L_{10}\mathbb{P}(H_0\mid x)\\
\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\frac{\mathbb{P}(H_0\mid x)}{\mathbb{P}(H_1\mid x)}
&>\frac{L_{01}}{L_{10}}.
\end{align*} Equal losses reduce the threshold to one. This separates the probability calculation from the decision rule.

title: Bayes action for two hypotheses
text:
Examples

Imperfect-fruit decision

Worked example from Bayesian hypotheses and model comparison

Let X_i be the number of imperfect pieces in box i, with about 100 pieces per box. “Imperfect” must be defined before the data are collected so that producer and analyst classify fruit in the same way. The model is

X_i\mid\theta\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Poisson}(\theta),
\qquad
H_0:\theta\leq10,
\quad H_1:\theta>10.

For the observed sample, n=20 and S=\sum_i x_i=177; the stated prior is \theta\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(12,1) in shape–rate form.
Question. Find the posterior distribution, the posterior probabilities and odds for H_0 and H_1, and an equal-tailed 95\% credible interval. Explain why the interval may cross 10 even when most posterior mass lies below it.
Solution. Because the posterior for \theta is continuous,

\mathbb{P}(\theta=10\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=0.

Consequently it makes no numerical difference whether equality is assigned to H_0 or H_1. This is a statement about the continuous parameter, even though the observed fruit counts are discrete.
For n boxes and S=\sum_i x_i, the likelihood is 
\begin{aligned}
p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta)
&=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{e^{-\theta}\theta^{x_i}}{x_i!}\\
&=\left(\prod_{i=1}^n\frac1{x_i!}\right)
   e^{-n\theta}\theta^{\sum_i x_i}\\
&\propto e^{-n\theta}\theta^S.
\end{aligned}
 The working total is S=177 for n=20.
The stated prior is \theta\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(12,1) in the standard shape–rate convention, so

p(\theta)=\frac1{\Gamma(12)}\theta^{12-1}e^{-\theta}
\propto\theta^{11}e^{-\theta}.

Multiplying by the likelihood gives \begin{align*}
p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto
\theta^S e^{-n\theta}\theta^{11}e^{-\theta}\\
&=\theta^{S+11}e^{-(n+1)\theta}\\
&=\theta^{189-1}e^{-21\theta}.
\end{align*} Therefore the internally consistent shape–rate update is 
\boxed{\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(189,21)}.
 Its posterior mean is

\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{189}{21}=9.

The MLE is S/n=177/20=8.85. Although the prior mean 12 lies above the boundary 10, the data move the posterior centre below it.
Let \gamma(a,z)=\int_0^zt^{a-1}e^{-t}\,\mathrm{d} t be the lower incomplete Gamma function. If T\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a,b), then

\mathbb{P}(T\leq t)=\frac{\gamma(a,bt)}{\Gamma(a)}.

Consequently, \begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}(H_0\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=\mathbb{P}(\theta\leq10\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\\
&=\frac{\gamma(189,21\cdot10)}{\Gamma(189)}\\
&=0.93298381,\\
\mathbb{P}(H_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})&=1-0.93298381=0.06701619.
\end{align*} The posterior odds are

\frac{\mathbb{P}(H_0\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})}{\mathbb{P}(H_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})}
=\frac{0.93298381}{0.06701619}
\approx13.92.

The equal-tailed 95\% credible interval is approximately (7.76,10.33). It crosses 10, while 93.3\% of posterior mass lies at or below 10. These are different summaries: interval inclusion does not produce a general accept/reject rule for an interval hypothesis.






Figure 1: The fruit posterior \operatorname{Gamma}(189,21), with the region \theta\leq10 shaded. The two summaries disagree in appearance only. The equal-tailed interval must leave 2.5\% in each tail, so its upper endpoint is pushed past 10; the shaded area answers a different question and puts 93.3\% of the mass at or below the boundary. Reading the crossing as a rejection substitutes one summary for the other.









Parameterisation check



A convention check uses the other Gamma convention. Writing a prior kernel p(\theta)\propto\theta^\alpha e^{-\beta\theta} with \alpha=12 describes \operatorname{Gamma}(13,1), not the stated \operatorname{Gamma}(12,1). That alternative gives \theta\mid x\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(190,21), posterior mean 190/21\approx9.05, \mathbb{P}(\theta\leq10\mid x)=0.92320087, odds 12.02, and interval (7.81,10.38). The main calculation above follows the stated shape–rate prior; the alternative is retained here so that neither that result nor the convention error is hidden.

title: Baseline-category logit model
text:
Definition taught in Categorical responses, part of Generalised linear models
For nominal categories 0,1,\ldots,K-1, the baseline-category logit model is 
\log\frac{p_k}{p_0}=\beta_{0k}+{\boldsymbol{x}}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}_k,
\qquad k=1,\ldots,K-1.
 The log-odds of category k against category k' are (\beta_{0k}-\beta_{0k'})+{\boldsymbol{x}}^\top(\boldsymbol{\beta}_k-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{k'}).

title: Baseline-category logit model
text:
Examples

Practice set: Q46. Multinomial logistic regression

Question page: Q46. Multinomial logistic regression

[10 marks]
A response has categories 0,1,2, with probabilities p_0(x),p_1(x),p_2(x). Consider \log\frac{p_1(x)}{p_0(x)}=\alpha_1+\beta_1x,
\qquad
\log\frac{p_2(x)}{p_0(x)}=\alpha_2+\beta_2x.
(a) Derive expressions for all three probabilities and verify that they sum to one. [4 marks]
(b) Interpret e^{\beta_1}. [2 marks]
(c) Derive \log[p_2(x)/p_1(x)]. [2 marks]
(d) If category 1 becomes the reference category, express the new intercepts and slopes in terms of the original parameters. Do the fitted probabilities change? [2 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. p_0(x),p_1(x),p_2(x) are probabilities of three mutually exclusive, exhaustive categories, summing to one. With category 0 as baseline, define \eta_j(x)=\log\{p_j(x)/p_0(x)\}=\alpha_j+\beta_jx, for j=1,2. These are baseline-category log ratios, not one-versus-rest logits \log\{p_j/(1-p_j)\}. The predictors are finite, so all fitted probabilities are positive.
(a) The three probabilities. Exponentiating the model equations gives p_1(x)=e^{\eta_1(x)}p_0(x),\qquad
p_2(x)=e^{\eta_2(x)}p_0(x). Since the probabilities sum to one, p_0(x)\{1+e^{\eta_1(x)}+e^{\eta_2(x)}\}=1. With D(x)=1+e^{\eta_1(x)}+e^{\eta_2(x)}, \boxed{p_0(x)=\frac1{D(x)},\qquad
p_1(x)=\frac{e^{\eta_1(x)}}{D(x)},\qquad
p_2(x)=\frac{e^{\eta_2(x)}}{D(x)}.} All are positive and their sum is D(x)/D(x)=1.
(b) Interpretation of e^{\beta_1}. For a one-unit increase in x, \boxed{
\frac{p_1(x+1)/p_0(x+1)}{p_1(x)/p_0(x)}=e^{\beta_1}.
} Thus e^{\beta_1} is the multiplicative change in the odds of category 1 relative to category 0. It is not generally the multiplier for p_1(x) itself, or for the odds of category 1 against all other categories combined.
(c) Comparing categories 2 and 1. Subtract the two original log-ratio equations: \boxed{
\log\frac{p_2(x)}{p_1(x)}
=\log\frac{p_2(x)}{p_0(x)}-\log\frac{p_1(x)}{p_0(x)}
=(\alpha_2-\alpha_1)+(\beta_2-\beta_1)x.
}
(d) Taking category 1 as the reference. The two new equations are \log\frac{p_0(x)}{p_1(x)}=-\alpha_1-\beta_1x,
\qquad
\log\frac{p_2(x)}{p_1(x)}
=(\alpha_2-\alpha_1)+(\beta_2-\beta_1)x. Thus the new intercept and slope are (-\alpha_1,-\beta_1) for category 0, and (\alpha_2-\alpha_1,\beta_2-\beta_1) for category 2. The fitted probabilities do not change: this is a reparametrisation. For example, p_1(x)=\frac1{1+e^{-\eta_1(x)}+e^{\eta_2(x)-\eta_1(x)}}
=\frac{e^{\eta_1(x)}}{D(x)}, which is the original expression, and the other probabilities follow by their corresponding ratios.





Concept check: C24. Categorical response types

Question page: C24. Categorical response types

What are nominal and ordinal responses? What probabilities does a baseline-category logit compare?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. Nominal categories have no intrinsic ordering; ordinal categories have an ordering but not necessarily meaningful numerical gaps. A baseline-category logit compares category probabilities with a fixed reference: \log(p_k/p_0)=\beta_{0k}+x^\top\beta_k, where p_k=\mathbb{P}(Y=k\mid x) and k\ne0.

title: A proper approximation to the flat prior
text:
Remark taught in Conjugate analysis for normal models, part of Bayesian statistics
The honest bounded version of the improper kernel p(\mu)\propto1 is
p_C(\mu)=\frac1{2C}\mathbf{1}\{-C\leq\mu\leq C\}.
Taking, for example, C=10^4 makes this density nearly constant over an ordinary data range while keeping it proper. It also exposes what “very diffuse” means. For any fixed 0<M<C,
\mathbb{P}_C(|\mu|\leq M)=\int_{-M}^{M}\frac1{2C}\,\mathrm{d}\mu=\frac MC
\longrightarrow0
\qquad(C\longrightarrow\infty).
Thus the limiting sequence puts essentially all of its probability beyond every fixed finite range; it does not converge to a uniform probability distribution on \mathbb{R}. Human height makes the point concrete: no observed person is three metres tall, yet a sufficiently broad uniform prior assigns almost no mass to the entire range of heights that have actually been encountered.

title: Bayes’ rule
text:
Theorem taught in Bayesian foundations, part of Bayesian statistics
For events A and B with \mathbb{P}(B)>0,
\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)=\frac{\mathbb{P}(B\mid A)\mathbb{P}(A)}{\mathbb{P}(B)}.
The density version follows from two factorizations of a joint density:
p(x,\theta)=p(x\mid\theta)p(\theta)
             =p(\theta\mid x)p(x).
Equating the right-hand sides and dividing by p(x) gives 
p(\theta\mid x)
  =\frac{p(x\mid\theta)p(\theta)}{p(x)}.

title: Bayes’ rule
text:
Examples

Practice set: Q15. Prior beliefs and conflicting data

Question page: Q15. Prior beliefs and conflicting data

[3 marks]
A researcher models independent observations as Bernoulli with unknown success probability \theta. The researcher chooses a prior that is uniform on (0,1/2).
Of 100 observed trials, 80 are successes. The researcher argues that these data should make the posterior probability of \theta>1/2 large.
Is this reasoning correct? Explain what happens and whether collecting more observations can overcome the restriction imposed by this prior.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Let L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})=p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta) and let m({\boldsymbol{x}})=\int L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})p(\theta)\,d\theta be the marginal likelihood. Bayes’ update is p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})p(\theta)/m({\boldsymbol{x}}), provided 0<m({\boldsymbol{x}})<\infty. The prior here excludes the entire region \theta>1/2, not merely a single value.
The reasoning is incorrect. The prior density is zero for every \theta>1/2. Bayes’ theorem gives p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
\propto p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta)p(\theta), so p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=0
\qquad\text{whenever }\theta>1/2. Hence \boxed{
\mathbb{P}(\theta>1/2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=0.
} This remains true regardless of how many observations are collected. The likelihood can redistribute posterior mass only among parameter values to which the prior assigns positive density; it cannot create support in a region excluded by the prior.
The observed proportion 80/100=0.8 instead reveals serious conflict between the data and the assumed model–prior combination. The researcher should reconsider the restricted prior, or investigate whether the Bernoulli model is appropriate. With the restriction left unchanged, additional data cannot make the posterior probability above 1/2 positive.

title: Beta–Binomial conjugacy
text:
Examples

Practice set: Q6. Beta-Binomial conjugacy and prior influence

Question page: Q6. Beta-Binomial conjugacy and prior influence

Suppose X\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,\theta),
  \qquad
  \theta\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a,b), where n\geq1, a,b>0, and the observed value of X is x.
(a) Derive the posterior density of \theta. Identify its distribution, parameters, and support. [3 marks]
(b) Express the posterior mean as a weighted average of the prior mean and x/n. Explain how the weight on the prior changes as n increases, with a and b fixed. [3 marks]
(c) Another statistician instead uses a prior uniform on (0,1/2). If x/n=4/5, can the posterior assign positive probability to \theta>1/2? Explain why or why not. [2 marks]
(d) Under squared-error loss, explain why the posterior mean is the Bayes estimate. Is it necessarily the Bayes estimate under a different loss? [2 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. For a,b>0, a \operatorname{Beta}(a,b) density is \theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}/B(a,b) on (0,1), where B(a,b)=\int_0^1u^{a-1}(1-u)^{b-1}\,du. Here x is a Binomial success count out of known n. A Bayes estimate is an action d minimising posterior expected loss. Part (c) substitutes a restricted prior; part (d) returns to the Beta prior from (a).

(a) Posterior distribution
The likelihood and prior kernels are p(x\mid\theta)\propto\theta^x(1-\theta)^{n-x},
  \qquad
  p(\theta)\propto\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}. Therefore, \begin{aligned}
  p(\theta\mid x)
  &\propto p(x\mid\theta)p(\theta)\\
  &\propto
    \theta^{a+x-1}(1-\theta)^{b+n-x-1},
    \qquad 0<\theta<1.
\end{aligned} Thus \boxed{
    \theta\mid x\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a+x,b+n-x)
  }. The normalised posterior density is p(\theta\mid x)
  =\frac{\theta^{a+x-1}(1-\theta)^{b+n-x-1}}
         {B(a+x,b+n-x)},
  \qquad 0<\theta<1.


(b) Posterior mean and prior influence
The posterior mean is \mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)=\frac{a+x}{a+b+n}. Since the prior mean is \mathbb{E}(\theta)=a/(a+b), \begin{aligned}
  \mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)
  &=
  \frac{a+b}{a+b+n}\frac{a}{a+b}
  +\frac{n}{a+b+n}\frac{x}{n}\\
  &=
  \boxed{
    \frac{a+b}{a+b+n}\mathbb{E}(\theta)
    +\frac{n}{a+b+n}\frac{x}{n}
  }.
\end{aligned} The two weights sum to one. With a and b fixed, the prior weight (a+b)/(a+b+n) decreases to zero as n\to\infty, while the data weight increases to one.


(c) Restricted prior support
No. A prior uniform on (0,1/2) has density zero for \theta>1/2. Because p(\theta\mid x)\propto p(x\mid\theta)p(\theta), the posterior is also zero wherever the prior is zero. Hence \boxed{\mathbb{P}(\theta>1/2\mid x)=0}, even when x/n=4/5. The likelihood can reweight values inside the prior support, but it cannot create posterior mass outside that support.


(d) Bayes estimate under squared-error loss
Write m=\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x) and expand \theta-d=(\theta-m)+(m-d). The cross term has posterior expectation 2(m-d)\mathbb{E}(\theta-m\mid x)=0. Consequently, for an estimate d, the posterior expected squared loss is \begin{aligned}
  \mathbb{E}\bigl[(\theta-d)^2\mid x\bigr]
  &=
  \operatorname{Var}(\theta\mid x)
  +\bigl\{\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)-d\bigr\}^2.
\end{aligned} The variance term does not depend on d, so this expression is minimised by \boxed{
  \widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{Bayes}}
  =\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)
  =\frac{a+x}{a+b+n}.
  } The Bayes estimate depends on the loss function: for example, absolute-error loss gives a posterior median rather than necessarily the posterior mean.






Practice set: Q17. Choosing a conjugate prior

Question page: Q17. Choosing a conjugate prior

[3 marks]
Explain what it means for a prior family to be conjugate to a sampling model, and give one practical advantage of using such a family.
A researcher instead chooses a nonconjugate prior because it better represents the available background information. Does this make the Bayesian analysis invalid? Explain what computational difficulty may arise.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. A prior family is conjugate when multiplication by the likelihood and normalisation return a member of that family. For the example below, the Binomial likelihood kernel is \theta^x(1-\theta)^{n-x} and the Beta prior kernel is \theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1} on (0,1), with a,b>0. A valid posterior requires a finite, positive normalising integral.
For example, multiplying the Binomial and Beta kernels adds their success and failure exponents. Thus X\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,\theta),
\qquad
\theta\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a,b) implies \theta\mid X=x
\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a+x,b+n-x). One practical advantage is that posterior updating reduces to updating the hyperparameters. Posterior summaries and predictive calculations can often be obtained analytically, without numerical integration.
A nonconjugate prior does not make the analysis invalid. It may be preferable when it represents the available prior information more faithfully. However, the posterior may not have a standard form, and its normalising constant or required expectations may be difficult to calculate. Numerical quadrature, grid approximation, importance sampling, or MCMC may then be required.
