The Beta distribution is the two-category Dirichlet

Main article: The Beta distribution is the two-category Dirichlet

When K=2, write p_1=p and p_2=1-p. Restricting the Dirichlet density to the one-dimensional simplex gives

p(p\mid\alpha_1,\alpha_2)
=\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_1+\alpha_2)}
        {\Gamma(\alpha_1)\Gamma(\alpha_2)}
   p^{\alpha_1-1}(1-p)^{\alpha_2-1},

which is exactly \operatorname{Beta}(\alpha_1,\alpha_2). The Dirichlet is therefore a genuine extension of the Beta family rather than merely a similar-looking density.


Beta–Binomial posterior prediction

Main article: Beta–Binomial posterior prediction

If \theta\mid x\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a,b) and, conditionally on \theta, \widetilde X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(m,\theta), then

\mathbb{P}(\widetilde X=k\mid x)
=\binom mk\frac{B(k+a,m-k+b)}{B(a,b)},
\qquad k=0,\ldots,m.

For one future Bernoulli observation, \mathbb{P}(\widetilde Y=1\mid x)=a/(a+b).


Two pseudo-count conventions

Main article: Two pseudo-count conventions

For posterior means, (\alpha,\beta) act as prior success and failure counts. For an interior posterior mode, the corresponding counts are (\alpha-1,\beta-1). A pseudo-count statement is incomplete unless the posterior summary being interpreted is also named.

title: Beta distribution
text:
Examples

Practice set: Q6. Beta-Binomial conjugacy and prior influence

Question page: Q6. Beta-Binomial conjugacy and prior influence

Suppose X\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,\theta),
  \qquad
  \theta\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a,b), where n\geq1, a,b>0, and the observed value of X is x.
(a) Derive the posterior density of \theta. Identify its distribution, parameters, and support. [3 marks]
(b) Express the posterior mean as a weighted average of the prior mean and x/n. Explain how the weight on the prior changes as n increases, with a and b fixed. [3 marks]
(c) Another statistician instead uses a prior uniform on (0,1/2). If x/n=4/5, can the posterior assign positive probability to \theta>1/2? Explain why or why not. [2 marks]
(d) Under squared-error loss, explain why the posterior mean is the Bayes estimate. Is it necessarily the Bayes estimate under a different loss? [2 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. For a,b>0, a \operatorname{Beta}(a,b) density is \theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}/B(a,b) on (0,1), where B(a,b)=\int_0^1u^{a-1}(1-u)^{b-1}\,du. Here x is a Binomial success count out of known n. A Bayes estimate is an action d minimising posterior expected loss. Part (c) substitutes a restricted prior; part (d) returns to the Beta prior from (a).

(a) Posterior distribution
The likelihood and prior kernels are p(x\mid\theta)\propto\theta^x(1-\theta)^{n-x},
  \qquad
  p(\theta)\propto\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}. Therefore, \begin{aligned}
  p(\theta\mid x)
  &\propto p(x\mid\theta)p(\theta)\\
  &\propto
    \theta^{a+x-1}(1-\theta)^{b+n-x-1},
    \qquad 0<\theta<1.
\end{aligned} Thus \boxed{
    \theta\mid x\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a+x,b+n-x)
  }. The normalised posterior density is p(\theta\mid x)
  =\frac{\theta^{a+x-1}(1-\theta)^{b+n-x-1}}
         {B(a+x,b+n-x)},
  \qquad 0<\theta<1.


(b) Posterior mean and prior influence
The posterior mean is \mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)=\frac{a+x}{a+b+n}. Since the prior mean is \mathbb{E}(\theta)=a/(a+b), \begin{aligned}
  \mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)
  &=
  \frac{a+b}{a+b+n}\frac{a}{a+b}
  +\frac{n}{a+b+n}\frac{x}{n}\\
  &=
  \boxed{
    \frac{a+b}{a+b+n}\mathbb{E}(\theta)
    +\frac{n}{a+b+n}\frac{x}{n}
  }.
\end{aligned} The two weights sum to one. With a and b fixed, the prior weight (a+b)/(a+b+n) decreases to zero as n\to\infty, while the data weight increases to one.


(c) Restricted prior support
No. A prior uniform on (0,1/2) has density zero for \theta>1/2. Because p(\theta\mid x)\propto p(x\mid\theta)p(\theta), the posterior is also zero wherever the prior is zero. Hence \boxed{\mathbb{P}(\theta>1/2\mid x)=0}, even when x/n=4/5. The likelihood can reweight values inside the prior support, but it cannot create posterior mass outside that support.


(d) Bayes estimate under squared-error loss
Write m=\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x) and expand \theta-d=(\theta-m)+(m-d). The cross term has posterior expectation 2(m-d)\mathbb{E}(\theta-m\mid x)=0. Consequently, for an estimate d, the posterior expected squared loss is \begin{aligned}
  \mathbb{E}\bigl[(\theta-d)^2\mid x\bigr]
  &=
  \operatorname{Var}(\theta\mid x)
  +\bigl\{\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)-d\bigr\}^2.
\end{aligned} The variance term does not depend on d, so this expression is minimised by \boxed{
  \widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{Bayes}}
  =\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)
  =\frac{a+x}{a+b+n}.
  } The Bayes estimate depends on the loss function: for example, absolute-error loss gives a posterior median rather than necessarily the posterior mean.






Practice set: Q23. Rat-tumour studies and hierarchical shrinkage

Question page: Q23. Rat-tumour studies and hierarchical shrinkage

[12 marks]
Suppose J related studies record tumour counts Y_j\mid\theta_j\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n_j,\theta_j),
\qquad j=1,\ldots,J, independently conditional on the study rates. Assume \theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta
\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta),
\qquad
\alpha\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1),\quad
\beta\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1), where the two hyperpriors are independent. Write \mathbf y=(y_1,\ldots,y_J); the sample sizes n_j are known. You may use B(a,b)=\int_0^1 t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}\,dt,
\qquad
f(\theta\mid a,b)=\frac{\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}}{B(a,b)}.
(a) [2 marks] Derive and identify the full conditional distribution \theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y.
(b) [3 marks] For this part only, fix \alpha=2 and \beta=8. Two studies report (y_1,n_1)=(4,10),\qquad (y_2,n_2)=(40,100). Calculate both posterior means. Although both observed proportions equal 0.4, explain why the posterior means differ and identify which study experiences stronger shrinkage.
(c) [4 marks] Return to unknown \alpha,\beta. Integrate out the study rates to derive:
(i) the marginal probability \mathbb{P}(Y_j=y_j\mid\alpha,\beta);
(ii) the marginal posterior kernel p(\alpha,\beta\mid\mathbf y).
Express your answers using Beta functions. Explain why the Beta prior’s normalising factor cannot be discarded when deriving this hyperparameter posterior.
(d) [3 marks] Explain how the full Bayesian model allows studies to share information. What uncertainty is omitted if \alpha,\beta are instead estimated from the data and then treated as known?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Study j has observed count y_j, known size n_j, and unknown rate \theta_j; \alpha,\beta>0 are shared hyperparameters. A \operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta) density is \theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1}/B(\alpha,\beta) on (0,1), where B(a,b)=\int_0^1u^{a-1}(1-u)^{b-1}\,du. \operatorname{Exp}(1) uses rate one. Partial pooling allows different study rates linked through a common population distribution.
Assumptions. The hierarchy assumes conditional independence of studies given their rates, and iid Beta rates given \alpha,\beta. Thus its joint density factors as p(\alpha)p(\beta)\prod_jp(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta)p(y_j\mid\theta_j), with independent rate-one exponential hyperpriors. Only in part (b) are the hyperparameters fixed at the supplied values.
(a) Full conditional for a study rate. Holding \alpha,\beta fixed, the factors involving \theta_j are \begin{aligned}
p(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y)
&\propto p(y_j\mid\theta_j)p(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta)\\
&\propto\theta_j^{y_j}(1-\theta_j)^{n_j-y_j}
\theta_j^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta_j)^{\beta-1}\\
&=\theta_j^{\alpha+y_j-1}(1-\theta_j)^{\beta+n_j-y_j-1}.
\end{aligned} Therefore \boxed{\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y
\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+y_j,\beta+n_j-y_j),\qquad 0<\theta_j<1.} Conditional on the hyperparameters and data, the study rates are independent. Other studies’ observations affect this study’s marginal posterior through learning \alpha,\beta, not through an additional factor in this full conditional.
(b) Posterior means and shrinkage. For fixed \alpha=2, \beta=8, the population mean is \frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}=\frac2{10}=0.2. The two posteriors are \theta_1\mid\alpha=2,\beta=8,\mathbf y\sim\operatorname{Beta}(6,14), \theta_2\mid\alpha=2,\beta=8,\mathbf y\sim\operatorname{Beta}(42,68). Thus their posterior means are \boxed{\mathbb{E}(\theta_1\mid\alpha=2,\beta=8,\mathbf y)=\frac6{20}=0.3,} \boxed{\mathbb{E}(\theta_2\mid\alpha=2,\beta=8,\mathbf y)=\frac{42}{110}
\approx0.3818.} To see the shrinkage explicitly, write \frac{\alpha+y_j}{\alpha+\beta+n_j}
=\frac{\alpha+\beta}{\alpha+\beta+n_j}
\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}
+\frac{n_j}{\alpha+\beta+n_j}\frac{y_j}{n_j}. Both sample proportions equal 0.4, but study 1 puts weight 10/20=1/2 on the population mean, whereas study 2 puts only 10/110=1/11 on it. The smaller study therefore experiences stronger shrinkage toward 0.2. The larger study has more information about its own rate, so its posterior mean remains closer to its observed proportion.
(c) Integrating out the study rates. For one study, retain the normalising factor of the Beta density: \begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(Y_j=y_j\mid\alpha,\beta)
&=\int_0^1 p(y_j\mid\theta_j)p(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta)\,d\theta_j\\
&=\binom{n_j}{y_j}\frac1{B(\alpha,\beta)}
\int_0^1\theta_j^{y_j+\alpha-1}
(1-\theta_j)^{n_j-y_j+\beta-1}\,d\theta_j\\
&=\boxed{\binom{n_j}{y_j}
\frac{B(\alpha+y_j,\beta+n_j-y_j)}{B(\alpha,\beta)}.}
\end{aligned} This is a Beta–Binomial marginal distribution, with y_j\in\{0,\ldots,n_j\}.
The independent rate-one exponential hyperpriors give p(\alpha,\beta)=e^{-\alpha-\beta},\qquad \alpha>0,\quad\beta>0. The studies remain independent conditional on the hyperparameters after their individual rates have been integrated out. Consequently, \begin{aligned}
p(\alpha,\beta\mid\mathbf y)
&\propto p(\alpha,\beta)
\prod_{j=1}^{J}\mathbb{P}(Y_j=y_j\mid\alpha,\beta)\\
&\propto e^{-(\alpha+\beta)}
\prod_{j=1}^{J}
\frac{B(\alpha+y_j,\beta+n_j-y_j)}{B(\alpha,\beta)}.
\end{aligned} Hence \boxed{
p(\alpha,\beta\mid\mathbf y)
\propto e^{-(\alpha+\beta)}B(\alpha,\beta)^{-J}
\prod_{j=1}^{J}B(\alpha+y_j,\beta+n_j-y_j),
\quad \alpha,\beta>0.
} The binomial coefficients can be dropped because the observed y_j and known n_j make them constant with respect to \alpha,\beta. However, 1/B(\alpha,\beta) depends on the hyperparameters, so it must remain. A factor constant in \theta_j need not be constant in \alpha,\beta.
(d) Sharing information and hyperparameter uncertainty. Every study contributes to the posterior for the common population parameters \alpha,\beta. That posterior then contributes to each study-specific posterior through p(\theta_j\mid\mathbf y)
=\int_0^\infty\!\int_0^\infty
p(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y)
p(\alpha,\beta\mid\mathbf y)\,d\alpha\,d\beta. This is partial pooling: study rates can differ, but they are connected by a population distribution learned from all the studies. The model does not force them to be identical, and it does not treat them as unrelated.
Replacing \alpha,\beta by fixed estimates is an empirical-Bayes plug-in analysis. It omits uncertainty about the population distribution’s parameters. For example, the law of total variance gives \begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(\theta_j\mid\mathbf y)
={}&\mathbb{E}\!\left[
\operatorname{Var}(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y)
\mid\mathbf y\right]\\
&+\operatorname{Var}\!\left[
\mathbb{E}(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y)
\mid\mathbf y\right].
\end{aligned} The second term represents variation in the conditional mean as the hyperparameters vary under their posterior. A plug-in calculation does not propagate this variation and can therefore give an overly precise account of uncertainty.

Key result. Conditional conjugacy does not eliminate uncertainty in the hyperparameters. Full Bayes learns their distribution and averages over it.

title: Canonical link
text:
Definition taught in Introduction to generalised linear models, part of Generalised linear models
The link g is canonical when the linear predictor is the natural parameter of the family: g(\mu_i)=b(\theta_i), in the notation of Equation (6) in Introduction to generalised linear models.

title: Canonical link
text:
Examples

Practice set: Q57. Negative-binomial canonical link

Question page: Q57. Negative-binomial canonical link

[6 marks]
Let Y have a negative-binomial distribution with probability mass function f(y;\theta)
=\binom{y+r-1}{r-1}\theta^r(1-\theta)^y,
\qquad y=0,1,2,\ldots, where r>0 is known and 0<\theta<1.
(a) Show that this distribution belongs to the linear exponential family by expressing its probability mass function in the form f(y;\theta)
        =\exp\left\{
        \frac{y\,b(\theta)+c(\theta)}{e(\phi)}+d(y;\phi)
        \right\}. Identify the natural parameter b(\theta). [3 marks]
(b) Given that \mu=\mathbb{E}(Y)=\frac{r(1-\theta)}{\theta}, derive the canonical link function g(\mu). [3 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Here Y counts failures, with support \{0,1,2,\ldots\}, known r>0, and 0<\theta<1. For non-integer r, interpret the binomial coefficient as \binom{y+r-1}{r-1}=\Gamma(y+r)/\{\Gamma(r)\Gamma(y+1)\}. In the stated linear exponential-family form, the natural parameter is b(\theta); the canonical link is g(\mu)=b\{\theta(\mu)\}. We use scale convention e(\phi)=1.
(a) Exponential-family representation. The support \{0,1,2,\ldots\} does not depend on \theta. Take logarithms of the supplied mass function: \begin{aligned}
\log f(y;\theta)
&=\log\left\{\binom{y+r-1}{r-1}\theta^r(1-\theta)^y\right\}\\
&=y\log(1-\theta)+r\log\theta
  +\log\binom{y+r-1}{r-1}.
\end{aligned} Since r is known, there is no free dispersion parameter to estimate here. Choose e(\phi)=1 and identify \boxed{
b(\theta)=\log(1-\theta),\qquad
c(\theta)=r\log\theta,\qquad e(\phi)=1,
} \boxed{d(y;\phi)=\log\binom{y+r-1}{r-1}.} The symbol \phi is redundant in this choice: d depends on the known r, not on the unknown \theta. Substitution gives f(y;\theta)
=\exp\left\{y\log(1-\theta)+r\log\theta+
\log\binom{y+r-1}{r-1}\right\}, exactly the required form. In particular, \boxed{\eta=b(\theta)=\log(1-\theta)<0.} The natural parameter is \log(1-\theta), not \log\theta: it is the coefficient multiplying the observation y.
The Gamma-function convention in Definitions makes this representation valid for every stated r>0.
(b) Canonical link. Start with the supplied mean and solve for the original parameter: \begin{aligned}
\mu&=\frac{r(1-\theta)}{\theta},\\
\mu\theta&=r-r\theta,\\
(\mu+r)\theta&=r,\\
\theta&=\frac r{\mu+r},\qquad
1-\theta=\frac{\mu}{\mu+r}.
\end{aligned} Now substitute into the natural parameter from part (a): \boxed{
g(\mu)=b\{\theta(\mu)\}
=\log\left(\frac{\mu}{\mu+r}\right)
=\log\mu-\log(\mu+r),\qquad\mu>0.
} Thus a canonical-link regression would set \eta_i=\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta=g(\mu_i), with \eta_i<0 to keep the means valid. Solving for the mean gives e^\eta=\frac{\mu}{\mu+r}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mu(1-e^\eta)=re^\eta
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\boxed{\mu=\frac{re^\eta}{1-e^\eta},\qquad\eta<0.}
Independent check from the normalising term. Write the log mass function as \log f(y;\eta)=y\eta-A(\eta)+d(y),
\qquad A(\eta)=-r\log(1-e^\eta). Differentiating the identity \sum_y f(y;\eta)=1 gives 0=\sum_y\{y-A'(\eta)\}f(y;\eta), so \mathbb{E}(Y)=A'(\eta). Here A'(\eta)=\frac{re^\eta}{1-e^\eta}, which is exactly the inverse link just derived.
A log link can be chosen for a negative-binomial regression, but it is not the canonical link derived here.





Concept check: C17. Links

Question page: C17. Links

What are a link function, an inverse link and a canonical link?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. The link g maps the conditional mean to the linear predictor, g(\mu_i)=\eta_i, and its inverse gives \mu_i=g^{-1}(\eta_i). A canonical link equates \eta_i with the natural parameter in the chosen linear exponential-family representation; it is a transformation of the mean, not of each observed response.

title: Conjugacy is optional
text:
Remark taught in The Beta–Binomial model, part of Bayesian statistics
Conjugacy is convenient, not compulsory. A prior concentrated around 1/2 could be obtained by truncating a Laplace density:
p(\theta)\propto
  \exp\!\left(-\frac{|\theta-1/2|}{b}\right)
  \mathbf{1}\{0\leq\theta\leq1\}.
The posterior kernel is then
p(\theta\mid x)
\propto
\theta^x(1-\theta)^{n-x}
\exp\!\left(-\frac{|\theta-1/2|}{b}\right)
\mathbf{1}\{0\leq\theta\leq1\}.
If equality rather than proportionality is needed, symmetry supplies the normalising constant without numerical integration: \begin{align*}
\int_0^1\exp\!\left(-\frac{|\theta-1/2|}{b}\right)\,\mathrm{d}\theta
&=2\int_0^{1/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{1/2-\theta}{b}\right)\,\mathrm{d}\theta\\
&=2\left[b\exp\!\left(-\frac{1/2-\theta}{b}\right)\right]_{\theta=0}^{1/2}\\
&=2b\left(1-e^{-1/(2b)}\right).
\end{align*} Thus the proper truncated-Laplace prior has multiplier ([2b{1-e^{-1/(2b)}}]^{-1}). The resulting posterior is not a named standard density, so its normalising integral and summaries must be evaluated numerically. The later MCMC chapters provide a general route when direct integration becomes difficult.

title: Conjugacy is optional
text:
Examples

Practice set: Q42. A nonconjugate prior and a change of variable

Question page: Q42. A nonconjugate prior and a change of variable

[12 marks]
Suppose X\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,\theta). Define Z=\log\frac{\theta}{1-\theta}, and assign the prior Z\sim N(1,1).
(a) Derive the prior density of \theta, including the Jacobian. [3 marks]
(b) Find the posterior kernel p(\theta\mid x). Is this prior conjugate? [2 marks]
(c) Derive the posterior kernel p(z\mid x). [3 marks]
(d) Construct a random-walk Metropolis–Hastings algorithm targeting p(z\mid x), using Z^*\mid Z^{(t)}=z\sim N(z,s^2). Explain how its output can estimate \mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x). [4 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. The sampling parameter is 0<\theta<1, and its logit coordinate is z=\log\{\theta/(1-\theta)\}. The prior is Z\sim N(1,1), where the second argument is variance. For an invertible transformation, densities obey p_\theta(\theta)=p_Z(z(\theta))|dz/d\theta|. A kernel is always defined relative to its coordinate and reference measure; here these are d\theta or dz.
(a) Prior density of \theta. The inverse transformation is \theta=g(z)=\frac{e^z}{1+e^z},\qquad z\in\mathbb R, and \frac{dz}{d\theta}
=\frac{d}{d\theta}\{\log\theta-\log(1-\theta)\}
=\frac1{\theta(1-\theta)}. Since Z\sim N(1,1), the change-of-variable formula gives \boxed{
p(\theta)
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\theta(1-\theta)}
\exp\left[-\frac12\left\{\log\frac{\theta}{1-\theta}-1\right\}^2\right],
\quad 0<\theta<1.
} The density is zero outside (0,1). This is a logit-normal prior.
(b) Posterior kernel for \theta. For an observed count x\in\{0,\ldots,n\}, L(\theta;x)=\binom nx\theta^x(1-\theta)^{n-x}. Multiplication by the prior gives \boxed{
p(\theta\mid x)\propto
\theta^{x-1}(1-\theta)^{n-x-1}
\exp\left[-\frac12\left\{\log\frac{\theta}{1-\theta}-1\right\}^2\right],
\quad 0<\theta<1.
} This prior is not conjugate: the posterior does not in general remain logit-normal. In particular, its logit-transformed posterior is not Normal, as the following kernel shows.
(c) Posterior kernel for z. Substituting \theta=g(z) in the likelihood, \theta^x(1-\theta)^{n-x}
=\frac{e^{xz}}{(1+e^z)^n}. Multiplying by the Normal prior density for z yields \boxed{
p(z\mid x)\propto
\exp\left\{xz-n\log(1+e^z)-\frac12(z-1)^2\right\},
\quad z\in\mathbb R.
} Alternatively, transforming the posterior from part (b) requires |d\theta/dz|=\theta(1-\theta), which cancels the prior’s Jacobian factor. Simply substituting \theta=g(z) into a density in \theta without this Jacobian would give the wrong density in z.
(d) Random-walk Metropolis–Hastings sampler. Define the log posterior kernel h(z)=xz-n\log(1+e^z)-\frac12(z-1)^2. The proposal density is symmetric because q(z^*\mid z)
=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi s^2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{(z^*-z)^2}{2s^2}\right\}
=q(z\mid z^*). Thus the acceptance probability is A(z,z^*)=\min\{1,\exp[h(z^*)-h(z)]\}. Equivalently, the log of the untruncated ratio is \begin{aligned}
\Delta=h(z^*)-h(z)
&=x(z^*-z)-n\{\log(1+e^{z^*})-\log(1+e^z)\}\\
&\quad-\frac12\{(z^*-1)^2-(z-1)^2\}.
\end{aligned}
Pseudocode. Choose any z^{(0)}\in\mathbb R and a fixed s>0. For t=0,\ldots,T-1:
1. Propose z^*\sim N(z^{(t)},s^2).
2. Calculate \Delta=h(z^*)-h(z^{(t)}).
3. Independently draw U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1).
4. If \log U\le\min\{0,\Delta\}, set z^{(t+1)}=z^*; otherwise set z^{(t+1)}=z^{(t)}.
This Markov chain has p(z\mid x) as its equilibrium density. Initial draws from an arbitrary start are not automatically posterior draws, and successive draws are generally dependent.
Estimating the requested posterior mean. After discarding a suitable initial burn-in of B iterations, transform each retained state and average: \theta^{(t)}=g(z^{(t)}),
\qquad
\boxed{
\widehat{\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)}
=\frac1{T-B}\sum_{t=B+1}^T\frac{e^{z^{(t)}}}{1+e^{z^{(t)}}}
}. With adequate convergence and a sufficiently long run, the ergodic average estimates the posterior expectation. Assess mixing and Monte Carlo error; the retained values are not independent.
For stable numerical evaluation, use \log(1+e^z)=\max\{0,z\}+\log(1+e^{-|z|}) and a stable logistic function.

Key result. Average the transformed draws. In general, \mathbb{E}\{g(Z)\mid x\}\ne g\{\mathbb{E}(Z\mid x)\}, so transforming the average of the z draws does not estimate the same quantity.






Book exercise: A logit-normal prior for a coin

Question page: A logit-normal prior for a coin

Suppose X\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,\theta) and prior knowledge favours heads. Consider the logit-normal prior

p(\theta)=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\theta(1-\theta)}
\exp\!\left[-\frac12\{\operatorname{logit}(\theta)-1\}^2\right],
\qquad 0<\theta<1,

where \operatorname{logit}(\theta)=\log\{\theta/(1-\theta)\}.

Plot the prior on a grid and describe its shape.
Generate 100{,}000 prior draws by taking Y\sim\operatorname{N}(1,1) and \theta=\exp(Y)/\{1+\exp(Y)\}. Add a kernel-density estimate from the draws to the exact prior curve.
Explain how the draws approximate the prior mean.
After observing x heads in n tosses, show that


p(\theta\mid x)\propto
\theta^{x-1}(1-\theta)^{n-x-1}
\exp\!\left[-\frac12\{\operatorname{logit}(\theta)-1\}^2\right].

Explain why this posterior is not Beta.






Worked answer (click to show)





Question. Suppose X\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,\theta) and prior knowledge favours heads. Consider the logit-normal prior

p(\theta)=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\theta(1-\theta)}
\exp\!\left[-\frac12\{\operatorname{logit}(\theta)-1\}^2\right],
\qquad 0<\theta<1,

where \operatorname{logit}(\theta)=\log\{\theta/(1-\theta)\}.

Plot the prior on a grid and describe its shape.
Generate 100{,}000 prior draws by taking Y\sim\operatorname{N}(1,1) and \theta=\exp(Y)/\{1+\exp(Y)\}. Add a kernel-density estimate from the draws to the exact prior curve.
Explain how the draws approximate the prior mean.
After observing x heads in n tosses, show that


p(\theta\mid x)\propto
\theta^{x-1}(1-\theta)^{n-x-1}
\exp\!\left[-\frac12\{\operatorname{logit}(\theta)-1\}^2\right].

Explain why this posterior is not Beta.
Solution. Let Y=\operatorname{logit}(\theta). Then

\theta=\frac{e^Y}{1+e^Y},
\qquad
\frac{\,\mathrm{d} Y}{\,\mathrm{d}\theta}
=\frac1\theta+\frac1{1-\theta}
=\frac1{\theta(1-\theta)}.

Transforming Y\sim\operatorname{N}(1,1) therefore produces exactly the stated prior.

The density is unimodal, concentrated above 1/2, and has a longer left tail than right tail. Its mode is near 0.84. The exact curve and a simulation check can be produced together by the following code.

dlogitnormal <- function(theta) {
  ok <- theta > 0 & theta < 1
  ans <- numeric(length(theta))
  ans[ok] <- dnorm(qlogis(theta[ok]), mean = 1, sd = 1) /
             (theta[ok] * (1 - theta[ok]))
  ans
}

set.seed(3500)
theta_grid <- seq(0.001, 0.999, length.out = 1000)
theta_draw <- plogis(rnorm(100000, mean = 1, sd = 1))

plot(theta_grid, dlogitnormal(theta_grid), type = "l",
     xlab = expression(theta), ylab = expression(p(theta)))
lines(density(theta_draw, from = 0, to = 1), col = "steelblue")

The overlaid kernel-density estimate should follow the exact curve. Agreement is a useful check both of the transformation and of the Jacobian in the displayed density.
By the law of large numbers,


\widehat{\mathbb{E}(\theta)}
=\frac1L\sum_{l=1}^L\theta^{(l)}
\longrightarrow \mathbb{E}(\theta).

For L=100{,}000 the answer varies slightly with the seed; numerical integration gives \mathbb{E}(\theta)\approx0.6967.

The binomial likelihood kernel is


p(x\mid\theta)\propto\theta^x(1-\theta)^{n-x}.

Multiplying by the prior gives \begin{align*}
p(\theta\mid x)
&\propto p(x\mid\theta)p(\theta)\\
&\propto
\theta^x(1-\theta)^{n-x}
\frac1{\theta(1-\theta)}
\exp\!\left[-\frac12\{\operatorname{logit}(\theta)-1\}^2\right]\\
&=\boxed{
\theta^{x-1}(1-\theta)^{n-x-1}
\exp\!\left[-\frac12\{\operatorname{logit}(\theta)-1\}^2\right]}.
\end{align*} A Beta kernel consists only of powers of \theta and 1-\theta. The extra factor involving the squared logit cannot be absorbed into those powers, so the posterior is not Beta.

title: Dirichlet distribution
text:
Definition taught in Categorical data and the Dirichlet distribution, part of Bayesian statistics · Also on the distribution sheet
The conjugate prior for {\boldsymbol{p}} is the Dirichlet distribution. Write
\alpha_0=\sum_{k=1}^K\alpha_k,
\qquad \alpha_k>0.
The multivariate Beta function is
B({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
=\frac{\prod_{k=1}^K\Gamma(\alpha_k)}
        {\Gamma(\alpha_0)}.
Then 
p({\boldsymbol{p}}\mid{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
=\frac1{B({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})}
   \prod_{k=1}^Kp_k^{\alpha_k-1},
\qquad {\boldsymbol{p}}\in\mathcal S_{K-1},
 where
\mathcal S_{K-1}
=\left\{{\boldsymbol{p}}:p_k\geq0,\ \sum_{k=1}^Kp_k=1\right\}
is the probability simplex.

title: Dirichlet distribution
text:
Properties

Dirichlet moments

Main article: Dirichlet moments

Standard Dirichlet integrals give \begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}(P_k)&=\frac{\alpha_k}{\alpha_0},\\
\mathbb{E}(P_k^2)&=\frac{\alpha_k(\alpha_k+1)}
                  {\alpha_0(\alpha_0+1)},\\
\mathbb{E}(P_jP_k)&=\frac{\alpha_j\alpha_k}
                  {\alpha_0(\alpha_0+1)},\qquad j\neq k.
\end{align*}


Interior Dirichlet mode

Main article: Interior Dirichlet mode

Consequently, 
\operatorname{mode}(P_k)
=\frac{\alpha_k-1}{\alpha_0-K}.
 This derivation requires every \alpha_k>1. Otherwise the mode may lie on a face or corner of the simplex.


Dirichlet–Multinomial conjugacy

Main article: Dirichlet–Multinomial conjugacy

After division by this evidence, 
\boxed{
{\boldsymbol{p}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1+x_1,\ldots,\alpha_K+x_K)}.



The Beta distribution is the two-category Dirichlet

Main article: The Beta distribution is the two-category Dirichlet

When K=2, write p_1=p and p_2=1-p. Restricting the Dirichlet density to the one-dimensional simplex gives

p(p\mid\alpha_1,\alpha_2)
=\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_1+\alpha_2)}
        {\Gamma(\alpha_1)\Gamma(\alpha_2)}
   p^{\alpha_1-1}(1-p)^{\alpha_2-1},

which is exactly \operatorname{Beta}(\alpha_1,\alpha_2). The Dirichlet is therefore a genuine extension of the Beta family rather than merely a similar-looking density.

Question. Use an unrestricted six-cell multinomial with the uniform prior

{\boldsymbol{p}}\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(1,1,1,1,1,1).

Find the posterior distribution and the posterior mean and MAP estimate of the male-negative cell probability.
Solution. The conjugate update gives

{\boldsymbol{p}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(54,58,148,94,39,114).

For the male-negative cell,

\mathbb{E}(P_{11}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{54}{501+6}=\frac{54}{507}
\approx0.1065,

while

\widehat p_{11,\mathrm{MAP}}
=\frac{54-1}{507-6}=\frac{53}{501}
\approx0.1058.

The MAP equals the maximum-likelihood cell proportion because every prior parameter equals one.

Question page: Q22. Advertising responses and Dirichlet inference

[10 marks]
An advertising campaign records responses from 60 independently sampled people:

Neutral
Positive




Male

6

4
14



Let \mathbf p=(p_{MN},p_{MU},p_{MP},p_{FN},p_{FU},p_{FP}) be the six population cell probabilities, with U denoting a neutral response. Model the counts as multinomial and use \mathbf p\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(1,1,1,1,1,1). You may use the Dirichlet kernel f(\mathbf p)\propto\prod_{k=1}^{K}p_k^{\alpha_k-1},
\qquad p_k>0,\quad \sum_{k=1}^{K}p_k=1.
(a) [2 marks] Derive the posterior distribution of \mathbf p, stating its parameters and support.
(b) [2 marks] Find the posterior mean of p_{MP} and its component of the joint MAP estimate of \mathbf p. Explain why that MAP component equals the observed cell proportion here.
(c) [2 marks] Find the posterior predictive probability that one new person responds positively, regardless of gender. Express it as a posterior expectation before calculating it.
(d) [2 marks] For that new person, calculate \mathbb{P}(\text{positive response}\mid\text{female},\text{data}). Explain why this differs from \mathbb{P}(\text{female and positive response}\mid\text{data}).
(e) [2 marks] Are the six components of \mathbf p independent under the posterior? Explain using their constraint.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Let D be the observed table and \mathbf p its six population cell probabilities. The labels M,F denote male and female; N,U,P denote negative, neutral, and positive. With parameters a_1,\ldots,a_K>0, a Dirichlet density has kernel \prod_k p_k^{a_k-1} on the simplex p_k>0, \sum_kp_k=1. The joint MAP maximises this density over the entire simplex, not a one-component marginal density.
(a) Posterior distribution. Write the counts in the stated order as \mathbf x=(8,6,16,12,4,14),\qquad n=60. The multinomial likelihood is L(\mathbf p;D)=\frac{60!}{\prod_{k=1}^{6}x_k!}
\prod_{k=1}^{6}p_k^{x_k}
\propto\prod_{k=1}^{6}p_k^{x_k}. The Dirichlet prior has kernel \prod_k p_k^{1-1}=1 on the simplex. Consequently, p(\mathbf p\mid D)\propto
\prod_{k=1}^{6}p_k^{x_k+1-1}, which is the Dirichlet kernel with parameters x_k+1. Thus \boxed{\mathbf p\mid D\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(9,7,17,13,5,15).} Its density is supported on the simplex p_k>0, \sum_{k=1}^6p_k=1; the boundary has probability zero. The posterior concentration is A=9+7+17+13+5+15=66.
(b) Posterior mean and MAP. For a Dirichlet vector with parameters a_1,\ldots,a_K and A=\sum_k a_k, \mathbb{E}(p_k)=\frac{a_k}{A},\qquad
\widehat p_{k,\mathrm{MAP}}=\frac{a_k-1}{A-K}
\quad\text{when every }a_k>1. Here every posterior parameter exceeds one, so \boxed{\mathbb{E}(p_{MP}\mid D)=\frac{17}{66}\approx0.2576,}
\qquad
\boxed{\widehat p_{MP,\mathrm{MAP}}=
\frac{17-1}{66-6}=\frac{16}{60}\approx0.2667.} The MAP component is taken from the mode of the joint posterior for \mathbf p. Since the prior density is constant on the simplex, maximising the posterior is equivalent to maximising the likelihood, giving the observed cell proportions.
(c) Predicting a positive response. Conditional on \mathbf p, the probability of a positive response is p_{MP}+p_{FP}. Averaging over posterior uncertainty gives \begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(\text{positive}\mid D)
&=\int (p_{MP}+p_{FP})p(\mathbf p\mid D)\,d\mathbf p\\
&=\mathbb{E}(p_{MP}+p_{FP}\mid D)\\
&=\frac{17}{66}+\frac{15}{66}
=\boxed{\frac{16}{33}\approx0.4848.}
\end{aligned} Prediction uses posterior averaging, not substitution of the MAP estimate.
(d) Conditioning on the new person being female. First calculate the two relevant posterior predictive probabilities: \mathbb{P}(\text{female and positive}\mid D)=\mathbb{E}(p_{FP}\mid D)=\frac{15}{66}, \mathbb{P}(\text{female}\mid D)
=\mathbb{E}(p_{FN}+p_{FU}+p_{FP}\mid D)
=\frac{13+5+15}{66}=\frac{33}{66}. By the definition of conditional probability, \boxed{
\mathbb{P}(\text{positive}\mid\text{female},D)
=\frac{15/66}{33/66}=\frac5{11}\approx0.4545.
} By contrast, the joint probability is \boxed{\mathbb{P}(\text{female and positive}\mid D)
=\frac{15}{66}=\frac5{22}\approx0.2273.} The conditional probability restricts attention to the female row; the joint probability refers to both events occurring for a person sampled from the whole population.
(e) Posterior dependence. No. The probabilities must satisfy \sum_k p_k=1 exactly. Increasing one component leaves less total probability for the others. More formally, if they were independent, then 0=\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^{6}p_k\,\middle|\,D\right)
=\sum_{k=1}^{6}\operatorname{Var}(p_k\mid D)>0, a contradiction, since each component has positive posterior variance. Indeed, distinct Dirichlet components have \operatorname{Cov}(p_j,p_k\mid D)
=-\frac{a_ja_k}{A^2(A+1)}<0,\qquad j\ne k.

Key result. Add counts to the Dirichlet parameters; average probabilities for prediction; and distinguish a joint cell probability from a probability conditional on a row.

Solution.

The Dirichlet–Multinomial update adds the observed cell counts to the corresponding concentration parameters. Since 63+19+3+38=123, \begin{align*}
{\boldsymbol{p}}&\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3,\alpha_4),\\
{\boldsymbol{x}}\mid{\boldsymbol{p}}&\sim\operatorname{Multinomial}(123,{\boldsymbol{p}}),\\
&\boxed{{\boldsymbol{p}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(63+\alpha_1,19+\alpha_2,3+\alpha_3,38+\alpha_4)}.
\end{align*}
Write last week’s proportions as


{\boldsymbol{q}}=(0.4479,0.2760,0.0736,0.2025).

A Dirichlet prior centred exactly at {\boldsymbol{q}} can be written {\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\kappa{\boldsymbol{q}}, where \kappa>0 is the total prior concentration. Increasing \kappa preserves the prior mean but increases the weight assigned to last week.
The construction used here instead combines 100 fractional counts with one baseline count in each category:

{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
=(44.79,27.60,7.36,20.25)+(1,1,1,1)
=(45.79,28.60,8.36,21.25).

Its concentration is 104 and its mean is {\boldsymbol{\alpha}}/104, which is slightly closer to (1/4,1/4,1/4,1/4) than {\boldsymbol{q}}. Thus the direction and concentration should both be reported; percentages alone determine only the direction.

The posterior parameters are \begin{align*}
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^\ast
&=(63,19,3,38)+(45.79,28.60,8.36,21.25)\\
&=\boxed{(108.79,47.60,11.36,59.25)},
\end{align*} with total concentration \alpha_0^\ast=108.79+47.60+11.36+59.25=227. Thus


\mathbb{E}(P_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{108.79}{227}=0.4793,
\qquad
\mathbb{E}(P_4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{59.25}{227}=0.2610.

Also,

\mathbb{E}(P_1+P_2+P_3\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=1-\mathbb{E}(P_4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=0.7390

and

\mathbb{E}(P_1-P_4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\frac{108.79-59.25}{227}=0.2182.

The Dirichlet marginal results give \begin{align*}
P_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}&\sim\operatorname{Beta}(108.79,118.21),\\
P_4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}&\sim\operatorname{Beta}(59.25,167.75),\\
P_1+P_2+P_3\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}&\sim\operatorname{Beta}(167.75,59.25).
\end{align*} Their intervals can therefore be obtained with Beta quantiles. The difference P_1-P_4 has no such Beta form, so simulation handles all four quantities uniformly:
rdirichlet_base <- function(n, alpha) {
  z <- sapply(alpha, function(a) rgamma(n, shape = a, rate = 1))
  z / rowSums(z)
}

set.seed(3500)
alpha_post <- c(108.79, 47.60, 11.36, 59.25)
p <- rdirichlet_base(100000, alpha_post)
summaries <- cbind(
  p1 = p[, 1],
  p4 = p[, 4],
  p123 = rowSums(p[, 1:3]),
  difference = p[, 1] - p[, 4]
)
rbind(
  mean = colMeans(summaries),
  lower = apply(summaries, 2, quantile, 0.025),
  upper = apply(summaries, 2, quantile, 0.975)
)

Let {\boldsymbol{p}}=(p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4) be the corresponding population proportions.

With {\boldsymbol{x}}\mid{\boldsymbol{p}}\sim\operatorname{Multinomial}(123,{\boldsymbol{p}}) and {\boldsymbol{p}}\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_4), identify the posterior.
Last week’s percentages were 44.79\%, 27.60\%, 7.36\%, and 20.25\%. Explain how to use these proportions to choose the direction of {\boldsymbol{\alpha}}, and how a chosen total concentration records the weight given to last week.
Using a prior equivalent, for posterior-mean purposes, to last week’s proportions plus one baseline count in each category, report posterior means and equal-tailed 95\% credible intervals for p_1, p_4, p_1+p_2+p_3, and p_1-p_4.

Solution.

The Dirichlet–Multinomial update adds the observed cell counts to the corresponding concentration parameters. Since 63+19+3+38=123, \begin{align*}
{\boldsymbol{p}}&\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3,\alpha_4),\\
{\boldsymbol{x}}\mid{\boldsymbol{p}}&\sim\operatorname{Multinomial}(123,{\boldsymbol{p}}),\\
&\boxed{{\boldsymbol{p}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(63+\alpha_1,19+\alpha_2,3+\alpha_3,38+\alpha_4)}.
\end{align*}
Write last week’s proportions as


{\boldsymbol{q}}=(0.4479,0.2760,0.0736,0.2025).

A Dirichlet prior centred exactly at {\boldsymbol{q}} can be written {\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\kappa{\boldsymbol{q}}, where \kappa>0 is the total prior concentration. Increasing \kappa preserves the prior mean but increases the weight assigned to last week.
The construction used here instead combines 100 fractional counts with one baseline count in each category:

{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
=(44.79,27.60,7.36,20.25)+(1,1,1,1)
=(45.79,28.60,8.36,21.25).

Its concentration is 104 and its mean is {\boldsymbol{\alpha}}/104, which is slightly closer to (1/4,1/4,1/4,1/4) than {\boldsymbol{q}}. Thus the direction and concentration should both be reported; percentages alone determine only the direction.

The posterior parameters are \begin{align*}
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^\ast
&=(63,19,3,38)+(45.79,28.60,8.36,21.25)\\
&=\boxed{(108.79,47.60,11.36,59.25)},
\end{align*} with total concentration \alpha_0^\ast=108.79+47.60+11.36+59.25=227. Thus


\mathbb{E}(P_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{108.79}{227}=0.4793,
\qquad
\mathbb{E}(P_4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{59.25}{227}=0.2610.

Also,

\mathbb{E}(P_1+P_2+P_3\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=1-\mathbb{E}(P_4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=0.7390

and

\mathbb{E}(P_1-P_4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\frac{108.79-59.25}{227}=0.2182.

The Dirichlet marginal results give \begin{align*}
P_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}&\sim\operatorname{Beta}(108.79,118.21),\\
P_4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}&\sim\operatorname{Beta}(59.25,167.75),\\
P_1+P_2+P_3\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}&\sim\operatorname{Beta}(167.75,59.25).
\end{align*} Their intervals can therefore be obtained with Beta quantiles. The difference P_1-P_4 has no such Beta form, so simulation handles all four quantities uniformly:
rdirichlet_base <- function(n, alpha) {
  z <- sapply(alpha, function(a) rgamma(n, shape = a, rate = 1))
  z / rowSums(z)
}

set.seed(3500)
alpha_post <- c(108.79, 47.60, 11.36, 59.25)
p <- rdirichlet_base(100000, alpha_post)
summaries <- cbind(
  p1 = p[, 1],
  p4 = p[, 4],
  p123 = rowSums(p[, 1:3]),
  difference = p[, 1] - p[, 4]
)
rbind(
  mean = colMeans(summaries),
  lower = apply(summaries, 2, quantile, 0.025),
  upper = apply(summaries, 2, quantile, 0.975)
)
For the displayed seed, rounding to three decimals gives

title: Error and residual
text:
Definition taught in Bayesian linear regression, part of Bayesian statistics
The true error is
\varepsilon_i=Y_i-{\boldsymbol{x}}_i^\top{\boldsymbol{\beta}},
which contains the unknown true coefficient vector. After fitting the model, the residual is
e_i=y_i-{\boldsymbol{x}}_i^\top\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}.
Errors are independent model variables under Equation (1) in Bayesian linear regression; residuals are observable functions of the entire fitted dataset and are not iid. The conventional name “sum of squared errors” is therefore slightly loose: the fitted quantity is a sum of squared residuals.

title: Exponential distribution
text:
Examples

Book exercise: Exponential observations parameterised by rate

Question page: Exponential observations parameterised by rate

For X\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\theta), take \theta to be the rate, so that

p(x\mid\theta)=\theta e^{-\theta x}\mathbf{1}_{\{x\geq0\}}.

Write this model in the chapter’s a(\theta), b(x), c(\theta), T(x) form and use that form to find a conjugate prior. Then give the posterior for an iid sample x_1,\ldots,x_n.






Worked answer (click to show)





Question. For X\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\theta), take \theta to be the rate, so that

p(x\mid\theta)=\theta e^{-\theta x}\mathbf{1}_{\{x\geq0\}}.

Write this model in the chapter’s a(\theta), b(x), c(\theta), T(x) form and use that form to find a conjugate prior. Then give the posterior for an iid sample x_1,\ldots,x_n.
Solution. For one observation,

p(x\mid\theta)=\theta e^{-\theta x}\mathbf{1}_{\{x\geq0\}}
=\frac{b(x)\exp\{c(\theta)T(x)\}}{a(\theta)}

with

\boxed{
b(x)=\mathbf{1}_{\{x\geq0\}},\quad
T(x)=x,\quad
c(\theta)=-\theta,\quad
a(\theta)=\frac1\theta}.

The chapter’s generic conjugate-prior kernel is therefore \begin{align*}
p(\theta\mid\alpha,\beta)
&\propto
\frac{\exp\{c(\theta)\alpha\}}{a(\theta)^\beta}\\
&=\frac{e^{-\alpha\theta}}{(1/\theta)^\beta}\\
&=\theta^\beta e^{-\alpha\theta}.
\end{align*} For \alpha>0 and \beta>-1, this is

\theta\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\beta+1,\alpha)

in the book’s shape–rate convention.
For an iid sample let S({\boldsymbol{x}})=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i. Then \begin{align*}
p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto
\left\{\prod_{i=1}^n\theta e^{-\theta x_i}\right\}
\theta^\beta e^{-\alpha\theta}\\
&=\theta^n e^{-\theta S({\boldsymbol{x}})}
\theta^\beta e^{-\alpha\theta}\\
&=\theta^{\beta+n}
e^{-\{\alpha+S({\boldsymbol{x}})\}\theta}.
\end{align*} Thus

\boxed{\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{Gamma}\bigl(\beta+n+1,\alpha+S({\boldsymbol{x}})\bigr)}.

Equivalently, if the prior is written in the standard shape–rate form \operatorname{Gamma}(a_0,b_0), then

\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim
\operatorname{Gamma}\bigl(a_0+n,b_0+S({\boldsymbol{x}})\bigr).






Final preparation: Question 8. Exponential versus gamma lifetimes

Question page: Question 8. Exponential versus gamma lifetimes

The lifetimes of n devices are {\boldsymbol{x}}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n). Two models are proposed,

M_1\colon X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda),
\qquad
M_2\colon X\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(3,\theta),

with priors \lambda\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(1,3) and \theta\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(1,1). Gamma and exponential distributions use the shape–rate sheet: a \operatorname{Gamma}(3,\theta) density is \theta^{3}x^{2}e^{-\theta x}/2.
(i) Find the marginal likelihood f({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_1). [6 marks]
(ii) Find the marginal likelihood f({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_2). [6 marks]
(iii) Obtain BF_{12}=f({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_1)/f({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_2). For these data BF_{12}=1.347. Interpret this number and state which model it prefers. [4 marks]
(iv) The researchers believe M_2 is three times as likely as M_1 a priori. What are the posterior odds? Which model is preferred? [4 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write S=\sum_i x_i and Q=\prod_i x_i^2. Both \lambda and \theta are rates. The marginal likelihood f({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_k) is the prior predictive density of the entire observed sample under model M_k. The Bayes factor BF_{12} is the ratio of these densities, in the stated order.
A marginal likelihood integrates the normalised likelihood against the normalised parameter prior, so factors involving only the data must be retained. Both integrations use \int_0^\infty t^{A-1}e^{-Bt}\,dt=\Gamma(A)/B^A for A,B>0. This identity follows by setting u=Bt in the defining gamma integral.
(i) The \operatorname{Exp}(\lambda) likelihood is \lambda^{n}e^{-\lambda\sum x_i}, and the \operatorname{Gamma}(1,3) prior density is 3e^{-3\lambda}. Hence

f({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_1)
=
3\int_0^{\infty}\lambda^{n}e^{-\lambda(\sum x_i+3)}\,d\lambda
=
\boxed{\dfrac{3\,n!}{\bigl(3+\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\bigr)^{n+1}}.}

(ii) A \operatorname{Gamma}(3,\theta) observation has density \theta^{3}x^{2}e^{-\theta x}/2. The prior density of \theta is e^{-\theta}. Therefore

\begin{aligned}
f({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_2)
&=
\frac{\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_i^{2}}{2^{n}}
\int_0^{\infty}\theta^{3n}e^{-\theta(\sum x_i+1)}\,d\theta\\
&=
\boxed{\dfrac{\bigl(\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_i^{2}\bigr)\,\Gamma(3n+1)}{2^{n}\bigl(1+\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\bigr)^{3n+1}}.}
\end{aligned}

(iii) Substituting (i) and (ii) into BF_{12}=f({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_1)/f({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_2) gives

\boxed{BF_{12}
=\frac{3\,2^n\Gamma(n+1)(S+1)^{3n+1}}
{\Gamma(3n+1)(S+3)^{n+1}Q}.}

For the observed sample this is 1.347: the marginal likelihood under M_1 is 1.347 times that under M_2. The data therefore favour M_1, but only slightly. The Bayes factor is not a posterior model probability.
For a continuous sample these are densities, not probabilities of the exact observed vector. Their ratio compares how strongly the two prior predictive distributions support the same observed data. Optimising each likelihood and taking the ratio would instead compare maximised likelihoods and would not calculate this Bayes factor.
(iv) Prior odds of M_1 to M_2 are 1/3. Posterior odds of M_1 to M_2 are BF_{12}/3=1.347/3=0.449:1, or about 2.23:1 in favour of M_2. Thus M_2 is preferred once the prior odds are included.
The governing identity is posterior odds = Bayes factor \times prior odds. The data shift the odds towards M_1, but the shift is too small to overcome the prior preference for M_2. If these are the only two models under consideration, their posterior probabilities are approximately 0.310 and 0.690, respectively.

title: Fisher–Neyman factorisation
text:
Theorem taught in Exponential families and conjugacy, part of Bayesian statistics
Suppose the family \{p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta):\theta\in\Omega\} is dominated by a common measure. Then T({\boldsymbol{X}}) is sufficient for \theta if and only if there are nonnegative functions g_\theta and h such that 
p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta)
=g_\theta\{T({\boldsymbol{x}})\}h({\boldsymbol{x}}),
\qquad \theta\in\Omega,
 where h does not depend on \theta.

title: Fisher–Neyman factorisation
text:
Examples

Sufficiency for a normal mean

Worked example from Exponential families and conjugacy

Suppose

X_1,\ldots,X_n\mid\mu
\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^2),
\qquad \sigma^2\text{ known}.

Question. Use the Fisher–Neyman factorisation theorem to find a sufficient statistic for \mu. Then identify a sufficient statistic when both \mu and \sigma^2 are unknown.
Solution. The joint density is \begin{align*}
p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\mu)
&=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}
   \exp\!\left\{-\frac1{2\sigma^2}
   \sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2\right\}.
\end{align*} Expand the quadratic: \begin{align*}
\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2
&=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i^2-2\mu x_i+\mu^2)\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^nx_i^2
   -2\mu\sum_{i=1}^nx_i
   +n\mu^2.
\end{align*} Substitution gives \begin{align*}
p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\mu)
&=\underbrace{
   (2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}
   \exp\!\left\{-\frac1{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^nx_i^2\right\}}
   _{h({\boldsymbol{x}})}\\
&\quad\times
   \underbrace{
   \exp\!\left\{
    \frac{\mu}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^nx_i
    -\frac{n\mu^2}{2\sigma^2}\right\}}
   _{g_\mu\{T({\boldsymbol{x}})\}}.
\end{align*} All dependence on \mu passes through

T({\boldsymbol{x}})=\sum_{i=1}^nx_i.

The factorisation theorem therefore proves that \sum_iX_i is sufficient for \mu. Since \overline X=T/n is a one-to-one function of T when n is fixed, \overline X is equivalent and is also sufficient.
If both \mu and \sigma^2 are unknown, the displayed factorisation no longer isolates all parameter dependence through \sum_iX_i. A sufficient statistic for (\mu,\sigma^2) is instead

\left(\sum_{i=1}^nX_i,\sum_{i=1}^nX_i^2\right),

or equivalently

\left(\overline X,\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\overline X)^2\right).

This is the nuisance-parameter warning in concrete form.


Book exercise: Sufficiency and the posterior

Question page: Sufficiency and the posterior

Let {\boldsymbol{X}}=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)^{\mathsf T} have likelihood p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta) and prior p(\theta). If U({\boldsymbol{X}}) is sufficient for \theta, use the Fisher–Neyman factorisation theorem and Bayes’ rule to show that the posterior depends on the observed sample only through U({\boldsymbol{x}}). Retain the normalising integral in the derivation.






Worked answer (click to show)





Question. Let {\boldsymbol{X}}=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)^{\mathsf T} have likelihood p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta) and prior p(\theta). If U({\boldsymbol{X}}) is sufficient for \theta, use the Fisher–Neyman factorisation theorem and Bayes’ rule to show that the posterior depends on the observed sample only through U({\boldsymbol{x}}). Retain the normalising integral in the derivation.
Solution. By the Fisher–Neyman factorisation theorem, sufficiency of U({\boldsymbol{X}}) implies that there are nonnegative functions g and h such that

p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta)=g\{U({\boldsymbol{x}}),\theta\}h({\boldsymbol{x}}),

where h does not depend on \theta. Bayes’ rule, including its normalising integral, gives \begin{align*}
p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=\frac{p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta)p(\theta)}
{\displaystyle\int p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid t)p(t)\,\mathrm{d} t}\\
&=\frac{g\{U({\boldsymbol{x}}),\theta\}h({\boldsymbol{x}})p(\theta)}
{\displaystyle\int g\{U({\boldsymbol{x}}),t\}h({\boldsymbol{x}})p(t)\,\mathrm{d} t}\\
&=\boxed{
\frac{g\{U({\boldsymbol{x}}),\theta\}p(\theta)}
{\displaystyle\int g\{U({\boldsymbol{x}}),t\}p(t)\,\mathrm{d} t}}.
\end{align*} Every occurrence of the observed sample is through U({\boldsymbol{x}}); the factor h({\boldsymbol{x}}) cancels because it is constant with respect to the integration variable and the parameter.

title: Gamma distribution
text:
Examples

Poisson natural form and Gamma conjugacy

Worked example from Exponential families and conjugacy

Question. For iid Poisson observations with mean \theta, write the model in the a(\theta), b(x), c(\theta), T(x) form, identify the sufficient statistic, and derive the corresponding conjugate prior and posterior update.
Solution. For one Poisson observation, \begin{align*}
p(x\mid\theta)
&=\frac{e^{-\theta}\theta^x}{x!}\\
&=\frac1{x!}\exp\{x\log\theta\}e^{-\theta}\\
&=\frac{b(x)\exp\{c(\theta)T(x)\}}{a(\theta)},
\end{align*} with

b(x)=\frac1{x!},
\qquad c(\theta)=\log\theta,
\qquad T(x)=x,
\qquad a(\theta)=e^\theta.

For the Poisson model, the definition Equation (4) in Exponential families and conjugacy gives S({\boldsymbol{x}})=\sum_i x_i. The joint likelihood is \begin{align*}
p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta)
&=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{e^{-\theta}\theta^{x_i}}{x_i!}\\
&=\left(\prod_{i=1}^n\frac1{x_i!}\right)
   \exp\{(\log\theta)S({\boldsymbol{x}})-n\theta\}.
\end{align*} The factorisation theorem shows that S({\boldsymbol{X}}) is sufficient for \theta. It is also minimal sufficient by the likelihood-ratio criterion. Because the natural parameter c(\theta)=\log\theta ranges over the open set \mathbb{R}, S({\boldsymbol{X}}) is complete as well.
The generic prior Equation (6) in Exponential families and conjugacy becomes \begin{align*}
p(\theta\mid\alpha,\beta)
&\propto
\frac{\exp\{\alpha\log\theta\}}{(e^\theta)^\beta}\\
&=\theta^\alpha e^{-\beta\theta}.
\end{align*} This is the kernel of \operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha+1,\beta), not \operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha,\beta). Using the sufficient statistic S({\boldsymbol{x}}), \begin{align*}
p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto
\theta^{S({\boldsymbol{x}})} e^{-n\theta}\theta^\alpha e^{-\beta\theta}\\
&=\theta^{S({\boldsymbol{x}})+\alpha}e^{-(n+\beta)\theta},
\end{align*} so 
\boxed{
\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha+S({\boldsymbol{x}})+1,\beta+n)}.
 Its posterior mean is \begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=\frac{\alpha+S({\boldsymbol{x}})+1}{\beta+n}\\
&=\frac{(\alpha+1)+n\overline x}{\beta+n}\\
&=\frac\beta{\beta+n}\frac{\alpha+1}{\beta}
  +\frac n{\beta+n}\overline x.
\end{align*} The prior therefore behaves, for the mean, as \beta prior observations with total count \alpha+1.


Practice set: Q48. Conjugate Bayesian inference for a Gamma rate

Question page: Q48. Conjugate Bayesian inference for a Gamma rate

[10 marks]
Let X_1,\ldots,X_n be conditionally independent given \lambda, with density f(x_i\mid\lambda)
=\frac{\lambda^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)}
x_i^{\alpha-1}e^{-\lambda x_i},\qquad x_i>0, where \alpha>0 is known and \lambda>0 is unknown.
Suppose \lambda\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a,b), where a,b>0, with prior density p(\lambda)=\frac{b^a}{\Gamma(a)}\lambda^{a-1}e^{-b\lambda}.
(a) Derive the posterior distribution of \lambda\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}, identifying its parameters. Show the likelihood and posterior kernels. [4 marks]
(b) State the posterior mean \mathbb{E}[\lambda\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}]. [1 mark]
(c) Derive the maximum likelihood estimator \widehat\lambda_{\mathrm{ML}}. [2 marks]
(d) Express the posterior mean in the form \mathbb{E}[\lambda\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}]
        =w_n\mathbb{E}[\lambda]+(1-w_n)\widehat\lambda_{\mathrm{ML}}. Identify w_n, verify that this is a convex combination, and determine the limits of the weights as n\to\infty, assuming \bar x_n\to m>0 and fixed prior parameters. [3 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. \operatorname{Gamma}(A,B) uses shape A and rate B, with kernel \lambda^{A-1}e^{-B\lambda} on \lambda>0 and mean A/B. The sampling shape \alpha>0 is known, while the rate \lambda is unknown. Write T_n=\sum_i x_i=n\bar x_n>0. The prior parameters a,b>0 are fixed; the asymptotic statement uses the specified \bar x_n\to m>0.
(a) Likelihood and posterior. Conditional independence gives \begin{aligned}
L(\lambda;{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=\prod_{i=1}^n
\left\{\frac{\lambda^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)}
x_i^{\alpha-1}e^{-\lambda x_i}\right\}\\
&=\frac{\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{\alpha-1}}{\Gamma(\alpha)^n}
\lambda^{n\alpha}e^{-\lambda T_n}.
\end{aligned} The leading factor does not involve \lambda, so \boxed{L(\lambda;{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto\lambda^{n\alpha}e^{-T_n\lambda},
\qquad\lambda>0.} Multiplying by the prior kernel, \begin{aligned}
p(\lambda\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto\lambda^{n\alpha}e^{-T_n\lambda}
\lambda^{a-1}e^{-b\lambda}\\
&=\lambda^{a+n\alpha-1}e^{-(b+T_n)\lambda}.
\end{aligned} Matching \lambda^{A-1}e^{-B\lambda} gives \boxed{\lambda\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim
\operatorname{Gamma}(a+n\alpha,\ b+T_n)
\quad\text{(shape--rate)},\qquad\lambda>0.} Thus the Gamma family is conjugate for the unknown rate.
(b) Posterior mean. A shape–rate Gamma distribution has mean shape divided by rate: \boxed{\mathbb{E}[\lambda\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}]=\frac{a+n\alpha}{b+T_n}.}
(c) Maximum likelihood estimator. The log-likelihood, up to a constant, is \ell(\lambda)=n\alpha\log\lambda-T_n\lambda+C. Its derivatives are \ell'(\lambda)=\frac{n\alpha}{\lambda}-T_n,
\qquad \ell''(\lambda)=-\frac{n\alpha}{\lambda^2}<0. Solving \ell'(\lambda)=0 therefore gives the unique maximiser \boxed{\widehat\lambda_{\mathrm{ML}}=\frac{n\alpha}{T_n}
=\frac{\alpha}{\bar x_n}.}
(d) Convex combination and limiting weights. The prior mean is \mathbb{E}[\lambda]=a/b. Split the posterior mean as follows: \begin{aligned}
\frac{a+n\alpha}{b+T_n}
&=\frac{b}{b+T_n}\frac ab
+\frac{T_n}{b+T_n}\frac{n\alpha}{T_n}\\
&=w_n\mathbb{E}[\lambda]+(1-w_n)\widehat\lambda_{\mathrm{ML}},
\end{aligned} where \boxed{w_n=\frac{b}{b+T_n}=\frac{b}{b+n\bar x_n},
\qquad 1-w_n=\frac{T_n}{b+T_n}.} Because b>0 and T_n>0, both weights are strictly between zero and one, and \frac{b}{b+T_n}+\frac{T_n}{b+T_n}=1. Hence this is a convex combination of the prior mean and the MLE. Notice that the weights depend on the observed total T_n, not just on n.
Under \bar x_n\to m>0, we have T_n=n\bar x_n\to\infty. With fixed prior parameters, \boxed{w_n\longrightarrow0,\qquad1-w_n\longrightarrow1.} The prior-mean contribution consequently vanishes and the data receive asymptotically all the weight. In fact, both estimates have the same limit: \widehat\lambda_{\mathrm{ML}}=\frac\alpha{\bar x_n}
\longrightarrow\frac\alpha m,
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[\lambda\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}]
=\frac{a/n+\alpha}{b/n+\bar x_n}
\longrightarrow\frac\alpha m.

Key result. For this rate parameter, the prior weight is b/(b+\sum_i x_i). Derive the weights from the actual posterior mean; they are not always “prior sample size divided by total sample size.”






Practice set: Q29. Comparing Exponential and Gamma lifetime models

Question page: Q29. Comparing Exponential and Gamma lifetime models

[20 marks]
Researchers observed lifetimes {\boldsymbol{x}}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n), with each x_i>0, for a sample of n medical devices. Two models are proposed, with conditionally iid observations under each model: M_1:\quad X_i\mid\lambda\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda),
\qquad
M_2:\quad X_i\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(3,\theta). Prior experiments suggest the parameter priors \lambda\mid M_1\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(1,3),
\qquad
\theta\mid M_2\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(1,1). Parameterisation: all Gamma distributions use shape–rate notation, and the exponential parameter is its rate.
(i) [6 marks] Find p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_1), the marginal likelihood of the data under model M_1.
(ii) [6 marks] Find p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_2), the marginal likelihood of the data under model M_2.
(iii) [4 marks] Obtain an expression for BF_{12}, the Bayes factor comparing M_1 with M_2. For the observed data, BF_{12}=1.347. Briefly interpret this number. Based on this evidence alone, which model is preferred?
(iv) [4 marks] Suppose the researchers’ prior belief is that M_2 is three times as likely as M_1. What are the posterior model odds? Which model is now preferred?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write S=\sum_i x_i and Q=\prod_i x_i^2. \operatorname{Exp}(\lambda) uses rate \lambda; \operatorname{Gamma}(a,b) uses shape a and rate b. For model M_j, the marginal likelihood is m_j({\boldsymbol{x}})=\int L_j(\vartheta;{\boldsymbol{x}})p_j(\vartheta)\,d\vartheta and BF_{12}=m_1/m_2. Use the same positive, conditionally independent lifetime sample and the stated proper priors in both models.
A marginal likelihood averages the fully normalised likelihood over the parameter prior. Unlike posterior kernel matching, this calculation must retain all multiplicative constants, including factors involving only the data.
Both calculations use the Gamma integral \int_0^\infty t^{A-1}e^{-Bt}\,dt
=\frac{\Gamma(A)}{B^A},\qquad A,B>0.
(i) Marginal likelihood under M_1. For an exponential distribution with rate \lambda, p(x_i\mid\lambda,M_1)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x_i},\qquad x_i>0. Therefore the likelihood and normalised prior are p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\lambda,M_1)=\lambda^n e^{-\lambda S},
\qquad p(\lambda\mid M_1)=3e^{-3\lambda},\quad\lambda>0. Integrating their product, \begin{aligned}
p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_1)
&=\int_0^\infty p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\lambda,M_1)
p(\lambda\mid M_1)\,d\lambda\\
&=3\int_0^\infty\lambda^n e^{-(S+3)\lambda}\,d\lambda\\
&=\boxed{\frac{3\Gamma(n+1)}{(S+3)^{n+1}}.}
\end{aligned} The power \lambda^n corresponds to Gamma shape n+1, not n. The leading 3 comes from the normalised prior and cannot be omitted.
(ii) Marginal likelihood under M_2. For a Gamma distribution with shape 3 and rate \theta, p(x_i\mid\theta,M_2)
=\frac{\theta^3}{\Gamma(3)}x_i^2e^{-\theta x_i}
=\frac{\theta^3}{2}x_i^2e^{-\theta x_i},\qquad x_i>0. Thus p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta,M_2)=\frac{Q}{2^n}\theta^{3n}e^{-\theta S},
\qquad p(\theta\mid M_2)=e^{-\theta},\quad\theta>0. Integrating gives \begin{aligned}
p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_2)
&=\int_0^\infty p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta,M_2)
p(\theta\mid M_2)\,d\theta\\
&=\frac{Q}{2^n}\int_0^\infty\theta^{3n}e^{-(S+1)\theta}\,d\theta\\
&=\boxed{\frac{Q\,\Gamma(3n+1)}{2^n(S+1)^{3n+1}}.}
\end{aligned} Although Q/2^n does not involve \theta, it remains part of the marginal likelihood. Dropping it would give the wrong model comparison.
(iii) Bayes factor and its interpretation. By definition, \begin{aligned}
BF_{12}
&=\frac{p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_1)}{p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_2)}\\
&=\frac{3\Gamma(n+1)}{(S+3)^{n+1}}
\frac{2^n(S+1)^{3n+1}}{Q\,\Gamma(3n+1)}.
\end{aligned} Hence \boxed{BF_{12}
=\frac{3\cdot2^n\Gamma(n+1)(S+1)^{3n+1}}
{\Gamma(3n+1)(S+3)^{n+1}\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_i^2}.} The observed value BF_{12}=1.347 means that the marginal likelihood of the data under M_1 is 1.347 times that under M_2, using the specified parameter priors. The data therefore favour M_1, but only slightly. This is not a posterior probability of either model.
Based on the marginal evidence alone, M_1 is preferred. If the prior model probabilities were equal, its posterior probability would be \mathbb{P}(M_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{1.347}{1+1.347}\approx0.574. Different prior model odds can reverse that posterior preference.
(iv) Unequal prior model probabilities. The prior belief in the question gives \frac{\mathbb{P}(M_1)}{\mathbb{P}(M_2)}=\frac13. Posterior odds equal the Bayes factor times prior odds, so \boxed{
\frac{\mathbb{P}(M_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})}{\mathbb{P}(M_2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})}
=1.347\left(\frac13\right)=0.449.
} Thus the posterior odds are 0.449:1 in favour of M_1 relative to M_2, or approximately 2.227:1 in favour of M_2. With these two models as the alternatives, \mathbb{P}(M_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{0.449}{1+0.449}\approx0.310, \mathbb{P}(M_2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac1{1+0.449}\approx0.690. Model M_2 is now preferred. The Bayes factor moves the odds toward M_1, but the evidence is too weak to overcome the prior three-to-one preference for M_2.

Key result. Keep the normalising constants when integrating likelihoods. A Bayes factor updates model odds; it is not itself a posterior model probability.

Observations Y_1,\ldots,Y_n follow a generalised linear model when all three of the following are specified.

title: Generalised linear model
text:
Definition

Random component. The Y_i are independent, and each belongs to the same exponential family. The functions a, b, c, d and e are common; the parameter \theta_i may depend on i.
Linear predictor. Covariate vectors {\boldsymbol{X}}_1,\ldots,{\boldsymbol{X}}_n and a coefficient vector \boldsymbol{\beta}=(\beta_0,\ldots,\beta_d)^\top form 
\eta_i={\boldsymbol{X}}_i^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}.

Link. A monotone function g connects the mean \mu_i=\mathrm{E}(Y_i) to that predictor, 
g(\mu_i)={\boldsymbol{X}}_i^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}.

title: Generalised linear model
text:
Examples

Practice set: Q30. Poisson regression model statement

Question page: Q30. Poisson regression model statement

[4 marks]
For 80 independent lakes, researchers record the number of fish species, distance from the coast in kilometres, and surface area in hectares. They fit:
glm(species ~ distance + log(area), family = poisson)
Write down explicitly the model corresponding to this code. Define your notation and state the independence assumption.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. For lake i=1,\ldots,80, let Y_i be its species count, d_i its distance from the coast in kilometres, and A_i>0 its area in hectares. Write \mu_i=\mathbb{E}(Y_i\mid d_i,A_i). The covariates are fixed; logarithms are natural. A GLM combines a response distribution with a link between this conditional mean and a linear predictor.
The model is \boxed{
Y_i\mid d_i,A_i\overset{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}
\operatorname{Poisson}(\mu_i),
\qquad
\log\mu_i=\beta_0+\beta_1d_i+\beta_2\log A_i.
} Thus the default link is the log link, and \mu_i=\exp\{\beta_0+\beta_1d_i+\beta_2\log A_i\}
     =e^{\beta_0}e^{\beta_1d_i}A_i^{\beta_2}. Under the Poisson assumption, \mathbb{E}(Y_i\mid d_i,A_i)
=\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid d_i,A_i)=\mu_i. The responses from different lakes are independent conditional on their covariates. They need not be identically distributed, because their means can differ.

Key result. A model statement needs a distribution and an independence assumption, as well as the equation linking the mean to the covariates.






Final preparation: Question 19. Poisson regression for fish species

Question page: Question 19. Poisson regression for fish species

2024 examination, Question 3 (20 marks).
Barbour and Brown recorded the number Y_i of fish species in n=70 lakes, together with latitude and area. The scatterplots show the observed counts against the two covariates.



Species counts against latitude and log lake area, as shown in the 2024 examination.


Consider

Y_i\mid X_i\stackrel{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}\operatorname{Poisson}(\mu_i=\exp(X_i^{\top}\beta)),
\qquad
X_i^{\top}\beta=\beta_0+\beta_1\,\mathrm{latitude}_i+\beta_2\log(\mathrm{area}_i).

(a) [1 mark] Briefly argue why \log(\mathrm{area}_i) is preferable to \mathrm{area}_i in the linear predictor.
(b) [2 marks] Show that the log-likelihood is

\ell(\beta\mid X,Y)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl\{Y_i(X_i^{\top}\beta)-\exp(X_i^{\top}\beta)\bigr\}+\text{constant}.

(c) [2 marks] Derive the score and show that

S(\beta)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Y_i-\mu_i(X_i^{\top}\beta)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid X_i)}\,\mu_i'(X_i^{\top}\beta)\,X_i.

(d) [1 mark] Show that S(\beta) is unbiased.
(e) [2 marks] Verify \operatorname{Var}(S(\beta))=-\mathbb{E}[\partial S(\beta)/\partial\beta].
The first statistician fits the linear Poisson model:
fit1 = glm(species ~ latitude + log(area), family=poisson)

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept)  2.5949644  0.0668158   38.84   <2e-16 ***
latitude    -0.0149475  0.0008788  -17.01   <2e-16 ***
log(area)    0.2092975  0.0068808   30.42   <2e-16 ***

(Dispersion parameter for poisson family taken to be 1)
Null deviance:     2646.1 on 69 degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 1249.9 on 67 degrees of freedom
AIC: 1616.4
(f) [5 marks] Interpret the intercept, the latitude and \log(\mathrm{area}) coefficients, the null deviance and the residual deviance.
The second statistician replaces the latitude slope with a smooth:
library(mgcv)
fit2 = gam(species ~ s(latitude) + log(area), family=poisson)

Parametric coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept)  2.064885   0.065793   31.39   <2e-16 ***
log(area)    0.202381   0.007701   26.28   <2e-16 ***

Approximate significance of smooth terms:
             edf Ref.df Chi.sq p-value
s(latitude) 8.881  8.996  463.2  <2e-16 ***



Fitted latitude smooth and uncertainty bands from the 2024 examination.


(g) [1 mark] Interpret the edf value 8.881.
(h) [2 marks] Comparing the two fits, is a linear function of latitude enough after accounting for lake area?
(i) [4 marks] Summarise the main findings in one short paragraph.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Y_i is the species count in lake i, and X_i=(1,\mathrm{latitude}_i,\log\mathrm{area}_i)^\top is its fixed covariate vector. The model assumes independent Y_i\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\mu_i) with \mu_i=\exp(X_i^\top\beta). Thus \mathbb{E}(Y_i\mid X_i)=\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid X_i)=\mu_i, with dispersion fixed at one. The score is the gradient of the log-likelihood, and Fisher information measures its expected curvature, or equivalently its covariance under the model.
(a) \log(\mathrm{area}) transforms a covariate; the log link transforms the response mean. These are separate choices. Logging area compresses its range and represents multiplicative area comparisons by additive differences: one unit of \log(\mathrm{area}) multiplies area by e. With a log link and a log-area predictor,

\mu_i=e^{\beta_0+\beta_1\mathrm{latitude}_i}\,
\mathrm{area}_i^{\beta_2}.

This is a power-law area effect, whereas using raw area in the same log-link GLM gives an exponential area effect. The observed plot and scientific context should guide that choice; logging a covariate does not by itself establish model adequacy. Neither choice requires taking \log Y_i, so zero species counts pose no transformation problem for the response.
(b) The Poisson log-likelihood contribution is Y_i\log\mu_i-\mu_i-\log(Y_i!). The factorial term does not depend on \beta. With the log link, \log\mu_i=X_i^{\top}\beta and \mu_i=\exp(X_i^{\top}\beta), so

\ell(\beta\mid X,Y)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl\{Y_i(X_i^{\top}\beta)-\exp(X_i^{\top}\beta)\bigr\}
+\text{constant}.

(c) Differentiate (b). Since \partial\mu_i/\partial\beta=\mu_i X_i,

S(\beta)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i-\mu_i)X_i.

For every GLM the score is the same residual, reweighted by the variance and by the slope of the mean:

S(\beta)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\frac{Y_i-\mu_i}{\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid X_i)}
\,\mu_i'(X_i^{\top}\beta)\,X_i.

Here \operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid X_i)=\mu_i. Under the log link, \mu_i'=\mu_i, so the weight equals 1 and the general score reduces to the sum above. Setting S(\beta)=0 is still nonlinear in \beta, because \mu_i=\exp(X_i^{\top}\beta). The fit is Fisher scoring of that equation, not a closed form.
(d) At the \beta in the model, \mathbb{E}(Y_i\mid X_i)=\mu_i. Each summand then has conditional mean zero, and \mathbb{E}[S(\beta)]=0.
Explicitly, with the design held fixed,

\mathbb{E}\{S(\beta)\mid X\}
=\sum_iX_i\{\mathbb{E}(Y_i\mid X)-\mu_i\}=0.

This identity concerns repeated samples at the true parameter. The fitted score S(\hat\beta)=0 instead follows from maximising the observed likelihood; the two zeroes arise for different reasons.
(e) From the reduced score and \partial\mu_i/\partial\beta^{\top}=\mu_i X_i^{\top},

\frac{\partial S(\beta)}{\partial\beta}
=
-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mu_i X_iX_i^{\top}.

The right-hand side does not depend on Y, so

-\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\partial S(\beta)}{\partial\beta}\right]
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mu_i X_iX_i^{\top}.

Calculate the score covariance separately. Conditional independence removes cross-covariances, and the Poisson variance is \operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid X)=\mu_i, so

\operatorname{Var}\{S(\beta)\mid X\}
=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid X)X_iX_i^{\top}
=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mu_iX_iX_i^{\top}.

This matches the negative expected Hessian above. The common matrix is the Fisher information. For the Poisson log link the observed and expected information agree; overdispersion or dependence would change the score covariance even if the mean formula remained correct.
(f) The intercept 2.595 is the log mean at latitude 0 (the equator) and \log(\mathrm{area})=0 (unit area), so the fitted mean there is \exp(2.595)\approx 13.4 species. This is the model’s reference lake, not a general mean for the sampled lakes.
The latitude coefficient -0.01495 is a multiplicative effect at fixed log area. One extra degree away from the equator multiplies the mean count by \exp(-0.01495)\approx 0.985. A degree is a small unit: ten degrees multiply the mean by \exp(-0.1495)\approx 0.861. Those are the same fit. The coefficient looks small because the unit is one degree.
The coefficient 0.2093 is the effect of one unit of \log(\mathrm{area}) at fixed latitude. Multiplying area by e multiplies the mean count by \exp(0.2093)\approx 1.233.
For any positive multiplier c, the fitted mean ratio is c^{0.2093}. Doubling area therefore multiplies the fitted mean by about 1.16, rather than by 1.23. The coefficient is an elasticity: a small 1\% increase in area corresponds to approximately a 0.2093\% increase in the expected count, holding latitude fixed.
The null deviance 2646.1 on 69 degrees of freedom is the deviance of the intercept-only model, one mean for every lake. The deviance is twice the drop in log-likelihood from the saturated fit to the model under discussion,

D(Y;\hat\mu)=2\bigl\{\ell(Y;Y)-\ell(\hat\mu;Y)\bigr\},

with Poisson dispersion fixed at 1. The degrees of freedom are n-1=69.
The residual deviance 1249.9 on 67 degrees of freedom is the deviance of the fitted three-parameter model, n-3=67. For the Poisson,

D
=
2\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left\{
Y_i\log\frac{Y_i}{\hat\mu_i}-(Y_i-\hat\mu_i)
\right\}.

The value is about 19 times its degrees of freedom, so the Poisson model fits poorly relative to its stated mean–variance assumptions. This can reflect overdispersion, a misspecified mean function, influential lakes or dependence; the deviance alone does not identify which. A quasi-Poisson fit with \operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid X_i)=\phi\mu_i would retain these fitted coefficients while adjusting their standard errors, but it would not repair a wrong mean function.
The saturated fit has one fitted mean per observation, \hat\mu_i=Y_i, and hence no residual degrees of freedom. The null and residual degrees of freedom reveal n=70 and three fitted regression coefficients. In the deviance formula use 0\log(0/\hat\mu_i)=0 when Y_i=0. Comparing deviance to degrees of freedom is a diagnostic, not a proof that one particular assumption failed; sparse counts can also make a nominal chi-squared approximation inaccurate.
(g) The value 8.881 is the effective degrees of freedom of the fitted latitude smooth. It measures the smooth’s effective flexibility after penalisation, roughly comparable to a high-order polynomial fit; the fitted function is not literally a polynomial of degree 8.881. A value near 1 would indicate an approximately straight effect on the log-mean scale. Here the fitted effect is substantially more flexible.
The GAM keeps the Poisson response distribution and log link but replaces \beta_1\mathrm{latitude} by a fitted function g(\mathrm{latitude}). A smooth can be represented by basis functions with a penalty discouraging excessive wiggliness. The edf describes the flexibility remaining after that penalty, rather than the number of knots or an ordinary polynomial degree. The plotted ordinate is the smooth’s contribution to the log mean; obtaining a predicted count also requires the intercept and log-area contribution.
(h) The plotted effect of latitude rises and falls several times, so a single straight line on the log-mean scale misses its shape. The edf of 8.881 is also far above the near-linear value of 1. The printed \chi^2 test concerns whether the smooth is absent, not specifically whether it departs from a line. A direct formal comparison of linear and smooth latitude fits would address that narrower hypothesis. The log-area coefficient is similar in the two fits, 0.209 and 0.202.
(i) At a fixed latitude, multiplying lake area by e multiplies the fitted mean species count by about 1.23; the log-area coefficient stays close to 0.20 in the GAM. The smooth suggests high diversity near the equator, a dip around 20–25 degrees away, a rise around 30–40 degrees, and lower diversity towards the poles. A single latitude slope misses this pattern. The linear Poisson fit reduces deviance from 2646.1 to 1249.9, but the residual deviance remains far above 67 degrees of freedom. Check the mean function, the Poisson variance assumption and influential lakes before relying on its printed standard errors and z tests.





Concept check: C16. The GLM components

Question page: C16. The GLM components

What are the three components of a GLM? State the usual conditional-independence assumption.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. A GLM specifies an exponential-family response distribution, a linear predictor \eta_i=x_i^\top\beta, and a link g(\mu_i)=\eta_i, where \mu_i=\mathbb{E}(Y_i\mid x_i). Responses are assumed independent conditional on the fixed covariates and model parameters.
