title: Geometric distribution
text:
Examples

Final preparation: Question 11. Geometric success probability

Question page: Question 11. Geometric success probability

Let x_1,\ldots,x_n be iid with

f(x\mid p)=(1-p)^{x}p,
\quad x=0,1,2,\ldots,

and p\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta).
(i) Find the posterior distribution of p and identify it. [3 marks]
(ii) Is this prior conjugate? [1 mark]
(iii) Show that a \operatorname{Beta}(a,b) mean equals a/(a+b). [2 marks]
(iv) Hence show that \mathbb{E}(p\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=(\alpha+n)/(\alpha+\beta+n+n\bar x). [1 mark]
(v) What happens to the posterior mean as n\to\infty? [1 mark]
(vi) What happens if \alpha,\beta\to 0? [1 mark]
(vii) Complete: “The effect of the prior hyperparameters \alpha,\beta on the posterior mean of p is like…” [2 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Here X_i counts failures before the first success, so its support begins at zero. Each observation represents one success and x_i failures. Put F=\sum_i x_i=n\bar x. The beta density is p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1}/B(\alpha,\beta) on 0<p<1. This geometric convention differs from the trial-count convention in Question 6 by one.
(i) The likelihood is p^{n}(1-p)^{\sum x_i}. The beta prior contributes p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1}, so

\boxed{p\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{Beta}\bigl(\alpha+n,\;\beta+\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\bigr).}

(ii) Yes. The posterior is beta, the same family as the prior.
(iii) For a>0 and b>0, the expectation integral is

\mathbb{E}(P)=\frac1{B(a,b)}\int_0^1 p^a(1-p)^{b-1}\,dp
=\frac{B(a+1,b)}{B(a,b)}.

Using B(a,b)=\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)/\Gamma(a+b) and \Gamma(a+1)=a\Gamma(a),

\frac{B(a+1,b)}{B(a,b)}
=
\frac{\Gamma(a+1)\Gamma(a+b)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(a+b+1)}
=
\frac{a}{a+b},

and this ratio is the beta mean.
(iv) By (i) and (iii),

\mathbb{E}(p\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=
\frac{\alpha+n}{\alpha+\beta+n+n\bar x}.

(v) Divide the numerator and denominator by n:

\mathbb{E}(p\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{1+\alpha/n}{1+\bar x+(\alpha+\beta)/n}.

For fixed prior parameters this approaches the data-based estimate 1/(1+\bar x). The log-likelihood is n\log p+F\log(1-p), and setting its derivative to zero gives \hat p=n/(n+F) when F>0. If the data come from the model at p_0, then \bar X_n\to(1-p_0)/p_0 and both estimates converge to p_0.
(vi) If \alpha,\beta\to 0, the posterior mean tends to n/(n+n\bar x)=1/(1+\bar x). The prior drops out.
This is a limit of proper beta priors, not substitution of \alpha=\beta=0 into a proper prior density. If F=0, the limiting estimate is the boundary value 1 and the limiting beta kernel is not a proper density; the posteriors for positive hyperparameters remain proper.
(vii) The effect is like \alpha prior successes and \beta prior failures, added to the n observed successes and \sum x_i observed failures.
An exact weighted-average expression makes that interpretation explicit:

\mathbb{E}(p\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\frac{\alpha+\beta}{\alpha+\beta+n+F}\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}
+\frac{n+F}{\alpha+\beta+n+F}\frac{n}{n+F}.

The beta prior mean and the observed success fraction are weighted by their respective total counts. These pseudo-counts describe the posterior-mean update; the powers in the prior density itself are \alpha-1 and \beta-1.





Book exercise: A geometric observation and a uniform prior

Question page: A geometric observation and a uniform prior

Let X be the number of coin tosses up to and including the first head. Thus

\mathbb{P}(X=x\mid\theta)=\theta(1-\theta)^{x-1},
\qquad x=1,2,\ldots,

where \theta is the probability of a head. Use the prior \theta\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1).

Find and identify p(\theta\mid x).
Discuss whether the prior was intended to be informative and whether it is conjugate.
Find the posterior mode.
Find \mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x).
Express the posterior mean as a convex combination of the prior mean and the maximum-likelihood estimate of \theta.
Give an equivalent-prior-observations interpretation, and state which pseudo-count convention you are using.







Worked answer (click to show)





Question. Let X be the number of coin tosses up to and including the first head. Thus

\mathbb{P}(X=x\mid\theta)=\theta(1-\theta)^{x-1},
\qquad x=1,2,\ldots,

where \theta is the probability of a head. Use the prior \theta\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1).

Find and identify p(\theta\mid x).
Discuss whether the prior was intended to be informative and whether it is conjugate.
Find the posterior mode.
Find \mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x).
Express the posterior mean as a convex combination of the prior mean and the maximum-likelihood estimate of \theta.
Give an equivalent-prior-observations interpretation, and state which pseudo-count convention you are using.

Solution.

The prior density is one on (0,1), so Bayes’ rule gives \begin{align*}
p(\theta\mid x)
&\propto \mathbb{P}(X=x\mid\theta)p(\theta)\\
&=\theta(1-\theta)^{x-1}\\
&=\theta^{2-1}(1-\theta)^{x-1}.
\end{align*} The normalising integral is


\int_0^1\theta(1-\theta)^{x-1}\,\mathrm{d}\theta
=B(2,x)
=\frac{\Gamma(2)\Gamma(x)}{\Gamma(x+2)}
=\frac{1}{x(x+1)}.

Consequently

p(\theta\mid x)=x(x+1)\theta(1-\theta)^{x-1},
\qquad
\boxed{\theta\mid x\sim\operatorname{Beta}(2,x)}.


The uniform prior was chosen to give equal density to equal-length intervals of \theta, so it was intended as a non-informative prior on this particular scale. That description is not invariant under a transformation of \theta. Since \operatorname{Unif}(0,1)=\operatorname{Beta}(1,1) and the Beta family is conjugate to this geometric likelihood, the prior is conjugate.
A \operatorname{Beta}(a,b) density has interior mode (a-1)/(a+b-2) when a,b>1. Here this gives


\operatorname{mode}(\theta\mid x)
=\frac{2-1}{2+x-2}=\boxed{\frac1x}.

For x=1 this is the boundary mode at one.

The posterior mean is


\boxed{\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)=\frac{2}{x+2}}.


The prior mean is 1/2. To obtain the maximum-likelihood estimator, differentiate the log likelihood: \begin{align*}
\ell(\theta)&=\log\theta+(x-1)\log(1-\theta),\\
\ell'(\theta)&=\frac1\theta-\frac{x-1}{1-\theta}.
\end{align*} Setting \ell'(\theta)=0 gives 1-\theta=(x-1)\theta, hence \widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}=1/x. With w=2/(x+2), \begin{align*}
w\mathbb{E}(\theta)+(1-w)\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}
&=\frac{2}{x+2}\frac12
   +\left(1-\frac{2}{x+2}\right)\frac1x\\
&=\frac1{x+2}+\frac{x}{x+2}\frac1x\\
&=\frac2{x+2}\\
&=\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x).
\end{align*}
Under the posterior-mean concentration convention, \operatorname{Beta}(1,1) has total prior weight two with one prior head and one prior tail: it behaves like one head among two prior tosses. Under the kernel exponent convention, however, the prior contributes \alpha-1=0 powers of \theta and \beta-1=0 powers of 1-\theta. These are two different pseudo-count conventions; the first is the one used in the requested linear combination.

title: Hierarchical Bayesian model
text:
Definition taught in Hierarchical Bayes, part of Bayesian statistics
Hierarchical Bayes is ordinary Bayes for data that arrive in related groups. Each group is allowed to have its own parameter, but those group parameters are modelled as draws from a common population distribution. This structure is useful whenever complete equality between groups is implausible, yet treating them as unrelated would discard real information.

title: Hierarchical Bayesian model
text:
Properties

Normal hierarchical shrinkage

Main article: Normal hierarchical shrinkage

The final term is constant in \theta_j. The remaining kernel is normal, so 
\theta_j\mid\overline y_j,\mu,\tau^2,\sigma^2
\sim\operatorname{N}\!\left(
   \frac{B_j}{A_j},\frac1{A_j}\right).
 Its variance is \begin{align*}
\frac1{A_j}
&=\frac1{n_j/\sigma^2+1/\tau^2}\\
&=\frac{\sigma^2\tau^2}{\sigma^2+n_j\tau^2},
\end{align*} and its mean can be rearranged without omitting any terms: \begin{align*}
\frac{B_j}{A_j}
&=\frac{n_j\overline y_j/\sigma^2+\mu/\tau^2}
         {n_j/\sigma^2+1/\tau^2}\\
&=\frac{n_j\tau^2\overline y_j+\sigma^2\mu}
         {\sigma^2+n_j\tau^2}\\
&=\frac{n_j\tau^2}{\sigma^2+n_j\tau^2}\overline y_j
   +\frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2+n_j\tau^2}\mu\\
&=w_j\overline y_j+(1-w_j)\mu,
\end{align*} where 
w_j=\frac{n_j\tau^2}{\sigma^2+n_j\tau^2},
\qquad
1-w_j=\frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2+n_j\tau^2}.
 Thus

\mathbb{E}(\theta_j\mid\overline y_j,\mu,\tau^2,\sigma^2)
=w_j\overline y_j+(1-w_j)\mu.



Marginal hyperposterior

Main article: Marginal hyperposterior

The binomial coefficient does not depend on (\alpha,\beta), so the hyperposterior kernel is 
\boxed{
p(\alpha,\beta\mid{\boldsymbol{y}})
\propto p(\alpha,\beta)
\prod_{j=1}^J
\frac{\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)
       \Gamma(y_j+\alpha)
       \Gamma(n_j-y_j+\beta)}
      {\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)
       \Gamma(n_j+\alpha+\beta)}}.
 This expression is available pointwise but is not a familiar normalised density.


Study-rate full conditional

Main article: Study-rate full conditional

Normalising gives 
\boxed{
\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,{\boldsymbol{y}}
\sim\operatorname{Beta}(y_j+\alpha,n_j-y_j+\beta)}.
 Conditional on the hyperparameters, the study rates are independent, so the joint conditional is the product of these J Beta densities.

title: Hierarchical Bayesian model
text:
Examples

TG5 cattle hierarchy

Worked example from Hierarchical Bayes

A cattle-genetics meta-analysis illustrates hierarchical Bayes. The search was not exhaustive, but it recovered 14 independent studies, many of them unpublished, which produced 19 standardised estimates of a TG5 genotype effect on beef marbling. The studies covered four breed groups and four marbling measurements, so treating every estimate as an exchangeable replicate would erase scientifically meaningful structure.
The original study-level analyses compared the CC and TT genotypes with CT, then divided each contrast by its residual standard deviation. A schematic version of the hierarchy is \begin{align*}
y_{ij}\mid\delta_i,w_{ij}
&\sim\operatorname{N}(\delta_i,w_{ij}^{-1}),\\
\delta_i\mid\mu_{b(i)},\tau_{\mathrm{study}}
&\sim\operatorname{N}(\mu_{b(i)},\tau_{\mathrm{study}}^{-1}),\\
\mu_b\mid\mu_0,\tau_{\mathrm{breed}}
&\sim\operatorname{N}(\mu_0,\tau_{\mathrm{breed}}^{-1}),\\
\mu_0&\sim\operatorname{N}(0,\xi^2),
\qquad \xi^2\text{ large}.
\end{align*} Here w_{ij} records the within-study information, \delta_i is a study effect, and \mu_b is a breed-group effect. Precision parameters were given diffuse scaled inverse-\chi^2-type priors in the applied analysis. The diagrammatic flow is

\text{overall effect}\longrightarrow
\text{breed effect}\longrightarrow
\text{study effect}\longrightarrow
\text{observed contrast}.

The hierarchy performs partial pooling at more than one level. The reported posterior for TT minus CC lay mostly above zero, with a smaller shift for one T copy, but the important methodological point is that every conclusion and every uncertainty interval came from one coherent multilevel fit. The example connects Bayesian random parameters to mixed models. The analysis was fitted in WinBUGS using a Gibbs sampler; the “GS” in the software name stands for Gibbs sampling.


Rat-tumour hierarchy

Worked example from Hierarchical Bayes

Tumour rates in female F344 rats supply a second hierarchical example. In a current control study, y=4 of n=14 rats developed one or more tumours over two years. A one-study model is

Y\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Bin}(14,\theta),
\qquad
\theta\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta),

giving

\theta\mid Y=4
\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+4,\beta+10).

The question is how to choose (\alpha,\beta) when 70 earlier control studies are available.
Let study j contribute y_j tumour-bearing rats from n_j animals. The hierarchical model is 
Y_j\mid\theta_j,n_j\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n_j,\theta_j),
\qquad
\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta
\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta),
\quad j=1,\ldots,J.
 Each study has its own rate, but all study rates are drawn from a common population distribution.


Practice set: Q23. Rat-tumour studies and hierarchical shrinkage

Question page: Q23. Rat-tumour studies and hierarchical shrinkage

[12 marks]
Suppose J related studies record tumour counts Y_j\mid\theta_j\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n_j,\theta_j),
\qquad j=1,\ldots,J, independently conditional on the study rates. Assume \theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta
\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta),
\qquad
\alpha\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1),\quad
\beta\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1), where the two hyperpriors are independent. Write \mathbf y=(y_1,\ldots,y_J); the sample sizes n_j are known. You may use B(a,b)=\int_0^1 t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}\,dt,
\qquad
f(\theta\mid a,b)=\frac{\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}}{B(a,b)}.
(a) [2 marks] Derive and identify the full conditional distribution \theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y.
(b) [3 marks] For this part only, fix \alpha=2 and \beta=8. Two studies report (y_1,n_1)=(4,10),\qquad (y_2,n_2)=(40,100). Calculate both posterior means. Although both observed proportions equal 0.4, explain why the posterior means differ and identify which study experiences stronger shrinkage.
(c) [4 marks] Return to unknown \alpha,\beta. Integrate out the study rates to derive:
(i) the marginal probability \mathbb{P}(Y_j=y_j\mid\alpha,\beta);
(ii) the marginal posterior kernel p(\alpha,\beta\mid\mathbf y).
Express your answers using Beta functions. Explain why the Beta prior’s normalising factor cannot be discarded when deriving this hyperparameter posterior.
(d) [3 marks] Explain how the full Bayesian model allows studies to share information. What uncertainty is omitted if \alpha,\beta are instead estimated from the data and then treated as known?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Study j has observed count y_j, known size n_j, and unknown rate \theta_j; \alpha,\beta>0 are shared hyperparameters. A \operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta) density is \theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1}/B(\alpha,\beta) on (0,1), where B(a,b)=\int_0^1u^{a-1}(1-u)^{b-1}\,du. \operatorname{Exp}(1) uses rate one. Partial pooling allows different study rates linked through a common population distribution.
Assumptions. The hierarchy assumes conditional independence of studies given their rates, and iid Beta rates given \alpha,\beta. Thus its joint density factors as p(\alpha)p(\beta)\prod_jp(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta)p(y_j\mid\theta_j), with independent rate-one exponential hyperpriors. Only in part (b) are the hyperparameters fixed at the supplied values.
(a) Full conditional for a study rate. Holding \alpha,\beta fixed, the factors involving \theta_j are \begin{aligned}
p(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y)
&\propto p(y_j\mid\theta_j)p(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta)\\
&\propto\theta_j^{y_j}(1-\theta_j)^{n_j-y_j}
\theta_j^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta_j)^{\beta-1}\\
&=\theta_j^{\alpha+y_j-1}(1-\theta_j)^{\beta+n_j-y_j-1}.
\end{aligned} Therefore \boxed{\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y
\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+y_j,\beta+n_j-y_j),\qquad 0<\theta_j<1.} Conditional on the hyperparameters and data, the study rates are independent. Other studies’ observations affect this study’s marginal posterior through learning \alpha,\beta, not through an additional factor in this full conditional.
(b) Posterior means and shrinkage. For fixed \alpha=2, \beta=8, the population mean is \frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}=\frac2{10}=0.2. The two posteriors are \theta_1\mid\alpha=2,\beta=8,\mathbf y\sim\operatorname{Beta}(6,14), \theta_2\mid\alpha=2,\beta=8,\mathbf y\sim\operatorname{Beta}(42,68). Thus their posterior means are \boxed{\mathbb{E}(\theta_1\mid\alpha=2,\beta=8,\mathbf y)=\frac6{20}=0.3,} \boxed{\mathbb{E}(\theta_2\mid\alpha=2,\beta=8,\mathbf y)=\frac{42}{110}
\approx0.3818.} To see the shrinkage explicitly, write \frac{\alpha+y_j}{\alpha+\beta+n_j}
=\frac{\alpha+\beta}{\alpha+\beta+n_j}
\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}
+\frac{n_j}{\alpha+\beta+n_j}\frac{y_j}{n_j}. Both sample proportions equal 0.4, but study 1 puts weight 10/20=1/2 on the population mean, whereas study 2 puts only 10/110=1/11 on it. The smaller study therefore experiences stronger shrinkage toward 0.2. The larger study has more information about its own rate, so its posterior mean remains closer to its observed proportion.
(c) Integrating out the study rates. For one study, retain the normalising factor of the Beta density: \begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(Y_j=y_j\mid\alpha,\beta)
&=\int_0^1 p(y_j\mid\theta_j)p(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta)\,d\theta_j\\
&=\binom{n_j}{y_j}\frac1{B(\alpha,\beta)}
\int_0^1\theta_j^{y_j+\alpha-1}
(1-\theta_j)^{n_j-y_j+\beta-1}\,d\theta_j\\
&=\boxed{\binom{n_j}{y_j}
\frac{B(\alpha+y_j,\beta+n_j-y_j)}{B(\alpha,\beta)}.}
\end{aligned} This is a Beta–Binomial marginal distribution, with y_j\in\{0,\ldots,n_j\}.
The independent rate-one exponential hyperpriors give p(\alpha,\beta)=e^{-\alpha-\beta},\qquad \alpha>0,\quad\beta>0. The studies remain independent conditional on the hyperparameters after their individual rates have been integrated out. Consequently, \begin{aligned}
p(\alpha,\beta\mid\mathbf y)
&\propto p(\alpha,\beta)
\prod_{j=1}^{J}\mathbb{P}(Y_j=y_j\mid\alpha,\beta)\\
&\propto e^{-(\alpha+\beta)}
\prod_{j=1}^{J}
\frac{B(\alpha+y_j,\beta+n_j-y_j)}{B(\alpha,\beta)}.
\end{aligned} Hence \boxed{
p(\alpha,\beta\mid\mathbf y)
\propto e^{-(\alpha+\beta)}B(\alpha,\beta)^{-J}
\prod_{j=1}^{J}B(\alpha+y_j,\beta+n_j-y_j),
\quad \alpha,\beta>0.
} The binomial coefficients can be dropped because the observed y_j and known n_j make them constant with respect to \alpha,\beta. However, 1/B(\alpha,\beta) depends on the hyperparameters, so it must remain. A factor constant in \theta_j need not be constant in \alpha,\beta.
(d) Sharing information and hyperparameter uncertainty. Every study contributes to the posterior for the common population parameters \alpha,\beta. That posterior then contributes to each study-specific posterior through p(\theta_j\mid\mathbf y)
=\int_0^\infty\!\int_0^\infty
p(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y)
p(\alpha,\beta\mid\mathbf y)\,d\alpha\,d\beta. This is partial pooling: study rates can differ, but they are connected by a population distribution learned from all the studies. The model does not force them to be identical, and it does not treat them as unrelated.
Replacing \alpha,\beta by fixed estimates is an empirical-Bayes plug-in analysis. It omits uncertainty about the population distribution’s parameters. For example, the law of total variance gives \begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(\theta_j\mid\mathbf y)
={}&\mathbb{E}\!\left[
\operatorname{Var}(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y)
\mid\mathbf y\right]\\
&+\operatorname{Var}\!\left[
\mathbb{E}(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y)
\mid\mathbf y\right].
\end{aligned} The second term represents variation in the conditional mean as the hyperparameters vary under their posterior. A plug-in calculation does not propagate this variation and can therefore give an overly precise account of uncertainty.

Key result. Conditional conjugacy does not eliminate uncertainty in the hyperparameters. Full Bayes learns their distribution and averages over it.






Final preparation: Question 17. Hierarchical Poisson model

Question page: Question 17. Hierarchical Poisson model

Suppose J factories manufacture components. Factory j produces n_j observations of the number of defective components per batch.
Assume

Y_{ij}\mid\theta_j\stackrel{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}\operatorname{Poisson}(\theta_j),
\qquad i=1,\ldots,n_j,\quad j=1,\ldots,J.

Here, \theta_j>0 represents the expected number of defects per batch in factory j.
Rather than modelling the factory rates independently, we assume

\theta_j\mid\lambda\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Gamma}(a,\lambda),

where a>0 is known and \lambda>0 is an unknown common hyperparameter.
Finally, assign the hyperprior

\lambda\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(c,d),

where c,d>0 are known.
All Gamma distributions use the shape–rate parameterisation:

f(x\mid a,b)=\frac{b^{a}}{\Gamma(a)}x^{a-1}e^{-bx},
\qquad x>0.

(a) Write down the joint density p({\boldsymbol{Y}},{\boldsymbol{\theta}},\lambda) up to proportionality in the unknown parameters.
(b) Derive the full conditional distribution p(\theta_j\mid\lambda,{\boldsymbol{Y}}) for each factory j. Identify its distribution and parameters.
(c) Derive the full conditional distribution p(\lambda\mid{\boldsymbol{\theta}},{\boldsymbol{Y}}). Identify its distribution and parameters.
(d) Using your results from (b) and (c), describe a Gibbs sampling algorithm targeting p({\boldsymbol{\theta}},\lambda\mid{\boldsymbol{Y}}).
(e) Explain how the hierarchical model allows observations from one factory to influence inference about another factory’s defect rate.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Y_{ij} is the count from batch i in factory j, \theta_j is that factory’s mean count, and \lambda is a shared unknown gamma rate. The known shape is a, while c,d define the shape–rate gamma hyperprior on \lambda. Write s_j=\sum_iY_{ij} and \bar Y_j=s_j/n_j. The conditional hierarchy is \lambda\longrightarrow{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\longrightarrow{\boldsymbol{Y}}.
(a) Let s_j=\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}Y_{ij}. Since {\boldsymbol{Y}}\perp\lambda\mid{\boldsymbol{\theta}},

p({\boldsymbol{Y}},{\boldsymbol{\theta}},\lambda)
=
p({\boldsymbol{Y}}\mid{\boldsymbol{\theta}})\,p({\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mid\lambda)\,p(\lambda).

For \theta_j>0 and \lambda>0,

\begin{aligned}
p({\boldsymbol{Y}}\mid{\boldsymbol{\theta}})
&=
\Biggl(\prod_{j=1}^{J}\prod_{i=1}^{n_j}\frac{1}{Y_{ij}!}\Biggr)
\prod_{j=1}^{J}e^{-n_j\theta_j}\theta_j^{s_j},\\
p({\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mid\lambda)
&=
\Biggl(\frac{\lambda^{a}}{\Gamma(a)}\Biggr)^{J}
\prod_{j=1}^{J}\theta_j^{a-1}e^{-\lambda\theta_j},\\
p(\lambda)
&=
\frac{d^{c}}{\Gamma(c)}\lambda^{c-1}e^{-d\lambda}.
\end{aligned}

The factors 1/Y_{ij}!, \Gamma(a)^{-J} and d^{c}/\Gamma(c) do not depend on ({\boldsymbol{\theta}},\lambda). Dropping them leaves

\boxed{
p({\boldsymbol{Y}},{\boldsymbol{\theta}},\lambda)
\propto
\lambda^{aJ+c-1}e^{-d\lambda}
\prod_{j=1}^{J}
\theta_j^{s_j+a-1}e^{-(n_j+\lambda)\theta_j}.
}

(b) In the kernel from (a), the factors containing \theta_j are

\theta_j^{s_j+a-1}e^{-(n_j+\lambda)\theta_j}
=
\theta_j^{(s_j+a)-1}e^{-(n_j+\lambda)\theta_j},
\qquad\theta_j>0.

No other rate appears. Here s_j+a>0 because a>0 and s_j\ge 0, and n_j+\lambda>0 because \lambda>0. This is a shape–rate gamma kernel, so

\boxed{
\theta_j\mid\lambda,{\boldsymbol{Y}}
\sim
\operatorname{Gamma}\!\left(a+\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}Y_{ij},\ n_j+\lambda\right).
}

(c) In the kernel from (a), the factors containing \lambda are

\lambda^{aJ+c-1}
\exp\Bigl(-\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{J}\theta_j\Bigr)e^{-d\lambda}
=
\lambda^{(aJ+c)-1}
\exp\Bigl(-\Bigl(d+\sum_{j=1}^{J}\theta_j\Bigr)\lambda\Bigr),

for \lambda>0. Given {\boldsymbol{\theta}}, the observations do not appear. The shape aJ+c>0, and the rate d+\sum_j\theta_j>0 because d>0. Thus

\boxed{
\lambda\mid{\boldsymbol{\theta}},{\boldsymbol{Y}}
\sim
\operatorname{Gamma}\!\left(c+aJ,\ d+\sum_{j=1}^{J}\theta_j\right).
}

(d) By (b) and (c), start from \lambda^{(0)}>0 and repeat the following sweep. For each j=1,\ldots,J, draw

\theta_j^{(t+1)}
\sim
\operatorname{Gamma}\!\left(a+\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}Y_{ij},\ n_j+\lambda^{(t)}\right),

using \lambda^{(t)} and factory j’s counts. By (b) this draw does not use the other rates, so the J draws may be made in any order from the same \lambda^{(t)}. Then draw

\lambda^{(t+1)}
\sim
\operatorname{Gamma}\!\left(c+aJ,\ d+\sum_{j=1}^{J}\theta_j^{(t+1)}\right),

using the updated rates and not \lambda^{(t)}.

\therefore
\text{these full-conditional updates are a Gibbs sampler targeting }
p({\boldsymbol{\theta}},\lambda\mid{\boldsymbol{Y}}).

(e) By (b), \theta_j depends on the other factories only through \lambda. Counts from factory k update \theta_k, and by (c) every rate enters the conditional distribution of the shared \lambda. That \lambda is the second parameter of \theta_j. This dependence through the common hyperparameter is borrowing strength: observations from one factory inform the defect rate at another.
At a fixed \lambda, the conditional posterior mean makes the shrinkage explicit:

\mathbb{E}(\theta_j\mid\lambda,{\boldsymbol{Y}})
=\frac{s_j+a}{n_j+\lambda}
=\frac{n_j}{n_j+\lambda}\bar Y_j
+\frac{\lambda}{n_j+\lambda}\frac a\lambda.

It averages factory j’s sample mean and the common prior mean a/\lambda. A small factory receives more pooling for a given \lambda. To obtain the marginal posterior mean, average this expression over p(\lambda\mid{\boldsymbol{Y}}); that hyperposterior is informed by every factory. Fixing \lambda externally would remove this particular route by which other factories’ observations influence \theta_j. Integrating a shared uncertain \lambda also makes the factory rates generally dependent in the joint posterior.

title: Interior Dirichlet mode
text:
Examples

Practice set: Q22. Advertising responses and Dirichlet inference

Question page: Q22. Advertising responses and Dirichlet inference

[10 marks]
An advertising campaign records responses from 60 independently sampled people:




Negative
Neutral
Positive




Male
8
6
16


Female
12
4
14



Let \mathbf p=(p_{MN},p_{MU},p_{MP},p_{FN},p_{FU},p_{FP}) be the six population cell probabilities, with U denoting a neutral response. Model the counts as multinomial and use \mathbf p\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(1,1,1,1,1,1). You may use the Dirichlet kernel f(\mathbf p)\propto\prod_{k=1}^{K}p_k^{\alpha_k-1},
\qquad p_k>0,\quad \sum_{k=1}^{K}p_k=1.
(a) [2 marks] Derive the posterior distribution of \mathbf p, stating its parameters and support.
(b) [2 marks] Find the posterior mean of p_{MP} and its component of the joint MAP estimate of \mathbf p. Explain why that MAP component equals the observed cell proportion here.
(c) [2 marks] Find the posterior predictive probability that one new person responds positively, regardless of gender. Express it as a posterior expectation before calculating it.
(d) [2 marks] For that new person, calculate \mathbb{P}(\text{positive response}\mid\text{female},\text{data}). Explain why this differs from \mathbb{P}(\text{female and positive response}\mid\text{data}).
(e) [2 marks] Are the six components of \mathbf p independent under the posterior? Explain using their constraint.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Let D be the observed table and \mathbf p its six population cell probabilities. The labels M,F denote male and female; N,U,P denote negative, neutral, and positive. With parameters a_1,\ldots,a_K>0, a Dirichlet density has kernel \prod_k p_k^{a_k-1} on the simplex p_k>0, \sum_kp_k=1. The joint MAP maximises this density over the entire simplex, not a one-component marginal density.
(a) Posterior distribution. Write the counts in the stated order as \mathbf x=(8,6,16,12,4,14),\qquad n=60. The multinomial likelihood is L(\mathbf p;D)=\frac{60!}{\prod_{k=1}^{6}x_k!}
\prod_{k=1}^{6}p_k^{x_k}
\propto\prod_{k=1}^{6}p_k^{x_k}. The Dirichlet prior has kernel \prod_k p_k^{1-1}=1 on the simplex. Consequently, p(\mathbf p\mid D)\propto
\prod_{k=1}^{6}p_k^{x_k+1-1}, which is the Dirichlet kernel with parameters x_k+1. Thus \boxed{\mathbf p\mid D\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(9,7,17,13,5,15).} Its density is supported on the simplex p_k>0, \sum_{k=1}^6p_k=1; the boundary has probability zero. The posterior concentration is A=9+7+17+13+5+15=66.
(b) Posterior mean and MAP. For a Dirichlet vector with parameters a_1,\ldots,a_K and A=\sum_k a_k, \mathbb{E}(p_k)=\frac{a_k}{A},\qquad
\widehat p_{k,\mathrm{MAP}}=\frac{a_k-1}{A-K}
\quad\text{when every }a_k>1. Here every posterior parameter exceeds one, so \boxed{\mathbb{E}(p_{MP}\mid D)=\frac{17}{66}\approx0.2576,}
\qquad
\boxed{\widehat p_{MP,\mathrm{MAP}}=
\frac{17-1}{66-6}=\frac{16}{60}\approx0.2667.} The MAP component is taken from the mode of the joint posterior for \mathbf p. Since the prior density is constant on the simplex, maximising the posterior is equivalent to maximising the likelihood, giving the observed cell proportions.
(c) Predicting a positive response. Conditional on \mathbf p, the probability of a positive response is p_{MP}+p_{FP}. Averaging over posterior uncertainty gives \begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(\text{positive}\mid D)
&=\int (p_{MP}+p_{FP})p(\mathbf p\mid D)\,d\mathbf p\\
&=\mathbb{E}(p_{MP}+p_{FP}\mid D)\\
&=\frac{17}{66}+\frac{15}{66}
=\boxed{\frac{16}{33}\approx0.4848.}
\end{aligned} Prediction uses posterior averaging, not substitution of the MAP estimate.
(d) Conditioning on the new person being female. First calculate the two relevant posterior predictive probabilities: \mathbb{P}(\text{female and positive}\mid D)=\mathbb{E}(p_{FP}\mid D)=\frac{15}{66}, \mathbb{P}(\text{female}\mid D)
=\mathbb{E}(p_{FN}+p_{FU}+p_{FP}\mid D)
=\frac{13+5+15}{66}=\frac{33}{66}. By the definition of conditional probability, \boxed{
\mathbb{P}(\text{positive}\mid\text{female},D)
=\frac{15/66}{33/66}=\frac5{11}\approx0.4545.
} By contrast, the joint probability is \boxed{\mathbb{P}(\text{female and positive}\mid D)
=\frac{15}{66}=\frac5{22}\approx0.2273.} The conditional probability restricts attention to the female row; the joint probability refers to both events occurring for a person sampled from the whole population.
(e) Posterior dependence. No. The probabilities must satisfy \sum_k p_k=1 exactly. Increasing one component leaves less total probability for the others. More formally, if they were independent, then 0=\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^{6}p_k\,\middle|\,D\right)
=\sum_{k=1}^{6}\operatorname{Var}(p_k\mid D)>0, a contradiction, since each component has positive posterior variance. Indeed, distinct Dirichlet components have \operatorname{Cov}(p_j,p_k\mid D)
=-\frac{a_ja_k}{A^2(A+1)}<0,\qquad j\ne k.

Key result. Add counts to the Dirichlet parameters; average probabilities for prediction; and distinguish a joint cell probability from a probability conditional on a row.

title: Marginal hyperposterior
text:
Proposition taught in Hierarchical Bayes, part of Bayesian statistics
The binomial coefficient does not depend on (\alpha,\beta), so the hyperposterior kernel is 
\boxed{
p(\alpha,\beta\mid{\boldsymbol{y}})
\propto p(\alpha,\beta)
\prod_{j=1}^J
\frac{\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)
       \Gamma(y_j+\alpha)
       \Gamma(n_j-y_j+\beta)}
      {\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)
       \Gamma(n_j+\alpha+\beta)}}.
 This expression is available pointwise but is not a familiar normalised density.

Definition taught in Marginal models, and two responses at once, part of Correlated data
A marginal model for clustered responses has three parts.

title: Marginal model
text:
Definition

A mean, g(\mathrm{E}(Y_{ji}\mid {\boldsymbol{X}}_{ji}))={\boldsymbol{X}}_{ji}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}, the same link and the same linear predictor as for independent data.
A variance, \mathrm{Var}(Y_{ji}\mid {\boldsymbol{X}}_{ji})=\phi V(\mu_{ji}), depending on the covariates only through the mean.
A working association within a cluster, allowed to depend on the two means and on further association parameters.

title: Marginal model
text:
Examples

Concept check: C38. Generalised estimating equations

Question page: C38. Generalised estimating equations

What are generalised estimating equations, and what mean-model parameters do they estimate?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. GEE are estimating equations for the coefficients of a marginal (population-average) mean model for correlated responses, constructed using derivatives of the mean and a working within-cluster covariance. They require no full joint response distribution, but assume independent clusters and, for consistency under standard regularity conditions, a correctly specified marginal mean.





Concept check: C40. Sandwich robustness

Question page: C40. Sandwich robustness

What misspecification can the GEE sandwich covariance estimator tolerate? Does it repair an incorrect mean model?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. The sandwich estimator estimates the sampling covariance of the GEE coefficient estimator using empirical cluster residual variation, allowing the working covariance to be misspecified. It does not repair an incorrect mean model: its usual robustness is asymptotic with many independent clusters, a correct marginal mean, valid estimating equations and regularity conditions, not a guarantee for small samples or informative missingness.

title: Marginal variance posterior
Marginal variance posterior
text:
Examples

Practice set: Q24. Bayesian regression and prediction

Question page: Q24. Bayesian regression and prediction

[12 marks]
Consider the regression model Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad
\varepsilon_i\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2), with reference prior p(\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma^2)\propto1/\sigma^2 for (\beta_0,\beta_1)\in\mathbb{R}^2 and \sigma^2>0. For n=10 observations, the design matrix has rows (1,x_i), and \widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
(X^\top X)^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1/10&0\\0&1/40\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \operatorname{SSE}=16. The observed predictor values range from -3 to 3.
You may use the standard regression posterior formulas under this prior. Use the inverse-Gamma convention f(v)\propto v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v}. Write t_\nu(m,s) for a Student-t distribution with location m and scale s, and use t_{0.975,8}=2.306.
(a) [2 marks] State the marginal posterior distribution of \sigma^2 and calculate \mathbb{E}(\sigma^2\mid\mathbf y,X).
(b) [3 marks] State the marginal posterior distribution of the slope \beta_1, and calculate its equal-tailed 95% credible interval.
(c) [4 marks] At x_*=0, derive the posterior distributions and equal-tailed 95% intervals for:
(i) the unknown mean response \mu_*=\beta_0+\beta_1x_*;
(ii) a new observation \widetilde Y.
Explain precisely why the second interval is wider.
(d) [3 marks] Calculate h(x_*)=(1,x_*)(X^\top X)^{-1}(1,x_*)^\top at x_*=0 and x_*=4. Compare the posterior predictive scales at these points and explain how the calculation reflects uncertainty from extrapolation.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write D=(\mathbf y,X), v=\sigma^2, and \operatorname{SSE}=\|\mathbf y-X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\|^2. The inverse-Gamma kernel is v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v} on v>0. t_\nu(m,s) denotes location m, scale s, and \nu degrees of freedom: (T-m)/s\sim t_\nu. A scale is not a variance; t_{q,\nu} denotes the q quantile of standard t_\nu.
Assumptions. Use independent Normal errors, fixed covariates, full column rank X, n>p, positive SSE, and the reference prior p(\boldsymbol\beta,v)\propto1/v with respect to d\boldsymbol\beta\,dv. These rank and residual conditions ensure a proper posterior despite the improper prior.
There are p=2 regression coefficients, including the intercept. Define \nu=n-p=8,\qquad
s^2=\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}{n-p}=\frac{16}{8}=2,
\qquad C=(X^\top X)^{-1}. Here s^2 is the residual variance estimate; it is not the posterior mean of \sigma^2.
Why the regression posterior has this form. The likelihood times the reference prior gives p(\boldsymbol\beta,v\mid D)
\propto v^{-n/2-1}
\exp\{-\|\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta\|^2/(2v)\},
\qquad v=\sigma^2>0. Expand about the least-squares estimate. The cross term vanishes because X^\top(\mathbf y-X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})=\mathbf0, giving \|\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta\|^2
=\operatorname{SSE}
+(\boldsymbol\beta-\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})^\top
X^\top X(\boldsymbol\beta-\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}). The second term is a Normal quadratic. At fixed v it identifies \boldsymbol\beta\mid v,D\sim
N_p(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},vC). Its unnormalised exponential integrates to (2\pi v)^{p/2}|X^\top X|^{-1/2}, which explains the v^{p/2} factor in the variance marginal below.
(a) Marginal variance posterior. Under the stated reference prior, \sigma^2\mid D\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\left(\frac{n-p}{2},
\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}2\right). Thus \boxed{\sigma^2\mid D\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(4,8),\qquad\sigma^2>0.} An \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b) variable has mean b/(a-1) when a>1, so \boxed{\mathbb{E}(\sigma^2\mid D)=\frac8{4-1}=\frac83\approx2.6667.} For completeness, integrating the coefficient kernel out of the joint posterior contributes a factor (\sigma^2)^{p/2}. Therefore p(\sigma^2\mid D)
\propto (\sigma^2)^{-(n/2+1)}(\sigma^2)^{p/2}
\exp\!\left(-\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}{2\sigma^2}\right)
=(\sigma^2)^{-5}e^{-8/\sigma^2}, confirming the shape 4, not n/2=5.
(b) Slope posterior and credible interval. The conditional coefficient posterior is \boldsymbol\beta\mid\sigma^2,D
\sim N_2(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},\sigma^2 C). The slope entry of C is 1/40, so \beta_1\mid\sigma^2,D\sim N\!\left(2,\frac{\sigma^2}{40}\right). Integrating over \sigma^2\mid D gives \boxed{\beta_1\mid D\sim t_8\!\left(2,\sqrt{\frac2{40}}\right)
=t_8(2,\sqrt{0.05}).} Equivalently, (\beta_1-2)/\sqrt{0.05}\mid D\sim t_8. The equal-tailed 95% credible interval is therefore 2\pm2.306\sqrt{0.05}=2\pm0.5156,
\qquad\boxed{(1.484,\,2.516).} The second argument of t_8 is a scale, not a variance. There is no additional division by \sqrt n: sample-size information is already in C.
(c) Mean response versus a new observation at x_*=0. For a general predictor value, set \mathbf z_*=(1,x_*)^\top and write m_*=\mathbf z_*^\top\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},
\qquad h(x_*)=\mathbf z_*^\top C\mathbf z_*. The linear-transformation rule for a normal vector gives \mu_*\mid\sigma^2,D
\sim N\bigl(m_*,\sigma^2 h(x_*)\bigr). For a new response \widetilde Y=\mu_*+\widetilde\varepsilon, the new error is independent of the coefficient uncertainty conditional on \sigma^2,D, and has variance \sigma^2. Thus \widetilde Y\mid\sigma^2,D,x_*
\sim N\bigl(m_*,\sigma^2\{1+h(x_*)\}\bigr). Integrating over the inverse-Gamma variance posterior gives \mu_*\mid D\sim t_8\bigl(m_*,s\sqrt{h(x_*)}\bigr), \widetilde Y\mid D,x_*\sim t_8\bigl(m_*,s\sqrt{1+h(x_*)}\bigr). At x_*=0, m_*=(1,0)\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}=1,
\qquad h(0)=\frac1{10}. Therefore the unknown mean response has posterior \boxed{\mu_*\mid D\sim t_8(1,\sqrt{0.2}),} with equal-tailed 95% credible interval 1\pm2.306\sqrt{0.2}=1\pm1.0313,
\qquad\boxed{(-0.031,\,2.031).} The new observation has posterior predictive distribution \boxed{\widetilde Y\mid D,x_*=0\sim t_8(1,\sqrt{2.2}),} with equal-tailed 95% predictive interval 1\pm2.306\sqrt{2.2}=1\pm3.4204,
\qquad\boxed{(-2.420,\,4.420).} Both intervals have the same centre and use the same t_8 quantile. The predictive interval is wider because a new observation includes both uncertainty about the regression mean and fresh observational noise. That additional noise produces the extra 1 in 1+h(x_*).
(d) Extrapolation and predictive scale. Using the supplied diagonal matrix, \begin{aligned}
h(x_*)&=(1,x_*)
\begin{pmatrix}1/10&0\\0&1/40\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}1\\x_*\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\frac1{10}+\frac{x_*^2}{40}.
\end{aligned} Hence \boxed{h(0)=0.1,\qquad h(4)=0.1+\frac{16}{40}=0.5.} The corresponding predictive scales are \boxed{s_{\mathrm{pred}}(0)=\sqrt{2(1+0.1)}=\sqrt{2.2}\approx1.4832,} \boxed{s_{\mathrm{pred}}(4)=\sqrt{2(1+0.5)}=\sqrt3\approx1.7321.} At x_*=4, the predicted centre is 1+2(4)=9, so the predictive distribution is t_8(9,\sqrt3). Its interval is wider than at x_*=0 because it has the same degrees of freedom but a larger scale.
The value 4 lies outside the observed range [-3,3]. Uncertainty about the slope has a greater effect on the fitted mean farther from the centred design, increasing h(x_*). The future-error contribution is unchanged; the increased width comes from greater parameter uncertainty in the prediction. This calculation assumes the linear model remains appropriate beyond the observed range; it does not account for possible failure of that model there.

Key result. The mean-response scale is s\sqrt h; the new-observation scale is s\sqrt{1+h}. The extra 1 represents new observational noise, while h measures uncertainty about the fitted mean.

title: Mean and variance of an exponential family
text:
Theorem taught in Introduction to generalised linear models, part of Generalised linear models
If Y has density or mass function Equation (7) in Introduction to generalised linear models, and if differentiation in \theta may be passed under the integral or the sum, then 
\mathrm{E}(Y)=-c'(\theta),
\qquad
\mathrm{Var}(Y)=-c''(\theta)\,e(\phi).

title: Mean and variance of an exponential family
text:
Examples

Practice set: Q45. Gamma regression from the exponential-family form

Question page: Q45. Gamma regression from the exponential-family form

[12 marks]
Independent positive responses have density f(y_i\mid\mu_i,k)
=\frac{k^k}{\Gamma(k)\mu_i^k}
y_i^{k-1}\exp\left(-\frac{ky_i}{\mu_i}\right),
\qquad y_i>0, where \mu_i>0 and k>0.
(a) Express the density in the course form f(y;\theta,\phi)
        =\exp\left\{
        \frac{a(y)b(\theta)+c(\theta)}{e(\phi)}+d(y;\phi)
        \right\}, taking \theta=\mu and \phi=1/k. Identify all five functions. [4 marks]
(b) Find \mathbb{E}(Y_i) and \operatorname{Var}(Y_i). [2 marks]
(c) Under the model \log\mu_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i, interpret \beta_1 and derive the ratio of expected responses at x+1 and x. [2 marks]
(d) Derive the score vector for \boldsymbol\beta, treating k as known. [3 marks]
(e) Explain why this model does not assert that \log Y_i is Normally distributed. [1 mark]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. A Gamma variable with shape k and rate k/\mu has mean \mu and variance \mu^2/k; set \phi=1/k. In the course’s exponential-family form, b(\theta) is the coefficient paired with the statistic a(y) after division by e(\phi). For regression, \mathbf X_i=(1,x_i)^\top, \boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_0,\beta_1)^\top, and \mu_i=e^{\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta}. Responses are independent and covariates fixed; the score calculation holds k>0 known.
(a) Exponential-family representation. For one observation, taking logarithms gives \log f(y\mid\mu,k)
=k\log k-\log\Gamma(k)-k\log\mu+(k-1)\log y-\frac{ky}{\mu}. With \theta=\mu and \phi=1/k, rearrange this as \log f(y;\theta,\phi)
=\frac{-y/\theta-\log\theta}{\phi}
+\frac1\phi\log\frac1\phi-\log\Gamma\!\left(\frac1\phi\right)
+\left(\frac1\phi-1\right)\log y. One valid identification of the five functions is \boxed{
a(y)=y,\qquad b(\theta)=-\frac1\theta,\qquad
c(\theta)=-\log\theta,\qquad e(\phi)=\phi,
} \boxed{
d(y;\phi)=\frac1\phi\log\frac1\phi
-\log\Gamma\!\left(\frac1\phi\right)
+\left(\frac1\phi-1\right)\log y.
} The support is y>0, with \theta>0 and \phi>0.
(b) Mean and variance. The given density is Gamma with shape k and rate k/\mu_i. Therefore \boxed{\mathbb{E}(Y_i)=\frac{k}{k/\mu_i}=\mu_i,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\frac{k}{(k/\mu_i)^2}
=\frac{\mu_i^2}{k}=\phi\mu_i^2.}
(c) Interpretation of the coefficient. The log link gives \mu(x)=e^{\beta_0+\beta_1x}, so \boxed{\frac{\mathbb{E}(Y\mid x+1)}{\mathbb{E}(Y\mid x)}
=\frac{e^{\beta_0+\beta_1(x+1)}}{e^{\beta_0+\beta_1x}}
=e^{\beta_1}.} Thus a one-unit increase in x multiplies the expected response by e^{\beta_1}, corresponding to a percentage change 100(e^{\beta_1}-1)\%. The coefficient \beta_1 itself is the change in the log of the mean, not an additive change in the response.
(d) Score vector. Let \mathbf X_i=(1,x_i)^\top and \boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_0,\beta_1)^\top, so that \mu_i=e^{\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta}. Treating k as known, \ell(\boldsymbol\beta)
=-k\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\log\mu_i+\frac{y_i}{\mu_i}\right)+C, where C does not depend on \boldsymbol\beta. Differentiate each summand with respect to its mean and apply the chain rule: \frac{\partial\ell_i}{\partial\mu_i}
=-\frac{k}{\mu_i}+\frac{ky_i}{\mu_i^2},
\qquad
\frac{\partial\mu_i}{\partial\boldsymbol\beta}=\mu_i\mathbf X_i. It follows that \begin{aligned}
S(\boldsymbol\beta)
&=\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(-\frac{k}{\mu_i}+\frac{ky_i}{\mu_i^2}\right)\mu_i\mathbf X_i\\
&=\boxed{k\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf X_i\left(\frac{y_i}{\mu_i}-1\right)}.
\end{aligned} In components, S(\boldsymbol\beta)
=k\begin{pmatrix}
\sum_i(y_i/\mu_i-1)\\[3pt]
\sum_i x_i(y_i/\mu_i-1)
\end{pmatrix}.
(e) Why this is not a lognormal model. The model specifies a Gamma distribution for Y_i and a linear predictor for \log\mu_i=\log\mathbb{E}(Y_i). It does not specify a Normal distribution for \log Y_i. Applying a log link to a conditional mean is not the same operation as transforming the response and assuming Normal errors.

Key result. Keep the response distribution and the link separate: Gamma response plus log link does not mean lognormal response.

title: Metropolis–Hastings update
Metropolis–Hastings update
text:
Properties

Metropolis–Hastings invariance

Main article: Metropolis–Hastings invariance

The Metropolis–Hastings transition defined by Equation (5) in Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings satisfies detailed balance with respect to \pi. Consequently, \pi is stationary.


Warm-up is not a convergence proof

Main article: Warm-up is not a convergence proof

The chain should be initialised in a plausible region when one is available. A start many standard deviations from the typical set can require a long time to return, while a start at the mean of a separated mixture can lie in a low-density gap. Multiple dispersed chains help reveal failure to explore all modes; they do not repair it automatically.
Discarding early draws is called warm-up or burn-in. It limits dependence on the chosen initial state, but it is not a proof of convergence. Strong posterior correlation produces staircase-like Gibbs paths and high autocorrelation. Separated modes are harder still because a coordinate-wise move may have to cross a low-density barrier.
Thinning by retaining every kth draw reduces storage and visible serial dependence, but usually throws away usable information. Unless storage or an expensive downstream calculation is the constraint, retain all post-warm-up draws and quantify their effective sample size. Posterior means, probabilities, and equal-tailed intervals are computed from those draws; a continuous MAP is found by optimisation, not by asking which simulated value occurred most often.

title: Metropolis–Hastings update
text:
Examples

Practice set: Q5. Random-walk Metropolis-Hastings

Question page: Q5. Random-walk Metropolis-Hastings

Let the target density be \pi(x)\propto x^2e^{-x},
  \qquad x>0. We wish to sample from \pi using a random-walk Metropolis-Hastings algorithm with proposal Y\mid X^{(t-1)}=x\sim\mathcal{N}(x,\sigma^2), where \sigma>0 is fixed.
(a) [3 marks] Show that the Metropolis-Hastings acceptance probability is \alpha(x,y)
          =
          \begin{cases}
            \displaystyle
            \min\left\{
              \left(\frac{y}{x}\right)^2 e^{-(y-x)},1
            \right\}, & y>0,\\[1.2em]
            0, & y\leq0.
          \end{cases} Explain why the proposal-density terms cancel.
(b) [2 marks] Calculate the acceptance probability for each proposed move. You may leave your answers in exact exponential form.
1. Current state x=2, proposed state y=3.
2. Current state x=3, proposed state y=2.
(c) [3 marks] Write pseudocode for a random-walk Metropolis-Hastings sampler generating T observations from the target distribution. Begin from a valid initial value x^{(0)}>0.
(d) [1 mark] Explain why the unknown normalising constant of \pi(x) is not required.
(e) [2 marks] Are the sampled values X^{(1)},X^{(2)},\ldots,X^{(T)} independent? Briefly explain.
(f) [2 marks] Explain what is likely to happen if:
1. \sigma is extremely small;
2. \sigma is extremely large.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write q(y\mid x) for the density of a proposal y from current state x, and \alpha(x,y) for its acceptance probability. The target kernel is x^2e^{-x} on x>0 and zero elsewhere. N(x,\sigma^2) uses variance \sigma^2, held fixed and positive throughout the run; start with x^{(0)}>0.
As a recognition check, \pi(x)\propto x^{3-1}e^{-1\cdot x},
  \qquad x>0, is the kernel of a \operatorname{Gamma}(3,1) distribution under the shape-rate convention. The exercise nevertheless asks us to construct a Metropolis-Hastings sampler for this target.

(a) Acceptance probability
For a proposal density q(y\mid x), the Metropolis-Hastings acceptance probability is \alpha(x,y)
  =\min\left\{
    \frac{\pi(y)q(x\mid y)}{\pi(x)q(y\mid x)},1
  \right\}. The normal random-walk proposal is symmetric because q(y\mid x)
  =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}
   \exp\left[-\frac{(y-x)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right]
  =q(x\mid y). The proposal-density terms therefore cancel. If y>0, the target-density ratio is \frac{\pi(y)}{\pi(x)}
  =\frac{y^2e^{-y}}{x^2e^{-x}}
  =\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)^2e^{-(y-x)}. If y\leq0, then y is outside the support of the target and the proposal must be rejected. Hence \boxed{
    \alpha(x,y)
    =
    \begin{cases}
      \displaystyle
      \min\left\{
        \left(\frac{y}{x}\right)^2e^{-(y-x)},1
      \right\}, & y>0,\\[1.2em]
      0, & y\leq0.
    \end{cases}
  }


(b) Acceptance probabilities for the two moves
1. For x=2 and y=3, \alpha(2,3)
          =\min\left\{\left(\frac32\right)^2e^{-1},1\right\}
          =\boxed{\frac{9}{4e}\approx0.828}, since 9/(4e)<1. Thus the move is accepted with probability about 82.8\%.
2. For x=3 and y=2, \alpha(3,2)
          =\min\left\{\left(\frac23\right)^2e,1\right\}
          =\min\left\{\frac{4e}{9},1\right\}
          =\boxed{1}, since 4e/9>1. This move goes to a point of higher target density and is always accepted.
This illustrates the basic Metropolis rule: moves to higher target density are accepted automatically, while moves to lower target density may still be accepted with positive probability.


(c) Random-walk Metropolis-Hastings pseudocode
Choose an initial state x^{(0)}>0. For t=1,2,\ldots,T:
1. Generate a proposal Y\sim\mathcal{N}\bigl(x^{(t-1)},\sigma^2\bigr).
2. Calculate a=
          \begin{cases}
            \displaystyle
            \min\left\{
              \left(\frac{Y}{x^{(t-1)}}\right)^2
              e^{-(Y-x^{(t-1)})},1
            \right\}, & Y>0,\\[1.2em]
            0, & Y\leq0.
          \end{cases}
3. Independently generate U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1).
4. Set X^{(t)}=
          \begin{cases}
            Y, & U\leq a,\\
            X^{(t-1)}, & U>a.
          \end{cases}
5. Store X^{(t)}.
A rejection does not mean that nothing is recorded: the chain stores the current value again, so X^{(t)}=X^{(t-1)}. After a suitable burn-in, the stored values are approximately distributed according to \pi.


(d) Unknown normalising constant
If \pi(x)=\widetilde{\pi}(x)/C, then \frac{\pi(y)}{\pi(x)}
  =\frac{\widetilde{\pi}(y)/C}{\widetilde{\pi}(x)/C}
  =\frac{\widetilde{\pi}(y)}{\widetilde{\pi}(x)}. Thus the same unknown constant appears in the numerator and denominator and cancels from the acceptance ratio. Metropolis-Hastings therefore requires the target only up to proportionality, which is especially useful for posterior distributions with an intractable marginal likelihood.


(e) Independence of the sampled values
No. Each proposal is generated from the previous state, and a rejected move gives X^{(t)}=X^{(t-1)}. The samples therefore form a Markov chain and are generally serially dependent, even after the chain has reached equilibrium. At equilibrium, each X^{(t)} has marginal distribution \pi, but having the correct marginal distribution does not imply independence.


(f) Effect of the proposal scale
1. If \sigma is extremely small, proposals stay close to the current state and are usually accepted. However, the chain moves slowly through the target distribution, producing high autocorrelation and poor mixing.
2. If \sigma is extremely large, many proposals fall outside the support or in regions of very low target density. The acceptance rate becomes small, so the chain often repeats its current value and again mixes poorly.






Practice set: Q10. Metropolis-Hastings with an asymmetric-proposal extension

Question page: Q10. Metropolis-Hastings with an asymmetric-proposal extension

A posterior density is known up to a normalising constant: p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto\theta^2e^{-\theta},
  \qquad \theta>0. From the current state \theta^{(t)}>0, propose \theta^*=\theta^{(t)}+\varepsilon,
  \qquad
  \varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,s^2), where s>0 is fixed.
(a) Derive the acceptance probability, including the case \theta^*\leq0. Explain why the unknown normalising constant is not needed. [3 marks]
(b) Give pseudocode for one iteration, including the acceptance decision and the next state after rejection. [3 marks]
(c) One run uses a very small s and accepts almost every proposal. Another uses a very large s and accepts very few. Explain why either run may be inefficient. [2 marks]
(d) If the proposal density were not symmetric, what additional factor would be required in the acceptance ratio? Define its numerator and denominator. [2 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. The target is proportional to \theta^2e^{-\theta} on \theta>0 and is zero otherwise. Let q(\theta^*\mid\theta) be the proposal density, \alpha(\theta,\theta^*) the acceptance probability, and (t) the iteration index. The proposal N(\theta,s^2) has variance s^2>0, fixed across states and iterations; the current state must lie in the target support.
The target density has kernel \pi(\theta)\propto \theta^2e^{-\theta},
\qquad \theta>0.

(a) Acceptance probability
For a random-walk proposal \theta^*\mid\theta^{(t)}\sim N\left(\theta^{(t)},s^2\right), the proposal is symmetric: q(\theta^*\mid\theta^{(t)})
=q(\theta^{(t)}\mid\theta^*). Consequently, the proposal-density terms cancel from the Metropolis–Hastings ratio. If \theta^*>0, \begin{aligned}
\alpha\left(\theta^{(t)},\theta^*\right)
&=
\min\left\{
\frac{\pi(\theta^*)}{\pi(\theta^{(t)})},1
\right\}\\
&=
\boxed{
\min\left\{
\left(\frac{\theta^*}{\theta^{(t)}}\right)^2
\exp\left[-\left(\theta^*-\theta^{(t)}\right)\right],
1
\right\}.
}
\end{aligned} If \theta^*\leq 0, then \pi(\theta^*)=0, so the proposal is rejected and \alpha=0.


(b) Normalising constant
The unknown normalising constant appears in both the numerator and denominator of the target-density ratio and therefore cancels. Only the target kernel is needed.


(c) One sampler iteration
One iteration of the algorithm is:
1. Generate a proposal \theta^*\sim N\left(\theta^{(t)},s^2\right).
2. Calculate \alpha(\theta^{(t)},\theta^*) as above.
3. Generate U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1).
4. Set \theta^{(t+1)}=
    \begin{cases}
    \theta^*, & U\leq\alpha(\theta^{(t)},\theta^*),\\
    \theta^{(t)}, & U>\alpha(\theta^{(t)},\theta^*).
    \end{cases}


(d) Proposal scale
If s is extremely small, proposals remain close to the current state and the acceptance rate will usually be high. However, the chain moves only in small steps, producing high autocorrelation and slow exploration.
If s is extremely large, many proposals will be negative or will fall in regions where the target density is very small. Most will be rejected, so the chain will repeatedly remain at the same state and again mix slowly.


(e) Asymmetric proposals
For an asymmetric proposal, the proposal terms do not cancel. The acceptance probability becomes \boxed{
\alpha(\theta,\theta^*)
=
\min\left\{
\frac{\pi(\theta^*)q(\theta\mid\theta^*)}
{\pi(\theta)q(\theta^*\mid\theta)},
1
\right\}.
} The additional factor is therefore \boxed{
\frac{q(\theta\mid\theta^*)}{q(\theta^*\mid\theta)},
} that is, the reverse-proposal density divided by the forward-proposal density.






Book exercise: Metropolis–Hastings for the logit-normal posterior

Question page: Metropolis–Hastings for the logit-normal posterior

Use the posterior kernel in the logit-normal prior exercise.

For n=40 and x=16, use a Metropolis–Hastings algorithm to retain 10{,}000 draws after a burn-in of 1{,}000. Plot a kernel-density estimate and describe it.
Estimate the posterior mean, compare it with the prior mean, and explain how the data have changed the distribution.
Estimate and interpret an equal-tailed 95\% credible interval.
Repeat the numerical summaries for n=400 and x=160. Explain why ten times as much data changes the spread far more than the centre.







Worked answer (click to show)





Question. For 0<\theta<1, take the posterior target

\pi(\theta\mid x,n)\propto
\theta^{x-1}(1-\theta)^{n-x-1}
\exp\!\left[-\frac12\{\operatorname{logit}(\theta)-1\}^2\right].


For n=40 and x=16, use a Metropolis–Hastings algorithm to retain 10{,}000 draws after a burn-in of 1{,}000. Plot a kernel-density estimate and describe it.
Estimate the posterior mean, compare it with the prior mean, and explain how the data have changed the distribution.
Estimate and interpret an equal-tailed 95\% credible interval.
Repeat the numerical summaries for n=400 and x=160. Explain why ten times as much data changes the spread far more than the centre.

Solution. For numerical stability define the log of the unnormalised target by

\ell(\theta;x,n)
=(x-1)\log\theta+(n-x-1)\log(1-\theta)
-\frac12\{\operatorname{logit}(\theta)-1\}^2.

Use an independent \operatorname{Beta}(A,B) proposal with density g. Since this is not a random walk, the proposal terms do not cancel. For current state \theta and proposal y, \begin{align*}
r(\theta,y)
&=\frac{\pi(y)g(\theta)}{\pi(\theta)g(y)},\\
\log r(\theta,y)
&=\ell(y;x,n)-\ell(\theta;x,n)
   +\log g(\theta)-\log g(y),\\
a(\theta,y)&=\min\{1,r(\theta,y)\}.
\end{align*} The following implementation uses \operatorname{Beta}(4,6) for (x,n)=(16,40) and \operatorname{Beta}(40,60) for (160,400).
log_posterior <- function(theta, x, n) {
  ifelse(theta <= 0 | theta >= 1, -Inf,
         (x - 1) * log(theta) +
         (n - x - 1) * log1p(-theta) -
         0.5 * (qlogis(theta) - 1)^2)
}
independent_mh <- function(x, n, A, B, keep = 10000, burn = 1000) {
  total <- keep + burn
  out <- numeric(total)
  out[1] <- x / n
  for (t in 2:total) {
    proposed <- rbeta(1, A, B)
    log_ratio <-
      log_posterior(proposed, x, n) -
      log_posterior(out[t - 1], x, n) +
      dbeta(out[t - 1], A, B, log = TRUE) -
      dbeta(proposed, A, B, log = TRUE)
    if (log(runif(1)) < min(0, log_ratio)) {
      out[t] <- proposed
    } else {
      out[t] <- out[t - 1]
    }
  }
  out[(burn + 1):total]
}
set.seed(3500)
draw40  <- independent_mh(16,  40,  4,  6)
draw400 <- independent_mh(160, 400, 40, 60)
mean(draw40)
quantile(draw40, c(0.025, 0.975))
mean(draw400)
quantile(draw400, c(0.025, 0.975))
plot(density(draw40, from = 0, to = 1),
     xlab = expression(theta), main = "n = 40")
For the displayed seed, the n=40 run gives

\widehat{\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)}=0.432,
\qquad
\text{$95\%$ interval }(0.294,0.578).

Direct numerical integration gives 0.4320 and (0.291,0.579), so the Monte Carlo discrepancy is of the expected size. The prior mean is approximately 0.6967: observing only 16/40=0.4 heads moves the posterior sharply towards 0.4 and makes it appreciably more concentrated. The interval means that, under the model and prior, the posterior probability that \theta lies between the reported endpoints is approximately 0.95.
For n=400 and x=160, the same seed gives

\widehat{\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)}=0.404,
\qquad
\text{$95\%$ interval }(0.355,0.453),

while numerical integration gives 0.4035 and (0.356,0.452). Both data sets have empirical proportion 0.4, so the centre changes little. The ten-fold increase in sample size makes the likelihood much more concentrated and leaves the prior with much less leverage.
The function dbeta in the Hastings ratio is essential: g is a proposal density. Replacing it by the distribution function pbeta changes the invariant distribution and produces incorrect posterior summaries.

title: Multinomial central limit theorem
text:
Proposition taught in Categorical data and the Dirichlet distribution, part of Bayesian statistics
Let {\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{Multinomial}(n,{\boldsymbol{p}}) and \widehat{\boldsymbol{p}}={\boldsymbol{x}}/n. For fixed interior {\boldsymbol{p}}, define the covariance matrix
{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}({\boldsymbol{p}})
=\operatorname{diag}({\boldsymbol{p}})-{\boldsymbol{p}}{\boldsymbol{p}}^{\mathsf T}.
Then
\sqrt n\,(\widehat{\boldsymbol{p}}-{\boldsymbol{p}})
\xrightarrow{\mathcal D}
\operatorname{N}_K\!\left(
  {\boldsymbol{0}},
  {\color{blue}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}({\boldsymbol{p}})
\right).
The covariance matrix is singular because the components of \widehat{\boldsymbol{p}}-{\boldsymbol{p}} sum to zero. On the (K-1)-dimensional simplex, the count cloud therefore tightens at the usual n^{-1/2} rate and becomes locally normal.

title: Natural exponential family
text:
Definition taught in Exponential families and conjugacy, part of Bayesian statistics
In the a–b–c–T notation used here, the natural or canonical form of an exponential-family density is 
p(x\mid\theta)
=\frac{b(x)\exp\{c(\theta)^{\mathsf T}T(x)\}}
        {a(\theta)},
 where c(\theta) is the natural or canonical parameter, T(x) is the natural statistic, b(x) does not depend on \theta, and a(\theta) is the normalising function.

title: Natural exponential family
text:
Properties

Log-partition moment identities

Main article: Log-partition moment identities

Whenever c(\theta) can be used as a local parameter and differentiation under the normalising integral is valid,

\nabla_c\log a(\theta)
=\mathbb{E}_\theta\{T(X)\},
\qquad
\nabla_c^2\log a(\theta)
=\operatorname{Cov}_\theta\{T(X)\}.

Here derivatives are taken with respect to c=c(\theta), so a(\theta) is regarded as a function of c through the chosen parametrisation. Consequently \log a(\theta) is convex as a function of c, and the one-observation Fisher information in the natural parameter is \nabla_c^2\log a(\theta).


Generic exponential-family conjugate update

Main article: Generic exponential-family conjugate update

The hyperparameters update as 
\boxed{
\alpha\leftarrow
\alpha+S({\boldsymbol{x}}),
\qquad
\beta\leftarrow\beta+n.}



Pitman–Koopman–Darmois, informal form

Main article: Pitman–Koopman–Darmois, informal form

For regular iid models with parameter-independent support, the theorem says, roughly, that the existence for every n of a sufficient statistic whose dimension stays fixed essentially characterises exponential families. The support condition matters: models such as \operatorname{Uniform}(0,\theta) can have a fixed-dimensional sufficient statistic without having the regular form Equation (3) in Exponential families and conjugacy.

title: Natural exponential family
text:
Examples

Poisson natural form and Gamma conjugacy

Worked example from Exponential families and conjugacy

Question. For iid Poisson observations with mean \theta, write the model in the a(\theta), b(x), c(\theta), T(x) form, identify the sufficient statistic, and derive the corresponding conjugate prior and posterior update.
Solution. For one Poisson observation, \begin{align*}
p(x\mid\theta)
&=\frac{e^{-\theta}\theta^x}{x!}\\
&=\frac1{x!}\exp\{x\log\theta\}e^{-\theta}\\
&=\frac{b(x)\exp\{c(\theta)T(x)\}}{a(\theta)},
\end{align*} with

b(x)=\frac1{x!},
\qquad c(\theta)=\log\theta,
\qquad T(x)=x,
\qquad a(\theta)=e^\theta.

For the Poisson model, the definition Equation (4) in Exponential families and conjugacy gives S({\boldsymbol{x}})=\sum_i x_i. The joint likelihood is \begin{align*}
p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta)
&=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{e^{-\theta}\theta^{x_i}}{x_i!}\\
&=\left(\prod_{i=1}^n\frac1{x_i!}\right)
   \exp\{(\log\theta)S({\boldsymbol{x}})-n\theta\}.
\end{align*} The factorisation theorem shows that S({\boldsymbol{X}}) is sufficient for \theta. It is also minimal sufficient by the likelihood-ratio criterion. Because the natural parameter c(\theta)=\log\theta ranges over the open set \mathbb{R}, S({\boldsymbol{X}}) is complete as well.
The generic prior Equation (6) in Exponential families and conjugacy becomes \begin{align*}
p(\theta\mid\alpha,\beta)
&\propto
\frac{\exp\{\alpha\log\theta\}}{(e^\theta)^\beta}\\
&=\theta^\alpha e^{-\beta\theta}.
\end{align*} This is the kernel of \operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha+1,\beta), not \operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha,\beta). Using the sufficient statistic S({\boldsymbol{x}}), \begin{align*}
p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto
\theta^{S({\boldsymbol{x}})} e^{-n\theta}\theta^\alpha e^{-\beta\theta}\\
&=\theta^{S({\boldsymbol{x}})+\alpha}e^{-(n+\beta)\theta},
\end{align*} so 
\boxed{
\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha+S({\boldsymbol{x}})+1,\beta+n)}.
 Its posterior mean is \begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=\frac{\alpha+S({\boldsymbol{x}})+1}{\beta+n}\\
&=\frac{(\alpha+1)+n\overline x}{\beta+n}\\
&=\frac\beta{\beta+n}\frac{\alpha+1}{\beta}
  +\frac n{\beta+n}\overline x.
\end{align*} The prior therefore behaves, for the mean, as \beta prior observations with total count \alpha+1.


Concept check: C4. Exponential family

Question page: C4. Exponential family

What is an exponential family? Identify its natural parameter and statistic.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. An exponential family has density or mass function f(x\mid\theta)=b(x)\exp\{c(\theta)^\top T(x)\}/a(\theta), where c(\theta) is the natural parameter, T(x) the natural statistic, b(x) a parameter-free base factor and a(\theta) the normalising function. In the regular form used here, the support is independent of \theta.





Practice set: Q57. Negative-binomial canonical link

Question page: Q57. Negative-binomial canonical link

[6 marks]
Let Y have a negative-binomial distribution with probability mass function f(y;\theta)
=\binom{y+r-1}{r-1}\theta^r(1-\theta)^y,
\qquad y=0,1,2,\ldots, where r>0 is known and 0<\theta<1.
(a) Show that this distribution belongs to the linear exponential family by expressing its probability mass function in the form f(y;\theta)
        =\exp\left\{
        \frac{y\,b(\theta)+c(\theta)}{e(\phi)}+d(y;\phi)
        \right\}. Identify the natural parameter b(\theta). [3 marks]
(b) Given that \mu=\mathbb{E}(Y)=\frac{r(1-\theta)}{\theta}, derive the canonical link function g(\mu). [3 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Here Y counts failures, with support \{0,1,2,\ldots\}, known r>0, and 0<\theta<1. For non-integer r, interpret the binomial coefficient as \binom{y+r-1}{r-1}=\Gamma(y+r)/\{\Gamma(r)\Gamma(y+1)\}. In the stated linear exponential-family form, the natural parameter is b(\theta); the canonical link is g(\mu)=b\{\theta(\mu)\}. We use scale convention e(\phi)=1.
(a) Exponential-family representation. The support \{0,1,2,\ldots\} does not depend on \theta. Take logarithms of the supplied mass function: \begin{aligned}
\log f(y;\theta)
&=\log\left\{\binom{y+r-1}{r-1}\theta^r(1-\theta)^y\right\}\\
&=y\log(1-\theta)+r\log\theta
  +\log\binom{y+r-1}{r-1}.
\end{aligned} Since r is known, there is no free dispersion parameter to estimate here. Choose e(\phi)=1 and identify \boxed{
b(\theta)=\log(1-\theta),\qquad
c(\theta)=r\log\theta,\qquad e(\phi)=1,
} \boxed{d(y;\phi)=\log\binom{y+r-1}{r-1}.} The symbol \phi is redundant in this choice: d depends on the known r, not on the unknown \theta. Substitution gives f(y;\theta)
=\exp\left\{y\log(1-\theta)+r\log\theta+
\log\binom{y+r-1}{r-1}\right\}, exactly the required form. In particular, \boxed{\eta=b(\theta)=\log(1-\theta)<0.} The natural parameter is \log(1-\theta), not \log\theta: it is the coefficient multiplying the observation y.
The Gamma-function convention in Definitions makes this representation valid for every stated r>0.
(b) Canonical link. Start with the supplied mean and solve for the original parameter: \begin{aligned}
\mu&=\frac{r(1-\theta)}{\theta},\\
\mu\theta&=r-r\theta,\\
(\mu+r)\theta&=r,\\
\theta&=\frac r{\mu+r},\qquad
1-\theta=\frac{\mu}{\mu+r}.
\end{aligned} Now substitute into the natural parameter from part (a): \boxed{
g(\mu)=b\{\theta(\mu)\}
=\log\left(\frac{\mu}{\mu+r}\right)
=\log\mu-\log(\mu+r),\qquad\mu>0.
} Thus a canonical-link regression would set \eta_i=\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta=g(\mu_i), with \eta_i<0 to keep the means valid. Solving for the mean gives e^\eta=\frac{\mu}{\mu+r}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mu(1-e^\eta)=re^\eta
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\boxed{\mu=\frac{re^\eta}{1-e^\eta},\qquad\eta<0.}
Independent check from the normalising term. Write the log mass function as \log f(y;\eta)=y\eta-A(\eta)+d(y),
\qquad A(\eta)=-r\log(1-e^\eta). Differentiating the identity \sum_y f(y;\eta)=1 gives 0=\sum_y\{y-A'(\eta)\}f(y;\eta), so \mathbb{E}(Y)=A'(\eta). Here A'(\eta)=\frac{re^\eta}{1-e^\eta}, which is exactly the inverse link just derived.
A log link can be chosen for a negative-binomial regression, but it is not the canonical link derived here.

title: Normal hierarchical shrinkage
text:
Proposition taught in Hierarchical Bayes, part of Bayesian statistics
The final term is constant in \theta_j. The remaining kernel is normal, so 
\theta_j\mid\overline y_j,\mu,\tau^2,\sigma^2
\sim\operatorname{N}\!\left(
   \frac{B_j}{A_j},\frac1{A_j}\right).
 Its variance is \begin{align*}
\frac1{A_j}
&=\frac1{n_j/\sigma^2+1/\tau^2}\\
&=\frac{\sigma^2\tau^2}{\sigma^2+n_j\tau^2},
\end{align*} and its mean can be rearranged without omitting any terms: \begin{align*}
\frac{B_j}{A_j}
&=\frac{n_j\overline y_j/\sigma^2+\mu/\tau^2}
         {n_j/\sigma^2+1/\tau^2}\\
&=\frac{n_j\tau^2\overline y_j+\sigma^2\mu}
         {\sigma^2+n_j\tau^2}\\
&=\frac{n_j\tau^2}{\sigma^2+n_j\tau^2}\overline y_j
   +\frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2+n_j\tau^2}\mu\\
&=w_j\overline y_j+(1-w_j)\mu,
\end{align*} where 
w_j=\frac{n_j\tau^2}{\sigma^2+n_j\tau^2},
\qquad
1-w_j=\frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2+n_j\tau^2}.
 Thus
\mathbb{E}(\theta_j\mid\overline y_j,\mu,\tau^2,\sigma^2)
=w_j\overline y_j+(1-w_j)\mu.

title: Normal hierarchical shrinkage
text:
Examples

Large and small tutorial classes

Worked example from Hierarchical Bayes

Suppose the overall mean is \mu=70, the within-class standard deviation is \sigma=10, and the between-class standard deviation is \tau=5. Class A has 100 students and \overline y_A=75, while Class B has only two students and \overline y_B=95.
Question. Compute the two shrinkage weights and posterior means, treating \mu, \sigma^2, and \tau^2 as fixed, and explain why the more extreme sample mean need not produce the more extreme posterior mean.
Solution. For Class A, \begin{align*}
w_A&=\frac{100(25)}{100+100(25)}=\frac{25}{26}\approx0.962,\\
\mathbb{E}(\theta_A\mid\overline y_A,\mu,\tau^2,\sigma^2)
&=\frac{25}{26}(75)+\frac1{26}(70)\approx74.81.
\end{align*} For Class B, \begin{align*}
w_B&=\frac{2(25)}{100+2(25)}=\frac13,\\
\mathbb{E}(\theta_B\mid\overline y_B,\mu,\tau^2,\sigma^2)
&=\frac13(95)+\frac23(70)\approx78.33.
\end{align*} The extreme average from the small class is not ignored, but it is recognised as much less precise.


Practice set: Q23. Rat-tumour studies and hierarchical shrinkage

Question page: Q23. Rat-tumour studies and hierarchical shrinkage

[12 marks]
Suppose J related studies record tumour counts Y_j\mid\theta_j\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n_j,\theta_j),
\qquad j=1,\ldots,J, independently conditional on the study rates. Assume \theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta
\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta),
\qquad
\alpha\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1),\quad
\beta\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1), where the two hyperpriors are independent. Write \mathbf y=(y_1,\ldots,y_J); the sample sizes n_j are known. You may use B(a,b)=\int_0^1 t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}\,dt,
\qquad
f(\theta\mid a,b)=\frac{\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}}{B(a,b)}.
(a) [2 marks] Derive and identify the full conditional distribution \theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y.
(b) [3 marks] For this part only, fix \alpha=2 and \beta=8. Two studies report (y_1,n_1)=(4,10),\qquad (y_2,n_2)=(40,100). Calculate both posterior means. Although both observed proportions equal 0.4, explain why the posterior means differ and identify which study experiences stronger shrinkage.
(c) [4 marks] Return to unknown \alpha,\beta. Integrate out the study rates to derive:
(i) the marginal probability \mathbb{P}(Y_j=y_j\mid\alpha,\beta);
(ii) the marginal posterior kernel p(\alpha,\beta\mid\mathbf y).
Express your answers using Beta functions. Explain why the Beta prior’s normalising factor cannot be discarded when deriving this hyperparameter posterior.
(d) [3 marks] Explain how the full Bayesian model allows studies to share information. What uncertainty is omitted if \alpha,\beta are instead estimated from the data and then treated as known?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Study j has observed count y_j, known size n_j, and unknown rate \theta_j; \alpha,\beta>0 are shared hyperparameters. A \operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta) density is \theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1}/B(\alpha,\beta) on (0,1), where B(a,b)=\int_0^1u^{a-1}(1-u)^{b-1}\,du. \operatorname{Exp}(1) uses rate one. Partial pooling allows different study rates linked through a common population distribution.
Assumptions. The hierarchy assumes conditional independence of studies given their rates, and iid Beta rates given \alpha,\beta. Thus its joint density factors as p(\alpha)p(\beta)\prod_jp(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta)p(y_j\mid\theta_j), with independent rate-one exponential hyperpriors. Only in part (b) are the hyperparameters fixed at the supplied values.
(a) Full conditional for a study rate. Holding \alpha,\beta fixed, the factors involving \theta_j are \begin{aligned}
p(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y)
&\propto p(y_j\mid\theta_j)p(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta)\\
&\propto\theta_j^{y_j}(1-\theta_j)^{n_j-y_j}
\theta_j^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta_j)^{\beta-1}\\
&=\theta_j^{\alpha+y_j-1}(1-\theta_j)^{\beta+n_j-y_j-1}.
\end{aligned} Therefore \boxed{\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y
\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+y_j,\beta+n_j-y_j),\qquad 0<\theta_j<1.} Conditional on the hyperparameters and data, the study rates are independent. Other studies’ observations affect this study’s marginal posterior through learning \alpha,\beta, not through an additional factor in this full conditional.
(b) Posterior means and shrinkage. For fixed \alpha=2, \beta=8, the population mean is \frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}=\frac2{10}=0.2. The two posteriors are \theta_1\mid\alpha=2,\beta=8,\mathbf y\sim\operatorname{Beta}(6,14), \theta_2\mid\alpha=2,\beta=8,\mathbf y\sim\operatorname{Beta}(42,68). Thus their posterior means are \boxed{\mathbb{E}(\theta_1\mid\alpha=2,\beta=8,\mathbf y)=\frac6{20}=0.3,} \boxed{\mathbb{E}(\theta_2\mid\alpha=2,\beta=8,\mathbf y)=\frac{42}{110}
\approx0.3818.} To see the shrinkage explicitly, write \frac{\alpha+y_j}{\alpha+\beta+n_j}
=\frac{\alpha+\beta}{\alpha+\beta+n_j}
\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}
+\frac{n_j}{\alpha+\beta+n_j}\frac{y_j}{n_j}. Both sample proportions equal 0.4, but study 1 puts weight 10/20=1/2 on the population mean, whereas study 2 puts only 10/110=1/11 on it. The smaller study therefore experiences stronger shrinkage toward 0.2. The larger study has more information about its own rate, so its posterior mean remains closer to its observed proportion.
(c) Integrating out the study rates. For one study, retain the normalising factor of the Beta density: \begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(Y_j=y_j\mid\alpha,\beta)
&=\int_0^1 p(y_j\mid\theta_j)p(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta)\,d\theta_j\\
&=\binom{n_j}{y_j}\frac1{B(\alpha,\beta)}
\int_0^1\theta_j^{y_j+\alpha-1}
(1-\theta_j)^{n_j-y_j+\beta-1}\,d\theta_j\\
&=\boxed{\binom{n_j}{y_j}
\frac{B(\alpha+y_j,\beta+n_j-y_j)}{B(\alpha,\beta)}.}
\end{aligned} This is a Beta–Binomial marginal distribution, with y_j\in\{0,\ldots,n_j\}.
The independent rate-one exponential hyperpriors give p(\alpha,\beta)=e^{-\alpha-\beta},\qquad \alpha>0,\quad\beta>0. The studies remain independent conditional on the hyperparameters after their individual rates have been integrated out. Consequently, \begin{aligned}
p(\alpha,\beta\mid\mathbf y)
&\propto p(\alpha,\beta)
\prod_{j=1}^{J}\mathbb{P}(Y_j=y_j\mid\alpha,\beta)\\
&\propto e^{-(\alpha+\beta)}
\prod_{j=1}^{J}
\frac{B(\alpha+y_j,\beta+n_j-y_j)}{B(\alpha,\beta)}.
\end{aligned} Hence \boxed{
p(\alpha,\beta\mid\mathbf y)
\propto e^{-(\alpha+\beta)}B(\alpha,\beta)^{-J}
\prod_{j=1}^{J}B(\alpha+y_j,\beta+n_j-y_j),
\quad \alpha,\beta>0.
} The binomial coefficients can be dropped because the observed y_j and known n_j make them constant with respect to \alpha,\beta. However, 1/B(\alpha,\beta) depends on the hyperparameters, so it must remain. A factor constant in \theta_j need not be constant in \alpha,\beta.
(d) Sharing information and hyperparameter uncertainty. Every study contributes to the posterior for the common population parameters \alpha,\beta. That posterior then contributes to each study-specific posterior through p(\theta_j\mid\mathbf y)
=\int_0^\infty\!\int_0^\infty
p(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y)
p(\alpha,\beta\mid\mathbf y)\,d\alpha\,d\beta. This is partial pooling: study rates can differ, but they are connected by a population distribution learned from all the studies. The model does not force them to be identical, and it does not treat them as unrelated.
Replacing \alpha,\beta by fixed estimates is an empirical-Bayes plug-in analysis. It omits uncertainty about the population distribution’s parameters. For example, the law of total variance gives \begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(\theta_j\mid\mathbf y)
={}&\mathbb{E}\!\left[
\operatorname{Var}(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y)
\mid\mathbf y\right]\\
&+\operatorname{Var}\!\left[
\mathbb{E}(\theta_j\mid\alpha,\beta,\mathbf y)
\mid\mathbf y\right].
\end{aligned} The second term represents variation in the conditional mean as the hyperparameters vary under their posterior. A plug-in calculation does not propagate this variation and can therefore give an overly precise account of uncertainty.

Key result. Conditional conjugacy does not eliminate uncertainty in the hyperparameters. Full Bayes learns their distribution and averages over it.
