title: Normal–inverse-Gamma prior
text:
Definition taught in Bayesian linear regression, part of Bayesian statistics
Full joint conjugacy is obtained from the scaled prior 
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid\sigma^2
\sim\operatorname{N}_p({\boldsymbol{m}}_0,\sigma^2{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{V}}_0),
\qquad
\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(a_0,b_0).

title: Normal–inverse-Gamma prior
Normal–inverse-Gamma prior
text:
Examples

Final preparation: Question 4. Jointly conjugate normal–inverse-gamma

Question page: Question 4. Jointly conjugate normal–inverse-gamma

Let X_i\mid\mu,\sigma^2\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^2), with the jointly conjugate prior

\mu\mid\sigma^2\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu_0,\sigma^2/\kappa_0),
\qquad
\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(\alpha_0,\beta_0),

where \kappa_0,\alpha_0,\beta_0>0. The inverse-gamma kernel is (\sigma^2)^{-\alpha_0-1}\exp(-\beta_0/\sigma^2).
(a) How does the jointly conjugate prior for (\mu,\sigma^2) differ from independent normal and inverse-gamma priors?
(b) What remains in the same family after updating, and what is the marginal posterior distribution of \mu?
(c) What has to be checked before an inverse-gamma moment, or a software default, is used?
(d) State the four updated posterior hyperparameters \kappa_n, \mu_n, \alpha_n, and \beta_n.
(e) State the joint posterior family and the conditional posterior of \mu\mid\sigma^2,{\boldsymbol{x}}.
(f) State the marginal posterior of \sigma^2.
(g) State the marginal posterior of \mu, including its degrees of freedom, location, and scale.
(h) Explain why integrating out \sigma^2 produces a Student-t distribution rather than a normal distribution.
(i) Interpret \kappa_0 and the weighted-average form of the posterior mean.
(j) Explain how this model differs from the independent-prior model in Question 3.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Let v=\sigma^2, S=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2, and \kappa_0>0. The normal–inverse-gamma family is defined by the factorisation p(\mu,v)=p(v)p(\mu\mid v), with v\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(\alpha_0,\beta_0) and \mu\mid v\sim\operatorname{N}(\mu_0,v/\kappa_0). A Student-t location–scale distribution t_\nu(m,s) means m+sT with T\sim t_\nu; s is a scale.
(a) The jointly conjugate prior scales the prior variance of the mean by the unknown variance:

\mu\mid\sigma^2\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu_0,\sigma^2/\kappa_0),
\qquad
\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(\alpha_0,\beta_0).

The independent prior uses a fixed \sigma_0^2, not \sigma^2/\kappa_0.
Thus this prior already makes the uncertainty in \mu depend on v: larger observation variance brings larger conditional prior variance for the mean. Conjugacy concerns this dependent joint family. It does not mean that updating preserves independence.
(b) The joint posterior stays normal–inverse-gamma. The marginal posterior of \mu is a Student-t distribution.
(c) Match the density in use,

f(\sigma^2)\propto(\sigma^2)^{-\alpha-1}\exp(-\beta/\sigma^2),

before a moment or a software default is used. Packages do not all take (\alpha,\beta) in this shape–rate order.
(d) Let S=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2. The updated hyperparameters are

\begin{aligned}
\kappa_n&=\kappa_0+n,\\
\mu_n&=\frac{\kappa_0\mu_0+n\bar x}{\kappa_0+n},\\
\alpha_n&=\alpha_0+\frac n2,\\
\beta_n
&=
\beta_0+\frac12 S+\frac{\kappa_0 n}{2(\kappa_0+n)}(\bar x-\mu_0)^2.
\end{aligned}

The update follows by combining the two quadratic penalties. The useful identity is

n(\mu-\bar x)^2+\kappa_0(\mu-\mu_0)^2
=\kappa_n(\mu-\mu_n)^2
+\frac{\kappa_0n}{\kappa_n}(\bar x-\mu_0)^2.

The last term records disagreement between the prior centre and the sample mean. This disagreement adds to the posterior scale for v, alongside the within-sample scatter S. Ignoring it would understate uncertainty when the prior centre and data differ.
(e) Multiplying the likelihood by the joint prior and using that identity gives

p(\mu,v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto
v^{-(\alpha_n+3/2)}
\exp\left\{-\frac{\beta_n+\kappa_n(\mu-\mu_n)^2/2}{v}\right\}.

This factors into a normal density in \mu\mid v and an inverse-gamma density in v, so the joint posterior remains normal–inverse-gamma. Conditionally,

\mu\mid\sigma^2,{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim
\operatorname{N}\bigl(\mu_n,\sigma^2/\kappa_n\bigr).

(f) Integrating out \mu leaves the inverse-gamma factor,

\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(\alpha_n,\beta_n).

The integral of the conditional normal density is one. Equivalently, integrating its unnormalised exponential kernel contributes \sqrt{2\pi v/\kappa_n}, cancelling the extra factor v^{-1/2} in the joint kernel. This is why the marginal shape is \alpha_n.
(g) The marginal posterior is Student-t, with 2\alpha_n degrees of freedom, location \mu_n, and scale \sqrt{\beta_n/(\alpha_n\kappa_n)}:

\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim
t_{2\alpha_n}\!\left(\mu_n,\sqrt{\frac{\beta_n}{\alpha_n\kappa_n}}\right).

The second argument is a scale, not a standard deviation.
When \alpha_n>1, its variance is \beta_n/[\kappa_n(\alpha_n-1)], which is larger than the squared scale. The marginal mean equals \mu_n when 2\alpha_n>1; when this moment does not exist, \mu_n is still the distribution’s location and symmetry centre.
(h) Given \sigma^2, \mu is normal with variance proportional to \sigma^2. Mixing that normal over the inverse-gamma posterior of \sigma^2 gives the Student-t kernel

\left(1+\frac{\kappa_n(\mu-\mu_n)^2}{2\beta_n}\right)^{-(2\alpha_n+1)/2}.

Uncertainty in \sigma^2 produces heavier tails than a normal distribution with the same location and scale.
Indeed, the integral over v is proportional to [\beta_n+\kappa_n(\mu-\mu_n)^2/2]^{-(\alpha_n+1/2)}. Matching this with [1+(\mu-m)^2/(\nu s^2)]^{-(\nu+1)/2} gives \nu=2\alpha_n and s^2=\beta_n/(\alpha_n\kappa_n). A plug-in normal posterior at an estimated variance would not reproduce these tails.
(i) The weight \kappa_0 is the prior equivalent sample size: \mu_0 is weighted as \kappa_0 observations. Thus

\mu_n=\frac{\kappa_0\mu_0+n\bar x}{\kappa_0+n}

is the sample-size-weighted average of the prior location and the sample mean. The prior location is also its marginal mean when that mean exists.
(j) In the prior variance of \mu is a fixed \sigma_0^2, and the joint posterior does not stay normal–inverse-gamma. Here the prior variance is \sigma^2/\kappa_0, so the joint posterior stays in that family. Both marginals are then available in closed form: inverse-gamma for \sigma^2, and Student-t for \mu.
The distinction is visible in the conditional update: in the independent-prior model the relative weights depend on the current v, whereas here both precision contributions share the factor 1/v. That factor cancels from \mu_n, leaving fixed weights n and \kappa_0.





Final preparation: Question 5. Normal–inverse-\chi^2 regression

Question page: Question 5. Normal–inverse-\chi^2 regression

Suppose

y\mid\beta,\sigma^2,X\sim \operatorname{N}_n(X\beta,\sigma^2 I_n),

with prior

\beta\mid\sigma^2\sim \operatorname{N}_p(\beta_0,\sigma^2\Sigma_0),
\qquad
\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{Inv\text{-}\chi^2}(\mu_0,\sigma_0^2).

Here X is known, \Sigma_0 is positive definite, and \mu_0,\sigma_0^2>0. The inverse-\chi^2 convention is

\frac{\mu_0\sigma_0^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_{\mu_0}.

(a) State the inverse-\chi^2 prior kernel and its equivalent inverse-gamma parameters.
(b) State the updated parameters \Sigma_n and \beta_n.
(c) State the updated parameters \mu_n and \sigma_n^2.
(d) Express the joint posterior through a conditional posterior for \beta and a marginal posterior for \sigma^2.
(e) Express the updated scale using a residual sum of squares and a prior penalty. Explain why it is positive.
(f) Is \Sigma_n the conditional covariance matrix of \beta? Is \sigma_n^2 the posterior mean of \sigma^2? Give the correct expressions and the posterior mode of \sigma^2.
(g) State the full conditional posterior of \sigma^2\mid\beta,y,X. How does it differ from its marginal posterior?
(h) Without consulting the updates, complete the square to reconstruct them. Explain why the marginal degrees of freedom are \mu_0+n.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. There are n responses and p regression coefficients; X is an n\times p known design matrix. Write v=\sigma^2. The matrix \Sigma_0 scales the conditional prior covariance v\Sigma_0. In this question \mu_0 denotes prior degrees of freedom, not a normal mean. Our \operatorname{Inv\text{-}\chi^2}(\nu,s^2) convention means \nu s^2/v\sim\chi^2_\nu, or equivalently v\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(\nu/2,\nu s^2/2).
(a) The transformation \mu_0\sigma_0^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_{\mu_0} has kernel

\pi(\sigma^2)
\propto
(\sigma^2)^{-\mu_0/2-1}
\exp\Bigl(-\frac{\mu_0\sigma_0^2}{2\sigma^2}\Bigr),
\qquad\sigma^2>0.

Matching (\sigma^2)^{-a-1}\exp(-b/\sigma^2) gives a=\mu_0/2 and b=\mu_0\sigma_0^2/2.
For completeness, if U=\mu_0\sigma_0^2/v, then |dU/dv|=\mu_0\sigma_0^2/v^2. Multiplying the \chi^2_{\mu_0} density at U by this Jacobian gives the displayed inverse-gamma kernel. The Jacobian supplies the power v^{-2} and must be retained.

\boxed{
\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\Bigl(\frac{\mu_0}{2},\frac{\mu_0\sigma_0^2}{2}\Bigr).
}

(b) Since \Sigma_0^{-1} is positive definite and X^\top X is positive semidefinite, \Sigma_n^{-1} is positive definite. Precision addition gives

\boxed{\Sigma_n^{-1}=X^\top X+\Sigma_0^{-1},}
\qquad
\boxed{\beta_n=\Sigma_n(X^\top y+\Sigma_0^{-1}\beta_0).}

The data and prior precision contributions add, and their combined precision determines the posterior centre.
At fixed v, the likelihood contributes X^\top X/v to the precision of \beta, and the prior contributes \Sigma_0^{-1}/v. Their sum is \Sigma_n^{-1}/v. A proper positive-definite prior therefore gives a proper conditional update even if X is not of full column rank; an unregularised least-squares inverse (X^\top X)^{-1} is not needed.
(c)

\boxed{\mu_n=\mu_0+n,}
\qquad
\boxed{
\sigma_n^2
=
\frac{
\mu_0\sigma_0^2+y^\top y+\beta_0^\top\Sigma_0^{-1}\beta_0
-\beta_n^\top\Sigma_n^{-1}\beta_n
}{\mu_n}.
}

(d)

\boxed{\beta\mid\sigma^2,y,X\sim \operatorname{N}_p(\beta_n,\sigma^2\Sigma_n),}
\qquad
\boxed{\sigma^2\mid y,X\sim\operatorname{Inv\text{-}\chi^2}(\mu_n,\sigma_n^2).}

Together these specify a normal–inverse-\chi^2 joint posterior.
This is a conditional–marginal factorisation. To draw an independent posterior pair, draw v from the marginal inverse-\chi^2 distribution and then \beta from its normal distribution conditional on that v. The components within a pair are dependent through the conditional covariance, even though different pairs can be generated independently.
(e) Equivalently,

\mu_n\sigma_n^2
=
\mu_0\sigma_0^2
+(y-X\beta_n)^\top(y-X\beta_n)
+(\beta_n-\beta_0)^\top\Sigma_0^{-1}(\beta_n-\beta_0).

Both quadratic forms are nonnegative and \mu_0\sigma_0^2>0, so \sigma_n^2>0. The algebra is completed in (h).
(f) No. The conditional covariance is \sigma^2\Sigma_n, not \Sigma_n:

\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(\beta\mid\sigma^2,y,X)=\sigma^2\Sigma_n.}

The parameter \sigma_n^2 is a scale. By the inverse-gamma equivalence in (a),

\boxed{
\mathbb{E}(\sigma^2\mid y,X)
=
\frac{\mu_n\sigma_n^2}{\mu_n-2},
\qquad\mu_n>2,
}

and

\boxed{
\operatorname{mode}(\sigma^2\mid y,X)
=
\frac{\mu_n\sigma_n^2}{\mu_n+2}.
}

(g)

\boxed{
\sigma^2\mid\beta,y,X
\sim
\operatorname{Inv\text{-}\chi^2}\!\left(
\mu_n+p,\;
\frac{\mu_n\sigma_n^2+(\beta-\beta_n)^\top\Sigma_n^{-1}(\beta-\beta_n)}{\mu_n+p}
\right).
}

The full conditional fixes \beta. The marginal posterior integrates \beta out, which removes p from the degrees of freedom.
The difference comes from the normal density’s factor v^{-p/2}. It remains when \beta is fixed and therefore adds p/2 to the inverse-gamma shape. Integrating over \beta instead contributes a factor v^{p/2}, cancelling it. Substituting \beta=\beta_n in the full conditional would leave the wrong degrees of freedom.
(h) Expand the likelihood quadratic and the prior quadratic:

\begin{aligned}
&(y-X\beta)^\top(y-X\beta)
+(\beta-\beta_0)^\top\Sigma_0^{-1}(\beta-\beta_0)\\
&\quad=
\beta^\top(X^\top X+\Sigma_0^{-1})\beta
-2\beta^\top(X^\top y+\Sigma_0^{-1}\beta_0)
+y^\top y+\beta_0^\top\Sigma_0^{-1}\beta_0\\
&\quad=
(\beta-\beta_n)^\top\Sigma_n^{-1}(\beta-\beta_n)
+y^\top y+\beta_0^\top\Sigma_0^{-1}\beta_0
-\beta_n^\top\Sigma_n^{-1}\beta_n.
\end{aligned}

Adding \mu_0\sigma_0^2, the terms free of \beta are the numerator of \mu_n\sigma_n^2 in (c), with \mu_n=\mu_0+n. Thus

\boxed{
Q(\beta)
=
(\beta-\beta_n)^\top\Sigma_n^{-1}(\beta-\beta_n)
+\mu_n\sigma_n^2.
}

The joint posterior kernel is

(\sigma^2)^{-(\mu_0+n+p)/2-1}
\exp\Bigl(-\frac{Q(\beta)}{2\sigma^2}\Bigr).

The integral over \beta of the normal kernel equals (2\pi\sigma^2)^{p/2}|\Sigma_n|^{1/2}. The remaining power of \sigma^2 is

-\frac{\mu_0+n+p}{2}-1+\frac p2
=
-\frac{\mu_0+n}{2}-1.


\therefore
\text{the marginal inverse-}\chi^2\text{ degrees of freedom are }\mu_0+n.

title: Normal–Normal conjugacy
Normal–Normal conjugacy
text:
Examples

Final preparation: Question 1. Normal mean, known variance

Question page: Question 1. Normal mean, known variance

Let

X_i\mid\mu\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^2),

with \sigma^2 known and \mu\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu_0,\sigma_0^2).
(a) Using only the precision-addition rule and the precision-weighted mean, write the two updated parameters of the posterior for \mu.
(b) Define the prior equivalent sample size, and state what it counts.
(c) Explain why the posterior mean is a precision-weighted average of the prior mean and the sample mean.
(d) State and interpret the limiting posterior mean and variance as n\to\infty, with the prior parameters fixed and \bar X_n\to\mu^{\ast}.
(e) State the posterior predictive distribution of one new observation X_{\mathrm{new}}, conditionally independent of the sample given \mu.
(f) Explain why the posterior predictive variance is larger than the posterior variance of \mu.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write \bar x=n^{-1}\sum_i x_i. A normal distribution \operatorname{N}(m,v) has mean m and variance v; its precision is 1/v. Here \sigma^2 is the known observation variance, \sigma_0^2 is the prior variance of the unknown mean, and \sigma_1^2 will be its posterior variance. These are variances of different objects.
(a) The data precision of n observations is n/\sigma^2, and the prior precision is 1/\sigma_0^2. Precision addition gives

\frac1{\sigma_1^2}
=
\frac n{\sigma^2}+\frac1{\sigma_0^2}.

The posterior mean is the precision-weighted average of \bar x and \mu_0:

\mu_1
=
\frac{(n/\sigma^2)\bar x+(1/\sigma_0^2)\mu_0}{n/\sigma^2+1/\sigma_0^2}
=
\frac{n\bar x\,\sigma_0^2+\mu_0\sigma^2}{n\sigma_0^2+\sigma^2}.


\boxed{\mu\mid x\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2).}

(b)

\kappa_0=\frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma_0^2}.

It counts how many observations of variance \sigma^2 have the same precision as the prior, since 1/\sigma_0^2=\kappa_0/\sigma^2.
Consequently, \mu_1=(n\bar x+\kappa_0\mu_0)/(n+\kappa_0) and \sigma_1^2=\sigma^2/(n+\kappa_0). The equivalent sample size measures information about the common mean. It need not be an integer or represent actual previous observations.
(c) Up to an additive constant free of \mu, the log posterior is

-\frac{n}{2\sigma^2}(\bar x-\mu)^2-\frac{1}{2\sigma_0^2}(\mu-\mu_0)^2.

Its derivative is (n/\sigma^2)(\bar x-\mu)-(1/\sigma_0^2)(\mu-\mu_0). Setting the derivative equal to zero balances the two pulls, so

\mu_1
=
\frac{(n/\sigma^2)\bar x+(1/\sigma_0^2)\mu_0}{n/\sigma^2+1/\sigma_0^2}.

The second derivative is -n/\sigma^2-1/\sigma_0^2<0, so this stationary point is the unique posterior mode. The posterior is normal, hence its mode equals its mean. This derives the weighting rule: moving away from a more precise source incurs a larger quadratic penalty. The two weights are nonnegative and sum to one, so the posterior mean lies between \bar x and \mu_0.
(d) Let w_n=(n/\sigma^2)/(n/\sigma^2+1/\sigma_0^2). Then w_n\to 1 and

\mu_1=w_n\bar X_n+(1-w_n)\mu_0\to\mu^{\ast},
\qquad
\sigma_1^2=\Bigl(\frac n{\sigma^2}+\frac1{\sigma_0^2}\Bigr)^{-1}\to 0.

With the prior held fixed, the data precision dominates. The posterior concentrates at the limiting sample mean.
This conclusion uses the stated convergence \bar X_n\to\mu^\ast. Under the iid normal model with true mean \mu^\ast, that convergence follows from the law of large numbers. A fixed prior contributes a fixed amount of precision, while the likelihood contributes an amount growing linearly with n.
(e) Given \mu, X_{\mathrm{new}} is independent of the sample and X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid\mu\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^2). Since \mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2),

\boxed{X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu_1,\sigma^2+\sigma_1^2).}

To see the distributional result, write X_{\mathrm{new}}=\mu+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{new}}, where \varepsilon_{\mathrm{new}}\sim\operatorname{N}(0,\sigma^2) is independent of the posterior draw of \mu. Conditional on the observed sample, this is a sum of two independent normal variables. Merely replacing \mu by \mu_1 would omit uncertainty about the unknown mean.
(f) By the law of total variance,

\operatorname{Var}(X_{\mathrm{new}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=
\mathbb{E}[\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}]+\operatorname{Var}(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=
\sigma^2+\sigma_1^2.

The term \sigma_1^2 is uncertainty about \mu. The term \sigma^2 is the variance of a new observation even if \mu is known. Both are positive, so the predictive variance exceeds the posterior variance of \mu.

title: Ordinary least squares

Ordinary least squares
text:
Examples

Eight-point regression

Worked example from Bayesian linear regression

Consider n=8 observations with one predictor and an intercept:

{\boldsymbol{x}}=(1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8)^{\mathsf T},
\qquad
{\boldsymbol{y}}=(2.05,3.40,4.55,5.10,7.20,8.05,9.60,10.80)^\top.

Question. Under the reference-prior analysis developed above, compute \widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}, the fitted sum of squared errors, the posterior distributions of \sigma^2 and {\boldsymbol{\beta}}, and marginal 95\% credible intervals for the two regression coefficients. Then derive posterior predictive distributions at \widetilde x=4.5 and \widetilde x=10 and explain the effect of extrapolation.
Solution. For this example put the intercept first, so the ith row of {\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}} is (1,x_i). Direct summation gives

\sum_i y_i=50.75,
\qquad
\sum_i x_i y_i=280.80,
\qquad
\sum_i y_i^2=387.9175.

Therefore

{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}=
\begin{pmatrix}8&36\\36&204\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\boldsymbol{y}}=
\begin{pmatrix}50.75\\280.80\end{pmatrix}.

The determinant is 8(204)-36^2=336, so

({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})^{-1}
=\frac1{336}\begin{pmatrix}204&-36\\-36&8\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}
0.607143&-0.107143\\
-0.107143&0.023810
\end{pmatrix}.

Multiplying by {\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\boldsymbol{y}}, \begin{align*}
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
&=\frac1{336}
\begin{pmatrix}204&-36\\-36&8\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}50.75\\280.80\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\frac1{336}
\begin{pmatrix}
204(50.75)-36(280.80)\\
-36(50.75)+8(280.80)
\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\begin{pmatrix}0.726786\\1.248214\end{pmatrix}.
\end{align*} The fitted SSE can be calculated without listing every residual: \begin{align*}
\operatorname{SSE}
&={\boldsymbol{y}}^\top{\boldsymbol{y}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\boldsymbol{y}}\\
&=387.9175
-\frac{244.2}{336}(50.75)-\frac{419.4}{336}(280.80)\\
&\approx0.534554.
\end{align*} The exact coefficients are kept here rather than the six-figure decimals printed above. The subtraction cancels almost everything: two quantities near 387.9 leave a remainder near 0.53, so rounding \widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} first costs about four significant figures in \operatorname{SSE}. Summing the squared residuals directly avoids the cancellation entirely.
Thus n-p=6 and

s^2=\frac{0.534554}{6}\approx0.089092.

Under the reference prior, \begin{align*}
\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{y}}
&\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(3,0.267277),\\
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid{\boldsymbol{y}}
&\sim t_6\!\left(
\begin{pmatrix}0.726786\\1.248214\end{pmatrix},
0.089092
\begin{pmatrix}
0.607143&-0.107143\\
-0.107143&0.023810
\end{pmatrix}\right).
\end{align*} The variance summaries illustrate why the loss function matters:

\mathbb{E}(\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{y}})=\frac{0.267277}{3-1}=0.133638,
\qquad
\operatorname{mode}(\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{y}})
=\frac{0.267277}{3+1}=0.066819,

while s^2=0.089092. Using t_{0.975,6}\approx2.447, the marginal 95\% credible intervals are approximately

\beta_0\mid{\boldsymbol{y}}:\ (0.158,1.296),
\qquad
\beta_1\mid{\boldsymbol{y}}:\ (1.136,1.361).

At \widetilde x=4.5, take \widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}=(1,4.5)^\top. Matrix multiplication gives

h(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}})
=(1,4.5)({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})^{-1}
\begin{pmatrix}1\\4.5\end{pmatrix}=0.125,

and the predicted centre is

\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}^\top\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
=0.726786+4.5(1.248214)=6.34375.

Consequently,

\widetilde Y\mid{\boldsymbol{y}},\widetilde x=4.5
\sim t_6\!\left(6.34375,
\sqrt{0.089092(1.125)}\right)
\approx t_6(6.344,0.317).

At \widetilde x=10, the centre is about 13.209 and h(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}})\approx0.845, giving predictive scale about 0.405. The increase from 0.317 is the uncertainty cost of extrapolating beyond the observed predictor range.






Figure 1: The eight observations, the fitted line, and the two bands. The inner band is for the mean response and the outer for a new observation; the gap between them is the extra 1 in the predictive scale, which is why they never meet however small the leverage term becomes. The vertical rules mark the two predictions computed above, at \widetilde x=4.5 inside the data and \widetilde x=10 beyond it. Both bands are narrowest near \overline x and flare outward, so the cost of extrapolation is a feature of the geometry rather than a separate warning to remember.





Practice set: Q24. Bayesian regression and prediction

Question page: Q24. Bayesian regression and prediction

[12 marks]
Consider the regression model Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad
\varepsilon_i\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2), with reference prior p(\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma^2)\propto1/\sigma^2 for (\beta_0,\beta_1)\in\mathbb{R}^2 and \sigma^2>0. For n=10 observations, the design matrix has rows (1,x_i), and \widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
(X^\top X)^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1/10&0\\0&1/40\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \operatorname{SSE}=16. The observed predictor values range from -3 to 3.
You may use the standard regression posterior formulas under this prior. Use the inverse-Gamma convention f(v)\propto v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v}. Write t_\nu(m,s) for a Student-t distribution with location m and scale s, and use t_{0.975,8}=2.306.
(a) [2 marks] State the marginal posterior distribution of \sigma^2 and calculate \mathbb{E}(\sigma^2\mid\mathbf y,X).
(b) [3 marks] State the marginal posterior distribution of the slope \beta_1, and calculate its equal-tailed 95% credible interval.
(c) [4 marks] At x_*=0, derive the posterior distributions and equal-tailed 95% intervals for:
(i) the unknown mean response \mu_*=\beta_0+\beta_1x_*;
(ii) a new observation \widetilde Y.
Explain precisely why the second interval is wider.
(d) [3 marks] Calculate h(x_*)=(1,x_*)(X^\top X)^{-1}(1,x_*)^\top at x_*=0 and x_*=4. Compare the posterior predictive scales at these points and explain how the calculation reflects uncertainty from extrapolation.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write D=(\mathbf y,X), v=\sigma^2, and \operatorname{SSE}=\|\mathbf y-X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\|^2. The inverse-Gamma kernel is v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v} on v>0. t_\nu(m,s) denotes location m, scale s, and \nu degrees of freedom: (T-m)/s\sim t_\nu. A scale is not a variance; t_{q,\nu} denotes the q quantile of standard t_\nu.
Assumptions. Use independent Normal errors, fixed covariates, full column rank X, n>p, positive SSE, and the reference prior p(\boldsymbol\beta,v)\propto1/v with respect to d\boldsymbol\beta\,dv. These rank and residual conditions ensure a proper posterior despite the improper prior.
There are p=2 regression coefficients, including the intercept. Define \nu=n-p=8,\qquad
s^2=\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}{n-p}=\frac{16}{8}=2,
\qquad C=(X^\top X)^{-1}. Here s^2 is the residual variance estimate; it is not the posterior mean of \sigma^2.
Why the regression posterior has this form. The likelihood times the reference prior gives p(\boldsymbol\beta,v\mid D)
\propto v^{-n/2-1}
\exp\{-\|\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta\|^2/(2v)\},
\qquad v=\sigma^2>0. Expand about the least-squares estimate. The cross term vanishes because X^\top(\mathbf y-X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})=\mathbf0, giving \|\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta\|^2
=\operatorname{SSE}
+(\boldsymbol\beta-\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})^\top
X^\top X(\boldsymbol\beta-\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}). The second term is a Normal quadratic. At fixed v it identifies \boldsymbol\beta\mid v,D\sim
N_p(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},vC). Its unnormalised exponential integrates to (2\pi v)^{p/2}|X^\top X|^{-1/2}, which explains the v^{p/2} factor in the variance marginal below.
(a) Marginal variance posterior. Under the stated reference prior, \sigma^2\mid D\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\left(\frac{n-p}{2},
\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}2\right). Thus \boxed{\sigma^2\mid D\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(4,8),\qquad\sigma^2>0.} An \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b) variable has mean b/(a-1) when a>1, so \boxed{\mathbb{E}(\sigma^2\mid D)=\frac8{4-1}=\frac83\approx2.6667.} For completeness, integrating the coefficient kernel out of the joint posterior contributes a factor (\sigma^2)^{p/2}. Therefore p(\sigma^2\mid D)
\propto (\sigma^2)^{-(n/2+1)}(\sigma^2)^{p/2}
\exp\!\left(-\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}{2\sigma^2}\right)
=(\sigma^2)^{-5}e^{-8/\sigma^2}, confirming the shape 4, not n/2=5.
(b) Slope posterior and credible interval. The conditional coefficient posterior is \boldsymbol\beta\mid\sigma^2,D
\sim N_2(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},\sigma^2 C). The slope entry of C is 1/40, so \beta_1\mid\sigma^2,D\sim N\!\left(2,\frac{\sigma^2}{40}\right). Integrating over \sigma^2\mid D gives \boxed{\beta_1\mid D\sim t_8\!\left(2,\sqrt{\frac2{40}}\right)
=t_8(2,\sqrt{0.05}).} Equivalently, (\beta_1-2)/\sqrt{0.05}\mid D\sim t_8. The equal-tailed 95% credible interval is therefore 2\pm2.306\sqrt{0.05}=2\pm0.5156,
\qquad\boxed{(1.484,\,2.516).} The second argument of t_8 is a scale, not a variance. There is no additional division by \sqrt n: sample-size information is already in C.
(c) Mean response versus a new observation at x_*=0. For a general predictor value, set \mathbf z_*=(1,x_*)^\top and write m_*=\mathbf z_*^\top\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},
\qquad h(x_*)=\mathbf z_*^\top C\mathbf z_*. The linear-transformation rule for a normal vector gives \mu_*\mid\sigma^2,D
\sim N\bigl(m_*,\sigma^2 h(x_*)\bigr). For a new response \widetilde Y=\mu_*+\widetilde\varepsilon, the new error is independent of the coefficient uncertainty conditional on \sigma^2,D, and has variance \sigma^2. Thus \widetilde Y\mid\sigma^2,D,x_*
\sim N\bigl(m_*,\sigma^2\{1+h(x_*)\}\bigr). Integrating over the inverse-Gamma variance posterior gives \mu_*\mid D\sim t_8\bigl(m_*,s\sqrt{h(x_*)}\bigr), \widetilde Y\mid D,x_*\sim t_8\bigl(m_*,s\sqrt{1+h(x_*)}\bigr). At x_*=0, m_*=(1,0)\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}=1,
\qquad h(0)=\frac1{10}. Therefore the unknown mean response has posterior \boxed{\mu_*\mid D\sim t_8(1,\sqrt{0.2}),} with equal-tailed 95% credible interval 1\pm2.306\sqrt{0.2}=1\pm1.0313,
\qquad\boxed{(-0.031,\,2.031).} The new observation has posterior predictive distribution \boxed{\widetilde Y\mid D,x_*=0\sim t_8(1,\sqrt{2.2}),} with equal-tailed 95% predictive interval 1\pm2.306\sqrt{2.2}=1\pm3.4204,
\qquad\boxed{(-2.420,\,4.420).} Both intervals have the same centre and use the same t_8 quantile. The predictive interval is wider because a new observation includes both uncertainty about the regression mean and fresh observational noise. That additional noise produces the extra 1 in 1+h(x_*).
(d) Extrapolation and predictive scale. Using the supplied diagonal matrix, \begin{aligned}
h(x_*)&=(1,x_*)
\begin{pmatrix}1/10&0\\0&1/40\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}1\\x_*\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\frac1{10}+\frac{x_*^2}{40}.
\end{aligned} Hence \boxed{h(0)=0.1,\qquad h(4)=0.1+\frac{16}{40}=0.5.} The corresponding predictive scales are \boxed{s_{\mathrm{pred}}(0)=\sqrt{2(1+0.1)}=\sqrt{2.2}\approx1.4832,} \boxed{s_{\mathrm{pred}}(4)=\sqrt{2(1+0.5)}=\sqrt3\approx1.7321.} At x_*=4, the predicted centre is 1+2(4)=9, so the predictive distribution is t_8(9,\sqrt3). Its interval is wider than at x_*=0 because it has the same degrees of freedom but a larger scale.
The value 4 lies outside the observed range [-3,3]. Uncertainty about the slope has a greater effect on the fitted mean farther from the centred design, increasing h(x_*). The future-error contribution is unchanged; the increased width comes from greater parameter uncertainty in the prediction. This calculation assumes the linear model remains appropriate beyond the observed range; it does not account for possible failure of that model there.

Key result. The mean-response scale is s\sqrt h; the new-observation scale is s\sqrt{1+h}. The extra 1 represents new observational noise, while h measures uncertainty about the fitted mean.

title: Poisson distribution
text:
Examples

Poisson natural form and Gamma conjugacy

Worked example from Exponential families and conjugacy

Question. For iid Poisson observations with mean \theta, write the model in the a(\theta), b(x), c(\theta), T(x) form, identify the sufficient statistic, and derive the corresponding conjugate prior and posterior update.
Solution. For one Poisson observation, \begin{align*}
p(x\mid\theta)
&=\frac{e^{-\theta}\theta^x}{x!}\\
&=\frac1{x!}\exp\{x\log\theta\}e^{-\theta}\\
&=\frac{b(x)\exp\{c(\theta)T(x)\}}{a(\theta)},
\end{align*} with

b(x)=\frac1{x!},
\qquad c(\theta)=\log\theta,
\qquad T(x)=x,
\qquad a(\theta)=e^\theta.

For the Poisson model, the definition Equation (4) in Exponential families and conjugacy gives S({\boldsymbol{x}})=\sum_i x_i. The joint likelihood is \begin{align*}
p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta)
&=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{e^{-\theta}\theta^{x_i}}{x_i!}\\
&=\left(\prod_{i=1}^n\frac1{x_i!}\right)
   \exp\{(\log\theta)S({\boldsymbol{x}})-n\theta\}.
\end{align*} The factorisation theorem shows that S({\boldsymbol{X}}) is sufficient for \theta. It is also minimal sufficient by the likelihood-ratio criterion. Because the natural parameter c(\theta)=\log\theta ranges over the open set \mathbb{R}, S({\boldsymbol{X}}) is complete as well.
The generic prior Equation (6) in Exponential families and conjugacy becomes \begin{align*}
p(\theta\mid\alpha,\beta)
&\propto
\frac{\exp\{\alpha\log\theta\}}{(e^\theta)^\beta}\\
&=\theta^\alpha e^{-\beta\theta}.
\end{align*} This is the kernel of \operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha+1,\beta), not \operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha,\beta). Using the sufficient statistic S({\boldsymbol{x}}), \begin{align*}
p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto
\theta^{S({\boldsymbol{x}})} e^{-n\theta}\theta^\alpha e^{-\beta\theta}\\
&=\theta^{S({\boldsymbol{x}})+\alpha}e^{-(n+\beta)\theta},
\end{align*} so 
\boxed{
\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha+S({\boldsymbol{x}})+1,\beta+n)}.
 Its posterior mean is \begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=\frac{\alpha+S({\boldsymbol{x}})+1}{\beta+n}\\
&=\frac{(\alpha+1)+n\overline x}{\beta+n}\\
&=\frac\beta{\beta+n}\frac{\alpha+1}{\beta}
  +\frac n{\beta+n}\overline x.
\end{align*} The prior therefore behaves, for the mean, as \beta prior observations with total count \alpha+1.


Practice set: Q53. Poisson flaws and posterior odds

Question page: Q53. Poisson flaws and posterior odds

[12 marks]
A textile manufacturer counts flaws in equal-length rolls of fabric. Assume X_i\mid\theta\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Poisson}(\theta),
\qquad i=1,\ldots,10, where \theta is the mean number of flaws per roll.
Ten inspected rolls contain 32 flaws in total. The prior is \theta\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(8,2), using the shape–rate convention: \pi(\theta)=\frac{2^8}{\Gamma(8)}\theta^7e^{-2\theta},
\qquad\theta>0. The manufacturer considers the process acceptable if \theta\le4.
(a) Form the likelihood and derive the posterior distribution of \theta. [4 marks]
(b) Find the posterior mean. Show that it lies between the prior mean and the observed sample mean. [2 marks]
(c) Define H_0:\theta\le4,\qquad H_1:\theta>4. Write an integral for \mathbb P(H_0\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}), including the normalising constant. Hence express the posterior odds in favour of H_0. You do not need to evaluate the integral. [3 marks]
(d) A colleague argues:

“The posterior mean is below 4, so the probability that the process is acceptable must be 1.”

Explain why this is incorrect. Would changing H_0 to \theta<4 change its posterior probability? Justify your answer. [3 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. For Gamma shape–rate parameters (A,B), the density is B^A\theta^{A-1}e^{-B\theta}/\Gamma(A) on \theta>0 and the mean is A/B. Here n=10, \sum_i x_i=32, and the prior is \operatorname{Gamma}(8,2). Write q=\mathbb P(\theta\le4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}). Posterior odds in favour of this event over its complement are q/(1-q).
(a) Likelihood and posterior. Conditional independence gives, for observed nonnegative integer counts, \begin{aligned}
L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=\prod_{i=1}^{10}\frac{e^{-\theta}\theta^{x_i}}{x_i!}
=\frac{\theta^{\sum_i x_i}e^{-10\theta}}{\prod_{i=1}^{10}x_i!}\\
&\propto\theta^{32}e^{-10\theta},\qquad\theta>0.
\end{aligned} The factorial term does not depend on \theta, so only the total count is needed for this likelihood kernel. Multiplying by the prior kernel, \begin{aligned}
\pi(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})\pi(\theta)\\
&\propto\theta^{32}e^{-10\theta}\theta^7e^{-2\theta}
=\theta^{39}e^{-12\theta}.
\end{aligned} Matching \theta^{A-1}e^{-B\theta} gives A=40 and B=12. Thus \boxed{\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(40,12)
\quad\text{(shape--rate)},\qquad\theta>0,} with normalised posterior density \boxed{\pi(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\frac{12^{40}}{\Gamma(40)}\theta^{39}e^{-12\theta},
\qquad\theta>0.}
(b) Posterior mean and shrinkage. The prior mean, sample mean, and posterior mean are respectively \mathbb{E}[\theta]=\frac82=4,\qquad
\bar x=\frac{32}{10}=3.2,\qquad
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}]=\frac{40}{12}=\frac{10}{3}.} In particular, 3.2<10/3<4. More explicitly, \mathbb{E}[\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}]
=\frac{8+32}{2+10}
=\frac{2}{12}\left(\frac82\right)
+\frac{10}{12}\left(\frac{32}{10}\right)
=\frac16\mathbb{E}[\theta]+\frac56\bar x. The weights are positive and sum to one, so the posterior mean lies strictly between the two distinct means.
(c) Posterior probability and odds. Let q=\mathbb P(H_0\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}). Integrating the normalised posterior density over the acceptable region gives \boxed{q=\mathbb P(\theta\le4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\frac{12^{40}}{\Gamma(40)}
\int_0^4\theta^{39}e^{-12\theta}\,d\theta.} The two hypotheses exhaust the parameter space, so \mathbb P(H_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=1-q. Therefore the posterior odds in favour of H_0 are q:(1-q), or, as a ratio, \boxed{
\frac{\mathbb P(H_0\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})}{\mathbb P(H_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})}
=\frac{q}{1-q}
=\frac{\displaystyle\int_0^4\theta^{39}e^{-12\theta}\,d\theta}
       {\displaystyle\int_4^\infty\theta^{39}e^{-12\theta}\,d\theta}.
} The common normalising constant cancels in the odds ratio, but it is required in the probability integral above. No numerical evaluation is needed.
(d) A mean below the threshold does not imply certainty. The posterior mean is an average of possible values of \theta, not an upper bound on them. Although \mathbb{E}[\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}]=10/3<4, the \operatorname{Gamma}(40,12) density is strictly positive for every \theta>0, including values above 4. Consequently, \mathbb P(\theta>4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\frac{12^{40}}{\Gamma(40)}
\int_4^\infty\theta^{39}e^{-12\theta}\,d\theta>0, so \mathbb P(\theta\le4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})<1. A point estimate below the threshold does not eliminate posterior uncertainty about acceptability.
Replacing \theta\le4 by \theta<4 does not change the posterior probability. The posterior is continuous, and hence \mathbb P(\theta=4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=0. Therefore \boxed{\mathbb P(\theta<4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\mathbb P(\theta\le4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}).}

Key result. The posterior mean answers “what is the posterior average of \theta?” The posterior probability of H_0 answers “how much posterior probability lies at or below 4?” These are different summaries.






Practice set: Q32. Deriving the Poisson log-likelihood

Question page: Q32. Deriving the Poisson log-likelihood

[3 marks]
Suppose, conditional on fixed covariates, Y_i\mid\mathbf X_i
\overset{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}\operatorname{Poisson}(\mu_i),
\qquad
\mu_i=\exp(\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta). Starting from the Poisson probability mass function, show that \ell(\boldsymbol\beta)
=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[
Y_i\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta
-\exp(\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta)
\right]+C. State exactly what C contains and why it can be ignored when maximising over \boldsymbol\beta.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Let \mathbf X_i be a fixed column vector of predictors and X the matrix with rows \mathbf X_i^\top. Write \eta_i=\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta and \mu_i=e^{\eta_i}. The likelihood is the joint Poisson mass function evaluated at observed counts \mathbf y, and \ell=\log L. An additive constant may depend on the data but not on the parameter \boldsymbol\beta being maximised over.
For observed counts y_i\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}, \mathbb{P}(Y_i=y_i\mid\mathbf X_i)
=\frac{e^{-\mu_i}\mu_i^{y_i}}{y_i!},
\qquad \mu_i=\exp(\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta). Conditional independence gives L(\boldsymbol\beta;\mathbf y,X)
=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{e^{-\mu_i}\mu_i^{y_i}}{y_i!}. Taking logarithms, \ell(\boldsymbol\beta)
=\sum_{i=1}^n\{-\mu_i+y_i\log\mu_i-\log(y_i!)\}. Since \log\mu_i=\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta, this becomes \boxed{
\ell(\boldsymbol\beta)
=\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[y_i\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta
-\exp(\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta)\right]+C,
\quad C=-\sum_{i=1}^n\log(y_i!).
} The constant C depends only on the observed responses, not on \boldsymbol\beta. Therefore adding or removing it does not change the maximiser over \boldsymbol\beta, and its derivatives with respect to \boldsymbol\beta are zero. Writing Y_i instead of y_i gives the random-data version in the question.

Key result. “Constant” means constant with respect to the parameter being optimised, not necessarily independent of the data.

\sim N\bigl(m_*,\sigma^2\{1+h(x_*)\}\bigr). Integrating over the inverse-Gamma variance posterior gives \mu_*\mid D\sim t_8\bigl(m_*,s\sqrt{h(x_*)}\bigr), \widetilde Y\mid D,x_*\sim t_8\bigl(m_*,s\sqrt{1+h(x_*)}\bigr). At x_*=0, m_*=(1,0)\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}=1,
\qquad h(0)=\frac1{10}. Therefore the unknown mean response has posterior \boxed{\mu_*\mid D\sim t_8(1,\sqrt{0.2}),} with equal-tailed 95% credible interval 1\pm2.306\sqrt{0.2}=1\pm1.0313,
\qquad\boxed{(-0.031,\,2.031).} The new observation has posterior predictive distribution \boxed{\widetilde Y\mid D,x_*=0\sim t_8(1,\sqrt{2.2}),} with equal-tailed 95% predictive interval 1\pm2.306\sqrt{2.2}=1\pm3.4204,
\qquad\boxed{(-2.420,\,4.420).} Both intervals have the same centre and use the same t_8 quantile. The predictive interval is wider because a new observation includes both uncertainty about the regression mean and fresh observational noise. That additional noise produces the extra 1 in 1+h(x_*).
(d) Extrapolation and predictive scale. Using the supplied diagonal matrix, \begin{aligned}
h(x_*)&=(1,x_*)
\begin{pmatrix}1/10&0\\0&1/40\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}1\\x_*\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\frac1{10}+\frac{x_*^2}{40}.
\end{aligned} Hence \boxed{h(0)=0.1,\qquad h(4)=0.1+\frac{16}{40}=0.5.} The corresponding predictive scales are \boxed{s_{\mathrm{pred}}(0)=\sqrt{2(1+0.1)}=\sqrt{2.2}\approx1.4832,} \boxed{s_{\mathrm{pred}}(4)=\sqrt{2(1+0.5)}=\sqrt3\approx1.7321.} At x_*=4, the predicted centre is 1+2(4)=9, so the predictive distribution is t_8(9,\sqrt3). Its interval is wider than at x_*=0 because it has the same degrees of freedom but a larger scale.
The value 4 lies outside the observed range [-3,3]. Uncertainty about the slope has a greater effect on the fitted mean farther from the centred design, increasing h(x_*). The future-error contribution is unchanged; the increased width comes from greater parameter uncertainty in the prediction. This calculation assumes the linear model remains appropriate beyond the observed range; it does not account for possible failure of that model there.

Key result. The mean-response scale is s\sqrt h; the new-observation scale is s\sqrt{1+h}. The extra 1 represents new observational noise, while h measures uncertainty about the fitted mean.

title: Posterior summaries from draws
text:
Proposition taught in Bayesian foundations, part of Bayesian statistics
Let \theta^{(1)},\ldots,\theta^{(L)} be posterior draws and let \theta_{(1)}\leq\cdots\leq\theta_{(L)} be their order statistics. Then \begin{align*}
\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(\theta\mid x)
&=\frac1L\sum_{l=1}^L\theta^{(l)},\\
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\theta\mid x)
&=\frac1{L-1}\sum_{l=1}^L
   \left(\theta^{(l)}-\overline\theta\right)^2,\\
\widehat{\mathbb{P}}(\theta<c\mid x)
&=\frac1L\sum_{l=1}^L\mathbf{1}\{\theta^{(l)}<c\}.
\end{align*} The posterior median and equal-tailed interval are estimated by the corresponding empirical quantiles. With L=1000, the median can be estimated by the average of \theta_{(500)} and \theta_{(501)}, and a direct 95\% interval approximation by [\theta_{(25)},\theta_{(975)}]. The precise indices vary slightly with a software package’s quantile convention.

title: Posterior summaries from draws
text:
Examples

Practice set: Q25. Gibbs, Metropolis–Hastings, and Monte Carlo error

Question page: Q25. Gibbs, Metropolis–Hastings, and Monte Carlo error

[25 marks]
Consider two random variables X and Y with joint density f(x,y)\propto x^3y\exp(-xy-2x-3y),
\qquad x>0,\quad y>0, and zero density elsewhere.
Support clarification: the supplied screenshot does not state the support. This question uses the positive quadrant.
(a) [10 marks] Describe a Gibbs sampler to generate samples from the above joint density.
(b) [10 marks] Describe a random-walk Metropolis–Hastings algorithm to generate samples from the above joint density, using proposal increments distributed as N_2(\mathbf 0,\sigma^2I_2), where I_2 is the identity matrix and \sigma>0 is fixed.
(c) [5 marks] Briefly describe how you would obtain an approximate 95% confidence interval for \mathbb{E}(Y) from the simulation output.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Take the joint support to be x,y>0. We use \operatorname{Gamma}(a,b) in shape–rate form, with kernel z^{a-1}e^{-bz} on z>0. N_2(\mathbf m,\Sigma) uses a covariance matrix \Sigma, and I_2 is the 2\times2 identity. The estimand in (c) is the fixed target mean \mu_Y=\mathbb{E}_f(Y); its simulation uncertainty is measured by a Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE).
(a) Gibbs sampler. For the conditional distribution of X, fix y>0 and retain all factors involving x: \begin{aligned}
f(x\mid y)&\propto x^3y\exp(-xy-2x-3y)\\
&\propto x^3\exp\{-(y+2)x\},\qquad x>0.
\end{aligned} The power 3=4-1 identifies shape 4, and the coefficient of x in the negative exponential is the rate y+2. Thus \boxed{X\mid Y=y\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(4,y+2).} Similarly, fixing x>0 gives f(y\mid x)\propto y\exp\{-(x+3)y\},\qquad y>0, and hence \boxed{Y\mid X=x\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(2,x+3).} The corresponding normalised conditional densities are f(x\mid y)=\frac{(y+2)^4}{\Gamma(4)}x^3e^{-(y+2)x},
\qquad
f(y\mid x)=\frac{(x+3)^2}{\Gamma(2)}y e^{-(x+3)y}.
Choose any valid initial pair (x^{(0)},y^{(0)}) with both coordinates positive. A systematic-scan Gibbs sampler is:
1. For t=1,\ldots,T, draw X^{(t)}\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(4,Y^{(t-1)}+2).
2. Using this newly drawn value, draw Y^{(t)}\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(2,X^{(t)}+3).
3. Record the pair (X^{(t)},Y^{(t)}) and repeat.
Every draw is from an exact full conditional, so there is no accept–reject step. Each conditional update preserves the target joint distribution; their composition therefore has f(x,y) as an equilibrium distribution. After checking convergence and allowing suitable warm-up, retained pairs can be used to approximate target expectations. Successive pairs are generally dependent, not iid.
(b) Random-walk Metropolis–Hastings. Let the current state be (x,y) with x,y>0. Draw an increment \boldsymbol\varepsilon\sim N_2(\mathbf 0,\sigma^2I_2) and propose (x',y')=(x,y)+\boldsymbol\varepsilon. Equivalently, the proposed state is N_2((x,y)^\top,\sigma^2I_2). The zero-mean normal distribution describes the increment, not an independence proposal centred at the origin.
The proposal is symmetric: q\bigl((x',y')\mid(x,y)\bigr)
=q\bigl((x,y)\mid(x',y')\bigr), because reversing the increment leaves its squared length unchanged. Thus the proposal densities cancel from the Metropolis–Hastings ratio. For a proposal in the positive quadrant, \begin{aligned}
r&=\frac{f(x',y')}{f(x,y)}\\
&=\frac{(x')^3y' e^{-x'y'-2x'-3y'}}{x^3y e^{-xy-2x-3y}}\\
&=\left(\frac{x'}x\right)^3\frac{y'}y
\exp\{-x'y'+xy-2(x'-x)-3(y'-y)\}.
\end{aligned} Therefore the acceptance probability is \boxed{
a\bigl((x,y),(x',y')\bigr)=
\begin{cases}
\min\{1,r\},&x'>0,\ y'>0,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}} The unknown normalising constant of f cancels in the target-density ratio.
Start from a valid positive pair. For each iteration t=1,\ldots,T:
1. Draw an independent N_2(\mathbf0,\sigma^2I_2) increment and add it to (X^{(t-1)},Y^{(t-1)}) to obtain (x',y').
2. If either proposed coordinate is nonpositive, reject the proposal. Otherwise compute a above and draw U\sim U(0,1) independently; accept if U\leq a.
3. On acceptance set (X^{(t)},Y^{(t)})=(x',y'); on rejection set (X^{(t)},Y^{(t)})=(X^{(t-1)},Y^{(t-1)}).
4. Record the state, including repeated states caused by rejection.
An out-of-support proposal is rejected, not repeatedly redrawn until it is positive: such redrawing would change the proposal distribution and its acceptance ratio. Assess convergence before using the retained output.
(c) A 95% confidence interval for \mathbb{E}(Y). The target is the fixed number \mu_Y=\mathbb{E}_f(Y), estimated using a Monte Carlo average. After suitable warm-up and convergence checks, retain N consecutive values Y_1,\ldots,Y_N and calculate \bar Y_N=\frac1N\sum_{t=1}^{N}Y_t. These values are generally autocorrelated, so the iid standard error s_Y/\sqrt N is not generally valid.
One practical method is batch means. Write N=ab, with a non-overlapping batches of length b, and calculate \bar Y_k^{\mathrm{batch}}=
\frac1b\sum_{t=(k-1)b+1}^{kb}Y_t,\qquad k=1,\ldots,a, s_B^2=\frac1{a-1}\sum_{k=1}^{a}
\bigl(\bar Y_k^{\mathrm{batch}}-\bar Y_N\bigr)^2. With batches long relative to the chain’s dependence and sufficiently many batches, the batch averages are approximately independent and approximately normal under the usual Markov-chain central limit conditions. An estimated Monte Carlo standard error is \widehat{\operatorname{MCSE}}(\bar Y_N)=\frac{s_B}{\sqrt a}. An approximate 95% confidence interval is then \boxed{\bar Y_N\ \pm\ t_{0.975,a-1}\frac{s_B}{\sqrt a}.} For large a, the t quantile can be replaced by 1.96. The simulation should be long enough for the interval to be reasonably stable when the batch length is increased.
Equivalently, for a stationary chain satisfying a central limit theorem, \sqrt N(\bar Y_N-\mu_Y)\ \xrightarrow{d}\ N(0,\tau_Y^2), where the long-run variance is \tau_Y^2=\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k,
\qquad \gamma_k=\operatorname{Cov}(Y_t,Y_{t+k}). Batch means estimates this variance by \widehat\tau_Y^2=b s_B^2, giving the same standard error \sqrt{\widehat\tau_Y^2/N}=s_B/\sqrt a.

Key result. This interval measures Monte Carlo error in estimating \mathbb{E}(Y). The empirical 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the Y_t values instead give an interval for the variable Y; they are not a confidence interval for its mean.






Concept check: C11. Monte Carlo estimation

Question page: C11. Monte Carlo estimation

What is a Monte Carlo estimate of \mathbb{E}_\pi[h(\Theta)], and what is Monte Carlo error?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. For a target distribution \pi and integrable function h, a Monte Carlo estimate is N^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^N h(\theta^{(t)}), using independent draws from \pi or suitable ergodic MCMC output. Monte Carlo error is the finite-simulation discrepancy from \mathbb{E}_\pi[h(\Theta)], not the posterior uncertainty about \Theta; its assessment must account for dependence when draws are correlated.

title: Predictive-variance decomposition
Predictive-variance decomposition
text:
Examples

Practice set: Q20. Estimation and prediction

Question page: Q20. Estimation and prediction

[4 marks]
Suppose measurements are conditionally independent with X_i\mid\mu\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2), where \sigma^2>0 is known, and a proper Normal prior is used for \mu.
Explain the difference between the posterior distribution of \mu and the posterior predictive distribution of one new measurement. As the number of observations becomes very large, would you expect uncertainty about both quantities to approach zero? Explain your reasoning.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. \mu is the population mean and \widetilde X is a new observation. Write \mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim N(m_n,v_n), where v_n is the posterior variance. The known observation variance is \sigma^2>0; conditional on \mu, the new Normal observation is independent of the original sample. A predictive distribution averages over parameter uncertainty as well as new-observation noise.
The posterior distribution p(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}) describes remaining uncertainty about the unknown population mean \mu after observing the data. The posterior predictive distribution p(\widetilde x\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\int p(\widetilde x\mid\mu)
p(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\,d\mu describes uncertainty about a future observation \widetilde X. It includes both uncertainty about \mu and the new observation’s sampling variation around \mu.
If \mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(m_n,v_n), then \boxed{
\widetilde X\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\mathcal{N}(m_n,\sigma^2+v_n).
} As n\to\infty, under the model and standard regularity conditions, v_n\longrightarrow0. Hence posterior uncertainty about \mu approaches zero. By contrast, \operatorname{Var}(\widetilde X\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{new-observation noise}}
+\underbrace{v_n}_{\text{parameter uncertainty}}
\longrightarrow\sigma^2. Predictive uncertainty therefore does not vanish: even if \mu were known exactly, a future measurement would still vary randomly around it.

title: Proper prior and proper posterior
text:
Definition taught in Bayesian foundations, part of Bayesian statistics
A prior is proper if it is a probability distribution, so its total mass is one. A posterior is proper if the product of likelihood and prior has a finite, nonzero normalising constant. An improper prior may sometimes produce a proper posterior, but this must be checked rather than assumed.

title: Proper prior and proper posterior
text:
Properties

A proper approximation to the flat prior

Main article: A proper approximation to the flat prior

The honest bounded version of the improper kernel p(\mu)\propto1 is

p_C(\mu)=\frac1{2C}\mathbf{1}\{-C\leq\mu\leq C\}.

Taking, for example, C=10^4 makes this density nearly constant over an ordinary data range while keeping it proper. It also exposes what “very diffuse” means. For any fixed 0<M<C,

\mathbb{P}_C(|\mu|\leq M)=\int_{-M}^{M}\frac1{2C}\,\mathrm{d}\mu=\frac MC
\longrightarrow0
\qquad(C\longrightarrow\infty).

Thus the limiting sequence puts essentially all of its probability beyond every fixed finite range; it does not converge to a uniform probability distribution on \mathbb{R}. Human height makes the point concrete: no observed person is three metres tall, yet a sufficiently broad uniform prior assigns almost no mass to the entire range of heights that have actually been encountered.

title: Proper prior and proper posterior
text:
Examples

Final preparation: Question 12. Improper prior for a normal sample

Question page: Question 12. Improper prior for a normal sample

The prior and the sample are

f(\mu,\sigma^{2})\propto 1/\sigma^{2},
\qquad
x_1,\ldots,x_n\mid\mu,\sigma^{2}\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2}),

with n\geq 2.
(i) Derive the joint posterior kernel of (\mu,\sigma^{2}). [2 marks]
(ii) Show that \sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\mu)^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar x)^{2}+n(\mu-\bar x)^{2}. [2 marks]
(iii) Show that \mu\mid\sigma^{2},{\boldsymbol{x}} is normal, and give its mean and variance. [2 marks]
(iv) Show that \sigma^{2}\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}} is inverse-gamma, and give its shape and rate. [2 marks]
(v) Describe how to sample from the joint posterior. [4 marks]
(vi) Describe 90\% posterior credible intervals for \mu and for \sigma^{2}. [2 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write v=\sigma^2, \bar x=n^{-1}\sum_i x_i and S=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2, the unnormalised sum of squares. The prior p(\mu,v)\propto1/v is a density kernel relative to d\mu\,dv, and \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b) has kernel v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v}. Take the observed sample to be nonconstant (S>0), as required for a proper posterior with this improper prior.
(i) The likelihood contributes (\sigma^{2})^{-n/2}\exp\bigl(-\sum(x_i-\mu)^{2}/(2\sigma^{2})\bigr), and the prior contributes \sigma^{-2}. For \sigma^{2}>0,

f(\mu,\sigma^{2}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
\propto
(\sigma^{2})^{-n/2-1}
\exp\Bigl(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\mu)^{2}\Bigr).

(ii)

\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\mu)^{2}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar x+\bar x-\mu)^{2}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar x)^{2}+n(\mu-\bar x)^{2},

because \sum(x_i-\bar x)=0.
(iii) Let S=\sum(x_i-\bar x)^{2}. By (ii), the kernel in \mu is \exp\bigl(-n(\mu-\bar x)^{2}/(2\sigma^{2})\bigr). Thus

\mu\mid\sigma^{2},{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim \operatorname{N}(\bar x,\,\sigma^{2}/n).

(iv) The kernel in \sigma^{2} is

(\sigma^{2})^{-(n/2)-1}
\exp\Bigl(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\mu)^{2}\Bigr).


\boxed{\sigma^{2}\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim
\operatorname{InvGamma}\Bigl(\frac n2,\;\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\mu)^{2}\Bigr).}

(v) The two full conditionals give a valid Gibbs sampler, but direct independent draws are available. Integrate the joint kernel over \mu. By (ii), the normal integral contributes \sqrt{2\pi v/n}, so

\begin{aligned}
p(v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto v^{-n/2-1}e^{-S/(2v)}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-n(\mu-\bar x)^2/(2v)}\,d\mu\\
&\propto v^{-(n-1)/2-1}e^{-S/(2v)}.
\end{aligned}

Thus v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}((n-1)/2,S/2) when S>0. For each independent posterior pair, draw v from this marginal and then \mu\mid v,{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{N}(\bar x,v/n). This samples p(\mu,v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=p(v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})p(\mu\mid v,{\boldsymbol{x}}) exactly, with no burn-in. The pairs are independent across draws, though \mu and v within a pair are dependent. The marginal shape (n-1)/2 differs from the full-conditional shape n/2 because integrating over \mu contributes v^{1/2}.
If using Gibbs instead, initialise v^{(0)}>0 and alternate

\mu^{(t)}\sim\operatorname{N}(\bar x,v^{(t-1)}/n),\qquad
v^{(t)}\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\left(\frac n2,\frac{S+n(\mu^{(t)}-\bar x)^2}{2}\right).

These are dependent Markov-chain draws, so convergence must be assessed. Setting \mu=\bar x in the variance full conditional would not give the marginal variance posterior: it would still have shape n/2 and would miss the integration factor above.
(vi) Let F_{\mathrm{IG}} be the CDF of \operatorname{InvGamma}((n-1)/2,S/2). A central 90\% credible interval for v=\sigma^2 is [F_{\mathrm{IG}}^{-1}(0.05),F_{\mathrm{IG}}^{-1}(0.95)]. Integrating v out gives \mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}} a Student-t distribution with n-1 degrees of freedom, centre \bar x and scale \sqrt{S/[n(n-1)]}. Hence its central 90\% interval is

\boxed{\bar x\ \pm\ t_{0.95,n-1}\sqrt{\frac{S}{n(n-1)}}.}

Empirical 5\% and 95\% quantiles of the direct draws are an alternative approximation to these intervals.





Practice set: Q43. Unknown Normal mean and variance: conditional versus marginal

Question page: Q43. Unknown Normal mean and variance: conditional versus marginal

[14 marks]
Suppose X_1,\ldots,X_n\mid\mu,v
\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(\mu,v),
\qquad p(\mu,v)\propto\frac1v, where \mu\in\mathbb R, v>0, n\ge2, and S=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2>0. Use the inverse-Gamma convention f(v)\propto v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v}.
(a) Establish the identity \sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2=S+n(\mu-\bar x)^2. [2 marks]
(b) Derive the full conditional distributions \mu\mid v,{\boldsymbol{x}} and v\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}}. [4 marks]
(c) Integrate out \mu to derive p(v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}). Explain why it differs from p(v\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}}). [4 marks]
(d) Describe a Gibbs sampler using part (b). A student instead samples v from its marginal posterior, then \mu conditional on that draw, repeating with fresh random numbers. Is this also a valid way to sample the joint posterior? Are its resulting pairs independent? [4 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write v=\sigma^2, \bar x=n^{-1}\sum_i x_i, and S=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2, the unnormalised sum of squares. We use N(m,v) with variance v and \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b) with kernel v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v} on v>0. A full conditional fixes the other parameter; a marginal posterior integrates it out.
Assumptions. The Normal observations are conditionally iid, with prior p(\mu,v)\propto1/v relative to d\mu\,dv. Because this prior is improper, require n\ge2 and S>0 for the posterior below to be proper.
(a) Sum-of-squares identity. Write x_i-\mu=(x_i-\bar x)+(\bar x-\mu) and expand: \begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2
&=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2
+2(\bar x-\mu)\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)
+n(\bar x-\mu)^2\\
&=\boxed{S+n(\mu-\bar x)^2},
\end{aligned} because \sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=0.
(b) Full conditional distributions. The likelihood and joint posterior kernels are L(\mu,v;{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto
v^{-n/2}\exp\left\{-\frac{S+n(\mu-\bar x)^2}{2v}\right\}, p(\mu,v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto
v^{-n/2-1}\exp\left\{-\frac{S+n(\mu-\bar x)^2}{2v}\right\},
\qquad \mu\in\mathbb R,\ v>0. For fixed v, retain only factors involving \mu: p(\mu\mid v,{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto
\exp\left\{-\frac{n(\mu-\bar x)^2}{2v}\right\}. Recognising a Normal kernel, \boxed{\mu\mid v,{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim N\!\left(\bar x,\frac vn\right).} For fixed \mu, retain all the v-dependent factors: p(v\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto
v^{-n/2-1}\exp\left\{-\frac{S+n(\mu-\bar x)^2}{2v}\right\}. Under the stated inverse-Gamma convention, \boxed{
v\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim
\operatorname{InvGamma}\!\left(\frac n2,\frac{S+n(\mu-\bar x)^2}{2}\right).
} Its support is v>0. In this conditional distribution, \mu is held fixed; it has not been replaced by \bar x or integrated out.
(c) Marginal posterior for v. Integrate the joint posterior kernel over all \mu\in\mathbb R: \begin{aligned}
p(v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto v^{-n/2-1}e^{-S/(2v)}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\exp\left\{-\frac{n(\mu-\bar x)^2}{2v}\right\}\,d\mu\\
&=v^{-n/2-1}e^{-S/(2v)}\sqrt{\frac{2\pi v}{n}}\\
&\propto v^{-(n-1)/2-1}e^{-S/(2v)}.
\end{aligned} Therefore \boxed{v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\!\left(\frac{n-1}{2},\frac S2\right),
\qquad v>0.} The assumptions n\ge2 and S>0 make both parameters positive, so the posterior is proper despite the improper prior.
The marginal distribution accounts for uncertainty in \mu by integrating over it. The integral contributes a factor v^{1/2}, changing the shape from n/2 to (n-1)/2. Even setting \mu=\bar x in the full conditional does not produce the marginal posterior, because it misses this factor.
(d) Gibbs sampling and direct joint sampling. Start from any \mu^{(0)}\in\mathbb R and v^{(0)}>0. At iteration t=1,\ldots,T, draw \mu^{(t)}\sim N\!\left(\bar x,\frac{v^{(t-1)}}n\right), v^{(t)}\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\!\left(
\frac n2,\frac{S+n(\mu^{(t)}-\bar x)^2}{2}\right). Each update uses the latest available value of the other parameter. The resulting Markov chain has the joint posterior as its equilibrium distribution; successive pairs are generally dependent, and convergence from the chosen starting value must be assessed.
The student’s alternative is also valid. Independently for each repetition, draw v^{(t)}\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\!\left(\frac{n-1}{2},\frac S2\right),
\qquad
\mu^{(t)}\mid v^{(t)}\sim N\!\left(\bar x,\frac{v^{(t)}}n\right). This samples the factorisation p(\mu,v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=p(v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})p(\mu\mid v,{\boldsymbol{x}}) directly. With fresh independent random numbers for each repetition, the pairs are iid joint-posterior draws, with no burn-in required. The two components within a pair are not independent: the conditional variance of \mu depends on v.

title: Quasi-score and quasi-likelihood
text:
Definition taught in Underdispersion, positive responses, and quasi-likelihood, part of Generalised linear models
If \mathrm{Var}(Y)=\phi V(\mu), the quasi-score in the mean is 
S_\mu=\frac{Y-\mu}{\phi V(\mu)}.
 If the mean depends on covariates through \mu({\boldsymbol{X}}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}), the quasi-score in \boldsymbol{\beta} is 
{\boldsymbol{S}}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
=\frac{Y-\mu}{\phi V(\mu)}\,\mu'({\boldsymbol{X}}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta})\,{\boldsymbol{X}}.

title: Quasi-score and quasi-likelihood
text:
Examples

Practice set: Q47. Overdispersion and quasi-Poisson inference

Question page: Q47. Overdispersion and quasi-Poisson inference

[10 marks]
For independent counts, suppose \mathbb{E}(Y_i)=\mu_i=\exp(\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta),
\qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\phi\mu_i.
(a) Explain what \phi>1 means relative to a Poisson model. [2 marks]
(b) Using the quasi-score U(\boldsymbol\beta)
        =\sum_i\frac{Y_i-\mu_i}{\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)}
        \frac{\partial\mu_i}{\partial\boldsymbol\beta}, show why the coefficient estimates coincide with the Poisson estimates when the data and mean model are unchanged. [3 marks]
(c) A coefficient has Poisson standard error 0.10. If \hat\phi=4, find its quasi-Poisson standard error. Explain the effect on a Wald statistic. [2 marks]
(d) Does specifying the mean and variance above determine a complete probability distribution? Explain why an ordinary likelihood-ratio test cannot automatically be applied. [3 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Let \mu_i=e^{\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta}, where \mathbf x_i is a fixed predictor column vector. The dispersion \phi>0 scales variance to \phi\mu_i. A quasi-score weights residuals by the inverse assumed variance and the derivative of the mean; it is an estimating equation, not necessarily the derivative of a full log-likelihood. Standard error is the square root of an estimated coefficient variance.
Assumptions. Compare fits to the same data using the same unpenalised log-linear mean, conditionally independent observations, and a common dispersion \phi. The design and fitted solution must support finite, identifiable coefficient estimates and the stated covariance calculation. Equality of estimates is not asserted for different mean models, penalties, or observation-specific dispersion.
(a) Meaning of \phi>1. A Poisson model has \operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\mathbb{E}(Y_i)=\mu_i. Here \operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\phi\mu_i, so \phi>1 means overdispersion: at the same expected count, the variance is \phi times the Poisson variance.
(b) Equality of the coefficient estimates. For \mu_i=e^{\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta}, \frac{\partial\mu_i}{\partial\boldsymbol\beta}=\mu_i\mathbf x_i. Substitution into the supplied quasi-score gives \begin{aligned}
U(\boldsymbol\beta)
&=\sum_i\frac{Y_i-\mu_i}{\phi\mu_i}\mu_i\mathbf x_i\\
&=\frac1\phi\sum_i\mathbf x_i(Y_i-\mu_i)
=\boxed{\frac1\phi S_{\mathrm{Poisson}}(\boldsymbol\beta)}.
\end{aligned} Because \phi>0 is a common scalar, U(\boldsymbol\beta)=\mathbf0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
S_{\mathrm{Poisson}}(\boldsymbol\beta)=\mathbf0. The same data and mean model therefore give the same fitted coefficients, when the estimates exist and are well defined. Estimating the common dispersion does not change these estimating equations’ roots.
(c) Standard error and Wald statistic. The usual model-based covariance matrix is multiplied by \hat\phi: \widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_{\mathrm{quasi}}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})
=\hat\phi(X^\top\widehat WX)^{-1},
\qquad \widehat W=\operatorname{diag}(\widehat\mu_i). Thus standard errors are multiplied by \sqrt{\hat\phi}, not by \hat\phi itself: \boxed{\operatorname{SE}_{\mathrm{quasi}}=\sqrt4(0.10)=0.20.} For a fixed null value \beta_{j,0}, the signed Wald statistic becomes z_{\mathrm{quasi}}
=\frac{\widehat\beta_j-\beta_{j,0}}{0.20}
=\frac12z_{\mathrm{Poisson}}. Its squared version is one quarter as large. Against the same reference distribution, this gives weaker evidence against the null; it does not necessarily change a particular reject/non-reject decision.
(d) Is a full probability distribution specified? No. A mean and variance alone do not determine all the count probabilities. Quasi-Poisson inference specifies these moments and an estimating equation, not a unique probability mass function. There is therefore no ordinary full likelihood supplied by these assumptions from which to construct an ordinary likelihood-ratio test automatically. A valid test needs an appropriate quasi-likelihood calibration or an additional fully specified distributional model; a Poisson likelihood-ratio test cannot simply ignore the overdispersion.





Concept check: C27. Quasilikelihood

Question page: C27. Quasilikelihood

What is a quasilikelihood model? What must be specified instead of a full response distribution?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. A quasilikelihood model specifies a mean \mu_i=g^{-1}(x_i^\top\beta) and variance \phi V(\mu_i), rather than a full response distribution. For independent responses its quasi-score is built from (Y_i-\mu_i)\{\phi V(\mu_i)\}^{-1}\partial\mu_i/\partial\beta, whose expectation is zero when the mean model is correct.

title: Stationarity and detailed balance
text:
Definition taught in Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings, part of Bayesian statistics
A distribution \pi is stationary if a state distributed as \pi remains distributed as \pi after one transition. The global balance equation is 
\pi(y)=\sum_x\pi(x)q(y\mid x)
\quad\text{or}\quad
\pi(y)=\int\pi(x)q(y\mid x)\,\mathrm{d} x.
 A stronger sufficient condition is detailed balance: 
\pi(x)q(y\mid x)=\pi(y)q(x\mid y)
\quad\text{for all }x,y.

title: Stationarity and detailed balance
text:
Properties

Detailed balance implies stationarity

Main article: Detailed balance implies stationarity

If a transition kernel q satisfies Equation (3) in Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings for a probability distribution \pi, then \pi satisfies global balance and is a stationary distribution of the chain.

title: Stationarity and detailed balance
text:
Examples

Four-state random walk

Worked example from Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings

Question. Consider states 1,2,3,4 arranged in a line. At every state the chain stays put with probability 1/2. From an endpoint it moves to the only neighbour with probability 1/2; from an interior state it moves left or right with probability 1/4 each. With columns indexing the current state and rows the next state, construct the transition matrix and find the stationary distribution.
Solution. The transition matrix is

{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{Q}}=
\begin{pmatrix}
1/2&1/4&0&0\\
1/2&1/2&1/4&0\\
0&1/4&1/2&1/2\\
0&0&1/4&1/2
\end{pmatrix}.

Detailed balance between states 1 and 2 requires

\pi_1\frac12=\pi_2\frac14
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\pi_2=2\pi_1.

Similarly,

\pi_2\frac14=\pi_3\frac14
\Longrightarrow\pi_3=\pi_2,
\qquad
\pi_3\frac14=\pi_4\frac12
\Longrightarrow\pi_3=2\pi_4.

Hence

{\boldsymbol{\pi}}=(\pi_1,\pi_2,\pi_3,\pi_4)^{\mathsf T}
\propto(1,2,2,1)^{\mathsf T}.

Normalising by 1+2+2+1=6 gives

\boxed{{\boldsymbol{\pi}}=(1/6,2/6,2/6,1/6)^{\mathsf T}}.



Concept check: C12. Markov property and invariance

Question page: C12. Markov property and invariance

What is the Markov property? What does it mean for a distribution to be invariant for a chain?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. The Markov property says that the conditional distribution of the next state, given the whole past, depends only on the current state. A distribution \pi is invariant if one transition preserves it: X^{(t)}\sim\pi implies X^{(t+1)}\sim\pi; this alone does not establish convergence from every initial state.

title: Sufficient statistic
text:
Definition taught in Exponential families and conjugacy, part of Bayesian statistics
A statistic T({\boldsymbol{X}}) is sufficient for \theta if the conditional distribution of {\boldsymbol{X}} given T({\boldsymbol{X}})=t does not depend on \theta.

title: Sufficient statistic
text:
Properties

Fisher–Neyman factorisation

Main article: Fisher–Neyman factorisation

Suppose the family \{p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta):\theta\in\Omega\} is dominated by a common measure. Then T({\boldsymbol{X}}) is sufficient for \theta if and only if there are nonnegative functions g_\theta and h such that 
p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta)
=g_\theta\{T({\boldsymbol{x}})\}h({\boldsymbol{x}}),
\qquad \theta\in\Omega,
 where h does not depend on \theta.


Basu’s theorem

Main article: Basu’s theorem

A complete sufficient statistic is independent of every ancillary statistic.


Pitman–Koopman–Darmois, informal form

Main article: Pitman–Koopman–Darmois, informal form

For regular iid models with parameter-independent support, the theorem says, roughly, that the existence for every n of a sufficient statistic whose dimension stays fixed essentially characterises exponential families. The support condition matters: models such as \operatorname{Uniform}(0,\theta) can have a fixed-dimensional sufficient statistic without having the regular form Equation (3) in Exponential families and conjugacy.

title: Sufficient statistic
text:
Examples

Sufficiency for a normal mean

Worked example from Exponential families and conjugacy

Suppose

X_1,\ldots,X_n\mid\mu
\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^2),
\qquad \sigma^2\text{ known}.

Question. Use the Fisher–Neyman factorisation theorem to find a sufficient statistic for \mu. Then identify a sufficient statistic when both \mu and \sigma^2 are unknown.
Solution. The joint density is \begin{align*}
p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\mu)
&=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}
   \exp\!\left\{-\frac1{2\sigma^2}
   \sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2\right\}.
\end{align*} Expand the quadratic: \begin{align*}
\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2
&=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i^2-2\mu x_i+\mu^2)\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^nx_i^2
   -2\mu\sum_{i=1}^nx_i
   +n\mu^2.
\end{align*} Substitution gives \begin{align*}
p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\mu)
&=\underbrace{
   (2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}
   \exp\!\left\{-\frac1{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^nx_i^2\right\}}
   _{h({\boldsymbol{x}})}\\
&\quad\times
   \underbrace{
   \exp\!\left\{
    \frac{\mu}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^nx_i
    -\frac{n\mu^2}{2\sigma^2}\right\}}
   _{g_\mu\{T({\boldsymbol{x}})\}}.
\end{align*} All dependence on \mu passes through

T({\boldsymbol{x}})=\sum_{i=1}^nx_i.

The factorisation theorem therefore proves that \sum_iX_i is sufficient for \mu. Since \overline X=T/n is a one-to-one function of T when n is fixed, \overline X is equivalent and is also sufficient.
If both \mu and \sigma^2 are unknown, the displayed factorisation no longer isolates all parameter dependence through \sum_iX_i. A sufficient statistic for (\mu,\sigma^2) is instead

\left(\sum_{i=1}^nX_i,\sum_{i=1}^nX_i^2\right),

or equivalently

\left(\overline X,\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\overline X)^2\right).

This is the nuisance-parameter warning in concrete form.


Book exercise: Sufficiency and the posterior

Question page: Sufficiency and the posterior

Let {\boldsymbol{X}}=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)^{\mathsf T} have likelihood p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta) and prior p(\theta). If U({\boldsymbol{X}}) is sufficient for \theta, use the Fisher–Neyman factorisation theorem and Bayes’ rule to show that the posterior depends on the observed sample only through U({\boldsymbol{x}}). Retain the normalising integral in the derivation.






Worked answer (click to show)





Question. Let {\boldsymbol{X}}=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)^{\mathsf T} have likelihood p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta) and prior p(\theta). If U({\boldsymbol{X}}) is sufficient for \theta, use the Fisher–Neyman factorisation theorem and Bayes’ rule to show that the posterior depends on the observed sample only through U({\boldsymbol{x}}). Retain the normalising integral in the derivation.
Solution. By the Fisher–Neyman factorisation theorem, sufficiency of U({\boldsymbol{X}}) implies that there are nonnegative functions g and h such that

p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta)=g\{U({\boldsymbol{x}}),\theta\}h({\boldsymbol{x}}),

where h does not depend on \theta. Bayes’ rule, including its normalising integral, gives \begin{align*}
p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=\frac{p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta)p(\theta)}
{\displaystyle\int p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid t)p(t)\,\mathrm{d} t}\\
&=\frac{g\{U({\boldsymbol{x}}),\theta\}h({\boldsymbol{x}})p(\theta)}
{\displaystyle\int g\{U({\boldsymbol{x}}),t\}h({\boldsymbol{x}})p(t)\,\mathrm{d} t}\\
&=\boxed{
\frac{g\{U({\boldsymbol{x}}),\theta\}p(\theta)}
{\displaystyle\int g\{U({\boldsymbol{x}}),t\}p(t)\,\mathrm{d} t}}.
\end{align*} Every occurrence of the observed sample is through U({\boldsymbol{x}}); the factor h({\boldsymbol{x}}) cancels because it is constant with respect to the integration variable and the parameter.





Concept check: C3. Sufficiency

Question page: C3. Sufficiency

What is a sufficient statistic, using the conditional-distribution definition?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. A statistic T(X) is a function of the sample alone and is sufficient for \theta if the conditional distribution of X given T(X) does not depend on \theta. Thus, within the assumed model, the remaining sample details add no information about \theta once T(X) is known.

title: The Beta distribution is the two-category Dirichlet
text:
Proposition taught in Categorical data and the Dirichlet distribution, part of Bayesian statistics
When K=2, write p_1=p and p_2=1-p. Restricting the Dirichlet density to the one-dimensional simplex gives
p(p\mid\alpha_1,\alpha_2)
=\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_1+\alpha_2)}
        {\Gamma(\alpha_1)\Gamma(\alpha_2)}
   p^{\alpha_1-1}(1-p)^{\alpha_2-1},
which is exactly \operatorname{Beta}(\alpha_1,\alpha_2). The Dirichlet is therefore a genuine extension of the Beta family rather than merely a similar-looking density.
