title: Smooth means
text:
Part of Smoothing · 5 questions on this topic · What links here
A coefficient is worth having when you can say what a unit change does. In a linear model, \beta_j is the change in the mean. In a log-linear model, e^{\beta_j} is the multiplicative change. In a logit model, \beta_j is the change in log-odds. Powers, logarithms, and products of covariates are still linear in the parameters, and they are still GLMs. The limitation is that you had to name the function before you saw the curve.
Sometimes nothing in the science names it. Dosage and exposure want a logarithm for a reason we have already used. A rate wants a log link because the natural parameter said so. A lidar return, plotted against distance, does not offer you that sentence in advance.

title: Smooth means
text:
Lidar
Ruppert, Wand, and Carroll’s lidar data take Y to be the log ratio of received light to emitted light, and x the range in feet. A perfect return would sit at 0. Some points sit above 0 because the room is not dark: the sensor records the laser plus whatever else is shining. Out to roughly 500 or 550 feet the mean is flat. Past that threshold it drops, sharply, and the scatter widens as the mean falls. A laser gets weaker with distance and it gets noisier. The variance is a GLM problem, and we already know how to write \mathrm{Var}=\phi V(\mu). The mean is not a quadratic we would have written down before seeing the plot, and we would not want to have to name the threshold.






Figure 1: Lidar log-ratio against range. The narrow window follows the noise. The 25-foot window keeps the drop. The 100-foot window smears it, and the scatter widens once the mean has fallen.



A moving window is the first smoother you are likely to have seen. In Figure 1, averaging within \pm 5 feet leaves a noisy curve. Within \pm 25 feet it is calmer but still jagged on the drop. Within \pm 100 feet it is smooth and it has smeared the drop. A single window width cannot be wide where the noise is large and narrow where the signal is sharp. The window also ignores the mean-variance relationship, so it oversmooths the precise part of the curve and undersmooths the noisy part. The penalty has to live on the likelihood scale, where a GLM already knows that a residual at a large mean is not the same as a residual at a small one.

title: Smooth means
text:
A roughness penalty
Green and Silverman’s formulation is the clean one, even though we no longer compute it with a knot at every x. Keep the exponential family. Replace the linear predictor by an unknown smooth function g(x), and keep the canonical link, so the mean is -c'(g(x)) in the sign convention of the first chapter. For the normal that is g(x) itself. For the Poisson it is \exp(g(x)), which stays positive whatever g does. For the Bernoulli it is the expit of g(x), which stays inside (0,1). For the gamma the canonical choice is 1/g(x), and that still requires g not to change sign. You may use a log link for the gamma instead. Nothing forces the canonical link once you have decided the mean is smooth rather than linear.
Maximise the log-likelihood and charge for curvature: 
\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl\{y_i g(x_i)-c(g(x_i))\bigr\}
-\frac{\lambda}{2}\int \{g''(x)\}^2\,\mathrm{d}x.
 The first piece wants g to pass through the data. The integral of the squared second derivative is large when the curve turns often. A straight line has second derivative zero and pays nothing. A sine wave pays on every oscillation. \lambda is the exchange rate between fidelity and smoothness. The half is cosmetic: for the normal likelihood it cancels the usual factor of one half.
The maximiser, for any fixed \lambda, is a cubic spline with a knot at each distinct x_i. Inside each interval the function is a cubic. At each knot the function, the first derivative, and the second derivative agree from the left and the right. Your eye can see those three. It cannot see a jump in the third derivative, which is why a cubic, rather than a higher piecewise polynomial, is the one this penalty produces.
Putting a knot at every x_i is expensive, and \lambda itself changes meaning when you change the likelihood. In practice we use a smaller set of knots, ten equally spaced between the smallest and largest x being the usual default, or knots at the deciles if the x values pile up at one end. More knots are available when the sample is in the thousands. And we do not quote \lambda. Cross-validation hides a fraction of the sample, fits on the rest, and scores the hidden points, rotating which fraction is hidden. The software reports the smoothness as an equivalent degrees of freedom: the polynomial degree the curve is about as flexible as. As \lambda\to\infty that degrees of freedom falls to 1, a straight line, which is the ordinary GLM. As \lambda\to 0 the fit interpolates, and if no x values are tied it interpolates perfectly. Interpolation fits noise. It does not predict the next point.

title: Smooth means
text:
Kyphosis and age
Eighty-one children were followed after spinal surgery to see whether kyphosis, a forward bend in the spine, was still present. Age is recorded in months, from infancy out to about 200 months. The ones and zeros rise through the middle ages and fall again. A logistic regression with age as a linear predictor can only ever increase, or only ever decrease. It cannot come back down. So keep the logistic mean, and let the inside be a smooth function centred at zero: 
\mathrm{P}(\text{kyphosis}\mid \text{age})
=\frac{\exp\{\beta_0+g(\text{age})\}}{1+\exp\{\beta_0+g(\text{age})\}},
 where g is constrained to average zero so that \beta_0 is the log-odds at the centre of the age effect. In mgcv,
need <- function(pkg) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  }
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(pkg, character.only = TRUE))
}
need("mgcv")
need("rpart")
data(kyphosis, package = "rpart")
kyphosis$Kyphosis <- as.numeric(kyphosis$Kyphosis == "present")
fit <- gam(Kyphosis ~ s(Age), family = binomial, data = kyphosis)
summary(fit)
s(Age) asks for the smooth. Knots and \lambda are chosen by cross-validation. The plotted smooth is labelled with equivalent degrees of freedom 2.22: more flexible than a quadratic, short of a cubic, and not itself a polynomial of degree 2.22. It is a piecewise cubic whose overall budget of wiggliness is 2.22. The intercept is -1.51 (z=-4.78), so at the centre of g the odds are e^{-1.51}. The smooth term has 
\mathrm{edf}=2.22,\qquad \chi^2=6.69,\qquad p=0.071.
 The equivalent degrees of freedom and the intercept -1.51 are what the code prints. The chi-squared statistic moves with the version of mgcv: one printout was 6.69 with p=0.071, and mgcv 1.8 reports about 6.36 with p=0.076. Either reading is the same decision.






Figure 2: Top: the centred age smooth on the log-odds scale, with the confidence band drawn by mgcv. The dashed line at zero is “age does nothing”, and it just about stays inside the band. Bottom: the fitted probability. The dashed line is a logistic regression that is linear in age, and it cannot come back down.



In Figure 2 a horizontal line at zero just about stays inside the band, and it just about fails to. We do not have a hard rule at 0.05. We keep age. The fitted probability, the expit of \beta_0+g, rises and then falls. That graph is the answer to “how does kyphosis depend on age?”. There is no unit-change sentence, and that is the price of not having specified the shape in advance.
The substantive reading we would offer, cautiously, is a mixture of biology and of who is sent to surgery. Very young children are operated on because the problem is serious, and they also recover more readily. Older adolescents are often milder cases, chosen for correction once the skeleton is more settled. The ages in the middle are the ones whose surgery was delayed and whose bones were no longer infant bones. You cannot randomise the age at which an elective operation happens. The curve is a description of this sample, not a pure age effect.
Number of vertebrae operated on, and where on the spine the operation started, are in the same data set. They are the next chapter. A smooth of age alone is the model this chapter stops on.

In the penalised criterion, what does the fitted g become as \lambda\to\infty, and what does it become as \lambda\to 0 if all the x_i are distinct?
The kyphosis smooth has equivalent degrees of freedom 2.22 and a p-value of about 0.07. Say what each of those numbers is measuring, and why a logistic regression that is linear in age cannot reproduce the shape in the plot.

title: Random intercepts
text:
Part of Correlated data · 1 question on this topic · What links here
Every model so far has taken the responses to be independent given the covariates. Clustering, proximity in space or time, and repeated measures on the same person all break that. Two trees in the same soil can be positively dependent because they share conditions, or negatively dependent because they compete. The negative case is real and, as a correlation matrix for a whole block, surprisingly rigid.
We generate the dependence with a mixed model rather than write down a correlation matrix and stop. A correlation matrix describes association. For a normal response, a mean and a covariance do define a distribution. For a Poisson or a binomial they do not: there is no unique multivariate Poisson with a given set of correlations. A mixed model gives a mechanism. The price is that the correlations it can produce are a narrower set.

title: Random intercepts
text:
A random intercept
Index the block by j and the unit inside the block by i: 
Y_{ji}=\beta_0+{\boldsymbol{X}}_{ji}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}+\alpha_j+\varepsilon_{ji},
 
\alpha_j\stackrel{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}\mathrm{N}(0,\sigma_A^2),
\qquad
\varepsilon_{ji}\stackrel{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}\mathrm{N}(0,\sigma^2),
 with the block effects independent of the residuals. Drop the distribution of \alpha_j and this is an ordinary model with a separate intercept for each block. The extra line says those intercepts are themselves a sample from a population of blocks.
The mean is still the straight line, because both \alpha_j and \varepsilon_{ji} have mean zero. The variance of one response is \sigma_A^2+\sigma^2. Two people in different blocks share nothing, so their covariance is zero. Two people in the same block share \alpha_j, so 
\mathrm{Cov}(Y_{ji},Y_{ji'})=\sigma_A^2,
\qquad
\mathrm{Corr}=\frac{\sigma_A^2}{\sigma_A^2+\sigma^2}.
 The correlation is between 0 and 1. If the blocks are identical, \sigma_A^2\to 0 and the correlation vanishes: it was one big sample. If the block effect swamps the person-to-person noise, the correlation tends to 1: everyone in the hospital looks the same. A linear mixed model of this form cannot produce a negative within-block correlation.
Negative dependence does happen, when units in a block compete for a fixed resource. It is an awkward correlation to write down for every pair at once. A 3\times 3 equicorrelation matrix is positive definite for any correlation in [0,1), but if every pair has correlation -\rho, the matrix is only valid for \rho\le 1/2. In a block of size K the lower bound is -1/(K-1). Add one more person to the block and a correlation that used to be legal becomes illegal. That dependence on the block size is why the random-intercept model’s refusal of negative correlations is acceptable. Competition can be modelled later by letting some pairs differ. A single negative number for every pair in a large block is not a structure worth having.

title: Random intercepts
section: What is fixed, and what is random
text:
What is fixed, and what is random
There is no theorem that sorts the factors. The question is whether the blocks in the study are a sample from a larger population of blocks that need not be named, or whether these particular blocks are the ones to compare.
Seven hospitals, twenty patients each, two treatments for skin cancer. If those seven were a draw from the hospitals in the region that could have run the trial, the hospital intercepts are random: one variance, not seven means, and the target is the treatment contrast in that population of hospitals. If they are the seven largest hospitals and the point of the study is to compare them, the intercepts are fixed. The first line of the model is the same either way. The second line is the decision.
Five fertilisers and six species, on three blocks of land, balanced so that every species meets every fertiliser once in each block. The blocks of land are almost always random. The trial did not set out to compare those three rectangles of soil, and next year it will move. The fertilisers are fixed if the point is to compare those five. They would be random only if five had been drawn from a long catalogue and the catalogue, not the five, was the target. The species are fixed if they are the six being sold, and random if they are six for which seed happened to be on hand. The data set does not answer that. It is a question to ask before the model is written.
Ten jokes, told to eight people in each of five ethnicity groups. The five ethnicity labels exhaust the classification used in the study, and the comparison across them is the point, so those effects are fixed. The jokes, if they were a sample from a book rather than the ten chosen as the funniest, are random: which joke is funnier is not the question. Each person also hears all ten jokes, so a person effect, nested inside ethnicity, belongs in the model as well. A person who does not laugh at the first joke may simply not be a laugher. That is a second random intercept, not a residual.
The estimation, for a normal mixed model, is not the closed form \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})^{-1}{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\boldsymbol{y}}, because the covariance is not a multiple of the identity and it depends on variance parameters that themselves depend on \boldsymbol{\beta}. Restricted maximum likelihood, which removes the fixed mean before estimating the variances, is the stable version of that loop. The next chapter is the one in which we fit the model and read the variances.

From the random-intercept model, derive \mathrm{Corr}(Y_{ji},Y_{ji'}) for i\neq i' in the same block, and check that it lies in [0,1).
A 3\times 3 correlation matrix with every off-diagonal entry equal to -\rho is positive definite only for \rho\le 1/2. Give the reason, in terms of three people who are all negatively correlated with each other, without a matrix calculation.
For the skin-cancer trial in seven hospitals, state one sampling story that makes the hospital effect random and one that makes it fixed. The treatment contrast is in the model either way.

title: Marginal models, and two responses at once
text:
Part of Correlated data · 6 questions on this topic · What links here
A mixed model explains the correlation: a shared intercept, a shared slope, something that can be simulated. A marginal model does not. It describes the average curve in the population and then corrects the standard errors for whatever dependence is left. This chapter is that second description, first for one response measured repeatedly, then for two different responses on the same person.
crumbs: Marginal models, and two responses at once

title: Marginal models, and two responses at once
text:
The average, and the person
Plot risk of a birth complication against the mother’s age and the cloud rises. Label the points by mother and the story reverses.






Figure 1: Schematic, not a recorded data set. Each red line is one mother: within a mother the risk falls a little as she ages. The blue line ignores which mother a birth belongs to, and it rises with age.



Within a mother, the second and third births are a little safer than the first, even though she is older. The red lines in Figure 1, one intercept and one slope per mother, are the subject-specific model of the previous chapter. The blue line through the whole cloud is the marginal, or population-average, model. They answer different questions. “What happens to this woman as she ages?” is the red line. “What does the risk look like, in this population, at a given age?” is the blue one. Which random-effects model is placed inside each mother can change the red slopes. The blue slope is the average association, and it does not have to move when the working correlation changes.
That is the attraction. We specify a mean that has an interpretation as a population average, a variance that depends on that mean, and a working association within each cluster. The working association does not have to be right. After the fit, a sandwich estimator replaces the model-based variance of \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} by one that uses the empirical residuals. If the mean is correctly specified, \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} is consistent, and so is the sandwich variance, even when the working correlation is wrong. The rate depends on how wrong it was. The guarantee is asymptotic in the number of clusters and, in the theory, in the size of each cluster. A handful of clusters, or one cluster with almost all the data, is not a setting in which the robust column should be trusted blindly.
For two binary variables the correlation cannot be chosen freely. A coin with success probability 0.2 and a coin with success probability 0.8 cannot be perfectly correlated. The largest correlation they can have is 0.25. A correlation is the wrong primitive once the margins are not normal. An odds ratio, or some other association that is free of that constraint, is the working model. And a mean plus a covariance does not determine a joint Poisson distribution. There is no unique bivariate Poisson. The marginal model does not need one.

Definition 1 A marginal model for clustered responses has three parts.

A mean, g(\mathrm{E}(Y_{ji}\mid {\boldsymbol{X}}_{ji}))={\boldsymbol{X}}_{ji}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}, the same link and the same linear predictor as for independent data.
A variance, \mathrm{Var}(Y_{ji}\mid {\boldsymbol{X}}_{ji})=\phi V(\mu_{ji}), depending on the covariates only through the mean.
A working association within a cluster, allowed to depend on the two means and on further association parameters.

Article: Marginal model →

The estimator solves the generalised estimating equations, the dependent version of the quasi-score. Liang and Zeger (1986) showed that the fit does not require integrating up to a likelihood. If the working variance happens to equal the truth, the sandwich collapses to the model-based inverse information, which is the best variance available. If it does not, the variance of \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} is the sandwich: model-based bread on the outside, the empirical residual covariance in the middle. Packages still call those pieces bread and meat.

title: Marginal models, and two responses at once
text:
Warp breaks
Yarn was spun at two factories, at low, medium, and high tension, and the number of breaks in a fixed length was recorded, nine replicates of each tension at each factory. Breaks are a count. Yarn from the same factory shares machines, material, and a standard, so the factory is the cluster. Two clusters is a small number for a sandwich. The model is still fitted. The robust column is the one the theory prefers, and it is not a precise standard error from a large number of factories.
An exchangeable working correlation says every pair of looms from the same factory has the same correlation. With a Poisson mean and a log link,
need <- function(pkg) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  }
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(pkg, character.only = TRUE))
}
need("gee")
data(warpbreaks)
warpbreaks$factory <- warpbreaks$wool
warpbreaks <- warpbreaks[order(warpbreaks$factory), ]
exchangeable <- gee(breaks ~ tension, id = factory, data = warpbreaks,
                    family = poisson, corstr = "exchangeable")
summary(exchangeable)
ar1 <- gee(breaks ~ tension, id = factory, data = warpbreaks,
           family = poisson, corstr = "AR-M", Mv = 1)
summary(ar1)
ar1$working.correlation[1:4, 1:4]
gaussian_ar <- gee(breaks ~ tension, id = factory, data = warpbreaks,
                   family = gaussian(link = "log"), corstr = "AR-M", Mv = 1)
summary(gaussian_ar)
            Estimate   Naive SE   Robust SE
(Intercept)   3.594     0.091       0.159
tensionM     -0.321     0.128       0.223
tensionH     -0.518     0.136       0.064
The scale estimate is 4.60, far from 1: these counts are more variable than a Poisson. The working correlation is about 0.021. Low tension, the baseline, has fitted mean \exp(3.594)\approx 36 breaks. Medium tension multiplies that mean by \exp(-0.321)=0.73. High tension multiplies it by \exp(-0.518)=0.60. On the naive standard errors, medium tension is detected (z=-2.51). On the robust standard errors it is not (z=-1.44). High tension is detected either way, and the robust standard error is about half the naive one. The two columns disagree, which is evidence that the Poisson variance and the exchangeable correlation are not the truth. The robust column is the one that remains consistent if the mean is right.
The looms were recorded in the order they came off the machine. Then exchangeable correlation is the wrong working model. An AR(1) working correlation sets 
\mathrm{Corr}(Y_t,Y_{t+k})=\gamma^{|k|}.
 The lag-1 value is 0.041, then 0.041^2 at lag 2 and 0.041^3 at lag 3. The coefficients barely move: intercept 3.595, medium -0.325, high -0.518. The naive standard errors move, because the working model moved. The robust standard errors stay where they were, to two decimals. That is the theorem, visible in one table. A third fit keeps the log mean and the AR(1) working correlation, and replaces the Poisson variance by a constant variance, a Gaussian family with a log link. A constant-variance model for counts is a poor variance story. The coefficients are again 3.595, -0.324, -0.518, and the robust standard errors again match the previous robust column. The scale estimate, 141, is a variance on the count scale and is not a quantity to interpret as a Poisson dispersion.






Key idea



If the mean is the right function of the covariates, the estimates of \boldsymbol{\beta} and the sandwich standard errors settle in the same place whatever working correlation the fit starts from. The naive standard errors move. A large gap between the two columns means the working variance was wrong. It does not, by itself, mean the robust column is wrong.


The gap here is large for every working model fitted above, so none of them is close to the true covariance. The robust standard errors are still the ones the asymptotic result licenses. They are not a substitute for having more than two factories.

title: Marginal models, and two responses at once
text:
Two responses, one person
A longitudinal study repeats the same measurement. A vector regression measures different things on the same unit, and each margin can have its own link and its own variance. Height and arm span, or burn area and death, are not repeated measures of one variable. Write component k on unit i as 
\mathrm{E}(Y_{ik}\mid {\boldsymbol{X}}_{ik})=\mu_k({\boldsymbol{X}}_{ik}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}_k),
\qquad
\mathrm{Var}(Y_{ik}\mid {\boldsymbol{X}}_{ik})=\phi_k V_k(\mu_{ik}).
 The \boldsymbol{\beta}_k are different parameters. A working association across components can be wrong, and the sandwich corrects it afterwards.
Fan and Gibbon’s burn data, as quoted by Song, have two responses of equal interest on each patient: the log of burn area plus one, a continuous severity, and an indicator of death. Age is the covariate. The margins, fitted independently, are 
\widehat{\mathrm{E}}(\text{severity}\mid \text{age})=6.7118+0.0035\,\text{age},
 
\widehat{\mathrm{P}}(\text{death}\mid \text{age})
=\frac{\exp(-3.6891+0.0508\,\text{age})}{1+\exp(-3.6891+0.0508\,\text{age})}.
 The sandwich standard errors of the two slopes are 0.0017 and 0.0051. The ratios are 
0.0035/0.0017=2.1,
\qquad
0.0508/0.0051=10.0.
 Age is associated with worse burns and with a higher chance of death. The direction is not the one a purely biological story about fragile infants would have suggested. Older children are the ones who get far enough into a kitchen, or a fire, to be burned this badly. The association is marginal and confounded with exposure.
The working model here was independence: two separate glm fits, stacked. The sandwich uses the cross-products of the two residuals on the same child, so the reported standard errors are not the independence standard errors.






Figure 2: The two burn slopes. The dashed rectangle is the pair of marginal 95% intervals from the standard errors reported above. The ellipse is the joint 95% region for those same standard errors if the slopes were uncorrelated. The sandwich covariance is not reported, so the ellipse drawn here is not rotated. A pair can sit inside the rectangle and outside the ellipse, and the corners of the rectangle sit outside the ellipse.



A joint confidence region for the two slopes is an ellipse, as in Figure 2, not the rectangle obtained by crossing the two marginal intervals. A pair that is acceptable one slope at a time can sit outside the ellipse. The ellipse puts more of its mass on “age matters for both” and less on “age matters strongly for severity and not at all for death”.
A genuine bivariate Poisson, when a distribution is wanted rather than a working covariance, is usually built by sharing a third Poisson: X_1=Y_1+Y_2, X_2=Y_2+Y_3, with Y_1,Y_2,Y_3 independent Poissons. The margins are Poisson and the correlation is positive. A minus sign can produce a negative correlation and can also produce a negative count, which is not a Poisson margin. The estimating-equation model simply declares two Poisson margins and a correlation in (-1,1), and does not claim that a joint distribution with those moments exists. That is the same descriptive licence as a quasi-likelihood.
The three plant species at a set of altitudes, where the association is an odds ratio rather than a correlation of two different kinds of measurement, are the next chapter.

From the exchangeable warp-break fit, compute \exp(3.594), \exp(-0.321) and \exp(-0.518), and state them as a baseline mean and two multiplicative comparisons with low tension.
Explain why the robust z-statistic for medium tension changes the conclusion that the naive z-statistic gave, and why the coefficients themselves did not have to move when the working correlation changed from exchangeable to AR(1).
The burn-severity slope is 0.0035 with sandwich standard error 0.0017. Compute the z-statistic and say what “marginal” means for that slope.
Why can two Bernoulli random variables with means 0.2 and 0.8 not have correlation 1?

title: Forecasting
text:
Part of Time series · 2 questions on this topic · What links here
The theory stopped at the Wold decomposition. This chapter is about using it. Rob Hyndman’s forecast package fits a model and returns a point forecast and a prediction interval. Once the package is installed, the function is left to choose the orders. The point is that the automatic choice does what the autocorrelation plots would have suggested by hand.

title: Forecasting
text:
Accidental deaths
USAccDeaths is a monthly count of accidental deaths in the United States, six years, 72 months, ending in December 1978.






Figure 1: Monthly accidental deaths in the United States, 1973 to 1978. The series is not white noise: deaths are higher in the northern summer, and the level sags and then recovers.



Plotting a series that R already knows is a time series puts time on the horizontal axis. Figure 1 is not white noise. Deaths are higher in the middle of the year, the northern summer, and lower in winter. A twelve-month cycle is the obvious feature. The overall level is not a straight trend. It sags and then recovers, the sort of slow movement produced when a temporary legal or behavioural change pulls a series down and then lets it drift back.
The autocorrelation and the partial autocorrelation both keep oscillating. An MA process would cut the autocorrelation off after a finite lag. An AR process would cut the partial autocorrelation off. Neither plot dies. That is the seasonality, still in the correlations.
Differencing at lag 12, 
\nabla_{12} X_t=X_t-X_{t-12},
 removes a twelve-month cycle and, as a side effect, a linear trend. The differenced series still slopes. A linear trend left after a seasonal difference means the original series had a quadratic trend. One further difference at lag 1 takes that slope out. What remains is closer to a constant mean and a constant scatter. The autocorrelation of that twice-differenced series still has a spike at the first lag, and a spike near one year. Those are the MA terms.






Figure 2: Autocorrelation and partial autocorrelation, in months. The top row is the raw series: neither plot dies, and the year shows up at lags 12 and 24. The bottom row is the series after a seasonal difference and a first difference. What remains is a spike at lag 1 and a spike near lag 12.



auto.arima, with the seasonal option left on, finds this without being told that the data are monthly.
need <- function(pkg) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  }
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(pkg, character.only = TRUE))
}
need("forecast")
fit <- auto.arima(USAccDeaths, seasonal = TRUE)
fit
fc <- forecast(fit, h = 12)
fc$mean[1]
sum(fc$mean)
The selected model differences once at lag 12, keeps a seasonal MA(1) on that yearly lag, differences once more at lag 1, and keeps an ordinary MA(1). There is no AR term. Both MA coefficients are negative. They are read as behaviour rather than as algebra. If last month was worse than the month before, this month is more careful, and the coefficient on that surprise is negative. If last year was worse than the year before, this year is more careful, and the seasonal coefficient is negative too. A good year, by the same arithmetic, is followed by a slack one. The AIC is what the function used to choose the orders. BIC is available and was not the default.






Figure 3: The forecast from January 1979. The darker band is the 80% interval and the lighter band is the 95% interval. The red point is the reported January total, 7798, inside the wider band and below the point forecast.



The series stops in December 1978. One step ahead, January 1979, the point forecast is 8336 deaths, with an 80% interval and a wider 95% interval. Figure 3 is that forecast. The same step, read more roughly, is about 8400. The two figures are the same forecast read at two moments. The reported January total is 7798, inside the 95% band and low relative to the point forecast. Twelve steps ahead, the forecasts trace one more seasonal shape, and the sum of those twelve monthly forecasts was about 109{,}000. A reported annual total for 1979 is near 105{,}000. Further out, past a few years, the local MA terms die and the forecast repeats the seasonal shape on top of the quadratic trend. A long-range forecast from this model is the mean structure. A short-range forecast still feels the last surprise.
The function was not told the period. It found 12. That is the part worth trusting the automation for: it matched the differencing the seasonal plot would have suggested.

title: Forecasting
text:
A hundred minutes of traffic
WWWusage counts hits on a server, one number per minute for 100 minutes. There is no season in a series that short.






Figure 4: Server hits, one number per minute. The autocorrelation dies slowly and then changes sign, because the series wanders. The partial autocorrelation is essentially one spike, at lag 1.



The autocorrelation in Figure 4 dies slowly. The partial autocorrelation dies after a lag or two. After one ordinary difference the series is closer to a flat mean, and auto.arima selects an ARMA(1,1) on that difference:
need <- function(pkg) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  }
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(pkg, character.only = TRUE))
}
need("forecast")
auto.arima(WWWusage, seasonal = TRUE)
The fit has no seasonal piece: one difference, one autoregressive coefficient, and one moving-average coefficient. Both coefficients are positive. A busy minute is followed by a busy minute, and a minute that was busy relative to the minute before it is followed by a minute that is busier still. That is a trend, of the sort a topic has when it is spreading, and it does not need a separate time covariate.






Figure 5: A twenty-minute forecast for the server traffic. The point forecast is nearly flat. The interval widens as the horizon moves away.



The forecast of the next minutes, in Figure 5, is a shallow line, and the interval widens as the horizon moves away. At a long horizon the forecast has forgotten the local level and sits on the mean that the difference implies.

title: Forecasting
section: What this chapter does not cover
text:
What this chapter does not cover
Autoregressive conditional heteroscedasticity, and its generalisations, put a time-series model on the variance rather than only on the mean. They are not developed here. Count-valued series are named and not developed, for a reason that has run through the earlier chapters: a Poisson observation is not a mean plus an innovation that can be separated off. Forecasting is the end of the material.

A linear trend, differenced at lag 12, leaves a constant. A quadratic trend, differenced at lag 12, leaves a linear trend. Explain why, for X_t=a+bt+ct^2, the seasonal difference X_t-X_{t-12} still depends on t.
Both MA coefficients in the accidental-death model are negative. State what a negative seasonal MA coefficient says about a year that was worse than the year before it.
Why is exponentiating a forecast made on the log scale not the same object as a forecast of the mean on the original scale?
auto.arima was not told that USAccDeaths is monthly. Which feature of the selected model shows that it found the season anyway?

title: Bayesian foundations
text: Part of Bayesian statistics · 15 questions on this topic · What links here

title: Bayesian foundations
text:
What is random?
Statistical inference is not exhausted by a contest between two schools. At least three traditions are worth distinguishing at the outset: classical or frequentist, Bayesian, and fiducial inference. Fiducial statistics takes a different route again to statements about unknown parameters, but it is now a much quieter and more specialised field. It is named here so that a useful comparison between frequentist and Bayesian reasoning is not mistaken for an exhaustive classification; we shall not develop fiducial methods in this book.
In a frequentist model the unknown parameter is fixed, while data are random under repeated sampling. For example, if

  X_1,\ldots,X_n\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^2),

then the sample mean and sample variance are random variables,

  \overline X=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i,
  \qquad
  S^2=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\overline X)^2,

but \mu is not. A theoretical 95\% confidence statement is

\mathbb{P}_{\mu}\!\left(
   \overline X-t_{0.975,n-1}\frac{S}{\sqrt n}
   <\mu<
   \overline X+t_{0.975,n-1}\frac{S}{\sqrt n}
\right)=0.95.

The randomness in this statement comes from repeating the entire sampling procedure. After observing x_1,\ldots,x_n, the realised interval is fixed; the frequentist statement is about the long-run coverage of the procedure.
A frequentist hypothesis test likewise refers to repeated sampling. Under a null hypothesis H_0, a p-value is the probability of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed value:

p_{\mathrm{value}}
=\mathbb{P}_{H_0}\{T(X)\text{ is at least as extreme as }T(x)\}.

It is not \mathbb{P}(H_0\mid x). Conventional design values such as type-I error 0.05 and type-II error 0.20 are choices about long-run performance, not probabilities that the realised decision is correct.
Bayesian and frequentist inference are not a contest for a single universal winner. Frequentist procedures often have excellent theory and fast computation; Bayesian statements are often easier to explain because they put probability directly on the uncertain quantity. A statistician should understand both languages well enough to say exactly what a reported interval or probability means. Statistics is usually a helper discipline, and an answer that cannot be communicated accurately to the scientist or decision-maker has not finished its job.

Definition 1 (Bayesian credible interval) Bayesian analysis introduces a probability distribution for the unknown parameter. Conditional on observed data x, a statement such as

  \mathbb{P}\!\left(a(x)<\mu<b(x)\mid x\right)=0.95

is meaningful. The interval (a(x),b(x)) is a 95\% credible interval. This is not a reworded confidence interval: the two calculations can coincide in large samples, but their probability statements condition on different objects.
Article: Bayesian credible interval →

title: Bayesian foundations
text:
Bayes’ rule for densities

Theorem 1 (Bayes’ rule) For events A and B with \mathbb{P}(B)>0,

  \mathbb{P}(A\mid B)=\frac{\mathbb{P}(B\mid A)\mathbb{P}(A)}{\mathbb{P}(B)}.

The density version follows from two factorizations of a joint density:

  p(x,\theta)=p(x\mid\theta)p(\theta)
             =p(\theta\mid x)p(x).

Equating the right-hand sides and dividing by p(x) gives 
p(\theta\mid x)
  =\frac{p(x\mid\theta)p(\theta)}{p(x)}.
\qquad(1)
Article: Bayes’ rule →

Here

p(x\mid\theta) is the sampling density, viewed as a likelihood in \theta after x is observed;
p(\theta) is the prior density;
p(\theta\mid x) is the posterior density; and
p(x) is the marginal likelihood, or evidence.

The evidence is the constant that normalises the posterior. For a continuous parameter, \begin{align*}
  p(x)
  &=\int p(x,\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta\\
  &=\int p(x\mid\theta)p(\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta.
\end{align*} For a discrete parameter taking values \theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m,

  p(x)=\sum_{j=1}^mp(x\mid\theta_j)p(\theta_j).

When only the posterior’s shape is needed, the denominator in Equation 1 does not depend on \theta, so 
p(\theta\mid x)\propto p(x\mid\theta)p(\theta).
\qquad(2)






Key idea



Bayesian calculation is the controlled multiplication of a likelihood by a prior, followed by normalisation or recognition of a known density kernel. The proportionality symbol removes constants in the variable being analysed, not arbitrary terms that still depend on that variable.

title: Bayesian foundations
text:
Priors and transparency

Definition 2 (Proper prior and proper posterior) A prior is proper if it is a probability distribution, so its total mass is one. A posterior is proper if the product of likelihood and prior has a finite, nonzero normalising constant. An improper prior may sometimes produce a proper posterior, but this must be checked rather than assumed.
Article: Proper prior and proper posterior →

A subjective prior encodes stated beliefs or expert information. An objective or weakly informative prior tries to limit the prior’s influence while still producing a mathematically usable model. Neither label removes judgement. Support, scale, invariance, tail behaviour, and parameterisation all matter. In particular, a prior that is exactly zero on part of the parameter space can never be rescued there by data:

p(\theta\mid x)\propto p(x\mid\theta)p(\theta)=0
\quad\text{whenever }p(\theta)=0.

A diffuse normal prior may be badly centred but still has nonzero tails; a bounded uniform prior that excludes the true value rules it out forever.
A prior does not remove judgement; it makes judgement visible. That is both a strength and a danger. The prior should be chosen before looking at the data being analysed, its scientific basis should be stated, and conclusions that move under other reasonable priors should be reported as sensitive. Prior influence is strongest precisely when the data are weakest, which is when good prior information can help most and an indefensible prior can do most damage. Formal expert elicitation is a standing reminder of the same caution: prior information is a double-edged sword, neither a defect nor an automatic virtue.
The practical discipline is:

state the prior family and every hyperparameter;
explain the scale on which it is intended to be weak or informative;
check whether it is proper, meaning that it integrates to one;
check whether the resulting posterior is proper; and
report sensitivity to other defensible priors when the conclusion depends materially on the choice.

title: Bayesian foundations
text:
Posterior summaries

Definition 3 (Posterior point summaries) For a scalar parameter, common point summaries include

  \mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)=\int\theta p(\theta\mid x)\,\mathrm{d}\theta,
  \qquad
  \widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MAP}}
  =\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\theta}p(\theta\mid x),

the posterior median, and posterior quantiles. These summaries need not agree for a skewed distribution.
Article: Posterior point summaries →


Definition 4 (Credible-region constructions) Three interval constructions are worth distinguishing. An equal-tailed 95\% credible interval (l,u) satisfies

  \mathbb{P}(\theta<l\mid x)=0.025,
  \qquad
  \mathbb{P}(\theta>u\mid x)=0.025.

The minimum-width interval solves

\min_{l<u}(u-l)
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\int_l^u p(\theta\mid x)\,\mathrm{d}\theta=0.95.

A highest-posterior-density set chooses a level c so that

\mathcal H_c=\{\theta:p(\theta\mid x)\geq c\},
\qquad
\int_{\mathcal H_c}p(\theta\mid x)\,\mathrm{d}\theta=0.95.

Every included point then has density at least as large as every excluded point. For a continuous unimodal posterior this gives the minimum-width interval; for a multimodal posterior the highest-density set can be disjoint. For a symmetric unimodal density, the mean, median, and mode coincide and the common interval constructions often agree.
Article: Credible-region constructions →







Figure 1: Two 95\% summaries of the same skewed \operatorname{Beta}(3,9) posterior. Equal tails force 2.5\% of the probability to each side. The minimum-width interval shifts toward the high-density part of the posterior; because this density is continuous and unimodal, it is also the HPD set and its two endpoints have equal density.



The MAP is a useful point, but a point alone discards the uncertainty that the posterior was introduced to represent. A posterior sample converts most summaries into ordinary sample calculations.

Proposition 1 (Posterior summaries from draws) Let \theta^{(1)},\ldots,\theta^{(L)} be posterior draws and let \theta_{(1)}\leq\cdots\leq\theta_{(L)} be their order statistics. Then \begin{align*}
\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(\theta\mid x)
&=\frac1L\sum_{l=1}^L\theta^{(l)},\\
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\theta\mid x)
&=\frac1{L-1}\sum_{l=1}^L
   \left(\theta^{(l)}-\overline\theta\right)^2,\\
\widehat{\mathbb{P}}(\theta<c\mid x)
&=\frac1L\sum_{l=1}^L\mathbf{1}\{\theta^{(l)}<c\}.
\end{align*} The posterior median and equal-tailed interval are estimated by the corresponding empirical quantiles. With L=1000, the median can be estimated by the average of \theta_{(500)} and \theta_{(501)}, and a direct 95\% interval approximation by [\theta_{(25)},\theta_{(975)}]. The precise indices vary slightly with a software package’s quantile convention.
Article: Posterior summaries from draws →

The mode is the exception. It is not an order statistic and, for continuous draws, looking for the most frequently repeated value is generally useless. One should maximise the posterior density or log-posterior, or deliberately construct and optimise a density estimate if the density itself is unavailable.

Remark 1 (R’s distribution interface). For a common distribution, R prefixes the distribution name by d for density, p for cumulative probability, q for quantile, and r for random generation. These are numerical calculations to run once the posterior distribution has been derived. For the \operatorname{Beta}(3,9) posterior in Figure 1, the following commands compute its median, a posterior probability, an equal-tailed interval, and Monte Carlo versions of the same summaries.
Article: R’s distribution interface →

# theta | x ~ Beta(3, 9)
qbeta(0.5, shape1 = 3, shape2 = 9)       # posterior median
pbeta(0.5, shape1 = 3, shape2 = 9)       # P(theta <= 0.5 | x)
qbeta(c(0.025, 0.975), 3, 9)             # equal-tailed interval

set.seed(3500)
theta <- rbeta(1000, shape1 = 3, shape2 = 9)
c(mean = mean(theta),
  median = median(theta),
  Pr_below_half = mean(theta < 0.5))
quantile(theta, c(0.025, 0.975))
The first three lines use the known Beta posterior directly and are preferable when the required function is available. The simulated calculation is the version that survives when the posterior is accessible only through a sampler. Increasing the number of draws reduces Monte Carlo error; it does not repair a sampler that targets the wrong distribution.

title: Bayesian foundations
text:
Prior and posterior prediction
The posterior p(\theta\mid x) describes uncertainty about an unknown parameter. Many scientific questions instead concern an observable outcome: the next patient’s response, tomorrow’s demand, the number of defects in a future batch, or the mean mark in a future class. These are not questions about \theta itself. They require a distribution for a future random quantity \widetilde X.
Prediction moves posterior uncertainty back onto the scale of the data. It serves at least three purposes:

forecasting future observations or future aggregates;
supporting decisions whose consequences depend on what will be observed, rather than on the parameter alone; and
checking whether replicated data generated by the fitted model resemble the observations that motivated the model.

The predictive target must be stated. The distribution of one new observation, a future sample mean, and a future count over m trials are different even when they use the same posterior for \theta.

Prior predictive and posterior predictive distributions

Definition 5 (Prior and posterior predictive distributions) Before data are observed, a new observation \widetilde x is generated by first drawing \theta from its prior and then drawing \widetilde x from the sampling model. Marginalising \theta gives the prior predictive density: \begin{align*}
  p(\widetilde x)
  &=\int p(\widetilde x,\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta\\
  &=\int p(\widetilde x\mid\theta)p(\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta.
\end{align*}
After observing x, the analogous calculation uses the posterior: \begin{align*}
  p(\widetilde x\mid x)
  &=\int p(\widetilde x,\theta\mid x)\,\mathrm{d}\theta\\
  &=\int p(\widetilde x\mid\theta,x)p(\theta\mid x)\,\mathrm{d}\theta\\
  &=\int p(\widetilde x\mid\theta)p(\theta\mid x)\,\mathrm{d}\theta.
\end{align*} The last equality uses conditional independence of future and observed data given \theta. Prediction therefore averages the sampling model over parameter uncertainty instead of plugging in a single estimate.
The prior predictive distribution asks what data the complete model regarded as plausible before seeing the observations. It is therefore useful for study design and for detecting a prior that places most of its mass on scientifically absurd data. The posterior predictive distribution asks what future data are plausible after learning from x. It is used for forecasting and for posterior predictive model checks. Although both are mixtures of the sampling distribution, they mix with different distributions for \theta: p(\theta) before the data and p(\theta\mid x) after the data.
Article: Prior and posterior predictive distributions →

One of the best ways to understand a probabilistic model is to run it in both directions. Fitting asks what parameter values are plausible after seeing the data; generation asks what data those parameter values would produce. Prior and posterior predictive simulation turn an abstract hierarchy of densities into observable consequences, which is why prediction is also a powerful model-checking habit.


Why a plug-in prediction is incomplete
Replacing \theta by one estimate \widehat\theta gives the plug-in distribution p(\widetilde x\mid\widehat\theta). This treats \widehat\theta as known and therefore omits parameter uncertainty. The omitted contribution is visible from the laws of total expectation and total variance. Define

m(\theta)=\mathbb{E}(\widetilde X\mid\theta),
\qquad
v(\theta)=\operatorname{Var}(\widetilde X\mid\theta).

Conditional independence gives \begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}(\widetilde X\mid x)
&=\mathbb{E}\!\left\{\mathbb{E}(\widetilde X\mid\theta,x)\mid x\right\}\\
&=\mathbb{E}\!\left\{\mathbb{E}(\widetilde X\mid\theta)\mid x\right\}\\
&=\mathbb{E}\{m(\theta)\mid x\}.
\end{align*} To derive the variance decomposition, let M=\mathbb{E}(\widetilde X\mid x). Then

\widetilde X-M
=\{\widetilde X-m(\theta)\}+\{m(\theta)-M\}.

Squaring and taking the posterior-predictive expectation gives \begin{align*}
\operatorname{Var}(\widetilde X\mid x)
&=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\{\widetilde X-m(\theta)\}^2\mid x\right]
   +\mathbb{E}\!\left[\{m(\theta)-M\}^2\mid x\right]\\
&\quad
   +2\mathbb{E}\!\left[
      \{\widetilde X-m(\theta)\}\{m(\theta)-M\}\mid x
   \right].
\end{align*} The cross-term is zero because \begin{align*}
&\mathbb{E}\!\left[
\{\widetilde X-m(\theta)\}\{m(\theta)-M\}\mid x
\right]\\
&\quad=
\mathbb{E}\!\left[
\mathbb{E}\{\widetilde X-m(\theta)\mid\theta,x\}
\{m(\theta)-M\}\mid x
\right]\\
&\quad=0.
\end{align*}

Proposition 2 (Predictive-variance decomposition) Under the conditional-independence assumption above, 
\boxed{
\operatorname{Var}(\widetilde X\mid x)
=\underbrace{\mathbb{E}\{v(\theta)\mid x\}}_{\textnormal{future-observation noise}}
+\underbrace{\operatorname{Var}\{m(\theta)\mid x\}}_{\textnormal{parameter uncertainty}}.}
\qquad(3)
Article: Predictive-variance decomposition →

A plug-in distribution keeps only the first kind of variation evaluated at \widehat\theta. Its intervals are therefore commonly too narrow. A credible interval for \theta and a predictive interval for \widetilde X answer different questions; the latter is usually wider because it must include the randomness of a new observation as well.


Prediction by simulation
A finite mixture provides a useful way to remember the simulation. To sample from a mixture, first select a component and then sample within that component. For a predictive distribution the parameter draw plays the role of the component: first select one plausible data-generating model, then generate an observation from it. The integral gives the same two-stage recipe:

before data, draw \theta^{(l)}\sim p(\theta); after data, draw \theta^{(l)}\sim p(\theta\mid x);
draw \widetilde x^{(l)}\sim p(\widetilde x\mid\theta^{(l)});
summarise the \widetilde x^{(l)} values.

The simulated future observations are not fed back into the posterior because they are not observed data. This algorithm remains valid when the predictive integral has no closed form and when \widetilde X is multivariate.






Key idea



The posterior predictive distribution is the Bayesian answer to what might we observe next? It averages over every plausible parameter value instead of behaving as though one estimate were exact. Its uncertainty contains both irreducible future-observation noise and uncertainty about the data-generating parameter.

title: Conjugate analysis for normal models
text:
Unknown mean, known variance

Definition 1 (Normal–Normal model) Assume

  X_1,\ldots,X_n\mid\mu
  \stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^2),

where \sigma^2 is known, and use the prior

  \mu\sim\operatorname{N}(\mu_0,\sigma_0^2).

Article: Normal–Normal model →

The normal prior respects the fact that \mu may be positive or negative. A log-normal prior would impose positivity, while a bounded uniform prior would assign permanent posterior probability zero outside its bounds. The normal prior can be badly centred, but its nonzero tails allow enough data eventually to overcome that error. It is often convenient to work in precisions \sigma^{-2} and \sigma_0^{-2} because independent information then adds.1
When the aim is to be weakly informative, it is safer to give the model room to recover than to impose a hard boundary that cannot be defended. A broad normal prior may put too much mass in uninteresting regions, but it does not make a plausible value impossible. A bounded prior that misses the truth cannot be repaired by any amount of data. Weak information is therefore about scale and support, not simply about making a variance enormous.

Remark 1 (A proper approximation to the flat prior). The honest bounded version of the improper kernel p(\mu)\propto1 is

p_C(\mu)=\frac1{2C}\mathbf{1}\{-C\leq\mu\leq C\}.

Taking, for example, C=10^4 makes this density nearly constant over an ordinary data range while keeping it proper. It also exposes what “very diffuse” means. For any fixed 0<M<C,

\mathbb{P}_C(|\mu|\leq M)=\int_{-M}^{M}\frac1{2C}\,\mathrm{d}\mu=\frac MC
\longrightarrow0
\qquad(C\longrightarrow\infty).

Thus the limiting sequence puts essentially all of its probability beyond every fixed finite range; it does not converge to a uniform probability distribution on \mathbb{R}. Human height makes the point concrete: no observed person is three metres tall, yet a sufficiently broad uniform prior assigns almost no mass to the entire range of heights that have actually been encountered.
Article: A proper approximation to the flat prior →

The likelihood is \begin{align*}
  p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\mu)
  &=\prod_{i=1}^n
    \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}
    \exp\!\left[-\frac{(x_i-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right]\\
  &=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}
    \exp\!\left[-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
      \sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2\right].
\end{align*} The prior density is

  p(\mu)=(2\pi\sigma_0^2)^{-1/2}
  \exp\!\left[-\frac{(\mu-\mu_0)^2}{2\sigma_0^2}\right].

Dropping factors that do not depend on \mu, \begin{align*}
  p(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
  &\propto p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\mu)p(\mu)\\
  &\propto
  \exp\!\left\{-\frac12\left[
    \frac1{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2
    +\frac1{\sigma_0^2}(\mu-\mu_0)^2
  \right]\right\}.
\end{align*}
To identify the density, expand every square: \begin{align*}
\frac1{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2
&=\frac1{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n
   (x_i^2-2x_i\mu+\mu^2)\\
&=\frac1{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^nx_i^2
   -2\mu\frac{\sum_i x_i}{\sigma^2}
   +\mu^2\frac{n}{\sigma^2},\\[3pt]
\frac1{\sigma_0^2}(\mu-\mu_0)^2
&=\frac{\mu^2}{\sigma_0^2}
   -2\mu\frac{\mu_0}{\sigma_0^2}
   +\frac{\mu_0^2}{\sigma_0^2}.
\end{align*} Collect the coefficients that involve \mu:

A\mu^2-2B\mu+C,
\qquad
A=\frac{n}{\sigma^2}+\frac1{\sigma_0^2},
\quad
B=\frac{\sum_i x_i}{\sigma^2}+\frac{\mu_0}{\sigma_0^2},

where C contains no variable \mu. Completing the square, \begin{align*}
A\mu^2-2B\mu+C
&=A\left(\mu^2-2\frac BA\mu\right)+C\\
&=A\left[\left(\mu-\frac BA\right)^2
           -\left(\frac BA\right)^2\right]+C\\
&=A\left(\mu-\frac BA\right)^2
   +C-\frac{B^2}{A}.
\end{align*} The last two terms are constant in \mu. Hence

  p(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
  \propto
  \exp\!\left[-\frac{A}{2}
    \left(\mu-\frac BA\right)^2\right],

Therefore:

Proposition 1 (Normal–Normal conjugacy) 
\boxed{
  \mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{N}(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)},
\qquad(1) with 
\begin{aligned}
\sigma_1^2
&=\frac1A
=\left(\frac n{\sigma^2}+\frac1{\sigma_0^2}\right)^{-1}
=\frac{\sigma^2\sigma_0^2}{n\sigma_0^2+\sigma^2},
\\
\mu_1
&=\frac BA
=\frac{\sum_i x_i/\sigma^2+\mu_0/\sigma_0^2}
        {n/\sigma^2+1/\sigma_0^2}\\
&=\frac{n\overline x\,\sigma_0^2+\mu_0\sigma^2}
        {n\sigma_0^2+\sigma^2}.
\end{aligned}
\qquad(2)
Article: Normal–Normal conjugacy →


Remark 2 (Precision weighting). Writing

w=\frac{\sigma^2}{n\sigma_0^2+\sigma^2}

turns Equation 2 into

\mu_1=(1-w)\overline x+w\mu_0.

The posterior mean is therefore a precision-weighted average. Equivalently, if \kappa_0=\sigma^2/\sigma_0^2, then

\mu_1=\frac{n\overline x+\kappa_0\mu_0}{n+\kappa_0}.

Thus the prior behaves like \kappa_0 observations whose mean is \mu_0. In the special case \sigma_0^2=\sigma^2, it behaves like one extra observation at \mu_0.
Article: Precision weighting →

The limiting cases check the algebra: \begin{align*}
n=0
&\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mu_1=\mu_0,
\quad \sigma_1^2=\sigma_0^2,\\
\sigma_0^2\to\infty
&\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mu_1\to\overline x,
\quad \sigma_1^2\to\frac{\sigma^2}{n},\\
\sigma^2\to0
&\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mu_1\to\overline x,
\quad \sigma_1^2\to0,\\
\sigma_0^2\to0
&\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mu_1\to\mu_0,
\quad \sigma_1^2\to0.
\end{align*}

title: Categorical data and the Dirichlet distribution
text:
From two categories to many

Definition 1 (Categorical and multinomial models) For two categories, a Bernoulli trial has probabilities (p,1-p) and an aggregated count has a binomial distribution. For K categories, let

{\boldsymbol{p}}=(p_1,\ldots,p_K)^{\mathsf T},
\qquad p_k\geq0,
\qquad \sum_{k=1}^Kp_k=1.

A single observation Y_i\in\{1,\ldots,K\} has

\mathbb{P}(Y_i=k\mid{\boldsymbol{p}})=p_k.

For n conditionally independent observations define

X_k=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf{1}\{Y_i=k\}.

Then \sum_kX_k=n and

{\boldsymbol{x}}\mid{\boldsymbol{p}}\sim\operatorname{Multinomial}(n,{\boldsymbol{p}}).

Article: Categorical and multinomial models →

To derive its mass function, first choose which x_1 positions receive category 1, then which x_2 of the remaining positions receive category 2, and so on: \begin{align*}
\binom{n}{x_1}
\binom{n-x_1}{x_2}\cdots
\binom{x_{K-1}+x_K}{x_{K-1}}
&=\frac{n!}{x_1!(n-x_1)!}
   \frac{(n-x_1)!}{x_2!(n-x_1-x_2)!}\cdots\\
&=\frac{n!}{x_1!\cdots x_K!}.
\end{align*} Every one of those sequences has probability \prod_kp_k^{x_k}, so 
p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid{\boldsymbol{p}})
=\frac{n!}{\prod_{k=1}^Kx_k!}
  \prod_{k=1}^Kp_k^{x_k}.
\qquad(1) As a likelihood in {\boldsymbol{p}},

L({\boldsymbol{p}};{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto\prod_{k=1}^Kp_k^{x_k}.
crumbs: Categorical data and the Dirichlet distribution

title: Categorical data and the Dirichlet distribution
text:
The Dirichlet prior

Definition 2 (Dirichlet distribution) The conjugate prior for {\boldsymbol{p}} is the Dirichlet distribution. Write

\alpha_0=\sum_{k=1}^K\alpha_k,
\qquad \alpha_k>0.

The multivariate Beta function is

B({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
=\frac{\prod_{k=1}^K\Gamma(\alpha_k)}
        {\Gamma(\alpha_0)}.

Then 
p({\boldsymbol{p}}\mid{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
=\frac1{B({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})}
   \prod_{k=1}^Kp_k^{\alpha_k-1},
\qquad {\boldsymbol{p}}\in\mathcal S_{K-1},
\qquad(2) where

\mathcal S_{K-1}
=\left\{{\boldsymbol{p}}:p_k\geq0,\ \sum_{k=1}^Kp_k=1\right\}

is the probability simplex.
Article: Dirichlet distribution →


Proposition 1 (The Beta distribution is the two-category Dirichlet) When K=2, write p_1=p and p_2=1-p. Restricting the Dirichlet density to the one-dimensional simplex gives

p(p\mid\alpha_1,\alpha_2)
=\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_1+\alpha_2)}
        {\Gamma(\alpha_1)\Gamma(\alpha_2)}
   p^{\alpha_1-1}(1-p)^{\alpha_2-1},

which is exactly \operatorname{Beta}(\alpha_1,\alpha_2). The Dirichlet is therefore a genuine extension of the Beta family rather than merely a similar-looking density.
Article: The Beta distribution is the two-category Dirichlet →

The prior cannot itself be multinomial. A multinomial distribution is a discrete distribution for a vector of counts, whereas the unknown {\boldsymbol{p}} varies continuously over the simplex. The likelihood may be discrete in the data while the prior and posterior are continuous in the parameter; these are different arguments of the same Bayesian calculation.
For K=3 the simplex is a triangle. Beginning with three categories and a triangle is easier than beginning with the general simplex, although the triangle eventually has to give way.






Figure 1: The three-category probability simplex.



If all \alpha_k=1, the density in Equation 2 is constant on the simplex. This means uniform density over valid probability vectors. It does not force p_1=\cdots=p_K=1/K.
For the Dirichlet distribution, separate location from concentration. The ratios \alpha_k/\alpha_0 describe the centre of the prior, while \alpha_0=\sum_k\alpha_k controls how tightly probability vectors cluster around it. Multiplying every \alpha_k by the same constant keeps the centre but changes the strength of the prior. That is a more useful way to reason about these parameters than trying to picture a high-dimensional density one coordinate at a time.
When every \alpha_k<1, the density favours sparse probability vectors near the boundary. For \alpha_1=\cdots=\alpha_K=0.1, typical draws put most of their mass on one category: a “winner takes all” prior. The density is singular along the boundary, so the careful statement is about the distribution of draws, not a finite interior mode located at a corner.






Figure 2: Draws from three symmetric Dirichlet distributions. The uniform \operatorname{Dirichlet}(1,1,1) fills the triangle; increasing the common concentration to 5 pulls probability vectors toward (1/3,1/3,1/3); reducing it to 0.1 puts most draws near an edge or corner. Symmetry fixes the same centre in all three panels, so the visible change is concentration rather than location.



One should be prepared to abandon a visualisation that is not helping.

Proposition 2 (Multinomial central limit theorem) Let {\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{Multinomial}(n,{\boldsymbol{p}}) and \widehat{\boldsymbol{p}}={\boldsymbol{x}}/n. For fixed interior {\boldsymbol{p}}, define the covariance matrix

{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}({\boldsymbol{p}})
=\operatorname{diag}({\boldsymbol{p}})-{\boldsymbol{p}}{\boldsymbol{p}}^{\mathsf T}.

Then

\sqrt n\,(\widehat{\boldsymbol{p}}-{\boldsymbol{p}})
\xrightarrow{\mathcal D}
\operatorname{N}_K\!\left(
  {\boldsymbol{0}},
  {\color{blue}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}({\boldsymbol{p}})
\right).

The covariance matrix is singular because the components of \widehat{\boldsymbol{p}}-{\boldsymbol{p}} sum to zero. On the (K-1)-dimensional simplex, the count cloud therefore tightens at the usual n^{-1/2} rate and becomes locally normal.
Article: Multinomial central limit theorem →
crumbs: Categorical data and the Dirichlet distribution

title: Categorical data and the Dirichlet distribution
text:
Moments and the mode

Proposition 3 (Dirichlet moments) Standard Dirichlet integrals give \begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}(P_k)&=\frac{\alpha_k}{\alpha_0},\\
\mathbb{E}(P_k^2)&=\frac{\alpha_k(\alpha_k+1)}
                  {\alpha_0(\alpha_0+1)},\\
\mathbb{E}(P_jP_k)&=\frac{\alpha_j\alpha_k}
                  {\alpha_0(\alpha_0+1)},\qquad j\neq k.
\end{align*}
Article: Dirichlet moments →

Therefore \begin{align*}
\operatorname{Var}(P_k)
&=\mathbb{E}(P_k^2)-\mathbb{E}(P_k)^2\\
&=\frac{\alpha_k(\alpha_k+1)}
          {\alpha_0(\alpha_0+1)}
   -\frac{\alpha_k^2}{\alpha_0^2}\\
&=\frac{\alpha_k\alpha_0(\alpha_k+1)
          -\alpha_k^2(\alpha_0+1)}
         {\alpha_0^2(\alpha_0+1)}\\
&=\frac{\alpha_k(\alpha_0-\alpha_k)}
         {\alpha_0^2(\alpha_0+1)},\\[4pt]
\operatorname{Cov}(P_j,P_k)
&=\mathbb{E}(P_jP_k)-\mathbb{E}(P_j)\mathbb{E}(P_k)\\
&=\frac{\alpha_j\alpha_k}{\alpha_0(\alpha_0+1)}
   -\frac{\alpha_j\alpha_k}{\alpha_0^2}\\
&=-\frac{\alpha_j\alpha_k}
          {\alpha_0^2(\alpha_0+1)}.
\end{align*} The negative covariance is forced by the sum-to-one constraint.
To derive the interior mode, maximise

\ell({\boldsymbol{p}})=\sum_{k=1}^K(\alpha_k-1)\log p_k

subject to \sum_kp_k=1. The Lagrangian is

\mathcal L({\boldsymbol{p}},\lambda)
=\sum_{k=1}^K(\alpha_k-1)\log p_k
  +\lambda\left(\sum_{k=1}^Kp_k-1\right).

Differentiating,

\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial p_k}
=\frac{\alpha_k-1}{p_k}+\lambda=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
p_k=-\frac{\alpha_k-1}{\lambda}.

Summing over k and imposing the constraint gives

1=\sum_kp_k
=-\frac1\lambda\sum_k(\alpha_k-1)
=-\frac{\alpha_0-K}{\lambda},

so \lambda=-(\alpha_0-K).

Proposition 4 (Interior Dirichlet mode) Consequently, 
\operatorname{mode}(P_k)
=\frac{\alpha_k-1}{\alpha_0-K}.
\qquad(3) This derivation requires every \alpha_k>1. Otherwise the mode may lie on a face or corner of the simplex.
Article: Interior Dirichlet mode →

Question. Use an unrestricted six-cell multinomial with the uniform prior

{\boldsymbol{p}}\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(1,1,1,1,1,1).

Find the posterior distribution and the posterior mean and MAP estimate of the male-negative cell probability.
Solution. The conjugate update gives

{\boldsymbol{p}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(54,58,148,94,39,114).

For the male-negative cell,

\mathbb{E}(P_{11}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{54}{501+6}=\frac{54}{507}
\approx0.1065,

while

\widehat p_{11,\mathrm{MAP}}
=\frac{54-1}{507-6}=\frac{53}{501}
\approx0.1058.

The MAP equals the maximum-likelihood cell proportion because every prior parameter equals one.
