title: Exponential families and conjugacy
text:
Part of Bayesian statistics · 18 questions on this topic · What links here
The conjugate calculations in the Beta–Binomial, Normal–Normal, and Gamma–Poisson models are not isolated coincidences. They are instances of a general pattern: the likelihood compresses the observations into sufficient statistics, and a matching prior allows those statistics to update a fixed number of hyperparameters. This chapter isolates that algebraic mechanism before the book turns to the different idea of linking related groups through a hierarchy.1

title: Exponential families and conjugacy
text:
Statistics and inferential reduction

Definition 1 (Statistic and estimator) Write the complete sample as {\boldsymbol{X}}=(X_1,\ldots,X_n) and its realised value as {\boldsymbol{x}}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n). A statistic is any function

T=T({\boldsymbol{X}})

of the random data alone. It cannot contain an unknown parameter. An estimator is a statistic used to estimate a parameter or a function of one, so every estimator is a statistic but not every statistic is introduced for estimation. For example, \overline X, \max_iX_i, and \sum_i(X_i-\overline X)^2 are all statistics.
Article: Statistic and estimator →

The same mathematical expression p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta) is viewed in two different ways:

as a sampling density, {\boldsymbol{x}} varies and \theta is fixed;
as a likelihood, the observed {\boldsymbol{x}} is fixed and \theta varies.

The likelihood is therefore a function of \theta; it is not generally a probability density in \theta. A prior is required before it can be normalised to form a posterior.
Statistical reduction asks whether the full data vector can be replaced by a lower-dimensional statistic without losing information about \theta under the assumed model. This is the role of sufficiency.
Sufficiency is not a claim that the discarded features are useless for every purpose. It says they add no information about the named parameter within the assumed model. Residual patterns can still be vital for checking that model. The parameter, the model, and the inferential purpose therefore belong in any careful statement that a statistic is sufficient.

title: Exponential families and conjugacy
text:
Sufficiency and the Fisher–Neyman theorem

Definition 2 A statistic T({\boldsymbol{X}}) is sufficient for \theta if the conditional distribution of {\boldsymbol{X}} given T({\boldsymbol{X}})=t does not depend on \theta.
Article: Sufficient statistic →

Once T is known, the remaining details of the sample may still be useful for checking the model or answering other questions, but they contain no further information about \theta within that model. Sufficiency is therefore model-relative. A statistic sufficient when a nuisance parameter is known need not remain sufficient when that parameter is also unknown.
The conditional definition is conceptually clean but awkward to verify directly. The standard practical tool is the following theorem.

Theorem 1 (Fisher–Neyman factorisation) Suppose the family \{p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta):\theta\in\Omega\} is dominated by a common measure. Then T({\boldsymbol{X}}) is sufficient for \theta if and only if there are nonnegative functions g_\theta and h such that 
p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta)
=g_\theta\{T({\boldsymbol{x}})\}h({\boldsymbol{x}}),
\qquad \theta\in\Omega,
\qquad(1) where h does not depend on \theta.
Article: Fisher–Neyman factorisation →

The factorisation says that every part of the likelihood that depends on \theta must pass through T({\boldsymbol{x}}). For a discrete sample, the easy direction of the theorem can be seen directly. If T({\boldsymbol{x}})=t, then \begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}_\theta({\boldsymbol{X}}={\boldsymbol{x}}\mid T=t)
&=\frac{p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta)}
         {\sum_{{\boldsymbol{u}}:T({\boldsymbol{u}})=t}
          p({\boldsymbol{u}}\mid\theta)}\\
&=\frac{g_\theta(t)h({\boldsymbol{x}})}
         {\sum_{{\boldsymbol{u}}:T({\boldsymbol{u}})=t}
          g_\theta(t)h({\boldsymbol{u}})}\\
&=\frac{h({\boldsymbol{x}})}
         {\sum_{{\boldsymbol{u}}:T({\boldsymbol{u}})=t}h({\boldsymbol{u}})}.
\end{align*} The final expression contains no \theta. The measure-theoretic theorem extends the same cancellation to continuous and mixed models.
The Bayesian consequence is immediate. If the prior density is \pi(\theta), then \begin{align*}
p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta)\pi(\theta)\\
&=g_\theta\{T({\boldsymbol{x}})\}h({\boldsymbol{x}})\pi(\theta)\\
&\propto g_\theta\{T({\boldsymbol{x}})\}\pi(\theta),
\end{align*} because h({\boldsymbol{x}}) is constant in \theta. Thus two samples having the same sufficient statistic produce the same posterior under the same prior. This is why conjugate updates can often be written using only a count, a sum, or a pair of sums.

title: Exponential families and conjugacy
text:
Worked factorisation: a normal mean

Example 1 (Sufficiency for a normal mean) Suppose

X_1,\ldots,X_n\mid\mu
\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^2),
\qquad \sigma^2\text{ known}.

Question. Use the Fisher–Neyman factorisation theorem to find a sufficient statistic for \mu. Then identify a sufficient statistic when both \mu and \sigma^2 are unknown.
Solution. The joint density is \begin{align*}
p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\mu)
&=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}
   \exp\!\left\{-\frac1{2\sigma^2}
   \sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2\right\}.
\end{align*} Expand the quadratic: \begin{align*}
\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2
&=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i^2-2\mu x_i+\mu^2)\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^nx_i^2
   -2\mu\sum_{i=1}^nx_i
   +n\mu^2.
\end{align*} Substitution gives \begin{align*}
p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\mu)
&=\underbrace{
   (2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}
   \exp\!\left\{-\frac1{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^nx_i^2\right\}}
   _{h({\boldsymbol{x}})}\\
&\quad\times
   \underbrace{
   \exp\!\left\{
    \frac{\mu}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^nx_i
    -\frac{n\mu^2}{2\sigma^2}\right\}}
   _{g_\mu\{T({\boldsymbol{x}})\}}.
\end{align*} All dependence on \mu passes through

T({\boldsymbol{x}})=\sum_{i=1}^nx_i.

The factorisation theorem therefore proves that \sum_iX_i is sufficient for \mu. Since \overline X=T/n is a one-to-one function of T when n is fixed, \overline X is equivalent and is also sufficient.
If both \mu and \sigma^2 are unknown, the displayed factorisation no longer isolates all parameter dependence through \sum_iX_i. A sufficient statistic for (\mu,\sigma^2) is instead

\left(\sum_{i=1}^nX_i,\sum_{i=1}^nX_i^2\right),

or equivalently

\left(\overline X,\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\overline X)^2\right).

This is the nuisance-parameter warning in concrete form.

title: Exponential families and conjugacy
text:
Minimal sufficiency, completeness, and ancillarity

Definition 3 (Minimal sufficiency) Sufficiency alone does not guarantee the greatest possible compression: the entire sample is trivially sufficient. A statistic T is minimal sufficient if it is a function of every other sufficient statistic.
Article: Minimal sufficiency →

Under common-support regularity conditions, a useful likelihood-ratio criterion is 
\frac{p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta)}{p({\boldsymbol{y}}\mid\theta)}
\text{ is constant in }\theta
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
T({\boldsymbol{x}})=T({\boldsymbol{y}}).
\qquad(2)
For the known-variance normal model, \begin{align*}
\frac{p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\mu)}{p({\boldsymbol{y}}\mid\mu)}
&=\exp\!\left\{
-\frac{\sum_i x_i^2-\sum_i y_i^2}{2\sigma^2}
+\frac{\mu}{\sigma^2}
  \left(\sum_i x_i-\sum_i y_i\right)
\right\}.
\end{align*} The first term is independent of \mu. The second is independent of \mu if and only if \sum_i x_i=\sum_i y_i. Therefore \sum_iX_i, or equivalently \overline X, is minimal sufficient for \mu.

Definition 4 A statistic T is complete for a family if

\mathbb{E}_\theta\{q(T)\}=0,\qquad \theta\in\Omega,

implies q(T)=0 almost surely for every \theta\in\Omega.
Article: Complete statistic →

Sufficiency concerns lossless data reduction; completeness concerns whether a nonzero function of the reduced data can have mean zero for every parameter value. A complete sufficient statistic is minimal sufficient. The Lehmann–Scheffé theorem further says that an unbiased estimator which is a function of a complete sufficient statistic is the unique uniformly minimum-variance unbiased estimator of its target.
Completeness must not be claimed merely because a model has been written in exponential-family notation. For a full-rank exponential family whose natural parameter space contains an open set of the appropriate dimension, the natural sufficient statistic is complete under standard integrability conditions. Curved or restricted subfamilies need not inherit this property.

Definition 5 (Ancillary statistic) A statistic A({\boldsymbol{X}}) is ancillary if its sampling distribution does not depend on \theta.
Article: Ancillary statistic →


Theorem 2 (Basu’s theorem) A complete sufficient statistic is independent of every ancillary statistic.
Article: Basu’s theorem →

In the normal model with known \sigma^2, \overline X carries the information about \mu while the centred residual pattern (X_1-\overline X,\ldots,X_n-\overline X) is ancillary for \mu. The distinction helps separate parameter information from model-diagnostic variation.

title: Exponential families and conjugacy
text:
Why exponential families keep appearing

Definition 6 (Natural exponential family) In the a–b–c–T notation used here, the natural or canonical form of an exponential-family density is 
p(x\mid\theta)
=\frac{b(x)\exp\{c(\theta)^{\mathsf T}T(x)\}}
        {a(\theta)},
\qquad(3) where c(\theta) is the natural or canonical parameter, T(x) is the natural statistic, b(x) does not depend on \theta, and a(\theta) is the normalising function.
Article: Natural exponential family →


Remark 1 (Translation to another common notation). Some books write the same density as

p(x\mid{\boldsymbol{\eta}})
=h(x)\exp\{{\boldsymbol{\eta}}^{\mathsf T}T(x)-A({\boldsymbol{\eta}})\}.

This is only a change of names: {\boldsymbol{\eta}}=c(\theta), h(x)=b(x), and A({\boldsymbol{\eta}})=\log a(\theta). We retain the a(\theta)–b(x)–c(\theta)–T(x) notation from this point onward.
Article: Translation to another common notation →

For an independent sample, define once and for all 
S({\boldsymbol{X}})=\sum_{i=1}^nT(X_i).
\qquad(4) Then \begin{align*}
p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta)
&=\prod_{i=1}^n
   \frac{b(x_i)\exp\{c(\theta)^{\mathsf T}T(x_i)\}}
        {a(\theta)}\\
&=\left\{\prod_{i=1}^n b(x_i)\right\}
   \frac{\exp\{c(\theta)^{\mathsf T}S({\boldsymbol{x}})\}}
        {a(\theta)^n}.
\end{align*} The Fisher–Neyman theorem therefore gives the fixed-dimensional sufficient statistic S({\boldsymbol{X}}). Its dimension does not grow with the sample size.
This is why exponential families keep reappearing in elementary Bayesian calculations. They turn an ever-growing data set into a fixed collection of updated totals, and conjugate priors update those totals by addition. The pattern explains the familiar formulas; it does not imply that every useful model must be exponential-family or that a nonconjugate prior is somehow illegitimate.

Proposition 1 (Log-partition moment identities) Whenever c(\theta) can be used as a local parameter and differentiation under the normalising integral is valid,

\nabla_c\log a(\theta)
=\mathbb{E}_\theta\{T(X)\},
\qquad
\nabla_c^2\log a(\theta)
=\operatorname{Cov}_\theta\{T(X)\}.

Here derivatives are taken with respect to c=c(\theta), so a(\theta) is regarded as a function of c through the chosen parametrisation. Consequently \log a(\theta) is convex as a function of c, and the one-observation Fisher information in the natural parameter is \nabla_c^2\log a(\theta).
Article: Log-partition moment identities →

The density must integrate to one, so the normalising function is

a(\theta)
=\int b(x)\exp\{c(\theta)^{\mathsf T}T(x)\}\,\mathrm{d} x.

Assuming differentiation under the integral is valid, \begin{align*}
\nabla_c\log a(\theta)
&=\frac{\nabla_ca(\theta)}{a(\theta)}\\
&=\frac{
   \int T(x)b(x)
   \exp\{c(\theta)^{\mathsf T}T(x)\}\,\mathrm{d} x}
   {a(\theta)}\\
&=\mathbb{E}_\theta\{T(X)\}.
\end{align*} Differentiating once more, \begin{align*}
\nabla_c^2\log a(\theta)
&=\mathbb{E}_\theta\{T(X)T(X)^{\mathsf T}\}
   -\mathbb{E}_\theta\{T(X)\}
    \mathbb{E}_\theta\{T(X)\}^{\mathsf T}\\
&=\operatorname{Cov}_\theta\{T(X)\}.
\end{align*} Consequently \log a(\theta) is convex as a function of c. For an iid sample the log-likelihood, score, and Fisher information in the natural parameter are \begin{align*}
\ell(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=c(\theta)^{\mathsf T}S({\boldsymbol{x}})
   -n\log a(\theta)+\text{constant},\\
\nabla_c\ell(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=S({\boldsymbol{x}})-n\nabla_c\log a(\theta),\\
\mathcal I_n(c)
&=-\mathbb{E}_\theta
   \{\nabla_c^2\ell(\theta;{\boldsymbol{X}})\}\\
&=n\nabla_c^2\log a(\theta)\\
&=n\operatorname{Cov}_\theta\{T(X)\}.
\end{align*} The likelihood equations therefore match the observed sufficient statistic to its model expectation:

S({\boldsymbol{x}})=n\mathbb{E}_{\widehat\theta}\{T(X)\}.


Theorem 3 (Pitman–Koopman–Darmois, informal form) For regular iid models with parameter-independent support, the theorem says, roughly, that the existence for every n of a sufficient statistic whose dimension stays fixed essentially characterises exponential families. The support condition matters: models such as \operatorname{Uniform}(0,\theta) can have a fixed-dimensional sufficient statistic without having the regular form Equation 3.
Article: Pitman–Koopman–Darmois, informal form →

title: Exponential families and conjugacy
section: Conjugate priors from the exponential-family form

title: Exponential families and conjugacy
text:
Poisson example and Gamma conventions

Example 2 (Poisson natural form and Gamma conjugacy) Question. For iid Poisson observations with mean \theta, write the model in the a(\theta), b(x), c(\theta), T(x) form, identify the sufficient statistic, and derive the corresponding conjugate prior and posterior update.
Solution. For one Poisson observation, \begin{align*}
p(x\mid\theta)
&=\frac{e^{-\theta}\theta^x}{x!}\\
&=\frac1{x!}\exp\{x\log\theta\}e^{-\theta}\\
&=\frac{b(x)\exp\{c(\theta)T(x)\}}{a(\theta)},
\end{align*} with

b(x)=\frac1{x!},
\qquad c(\theta)=\log\theta,
\qquad T(x)=x,
\qquad a(\theta)=e^\theta.

For the Poisson model, the definition Equation 4 gives S({\boldsymbol{x}})=\sum_i x_i. The joint likelihood is \begin{align*}
p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta)
&=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{e^{-\theta}\theta^{x_i}}{x_i!}\\
&=\left(\prod_{i=1}^n\frac1{x_i!}\right)
   \exp\{(\log\theta)S({\boldsymbol{x}})-n\theta\}.
\end{align*} The factorisation theorem shows that S({\boldsymbol{X}}) is sufficient for \theta. It is also minimal sufficient by the likelihood-ratio criterion. Because the natural parameter c(\theta)=\log\theta ranges over the open set \mathbb{R}, S({\boldsymbol{X}}) is complete as well.
The generic prior Equation 6 becomes \begin{align*}
p(\theta\mid\alpha,\beta)
&\propto
\frac{\exp\{\alpha\log\theta\}}{(e^\theta)^\beta}\\
&=\theta^\alpha e^{-\beta\theta}.
\end{align*} This is the kernel of \operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha+1,\beta), not \operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha,\beta). Using the sufficient statistic S({\boldsymbol{x}}), \begin{align*}
p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto
\theta^{S({\boldsymbol{x}})} e^{-n\theta}\theta^\alpha e^{-\beta\theta}\\
&=\theta^{S({\boldsymbol{x}})+\alpha}e^{-(n+\beta)\theta},
\end{align*} so 
\boxed{
\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha+S({\boldsymbol{x}})+1,\beta+n)}.
\qquad(8) Its posterior mean is \begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=\frac{\alpha+S({\boldsymbol{x}})+1}{\beta+n}\\
&=\frac{(\alpha+1)+n\overline x}{\beta+n}\\
&=\frac\beta{\beta+n}\frac{\alpha+1}{\beta}
  +\frac n{\beta+n}\overline x.
\end{align*} The prior therefore behaves, for the mean, as \beta prior observations with total count \alpha+1.







Parameterisation check



In this exponent convention, letting \alpha\to0 and \beta\to0 produces the improper flat kernel p(\theta)\propto1. The Poisson Jeffreys prior is p(\theta)\propto\theta^{-1/2}, corresponding to \alpha=-1/2,\beta=0. The scale-invariant kernel p(\theta)\propto1/\theta corresponds to \alpha=-1,\beta=0. These three improper priors are different and lead to Gamma shapes S+1, S+1/2, and S, respectively.


Improper priors can be useful limiting devices, but they create enough risks that posterior propriety must be checked rather than admired.






Key idea



Conjugacy in an exponential family updates a fixed number of hyperparameters with sufficient statistics. Hierarchical Bayes, developed next, addresses a separate modelling problem: how to represent and learn from variation among related groups.

title: Exponential families and conjugacy
text:
Footnotes


Conjugacy is not needed for Bayesian inference. Metropolis–Hastings mostly asks for ratios of target densities; Gibbs sampling benefits more directly from named full conditional distributions. That computational distinction is a better reason to value conjugacy than mere nostalgia for closed forms.↩︎

title: Bayesian linear regression
text:
Part of Bayesian statistics · 8 questions on this topic · What links here
Linear regression extends the earlier normal model with unknown mean and variance. Instead of giving every observation the same mean \mu, it gives observation i the mean {\boldsymbol{x}}_i^\top{\boldsymbol{\beta}}. The central calculations are therefore familiar normal–inverse-Gamma calculations, but now in p dimensions and with the geometry of least squares doing the algebraic work.
This chapter develops the model, the least-squares reference calculation, the improper-prior posterior kernel and its quadratic decomposition, the conditional posterior families, and independent informative priors, and then carries the marginalisation, simulation, and prediction arguments through in full.
Least squares is the reference calculation to learn first. It is fast, widely available, and provides the least-squares coordinates and checks used below. Bayesian regression retains that sampling model and adds probability distributions for the unknown coefficients and variance.1

title: Bayesian linear regression
text:
The Gaussian linear model
Regression allows the mean response to change with measured predictors. Let there be n observations and k measured predictors, together with an intercept. There are therefore p=k+1 regression coefficients. For observation i, the scalar model is 
Y_i
=x_{i1}\beta_1+\cdots+x_{ik}\beta_k+\beta_0+\varepsilon_i.
\qquad(1) Here x_{ij} is the recorded value of predictor j for observation i. Before the response is observed, Y_i is random; the x_{ij} are known numbers in the model; and the coefficients \beta_0,\ldots,\beta_k are unknown. The term \varepsilon_i represents the part of the response not explained by its mean.
Stacking the scalar equations introduces no new statistical assumption. It is bookkeeping that lets one equation describe all n observations. Using the convention that the intercept comes last, define

{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}=
\begin{pmatrix}
  x_{11}&x_{12}&\cdots&x_{1k}&1\\
  x_{21}&x_{22}&\cdots&x_{2k}&1\\
  \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\
  x_{n1}&x_{n2}&\cdots&x_{nk}&1
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=
\begin{pmatrix}
  \beta_1\\ \beta_2\\ \vdots\\ \beta_k\\ \beta_0
\end{pmatrix}.

Thus {\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p} is known, while {\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathbb{R}^p is unknown. The column of ones supplies the intercept in every row. Placing that column first, and \beta_0 first in {\boldsymbol{\beta}}, changes only the ordering of the coefficients.
Now stack the random responses and errors:

{\boldsymbol{Y}}=
\begin{pmatrix}Y_1\\ \vdots\\Y_n\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}=
\begin{pmatrix}\varepsilon_1\\ \vdots\\\varepsilon_n\end{pmatrix}.

Matrix multiplication produces the complete vector of true mean responses: \begin{align*}
{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
&=
\begin{pmatrix}
  \beta_0+x_{11}\beta_1+\cdots+x_{1k}\beta_k\\
  \beta_0+x_{21}\beta_1+\cdots+x_{2k}\beta_k\\
  \vdots\\
  \beta_0+x_{n1}\beta_1+\cdots+x_{nk}\beta_k
\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\mathbb{E}({\boldsymbol{Y}}\mid{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2,{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}).
\end{align*} The adjective true here means “under the model at the unknown parameter value.” It does not mean that these means have been observed.

Definition 1 (Gaussian linear model) Let {\boldsymbol{x}}_i^\top denote row i of {\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}. The Gaussian linear model is 
{\boldsymbol{Y}}={\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}},
\qquad
{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}\mid\sigma^2
\sim\operatorname{N}_n({\boldsymbol{0}},\sigma^2{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{I}}_n),
\qquad(2) and hence 
{\boldsymbol{Y}}\mid{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2,{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}
\sim\operatorname{N}_n({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{I}}_n).
\qquad(3) Equivalently, the errors are independent with \varepsilon_i\sim\operatorname{N}(0,\sigma^2), so every response has variance \sigma^2 and distinct responses have zero covariance.
The design matrix is conditioned on and treated as fixed. This does not claim that its entries were never measured; it says that their uncertainty is not part of this particular model.
Article: Gaussian linear model →


From random responses to fitted values
Once the responses have been observed, their realised values are written without capital letters and without hats:

{\boldsymbol{y}}=
\begin{pmatrix}y_1\\y_2\\\vdots\\y_n\end{pmatrix}.

These are the actual measured responses. We use {\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}} and {\boldsymbol{y}} to estimate the unknown coefficient vector, obtaining

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=
\begin{pmatrix}
  \widehat\beta_1\\ \widehat\beta_2\\ \vdots\\
  \widehat\beta_k\\ \widehat\beta_0
\end{pmatrix}.

The fitted mean responses are then 
\widehat{{\boldsymbol{y}}}={\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},
\qquad
\widehat y_i
=x_{i1}\widehat\beta_1+\cdots+x_{ik}\widehat\beta_k
  +\widehat\beta_0.
\qquad(4) No new noise is added to these fitted means: \widehat{{\boldsymbol{y}}} estimates the conditional mean {\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}, not a new random response. Notice also that {\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}} still has no hat. We use the same recorded predictors after fitting that we used to specify the model.
Subtracting fitted responses from measured responses gives the residual vector 
\widehat{{\boldsymbol{e}}}
={\boldsymbol{y}}-\widehat{{\boldsymbol{y}}}
={\boldsymbol{y}}-{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
  y_1-\widehat y_1\\ y_2-\widehat y_2\\ \vdots\\
  y_n-\widehat y_n
\end{pmatrix}.
\qquad(5) The two equations worth keeping side by side are

\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
  {\boldsymbol{Y}}&={\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}
   &&\text{(probability model)},\\[2pt]
  {\boldsymbol{y}}&={\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+\widehat{{\boldsymbol{e}}}
   &&\text{(observed data = fitted means + residuals)}.
\end{aligned}}

The first equation contains the unknown true coefficients and random errors. The second contains estimated coefficients and calculated residuals, and it holds exactly because of the definition \widehat{{\boldsymbol{e}}}={\boldsymbol{y}}-{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}.


Errors are not residuals

Definition 2 (Error and residual) The true error is

\varepsilon_i=Y_i-{\boldsymbol{x}}_i^\top{\boldsymbol{\beta}},

which contains the unknown true coefficient vector. After fitting the model, the residual is

e_i=y_i-{\boldsymbol{x}}_i^\top\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}.

Errors are independent model variables under Equation 1; residuals are observable functions of the entire fitted dataset and are not iid. The conventional name “sum of squared errors” is therefore slightly loose: the fitted quantity is a sum of squared residuals.
Article: Error and residual →







Key idea



Whenever {\boldsymbol{\beta}} is still a free argument, \sum_i(y_i-{\boldsymbol{x}}_i^\top{\boldsymbol{\beta}})^2 is a function of {\boldsymbol{\beta}}. It becomes the fitted residual sum of squares only after setting {\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}.

title: Bayesian linear regression
text:
Classical calculations as a reference
In the repeated-sampling argument, {\boldsymbol{\beta}} denotes the fixed, true coefficient vector. The conditioning bar shows when that vector is treated as fixed.
For a proposed coefficient vector {\boldsymbol{b}}, define 
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{SSE}({\boldsymbol{b}})
&=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-{\boldsymbol{x}}_i^\top{\boldsymbol{b}})^2\\
&=({\boldsymbol{y}}-{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}{\boldsymbol{b}})^\top
    ({\boldsymbol{y}}-{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}{\boldsymbol{b}})\\
&=\lVert{\boldsymbol{y}}-{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}{\boldsymbol{b}}\rVert_2^2.
\end{aligned}
\qquad(6) Multiplying out every term gives \begin{align*}
\operatorname{SSE}({\boldsymbol{b}})
&={\boldsymbol{y}}^\top{\boldsymbol{y}}
   -{\boldsymbol{y}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}{\boldsymbol{b}}
   -{\boldsymbol{b}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\boldsymbol{y}}
   +{\boldsymbol{b}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}{\boldsymbol{b}}\\
&={\boldsymbol{y}}^\top{\boldsymbol{y}}
   -2{\boldsymbol{b}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\boldsymbol{y}}
   +{\boldsymbol{b}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}{\boldsymbol{b}},
\end{align*} because the two middle terms are equal scalars. Differentiating with respect to {\boldsymbol{b}},

\frac{\partial}{\partial{\boldsymbol{b}}}
\operatorname{SSE}({\boldsymbol{b}})
=-2{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\boldsymbol{y}}+2{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}{\boldsymbol{b}}.

At the minimiser this gradient is zero, so the normal equations are

{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
={\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\boldsymbol{y}}.


Proposition 1 (Ordinary least squares) Assume that \operatorname{rank}({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})=p. Then {\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}} is invertible and 
\boxed{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
  =({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})^{-1}{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\boldsymbol{y}}.}
\qquad(7) The fitted residual vector and residual sum of squares are 
\widehat{{\boldsymbol{e}}}={\boldsymbol{y}}-{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},
\qquad
\operatorname{SSE}
=\widehat{{\boldsymbol{e}}}^{\top}\widehat{{\boldsymbol{e}}}
=\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{e}}}\rVert_2^2
=\operatorname{SSE}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}).
\qquad(8)
The maximum-likelihood estimator of \sigma^2 is \operatorname{SSE}/n. Estimating p coefficients consumes p degrees of freedom, so the usual unbiased estimator is 
s^2=\widehat\sigma^2=\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}{n-p}.
\qquad(9)
Article: Ordinary least squares →

To see the sampling distribution of the OLS estimator, substitute {\boldsymbol{Y}}={\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}} into Equation 7: \begin{align*}
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
&=({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})^{-1}{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top
   ({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}})\\
&=({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})^{-1}{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
   +({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})^{-1}{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top
     {\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}\\
&={\boldsymbol{\beta}}+({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})^{-1}{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top
     {\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}.
\end{align*} It is a linear transformation of a normal vector. Its expectation is {\boldsymbol{\beta}}, and its covariance is \begin{align*}
\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2)
&=({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})^{-1}{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top
   (\sigma^2{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{I}}_n){\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}
   ({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})^{-1}\\
&=\sigma^2({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})^{-1}.
\end{align*} Therefore the following result holds.

Proposition 2 (Sampling distribution of the OLS estimator) 
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2,{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}
\sim\operatorname{N}_p\!\left(
   {\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})^{-1}\right).
\qquad(10) Also, 
\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_{n-p},
\qquad
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\ \text{is independent of }\operatorname{SSE}.
\qquad(11)
Article: Sampling distribution of the OLS estimator →

If c_{jj}=[({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})^{-1}]_{jj}, then

Corollary 1 (Studentised coefficient pivot) 
\frac{\widehat\beta_j-\beta_j}{s\sqrt{c_{jj}}}
\sim t_{n-p}.
\qquad(12) Thus \widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} itself has the normal distribution Equation 10; the Student distribution appears only after replacing the unknown \sigma by s and standardising.
Article: Studentised coefficient pivot →

title: Bayesian linear regression
text:
Likelihood and reference prior
Conditional independence in Equation 1 gives 
\begin{aligned}
p({\boldsymbol{y}}\mid{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2,{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})
&=\prod_{i=1}^n
   \frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}
   \exp\!\left\{-\frac{(y_i-{\boldsymbol{x}}_i^\top{\boldsymbol{\beta}})^2}
                         {2\sigma^2}\right\}\\
&=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}
   \exp\!\left\{-\frac{\operatorname{SSE}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})}
                         {2\sigma^2}\right\}.
\end{aligned}
\qquad(13) The standard improper reference prior is 
p({\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2)\propto\frac1{\sigma^2},
\qquad {\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathbb{R}^p,\quad\sigma^2>0.
\qquad(14) It is flat in {\boldsymbol{\beta}} and flat in \log\sigma^2, since \,\mathrm{d}(\log\sigma^2)=\,\mathrm{d}\sigma^2/\sigma^2. Neither factor integrates to one, so “uninformative” is a modelling convention, not the absence of assumptions.
An improper reference prior is usable only when the posterior is proper. Here that requires enough information to identify all p regression coefficients, including full column rank and, in the ordinary derivation, n>p. The prior is a limiting device rather than a population from which parameters could literally be simulated, so prior prediction is unavailable under it even when posterior inference is valid.
Bayes’ rule gives the joint posterior kernel 
p({\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{y}},{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})
\propto
(\sigma^2)^{-(n/2+1)}
\exp\!\left\{-\frac{\operatorname{SSE}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})}
                         {2\sigma^2}\right\}.
\qquad(15) This kernel defines a proper posterior when

\operatorname{rank}({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})=p,
\qquad n>p,
\qquad \operatorname{SSE}>0.

For continuous Gaussian data, the last condition holds with probability one under full rank and n>p.

title: Bayesian linear regression
Bayesian linear regression
Bayesian linear regression
section: Direct simulation and genuine Gibbs sampling
text:
Direct simulation and genuine Gibbs sampling
The posterior factorisation

p({\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{y}})
=p({\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid\sigma^2,{\boldsymbol{y}})
  p(\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{y}})

gives direct ancestral simulation. For m=1,\ldots,M:

Proposition 5 (Direct posterior simulation)  

draw


  \sigma^{2(m)}\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\!\left(
  \frac{n-p}{2},\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}2\right);


conditional on that draw, draw


  {\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(m)}\sim\operatorname{N}_p\!\left(
  \widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},
  \sigma^{2(m)}({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})^{-1}\right).

The resulting pairs are iid joint-posterior draws. There is no burn-in, serial dependence, or convergence diagnostic.
Article: Direct posterior simulation →

The following base-R calculation implements the proposition. The design matrix X includes the intercept column and y is the response vector. The derivation has already supplied the inverse-Gamma parameters and the coefficient covariance; the computer now performs the random generation and the matrix arithmetic. The final two lines produce the posterior predictive distribution at \widetilde x=4.5 by adding a new observation’s noise to every coefficient draw.
fit <- lm.fit(X, y)
beta_hat <- fit$coefficients
SSE <- sum(fit$residuals^2)
p <- ncol(X)
nu <- nrow(X) - p
XtX_inv <- solve(crossprod(X))

set.seed(3500)
M <- 10000L
sigma2 <- 1 / rgamma(M, shape = nu / 2, rate = SSE / 2)
Z <- matrix(rnorm(M * p), M, p)
beta <- sweep(Z %*% chol(XtX_inv), 1, sqrt(sigma2), "*")
beta <- sweep(beta, 2, beta_hat, "+")

x_new <- c(1, 4.5)
mu_new <- drop(beta %*% x_new)
y_new <- rnorm(M, mean = mu_new, sd = sqrt(sigma2))
quantile(y_new, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
These are independent ancestral draws. Running generic MCMC here would add dependence and convergence questions to a problem that already has a direct solution. The distinction is computationally important as well as terminological.
If one deliberately constructs a Gibbs sampler, the variance must instead be conditioned on the current coefficient vector. From Equation 15, 
\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{y}},{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}
\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\!\left(
\frac n2,\frac{\operatorname{SSE}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})}2\right).
\qquad(25) A Gibbs sweep alternates Equation 19 and Equation 25. For this model the direct sampler is simpler. The two variance distributions should not be confused:








Posterior
Shape
Sum of squares




\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{y}}
(n-p)/2
fitted \operatorname{SSE}


\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{y}}
n/2
\operatorname{SSE}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})

title: Bayesian linear regression
text:
Informative priors and regularisation
The independent priors are

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\sim\operatorname{N}_p({\boldsymbol{m}}_0,{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{V}}_0),
\qquad
\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(a_0,b_0).

Under this specification the model is conditionally conjugate. Collecting quadratic terms in {\boldsymbol{\beta}} gives \begin{align*}
{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{V}}_\beta^{-1}
&=\frac{{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}}{\sigma^2}+{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{V}}_0^{-1},\\
{\boldsymbol{m}}_\beta
&={\color{blue}\boldsymbol{V}}_\beta\left(
   \frac{{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\boldsymbol{y}}}{\sigma^2}
   +{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{V}}_0^{-1}{\boldsymbol{m}}_0\right),
\end{align*} and hence 
\begin{aligned}
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid\sigma^2,{\boldsymbol{y}}
&\sim\operatorname{N}_p({\boldsymbol{m}}_\beta,{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{V}}_\beta),
\\
\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{y}}
&\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\!\left(
  a_0+\frac n2,
  b_0+\frac12\operatorname{SSE}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right).
\end{aligned}
\qquad(26) These full conditionals define a Gibbs sampler, but prior independence is not the usual jointly conjugate normal–inverse-Gamma family.

Definition 3 (Normal–inverse-Gamma prior) Full joint conjugacy is obtained from the scaled prior 
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid\sigma^2
\sim\operatorname{N}_p({\boldsymbol{m}}_0,\sigma^2{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{V}}_0),
\qquad
\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(a_0,b_0).
\qquad(27)
Article: Normal–inverse-Gamma prior →

Define 
\begin{aligned}
{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{V}}_n^{-1}&={\color{blue}\boldsymbol{V}}_0^{-1}+{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}},
\\
{\boldsymbol{m}}_n&={\color{blue}\boldsymbol{V}}_n
({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{V}}_0^{-1}{\boldsymbol{m}}_0+{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\boldsymbol{y}}).
\end{aligned}
\qquad(28) The two quadratic forms combine as \begin{align*}
&({\boldsymbol{y}}-{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})^\top({\boldsymbol{y}}-{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
+({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{m}}_0)^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{V}}_0^{-1}
  ({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{m}}_0)\\
&\quad={\boldsymbol{y}}^\top{\boldsymbol{y}}+{\boldsymbol{m}}_0^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{V}}_0^{-1}
{\boldsymbol{m}}_0
-2{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^\top({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\boldsymbol{y}}+{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{V}}_0^{-1}{\boldsymbol{m}}_0)
+{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{V}}_n^{-1}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\\
&\quad=({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{m}}_n)^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{V}}_n^{-1}
({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{m}}_n)
+{\boldsymbol{y}}^\top{\boldsymbol{y}}+{\boldsymbol{m}}_0^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{V}}_0^{-1}{\boldsymbol{m}}_0
-{\boldsymbol{m}}_n^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{V}}_n^{-1}{\boldsymbol{m}}_n.
\end{align*} The first line has the geometric reading

\lVert{\boldsymbol{y}}-{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\rVert_2^2
+\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{m}}_0\rVert_{{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{V}}_0^{-1}}^2.

It adds squared data-space misfit to squared distance from the prior centre, measured in the prior-precision geometry. After completing the square, the coefficient-dependent term on the final line is \lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{m}}_n\rVert_{{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{V}}_n^{-1}}^2. Therefore, with \begin{align*}
a_n&=a_0+\frac n2,\\
b_n&=b_0+\frac12\left(
{\boldsymbol{y}}^\top{\boldsymbol{y}}
+{\boldsymbol{m}}_0^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{V}}_0^{-1}{\boldsymbol{m}}_0
-{\boldsymbol{m}}_n^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{V}}_n^{-1}{\boldsymbol{m}}_n
\right),
\end{align*} the posterior remains normal–inverse-Gamma.

Theorem 2 (Normal–inverse-Gamma conjugacy) 
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid\sigma^2,{\boldsymbol{y}}
\sim\operatorname{N}_p({\boldsymbol{m}}_n,\sigma^2{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{V}}_n),
\qquad
\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{y}}\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(a_n,b_n).
\qquad(29)
Article: Normal–inverse-Gamma conjugacy →

A centred normal prior also explains ridge regularisation. If \sigma^2 is fixed and {\boldsymbol{\beta}}\sim\operatorname{N}_p({\boldsymbol{0}},\tau^2{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{I}}_p), then \begin{align*}
-2\sigma^2\log p({\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid{\boldsymbol{y}})
&=\operatorname{SSE}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
   +\frac{\sigma^2}{\tau^2}\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\rVert^2
   +\text{a constant}\\
&=\lVert{\boldsymbol{y}}-{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\rVert_2^2
   +\frac{\sigma^2}{\tau^2}\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\rVert_2^2
   +\text{the same constant}.
\end{align*} The MAP therefore minimises a ridge objective: Euclidean data-space error is balanced against squared Euclidean distance of the coefficient vector from the prior centre, here {\boldsymbol{0}}. A Laplace prior similarly produces an L^1 penalty related to the lasso. MAP keeps only the posterior mode; full Bayes retains coefficient uncertainty and averages predictions over the posterior.
In machine learning, priors are often introduced mainly as regularisers. That is a legitimate computational use, but it changes the emphasis: the MAP acts like a penalised estimate, while the rest of the posterior may be ignored. For statistical inference the posterior is reported, rather than only a penalised point estimate, because coefficient uncertainty and its dependence feed directly into predictions.

title: Bayesian linear regression
text:
Posterior prediction

Definition 4 (Posterior predictive target) Prediction requires a new random quantity; estimating a fitted mean and predicting a new observation are not the same problem. For a new predictor vector \widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}, suppose 
\widetilde Y\mid{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2,\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{N}(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}^\top{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2).
\qquad(30) The posterior predictive density is 
p(\widetilde y\mid{\boldsymbol{y}},{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}},\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\int_0^\infty\int_{\mathbb{R}^p}
p(\widetilde y\mid{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2,\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}})
p({\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{y}},{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})
\,\mathrm{d}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\,\mathrm{d}\sigma^2.
\qquad(31)
Article: Posterior predictive target →

If the goal is a new response, posterior prediction is not optional decoration. A fitted mean describes uncertainty about the regression surface; a future observation also contains a new error term. Averaging over ({\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2) carries both sources of uncertainty forward, which is why a predictive interval is wider than an interval for the mean response at the same predictor value.
Let

h(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}^\top({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})^{-1}
  \widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}
=\lVert\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}\rVert_{({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})^{-1}}^2.

Thus leverage is the squared length of the new predictor in the covariance geometry of the fitted coefficients, before multiplying by \sigma^2. By the linear-transformation rule applied to Equation 19, 
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}^\top{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid\sigma^2,{\boldsymbol{y}},{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}
\sim\operatorname{N}\!\left(
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}^\top\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},
\sigma^2h(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}})\right).
\qquad(32) For a future response, the independent new error contributes another \sigma^2, so integrating {\boldsymbol{\beta}} first gives 
\widetilde Y\mid\sigma^2,{\boldsymbol{y}},{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}},\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{N}\!\left(
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}^\top\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},
\sigma^2\{1+h(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}})\}\right).
\qquad(33) Finally integrate \sigma^2 using Equation 20. The same normal–inverse-Gamma mixture that produced Equation 22 gives

Theorem 3 (Posterior prediction under the reference prior) 
\boxed{
\widetilde Y\mid{\boldsymbol{y}},{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}},\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim t_{n-p}\!\left(
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}^\top\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},
s\sqrt{1+h(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}})}\right).}
\qquad(34) For the unknown mean response itself, there is no new observational error: 
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}^\top{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid{\boldsymbol{y}},{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}
\sim t_{n-p}\!\left(
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}^\top\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},
s\sqrt{h(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}})}\right).
\qquad(35)
Article: Posterior prediction under the reference prior →

The distinction is summarised by the scale terms.








Target
Posterior centre
Squared scale




Coefficient \beta_j
\widehat\beta_j
s^2 c_{jj}


Mean at \widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}^\top\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
s^2 h(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}})


New response at \widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}^\top\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
s^2\{1+h(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}})\}



The extra 1 is irreducible future observational noise. The leverage term h(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}) measures uncertainty about the fitted line and typically grows during extrapolation. Posterior predictive simulation provides the same answer without closed-form algebra: for every posterior draw, generate

\widetilde Y^{(m)}\sim\operatorname{N}\!\left(
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}^\top{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(m)},\sigma^{2(m)}\right).

The empirical distribution of these values approximates the posterior predictive distribution and directly supplies predictive means, quantiles, and intervals.

title: Bayesian linear regression
text:
Worked regression example

Example 1 (Eight-point regression) Consider n=8 observations with one predictor and an intercept:

{\boldsymbol{x}}=(1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8)^{\mathsf T},
\qquad
{\boldsymbol{y}}=(2.05,3.40,4.55,5.10,7.20,8.05,9.60,10.80)^\top.

Question. Under the reference-prior analysis developed above, compute \widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}, the fitted sum of squared errors, the posterior distributions of \sigma^2 and {\boldsymbol{\beta}}, and marginal 95\% credible intervals for the two regression coefficients. Then derive posterior predictive distributions at \widetilde x=4.5 and \widetilde x=10 and explain the effect of extrapolation.
Solution. For this example put the intercept first, so the ith row of {\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}} is (1,x_i). Direct summation gives

\sum_i y_i=50.75,
\qquad
\sum_i x_i y_i=280.80,
\qquad
\sum_i y_i^2=387.9175.

Therefore

{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}=
\begin{pmatrix}8&36\\36&204\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\boldsymbol{y}}=
\begin{pmatrix}50.75\\280.80\end{pmatrix}.

The determinant is 8(204)-36^2=336, so

({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})^{-1}
=\frac1{336}\begin{pmatrix}204&-36\\-36&8\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}
0.607143&-0.107143\\
-0.107143&0.023810
\end{pmatrix}.

Multiplying by {\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\boldsymbol{y}}, \begin{align*}
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
&=\frac1{336}
\begin{pmatrix}204&-36\\-36&8\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}50.75\\280.80\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\frac1{336}
\begin{pmatrix}
204(50.75)-36(280.80)\\
-36(50.75)+8(280.80)
\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\begin{pmatrix}0.726786\\1.248214\end{pmatrix}.
\end{align*} The fitted SSE can be calculated without listing every residual: \begin{align*}
\operatorname{SSE}
&={\boldsymbol{y}}^\top{\boldsymbol{y}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\boldsymbol{y}}\\
&=387.9175
-\frac{244.2}{336}(50.75)-\frac{419.4}{336}(280.80)\\
&\approx0.534554.
\end{align*} The exact coefficients are kept here rather than the six-figure decimals printed above. The subtraction cancels almost everything: two quantities near 387.9 leave a remainder near 0.53, so rounding \widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} first costs about four significant figures in \operatorname{SSE}. Summing the squared residuals directly avoids the cancellation entirely.
Thus n-p=6 and

s^2=\frac{0.534554}{6}\approx0.089092.

Under the reference prior, \begin{align*}
\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{y}}
&\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(3,0.267277),\\
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid{\boldsymbol{y}}
&\sim t_6\!\left(
\begin{pmatrix}0.726786\\1.248214\end{pmatrix},
0.089092
\begin{pmatrix}
0.607143&-0.107143\\
-0.107143&0.023810
\end{pmatrix}\right).
\end{align*} The variance summaries illustrate why the loss function matters:

\mathbb{E}(\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{y}})=\frac{0.267277}{3-1}=0.133638,
\qquad
\operatorname{mode}(\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{y}})
=\frac{0.267277}{3+1}=0.066819,

while s^2=0.089092. Using t_{0.975,6}\approx2.447, the marginal 95\% credible intervals are approximately

\beta_0\mid{\boldsymbol{y}}:\ (0.158,1.296),
\qquad
\beta_1\mid{\boldsymbol{y}}:\ (1.136,1.361).

At \widetilde x=4.5, take \widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}=(1,4.5)^\top. Matrix multiplication gives

h(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}})
=(1,4.5)({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})^{-1}
\begin{pmatrix}1\\4.5\end{pmatrix}=0.125,

and the predicted centre is

\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}^\top\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
=0.726786+4.5(1.248214)=6.34375.

Consequently,

\widetilde Y\mid{\boldsymbol{y}},\widetilde x=4.5
\sim t_6\!\left(6.34375,
\sqrt{0.089092(1.125)}\right)
\approx t_6(6.344,0.317).

At \widetilde x=10, the centre is about 13.209 and h(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}})\approx0.845, giving predictive scale about 0.405. The increase from 0.317 is the uncertainty cost of extrapolating beyond the observed predictor range.






Figure 1: The eight observations, the fitted line, and the two bands. The inner band is for the mean response and the outer for a new observation; the gap between them is the extra 1 in the predictive scale, which is why they never meet however small the leverage term becomes. The vertical rules mark the two predictions computed above, at \widetilde x=4.5 inside the data and \widetilde x=10 beyond it. Both bands are narrowest near \overline x and flare outward, so the cost of extrapolation is a feature of the geometry rather than a separate warning to remember.

title: Bayesian linear regression
section: Three corrections and a problem-solving checklist
text:
Three corrections and a problem-solving checklist
Three distinctions are worth making explicit.

Remark 1 (Three easy confusions). 

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} has an exact normal sampling distribution when \sigma^2 is known. The t distribution applies after studentisation by s.
The marginal variance posterior has inverse-Gamma shape (n-p)/2, not (n+p)/2. The p/2 belongs to the coefficient normalising constant and must be subtracted from the original power.
Drawing first from p(\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{y}}) and then from p({\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid\sigma^2,{\boldsymbol{y}}) produces iid posterior draws. A genuine Gibbs sampler instead uses p(\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{y}}) and therefore produces a Markov chain.

Article: Three easy confusions →

For an unseen problem, the reliable route is:

state the model using errors, and state whether {\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}} is fixed;
check \operatorname{rank}({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}})=p and n>p;
form the likelihood using the free {\boldsymbol{\beta}}, not \widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}};
decompose the candidate SSE with Equation 17;
read off Equation 19 and derive Equation 20 by accounting for the normalising power;
decide whether the target is a coefficient, a fitted mean, or a future response; and
use direct posterior simulation when it is available rather than introducing unnecessary MCMC dependence.







Key idea



Bayesian linear regression is the unknown-mean normal model in p dimensions. Least-squares geometry supplies the quadratic decomposition; Bayesian conditioning turns it into normal, inverse-Gamma, and Student posteriors; and posterior prediction adds future observational noise to parameter uncertainty.

title: Topics
text:
About the book
This book is a self-contained course in modern applied statistics for advanced undergraduates and beginning postgraduates. It assumes a working knowledge of probability, the linear model, and elementary calculus, and it is written so that a careful reader can reconstruct every calculation.
The book has five parts. The first develops Bayesian inference from first principles: credible intervals, conjugate updating, Markov chain Monte Carlo, categorical models, hypothesis comparison, exponential families, hierarchical models, and Bayesian linear regression. The later parts leave the normal linear model. Generalised linear models separate the mean, the variance, and the link. Smoothing replaces a straight line with a function the data are allowed to bend. Models for correlated data then drop independence, first with random effects and then with marginal estimating equations. The last part treats dependence along a time series, and forecasting from that dependence.
Two conventions hold throughout.

Scalars are ordinary italic (a, \theta, \sigma^2). Vectors are bold black ({\boldsymbol{x}}, \boldsymbol{\beta}). Matrices are bold blue ({\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}}). A component such as \beta_j or X_{ij} is a scalar again. The covariate vector of one unit is {\boldsymbol{X}}_i, and {\color{blue}\boldsymbol{X}} is the matrix with ith row {\boldsymbol{X}}_i^\top.
\mathrm{Gamma}(a,b) means shape a and rate b, 
f(t)=\frac{b^a}{\Gamma(a)}t^{a-1}e^{-bt},\qquad t>0,
 unless a displayed convention is labelled otherwise. The mean is then a/b and the variance is a/b^2. \mathrm{InvGamma}(a,b) means 1/T\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(a,b). Where another parameterisation appears, it is named before it is used.

Software comes after the probability target is already clear. When a fit is shown, it is in R. The code is a translation of a derivation, not a substitute for it.
Each chapter ends with exercises. Applied problems are gathered with the chapter that supplies the method, and worked solutions are collected in one place at the end of the Bayesian part. A solution link after an applied problem jumps to that solution; the solution title jumps back to the problem.

title: Topics
text:
What is written

Bayesian statistics

Bayesian foundations. What a credible interval says, Bayes’ rule for densities, and prior and posterior prediction.
The Beta–Binomial model. Conjugacy, pseudo-counts, prior sensitivity, and prediction of further tosses.
Conjugate analysis for normal models. A normal mean, an inverse-Gamma variance, and the two full conditionals.
Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings. Detailed balance, then two samplers worth implementing.
Categorical data and the Dirichlet distribution. The simplex, Dirichlet–Multinomial conjugacy, and the multinomial central limit theorem.
Bayesian hypotheses and model comparison. Posterior odds, Bayes factors, and the imperfect-fruit calculation.
Exponential families and conjugacy. Sufficiency, the natural exponential family, and the generic conjugate update.
Hierarchical Bayes. Exchangeability, partial pooling, and a grid approximation for a hyperposterior.
Bayesian linear regression. The reference prior, direct simulation, and posterior prediction.
Reference formulas and a problem-solving workflow. The distribution kernels used in the Bayesian chapters, gathered in one place.
Solutions to the applied exercises. Worked solutions, placed with the chapter that supplies the method.



Generalised linear models

Introduction to generalised linear models. Exponential families, the three components, binary links, and Fisher scoring.
Standard errors, and models for counts. Standard errors, dose–response data, Poisson and quasi-Poisson fits, the negative binomial, and the two Conway–Maxwell–Poisson parameterisations.
Underdispersion, positive responses, and quasi-likelihood. Gamma and inverse-Gaussian models for positive measurements, and a variance function that is not an exponential-family variance.
Categorical responses. Proportional odds, proportional hazards, and the baseline-category logit.
Paired comparisons and deviance. Odds ratios, the Bradley–Terry model, and deviance residuals.
Probability-integral residuals. A uniform plot that does not require a normal residual.



Smoothing

Smooth means. The roughness penalty, and a smooth for a probability that need not be monotone.
Additive smooths. Several smooth functions of one covariate at a time, including a partially linear model.



Correlated data

Random intercepts. Blocks, the induced correlation, and fixed versus random effects.
Random slopes, and a binary mixed model. A slope that varies between subjects, and a logit with random effects.
Marginal models. Population averages, working correlation, and sandwich standard errors.
Several responses on one unit. A multivariate margin, and why the sandwich interval is not a rectangle.



Time series

Dependence along a series. Autoregression, moving averages, stationarity, and the Wold decomposition.
Forecasting. Automatic selection for a seasonal series and for a wandering count of server traffic. Models for changing variance, and for counts, are named and left for later work.

title: Random-walk Metropolis for a correlated normal
text:
Topic: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings · more questions on this topic
Source: Book exercise from Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings ‹ Metropolis–Hastings for the logit-normal posterior An independent Gamma proposal ›

For the bivariate-normal target of the bivariate-normal Gibbs exercise, describe a random-walk Metropolis–Hastings sampler using increments

{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}\sim\operatorname{N}_2({\boldsymbol{0}},{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{\Psi}}),
\qquad
{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{\Psi}}=
\begin{bmatrix}a^2&0\\0&b^2\end{bmatrix}.

Give the proposal, the acceptance probability in explicit quadratic form and its equivalent norm/distance reading, and the accept–reject update. Discuss what a and b control.






Worked answer (click to show)





Question. Let the target be the bivariate normal distribution

{\boldsymbol{Z}}\sim\operatorname{N}_2\!\left(
\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\end{bmatrix},
\begin{bmatrix}1&\rho\\ \rho&1\end{bmatrix}
\right),\qquad |\rho|<1.

Describe a random-walk Metropolis–Hastings sampler using increments

{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}\sim\operatorname{N}_2({\boldsymbol{0}},{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{\Psi}}),
\qquad
{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{\Psi}}=
\begin{bmatrix}a^2&0\\0&b^2\end{bmatrix}.

Give the proposal, the acceptance probability in explicit quadratic form and its equivalent norm/distance reading, and the accept–reject update. Discuss what a and b control.
Solution. Let {\boldsymbol{z}}_t=(x_t,y_t)^{\mathsf T}. Generate an increment

{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}_t\sim
\operatorname{N}_2({\boldsymbol{0}},{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{\Psi}}),
\qquad
{\boldsymbol{z}}^\ast={\boldsymbol{z}}_t+{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}_t.

The proposal density satisfies q({\boldsymbol{z}}^\ast\mid{\boldsymbol{z}}_t)
=q({\boldsymbol{z}}_t\mid{\boldsymbol{z}}^\ast), so the Hastings correction cancels. Since

{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}
=\frac1{1-\rho^2}
\begin{bmatrix}1&-\rho\\-\rho&1\end{bmatrix},

For a generic state {\boldsymbol{z}}=(x,y)^{\mathsf T}, define \begin{align*}
Q(x,y)
&=\frac{x^2-2\rho xy+y^2}{1-\rho^2}\\
&={\boldsymbol{z}}^\top{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}{\boldsymbol{z}}\\
&=\lVert{\boldsymbol{z}}\rVert_{{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}}^2.
\end{align*} The same scalar is therefore the explicit coordinate quadratic, the matrix quadratic form, and squared Mahalanobis distance from the origin. Its level sets are the target’s elliptical density contours. The target ratio is \begin{align*}
\frac{\pi({\boldsymbol{z}}^\ast)}{\pi({\boldsymbol{z}}_t)}
&=\frac{\exp\{-Q(x^\ast,y^\ast)/2\}}
{\exp\{-Q(x_t,y_t)/2\}}\\
&=\exp\!\left[-\frac12
\{Q(x^\ast,y^\ast)-Q(x_t,y_t)\}\right]\\
&=\exp\!\left[-\frac12\left\{
\lVert{\boldsymbol{z}}^\ast\rVert_{{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}}^2
-\lVert{\boldsymbol{z}}_t\rVert_{{\color{blue}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}}^2
\right\}\right].
\end{align*} Thus

a({\boldsymbol{z}}_t,{\boldsymbol{z}}^\ast)
=\min\!\left(1,
\exp\!\left[-\frac12
\{Q(x^\ast,y^\ast)-Q(x_t,y_t)\}\right]
\right).

Draw U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1); set {\boldsymbol{z}}_{t+1}={\boldsymbol{z}}^\ast if U<a, and otherwise repeat the current state. The constants a and b are the proposal standard deviations in the two coordinate directions. If they are too small, acceptance is high but travel is slow; if too large, rejections dominate. For |\rho| near one, a diagonal proposal also ignores the target’s rotated geometry, so a proposal covariance aligned with {\color{blue}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} can be much more efficient.

title: Exponential observations parameterised by mean
text:
Topic: Exponential families and conjugacy · more questions on this topic
Source: Book exercise from Exponential families and conjugacy ‹ Exponential observations parameterised by rate Pooling ›

Let X_1,\ldots,X_n be iid \operatorname{Exp}(1/\theta) observations, so that \theta>0 is the mean and

p(x_i\mid\theta)=\theta^{-1}e^{-x_i/\theta}\mathbf{1}_{\{x_i\geq0\}}.

Use the exponential-family form to find a conjugate prior and derive its posterior parameters.






Worked answer (click to show)





Question. Let X_1,\ldots,X_n be iid \operatorname{Exp}(1/\theta) observations, so that \theta>0 is the mean and

p(x_i\mid\theta)=\theta^{-1}e^{-x_i/\theta}\mathbf{1}_{\{x_i\geq0\}}.

Use the exponential-family form to find a conjugate prior and derive its posterior parameters.
Solution. Now

p(x\mid\theta)=\theta^{-1}e^{-x/\theta}\mathbf{1}_{\{x\geq0\}}
=\frac{b(x)\exp\{c(\theta)T(x)\}}{a(\theta)}

with

\boxed{
b(x)=\mathbf{1}_{\{x\geq0\}},\quad
T(x)=x,\quad
c(\theta)=-\frac1\theta,\quad
a(\theta)=\theta}.

The generic prior kernel becomes \begin{align*}
p(\theta\mid\alpha,\beta)
&\propto
\frac{\exp(-\alpha/\theta)}{\theta^\beta}\\
&=\theta^{-\beta}e^{-\alpha/\theta}.
\end{align*} Since an \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b) density has kernel \theta^{-a-1}e^{-b/\theta}, this prior is

\theta\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(\beta-1,\alpha),
\qquad \alpha>0,\quad\beta>1.

The sample likelihood is

p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta)
\propto\theta^{-n}
\exp\!\left[-\frac{S({\boldsymbol{x}})}{\theta}\right].

Therefore \begin{align*}
p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto
\theta^{-n}e^{-S({\boldsymbol{x}})/\theta}
\theta^{-\beta}e^{-\alpha/\theta}\\
&=\theta^{-(\beta+n)}
\exp\!\left[-\frac{\alpha+S({\boldsymbol{x}})}{\theta}\right],
\end{align*} and hence

\boxed{\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\bigl(\beta+n-1,\alpha+S({\boldsymbol{x}})\bigr)}.

Equivalently, a standard prior \operatorname{InvGamma}(a_0,b_0) updates to

\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim
\operatorname{InvGamma}\bigl(a_0+n,b_0+S({\boldsymbol{x}})\bigr).







Parameterisation check



\operatorname{Exp}(\theta) in the preceding exercise used \theta as a rate, whereas \operatorname{Exp}(1/\theta) here makes \theta the mean. The first likelihood is conjugate to a Gamma prior for \theta; the second is conjugate to an inverse-Gamma prior. Interchanging rate and mean without rewriting the density would interchange the two answers.

title: A geometric observation and a uniform prior
text:
Topic: The Beta–Binomial model · more questions on this topic
Source: Book exercise from The Beta–Binomial model ‹ A future run of tosses A logit-normal prior for a coin ›

Let X be the number of coin tosses up to and including the first head. Thus

\mathbb{P}(X=x\mid\theta)=\theta(1-\theta)^{x-1},
\qquad x=1,2,\ldots,

where \theta is the probability of a head. Use the prior \theta\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1).

Find and identify p(\theta\mid x).
Discuss whether the prior was intended to be informative and whether it is conjugate.
Find the posterior mode.
Find \mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x).
Express the posterior mean as a convex combination of the prior mean and the maximum-likelihood estimate of \theta.
Give an equivalent-prior-observations interpretation, and state which pseudo-count convention you are using.







Worked answer (click to show)





Question. Let X be the number of coin tosses up to and including the first head. Thus

\mathbb{P}(X=x\mid\theta)=\theta(1-\theta)^{x-1},
\qquad x=1,2,\ldots,

where \theta is the probability of a head. Use the prior \theta\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1).

Find and identify p(\theta\mid x).
Discuss whether the prior was intended to be informative and whether it is conjugate.
Find the posterior mode.
Find \mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x).
Express the posterior mean as a convex combination of the prior mean and the maximum-likelihood estimate of \theta.
Give an equivalent-prior-observations interpretation, and state which pseudo-count convention you are using.

Solution.

The prior density is one on (0,1), so Bayes’ rule gives \begin{align*}
p(\theta\mid x)
&\propto \mathbb{P}(X=x\mid\theta)p(\theta)\\
&=\theta(1-\theta)^{x-1}\\
&=\theta^{2-1}(1-\theta)^{x-1}.
\end{align*} The normalising integral is


\int_0^1\theta(1-\theta)^{x-1}\,\mathrm{d}\theta
=B(2,x)
=\frac{\Gamma(2)\Gamma(x)}{\Gamma(x+2)}
=\frac{1}{x(x+1)}.

Consequently

p(\theta\mid x)=x(x+1)\theta(1-\theta)^{x-1},
\qquad
\boxed{\theta\mid x\sim\operatorname{Beta}(2,x)}.


The uniform prior was chosen to give equal density to equal-length intervals of \theta, so it was intended as a non-informative prior on this particular scale. That description is not invariant under a transformation of \theta. Since \operatorname{Unif}(0,1)=\operatorname{Beta}(1,1) and the Beta family is conjugate to this geometric likelihood, the prior is conjugate.
A \operatorname{Beta}(a,b) density has interior mode (a-1)/(a+b-2) when a,b>1. Here this gives


\operatorname{mode}(\theta\mid x)
=\frac{2-1}{2+x-2}=\boxed{\frac1x}.

For x=1 this is the boundary mode at one.

The posterior mean is


\boxed{\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)=\frac{2}{x+2}}.


The prior mean is 1/2. To obtain the maximum-likelihood estimator, differentiate the log likelihood: \begin{align*}
\ell(\theta)&=\log\theta+(x-1)\log(1-\theta),\\
\ell'(\theta)&=\frac1\theta-\frac{x-1}{1-\theta}.
\end{align*} Setting \ell'(\theta)=0 gives 1-\theta=(x-1)\theta, hence \widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}=1/x. With w=2/(x+2), \begin{align*}
w\mathbb{E}(\theta)+(1-w)\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}
&=\frac{2}{x+2}\frac12
   +\left(1-\frac{2}{x+2}\right)\frac1x\\
&=\frac1{x+2}+\frac{x}{x+2}\frac1x\\
&=\frac2{x+2}\\
&=\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x).
\end{align*}
Under the posterior-mean concentration convention, \operatorname{Beta}(1,1) has total prior weight two with one prior head and one prior tail: it behaves like one head among two prior tosses. Under the kernel exponent convention, however, the prior contributes \alpha-1=0 powers of \theta and \beta-1=0 powers of 1-\theta. These are two different pseudo-count conventions; the first is the one used in the requested linear combination.

title: Metropolis–Hastings for the logit-normal posterior
text:
Topic: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings · more questions on this topic
Source: Book exercise from Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings ‹ A bivariate-normal Gibbs sampler Random-walk Metropolis for a correlated normal ›

Use the posterior kernel in the logit-normal prior exercise.

For n=40 and x=16, use a Metropolis–Hastings algorithm to retain 10{,}000 draws after a burn-in of 1{,}000. Plot a kernel-density estimate and describe it.
Estimate the posterior mean, compare it with the prior mean, and explain how the data have changed the distribution.
Estimate and interpret an equal-tailed 95\% credible interval.
Repeat the numerical summaries for n=400 and x=160. Explain why ten times as much data changes the spread far more than the centre.







Worked answer (click to show)





Question. For 0<\theta<1, take the posterior target

\pi(\theta\mid x,n)\propto
\theta^{x-1}(1-\theta)^{n-x-1}
\exp\!\left[-\frac12\{\operatorname{logit}(\theta)-1\}^2\right].


For n=40 and x=16, use a Metropolis–Hastings algorithm to retain 10{,}000 draws after a burn-in of 1{,}000. Plot a kernel-density estimate and describe it.
Estimate the posterior mean, compare it with the prior mean, and explain how the data have changed the distribution.
Estimate and interpret an equal-tailed 95\% credible interval.
Repeat the numerical summaries for n=400 and x=160. Explain why ten times as much data changes the spread far more than the centre.

Solution. For numerical stability define the log of the unnormalised target by

\ell(\theta;x,n)
=(x-1)\log\theta+(n-x-1)\log(1-\theta)
-\frac12\{\operatorname{logit}(\theta)-1\}^2.

Use an independent \operatorname{Beta}(A,B) proposal with density g. Since this is not a random walk, the proposal terms do not cancel. For current state \theta and proposal y, \begin{align*}
r(\theta,y)
&=\frac{\pi(y)g(\theta)}{\pi(\theta)g(y)},\\
\log r(\theta,y)
&=\ell(y;x,n)-\ell(\theta;x,n)
   +\log g(\theta)-\log g(y),\\
a(\theta,y)&=\min\{1,r(\theta,y)\}.
\end{align*} The following implementation uses \operatorname{Beta}(4,6) for (x,n)=(16,40) and \operatorname{Beta}(40,60) for (160,400).
log_posterior <- function(theta, x, n) {
  ifelse(theta <= 0 | theta >= 1, -Inf,
         (x - 1) * log(theta) +
         (n - x - 1) * log1p(-theta) -
         0.5 * (qlogis(theta) - 1)^2)
}
independent_mh <- function(x, n, A, B, keep = 10000, burn = 1000) {
  total <- keep + burn
  out <- numeric(total)
  out[1] <- x / n
  for (t in 2:total) {
    proposed <- rbeta(1, A, B)
    log_ratio <-
      log_posterior(proposed, x, n) -
      log_posterior(out[t - 1], x, n) +
      dbeta(out[t - 1], A, B, log = TRUE) -
      dbeta(proposed, A, B, log = TRUE)
    if (log(runif(1)) < min(0, log_ratio)) {
      out[t] <- proposed
    } else {
      out[t] <- out[t - 1]
    }
  }
  out[(burn + 1):total]
}
set.seed(3500)
draw40  <- independent_mh(16,  40,  4,  6)
draw400 <- independent_mh(160, 400, 40, 60)
mean(draw40)
quantile(draw40, c(0.025, 0.975))
mean(draw400)
quantile(draw400, c(0.025, 0.975))
plot(density(draw40, from = 0, to = 1),
     xlab = expression(theta), main = "n = 40")
For the displayed seed, the n=40 run gives

\widehat{\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)}=0.432,
\qquad
\text{$95\%$ interval }(0.294,0.578).

Direct numerical integration gives 0.4320 and (0.291,0.579), so the Monte Carlo discrepancy is of the expected size. The prior mean is approximately 0.6967: observing only 16/40=0.4 heads moves the posterior sharply towards 0.4 and makes it appreciably more concentrated. The interval means that, under the model and prior, the posterior probability that \theta lies between the reported endpoints is approximately 0.95.
For n=400 and x=160, the same seed gives

\widehat{\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)}=0.404,
\qquad
\text{$95\%$ interval }(0.355,0.453),

while numerical integration gives 0.4035 and (0.356,0.452). Both data sets have empirical proportion 0.4, so the centre changes little. The ten-fold increase in sample size makes the likelihood much more concentrated and leaves the prior with much less leverage.
The function dbeta in the Hastings ratio is essential: g is a proposal density. Replacing it by the distribution function pbeta changes the invariant distribution and produces incorrect posterior summaries.

title: Posterior mean under squared-error loss
text:
Topic: Bayesian foundations · more questions on this topic
Source: Book exercise from Bayesian foundations ‹ The missing variance The pseudo-count trap ›

For observed data {\boldsymbol{x}}, consider the posterior mean squared error of a point estimate d=d({\boldsymbol{x}}),

R(d\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(d-\theta)^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\bigr].

Show, without omitting the quadratic expansion or the minimisation step, that the posterior mean d=\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}) is the minimum-mean-square-error estimator of \theta.






Worked answer (click to show)





Question. For observed data {\boldsymbol{x}}, consider the posterior mean squared error of a point estimate d=d({\boldsymbol{x}}),

R(d\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(d-\theta)^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\bigr].

Show, without omitting the quadratic expansion or the minimisation step, that the posterior mean d=\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}) is the minimum-mean-square-error estimator of \theta.
Solution. Once {\boldsymbol{x}} has been observed, d=d({\boldsymbol{x}}) is a fixed number and only \theta is random under the posterior. Therefore \begin{align*}
R(d\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(d-\theta)^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\bigr]\\
&=\mathbb{E}\bigl[d^2-2d\theta+\theta^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\bigr]\\
&=d^2-2d\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})+\mathbb{E}(\theta^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}).
\end{align*} Put m=\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}). Adding and subtracting m^2 gives \begin{align*}
R(d\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=d^2-2dm+m^2+\mathbb{E}(\theta^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})-m^2\\
&=(d-m)^2+\operatorname{Var}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}).
\end{align*} The posterior variance does not depend on d, and (d-m)^2\geq0 with equality exactly when d=m. Equivalently,

\frac{\partial R}{\partial d}=2d-2m,
\qquad
\frac{\partial^2 R}{\partial d^2}=2>0.

Thus the unique minimiser is

\boxed{d_{\mathrm{MMSE}}({\boldsymbol{x}})=\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})}.

title: Restaurant ordering methods
text:
Topic: Categorical data and the Dirichlet distribution · more questions on this topic
Source: Book exercise from Categorical data and the Dirichlet distribution ‹ Dirichlet updating Who owns the boundary? ›

A restaurant observed the following numbers of orders yesterday:




Dine-in
Take-away
Pick-up
Delivery




Count
63
19
3
38



Let {\boldsymbol{p}}=(p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4) be the corresponding population proportions.

With {\boldsymbol{x}}\mid{\boldsymbol{p}}\sim\operatorname{Multinomial}(123,{\boldsymbol{p}}) and {\boldsymbol{p}}\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_4), identify the posterior.
Last week’s percentages were 44.79\%, 27.60\%, 7.36\%, and 20.25\%. Explain how to use these proportions to choose the direction of {\boldsymbol{\alpha}}, and how a chosen total concentration records the weight given to last week.
Using a prior equivalent, for posterior-mean purposes, to last week’s proportions plus one baseline count in each category, report posterior means and equal-tailed 95\% credible intervals for p_1, p_4, p_1+p_2+p_3, and p_1-p_4.







Worked answer (click to show)





Question. A restaurant observed the following numbers of orders yesterday:




Dine-in
Take-away
Pick-up
Delivery




Count
63
19
3
38



Let {\boldsymbol{p}}=(p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4) be the corresponding population proportions.

With {\boldsymbol{x}}\mid{\boldsymbol{p}}\sim\operatorname{Multinomial}(123,{\boldsymbol{p}}) and {\boldsymbol{p}}\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_4), identify the posterior.
Last week’s percentages were 44.79\%, 27.60\%, 7.36\%, and 20.25\%. Explain how to use these proportions to choose the direction of {\boldsymbol{\alpha}}, and how a chosen total concentration records the weight given to last week.
Using a prior equivalent, for posterior-mean purposes, to last week’s proportions plus one baseline count in each category, report posterior means and equal-tailed 95\% credible intervals for p_1, p_4, p_1+p_2+p_3, and p_1-p_4.

Solution.

The Dirichlet–Multinomial update adds the observed cell counts to the corresponding concentration parameters. Since 63+19+3+38=123, \begin{align*}
{\boldsymbol{p}}&\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3,\alpha_4),\\
{\boldsymbol{x}}\mid{\boldsymbol{p}}&\sim\operatorname{Multinomial}(123,{\boldsymbol{p}}),\\
&\boxed{{\boldsymbol{p}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(63+\alpha_1,19+\alpha_2,3+\alpha_3,38+\alpha_4)}.
\end{align*}
Write last week’s proportions as


{\boldsymbol{q}}=(0.4479,0.2760,0.0736,0.2025).

A Dirichlet prior centred exactly at {\boldsymbol{q}} can be written {\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\kappa{\boldsymbol{q}}, where \kappa>0 is the total prior concentration. Increasing \kappa preserves the prior mean but increases the weight assigned to last week.
The construction used here instead combines 100 fractional counts with one baseline count in each category:

{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
=(44.79,27.60,7.36,20.25)+(1,1,1,1)
=(45.79,28.60,8.36,21.25).

Its concentration is 104 and its mean is {\boldsymbol{\alpha}}/104, which is slightly closer to (1/4,1/4,1/4,1/4) than {\boldsymbol{q}}. Thus the direction and concentration should both be reported; percentages alone determine only the direction.

The posterior parameters are \begin{align*}
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^\ast
&=(63,19,3,38)+(45.79,28.60,8.36,21.25)\\
&=\boxed{(108.79,47.60,11.36,59.25)},
\end{align*} with total concentration \alpha_0^\ast=108.79+47.60+11.36+59.25=227. Thus


\mathbb{E}(P_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{108.79}{227}=0.4793,
\qquad
\mathbb{E}(P_4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{59.25}{227}=0.2610.

Also,

\mathbb{E}(P_1+P_2+P_3\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=1-\mathbb{E}(P_4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=0.7390

and

\mathbb{E}(P_1-P_4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\frac{108.79-59.25}{227}=0.2182.

The Dirichlet marginal results give \begin{align*}
P_1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}&\sim\operatorname{Beta}(108.79,118.21),\\
P_4\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}&\sim\operatorname{Beta}(59.25,167.75),\\
P_1+P_2+P_3\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}&\sim\operatorname{Beta}(167.75,59.25).
\end{align*} Their intervals can therefore be obtained with Beta quantiles. The difference P_1-P_4 has no such Beta form, so simulation handles all four quantities uniformly:
rdirichlet_base <- function(n, alpha) {
  z <- sapply(alpha, function(a) rgamma(n, shape = a, rate = 1))
  z / rowSums(z)
}

set.seed(3500)
alpha_post <- c(108.79, 47.60, 11.36, 59.25)
p <- rdirichlet_base(100000, alpha_post)
summaries <- cbind(
  p1 = p[, 1],
  p4 = p[, 4],
  p123 = rowSums(p[, 1:3]),
  difference = p[, 1] - p[, 4]
)
rbind(
  mean = colMeans(summaries),
  lower = apply(summaries, 2, quantile, 0.025),
  upper = apply(summaries, 2, quantile, 0.975)
)
For the displayed seed, rounding to three decimals gives



Quantity
Posterior mean
2.5%
97.5%




p_1
0.479
0.415
0.544


p_4
0.261
0.206
0.320


p_1+p_2+p_3
0.739
0.680
0.794


p_1-p_4
0.218
0.109
0.325



The first three intervals agree, apart from Monte Carlo rounding, with the corresponding exact Beta quantiles.
