title: C1. Likelihood, prior and posterior
text:
Topic: Bayesian foundations · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 1 of 50 C2 ›

What are a likelihood, a prior and a posterior? Which variable is the likelihood a function of after observing the data?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. For observed data x and parameter \theta, the likelihood L(\theta;x)=p(x\mid\theta) is a function of \theta, the prior p(\theta) describes parameter uncertainty before these data, and the posterior p(\theta\mid x)\propto L(\theta;x)p(\theta) describes it after observing them. The likelihood need not integrate to one over \theta.

title: C3. Sufficiency
text:
Topic: Exponential families and conjugacy · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 3 of 50 ‹ C2 C4 ›

What is a sufficient statistic, using the conditional-distribution definition?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. A statistic T(X) is a function of the sample alone and is sufficient for \theta if the conditional distribution of X given T(X) does not depend on \theta. Thus, within the assumed model, the remaining sample details add no information about \theta once T(X) is known.

title: C5. Posterior prediction
text:
Topic: Bayesian foundations · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 5 of 50 ‹ C4 C6 ›

Why average over the posterior when predicting? What uncertainty does a plug-in prediction omit?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. Let \tilde Y be a future response and let \theta contain all unknown model parameters; with covariates suppressed and future and observed data conditionally independent given \theta, p(\tilde y\mid x)=\int p(\tilde y\mid\theta)p(\theta\mid x)\,d\theta. This averages over posterior parameter uncertainty; a plug-in distribution p(\tilde y\mid\hat\theta) retains response randomness but treats the fitted parameters as known.

title: C7. MAP and squared-error loss
text:
Topic: Bayesian foundations · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 7 of 50 ‹ C6 C8 ›

How does a MAP estimate differ from a Bayes estimate under squared-error loss?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. The MAP maximises p(\theta\mid x), whereas a Bayes estimate minimises the posterior expected loss for a specified loss function. Under squared-error loss and a finite posterior second moment, \mathbb{E}[(\theta-d)^2\mid x]=\operatorname{Var}(\theta\mid x)+(\mathbb{E}[\theta\mid x]-d)^2, so the Bayes estimate is the posterior mean, not generally the mode.

title: C9. Pooling
text:
Topic: Hierarchical Bayes · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 9 of 50 ‹ C8 C10 ›

How does partial pooling in a hierarchical model differ from complete pooling and no pooling?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. Complete pooling uses one common group parameter, no pooling estimates each group separately, and partial pooling connects distinct group parameters through a shared population distribution. This hierarchy allows information to be shared, typically shrinking less precisely estimated group effects more strongly toward the population centre.

title: C11. Monte Carlo estimation
text:
Topic: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 11 of 50 ‹ C10 C12 ›

What is a Monte Carlo estimate of \mathbb{E}_\pi[h(\Theta)], and what is Monte Carlo error?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. For a target distribution \pi and integrable function h, a Monte Carlo estimate is N^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^N h(\theta^{(t)}), using independent draws from \pi or suitable ergodic MCMC output. Monte Carlo error is the finite-simulation discrepancy from \mathbb{E}_\pi[h(\Theta)], not the posterior uncertainty about \Theta; its assessment must account for dependence when draws are correlated.

title: C13. Full conditionals and Gibbs
text:
Topic: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 13 of 50 ‹ C12 C14 ›

What is a full conditional distribution, and how does a Gibbs sampler use full conditionals?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. For a target \pi(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_p), a full conditional \pi(\theta_j\mid\theta_{-j}) conditions on all other coordinates, denoted \theta_{-j}. A systematic Gibbs sweep draws each coordinate from its exact full conditional using the latest available values of the others; each such coordinate update is accepted automatically.

title: C15. Warm-up and dependence
text:
Topic: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 15 of 50 ‹ C14 C16 ›

Does discarding MCMC warm-up guarantee convergence or make the retained draws independent? Explain briefly.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. Warm-up (burn-in) is an initial segment discarded to reduce the influence of initialisation. Discarding it neither proves convergence nor removes serial dependence: even a chain at equilibrium generally has dependent successive states, so mixing and Monte Carlo precision still need assessment.

title: C17. Links
text:
Topic: Introduction to generalised linear models · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 17 of 50 ‹ C16 C18 ›

What are a link function, an inverse link and a canonical link?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. The link g maps the conditional mean to the linear predictor, g(\mu_i)=\eta_i, and its inverse gives \mu_i=g^{-1}(\eta_i). A canonical link equates \eta_i with the natural parameter in the chosen linear exponential-family representation; it is a transformation of the mean, not of each observed response.

title: C19. Fisher scoring and IRLS
text:
Topic: Introduction to generalised linear models · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 19 of 50 ‹ C18 C20 ›

What is Fisher scoring, and how is it related to iteratively reweighted least squares in GLMs?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. With score S and nonsingular expected information I, Fisher scoring iterates \beta^{(t+1)}=\beta^{(t)}+
I(\beta^{(t)})^{-1}S(\beta^{(t)}). For GLMs this can be written as iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS): repeatedly update working responses and weights, then solve the resulting weighted least-squares problem.

title: C21. A log-link coefficient
text:
Topic: Standard errors, and models for counts · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 21 of 50 ‹ C20 C22 ›

In a Poisson regression with a log link and no interactions, what does e^{\beta_j} represent?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. In \log\mu=x^\top\beta, \mu is the expected count and \beta_j is the coefficient of predictor x_j, with no interactions involving it. Holding other predictors fixed, a one-unit increase in x_j multiplies the expected count by e^{\beta_j}, a 100(e^{\beta_j}-1)\% change; this is an association, not automatically a causal effect.

title: C23. Positive continuous responses
text:
Topic: Underdispersion, positive responses, and quasi-likelihood · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 23 of 50 ‹ C22 C24 ›

What response support and mean–variance relationships define Gamma and inverse-Gaussian GLMs?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. Both families have support y>0, conditional mean \mu_i>0 and dispersion \phi>0: Gamma variance is \phi\mu_i^2, whereas inverse-Gaussian variance is \phi\mu_i^3. In shape–rate notation the Gamma distribution is \operatorname{Gamma}(1/\phi,1/(\phi\mu_i)); the inverse-Gaussian family is distinct from the inverse-Gamma family.

title: C25. Proportional odds
text:
Topic: Categorical responses · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 25 of 50 ‹ C24 C26 ›

What is the proportional-odds assumption in an ordinal regression model?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. For ordered categories 1,\ldots,K, use the lecture’s upper-tail convention \gamma_k(x)=\mathbb{P}(Y\ge k\mid x) and \operatorname{logit}\gamma_k(x)=a_k+x^\top\beta, k=2,\ldots,K. The slope vector \beta is common to all cutpoints, so a unit change in x_j multiplies every cumulative odds by e^{\beta_j}, holding the other covariates fixed.

title: C27. Quasilikelihood
text:
Topic: Underdispersion, positive responses, and quasi-likelihood · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 27 of 50 ‹ C26 C28 ›

What is a quasilikelihood model? What must be specified instead of a full response distribution?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. A quasilikelihood model specifies a mean \mu_i=g^{-1}(x_i^\top\beta) and variance \phi V(\mu_i), rather than a full response distribution. For independent responses its quasi-score is built from (Y_i-\mu_i)\{\phi V(\mu_i)\}^{-1}\partial\mu_i/\partial\beta, whose expectation is zero when the mean model is correct.

title: C29. Saturated model and deviance
text:
Topic: Paired comparisons, and how far a fit is from the data · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 29 of 50 ‹ C28 C30 ›

What is a saturated model, and what does deviance compare? Distinguish deviance from scaled deviance.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. A saturated mean model fits each observed response exactly (\tilde\mu_i=y_i, possibly as a boundary limit); at common dispersion \phi, the scaled deviance is D/\phi=2\{\ell(\tilde\mu;y,\phi)-\ell(\hat\mu;y,\phi)\}. Thus the lecture’s unscaled deviance D is \phi times that log-likelihood-ratio discrepancy, and equals the scaled deviance when \phi=1.

title: C31. Cubic splines and knots
text:
Topic: Smooth means · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 31 of 50 ‹ C30 C32 ›

What is a cubic spline, and what is a knot?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. A cubic spline is a piecewise polynomial of degree at most three, joined at specified locations called knots, with the function and its first two derivatives continuous at ordinary interior knots. The knots divide the covariate domain into pieces without introducing jumps in the fitted curve or its first two derivatives.

title: C33. GAMs and effective degrees of freedom
text:
Topic: Additive smooths · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 33 of 50 ‹ C32 C34 ›

What is a GAM, and what do the effective degrees of freedom of a fitted smooth measure?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. A GAM models the conditional mean through g(\mu_i)=\beta_0+\sum_j f_j(x_{ij}), possibly with additional parametric terms, so effects are additive on the link scale. A smooth’s effective degrees of freedom (edf) measure its fitted flexibility after penalisation, not its polynomial degree; for an ordinary centred univariate smooth, edf near one is approximately linear.

title: C35. Random intercepts and slopes
text:
Topic: Random slopes, and a binary mixed model · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 35 of 50 ‹ C34 C36 ›

What are a random intercept and a random slope? On which scale do they enter a GLMM?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. A random intercept gives each group its own baseline deviation; a random slope gives it its own deviation in a covariate slope, and the two may be correlated. In a GLMM they enter the conditional linear predictor g\{\mathbb{E}(Y_{ij}\mid x_{ij},b_i)\}=x_{ij}^\top\beta+z_{ij}^\top b_i, where i indexes groups, j observations, b_i random effects, and x_{ij},z_{ij} the corresponding covariate vectors.

title: C37. Conditional versus marginal effects
text:
Topic: Marginal models, and two responses at once · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 37 of 50 ‹ C36 C38 ›

Why is a logistic GLMM coefficient not generally the same as a population-average logistic coefficient?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. A logistic GLMM coefficient describes a log-odds change conditional on a fixed random-effect value; a population-average coefficient describes the marginal mean after averaging over random effects. Because the inverse-logit is nonlinear, averaging conditional probabilities generally does not preserve the same logistic coefficients.

title: C39. Working correlation
text:
Topic: Marginal models, and two responses at once · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 39 of 50 ‹ C38 C40 ›

What is a working correlation structure in GEE? Give two examples.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. A working correlation matrix is an assumed pattern of within-cluster correlations used to construct the GEE weights. Examples are exchangeable correlation (one common off-diagonal correlation) and AR(1) correlation (\rho^{|j-k|} for equally spaced visits j,k, with lag-one correlation \rho, |\rho|<1); the working matrix need not be the true matrix.

title: C41. Vector-response regression
text:
Topic: Marginal models, and two responses at once · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 41 of 50 ‹ C40 C42 ›

What is vector-response regression, and how can GEE accommodate different response types within one observational unit?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. A response vector Y_i=(Y_{i1},\ldots,Y_{iK})^\top records several, possibly different kinds of outcome on unit i. GEE can assign each component its own marginal link and variance function, combine them with a working within-vector association model, and treat vectors from different units as independent.

title: C43. Two stationarity definitions
text:
Topic: Dependence along a series · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 43 of 50 ‹ C42 C44 ›

What are strict stationarity and weak stationarity? State the moment conditions in the latter.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. Strict stationarity means every finite-dimensional joint distribution is unchanged by a common time shift. Weak stationarity requires finite second moments, constant \mathbb{E}(X_t)=\mu, and covariance \operatorname{Cov}(X_t,X_{t-k})=\gamma(k) depending only on lag k; neither definition requires independence.

title: C45. ACF and PACF
text:
Topic: Dependence along a series · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 45 of 50 ‹ C44 C46 ›

What do the autocorrelation function (ACF) and partial autocorrelation function (PACF) measure?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. For a weakly stationary process with positive variance, the ACF at lag k is \rho(k)=\operatorname{Corr}(X_t,X_{t-k})=\gamma(k)/\gamma(0), where \gamma(k) is the autocovariance. The PACF is the correlation between the two endpoints’ residuals after their linear projections on the intervening observations X_{t-1},\ldots,X_{t-k+1} (no intervening adjustment at lag one).

title: C47. Unit roots and ARIMA
text:
Topic: Forecasting · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 47 of 50 ‹ C46 C48 ›

What is a unit root at one? What do p,d,q mean in an ARIMA(p,d,q) model?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. A unit root at one means the autoregressive polynomial has a factor (1-z); the corresponding first-difference operator is (1-B)X_t=X_t-X_{t-1}, where B is the backshift operator. In ARIMA(p,d,q), differencing d times produces a stationary ARMA(p,q) series; p and q are its AR and MA orders and d is its integration order (d=0 gives ARMA).

title: C49. Identification and residual checks
text:
Topic: Forecasting · more questions on this topic
Source: Concept check 49 of 50 ‹ C48 C50 ›

How can ACF/PACF patterns suggest AR or MA orders? What should the fitted residual ACF be checked for?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions/notation. For the usual causal stationary AR(p) model the population PACF vanishes beyond lag p; for MA(q), the population ACF vanishes beyond lag q. Sample patterns are noisy clues rather than proofs of order, and the residual ACF should be checked for remaining serial correlation that the fitted model has not captured.

title: Question 15. Battery lifetimes and a Bayes factor
text:
Topic: Bayesian hypotheses and model comparison · more questions on this topic
Source: Final preparation, question 15 of 22 ‹ Question 14 Question 16 ›

Researchers are attempting to determine the distribution of lifetimes of a type of battery. They have measured the lifetimes (years) of n of these batteries, recorded as x_1,\ldots,x_n, which we assume were the result of a random sample and we will assume that the observations could be considered independent and identically distributed. Two models were proposed:

M_1\colon x\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\theta)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
M_2\colon x\sim\operatorname{Weibull}(5,\theta).

This Weibull density is given by

f(x)=5\theta x^{4}e^{-\theta x^{5}},
\qquad\text{for }x>0.

Consider the prior distribution \theta\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1).
(a) Find the marginal likelihood under model M_1. [3 marks]
(b) Find the marginal likelihood under model M_2. [3 marks]
(c) Obtain an expression for the Bayes factor comparing M_1 to M_2. [2 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Under M_1, \theta is an exponential rate. Under M_2, its meaning is fixed by the supplied Weibull density 5\theta x^4e^{-\theta x^5}, rather than by a software scale convention. In both models the prior density is e^{-\theta} on \theta>0. Write S_1=\sum_i x_i, S_5=\sum_i x_i^5 and P_4=\prod_i x_i^4. The marginal likelihood averages a sampling density over the specified parameter prior.
(a) Let S_1=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i. Independence gives, for \theta>0,

p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta,M_1)
=
\prod_{i=1}^{n}\theta e^{-\theta x_i}
=
\theta^{n}e^{-\theta S_1}.

Since S_1+1>0,

p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_1)
=
\int_0^{\infty}\theta^{n}e^{-\theta(S_1+1)}\,d\theta.

Put u=(S_1+1)\theta. Then d\theta=du/(S_1+1) and u runs over (0,\infty), so

\begin{aligned}
p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_1)
&=
(S_1+1)^{-(n+1)}\int_0^{\infty}u^{n}e^{-u}\,du
=
\frac{\Gamma(n+1)}{(S_1+1)^{n+1}}.
\end{aligned}

Here n is a positive integer, so \Gamma(n+1)=n!.

\boxed{p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_1)
=
\dfrac{n!}{\bigl(1+\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\bigr)^{n+1}}.}

(b) Let P_4=\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_i^{4} and S_5=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i^{5}. The given density and independence give

p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid\theta,M_2)
=
\prod_{i=1}^{n}5\theta x_i^{4}e^{-\theta x_i^{5}}
=
5^{n}\theta^{n}P_4 e^{-\theta S_5},
\qquad\theta>0.

Thus

p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_2)
=
5^{n}P_4\int_0^{\infty}\theta^{n}e^{-(S_5+1)\theta}\,d\theta.

Now S_5+1>0. The same substitution as in (a) gives \int_0^{\infty}\theta^{n}e^{-(S_5+1)\theta}\,d\theta=n!/(S_5+1)^{n+1}. The factor 5^{n}P_4 does not depend on \theta, but it belongs to the normalised sampling density, so it remains in the marginal likelihood.

\boxed{p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_2)
=
\dfrac{5^{n}\,n!\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_i^{4}}{\bigl(1+\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i^{5}\bigr)^{n+1}}.}

(c) By (a) and (b),

\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{BF}_{12}
&=
\frac{p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_1)}{p({\boldsymbol{x}}\mid M_2)}
=
\frac{n!/(1+S_1)^{n+1}}{5^{n}n!\,P_4/(1+S_5)^{n+1}}
=
\frac{1}{5^{n}P_4}
\Biggl(\frac{1+S_5}{1+S_1}\Biggr)^{n+1}.
\end{aligned}


\boxed{\operatorname{BF}_{12}
=
\dfrac{1}{5^{n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_i^{4}}
\Biggl(
\dfrac{1+\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i^{5}}{1+\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i}
\Biggr)^{n+1}.}

Thus \operatorname{BF}_{12}>1 favours M_1, and \operatorname{BF}_{12}<1 favours M_2.
The transformation U=X^5 clarifies the second integration: under M_2, U\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\theta). However, the observed data are the x_i, so the transformation Jacobian \prod_i5x_i^4=5^nP_4 remains in their likelihood. Dropping it would compare densities expressed for different observed variables. In posterior inference within M_2 it is constant in \theta and can be omitted; in this model comparison it cannot.
The prior in each model must also be normalised. Using a density proportional to one on the positive line in place of \operatorname{Exp}(1) would introduce an unspecified multiplicative constant into each marginal likelihood. The stated proper priors avoid that ambiguity. Posterior model odds are obtained only after multiplying BF_{12} by the prior model odds.

title: Question 10. Beta downtime
text:
Topic: Exponential families and conjugacy · more questions on this topic
Source: Final preparation, question 10 of 22 ‹ Question 9 Question 11 ›

The proportion of downtime has density

f(x\mid\theta)=\theta(1-x)^{\theta-1},
\quad 0<x<1,\ \theta>0,

and \theta\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha,\beta) with density \beta^{\alpha}\theta^{\alpha-1}e^{-\beta\theta}/\Gamma(\alpha). Let x_1,\ldots,x_n be an iid sample.
(a) State the prior mean. [1 mark]
(b) Obtain the posterior distribution of \theta and identify it. [8 marks]
(c) State the posterior mean. [2 marks]
(d) Explain the posterior mean as n\to\infty; as \alpha,\beta\to 0; and as \alpha,\beta\to\infty with \alpha/\beta fixed. [9 marks]
(e) Complete the sentence: “The effect of the prior hyperparameters \alpha and \beta on the posterior mean of \theta is like…” [5 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. The observations are downtime proportions, while \theta>0 is the unknown shape parameter. The prior \operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha,\beta) uses rate \beta, so its mean is \alpha/\beta and variance \alpha/\beta^2. Define the transformed exposure S=-\sum_i\log(1-x_i)>0; it is not the sum of the original downtime proportions.
(a)

\mathbb{E}(\theta)=\alpha/\beta.

(b) The likelihood is \theta^{n}\exp\bigl(\theta\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log(1-x_i)\bigr) times a factor free of \theta. Multiplying by the gamma prior gives

\theta^{\alpha+n-1}
\exp\Bigl(-\theta\Bigl(\beta-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log(1-x_i)\Bigr)\Bigr).

Since \log(1-x_i)<0, the rate is positive.

\boxed{\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{Gamma}\Bigl(\alpha+n,\;\beta-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log(1-x_i)\Bigr).}

(c)

\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=
\frac{\alpha+n}{\beta-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log(1-x_i)}.

(d) Write S_n=-\sum_{i=1}^n\log(1-x_i)>0. The log-likelihood is n\log\theta-S_n\theta+\text{constant}, whose derivative gives \hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}=n/S_n. The posterior mean is

\frac{\alpha+n}{\beta+S_n}
=\frac{1+\alpha/n}{S_n/n+\beta/n}.

If observations come from the stated model at \theta_0>0, the transformed values -\log(1-X_i) are iid \operatorname{Exp}(\theta_0), so S_n/n\to1/\theta_0 and the posterior mean tends to \theta_0, as does the MLE. With the observed data fixed, \alpha,\beta\to0 gives n/S_n; this is a limit of proper priors, whose limiting kernel 1/\theta is improper. If \alpha,\beta\to\infty while \alpha/\beta\to m>0, the posterior mean tends to m, the limiting prior mean. Without a limit for \alpha/\beta, there is no unique limiting posterior mean.
(e) The effect is like adding \alpha to the observation count and \beta to the transformed total exposure S=-\sum\log(1-x_i), not to the raw downtime sum. Indeed,

\boxed{
\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\frac{\beta}{\beta+S}\frac{\alpha}{\beta}
+\frac{S}{\beta+S}\frac nS.}

The prior mean \alpha/\beta and the MLE n/S therefore receive nonnegative weights that sum to one.
The transformation explains the form of the update. For Z=-\log(1-X), we have x=1-e^{-z} and dx/dz=e^{-z}, so

f_Z(z\mid\theta)
=\theta(e^{-z})^{\theta-1}e^{-z}
=\theta e^{-\theta z},\qquad z>0.

Thus the problem is exponential-rate inference on the transformed scale: n counts observations and S is their total exposure. The prior adds information in exactly those two positions. In the strong-prior limit with \alpha/\beta=m fixed, the prior variance is m/\beta\to0, explaining why the posterior mean is forced towards m.

title: Question 11. Geometric success probability
text:
Topic: Exponential families and conjugacy · more questions on this topic
Source: Final preparation, question 11 of 22 ‹ Question 10 Question 12 ›

Let x_1,\ldots,x_n be iid with

f(x\mid p)=(1-p)^{x}p,
\quad x=0,1,2,\ldots,

and p\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta).
(i) Find the posterior distribution of p and identify it. [3 marks]
(ii) Is this prior conjugate? [1 mark]
(iii) Show that a \operatorname{Beta}(a,b) mean equals a/(a+b). [2 marks]
(iv) Hence show that \mathbb{E}(p\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=(\alpha+n)/(\alpha+\beta+n+n\bar x). [1 mark]
(v) What happens to the posterior mean as n\to\infty? [1 mark]
(vi) What happens if \alpha,\beta\to 0? [1 mark]
(vii) Complete: “The effect of the prior hyperparameters \alpha,\beta on the posterior mean of p is like…” [2 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Here X_i counts failures before the first success, so its support begins at zero. Each observation represents one success and x_i failures. Put F=\sum_i x_i=n\bar x. The beta density is p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1}/B(\alpha,\beta) on 0<p<1. This geometric convention differs from the trial-count convention in Question 6 by one.
(i) The likelihood is p^{n}(1-p)^{\sum x_i}. The beta prior contributes p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1}, so

\boxed{p\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{Beta}\bigl(\alpha+n,\;\beta+\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\bigr).}

(ii) Yes. The posterior is beta, the same family as the prior.
(iii) For a>0 and b>0, the expectation integral is

\mathbb{E}(P)=\frac1{B(a,b)}\int_0^1 p^a(1-p)^{b-1}\,dp
=\frac{B(a+1,b)}{B(a,b)}.

Using B(a,b)=\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)/\Gamma(a+b) and \Gamma(a+1)=a\Gamma(a),

\frac{B(a+1,b)}{B(a,b)}
=
\frac{\Gamma(a+1)\Gamma(a+b)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(a+b+1)}
=
\frac{a}{a+b},

and this ratio is the beta mean.
(iv) By (i) and (iii),

\mathbb{E}(p\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=
\frac{\alpha+n}{\alpha+\beta+n+n\bar x}.

(v) Divide the numerator and denominator by n:

\mathbb{E}(p\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{1+\alpha/n}{1+\bar x+(\alpha+\beta)/n}.

For fixed prior parameters this approaches the data-based estimate 1/(1+\bar x). The log-likelihood is n\log p+F\log(1-p), and setting its derivative to zero gives \hat p=n/(n+F) when F>0. If the data come from the model at p_0, then \bar X_n\to(1-p_0)/p_0 and both estimates converge to p_0.
(vi) If \alpha,\beta\to 0, the posterior mean tends to n/(n+n\bar x)=1/(1+\bar x). The prior drops out.
This is a limit of proper beta priors, not substitution of \alpha=\beta=0 into a proper prior density. If F=0, the limiting estimate is the boundary value 1 and the limiting beta kernel is not a proper density; the posteriors for positive hyperparameters remain proper.
(vii) The effect is like \alpha prior successes and \beta prior failures, added to the n observed successes and \sum x_i observed failures.
An exact weighted-average expression makes that interpretation explicit:

\mathbb{E}(p\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\frac{\alpha+\beta}{\alpha+\beta+n+F}\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}
+\frac{n+F}{\alpha+\beta+n+F}\frac{n}{n+F}.

The beta prior mean and the observed success fraction are weighted by their respective total counts. These pseudo-counts describe the posterior-mean update; the powers in the prior density itself are \alpha-1 and \beta-1.

title: Question 9. Gibbs and random-walk Metropolis–Hastings
text:
Topic: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings · more questions on this topic
Source: Final preparation, question 9 of 22 ‹ Question 8 Question 10 ›

Consider the joint density on x>0, y>0,

f(x,y)\propto x^{3}ye^{-xy-2x-3y}.

(a) Describe a Gibbs sampler for this density. [10 marks]
(b) Describe a random-walk Metropolis–Hastings algorithm with increment distribution \operatorname{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I_2). [10 marks]
(c) Describe how to obtain a 95\% confidence interval for \mathbb{E}(Y). [5 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. The target is the normalised version of q(x,y)=x^3y\exp(-xy-2x-3y) on the positive quadrant. A \operatorname{Gamma}(a,b) full conditional has shape a and rate b. Gibbs sampling redraws coordinates from exact full conditionals; Metropolis–Hastings proposes a move and corrects it with an acceptance probability. In part (c), the target is the fixed expectation \mu_Y=\mathbb{E}_f(Y), and the interval measures numerical error in estimating it.
(a) Given x, the factors in y are y\,e^{-(x+3)y}, so

Y\mid x\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(2,\,x+3).

Given y, the factors in x are x^{3}e^{-(y+2)x}, so

X\mid y\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(4,\,y+2).

Each draw uses the newest available value and comes from an exact full conditional, so it needs no acceptance step. The pairs across sweeps are generally dependent. Both gamma distributions use rates, not scales.
(b) From the current point (x,y), draw an increment Z\sim \operatorname{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I_2) and set (x',y')=(x,y)+Z. This proposal is symmetric. If x'\leq 0 or y'\leq 0, reject. Otherwise accept with probability

\min\Bigl(1,\frac{f(x',y')}{f(x,y)}\Bigr)
=
\min\Bigl(1,\frac{(x')^{3}y'}{x^{3}y}
\exp\bigl(-(x'y'-xy)-2(x'-x)-3(y'-y)\bigr)\Bigr).

Draw an independent U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1) and accept the valid proposal if U is no greater than this probability; otherwise retain and record the current point. A proposal outside the support is rejected, not redrawn until positive, because repeated redrawing would change the proposal kernel. The target’s unknown normalising constant cancels from the ratio.
Symmetry means equality of the forward and reverse density values: a centred normal increment has the same density at Z and -Z. Hence the proposal ratio in the general Metropolis–Hastings formula is one. The scale \sigma^2 affects exploration, not the target distribution: very small moves can mix slowly, while very large moves can cause many rejections. Repeated states after rejection are part of the chain and must be retained in averages.
For a general proposal density g(u'\mid u), the acceptance ratio includes g(u\mid u')/g(u'\mid u). The following algorithm uses the symmetric proposal in this question, so that factor cancels. Define the log kernel h(x,y)=3\log x+\log y-xy-2x-3y on the positive quadrant. Evaluating acceptance on the log scale avoids exponentiating a potentially extreme density ratio.
An invalid proposal or failed acceptance test leaves the current state unchanged. In particular, do not keep proposing until a move is accepted, and do not save only accepted moves: either action changes the sampling procedure. Check traces, exploration and autocorrelation before using the retained states in part (c).
(c) After checking convergence and allowing suitable warm-up, retain N=ab draws of Y in a non-overlapping batches of length b. Let \bar Y_N be their overall mean and \bar Y_k^{\mathrm{batch}} the mean in batch k. With

s_B^2=\frac{1}{a-1}\sum_{k=1}^a
\bigl(\bar Y_k^{\mathrm{batch}}-\bar Y_N\bigr)^2,
\qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{MCSE}}(\bar Y_N)=\frac{s_B}{\sqrt a},

an approximate 95\% confidence interval for the fixed target \mathbb{E}(Y) is \bar Y_N\pm t_{0.975,a-1}s_B/\sqrt a (or 1.96 in place of the t quantile for many batches). Batches must be long enough to weaken within-chain dependence. The iid standard error s_Y/\sqrt N ignores autocorrelation, and quantiles of the Y-draws describe Y, not uncertainty in its mean.
The reason for batching is that Monte Carlo uncertainty depends on the whole autocovariance sequence. Under a stationary Markov-chain central limit theorem,

\sqrt N(\bar Y_N-\mu_Y)\ \overset{d}{\longrightarrow}\ \operatorname{N}(0,\tau_Y^2),
\qquad
\tau_Y^2=\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k,

where \gamma_k=\operatorname{Cov}(Y_t,Y_{t+k}). Batch means estimates \tau_Y^2 by bs_B^2, giving \sqrt{bs_B^2/N}=s_B/\sqrt a. There must be enough batches to estimate their variance and enough observations within each batch to account for dependence. Check that the reported error is reasonably stable as the simulation and batch length are increased; discarding warm-up alone does not remove autocorrelation.

title: Question 7. Lognormal variance
text:
Topic: Conjugate analysis for normal models · more questions on this topic
Source: Final preparation, question 7 of 22 ‹ Question 6 Question 8 ›

The size X of a particle has density

f(x\mid\mu,\sigma^{2})
=
\frac{1}{x\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}
\exp\Bigl(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}(\log x-\mu)^{2}\Bigr),
\quad x>0.

If X\sim\operatorname{logN}(\mu,\sigma^{2}), then \log X\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2}). Assume \mu is known, and let x_1,\ldots,x_n be an iid sample.
(i) Show that this lognormal model belongs to the exponential family. [4 marks]
(ii) Find the form of the conjugate prior for \sigma^{2} and identify the distribution. [4 marks]
(iii) Find the posterior distribution of \sigma^{2}. [5 marks]
(iv) State, without derivation, the posterior mean and the posterior mode. Explain their behaviour as n\to\infty. [4 marks]
(v) Briefly describe how you would construct a 90\% credible interval for \sigma^{2}. [3 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. The unknown v=\sigma^2 is the variance of \log X, not the variance of X. The value \mu is known. Write Q=\sum_i(\log x_i-\mu)^2 and use the inverse-gamma kernel v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v} on v>0. All observed x_i must be positive.
(i) Put v=\sigma^2. In the course’s exponential-family form f(x\mid v)=b(x)\exp\{c(v)T(x)\}/a(v), take

b(x)=\frac1{x\sqrt{2\pi}},\qquad
T(x)=\frac{(\log x-\mu)^2}{2},\qquad
c(v)=-\frac1v,\qquad a(v)=\sqrt v.

The known \mu makes T(x) a statistic, and the support x>0 is independent of v. This is a one-parameter exponential family.
The same structure can be seen by setting Z_i=\log X_i. Then Z_i\sim\operatorname{N}(\mu,v), so inference about v is a normal known-mean variance problem on the log scale. The factor 1/x in the lognormal density is the transformation Jacobian; it depends on the data, so it does not change the posterior kernel in v.
(ii) For an iid sample the likelihood is

L(\sigma^{2})
\propto
(\sigma^{2})^{-n/2}
\exp\Bigl(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\log x_i-\mu)^{2}\Bigr).

The general conjugate kernel from (i) is a(v)^{-\kappa}\exp\{\eta c(v)\}=v^{-\kappa/2}e^{-\eta/v}. Matching it to (\sigma^{2})^{-a-1}\exp(-b/\sigma^{2}) gives a=\kappa/2-1 and b=\eta. Thus \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b), with a,b>0, is a proper conjugate prior on the variance, not on the standard deviation.
(iii) Let Q=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\log x_i-\mu)^{2}. Then

\begin{aligned}
p(v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto v^{-n/2}e^{-Q/(2v)}v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v}\\
&=v^{-(a+n/2)-1}e^{-(b+Q/2)/v}.
\end{aligned}

Recognising the inverse-gamma kernel,

\boxed{\sigma^{2}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\bigl(a+n/2,\; b+Q/2\bigr).}

(iv) With \alpha_n=a+n/2 and \beta_n=b+Q/2,

\mathbb{E}(\sigma^{2}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{\beta_n}{\alpha_n-1}\quad(\alpha_n>1),
\qquad
\operatorname{mode}(\sigma^{2}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{\beta_n}{\alpha_n+1}.

As n\to\infty with fixed prior parameters, both are asymptotic to Q/n, the maximum likelihood estimator of \sigma^{2}. If the data come from this model at variance v_0, the law of large numbers gives Q/n\to v_0; the prior’s influence vanishes.
For finite n the posterior mean exceeds the mode whenever the mean exists, reflecting the inverse-gamma right tail. The two become close as the shape grows. In the large-sample statement, Q grows with the sample; it is Q/n, rather than a fixed observed Q, that converges to the true log-scale variance.
(v) Take the 0.05 and 0.95 quantiles of this inverse-gamma posterior. That interval is a central 90\% credible interval for the unknown variance. Equivalently, if W=1/\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha_n,\beta_n) in shape–rate form and q_u is its u-quantile, the interval is [1/q_{0.95},\,1/q_{0.05}]. Taking reciprocals reverses the order of the endpoints.
Conditional on the observed sample and the model, the posterior probability between these endpoints is 0.90, with 0.05 in each tail. These are quantiles of the parameter posterior; quantiles of lognormal observations would answer a predictive question instead. If an interval for \sigma is wanted, take square roots of both endpoints.

title: Question 16. Mixed binomial–beta Gibbs sampler
text:
Topic: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings · more questions on this topic
Source: Final preparation, question 16 of 22 ‹ Question 15 Question 17 ›

Consider the mixed probability function

f(x,y,z)\propto
\binom{n}{x}\binom{m}{y}
z^{x+y+\alpha-1}(1-z)^{n+m-x-y+\beta-1}
\gamma^{m-y}(1-\gamma)^{n-x}\delta^{x}(1-\delta)^{y},

for x=0,1,\ldots,n, y=0,1,\ldots,m, and 0<z<1, where \alpha,\beta>0 and 0<\gamma,\delta<1. Identify the full conditionals and give a Gibbs sampler; implement and run it for 100{,}000 iterations, reporting marginal plots and summaries; and, for \alpha=2, \beta=4, \gamma=0.3, \delta=0.6, n=10, and m=20, apply conditional-mode updates until they no longer change.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. X and Y are bounded counts, while Z is a probability in (0,1). The positive values \alpha,\beta and probabilities \gamma,\delta are fixed hyperparameters. A full conditional holds the other two coordinates fixed. A conditional mode maximises that conditional distribution; replacing random draws by modes produces a deterministic optimisation procedure rather than a sampler.
The question gives numerical values only for the mode updates, and it gives no initial state. The run and the mode iteration below use those values and the initial state (x,y,z)=(5,10,1/2).
Full conditionals. Write q for the displayed kernel, so f=q/C on x\in\{0,\ldots,n\}, y\in\{0,\ldots,m\} and z\in(0,1). A full conditional is q renormalised in the target coordinate. Factors free of that coordinate cancel.
For x, split (1-z)^{n+m-x-y+\beta-1}=(1-z)^{n-x}(1-z)^{m-y+\beta-1}. The factors containing x are

\binom{n}{x}(z\delta)^{x}\bigl[(1-z)(1-\gamma)\bigr]^{n-x}.

For z\in(0,1) and \gamma,\delta\in(0,1), both A_x=z\delta and B_x=(1-z)(1-\gamma) are positive. Then

\binom{n}{x}A_x^{x}B_x^{n-x}
=
(A_x+B_x)^{n}
\binom{n}{x}p_x^{x}(1-p_x)^{n-x},
\quad
p_x=\frac{A_x}{A_x+B_x},

and (A_x+B_x)^{n} does not depend on x. Therefore

\boxed{X\mid y,z
\sim
\operatorname{Bin}\!\left(n,\
\frac{z\delta}{z\delta+(1-z)(1-\gamma)}\right).}

This conditional does not depend on y.
For y, split (1-z)^{n+m-x-y+\beta-1}=(1-z)^{m-y}(1-z)^{n-x+\beta-1}. The factors containing y are

\binom{m}{y}\bigl[z(1-\delta)\bigr]^{y}\bigl[(1-z)\gamma\bigr]^{m-y}.

The same binomial argument, with both bases positive, gives

\boxed{Y\mid x,z
\sim
\operatorname{Bin}\!\left(m,\
\frac{z(1-\delta)}{z(1-\delta)+(1-z)\gamma}\right).}

This conditional does not depend on x.
For z, the factors containing z are z^{x+y+\alpha-1}(1-z)^{n+m-x-y+\beta-1} on (0,1). Since \alpha,\beta>0 and 0\le x\le n, 0\le y\le m,

a_z:=x+y+\alpha>0,
\qquad
b_z:=n+m-x-y+\beta>0.

This is the \operatorname{Beta}(a_z,b_z) kernel, whose integral is the beta function \mathrm{B}(a_z,b_z). Hence

\boxed{Z\mid x,y
\sim
\operatorname{Beta}(x+y+\alpha,\ n+m-x-y+\beta).}

Gibbs sampler. From (x,y,z), draw

\begin{aligned}
X'&\sim\operatorname{Bin}\!\left(n,\ p_X(z)\right),\\
Y'&\sim\operatorname{Bin}\!\left(m,\ p_Y(z)\right),\\
Z'&\sim\operatorname{Beta}(X'+Y'+\alpha,\ n+m-X'-Y'+\beta),
\end{aligned}

where p_X(z) and p_Y(z) are the success probabilities above. The two binomial draws both use the current z, and neither uses the other count. The beta draw uses the new counts. One sweep replaces (x,y,z) by (X',Y',Z').
In fact, X and Y are conditionally independent given Z: at a fixed z, the joint kernel factors into a function of x and a function of y. They need not be independent marginally, since both success probabilities vary with the shared Z. Recording only one coordinate from the joint chain approximates its marginal distribution, automatically averaging over the other coordinates.
Run. Use \alpha=2, \beta=4, \gamma=0.3, \delta=0.6, n=10, m=20, and the sweeps above, for 100{,}000 iterations from (5,10,1/2), with generator seed 3500. Discard the first 1{,}000 iterations. The marginal summaries of the remaining 99{,}000 draws are

Conditional modes. For 0<p<1 and k=1,\ldots,n,

\frac{\mathbb{P}(W=k)}{\mathbb{P}(W=k-1)}
=
\frac{n-k+1}{k}\cdot\frac{p}{1-p}
\ge 1
\iff
k\le (n+1)p,

when W\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p). Thus the pmf is maximised at \lfloor(n+1)p\rfloor. If (n+1)p is an integer, that value and the integer one smaller are both modes.
For the beta coordinate, a=x+y+\alpha\ge 2>1 and b=n+m-x-y+\beta\ge 4>1 at these parameter values, for every feasible (x,y). The log conditional density has derivative (a-1)/z-(b-1)/(1-z) and second derivative -(a-1)/z^{2}-(b-1)/(1-z)^{2}<0, so the conditional mode is

z=\frac{a-1}{a+b-2}
=
\frac{x+y+\alpha-1}{n+m+\alpha+\beta-2}
=
\frac{x+y+1}{34}.

Update in the Gibbs order, using the latest value of each conditioning variable. At a binomial tie, take the larger mode \lfloor(n+1)p\rfloor. Starting at (5,10,1/2), with \delta=3/5 and \gamma=3/10,

p_X(1/2)=\frac{6}{13},
\qquad
11\cdot\frac{6}{13}=\frac{66}{13}\notin\mathbb{Z},

so the x-mode is 5. Also

p_Y(1/2)=\frac{4}{7},
\qquad
21\cdot\frac{4}{7}=12\in\mathbb{Z},

so y has modes 11 and 12. The larger mode is 12, and then

z=\frac{5+12+1}{34}=\frac{9}{17}.

At this state,

p_X(9/17)=\frac{27}{55},
\quad
11\cdot\frac{27}{55}=\frac{27}{5},
\quad
\lfloor 27/5\rfloor=5,

and

p_Y(9/17)=\frac{3}{5},
\quad
21\cdot\frac{3}{5}=\frac{63}{5},
\quad
\lfloor 63/5\rfloor=12,

neither success probability giving an integer (n+1)p. The beta mode is again 9/17.

\therefore
\text{the iteration stops at }
\Bigl(5,\ 12,\ \tfrac{9}{17}\Bigr).

Note: selecting the smaller y-mode at the tie stops at (5,11,1/2) instead. Other initial states can stop at other conditional-mode fixed points.
Each mode update can only increase or preserve the joint density with the other coordinates fixed. That explains the coordinate-ascent interpretation, but it does not prove that the terminal point is a global joint mode. More importantly, these terminal values do not quantify marginal uncertainty: the simulated spread and quantiles above come from random full-conditional draws, not from the mode iteration. Warm-up removal is a starting-point precaution; trace plots and autocorrelation checks are still needed to assess the simulation.

title: Question 3. Normal mean and variance
text:
Topic: Conjugate analysis for normal models · more questions on this topic
Source: Final preparation, question 3 of 22 ‹ Question 2 Question 4 ›

Let X_i\mid\mu,\sigma^2\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^2), with independent priors

\mu\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu_0,\sigma_0^2),
\qquad
\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(\alpha_0,\beta_0).

(a) Does the joint posterior have this same product form?
(b) Write the full conditional distributions of \mu and of \sigma^2.
(c) Which updating algorithm uses these two distributions as its steps?
(d) Explain why independent priors for \mu and \sigma^2 do not generally give independent posteriors.
(e) Distinguish a full conditional posterior from a marginal posterior.
(f) Explain why a standard full conditional distribution does not imply that the corresponding marginal posterior belongs to the same family.
(g) Explain how a Gibbs sampler uses these full conditional distributions.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write v=\sigma^2, S=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2, and use \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b) with kernel v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v}. Prior independence means p(\mu,v)=p(\mu)p(v). A full conditional fixes the other unknown parameter; a marginal posterior averages over its posterior uncertainty.
(a) No. After the data are observed, \mu and \sigma^2 are dependent, so the joint posterior is not an independent normal times an independent inverse-gamma.
Bayes’ theorem gives the joint kernel

p(\mu,v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto
v^{-(\alpha_0+n/2)-1}
\exp\left\{-\frac{\beta_0+\{S+n(\mu-\bar x)^2\}/2}{v}
-\frac{(\mu-\mu_0)^2}{2\sigma_0^2}\right\}.

The term (\mu-\bar x)^2/v couples the two unknowns. The same discrepancy between \mu and the data is more plausible when the observation variance is larger.
(b) With the other parameter held fixed, the updates are the univariate conjugate posteriors:

\begin{aligned}
\mu\mid\sigma^2,x
&\sim
N\Biggl(
\frac{n\bar x\,\sigma_0^2+\mu_0\sigma^2}{n\sigma_0^2+\sigma^2},\;
\frac{\sigma^2\sigma_0^2}{n\sigma_0^2+\sigma^2}
\Biggr),\\[4pt]
\sigma^2\mid\mu,x
&\sim
\operatorname{InvGamma}\Bigl(
\alpha_0+\frac n2,\;
\beta_0+\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2
\Bigr).
\end{aligned}

The normal variance equals \sigma_1^2 from the known-variance update, because

\Bigl(\frac n{\sigma^2}+\frac1{\sigma_0^2}\Bigr)^{-1}
=
\frac{\sigma^2\sigma_0^2}{n\sigma_0^2+\sigma^2}.

(c) A Gibbs sampler uses these two distributions. Choose v^{(0)}>0. At sweep t, draw \mu^{(t)} from the normal full conditional using v^{(t-1)}, then draw v^{(t)} from the inverse-gamma full conditional using \mu^{(t)}. Record the completed pair. The second draw uses the newly updated mean, rather than its value from the previous sweep.
For compact notation in the algorithm, define

m(v)=\frac{n\bar x/v+\mu_0/\sigma_0^2}{n/v+1/\sigma_0^2},
\qquad V(v)=\left(\frac n v+\frac1{\sigma_0^2}\right)^{-1},
\qquad b(\mu)=\beta_0+\frac12\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2.

Here B is the number of initial sweeps discarded as warm-up, not a guarantee of convergence. Assess mixing from multiple valid starting values, trace plots and autocorrelation, and account for dependence when computing Monte Carlo error. An exact full-conditional draw needs no Metropolis acceptance step.
(d) The prior density factors as p(\mu)\,p(\sigma^2). The likelihood does not. The factor \sigma^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2 depends on both parameters, so

p(\mu,\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})

does not factor into a function of \mu alone times a function of \sigma^2 alone.
(e) A full conditional treats the other parameter as known:

p(\mu\mid\sigma^2,{\boldsymbol{x}})
\quad\text{and}\quad
p(\sigma^2\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}}).

The marginal posteriors integrate that parameter out,

p(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=
\int p(\mu\mid\sigma^2,{\boldsymbol{x}})\,p(\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\,d\sigma^2,
\qquad
p(\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=
\int p(\sigma^2\mid\mu,{\boldsymbol{x}})\,p(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\,d\mu.

(f) The full conditional p(\mu\mid\sigma^2,{\boldsymbol{x}}) is normal at each fixed \sigma^2. The marginal p(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}) mixes those normals over the posterior distribution of \sigma^2; a mixture need not belong to the component family. Here, integrating the joint kernel over v gives

p(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto
\exp\left\{-\frac{(\mu-\mu_0)^2}{2\sigma_0^2}\right\}
\left\{\beta_0+\frac{S+n(\mu-\bar x)^2}{2}\right\}^{-(\alpha_0+n/2)}.

This is generally neither a normal nor a Student-t kernel. Likewise, the marginal variance posterior is a mixture of inverse-gamma full conditionals and is not generally inverse-gamma. Substituting a point estimate for the other unknown does not perform the required integration.
(g) Each Gibbs step draws from one full conditional, using the most recent value of the conditioned parameter. The stationary distribution of the pair is the joint posterior p(\mu,\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}). A marginal posterior is represented by the simulated values of one coordinate, not by a single full-conditional distribution.
After suitable convergence assessment and warm-up, averages of functions of the retained pairs approximate joint-posterior expectations. Keeping only the \mu coordinate approximates its marginal posterior automatically: uncertainty in v has been propagated through the chain. Successive draws are generally correlated, so Monte Carlo standard errors must account for that dependence.

title: Question 4. Jointly conjugate normal–inverse-gamma
text:
Topic: Conjugate analysis for normal models · more questions on this topic
Source: Final preparation, question 4 of 22 ‹ Question 3 Question 5 ›

Let X_i\mid\mu,\sigma^2\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^2), with the jointly conjugate prior

\mu\mid\sigma^2\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu_0,\sigma^2/\kappa_0),
\qquad
\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(\alpha_0,\beta_0),

where \kappa_0,\alpha_0,\beta_0>0. The inverse-gamma kernel is (\sigma^2)^{-\alpha_0-1}\exp(-\beta_0/\sigma^2).
(a) How does the jointly conjugate prior for (\mu,\sigma^2) differ from independent normal and inverse-gamma priors?
(b) What remains in the same family after updating, and what is the marginal posterior distribution of \mu?
(c) What has to be checked before an inverse-gamma moment, or a software default, is used?
(d) State the four updated posterior hyperparameters \kappa_n, \mu_n, \alpha_n, and \beta_n.
(e) State the joint posterior family and the conditional posterior of \mu\mid\sigma^2,{\boldsymbol{x}}.
(f) State the marginal posterior of \sigma^2.
(g) State the marginal posterior of \mu, including its degrees of freedom, location, and scale.
(h) Explain why integrating out \sigma^2 produces a Student-t distribution rather than a normal distribution.
(i) Interpret \kappa_0 and the weighted-average form of the posterior mean.
(j) Explain how this model differs from the independent-prior model in Question 3.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Let v=\sigma^2, S=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2, and \kappa_0>0. The normal–inverse-gamma family is defined by the factorisation p(\mu,v)=p(v)p(\mu\mid v), with v\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(\alpha_0,\beta_0) and \mu\mid v\sim\operatorname{N}(\mu_0,v/\kappa_0). A Student-t location–scale distribution t_\nu(m,s) means m+sT with T\sim t_\nu; s is a scale.
(a) The jointly conjugate prior scales the prior variance of the mean by the unknown variance:

\mu\mid\sigma^2\sim \operatorname{N}(\mu_0,\sigma^2/\kappa_0),
\qquad
\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(\alpha_0,\beta_0).

The independent prior uses a fixed \sigma_0^2, not \sigma^2/\kappa_0.
Thus this prior already makes the uncertainty in \mu depend on v: larger observation variance brings larger conditional prior variance for the mean. Conjugacy concerns this dependent joint family. It does not mean that updating preserves independence.
(b) The joint posterior stays normal–inverse-gamma. The marginal posterior of \mu is a Student-t distribution.
(c) Match the density in use,

f(\sigma^2)\propto(\sigma^2)^{-\alpha-1}\exp(-\beta/\sigma^2),

before a moment or a software default is used. Packages do not all take (\alpha,\beta) in this shape–rate order.
(d) Let S=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2. The updated hyperparameters are

\begin{aligned}
\kappa_n&=\kappa_0+n,\\
\mu_n&=\frac{\kappa_0\mu_0+n\bar x}{\kappa_0+n},\\
\alpha_n&=\alpha_0+\frac n2,\\
\beta_n
&=
\beta_0+\frac12 S+\frac{\kappa_0 n}{2(\kappa_0+n)}(\bar x-\mu_0)^2.
\end{aligned}

The update follows by combining the two quadratic penalties. The useful identity is

n(\mu-\bar x)^2+\kappa_0(\mu-\mu_0)^2
=\kappa_n(\mu-\mu_n)^2
+\frac{\kappa_0n}{\kappa_n}(\bar x-\mu_0)^2.

The last term records disagreement between the prior centre and the sample mean. This disagreement adds to the posterior scale for v, alongside the within-sample scatter S. Ignoring it would understate uncertainty when the prior centre and data differ.
(e) Multiplying the likelihood by the joint prior and using that identity gives

p(\mu,v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto
v^{-(\alpha_n+3/2)}
\exp\left\{-\frac{\beta_n+\kappa_n(\mu-\mu_n)^2/2}{v}\right\}.

This factors into a normal density in \mu\mid v and an inverse-gamma density in v, so the joint posterior remains normal–inverse-gamma. Conditionally,

\mu\mid\sigma^2,{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim
\operatorname{N}\bigl(\mu_n,\sigma^2/\kappa_n\bigr).

(f) Integrating out \mu leaves the inverse-gamma factor,

\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(\alpha_n,\beta_n).

The integral of the conditional normal density is one. Equivalently, integrating its unnormalised exponential kernel contributes \sqrt{2\pi v/\kappa_n}, cancelling the extra factor v^{-1/2} in the joint kernel. This is why the marginal shape is \alpha_n.
(g) The marginal posterior is Student-t, with 2\alpha_n degrees of freedom, location \mu_n, and scale \sqrt{\beta_n/(\alpha_n\kappa_n)}:

\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim
t_{2\alpha_n}\!\left(\mu_n,\sqrt{\frac{\beta_n}{\alpha_n\kappa_n}}\right).

The second argument is a scale, not a standard deviation.
When \alpha_n>1, its variance is \beta_n/[\kappa_n(\alpha_n-1)], which is larger than the squared scale. The marginal mean equals \mu_n when 2\alpha_n>1; when this moment does not exist, \mu_n is still the distribution’s location and symmetry centre.
(h) Given \sigma^2, \mu is normal with variance proportional to \sigma^2. Mixing that normal over the inverse-gamma posterior of \sigma^2 gives the Student-t kernel

\left(1+\frac{\kappa_n(\mu-\mu_n)^2}{2\beta_n}\right)^{-(2\alpha_n+1)/2}.

Uncertainty in \sigma^2 produces heavier tails than a normal distribution with the same location and scale.
Indeed, the integral over v is proportional to [\beta_n+\kappa_n(\mu-\mu_n)^2/2]^{-(\alpha_n+1/2)}. Matching this with [1+(\mu-m)^2/(\nu s^2)]^{-(\nu+1)/2} gives \nu=2\alpha_n and s^2=\beta_n/(\alpha_n\kappa_n). A plug-in normal posterior at an estimated variance would not reproduce these tails.
(i) The weight \kappa_0 is the prior equivalent sample size: \mu_0 is weighted as \kappa_0 observations. Thus

\mu_n=\frac{\kappa_0\mu_0+n\bar x}{\kappa_0+n}

is the sample-size-weighted average of the prior location and the sample mean. The prior location is also its marginal mean when that mean exists.
(j) In the prior variance of \mu is a fixed \sigma_0^2, and the joint posterior does not stay normal–inverse-gamma. Here the prior variance is \sigma^2/\kappa_0, so the joint posterior stays in that family. Both marginals are then available in closed form: inverse-gamma for \sigma^2, and Student-t for \mu.
The distinction is visible in the conditional update: in the independent-prior model the relative weights depend on the current v, whereas here both precision contributions share the factor 1/v. That factor cancels from \mu_n, leaving fixed weights n and \kappa_0.

title: Question 22. Orthodontic growth curves
text:
Topic: Random slopes, and a binary mixed model · more questions on this topic
Source: Final preparation, question 22 of 22 ‹ Question 21

2025 examination, Question 4 (20 marks).
Distance from pituitary to pterygomaxillary fissure was measured every two years from age 8 to 14 on 27 subjects. The individual trajectories are shown below.



Individual orthodontic trajectories from the 2025 examination.


The random-slope fit fit1 = lmer(distance ~ age + Sex + (age|Subject)) has the following summary output:
Random effects:
 Groups   Name        Variance Std.Dev. Corr
 Subject  (Intercept)  7.82249   2.7969
          age          0.05126   0.2264 -0.77
 Residual              1.71621   1.3100
Number of obs: 108, groups: Subject, 27

Fixed effects:
             Estimate Std. Error t value
(Intercept)  17.63518    0.88623  19.899
age           0.66019    0.07125   9.265
SexFemale    -2.14544    0.75746  -2.832
(a) [6 marks] Write the statistical model for the random-slope command.
(b) [6 marks] Interpret the three fixed-effect estimates and the three standard deviations above.
ranef(fit1)$Subject
       (Intercept)         age
M16     -0.96698456 -0.06544230
F10     -2.31273350 -0.13319695
(c) [4 marks] Interpret the two pairs of predicted random effects.
fit2 = lmer(distance ~ age + Sex + (1|Subject))
anova(fit2, fit1)

      npar    AIC    BIC  logLik deviance  Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq)
fit2     5 444.86 458.27 -217.43   434.86
fit1     7 446.84 465.61 -216.42   432.84 2.0213  2     0.364
(d) [2 marks] Write the model for distance ~ age + Sex + (1|Subject).
(e) [2 marks] Is the random-intercept model an acceptable simplification?






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Y_{ji} is the orthodontic distance in millimetres for child j at occasion i, and age is in years. Set F_j=1 for female and 0 for male. A random-intercept-and-slope model has a child-specific pair (\alpha_{0j},\alpha_{1j}) with mean zero and covariance \Sigma_A. The residual error represents occasion-specific variation after the child’s own line has been accounted for. All variance components have units determined by the quantity they vary.
(a) Index the subject by j and the occasion by i. Male is the reference level of sex. The command (age|Subject) is a random intercept and a random slope on age, with a covariance between them:

\begin{aligned}
Y_{ji}
&=
\beta_0+\beta_1\,\mathrm{age}_{ji}+\beta_2\,\mathrm{Female}_j
+
\alpha_{0j}+\alpha_{1j}\,\mathrm{age}_{ji}
+\varepsilon_{ji},\\[4pt]
\begin{pmatrix}\alpha_{0j}\\ \alpha_{1j}\end{pmatrix}
&\sim
\operatorname{N}(0,\Sigma_A),
\qquad
\varepsilon_{ji}\sim \operatorname{N}(0,\sigma^2),
\end{aligned}

independently across subjects, with the errors independent of the random effects. From the fit,

\Sigma_A
=
\begin{pmatrix}
7.822 & -0.488\\
-0.488 & 0.0513
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\sigma=1.310,

where -0.488\approx-0.77\times2.797\times0.226. Fixed effects are unknown population constants; random effects are realised child-specific departures modelled as draws from a population distribution. A new sample of children would have new realised departures, while the model’s population parameters describe the same population. The fit estimates both the mean structure and its variance components, using restricted maximum likelihood for the displayed fit.
The correlation -0.77 says that a child with a higher intercept tends to have a flatter slope. The intercept in this parameterisation is the value at age 0.
For distinct occasions at ages s and t on the same child, the model implies

\operatorname{Cov}\{Y_j(s),Y_j(t)\}
=\tau_0^2+(s+t)\tau_{01}+st\tau_1^2,

where \tau_0^2,\tau_1^2,\tau_{01} are the entries of \Sigma_A. At a single occasion the variance additionally includes \sigma^2. This follows by expanding \operatorname{Cov}(\alpha_{0j}+s\alpha_{1j},\alpha_{0j}+t\alpha_{1j}); independent residual errors contribute no covariance between distinct occasions. It explains why ordinary independent-error regression is not the stated model.
(b) These six numbers are statements about the population, not about the 27 children in the file.
The intercept 17.635 mm is the extrapolated male mean at age 0. The measured ages run from 8 to 14, so this is outside the observed age range and should not be presented as a typical observed distance. At age 12, for example, the fitted male population mean is 17.635+0.660(12)=25.555 mm, a comparison within the measured range.
The age coefficient 0.660 mm per year is the population mean change for one extra year of age, the same slope for both sexes. The female coefficient -2.145 mm is the female mean minus the male mean at the same age.
The intercept standard deviation 2.797 mm says that a typical child sits about 2.8 mm away from the population intercept. That intercept is the age-0 value. The age standard deviation 0.226 mm per year says that a typical slope sits about 0.23 mm per year away from 0.660. The residual standard deviation 1.310 mm is the within-child scatter about that child’s own line.
The first two standard deviations describe between-child heterogeneity in line parameters; the last describes variation of measurements around a given child’s line. They are not standard errors of the fixed effects. Recentring age at 12 would make the intercept refer to a meaningful age and would change the random-intercept variance and intercept–slope correlation, while leaving fitted trajectories unchanged. Consequently the negative correlation must be interpreted with its age-0 reference in mind.
(c) The pairs (-0.967,-0.065) and (-2.313,-0.133) are predicted random effects for the sampled children. With the variances estimated, they are empirical best linear unbiased predictors. These values are departures from the appropriate population intercept and slope, so they must be added to the fixed part before a child’s fitted line is obtained.
For M16 the predicted line lies 0.967 mm below the male population intercept and 0.065 mm per year below the population slope:

(17.635-0.967)+(0.660-0.065)\,\mathrm{age}
=
16.67+0.595\,\mathrm{age}.

For F10 the sex contrast is already in the fixed part. The predicted line lies a further 2.313 mm below the female intercept and 0.133 mm per year below the population slope:

(17.635-2.145-2.313)+(0.660-0.133)\,\mathrm{age}
=
13.18+0.527\,\mathrm{age}.

These predictions pool each child’s measurements with the population model, shrinking poorly determined individual departures towards zero. They are not four additional fixed-effect coefficients. The fitted line predicts the child’s conditional mean; a future observed distance also has residual variation with standard deviation \sigma and uncertainty in the predicted line.
(d) Dropping the random slope leaves a common age slope and one random intercept:

Y_{ji}
=
\beta_0+\beta_1\,\mathrm{age}_{ji}+\beta_2\,\mathrm{Female}_j
+\alpha_{0j}+\varepsilon_{ji},

with \alpha_{0j}\sim \operatorname{N}(0,\sigma_A^2) and \varepsilon_{ji}\sim \operatorname{N}(0,\sigma^2), independent across subjects. Two occasions on the same child then have covariance \sigma_A^2.
The corresponding within-child correlation is \sigma_A^2/(\sigma_A^2+\sigma^2) and is constant across pairs of distinct ages. Removing the random slope therefore imposes both a common age slope and a simpler covariance pattern. It still allows children to have persistently higher or lower distances through their random intercepts.
(e) Start from the larger model and delete. The likelihood-ratio statistic for the random slope and its covariance is 2.02 on 2 degrees of freedom, and the printed tail probability is 0.364. The random-intercept model has the smaller AIC, 444.86 against 446.84.
The null sets a variance to zero, a boundary of the parameter space, so the ordinary chi-squared reference used for the printed p-value is only approximate here. The large printed value and the lower AIC of the simpler model both support using the random-intercept model as an acceptable simplification for these data. This is not evidence that every subject has exactly the same age slope.
The larger model adds a slope variance and its covariance with the intercept, accounting for the two-parameter difference in the printed comparison. Both models must be fitted to the same observations and use a comparable likelihood criterion. Here the fixed-effects structure is the same, which permits a REML comparison of their random-effects structures. If fixed effects were being changed, the models should instead be compared using maximum likelihood. The statistical conclusion is that the extra random-slope structure is not sufficiently supported by these data, rather than that individual growth rates are known to be identical.

title: Question 5. Normal–inverse-\chi^2 regression
text:
Topic: Bayesian linear regression · more questions on this topic
Source: Final preparation, question 5 of 22 ‹ Question 4 Question 6 ›

Suppose

y\mid\beta,\sigma^2,X\sim \operatorname{N}_n(X\beta,\sigma^2 I_n),

with prior

\beta\mid\sigma^2\sim \operatorname{N}_p(\beta_0,\sigma^2\Sigma_0),
\qquad
\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{Inv\text{-}\chi^2}(\mu_0,\sigma_0^2).

Here X is known, \Sigma_0 is positive definite, and \mu_0,\sigma_0^2>0. The inverse-\chi^2 convention is

\frac{\mu_0\sigma_0^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_{\mu_0}.

(a) State the inverse-\chi^2 prior kernel and its equivalent inverse-gamma parameters.
(b) State the updated parameters \Sigma_n and \beta_n.
(c) State the updated parameters \mu_n and \sigma_n^2.
(d) Express the joint posterior through a conditional posterior for \beta and a marginal posterior for \sigma^2.
(e) Express the updated scale using a residual sum of squares and a prior penalty. Explain why it is positive.
(f) Is \Sigma_n the conditional covariance matrix of \beta? Is \sigma_n^2 the posterior mean of \sigma^2? Give the correct expressions and the posterior mode of \sigma^2.
(g) State the full conditional posterior of \sigma^2\mid\beta,y,X. How does it differ from its marginal posterior?
(h) Without consulting the updates, complete the square to reconstruct them. Explain why the marginal degrees of freedom are \mu_0+n.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. There are n responses and p regression coefficients; X is an n\times p known design matrix. Write v=\sigma^2. The matrix \Sigma_0 scales the conditional prior covariance v\Sigma_0. In this question \mu_0 denotes prior degrees of freedom, not a normal mean. Our \operatorname{Inv\text{-}\chi^2}(\nu,s^2) convention means \nu s^2/v\sim\chi^2_\nu, or equivalently v\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(\nu/2,\nu s^2/2).
(a) The transformation \mu_0\sigma_0^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_{\mu_0} has kernel

\pi(\sigma^2)
\propto
(\sigma^2)^{-\mu_0/2-1}
\exp\Bigl(-\frac{\mu_0\sigma_0^2}{2\sigma^2}\Bigr),
\qquad\sigma^2>0.

Matching (\sigma^2)^{-a-1}\exp(-b/\sigma^2) gives a=\mu_0/2 and b=\mu_0\sigma_0^2/2.
For completeness, if U=\mu_0\sigma_0^2/v, then |dU/dv|=\mu_0\sigma_0^2/v^2. Multiplying the \chi^2_{\mu_0} density at U by this Jacobian gives the displayed inverse-gamma kernel. The Jacobian supplies the power v^{-2} and must be retained.

\boxed{
\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\Bigl(\frac{\mu_0}{2},\frac{\mu_0\sigma_0^2}{2}\Bigr).
}

(b) Since \Sigma_0^{-1} is positive definite and X^\top X is positive semidefinite, \Sigma_n^{-1} is positive definite. Precision addition gives

\boxed{\Sigma_n^{-1}=X^\top X+\Sigma_0^{-1},}
\qquad
\boxed{\beta_n=\Sigma_n(X^\top y+\Sigma_0^{-1}\beta_0).}

The data and prior precision contributions add, and their combined precision determines the posterior centre.
At fixed v, the likelihood contributes X^\top X/v to the precision of \beta, and the prior contributes \Sigma_0^{-1}/v. Their sum is \Sigma_n^{-1}/v. A proper positive-definite prior therefore gives a proper conditional update even if X is not of full column rank; an unregularised least-squares inverse (X^\top X)^{-1} is not needed.
(c)

\boxed{\mu_n=\mu_0+n,}
\qquad
\boxed{
\sigma_n^2
=
\frac{
\mu_0\sigma_0^2+y^\top y+\beta_0^\top\Sigma_0^{-1}\beta_0
-\beta_n^\top\Sigma_n^{-1}\beta_n
}{\mu_n}.
}

(d)

\boxed{\beta\mid\sigma^2,y,X\sim \operatorname{N}_p(\beta_n,\sigma^2\Sigma_n),}
\qquad
\boxed{\sigma^2\mid y,X\sim\operatorname{Inv\text{-}\chi^2}(\mu_n,\sigma_n^2).}

Together these specify a normal–inverse-\chi^2 joint posterior.
This is a conditional–marginal factorisation. To draw an independent posterior pair, draw v from the marginal inverse-\chi^2 distribution and then \beta from its normal distribution conditional on that v. The components within a pair are dependent through the conditional covariance, even though different pairs can be generated independently.
(e) Equivalently,

\mu_n\sigma_n^2
=
\mu_0\sigma_0^2
+(y-X\beta_n)^\top(y-X\beta_n)
+(\beta_n-\beta_0)^\top\Sigma_0^{-1}(\beta_n-\beta_0).

Both quadratic forms are nonnegative and \mu_0\sigma_0^2>0, so \sigma_n^2>0. The algebra is completed in (h).
(f) No. The conditional covariance is \sigma^2\Sigma_n, not \Sigma_n:

\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(\beta\mid\sigma^2,y,X)=\sigma^2\Sigma_n.}

The parameter \sigma_n^2 is a scale. By the inverse-gamma equivalence in (a),

\boxed{
\mathbb{E}(\sigma^2\mid y,X)
=
\frac{\mu_n\sigma_n^2}{\mu_n-2},
\qquad\mu_n>2,
}

and

\boxed{
\operatorname{mode}(\sigma^2\mid y,X)
=
\frac{\mu_n\sigma_n^2}{\mu_n+2}.
}

(g)

\boxed{
\sigma^2\mid\beta,y,X
\sim
\operatorname{Inv\text{-}\chi^2}\!\left(
\mu_n+p,\;
\frac{\mu_n\sigma_n^2+(\beta-\beta_n)^\top\Sigma_n^{-1}(\beta-\beta_n)}{\mu_n+p}
\right).
}

The full conditional fixes \beta. The marginal posterior integrates \beta out, which removes p from the degrees of freedom.
The difference comes from the normal density’s factor v^{-p/2}. It remains when \beta is fixed and therefore adds p/2 to the inverse-gamma shape. Integrating over \beta instead contributes a factor v^{p/2}, cancelling it. Substituting \beta=\beta_n in the full conditional would leave the wrong degrees of freedom.
(h) Expand the likelihood quadratic and the prior quadratic:

\begin{aligned}
&(y-X\beta)^\top(y-X\beta)
+(\beta-\beta_0)^\top\Sigma_0^{-1}(\beta-\beta_0)\\
&\quad=
\beta^\top(X^\top X+\Sigma_0^{-1})\beta
-2\beta^\top(X^\top y+\Sigma_0^{-1}\beta_0)
+y^\top y+\beta_0^\top\Sigma_0^{-1}\beta_0\\
&\quad=
(\beta-\beta_n)^\top\Sigma_n^{-1}(\beta-\beta_n)
+y^\top y+\beta_0^\top\Sigma_0^{-1}\beta_0
-\beta_n^\top\Sigma_n^{-1}\beta_n.
\end{aligned}

Adding \mu_0\sigma_0^2, the terms free of \beta are the numerator of \mu_n\sigma_n^2 in (c), with \mu_n=\mu_0+n. Thus

\boxed{
Q(\beta)
=
(\beta-\beta_n)^\top\Sigma_n^{-1}(\beta-\beta_n)
+\mu_n\sigma_n^2.
}

The joint posterior kernel is

(\sigma^2)^{-(\mu_0+n+p)/2-1}
\exp\Bigl(-\frac{Q(\beta)}{2\sigma^2}\Bigr).

The integral over \beta of the normal kernel equals (2\pi\sigma^2)^{p/2}|\Sigma_n|^{1/2}. The remaining power of \sigma^2 is

-\frac{\mu_0+n+p}{2}-1+\frac p2
=
-\frac{\mu_0+n}{2}-1.


\therefore
\text{the marginal inverse-}\chi^2\text{ degrees of freedom are }\mu_0+n.
