title: Q2. Gamma waiting times with an inverse-Gamma prior
Q4. Gibbs sampling from full conditionals
text:
Topic: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 4 of 59 ‹ Q3 Q5 ›

Let X\in\{0,1,\ldots,10\} and 0<\theta<1 have joint density/mass function \pi(x,\theta)
  \propto
  \binom{10}{x}\theta^{x+1}(1-\theta)^{12-x}.
(a) [2 marks] Find and identify the conditional distribution of X\mid\theta.
(b) [2 marks] Find and identify the conditional distribution of \theta\mid X=x.
(c) [3 marks] Hence write pseudocode for a Gibbs sampler that generates a Markov chain with equilibrium distribution \pi(x,\theta). Begin from an arbitrary valid starting value (x^{(0)},\theta^{(0)}).
(d) [2 marks] Explain why there is no accept-reject step in this Gibbs sampler.
(e) [1 mark] Are the resulting pairs \bigl(X^{(1)},\theta^{(1)}\bigr),
          \bigl(X^{(2)},\theta^{(2)}\bigr),\ldots independent? Briefly explain.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. A full conditional is obtained by normalising the joint in the variable being updated; the other variable is fixed. The relevant kernels are \operatorname{Bin}(n,p):\ \binom nx p^x(1-p)^{n-x},\quad x=0,\ldots,n, \operatorname{Beta}(a,b):\ u^{a-1}(1-u)^{b-1},\quad 0<u<1,\quad a,b>0. Here n=10; superscript (t) denotes a completed Gibbs iteration.

(a) Conditional distribution of X\mid\theta
Holding \theta fixed and retaining the terms that depend on x, \begin{aligned}
  \pi(x\mid\theta)
  &\propto
    \binom{10}{x}\theta^{x+1}(1-\theta)^{12-x}\\
  &=\theta(1-\theta)^2
    \binom{10}{x}\theta^x(1-\theta)^{10-x}\\
  &\propto
    \binom{10}{x}\theta^x(1-\theta)^{10-x}.
\end{aligned} The discarded factor \theta(1-\theta)^2 is constant with respect to x. Therefore, \boxed{X\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Bin}(10,\theta)}.


(b) Conditional distribution of \theta\mid X=x
Holding x fixed, \pi(\theta\mid x)
  \propto
  \theta^{x+1}(1-\theta)^{12-x},
  \qquad 0<\theta<1. The kernel of a \operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta) distribution is \theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1}. Matching powers gives \alpha=x+2,
  \qquad
  \beta=13-x. Hence, \boxed{
    \theta\mid X=x
    \sim\operatorname{Beta}(x+2,13-x)
  }.


(c) Gibbs-sampler pseudocode
Choose any valid starting values x^{(0)}\in\{0,1,\ldots,10\},
  \qquad
  \theta^{(0)}\in(0,1). For t=1,2,\ldots,T:
1. Generate X^{(t)}
          \sim\operatorname{Bin}\bigl(10,\theta^{(t-1)}\bigr).
2. Using the newly generated X^{(t)}, generate \theta^{(t)}
          \sim\operatorname{Beta}\bigl(X^{(t)}+2,13-X^{(t)}\bigr).
3. Store \bigl(X^{(t)},\theta^{(t)}\bigr).
After a suitable burn-in, the stored states have approximately the target equilibrium distribution \pi(x,\theta).


(d) Why there is no accept-reject step
Each update is sampled directly from its exact full conditional distribution. The generated value therefore already has the required conditional distribution and is always accepted. Equivalently, Gibbs sampling is a special case of Metropolis-Hastings whose acceptance probability is 1.


(e) Independence of the sampled pairs
No. The update X^{(t)} depends on \theta^{(t-1)}, and \theta^{(t)} then depends on X^{(t)}. Successive states therefore form a Markov chain and are generally serially dependent. Once the chain is in equilibrium, each individual state has marginal distribution \pi(x,\theta), but this does not make the states independent.

Key result. The two full conditionals are \boxed{
    X\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Bin}(10,\theta),
    \qquad
    \theta\mid X=x\sim\operatorname{Beta}(x+2,13-x)
  }. At each iteration, sample from these in order using the newest available value. Exact full-conditional draws require no rejection, but successive Gibbs states are not independent.

title: Q6. Beta-Binomial conjugacy and prior influence
text:
Topic: The Beta–Binomial model · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 6 of 59 ‹ Q5 Q7 ›

Suppose X\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,\theta),
  \qquad
  \theta\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a,b), where n\geq1, a,b>0, and the observed value of X is x.
(a) Derive the posterior density of \theta. Identify its distribution, parameters, and support. [3 marks]
(b) Express the posterior mean as a weighted average of the prior mean and x/n. Explain how the weight on the prior changes as n increases, with a and b fixed. [3 marks]
(c) Another statistician instead uses a prior uniform on (0,1/2). If x/n=4/5, can the posterior assign positive probability to \theta>1/2? Explain why or why not. [2 marks]
(d) Under squared-error loss, explain why the posterior mean is the Bayes estimate. Is it necessarily the Bayes estimate under a different loss? [2 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. For a,b>0, a \operatorname{Beta}(a,b) density is \theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}/B(a,b) on (0,1), where B(a,b)=\int_0^1u^{a-1}(1-u)^{b-1}\,du. Here x is a Binomial success count out of known n. A Bayes estimate is an action d minimising posterior expected loss. Part (c) substitutes a restricted prior; part (d) returns to the Beta prior from (a).

(a) Posterior distribution
The likelihood and prior kernels are p(x\mid\theta)\propto\theta^x(1-\theta)^{n-x},
  \qquad
  p(\theta)\propto\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}. Therefore, \begin{aligned}
  p(\theta\mid x)
  &\propto p(x\mid\theta)p(\theta)\\
  &\propto
    \theta^{a+x-1}(1-\theta)^{b+n-x-1},
    \qquad 0<\theta<1.
\end{aligned} Thus \boxed{
    \theta\mid x\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a+x,b+n-x)
  }. The normalised posterior density is p(\theta\mid x)
  =\frac{\theta^{a+x-1}(1-\theta)^{b+n-x-1}}
         {B(a+x,b+n-x)},
  \qquad 0<\theta<1.


(b) Posterior mean and prior influence
The posterior mean is \mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)=\frac{a+x}{a+b+n}. Since the prior mean is \mathbb{E}(\theta)=a/(a+b), \begin{aligned}
  \mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)
  &=
  \frac{a+b}{a+b+n}\frac{a}{a+b}
  +\frac{n}{a+b+n}\frac{x}{n}\\
  &=
  \boxed{
    \frac{a+b}{a+b+n}\mathbb{E}(\theta)
    +\frac{n}{a+b+n}\frac{x}{n}
  }.
\end{aligned} The two weights sum to one. With a and b fixed, the prior weight (a+b)/(a+b+n) decreases to zero as n\to\infty, while the data weight increases to one.


(c) Restricted prior support
No. A prior uniform on (0,1/2) has density zero for \theta>1/2. Because p(\theta\mid x)\propto p(x\mid\theta)p(\theta), the posterior is also zero wherever the prior is zero. Hence \boxed{\mathbb{P}(\theta>1/2\mid x)=0}, even when x/n=4/5. The likelihood can reweight values inside the prior support, but it cannot create posterior mass outside that support.


(d) Bayes estimate under squared-error loss
Write m=\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x) and expand \theta-d=(\theta-m)+(m-d). The cross term has posterior expectation 2(m-d)\mathbb{E}(\theta-m\mid x)=0. Consequently, for an estimate d, the posterior expected squared loss is \begin{aligned}
  \mathbb{E}\bigl[(\theta-d)^2\mid x\bigr]
  &=
  \operatorname{Var}(\theta\mid x)
  +\bigl\{\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)-d\bigr\}^2.
\end{aligned} The variance term does not depend on d, so this expression is minimised by \boxed{
  \widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{Bayes}}
  =\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid x)
  =\frac{a+x}{a+b+n}.
  } The Bayes estimate depends on the loss function: for example, absolute-error loss gives a posterior median rather than necessarily the posterior mean.

title: Q8. Equal-tailed and highest-density intervals
text:
Topic: Bayesian foundations · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 8 of 59 ‹ Q7 Q9 ›

Suppose a continuous parameter \theta has posterior density p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=2\theta,
  \qquad 0<\theta<1, and zero elsewhere.
(a) Find a 75% equal-tailed posterior credible interval. [3 marks]
(b) Find a minimum-width 75% posterior credible interval. Sketch the posterior density and explain why your interval is a highest-density interval. Exact expressions are sufficient. [3 marks]
(c) A frequentist confidence-interval procedure happens to return the same endpoints as one of your intervals. Explain the difference between a 75% confidence statement and a 75% posterior credible statement. [2 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. For a continuous posterior, F(u)=\mathbb P(\theta\le u\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}) and F^{-1} is its quantile function. An equal-tailed interval puts half the omitted probability in each tail. A highest-density interval (HDI, also called HPD) includes points of at least as high density as those excluded. Here the posterior density is 2\theta on (0,1) and the required probability is 0.75.
For 0<\theta<1, the posterior distribution function is F(\theta)=\int_0^\theta 2u\,du=\theta^2,
  \qquad
  F^{-1}(p)=\sqrt{p}.

(a) Equal-tailed 75% credible interval
An equal-tailed 75% interval leaves probability 0.125 in each tail. Therefore its endpoints are F^{-1}(0.125)=\sqrt{\frac18},
  \qquad
  F^{-1}(0.875)=\sqrt{\frac78}. Thus \boxed{
    \left[\sqrt{\frac18},\sqrt{\frac78}\right]
  } is the 75% equal-tailed posterior credible interval.


(b) Minimum-width 75% credible interval
The posterior density 2\theta increases throughout (0,1), so the highest-density interval must contain the largest values of \theta and end at 1. Let it be [c,1]. Then \mathbb{P}(c\leq\theta\leq1\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
  =1-F(c)=1-c^2=0.75, which gives c=1/2. Hence the minimum-width interval is \boxed{\left[\frac12,1\right]}.



Every included point has density at least as large as every excluded point, so [1/2,1] is a highest-density interval. Equivalently, among intervals [a,b] satisfying b^2-a^2=0.75, its width (b-a)=0.75/(a+b) is minimised by taking the largest possible a+b, namely b=1 and a=1/2.


(c) Confidence versus credibility
A 75% confidence procedure has repeated-sampling coverage \mathbb{P}_{\theta}\{L(X)\leq\theta\leq U(X)\}=0.75. The probability refers to the random interval procedure; after observing the data, the realised frequentist interval is fixed.
A 75% credible interval [a,b] satisfies \mathbb{P}(a\leq\theta\leq b\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=0.75. This probability refers directly to the posterior distribution of \theta given the observed data, prior, and model. Identical numerical endpoints do not change these different interpretations.

title: Q10. Metropolis-Hastings with an asymmetric-proposal extension
text:
Topic: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 10 of 59 ‹ Q9 Q11 ›

A posterior density is known up to a normalising constant: p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto\theta^2e^{-\theta},
  \qquad \theta>0. From the current state \theta^{(t)}>0, propose \theta^*=\theta^{(t)}+\varepsilon,
  \qquad
  \varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,s^2), where s>0 is fixed.
(a) Derive the acceptance probability, including the case \theta^*\leq0. Explain why the unknown normalising constant is not needed. [3 marks]
(b) Give pseudocode for one iteration, including the acceptance decision and the next state after rejection. [3 marks]
(c) One run uses a very small s and accepts almost every proposal. Another uses a very large s and accepts very few. Explain why either run may be inefficient. [2 marks]
(d) If the proposal density were not symmetric, what additional factor would be required in the acceptance ratio? Define its numerator and denominator. [2 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. The target is proportional to \theta^2e^{-\theta} on \theta>0 and is zero otherwise. Let q(\theta^*\mid\theta) be the proposal density, \alpha(\theta,\theta^*) the acceptance probability, and (t) the iteration index. The proposal N(\theta,s^2) has variance s^2>0, fixed across states and iterations; the current state must lie in the target support.
The target density has kernel \pi(\theta)\propto \theta^2e^{-\theta},
\qquad \theta>0.

(a) Acceptance probability
For a random-walk proposal \theta^*\mid\theta^{(t)}\sim N\left(\theta^{(t)},s^2\right), the proposal is symmetric: q(\theta^*\mid\theta^{(t)})
=q(\theta^{(t)}\mid\theta^*). Consequently, the proposal-density terms cancel from the Metropolis–Hastings ratio. If \theta^*>0, \begin{aligned}
\alpha\left(\theta^{(t)},\theta^*\right)
&=
\min\left\{
\frac{\pi(\theta^*)}{\pi(\theta^{(t)})},1
\right\}\\
&=
\boxed{
\min\left\{
\left(\frac{\theta^*}{\theta^{(t)}}\right)^2
\exp\left[-\left(\theta^*-\theta^{(t)}\right)\right],
1
\right\}.
}
\end{aligned} If \theta^*\leq 0, then \pi(\theta^*)=0, so the proposal is rejected and \alpha=0.


(b) Normalising constant
The unknown normalising constant appears in both the numerator and denominator of the target-density ratio and therefore cancels. Only the target kernel is needed.


(c) One sampler iteration
One iteration of the algorithm is:
1. Generate a proposal \theta^*\sim N\left(\theta^{(t)},s^2\right).
2. Calculate \alpha(\theta^{(t)},\theta^*) as above.
3. Generate U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1).
4. Set \theta^{(t+1)}=
    \begin{cases}
    \theta^*, & U\leq\alpha(\theta^{(t)},\theta^*),\\
    \theta^{(t)}, & U>\alpha(\theta^{(t)},\theta^*).
    \end{cases}


(d) Proposal scale
If s is extremely small, proposals remain close to the current state and the acceptance rate will usually be high. However, the chain moves only in small steps, producing high autocorrelation and slow exploration.
If s is extremely large, many proposals will be negative or will fall in regions where the target density is very small. Most will be rejected, so the chain will repeatedly remain at the same state and again mix slowly.


(e) Asymmetric proposals
For an asymmetric proposal, the proposal terms do not cancel. The acceptance probability becomes \boxed{
\alpha(\theta,\theta^*)
=
\min\left\{
\frac{\pi(\theta^*)q(\theta\mid\theta^*)}
{\pi(\theta)q(\theta^*\mid\theta)},
1
\right\}.
} The additional factor is therefore \boxed{
\frac{q(\theta\mid\theta^*)}{q(\theta^*\mid\theta)},
} that is, the reverse-proposal density divided by the forward-proposal density.

title: Q12. Pareto likelihood and Gamma posterior
text:
Topic: Exponential families and conjugacy · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 12 of 59 ‹ Q11 Q13 ›

Suppose X_1,\ldots,X_n are conditionally iid with density p(x_i\mid\theta)
  =\theta m^\theta x_i^{-(\theta+1)},
  \qquad x_i\geq m, where m>0 is known and \theta>0 is unknown. Use the prior p(\theta)=\theta e^{-\theta},
  \qquad \theta>0. You may use the fact that a \operatorname{Gamma}(A,B) distribution in shape–rate form has kernel \theta^{A-1}e^{-B\theta}, mean A/B, and mode (A-1)/B when A>1.
[8 marks]
(a) Show that the likelihood can be written L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto\theta^n e^{-\theta S},
          \qquad
          S=\sum_{i=1}^n\log\left(\frac{x_i}{m}\right). [3 marks]
(b) Derive the posterior distribution of \theta. Identify its distribution, parameters, and support. [3 marks]
(c) State the posterior mean and MAP estimate. [2 marks]
Start with part (a). The target expression is supplied, so the task is to show how multiplying the densities produces it.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. The known lower endpoint is m>0, and the observed data satisfy x_i\ge m. We use the shape–rate Gamma kernel \theta^{A-1}e^{-B\theta} for \theta>0, A,B>0, with mean A/B and mode (A-1)/B when A>1. The MAP estimate is this posterior mode. The prior \theta e^{-\theta} is \operatorname{Gamma}(2,1).
Since m is known and the observed sample is valid, the support indicator does not depend on \theta.

(a) Likelihood
By conditional independence, \begin{aligned}
L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=\prod_{i=1}^n
  \left[\theta m^\theta x_i^{-(\theta+1)}\right]\\
&=\theta^n m^{n\theta}
  \prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{-(\theta+1)}.
\end{aligned} The factor m^{n\theta} must be retained because it depends on \theta. Using a^b=e^{b\log a}, \begin{aligned}
L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=\theta^n
  \exp\left(n\theta\log m\right)
  \exp\left[-(\theta+1)\sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i\right]\\
&=\theta^n
  \exp\left[-\sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i\right]
  \exp\left[-\theta\left\{
    \sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i-n\log m
  \right\}\right].
\end{aligned} The first exponential in the final line does not depend on \theta and may be absorbed into the proportionality constant. Also, \sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i-n\log m
=\sum_{i=1}^n\log\left(\frac{x_i}{m}\right)
=S. Therefore, \boxed{
L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto\theta^n e^{-\theta S},
\qquad \theta>0.
}


(b) Posterior distribution
Multiplying the likelihood by the prior gives \begin{aligned}
p(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto L(\theta;{\boldsymbol{x}})p(\theta)\\
&\propto
\theta^n e^{-\theta S}\,
\theta e^{-\theta}\\
&=\theta^{n+1}e^{-(S+1)\theta},
\qquad \theta>0.
\end{aligned} Comparing this with the shape–rate Gamma kernel \theta^{A-1}e^{-B\theta}, we obtain A-1=n+1,
\qquad
B=S+1. Hence \boxed{
\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(n+2,S+1)
\quad\text{in shape--rate form},
\qquad \theta>0.
} Because x_i\geq m, each \log(x_i/m)\geq0, so S+1>0 as required.


(c) Posterior mean and MAP estimate
For a shape–rate \operatorname{Gamma}(A,B) distribution, the mean is A/B. Therefore, \boxed{
\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{n+2}{S+1}.
} The MAP estimate is the posterior mode. Since A=n+2>1, \boxed{
\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MAP}}
=\frac{A-1}{B}
=\frac{n+1}{S+1}.
}

title: Q14. Marginal and conditional distributions
Q16. Interpreting identical interval endpoints
text:
Topic: Bayesian foundations · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 16 of 59 ‹ Q15 Q17 ›

[4 marks]
A Bayesian analysis produces a 95% posterior credible interval [0.3,0.6] for a parameter \theta. A frequentist analysis happens to produce a 95% confidence interval with the same endpoints.
Explain the interpretation of each interval. Identify what is treated as random in each probability statement and explain why identical endpoints do not imply identical interpretations.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. C(X) denotes an interval computed from a random sample X; C({\boldsymbol{x}}) is its realised value. \mathbb P_\theta describes repeated sampling with \theta fixed. In contrast, \mathbb P(\,\cdot\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}) for the parameter is calculated from its posterior under the chosen model and prior. The stated 95% levels refer respectively to coverage and posterior probability.
For the Bayesian interval, \boxed{
\mathbb{P}(0.3\leq\theta\leq0.6\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=0.95.
} Conditional on the observed data, the assumed model, and the prior, there is 95% posterior probability that \theta lies between 0.3 and 0.6. The observed data are fixed, while uncertainty about \theta is represented by its posterior distribution.
For a frequentist 95% confidence-interval procedure C(X), \boxed{
\mathbb{P}_{\theta}\{\theta\in C(X)\}=0.95.
} Here \theta is fixed and the interval is random because it is calculated from the random sample X. Under repeated sampling at the same true value of \theta, 95% of the intervals generated by the procedure would contain \theta. Once the data have been observed, the realised interval is fixed; the frequentist statement is not that this particular interval contains \theta with probability 0.95.
Therefore identical endpoints do not imply identical interpretations. The credible interval assigns posterior probability to values of \theta given the observed data, whereas the confidence interval describes the long-run coverage of a random interval-producing procedure.

title: Q18. Equilibrium and independence
text:
Topic: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 18 of 59 ‹ Q17 Q19 ›

[4 marks]
A Gibbs sampler targets a bivariate posterior in which the two parameters are strongly correlated. Its initial state is drawn exactly from the target posterior. A student states:

“The chain starts at equilibrium, so its successive sampled pairs can be treated as independent posterior observations.”

Explain what starting at equilibrium guarantees. Does independence follow? Justify your answer by referring to how Gibbs updates are generated.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. An invariant or equilibrium distribution is preserved by the chain’s transition. Starting from it makes the chain stationary: every iteration has the same marginal target distribution. This is weaker than independence across iterations. Here one Gibbs sweep updates each coordinate once from its exact full conditional, using the newest available conditioning value.
To see invariance directly, start with a pair having density p(\theta_1,\theta_2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}). Updating \theta_1 while leaving \theta_2 unchanged gives density p(\theta_2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\,
p(\theta_1'\mid\theta_2,{\boldsymbol{x}})
=p(\theta_1',\theta_2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}). The second conditional update reconstructs the same joint density in the same way. Therefore the full sweep preserves the target. Starting at equilibrium guarantees stationarity. If (\theta_1^{(0)},\theta_2^{(0)})
\sim p(\theta_1,\theta_2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}), then \boxed{
(\theta_1^{(t)},\theta_2^{(t)})
\sim p(\theta_1,\theta_2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
\quad\text{for every }t\geq0.
} Thus no convergence from an incorrectly distributed initial state is needed.
Independence does not follow. A systematic Gibbs update has the form \theta_1^{(t+1)}
\sim p(\theta_1\mid\theta_2^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{x}}), followed by \theta_2^{(t+1)}
\sim p(\theta_2\mid\theta_1^{(t+1)},{\boldsymbol{x}}). The new pair is generated using components of the current pair, so successive states are generally serially dependent. This dependence can be particularly strong when the target parameters are strongly correlated. Starting at equilibrium gives the correct marginal distribution at every iteration, but it does not turn the Markov chain into independent posterior draws.

title: Q20. Estimation and prediction
text:
Topic: Conjugate analysis for normal models · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 20 of 59 ‹ Q19 Q21 ›

[4 marks]
Suppose measurements are conditionally independent with X_i\mid\mu\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2), where \sigma^2>0 is known, and a proper Normal prior is used for \mu.
Explain the difference between the posterior distribution of \mu and the posterior predictive distribution of one new measurement. As the number of observations becomes very large, would you expect uncertainty about both quantities to approach zero? Explain your reasoning.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. \mu is the population mean and \widetilde X is a new observation. Write \mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim N(m_n,v_n), where v_n is the posterior variance. The known observation variance is \sigma^2>0; conditional on \mu, the new Normal observation is independent of the original sample. A predictive distribution averages over parameter uncertainty as well as new-observation noise.
The posterior distribution p(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}) describes remaining uncertainty about the unknown population mean \mu after observing the data. The posterior predictive distribution p(\widetilde x\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\int p(\widetilde x\mid\mu)
p(\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\,d\mu describes uncertainty about a future observation \widetilde X. It includes both uncertainty about \mu and the new observation’s sampling variation around \mu.
If \mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(m_n,v_n), then \boxed{
\widetilde X\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}
\sim\mathcal{N}(m_n,\sigma^2+v_n).
} As n\to\infty, under the model and standard regularity conditions, v_n\longrightarrow0. Hence posterior uncertainty about \mu approaches zero. By contrast, \operatorname{Var}(\widetilde X\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{new-observation noise}}
+\underbrace{v_n}_{\text{parameter uncertainty}}
\longrightarrow\sigma^2. Predictive uncertainty therefore does not vanish: even if \mu were known exactly, a future measurement would still vary randomly around it.

title: Q22. Advertising responses and Dirichlet inference
text:
Topic: Categorical data and the Dirichlet distribution · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 22 of 59 ‹ Q21 Q23 ›

[10 marks]
An advertising campaign records responses from 60 independently sampled people:




Negative
Neutral
Positive




Male
8
6
16


Female
12
4
14



Let \mathbf p=(p_{MN},p_{MU},p_{MP},p_{FN},p_{FU},p_{FP}) be the six population cell probabilities, with U denoting a neutral response. Model the counts as multinomial and use \mathbf p\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(1,1,1,1,1,1). You may use the Dirichlet kernel f(\mathbf p)\propto\prod_{k=1}^{K}p_k^{\alpha_k-1},
\qquad p_k>0,\quad \sum_{k=1}^{K}p_k=1.
(a) [2 marks] Derive the posterior distribution of \mathbf p, stating its parameters and support.
(b) [2 marks] Find the posterior mean of p_{MP} and its component of the joint MAP estimate of \mathbf p. Explain why that MAP component equals the observed cell proportion here.
(c) [2 marks] Find the posterior predictive probability that one new person responds positively, regardless of gender. Express it as a posterior expectation before calculating it.
(d) [2 marks] For that new person, calculate \mathbb{P}(\text{positive response}\mid\text{female},\text{data}). Explain why this differs from \mathbb{P}(\text{female and positive response}\mid\text{data}).
(e) [2 marks] Are the six components of \mathbf p independent under the posterior? Explain using their constraint.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Let D be the observed table and \mathbf p its six population cell probabilities. The labels M,F denote male and female; N,U,P denote negative, neutral, and positive. With parameters a_1,\ldots,a_K>0, a Dirichlet density has kernel \prod_k p_k^{a_k-1} on the simplex p_k>0, \sum_kp_k=1. The joint MAP maximises this density over the entire simplex, not a one-component marginal density.
(a) Posterior distribution. Write the counts in the stated order as \mathbf x=(8,6,16,12,4,14),\qquad n=60. The multinomial likelihood is L(\mathbf p;D)=\frac{60!}{\prod_{k=1}^{6}x_k!}
\prod_{k=1}^{6}p_k^{x_k}
\propto\prod_{k=1}^{6}p_k^{x_k}. The Dirichlet prior has kernel \prod_k p_k^{1-1}=1 on the simplex. Consequently, p(\mathbf p\mid D)\propto
\prod_{k=1}^{6}p_k^{x_k+1-1}, which is the Dirichlet kernel with parameters x_k+1. Thus \boxed{\mathbf p\mid D\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(9,7,17,13,5,15).} Its density is supported on the simplex p_k>0, \sum_{k=1}^6p_k=1; the boundary has probability zero. The posterior concentration is A=9+7+17+13+5+15=66.
(b) Posterior mean and MAP. For a Dirichlet vector with parameters a_1,\ldots,a_K and A=\sum_k a_k, \mathbb{E}(p_k)=\frac{a_k}{A},\qquad
\widehat p_{k,\mathrm{MAP}}=\frac{a_k-1}{A-K}
\quad\text{when every }a_k>1. Here every posterior parameter exceeds one, so \boxed{\mathbb{E}(p_{MP}\mid D)=\frac{17}{66}\approx0.2576,}
\qquad
\boxed{\widehat p_{MP,\mathrm{MAP}}=
\frac{17-1}{66-6}=\frac{16}{60}\approx0.2667.} The MAP component is taken from the mode of the joint posterior for \mathbf p. Since the prior density is constant on the simplex, maximising the posterior is equivalent to maximising the likelihood, giving the observed cell proportions.
(c) Predicting a positive response. Conditional on \mathbf p, the probability of a positive response is p_{MP}+p_{FP}. Averaging over posterior uncertainty gives \begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(\text{positive}\mid D)
&=\int (p_{MP}+p_{FP})p(\mathbf p\mid D)\,d\mathbf p\\
&=\mathbb{E}(p_{MP}+p_{FP}\mid D)\\
&=\frac{17}{66}+\frac{15}{66}
=\boxed{\frac{16}{33}\approx0.4848.}
\end{aligned} Prediction uses posterior averaging, not substitution of the MAP estimate.
(d) Conditioning on the new person being female. First calculate the two relevant posterior predictive probabilities: \mathbb{P}(\text{female and positive}\mid D)=\mathbb{E}(p_{FP}\mid D)=\frac{15}{66}, \mathbb{P}(\text{female}\mid D)
=\mathbb{E}(p_{FN}+p_{FU}+p_{FP}\mid D)
=\frac{13+5+15}{66}=\frac{33}{66}. By the definition of conditional probability, \boxed{
\mathbb{P}(\text{positive}\mid\text{female},D)
=\frac{15/66}{33/66}=\frac5{11}\approx0.4545.
} By contrast, the joint probability is \boxed{\mathbb{P}(\text{female and positive}\mid D)
=\frac{15}{66}=\frac5{22}\approx0.2273.} The conditional probability restricts attention to the female row; the joint probability refers to both events occurring for a person sampled from the whole population.
(e) Posterior dependence. No. The probabilities must satisfy \sum_k p_k=1 exactly. Increasing one component leaves less total probability for the others. More formally, if they were independent, then 0=\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^{6}p_k\,\middle|\,D\right)
=\sum_{k=1}^{6}\operatorname{Var}(p_k\mid D)>0, a contradiction, since each component has positive posterior variance. Indeed, distinct Dirichlet components have \operatorname{Cov}(p_j,p_k\mid D)
=-\frac{a_ja_k}{A^2(A+1)}<0,\qquad j\ne k.

Key result. Add counts to the Dirichlet parameters; average probabilities for prediction; and distinguish a joint cell probability from a probability conditional on a row.

title: Q24. Bayesian regression and prediction
text:
Topic: Bayesian linear regression · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 24 of 59 ‹ Q23 Q25 ›

[12 marks]
Consider the regression model Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad
\varepsilon_i\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2), with reference prior p(\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma^2)\propto1/\sigma^2 for (\beta_0,\beta_1)\in\mathbb{R}^2 and \sigma^2>0. For n=10 observations, the design matrix has rows (1,x_i), and \widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
(X^\top X)^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1/10&0\\0&1/40\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \operatorname{SSE}=16. The observed predictor values range from -3 to 3.
You may use the standard regression posterior formulas under this prior. Use the inverse-Gamma convention f(v)\propto v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v}. Write t_\nu(m,s) for a Student-t distribution with location m and scale s, and use t_{0.975,8}=2.306.
(a) [2 marks] State the marginal posterior distribution of \sigma^2 and calculate \mathbb{E}(\sigma^2\mid\mathbf y,X).
(b) [3 marks] State the marginal posterior distribution of the slope \beta_1, and calculate its equal-tailed 95% credible interval.
(c) [4 marks] At x_*=0, derive the posterior distributions and equal-tailed 95% intervals for:
(i) the unknown mean response \mu_*=\beta_0+\beta_1x_*;
(ii) a new observation \widetilde Y.
Explain precisely why the second interval is wider.
(d) [3 marks] Calculate h(x_*)=(1,x_*)(X^\top X)^{-1}(1,x_*)^\top at x_*=0 and x_*=4. Compare the posterior predictive scales at these points and explain how the calculation reflects uncertainty from extrapolation.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write D=(\mathbf y,X), v=\sigma^2, and \operatorname{SSE}=\|\mathbf y-X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\|^2. The inverse-Gamma kernel is v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v} on v>0. t_\nu(m,s) denotes location m, scale s, and \nu degrees of freedom: (T-m)/s\sim t_\nu. A scale is not a variance; t_{q,\nu} denotes the q quantile of standard t_\nu.
Assumptions. Use independent Normal errors, fixed covariates, full column rank X, n>p, positive SSE, and the reference prior p(\boldsymbol\beta,v)\propto1/v with respect to d\boldsymbol\beta\,dv. These rank and residual conditions ensure a proper posterior despite the improper prior.
There are p=2 regression coefficients, including the intercept. Define \nu=n-p=8,\qquad
s^2=\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}{n-p}=\frac{16}{8}=2,
\qquad C=(X^\top X)^{-1}. Here s^2 is the residual variance estimate; it is not the posterior mean of \sigma^2.
Why the regression posterior has this form. The likelihood times the reference prior gives p(\boldsymbol\beta,v\mid D)
\propto v^{-n/2-1}
\exp\{-\|\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta\|^2/(2v)\},
\qquad v=\sigma^2>0. Expand about the least-squares estimate. The cross term vanishes because X^\top(\mathbf y-X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})=\mathbf0, giving \|\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta\|^2
=\operatorname{SSE}
+(\boldsymbol\beta-\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})^\top
X^\top X(\boldsymbol\beta-\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}). The second term is a Normal quadratic. At fixed v it identifies \boldsymbol\beta\mid v,D\sim
N_p(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},vC). Its unnormalised exponential integrates to (2\pi v)^{p/2}|X^\top X|^{-1/2}, which explains the v^{p/2} factor in the variance marginal below.
(a) Marginal variance posterior. Under the stated reference prior, \sigma^2\mid D\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}\left(\frac{n-p}{2},
\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}2\right). Thus \boxed{\sigma^2\mid D\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(4,8),\qquad\sigma^2>0.} An \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b) variable has mean b/(a-1) when a>1, so \boxed{\mathbb{E}(\sigma^2\mid D)=\frac8{4-1}=\frac83\approx2.6667.} For completeness, integrating the coefficient kernel out of the joint posterior contributes a factor (\sigma^2)^{p/2}. Therefore p(\sigma^2\mid D)
\propto (\sigma^2)^{-(n/2+1)}(\sigma^2)^{p/2}
\exp\!\left(-\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}{2\sigma^2}\right)
=(\sigma^2)^{-5}e^{-8/\sigma^2}, confirming the shape 4, not n/2=5.
(b) Slope posterior and credible interval. The conditional coefficient posterior is \boldsymbol\beta\mid\sigma^2,D
\sim N_2(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},\sigma^2 C). The slope entry of C is 1/40, so \beta_1\mid\sigma^2,D\sim N\!\left(2,\frac{\sigma^2}{40}\right). Integrating over \sigma^2\mid D gives \boxed{\beta_1\mid D\sim t_8\!\left(2,\sqrt{\frac2{40}}\right)
=t_8(2,\sqrt{0.05}).} Equivalently, (\beta_1-2)/\sqrt{0.05}\mid D\sim t_8. The equal-tailed 95% credible interval is therefore 2\pm2.306\sqrt{0.05}=2\pm0.5156,
\qquad\boxed{(1.484,\,2.516).} The second argument of t_8 is a scale, not a variance. There is no additional division by \sqrt n: sample-size information is already in C.
(c) Mean response versus a new observation at x_*=0. For a general predictor value, set \mathbf z_*=(1,x_*)^\top and write m_*=\mathbf z_*^\top\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},
\qquad h(x_*)=\mathbf z_*^\top C\mathbf z_*. The linear-transformation rule for a normal vector gives \mu_*\mid\sigma^2,D
\sim N\bigl(m_*,\sigma^2 h(x_*)\bigr). For a new response \widetilde Y=\mu_*+\widetilde\varepsilon, the new error is independent of the coefficient uncertainty conditional on \sigma^2,D, and has variance \sigma^2. Thus \widetilde Y\mid\sigma^2,D,x_*
\sim N\bigl(m_*,\sigma^2\{1+h(x_*)\}\bigr). Integrating over the inverse-Gamma variance posterior gives \mu_*\mid D\sim t_8\bigl(m_*,s\sqrt{h(x_*)}\bigr), \widetilde Y\mid D,x_*\sim t_8\bigl(m_*,s\sqrt{1+h(x_*)}\bigr). At x_*=0, m_*=(1,0)\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}=1,
\qquad h(0)=\frac1{10}. Therefore the unknown mean response has posterior \boxed{\mu_*\mid D\sim t_8(1,\sqrt{0.2}),} with equal-tailed 95% credible interval 1\pm2.306\sqrt{0.2}=1\pm1.0313,
\qquad\boxed{(-0.031,\,2.031).} The new observation has posterior predictive distribution \boxed{\widetilde Y\mid D,x_*=0\sim t_8(1,\sqrt{2.2}),} with equal-tailed 95% predictive interval 1\pm2.306\sqrt{2.2}=1\pm3.4204,
\qquad\boxed{(-2.420,\,4.420).} Both intervals have the same centre and use the same t_8 quantile. The predictive interval is wider because a new observation includes both uncertainty about the regression mean and fresh observational noise. That additional noise produces the extra 1 in 1+h(x_*).
(d) Extrapolation and predictive scale. Using the supplied diagonal matrix, \begin{aligned}
h(x_*)&=(1,x_*)
\begin{pmatrix}1/10&0\\0&1/40\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}1\\x_*\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\frac1{10}+\frac{x_*^2}{40}.
\end{aligned} Hence \boxed{h(0)=0.1,\qquad h(4)=0.1+\frac{16}{40}=0.5.} The corresponding predictive scales are \boxed{s_{\mathrm{pred}}(0)=\sqrt{2(1+0.1)}=\sqrt{2.2}\approx1.4832,} \boxed{s_{\mathrm{pred}}(4)=\sqrt{2(1+0.5)}=\sqrt3\approx1.7321.} At x_*=4, the predicted centre is 1+2(4)=9, so the predictive distribution is t_8(9,\sqrt3). Its interval is wider than at x_*=0 because it has the same degrees of freedom but a larger scale.
The value 4 lies outside the observed range [-3,3]. Uncertainty about the slope has a greater effect on the fitted mean farther from the centred design, increasing h(x_*). The future-error contribution is unchanged; the increased width comes from greater parameter uncertainty in the prediction. This calculation assumes the linear model remains appropriate beyond the observed range; it does not account for possible failure of that model there.

Key result. The mean-response scale is s\sqrt h; the new-observation scale is s\sqrt{1+h}. The extra 1 represents new observational noise, while h measures uncertainty about the fitted mean.

title: Q26. General Beta–Binomial Gibbs sampler
text:
Topic: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 26 of 59 ‹ Q25 Q27 ›

[15 marks]
Consider the joint density/mass function, given up to proportionality, f(x,\theta)\propto
\binom{n}{x}\theta^{x+\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{n-x+\beta-1}, for x=0,1,\ldots,n, 0\leq\theta\leq1, with n a known positive integer and \alpha,\beta>0 known.
Normalisation clarification: the expression in the screenshot is treated as a kernel, since a constant is needed to make its total mass one.
(i) [4 marks] Find the conditional distribution of X given \theta and name the distribution. It is sufficient to work out the kernel, without specifying the normalising constant.
(ii) [4 marks] Find the conditional distribution of \theta given X=x and name the distribution. As in part (i), you may omit the normalising constant.
(iii) [7 marks] Using parts (i) and (ii), or otherwise, describe how you would construct a Gibbs sampler to sample from f(x,\theta).






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. A \operatorname{Binomial}(n,p) mass function is \binom nx p^x(1-p)^{n-x} for x=0,\ldots,n. A \operatorname{Beta}(a,b) density has kernel \theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1} on (0,1) and normalising integral B(a,b). Here n is a known positive integer and \alpha,\beta>0. A full conditional treats the other variable as fixed; (t) indexes complete Gibbs sweeps.
(i) Conditional distribution of X\mid\theta. For fixed 0<\theta<1, factor the joint kernel as f(x,\theta)\propto
\underbrace{\theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1}}_{\text{constant in }x}
\binom nx\theta^x(1-\theta)^{n-x}. The first factor can be dropped when finding the conditional distribution of X, but \binom nx must remain because it depends on x. Thus f(x\mid\theta)\propto\binom nx\theta^x(1-\theta)^{n-x},
\qquad x=0,1,\ldots,n. This is the Binomial kernel, so \boxed{X\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,\theta).} Indeed, the displayed Binomial probabilities already sum to one by the binomial theorem. At the endpoints the corresponding conditional is degenerate at 0 or n; these endpoints have zero probability under the continuous Beta marginal.
(ii) Conditional distribution of \theta\mid X=x. Now fix x. The binomial coefficient is constant with respect to \theta, giving f(\theta\mid x)\propto
\theta^{x+\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{n-x+\beta-1},\qquad 0<\theta<1. Matching the exponents to a Beta density yields \boxed{\theta\mid X=x\sim
\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+x,\beta+n-x).} Both shape parameters are positive because \alpha,\beta>0 and 0\leq x\leq n.
Normalisation check. Summing the joint kernel over x gives \begin{aligned}
\sum_{x=0}^{n}\binom nx
\theta^{x+\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{n-x+\beta-1}
&=\theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1}
\sum_{x=0}^{n}\binom nx\theta^x(1-\theta)^{n-x}\\
&=\theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1}.
\end{aligned} Integrating this over \theta gives B(\alpha,\beta). The normalised joint density/mass function is therefore the supplied expression divided by B(\alpha,\beta). This missing constant does not affect either conditional distribution.
(iii) Gibbs sampler. Choose x^{(0)}\in\{0,\ldots,n\} and 0<\theta^{(0)}<1. For t=1,\ldots,T:
1. Draw X^{(t)}\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,\theta^{(t-1)}).
2. Using the new count, draw \theta^{(t)}\sim
        \operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+X^{(t)},\beta+n-X^{(t)}).
3. Record (X^{(t)},\theta^{(t)}) and repeat.
The second update must use X^{(t)}, not the old value X^{(t-1)}. Each update samples exactly from a full conditional, so every draw is accepted and there is no Metropolis–Hastings acceptance step.
To see why the target is invariant, suppose a current pair has joint distribution f. Updating X conditional on its current \theta gives the joint distribution f(\theta)f(x\mid\theta)=f(x,\theta) again. Updating \theta conditional on that newly drawn X likewise preserves the same joint distribution. Thus the full sweep has f as its equilibrium distribution.
Run the chain for sufficient warm-up, assess convergence, and retain subsequent pairs for inference. The retained pairs are generally dependent; their empirical averages approximate joint expectations as the run length increases under the usual ergodicity conditions.

Key result. Hold one variable fixed, retain every factor involving the other, and then alternate exact Binomial and Beta draws using the most recently updated value.

title: Q28. Lognormal variance and conjugate inference
text:
Topic: Conjugate analysis for normal models · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 28 of 59 ‹ Q27 Q29 ›

[20 marks]
The size X of a certain type of particle can be modelled by a lognormal distribution with density f(x\mid\mu,\sigma^2)
=\frac1{x\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}
\exp\!\left\{-\frac{(\log x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right\},
\qquad x>0. Note that if X\sim\operatorname{logN}(\mu,\sigma^2), then Y=\log X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2). Assume that \mu is known and \sigma^2>0 is unknown. For the posterior calculations, let X_1,\ldots,X_n be conditionally iid observations from this model.
(i) [4 marks] Show that this lognormal model belongs to the exponential family.
(ii) [4 marks] Find the form of a conjugate prior for \sigma^2 and identify the distribution.
(iii) [5 marks] Find the posterior distribution of \sigma^2 given the observed data {\boldsymbol{x}}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n).
(iv) [4 marks] State, without derivation, the posterior mean and posterior mode. Explain their behaviour as n\to\infty, with the prior fixed.
(v) [3 marks] Briefly describe how you would construct a 90% credible interval for \sigma^2.






Worked answer (click to show)





Taking logs converts this to a Normal model with known mean and unknown variance.
Definitions. Write v=\sigma^2 and S=\sum_i(\log x_i-\mu)^2. The log observations have Normal mean \mu and variance v; \mu is known. An \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b) density has kernel v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v} on v>0. Throughout, Gamma distributions of the precision 1/v use shape–rate parameters. The positive observations are conditionally iid; prior propriety and moment conditions are stated below.
(i) Exponential-family form. The density can be written as f(x\mid v)
=\frac1{x\sqrt{2\pi}}
\frac{\exp\!\left\{-\dfrac1v\,
\dfrac{(\log x-\mu)^2}{2}\right\}}{\sqrt v},
\qquad x>0,\quad v>0. Comparing with the course’s form f(x\mid v)=b(x)\frac{\exp\{c(v)T(x)\}}{a(v)}, we identify \boxed{
\begin{gathered}
b(x)=\frac1{x\sqrt{2\pi}},\qquad
T(x)=\frac{(\log x-\mu)^2}{2},\\
c(v)=-\frac1v,\qquad a(v)=\sqrt v.
\end{gathered}} Here \mu is known, so T(x) involves no unknown parameter. The support x>0 also does not depend on v. This establishes the required one-parameter exponential-family representation.
(ii) Conjugate prior. For this representation, the general conjugate prior has kernel \pi(v)\propto\frac{\exp\{\eta c(v)\}}{a(v)^\kappa}
=v^{-\kappa/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac\eta v\right),\qquad v>0. Compare this with the inverse-Gamma kernel \pi(v)\propto v^{-a_0-1}e^{-b_0/v}. Matching the power and exponential term gives a_0=\frac\kappa2-1,\qquad b_0=\eta. Thus a convenient parameterisation of the conjugate prior is \boxed{\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(a_0,b_0),\qquad a_0,b_0>0,} with normalised density \pi(v)=\frac{b_0^{a_0}}{\Gamma(a_0)}
v^{-a_0-1}e^{-b_0/v},\qquad v>0. In the general conjugacy parameters, propriety requires \eta>0 and \kappa>2. The prior is on the variance \sigma^2, not on the standard deviation \sigma.
(iii) Posterior distribution. Define the sum of squared deviations on the log scale, S=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\log x_i-\mu)^2. The likelihood is \begin{aligned}
L(v;{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac1{x_i\sqrt{2\pi v}}
\exp\!\left\{-\frac{(\log x_i-\mu)^2}{2v}\right\}\\
&=(2\pi)^{-n/2}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac1{x_i}\right)
v^{-n/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{S}{2v}\right)\\
&\propto v^{-n/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{S}{2v}\right).
\end{aligned} The factors omitted in the last line do not depend on v. Multiplying by the inverse-Gamma prior, \begin{aligned}
\pi(v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto v^{-n/2}e^{-S/(2v)}v^{-a_0-1}e^{-b_0/v}\\
&=v^{-(a_0+n/2)-1}
\exp\!\left\{-\frac{b_0+S/2}{v}\right\}.
\end{aligned} Let A_n=a_0+\frac n2,\qquad B_n=b_0+\frac S2. Recognising the inverse-Gamma kernel gives \boxed{\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(A_n,B_n),\qquad\sigma^2>0.} Its normalised density is \pi(v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{B_n^{A_n}}{\Gamma(A_n)}
v^{-A_n-1}e^{-B_n/v},\qquad v>0.
(iv) Posterior mean, mode, and large-sample behaviour. The posterior summaries are \boxed{\mathbb{E}(\sigma^2\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{B_n}{A_n-1}
=\frac{b_0+S/2}{a_0+n/2-1},\qquad A_n>1,} \boxed{\widehat{\sigma^2}_{\mathrm{MAP}}=\frac{B_n}{A_n+1}
=\frac{b_0+S/2}{a_0+n/2+1}.} If A_n\leq1, the posterior mean is not finite; the mode exists for all A_n,B_n>0.
For fixed prior parameters and data generated at true variance \sigma_0^2, the law of large numbers gives \frac{S_n}{n}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\log X_i-\mu)^2
\longrightarrow\sigma_0^2. Both posterior summaries approach S_n/n and hence \sigma_0^2: the fixed prior’s influence vanishes. Since \mu is known, S_n/n is the usual likelihood estimate; there is no need to estimate \mu or replace it by the sample log-mean.
(v) A 90% credible interval for the variance. One valid choice is an equal-tailed interval. Let F_{\mathrm{IG}} be the CDF of the posterior \operatorname{InvGamma}(A_n,B_n). Choose its 5% and 95% quantiles: \boxed{\left[F_{\mathrm{IG}}^{-1}(0.05),
F_{\mathrm{IG}}^{-1}(0.95)\right].} This leaves posterior probability 0.05 below the interval and 0.05 above it, so the interval contains 0.90 posterior probability.
Equivalently, use the reciprocal precision W=\frac1{\sigma^2},\qquad
W\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(A_n,B_n)
\quad\text{in shape--rate form}. If q_{0.05} and q_{0.95} are the corresponding Gamma quantiles, then \mathbb{P}(q_{0.05}\leq W\leq q_{0.95}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=0.90. Taking reciprocals reverses the inequalities, giving \boxed{\left[\frac1{q_{0.95}},\frac1{q_{0.05}}\right]} as the same 90% credible interval for \sigma^2. The quantiles can be computed numerically, or approximated by the empirical 5% and 95% quantiles of a large sample drawn from the inverse-Gamma posterior.
This interval is for the unknown variance, not for a new particle size. It is an equal-tailed interval; it need not be the shortest or highest-posterior-density interval.

Key result. Take logs, recognise a normal model with known mean, and update a_0\mapsto a_0+n/2 and b_0\mapsto b_0+\tfrac12\sum_i(\log x_i-\mu)^2.

title: Q30. Poisson regression model statement
text:
Topic: Standard errors, and models for counts · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 30 of 59 ‹ Q29 Q31 ›

[4 marks]
For 80 independent lakes, researchers record the number of fish species, distance from the coast in kilometres, and surface area in hectares. They fit:
glm(species ~ distance + log(area), family = poisson)
Write down explicitly the model corresponding to this code. Define your notation and state the independence assumption.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. For lake i=1,\ldots,80, let Y_i be its species count, d_i its distance from the coast in kilometres, and A_i>0 its area in hectares. Write \mu_i=\mathbb{E}(Y_i\mid d_i,A_i). The covariates are fixed; logarithms are natural. A GLM combines a response distribution with a link between this conditional mean and a linear predictor.
The model is \boxed{
Y_i\mid d_i,A_i\overset{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}
\operatorname{Poisson}(\mu_i),
\qquad
\log\mu_i=\beta_0+\beta_1d_i+\beta_2\log A_i.
} Thus the default link is the log link, and \mu_i=\exp\{\beta_0+\beta_1d_i+\beta_2\log A_i\}
     =e^{\beta_0}e^{\beta_1d_i}A_i^{\beta_2}. Under the Poisson assumption, \mathbb{E}(Y_i\mid d_i,A_i)
=\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid d_i,A_i)=\mu_i. The responses from different lakes are independent conditional on their covariates. They need not be identically distributed, because their means can differ.

Key result. A model statement needs a distribution and an independence assumption, as well as the equation linking the mean to the covariates.

title: Q32. Deriving the Poisson log-likelihood
text:
Topic: Standard errors, and models for counts · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 32 of 59 ‹ Q31 Q33 ›

[3 marks]
Suppose, conditional on fixed covariates, Y_i\mid\mathbf X_i
\overset{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}\operatorname{Poisson}(\mu_i),
\qquad
\mu_i=\exp(\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta). Starting from the Poisson probability mass function, show that \ell(\boldsymbol\beta)
=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[
Y_i\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta
-\exp(\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta)
\right]+C. State exactly what C contains and why it can be ignored when maximising over \boldsymbol\beta.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Let \mathbf X_i be a fixed column vector of predictors and X the matrix with rows \mathbf X_i^\top. Write \eta_i=\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta and \mu_i=e^{\eta_i}. The likelihood is the joint Poisson mass function evaluated at observed counts \mathbf y, and \ell=\log L. An additive constant may depend on the data but not on the parameter \boldsymbol\beta being maximised over.
For observed counts y_i\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}, \mathbb{P}(Y_i=y_i\mid\mathbf X_i)
=\frac{e^{-\mu_i}\mu_i^{y_i}}{y_i!},
\qquad \mu_i=\exp(\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta). Conditional independence gives L(\boldsymbol\beta;\mathbf y,X)
=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{e^{-\mu_i}\mu_i^{y_i}}{y_i!}. Taking logarithms, \ell(\boldsymbol\beta)
=\sum_{i=1}^n\{-\mu_i+y_i\log\mu_i-\log(y_i!)\}. Since \log\mu_i=\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta, this becomes \boxed{
\ell(\boldsymbol\beta)
=\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[y_i\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta
-\exp(\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta)\right]+C,
\quad C=-\sum_{i=1}^n\log(y_i!).
} The constant C depends only on the observed responses, not on \boldsymbol\beta. Therefore adding or removing it does not change the maximiser over \boldsymbol\beta, and its derivatives with respect to \boldsymbol\beta are zero. Writing Y_i instead of y_i gives the random-data version in the question.

Key result. “Constant” means constant with respect to the parameter being optimised, not necessarily independent of the data.

title: Q34. Deviance and model adequacy
text:
Topic: Paired comparisons, and how far a fit is from the data · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 34 of 59 ‹ Q33 Q35 ›

[5 marks]
A Poisson regression gives:
Null deviance:      410.0 on 79 degrees of freedom
Residual deviance:  310.0 on 77 degrees of freedom
(a) Deduce the number of observations and the number of estimated regression coefficients, including the intercept.
(b) Explain which two models are being compared by the null deviance, and which two are being compared by the residual deviance.
(c) Test whether adding the predictors improves on an intercept-only model. You may use \chi^2_{2,0.95}=5.99.
(d) A researcher concludes: “The predictors are significant, so the model fits adequately.” Assess this conclusion using the output.
For this question, assume the usual large-sample deviance approximations are appropriate.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. The saturated model fits a separate mean to each observation. Deviance is 2(\ell_{\mathrm{sat}}-\ell_{\mathrm{fit}}), using maximised log-likelihoods. Null deviance uses an intercept-only fit; residual deviance uses the stated predictor model. A difference in deviances compares nested models fitted to the same data. Let n count observations and q count estimated regression coefficients, including the intercept.
Assumptions. As stipulated in the question, the large-sample chi-squared deviance approximations are appropriate. Test at 5%, using models fitted to the same observations. The goodness-of-fit calibration also relies on the specified Poisson variance model.
(a) Numbers of observations and coefficients. The intercept-only model has one coefficient, so its residual degrees of freedom give n-1=79\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\boxed{n=80}. If the fitted model has q regression coefficients including the intercept, n-q=77\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\boxed{q=3}.
(b) What the deviances compare. Write \ell_{\mathrm{sat}}, \ell_0, and \ell_1 for the maximised log-likelihoods of the saturated, intercept-only, and fitted predictor models, respectively. Then D_{\mathrm{null}}=2(\ell_{\mathrm{sat}}-\ell_0)=410,
\qquad
D_{\mathrm{res}}=2(\ell_{\mathrm{sat}}-\ell_1)=310. The saturated model fits a separate mean to each observation. Null deviance compares it with the intercept-only model; residual deviance compares it with the model containing the predictors.
(c) Test whether adding the predictors helps. With two predictor coefficients, test H_0:\beta_1=\beta_2=0,
\qquad H_1:\text{at least one of these coefficients is nonzero}. The likelihood-ratio statistic is G^2=2(\ell_1-\ell_0)
=D_{\mathrm{null}}-D_{\mathrm{res}}
=410-310=100. Under H_0, use the stipulated approximation G^2\sim\chi^2_2. Since 100>5.99, reject H_0 at the 5\% level. Conclusion: Under the Poisson assumptions, adding the predictors significantly improves fit compared with the intercept-only model.
(d) Does this establish adequate fit? No. Under an adequate fitted model and the stated approximation, the residual deviance is compared with \chi^2_{77}. The observed deviance 310 exceeds the 95th percentile \chi^2_{77,0.95}\approx98.48, so reject adequacy at the 5\% level. It is also large relative to the degrees of freedom: \frac{D_{\mathrm{res}}}{77}=\frac{310}{77}\approx4.03. This indicates lack of fit, despite the improvement in part (c). Possible causes include an incorrect mean structure or overdispersion; these two numbers alone do not identify the cause. Model inadequacy can also undermine the reliability of nominal model-based tests and standard errors, so the part (c) conclusion is conditional on its assumptions.

Key result. A model can be significantly better than a poor baseline and still fit the data badly. Improvement is not adequacy.

The same patients are analysed using:
