title: Q38. Changing from a logit to a probit link
text:
Topic: Smooth means · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 38 of 59 ‹ Q37 Q39 ›

[3 marks]
Another researcher fits:
gam(
  disease ~ s(cholesterol),
  family = binomial(link = "probit")
)
Write down explicitly the model statement, defining any additional mathematical function you use.
Identify precisely which component changes relative to the corresponding model with a logit link.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Let Y_i indicate disease, c_i denote fixed cholesterol, and p_i=\mathbb P(Y_i=1\mid c_i). For Z\sim N(0,1), \Phi(z)=\mathbb P(Z\le z); the probit link is \Phi^{-1}(p). Tildes on the intercept and smooth distinguish a refitted probit model from its logit counterpart. The Bernoulli responses are independent conditional on their covariates.
The model is Y_i\mid c_i\overset{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_i), \boxed{\Phi^{-1}(p_i)=\widetilde\beta_0+\widetilde s(c_i).} Equivalently, \boxed{p_i=\Phi\{\widetilde\beta_0+\widetilde s(c_i)\}.} Use a centring constraint such as \sum_i\widetilde s(c_i)=0 to separate the smooth from the intercept.
The comparison is with the corresponding intercept-plus-smooth logit model:



Component
Logit GAM
Probit GAM




Response distribution
Bernoulli
Bernoulli


Additive structure
Intercept plus smooth
Intercept plus smooth


Link
\log\{p/(1-p)\}
\Phi^{-1}(p)


Inverse link
e^\eta/(1+e^\eta)
\Phi(\eta)



The component that changes is the link function, and therefore the inverse link converting the predictor into a probability. The tildes emphasise that the intercept and smooth are fitted anew: their numerical values need not equal those obtained using the logit link.

Key result. A probit GAM models \Phi^{-1}(p), not log odds. Changing the link does not change the Bernoulli response distribution.

title: Q40. Interpreting a treatment–time interaction
text:
Topic: Random slopes, and a binary mixed model · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 40 of 59 ‹ Q39 Q41 ›

[6 marks]
The model in Question 39 produces:
Random effects:
Group       Term          Std.Dev.
patientID   Intercept       1.20



Fixed effect
Estimate
Standard error
p-value




Intercept
-0.80
0.20
0.000063


treatmentB
0.10
0.25
0.689


weeks
-0.10
0.02
<0.000001


treatmentB:weeks
-0.08
0.03
0.0077



(a) Interpret the random-intercept standard deviation of 1.20.
(b) Interpret the weeks coefficient and the treatmentB:weeks coefficient.
(c) Calculate the fitted conditional odds ratio for treatment B versus treatment A at week 8, comparing patients with the same random-intercept value.
(d) Assess this conclusion:

“The treatment p-value is 0.689, so there is no evidence that the treatments differ.”







Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. G_i=0 or 1 codes treatment A or B; t_{ij} is the visit week and b_i the patient random intercept. The coefficients \beta_G,\beta_T,\beta_{GT} multiply treatment, time, and their interaction. The linear predictor is a conditional log odds, so subtracting two predictors and exponentiating gives a conditional odds ratio. The treatment comparison holds week and random-intercept value fixed.
The fitted linear predictor is \widehat\eta_{ij}
=-0.80+0.10G_i-0.10t_{ij}-0.08G_it_{ij}+b_i.
(a) Random-intercept standard deviation. The unexplained patient-specific intercepts have estimated standard deviation 1.20 on the log-odds scale; their estimated variance is 1.20^2=1.44. This is not a standard deviation of disease probabilities.
For equal fixed covariates, increasing b_i by one standard deviation changes conditional odds by the factor \frac{\operatorname{odds}(b_i+1.20)}{\operatorname{odds}(b_i)}
=e^{1.20}\approx3.32.
(b) Weeks and interaction coefficients. For treatment A (G_i=0), the fitted predictor is \widehat\eta_A(t,b)=-0.80-0.10t+b. Thus, within a patient, an additional week changes the conditional log odds by -0.10 and multiplies the odds by e^{-0.10}\approx0.905, approximately a 9.52\% reduction in odds per week.
For treatment B (G_i=1), \widehat\eta_B(t,b)
=(-0.80+0.10)+(-0.10-0.08)t+b
=-0.70-0.18t+b. The time coefficient for B is therefore -0.18, giving a weekly odds multiplier e^{-0.18}\approx0.835, or approximately a 16.47\% reduction.
The interaction coefficient -0.08 is the difference between the B and A slopes on the log-odds scale. Equivalently, the ratio of their weekly odds multipliers is \frac{e^{-0.18}}{e^{-0.10}}=e^{-0.08}\approx0.923. It is not an extra 8-percentage-point weekly reduction in probability.
(c) Conditional odds ratio at week 8. Comparing patients with the same random-intercept value b, \begin{aligned}
\log\{\widehat{\operatorname{OR}}_{B:A}(t)\}
&=\widehat\eta_B(t,b)-\widehat\eta_A(t,b)\\
&=0.10-0.08t.
\end{aligned} The random intercept cancels. At week 8, \boxed{
\widehat{\operatorname{OR}}_{B:A}(8)
=\exp\{0.10-0.08(8)\}=e^{-0.54}\approx0.583.
} Conclusion: At week 8, treatment B has approximately 41.7\% lower fitted conditional odds of infection than treatment A, comparing patients with the same random-intercept value. This is an estimated odds ratio, not a probability ratio or a test of the week-8 contrast.
(d) Assessing the treatment p-value claim. The main treatment coefficient is the B–A difference at week zero, because the interaction term is then zero. Its p-value 0.689 tests H_0:\beta_G=0, not whether the treatment curves agree at every week. It supplies insufficient evidence of a baseline difference.
The interaction p-value 0.0077<0.05 tests H_0:\beta_{GT}=0, and provides evidence that the treatment groups have different time slopes on the conditional log-odds scale. Equality of the entire treatment-specific predictors would require both \beta_G=0 and \beta_{GT}=0, which is a joint hypothesis.

Key result. With an interaction, a main-effect test concerns the reference value of the other predictor. A nonsignificant baseline treatment effect does not rule out a treatment difference that changes over time.

title: Q42. A nonconjugate prior and a change of variable
Q44. Testing whether a coin is fair
Q46. Multinomial logistic regression
text:
Topic: Categorical responses · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 46 of 59 ‹ Q45 Q47 ›

[10 marks]
A response has categories 0,1,2, with probabilities p_0(x),p_1(x),p_2(x). Consider \log\frac{p_1(x)}{p_0(x)}=\alpha_1+\beta_1x,
\qquad
\log\frac{p_2(x)}{p_0(x)}=\alpha_2+\beta_2x.
(a) Derive expressions for all three probabilities and verify that they sum to one. [4 marks]
(b) Interpret e^{\beta_1}. [2 marks]
(c) Derive \log[p_2(x)/p_1(x)]. [2 marks]
(d) If category 1 becomes the reference category, express the new intercepts and slopes in terms of the original parameters. Do the fitted probabilities change? [2 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. p_0(x),p_1(x),p_2(x) are probabilities of three mutually exclusive, exhaustive categories, summing to one. With category 0 as baseline, define \eta_j(x)=\log\{p_j(x)/p_0(x)\}=\alpha_j+\beta_jx, for j=1,2. These are baseline-category log ratios, not one-versus-rest logits \log\{p_j/(1-p_j)\}. The predictors are finite, so all fitted probabilities are positive.
(a) The three probabilities. Exponentiating the model equations gives p_1(x)=e^{\eta_1(x)}p_0(x),\qquad
p_2(x)=e^{\eta_2(x)}p_0(x). Since the probabilities sum to one, p_0(x)\{1+e^{\eta_1(x)}+e^{\eta_2(x)}\}=1. With D(x)=1+e^{\eta_1(x)}+e^{\eta_2(x)}, \boxed{p_0(x)=\frac1{D(x)},\qquad
p_1(x)=\frac{e^{\eta_1(x)}}{D(x)},\qquad
p_2(x)=\frac{e^{\eta_2(x)}}{D(x)}.} All are positive and their sum is D(x)/D(x)=1.
(b) Interpretation of e^{\beta_1}. For a one-unit increase in x, \boxed{
\frac{p_1(x+1)/p_0(x+1)}{p_1(x)/p_0(x)}=e^{\beta_1}.
} Thus e^{\beta_1} is the multiplicative change in the odds of category 1 relative to category 0. It is not generally the multiplier for p_1(x) itself, or for the odds of category 1 against all other categories combined.
(c) Comparing categories 2 and 1. Subtract the two original log-ratio equations: \boxed{
\log\frac{p_2(x)}{p_1(x)}
=\log\frac{p_2(x)}{p_0(x)}-\log\frac{p_1(x)}{p_0(x)}
=(\alpha_2-\alpha_1)+(\beta_2-\beta_1)x.
}
(d) Taking category 1 as the reference. The two new equations are \log\frac{p_0(x)}{p_1(x)}=-\alpha_1-\beta_1x,
\qquad
\log\frac{p_2(x)}{p_1(x)}
=(\alpha_2-\alpha_1)+(\beta_2-\beta_1)x. Thus the new intercept and slope are (-\alpha_1,-\beta_1) for category 0, and (\alpha_2-\alpha_1,\beta_2-\beta_1) for category 2. The fitted probabilities do not change: this is a reparametrisation. For example, p_1(x)=\frac1{1+e^{-\eta_1(x)}+e^{\eta_2(x)-\eta_1(x)}}
=\frac{e^{\eta_1(x)}}{D(x)}, which is the original expression, and the other probabilities follow by their corresponding ratios.

title: Q48. Conjugate Bayesian inference for a Gamma rate
text:
Topic: Exponential families and conjugacy · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 48 of 59 ‹ Q47 Q49 ›

[10 marks]
Let X_1,\ldots,X_n be conditionally independent given \lambda, with density f(x_i\mid\lambda)
=\frac{\lambda^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)}
x_i^{\alpha-1}e^{-\lambda x_i},\qquad x_i>0, where \alpha>0 is known and \lambda>0 is unknown.
Suppose \lambda\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a,b), where a,b>0, with prior density p(\lambda)=\frac{b^a}{\Gamma(a)}\lambda^{a-1}e^{-b\lambda}.
(a) Derive the posterior distribution of \lambda\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}, identifying its parameters. Show the likelihood and posterior kernels. [4 marks]
(b) State the posterior mean \mathbb{E}[\lambda\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}]. [1 mark]
(c) Derive the maximum likelihood estimator \widehat\lambda_{\mathrm{ML}}. [2 marks]
(d) Express the posterior mean in the form \mathbb{E}[\lambda\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}]
        =w_n\mathbb{E}[\lambda]+(1-w_n)\widehat\lambda_{\mathrm{ML}}. Identify w_n, verify that this is a convex combination, and determine the limits of the weights as n\to\infty, assuming \bar x_n\to m>0 and fixed prior parameters. [3 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. \operatorname{Gamma}(A,B) uses shape A and rate B, with kernel \lambda^{A-1}e^{-B\lambda} on \lambda>0 and mean A/B. The sampling shape \alpha>0 is known, while the rate \lambda is unknown. Write T_n=\sum_i x_i=n\bar x_n>0. The prior parameters a,b>0 are fixed; the asymptotic statement uses the specified \bar x_n\to m>0.
(a) Likelihood and posterior. Conditional independence gives \begin{aligned}
L(\lambda;{\boldsymbol{x}})
&=\prod_{i=1}^n
\left\{\frac{\lambda^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)}
x_i^{\alpha-1}e^{-\lambda x_i}\right\}\\
&=\frac{\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{\alpha-1}}{\Gamma(\alpha)^n}
\lambda^{n\alpha}e^{-\lambda T_n}.
\end{aligned} The leading factor does not involve \lambda, so \boxed{L(\lambda;{\boldsymbol{x}})\propto\lambda^{n\alpha}e^{-T_n\lambda},
\qquad\lambda>0.} Multiplying by the prior kernel, \begin{aligned}
p(\lambda\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
&\propto\lambda^{n\alpha}e^{-T_n\lambda}
\lambda^{a-1}e^{-b\lambda}\\
&=\lambda^{a+n\alpha-1}e^{-(b+T_n)\lambda}.
\end{aligned} Matching \lambda^{A-1}e^{-B\lambda} gives \boxed{\lambda\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim
\operatorname{Gamma}(a+n\alpha,\ b+T_n)
\quad\text{(shape--rate)},\qquad\lambda>0.} Thus the Gamma family is conjugate for the unknown rate.
(b) Posterior mean. A shape–rate Gamma distribution has mean shape divided by rate: \boxed{\mathbb{E}[\lambda\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}]=\frac{a+n\alpha}{b+T_n}.}
(c) Maximum likelihood estimator. The log-likelihood, up to a constant, is \ell(\lambda)=n\alpha\log\lambda-T_n\lambda+C. Its derivatives are \ell'(\lambda)=\frac{n\alpha}{\lambda}-T_n,
\qquad \ell''(\lambda)=-\frac{n\alpha}{\lambda^2}<0. Solving \ell'(\lambda)=0 therefore gives the unique maximiser \boxed{\widehat\lambda_{\mathrm{ML}}=\frac{n\alpha}{T_n}
=\frac{\alpha}{\bar x_n}.}
(d) Convex combination and limiting weights. The prior mean is \mathbb{E}[\lambda]=a/b. Split the posterior mean as follows: \begin{aligned}
\frac{a+n\alpha}{b+T_n}
&=\frac{b}{b+T_n}\frac ab
+\frac{T_n}{b+T_n}\frac{n\alpha}{T_n}\\
&=w_n\mathbb{E}[\lambda]+(1-w_n)\widehat\lambda_{\mathrm{ML}},
\end{aligned} where \boxed{w_n=\frac{b}{b+T_n}=\frac{b}{b+n\bar x_n},
\qquad 1-w_n=\frac{T_n}{b+T_n}.} Because b>0 and T_n>0, both weights are strictly between zero and one, and \frac{b}{b+T_n}+\frac{T_n}{b+T_n}=1. Hence this is a convex combination of the prior mean and the MLE. Notice that the weights depend on the observed total T_n, not just on n.
Under \bar x_n\to m>0, we have T_n=n\bar x_n\to\infty. With fixed prior parameters, \boxed{w_n\longrightarrow0,\qquad1-w_n\longrightarrow1.} The prior-mean contribution consequently vanishes and the data receive asymptotically all the weight. In fact, both estimates have the same limit: \widehat\lambda_{\mathrm{ML}}=\frac\alpha{\bar x_n}
\longrightarrow\frac\alpha m,
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[\lambda\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}]
=\frac{a/n+\alpha}{b/n+\bar x_n}
\longrightarrow\frac\alpha m.

Key result. For this rate parameter, the prior weight is b/(b+\sum_i x_i). Derive the weights from the actual posterior mean; they are not always “prior sample size divided by total sample size.”

title: Q50. Metropolis–Hastings with a Cauchy prior
Q52. Bayesian logistic regression
text:
Topic: Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis–Hastings · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 52 of 59 ‹ Q51 Q53 ›

[12 marks]
A researcher models whether a manufactured component fails a stress test. For component i, let y_i=1 indicate failure and let x_i denote its centred test temperature. Conditional on \boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_0,\beta_1)^\top, assume Y_i\mid\boldsymbol\beta\overset{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}
\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_i),\qquad
p_i=\frac1{1+\exp[-(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)]},\quad i=1,\ldots,n. Assign independent priors \beta_0\sim N(0,4),\qquad\beta_1\sim N(0,9), where the second parameter denotes the variance. Treat the x_i as fixed.
(a) Write down the likelihood L(\boldsymbol\beta;\mathbf y,{\boldsymbol{x}}). [2 marks]
(b) Derive the posterior density of \boldsymbol\beta, up to proportionality. Hence obtain its log density up to an additive constant, expressed explicitly in terms of \beta_0,\beta_1,x_i,y_i. [3 marks]
A random-walk Metropolis–Hastings sampler proposes \boldsymbol\beta^*\mid\boldsymbol\beta^{(t)}
\sim N_2\!\left(\boldsymbol\beta^{(t)},s^2I_2\right), where s>0 is fixed and I_2 is the 2\times2 identity matrix.
(a) Starting from the general Metropolis–Hastings acceptance probability, simplify it for this proposal. Explain any cancellations and express your answer using the log posterior from part (b). [3 marks]
(b) Give pseudocode for the sampler. Specify what happens after both an accepted proposal and a rejected proposal. [2 marks]
(c) Explain how choosing s extremely small or extremely large can impair the sampler’s efficiency. [2 marks]
No implementation or numerical simulation is required.






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write \boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_0,\beta_1)^\top, \eta_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i, and p_i=e^{\eta_i}/(1+e^{\eta_i}). A Bernoulli observation contributes p_i^{y_i}(1-p_i)^{1-y_i} to the likelihood. The fixed x_i are covariates, the binary outcomes are conditionally independent, and the independent Normal priors have variances 4 and 9. I_2 is the identity matrix; the proposal covariance is fixed at s^2I_2.
The logistic probabilities satisfy p_i=\frac{e^{\eta_i}}{1+e^{\eta_i}},\qquad
1-p_i=\frac1{1+e^{\eta_i}}.
(a) Likelihood. For observed y_i\in\{0,1\}, conditional independence gives \boxed{
L(\boldsymbol\beta;\mathbf y,{\boldsymbol{x}})
=\prod_{i=1}^n p_i^{y_i}(1-p_i)^{1-y_i}
=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{\exp\{y_i(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)\}}
                          {1+\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)}.
} The covariates are fixed, so no probability density for the x_i is included in this likelihood.
(b) Posterior and log posterior. Independence of the priors gives p(\boldsymbol\beta)=p(\beta_0)p(\beta_1)
\propto\exp\left(-\frac{\beta_0^2}{2(4)}
                 -\frac{\beta_1^2}{2(9)}\right)
=\exp\left(-\frac{\beta_0^2}{8}-\frac{\beta_1^2}{18}\right). The denominators use the stated variances 4 and 9, not their squares. Multiplying this prior kernel by the likelihood yields \boxed{
\pi(\boldsymbol\beta\mid\mathbf y,{\boldsymbol{x}})
\propto
\left[\prod_{i=1}^n
\frac{\exp\{y_i(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)\}}
     {1+\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)}\right]
\exp\left(-\frac{\beta_0^2}{8}-\frac{\beta_1^2}{18}\right),
} with support \boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^2. Taking logarithms, \log\pi(\boldsymbol\beta\mid\mathbf y,{\boldsymbol{x}})
=h(\boldsymbol\beta)+C, where C does not depend on \boldsymbol\beta and \boxed{
h(\boldsymbol\beta)
=\sum_{i=1}^n\left[
y_i(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)
-\log\{1+\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)\}\right]
-\frac{\beta_0^2}{8}-\frac{\beta_1^2}{18}.
} Thus h is the log posterior up to an additive constant; it includes the log likelihood and the log prior.
(c) Acceptance probability. For current state \boldsymbol\beta and proposed state \boldsymbol\beta^*, the general rule is A(\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\beta^*)
=\min\left\{1,
\frac{\pi(\boldsymbol\beta^*\mid\mathbf y,{\boldsymbol{x}})
      q(\boldsymbol\beta\mid\boldsymbol\beta^*)}
     {\pi(\boldsymbol\beta\mid\mathbf y,{\boldsymbol{x}})
      q(\boldsymbol\beta^*\mid\boldsymbol\beta)}\right\}. The bivariate Normal random-walk proposal has density q(\boldsymbol\beta^*\mid\boldsymbol\beta)
=\frac1{2\pi s^2}
\exp\left[-\frac{\|\boldsymbol\beta^*-\boldsymbol\beta\|^2}{2s^2}\right]. Since the squared Euclidean distance is unchanged when the two states are exchanged, and s^2I_2 is fixed, q(\boldsymbol\beta^*\mid\boldsymbol\beta)
=q(\boldsymbol\beta\mid\boldsymbol\beta^*). The proposal-density terms therefore cancel. The posterior’s normalising constant also cancels, giving \boxed{
A(\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\beta^*)
=\min\{1,\exp[h(\boldsymbol\beta^*)-h(\boldsymbol\beta)]\}.
}
(d) Pseudocode. Start from any finite \boldsymbol\beta^{(0)}\in\mathbb R^2, for example (0,0)^\top, and choose fixed s>0. For t=0,\ldots,T-1:
1. Draw \boldsymbol\beta^*\sim
        N_2(\boldsymbol\beta^{(t)},s^2I_2).
2. Compute \Delta=h(\boldsymbol\beta^*)-h(\boldsymbol\beta^{(t)}).
3. Independently draw U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1).
4. If \log U\le\min\{0,\Delta\}, accept and set \boldsymbol\beta^{(t+1)}=\boldsymbol\beta^*. Otherwise reject and set \boldsymbol\beta^{(t+1)}=\boldsymbol\beta^{(t)}.
5. Store \boldsymbol\beta^{(t+1)}, including repeated states following rejection.
The log-scale comparison avoids exponentiating \Delta. Keeping only accepted proposals would not give the intended sequence of posterior Markov-chain states. Allow for convergence from the initial state before using the output for posterior summaries.
(e) Effect of proposal scale.

Extremely small s: proposals tend to be accepted often, but move only a short distance. The chain explores the posterior slowly and successive states are highly correlated, so many iterations provide little additional information.
Extremely large s: proposals often land in regions of much lower posterior density and are rejected. The chain then repeats its current state many times, again exploring slowly.

Both extremes reduce efficiency. A high acceptance rate alone is not evidence of efficient sampling; useful movement and mixing also matter. For any fixed s>0, the algorithm still targets the same posterior—the choice changes how efficiently it explores that distribution.

title: Q54. Poisson regression and overdispersion
text:
Topic: Standard errors, and models for counts · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 54 of 59 ‹ Q53 Q55 ›

[12 marks]
A manufacturing company records the number Y_i of machine failures during one month for machine i. Let x_i denote the age of the machine in years. A statistician proposes the model Y_i\mid x_i\overset{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}\operatorname{Poisson}(\mu_i),
\qquad i=1,\ldots,n, with \log(\mu_i)=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i. Treat the machine ages as fixed covariates.
(a) Write the model explicitly in terms of the conditional mean and conditional variance of Y_i. [2 marks]
(b) Starting from the Poisson probability mass function, \mathbb P(Y_i=y_i\mid x_i)
        =\frac{\mu_i^{y_i}e^{-\mu_i}}{y_i!}, derive the log-likelihood for \boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_0,\beta_1)^\top, up to an additive constant. Then derive the score vector S(\boldsymbol\beta)
        =\frac{\partial\ell(\boldsymbol\beta)}{\partial\boldsymbol\beta}. Your final answer should be written in vector form. [4 marks]
(c) Suppose the fitted model gives \hat\beta_1=\log(1.2). Interpret \hat\beta_1 in context. [2 marks]
(d) After fitting the model, the statistician estimates the dispersion parameter as \hat\phi=2.25. What does this suggest about the Poisson variance assumption? [2 marks]
(e) The statistician refits the same mean model using a quasi-Poisson model. State:
1. the new variance assumption;
2. whether the estimate \hat{\boldsymbol\beta} changes;
3. how the standard errors of the regression coefficients are affected.
[2 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write \mathbf x_i=(1,x_i)^\top, \boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_0,\beta_1)^\top, and \mu_i=\exp(\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta). Poisson equidispersion means \operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid x_i)=\mu_i; quasi-Poisson instead specifies \phi\mu_i. The comparisons use independent observations, fixed ages, the same unpenalised mean model and data, and a common dispersion \phi>0.
(a) Conditional mean and variance. The observations are independent conditional on the fixed machine ages, and the Poisson model gives \boxed{
\mathbb{E}[Y_i\mid x_i]=\mu_i=\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i),\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid x_i)=\mu_i=\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i).
} Equality of the conditional mean and variance is the Poisson equidispersion assumption.
(b) Log-likelihood and score vector. For observed nonnegative integer counts y_i, conditional independence gives L(\boldsymbol\beta)
=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{\mu_i^{y_i}e^{-\mu_i}}{y_i!}. Taking logarithms and substituting the log link, \begin{aligned}
\ell(\boldsymbol\beta)
&=\sum_{i=1}^n\{y_i\log\mu_i-\mu_i-\log(y_i!)\}\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^n\left[
y_i\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta
-\exp(\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta)\right]+C,
\end{aligned} where C=-\sum_{i=1}^n\log(y_i!) depends on the data but not on \boldsymbol\beta. It can therefore be ignored when maximising or differentiating with respect to \boldsymbol\beta.
The derivative of \mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta is \mathbf x_i, and the chain rule gives \frac{\partial}{\partial\boldsymbol\beta}
\exp(\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta)
=\exp(\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta)\mathbf x_i
=\mu_i\mathbf x_i. Hence \boxed{
S(\boldsymbol\beta)
=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf x_i(y_i-\mu_i)
=\begin{pmatrix}
\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\mu_i)\\[3pt]
\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(y_i-\mu_i)
\end{pmatrix}
=X^\top(\mathbf y-\boldsymbol\mu).
} Here X is the n\times2 design matrix with row i equal to \mathbf x_i^\top, while \mathbf y=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)^\top and \boldsymbol\mu=(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_n)^\top. Thus the score is a 2\times1 vector.
As a check, under the assumed model, \mathbb{E}[S(\boldsymbol\beta)\mid X]
=X^\top\{\mathbb{E}[\mathbf Y\mid X]-\boldsymbol\mu\}
=\mathbf0.
(c) Interpretation of the age coefficient. For two machine ages differing by one year, the ratio of fitted means is \frac{\hat\mu(x+1)}{\hat\mu(x)}
=\frac{\exp\{\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1(x+1)\}}
       {\exp(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x)}
=e^{\hat\beta_1}=1.2. Each additional year of machine age is associated with a 20% higher fitted mean number of failures per month. This is a multiplicative effect on the expected count, not an increase of 0.2 failures or a statement that every machine’s realised count rises by 20%.
(d) Estimated dispersion. An ordinary Poisson model imposes \phi=1. Since \hat\phi=2.25>1, the estimate suggests overdispersion: conditional variability is greater than the Poisson mean–variance relationship allows. Under the fitted dispersion model, the variance is estimated as 2.25\hat\mu_i, compared with the Poisson value \hat\mu_i. This raises concern about Poisson-based standard errors; it does not by itself establish that the log-linear mean model is correct.
(e) Quasi-Poisson refit.
1. Variance assumption. Keep \mathbb{E}[Y_i\mid x_i]=\mu_i=\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i), but use \boxed{\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid x_i)=\phi\mu_i,\qquad\phi>0.} Quasi-Poisson specifies this mean–variance relationship rather than a full Poisson probability mass function.
2. Coefficient estimates. For the same data and unpenalised mean model with the same log link, the estimates are unchanged. With a common positive dispersion parameter, the quasi-score is U_Q(\boldsymbol\beta)
        =\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{y_i-\mu_i}{\phi\mu_i}
          \frac{\partial\mu_i}{\partial\boldsymbol\beta}
        =\frac1\phi\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf x_i(y_i-\mu_i)
        =\frac1\phi S(\boldsymbol\beta). Thus U_Q=\mathbf0 and S=\mathbf0 have the same solutions; the fitted coefficients and fitted means agree, assuming the usual finite, identifiable fit.
3. Standard errors. Let \widehat W=\operatorname{diag}(\hat\mu_1,\ldots,\hat\mu_n). The usual estimated coefficient covariance matrices are \widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_P(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})
        =(X^\top\widehat W X)^{-1},\qquad
        \widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_Q(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})
        =\hat\phi(X^\top\widehat W X)^{-1}. Taking square roots of their diagonal entries gives \boxed{
        \operatorname{SE}_Q(\hat\beta_j)
        =\sqrt{\hat\phi}\,\operatorname{SE}_P(\hat\beta_j)
        =1.5\,\operatorname{SE}_P(\hat\beta_j),\quad j=0,1.
        } Thus the estimated variances are multiplied by 2.25, whereas the standard errors increase by 50%.

Key result. Same log-linear mean model and coefficient estimates; variance \phi\mu_i instead of \mu_i; standard errors multiplied by \sqrt{\hat\phi}, not by \hat\phi.

title: Q56. Exponential regression and the score
text:
Topic: Introduction to generalised linear models · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 56 of 59 ‹ Q55 Q57 ›

[5 marks]
Researchers study how long electronic components last. Let Y_i>0 be the lifetime of component i, and x_i its operating temperature. Assume independent responses with density f(y_i\mid\mu_i)
=\frac1{\mu_i}\exp\left(-\frac{y_i}{\mu_i}\right),
\qquad y_i>0, and a log link for the mean: \log\mu_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i
=\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta,\qquad
\mathbf X_i=(1,x_i)^\top,\qquad i=1,\ldots,n. Treat the operating temperatures as fixed. Here \mu_i=\mathbb{E}[Y_i\mid x_i]; the exponential rate is 1/\mu_i.
(a) Starting from the density, form the likelihood and show that \ell(\boldsymbol\beta)
        =-\sum_{i=1}^n\left[
        \mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta
        +Y_i e^{-\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta}\right]. [2 marks]
(b) Derive the score vector \mathbf S(\boldsymbol\beta)
        =\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\boldsymbol\beta}. Express your answer using Y_i,\mu_i,\mathbf X_i. [2 marks]
(c) Show that \mathbb{E}[\mathbf S(\boldsymbol\beta)]=\mathbf0. [1 mark]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. The exponential distribution is parameterised by mean \mu_i>0, so its rate is 1/\mu_i, not \mu_i. Let \mathbf X_i=(1,x_i)^\top, \boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_0,\beta_1)^\top, and \eta_i=\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta. The score is \mathbf S=\partial\ell/\partial\boldsymbol\beta, differentiating with the observed lifetimes fixed. Sampling is independent conditional on the fixed covariates.
(a) Likelihood and log-likelihood. Write \eta_i=\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta. The log link implies \mu_i=e^{\eta_i},\qquad\frac1{\mu_i}=e^{-\eta_i},
\qquad\log\mu_i=\eta_i. Independence gives, for the observed positive lifetimes, L(\boldsymbol\beta)
=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac1{\mu_i}\exp\left(-\frac{Y_i}{\mu_i}\right)
=\exp\left[-\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\log\mu_i+\frac{Y_i}{\mu_i}\right)\right]. The observed Y_i are held fixed when differentiating the likelihood. Taking logarithms and substituting the log link gives \boxed{
\ell(\boldsymbol\beta)
=-\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\log\mu_i+\frac{Y_i}{\mu_i}\right)
=-\sum_{i=1}^n\left[
\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta
+Y_i e^{-\mathbf X_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta}\right].
} This is the exact log-likelihood for positive observations; the support does not depend on \boldsymbol\beta.
(b) Score vector. Since \partial\eta_i/\partial\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf X_i, the chain rule gives \frac{\partial}{\partial\boldsymbol\beta}
\left[-\eta_i-Y_i e^{-\eta_i}\right]
=-\mathbf X_i+Y_i e^{-\eta_i}\mathbf X_i. The second term is positive because differentiating e^{-\eta_i} introduces a second minus sign. Summing and using e^{-\eta_i}=1/\mu_i, \boxed{
\mathbf S(\boldsymbol\beta)
=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf X_i\left(\frac{Y_i}{\mu_i}-1\right)
=\begin{pmatrix}
\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i/\mu_i-1)\\[3pt]
\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(Y_i/\mu_i-1)
\end{pmatrix}.
} This is a 2\times1 vector. Unlike the Poisson log-link score, it uses the relative residual Y_i/\mu_i-1=(Y_i-\mu_i)/\mu_i.
(c) Expected score. Let X denote the fixed design matrix whose ith row is \mathbf X_i^\top. Under the assumed model, \mathbb{E}[Y_i\mid X]=\mu_i. For fixed \boldsymbol\beta, both \mathbf X_i and \mu_i are nonrandom, so linearity of expectation gives \begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[\mathbf S(\boldsymbol\beta)\mid X]
&=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf X_i
  \left(\frac{\mathbb{E}[Y_i\mid X]}{\mu_i}-1\right)\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf X_i
  \left(\frac{\mu_i}{\mu_i}-1\right)
=\boxed{\mathbf0}.
\end{aligned} Since the covariates are fixed, this is the requested \mathbb{E}[\mathbf S(\boldsymbol\beta)]=\mathbf0: expectation is over repeated responses generated at the same parameter \boldsymbol\beta.

title: Q58. Joint Normal conjugacy and exact sampling
text:
Topic: Conjugate analysis for normal models · more questions on this topic
Source: Practice set, question 58 of 59 ‹ Q57 Q59 ›

[20 marks; approximately 25 minutes]
Let X_1,\ldots,X_n\mid\mu,\sigma^2
\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(\mu,\sigma^2), with both \mu\in\mathbb R and \sigma^2>0 unknown, and n\ge1. Write \theta=(\mu,\sigma^2). Prior densities below are with respect to d\mu\,d\sigma^2. Use the inverse-Gamma convention p(v)\propto v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v} for v>0.
(i) Show the Normal belongs to the exponential family in the form f(x\mid\theta)
        =\frac{b(x)\exp\{c_1(\theta)T_1(x)+c_2(\theta)T_2(x)\}}
        {a(\theta)}. Identify b,a,c_1,c_2,T_1,T_2 (signs go in the c_j). Hence write the likelihood of the whole sample in terms of \sum_i x_i and \sum_i x_i^2. [4 marks]
(ii) The conjugate prior for this family is \pi(\theta)\propto
        \frac{\exp\{c_1(\theta)\alpha_1+c_2(\theta)\alpha_2\}}
        {a(\theta)^\beta}. Write it out explicitly in \mu and \sigma^2. By completing the square in \mu, show it factorises as \mu\mid\sigma^2\sim N\!\left(m_0,\frac{\sigma^2}{\kappa_0}\right),
        \qquad\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(a_0,b_0), and find m_0,\kappa_0,a_0,b_0 in terms of \alpha_1,\alpha_2,\beta. State the conditions on the hyperparameters for a proper distribution. [6 marks]
(iii) Show that the posterior is in the same family, with hyperparameters (\alpha_1+\sum_i x_i,\,\alpha_2+\sum_i x_i^2,\,\beta+n). Then give the posterior m_n,\kappa_n,a_n,b_n in terms of \bar x, s^2=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2, and the prior quantities. Here s^2 denotes the unnormalised sum of squares, not the sample variance. [4 marks]
(iv) Show that \mathbb{E}[\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}] is a weighted average of m_0 and \bar x, and give the weights. What happens as n\to\infty with fixed prior hyperparameters? [3 marks]
(v) Describe how to draw exact (non-MCMC) samples from the joint posterior of (\mu,\sigma^2), and explain why it works. Assess the claim: “With a flat prior on \mu and an independent inverse-Gamma prior on \sigma^2, exact sampling is unavailable and a Gibbs sampler is necessary.” [3 marks]






Worked answer (click to show)





Definitions. Write v=\sigma^2, \bar x=n^{-1}\sum_i x_i, and s^2=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2. Here s^2 is the unnormalised sum of squares, not the sample variance. N(m,v) uses variance v; \operatorname{InvGamma}(a,b) has kernel v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v} on v>0. A Normal–inverse-Gamma factorisation means p(\mu,v)=p(v)p(\mu\mid v), not independence of \mu and v.
Assumptions. Use the specified conditionally iid Normal model with n\ge1. The joint prior density is with respect to d\mu\,dv and has exactly the kernel stated in the question. Changing to precision, or starting with a density in natural-parameter coordinates, would require a Jacobian; no such change is made here.
(i) Exponential-family form and likelihood. Expanding (x-\mu)^2=x^2-2\mu x+\mu^2 gives f(x\mid\mu,v)
=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi v}}
\exp\left(-\frac{x^2}{2v}+\frac{\mu x}{v}-\frac{\mu^2}{2v}\right)
=\frac{(2\pi)^{-1/2}\exp\{(\mu/v)x-x^2/(2v)\}}
{\sqrt v\exp\{\mu^2/(2v)\}}. One valid identification, with signs in the c_j, is \boxed{\begin{aligned}
b(x)&=(2\pi)^{-1/2},& a(\theta)&=\sqrt v\exp\{\mu^2/(2v)\},\\
T_1(x)&=x,&c_1(\theta)&=\frac\mu v,\\
T_2(x)&=x^2,&c_2(\theta)&=-\frac1{2v}.
\end{aligned}} Let S_1=\sum_i x_i and S_2=\sum_i x_i^2. Then \boxed{L(\mu,v;{\boldsymbol{x}})
=(2\pi v)^{-n/2}
\exp\left[-\frac{S_2-2\mu S_1+n\mu^2}{2v}\right].} Thus the sample enters the likelihood through (S_1,S_2).
(ii) Conjugate prior and parameter matching. Substitution into the given prior formula yields the joint density kernel \pi(\mu,v)
\propto v^{-\beta/2}
\exp\left[-\frac{\beta\mu^2-2\alpha_1\mu+\alpha_2}{2v}\right]. For \beta>0, complete the square: \beta\mu^2-2\alpha_1\mu+\alpha_2
=\beta\left(\mu-\frac{\alpha_1}{\beta}\right)^2
+\alpha_2-\frac{\alpha_1^2}{\beta}. Set \boxed{m_0=\frac{\alpha_1}{\beta},\qquad
\kappa_0=\beta,\qquad a_0=\frac{\beta-3}{2},\qquad
b_0=\frac12\left(\alpha_2-\frac{\alpha_1^2}{\beta}\right).} To see the shape parameter, factor the kernel as \pi(\mu,v)\propto
\underbrace{v^{-1/2}
\exp\left[-\frac{\kappa_0(\mu-m_0)^2}{2v}\right]}
_{\text{Normal conditional kernel, including its }v^{-1/2}\text{ factor}}
\underbrace{v^{-(\beta-1)/2}e^{-b_0/v}}
_{\text{inverse-Gamma marginal kernel}}. The Normal factor has a normalising multiplier \sqrt{\kappa_0/(2\pi)} that does not depend on v. The remaining exponent therefore satisfies a_0+1=(\beta-1)/2, giving a_0=(\beta-3)/2. Hence \mu\mid v\sim N(m_0,v/\kappa_0) and v\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(a_0,b_0).
The necessary and sufficient conditions for a proper prior are \boxed{\alpha_1\in\mathbb R,\qquad\beta>3,\qquad
\alpha_2>\frac{\alpha_1^2}{\beta}.} They ensure \kappa_0,a_0,b_0>0. The specified three-hyperparameter prior is a subfamily of the general Normal–inverse-Gamma family: it imposes \kappa_0=2a_0+3.
(iii) Posterior update. Multiplying the prior kernel by the likelihood gives \pi(\mu,v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
\propto v^{-(\beta+n)/2}
\exp\left[-\frac{(\beta+n)\mu^2
-2(\alpha_1+S_1)\mu+(\alpha_2+S_2)}{2v}\right]. This has exactly the same form, with \boxed{\alpha_1'=\alpha_1+S_1,\qquad
\alpha_2'=\alpha_2+S_2,\qquad\beta'=\beta+n.} Using S_1=n\bar x, S_2=s^2+n\bar x^2, and the prior identities \alpha_1=\kappa_0m_0 and \alpha_2=2b_0+\kappa_0m_0^2, we obtain \boxed{\begin{aligned}
\kappa_n&=\kappa_0+n,\\
m_n&=\frac{\kappa_0m_0+n\bar x}{\kappa_0+n},\\
a_n&=a_0+\frac n2,\\
b_n&=b_0+\frac12\left[s^2+
\frac{\kappa_0n}{\kappa_0+n}(\bar x-m_0)^2\right].
\end{aligned}} In particular, the final update follows from \begin{aligned}
b_n
&=\frac12\left[\alpha_2+S_2-
\frac{(\alpha_1+S_1)^2}{\beta+n}\right]\\
&=b_0+\frac12\left[s^2+\kappa_0m_0^2+n\bar x^2
-\frac{(\kappa_0m_0+n\bar x)^2}{\kappa_0+n}\right]\\
&=b_0+\frac12\left[s^2+
\frac{\kappa_0n}{\kappa_0+n}(\bar x-m_0)^2\right].
\end{aligned} Therefore \boxed{\mu\mid v,{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim N(m_n,v/\kappa_n),\qquad
v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(a_n,b_n).} The v distribution here is the marginal posterior, with \mu integrated out. All updates remain proper when the prior is proper.
(iv) Posterior mean and weights. For n\ge1 and a proper prior, a_n=a_0+n/2>1/2, which ensures that the marginal posterior mean of \mu exists. Iterated expectation gives \mathbb{E}[\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}]
=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathbb{E}[\mu\mid v,{\boldsymbol{x}}]\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\right]
=m_n. Consequently, \boxed{\mathbb{E}[\mu\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}]
=\underbrace{\frac{\kappa_0}{\kappa_0+n}}_{w_0}m_0
+\underbrace{\frac n{\kappa_0+n}}_{w_x}\bar x.} The weights are positive and sum to one. For fixed prior hyperparameters, w_0\to0 and w_x\to1: the prior contribution vanishes and the posterior mean approaches the sample mean. Under iid sampling at fixed true parameters, \bar x\to\mu_{\mathrm{true}} almost surely, so m_n\to\mu_{\mathrm{true}} almost surely as well.
(v) Exact joint-posterior sampling. For each j=1,\ldots,M, independently of all previous pairs:
1. Draw v^{(j)}\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(a_n,b_n) from the marginal posterior of v=\sigma^2.
2. Draw \mu^{(j)}\sim N(m_n,v^{(j)}/\kappa_n), conditional on that newly drawn variance.
3. Store (\mu^{(j)},v^{(j)}).
For example, step 1 can use G^{(j)}\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a_n,b_n) in shape–rate form and set v^{(j)}=1/G^{(j)}. With fresh random numbers in each repetition, this produces iid pairs from the joint posterior because p(\mu,v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})=p(v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})\,p(\mu\mid v,{\boldsymbol{x}}). The two coordinates within a pair are generally dependent, but distinct pairs are independent. There is no Markov-chain convergence, burn-in, or accept/reject step to manage in this construction.
Assessing the flat-prior claim. The claim is false for a flat mean prior and an independent inverse-Gamma variance prior. To distinguish its hyperparameters from those above, suppose p(\mu)\propto1,\qquad
v\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(a_*,b_*),\qquad a_*,b_*>0. Although this joint prior is improper in \mu, for n\ge1 the posterior is proper. Using \sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2=s^2+n(\mu-\bar x)^2, its kernel is p(\mu,v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}})
\propto v^{-a_*-1-n/2}
\exp\left[-\frac{b_*+s^2/2}{v}
          -\frac{n(\mu-\bar x)^2}{2v}\right]. Integrating over \mu contributes a factor proportional to \sqrt v, since \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\exp\left[-\frac{n(\mu-\bar x)^2}{2v}\right]d\mu
=\sqrt{\frac{2\pi v}{n}}. Hence \boxed{v\mid{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim
\operatorname{InvGamma}\!\left(a_*+\frac{n-1}{2},\ b_*+\frac{s^2}{2}\right),
\qquad\mu\mid v,{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim N(\bar x,v/n).} One can again draw from the variance marginal and then the Normal conditional, producing independent exact posterior pairs. Gibbs sampling is valid here, but not necessary. The same distinction appears in Question 43 for p(\mu,v)\propto1/v, with its stated propriety conditions.

Key result. Exact direct sampling uses a marginal then a conditional. Gibbs sampling alternates full conditionals. The key issue is whether the needed marginal is available for direct sampling, not merely whether the prior was described as independent.

title: Common distributions
text:
Continuous

Beta







Distribution
x\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)


Parameters
\alpha,\beta>0


Support
0<x<1


Probability density
p(x)=\frac{\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)}{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)}x^{\alpha-1}(1-x)^{\beta-1}


Expectation
\mathbb{E}(x)=\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)


Variance
\operatorname{Var}(x)=\alpha\beta/((\alpha+\beta)^{2}(\alpha+\beta+1))



Article: Beta distribution →


Dirichlet







Distribution
x\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha)


Parameters
\alpha\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{K}, \alpha_0=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\alpha_k


Support
x_k>0, \sum_{k=1}^{K}x_k=1


Probability density
p(x)=\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_0)}{\prod_{k=1}^{K}\Gamma(\alpha_k)}\prod_{k=1}^{K}x_k^{\alpha_k-1}


Expectation
\mathbb{E}(x)=\alpha/\alpha_0


Variance
\operatorname{Var}(x_k)=\alpha_k(\alpha_0-\alpha_k)/(\alpha_0^{2}(\alpha_0+1))



Article: Dirichlet distribution →


Exponential



Distribution
x\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)


Parameters
\lambda>0


Support
x>0


Probability density
p(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}


Expectation
\mathbb{E}(x)=1/\lambda


Variance
\operatorname{Var}(x)=1/\lambda^{2}



Article: Exponential distribution →


Gamma







Distribution
x\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha,\beta)


Parameters
\alpha,\beta>0, shape–rate


Support
x>0


Probability density
p(x)=\frac{\beta^{\alpha}}{\Gamma(\alpha)}x^{\alpha-1}e^{-\beta x}


Expectation
\mathbb{E}(x)=\alpha/\beta


Variance
\operatorname{Var}(x)=\alpha/\beta^{2}



Article: Gamma distribution →


Inverse gamma







Distribution
x\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(\alpha,\beta)


Parameters
\alpha,\beta>0


Support
x>0


Probability density
p(x)=\frac{\beta^{\alpha}}{\Gamma(\alpha)}x^{-\alpha-1}e^{-\beta/x}


Expectation
\mathbb{E}(x)=\beta/(\alpha-1) for \alpha>1


Variance
\operatorname{Var}(x)=\beta^{2}/((\alpha-1)^{2}(\alpha-2)) for \alpha>2



The mode is \beta/(\alpha+1), which is not the variance.

Normal







Distribution
X\sim\operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})


Parameters
\mu\in\mathbb{R}, \sigma>0


Support
x\in\mathbb{R}


Probability density
p(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}\exp\Bigl(-\frac{(x-\mu)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\Bigr)


Expectation
\mathbb{E}(X)=\mu


Variance
\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^{2}
